text:
Latest News Report

Friday, July 31, 2026 — updated around 11:00 a.m. Pacific Time

Gaza agreement offers hope, with major obstacles remaining

The most significant diplomatic development is a newly announced framework under which Hamas says it will begin disarming while Israel would end military operations and withdraw its forces from Gaza. President Donald Trump announced the agreement, and Hamas officials confirmed accepting the road map. Israel had not issued a full official response by the time of this report.

The sequence of events remains unresolved. Hamas says Israel must stop its strikes and begin withdrawing before heavy weapons are surrendered. Israeli officials have previously insisted that meaningful disarmament must come first. Hamas has also linked the eventual surrender of heavy weapons to progress toward a Palestinian state—something Israel’s current government strongly opposes. The agreement is therefore a potentially historic opening, not yet a completed peace settlement.

U.S.–Iran conflict pauses briefly, while maritime attacks continue

No new American strikes inside Iran were reported overnight Friday, giving the region a limited pause after several days of renewed escalation. However, the broader conflict remains extremely dangerous.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said it attacked two more oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. Kuwait reported intercepting Iranian drones directed toward military facilities. These developments keep commercial shipping, energy infrastructure and American-allied bases at risk even during a pause in direct U.S. bombing. Iran had earlier indicated that it would halt attacks as long as the United States maintained its bombing pause, though events at sea show that the definition and durability of that understanding remain uncertain.

Saudi Arabia has proposed a 14-country maritime-defense alliance intended to protect shipping and energy routes through the Red Sea. Turkey, Egypt and Pakistan are among the countries supporting the proposal. The initiative reflects fears that instability around both the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea could simultaneously threaten two of the world’s most important trade corridors.

Russia and Ukraine intensify long-range attacks

Ukraine urgently wants additional Patriot anti-ballistic missiles as Russia increases the scale and frequency of missile attacks. Ukraine’s ambassador to Washington said recent Russian barrages have included roughly 30 to 40 ballistic missiles in a single night. Ukraine is discussing eventually producing PAC-3 interceptor missiles domestically, though establishing production could take years.

Poland summoned Russia’s ambassador after authorities concluded that a recently manufactured Russian Kh-101 cruise missile landed in eastern Poland. The incident is especially serious because Poland is a NATO member. Polish officials called it a threat to national sovereignty, civilians and aviation safety. No deliberate Russian attack on Poland has been established, though the missile’s arrival again demonstrates the danger of the war spilling across Ukraine’s borders.

Ukraine, meanwhile, continued striking targets inside Russia. A drone attack ignited fires at an energy facility and warehouses in the Volgograd region and reportedly injured five people. Another attack injured a woman in Russia’s Rostov region. Ukraine describes strikes on Russian energy and logistics sites as an attempt to weaken Moscow’s ability to sustain the war.

Concerns are also growing about Black Sea food exports. Russia’s grain industry warned that continuing attacks on ships and ports could severely disrupt wheat shipments. Because Russia and Ukraine are both major grain exporters, prolonged disruption could raise food prices and particularly hurt import-dependent countries in Africa and the Middle East. The warning comes from a Russian industry group and should be understood within the broader wartime information struggle, though the underlying risk to shipping is real.

Japan continues recovering from powerful earthquake

Thousands of people in southwestern Japan remained in shelters or slept in vehicles following the major earthquake that struck the region. Survivors are dealing with damaged buildings, disrupted services, continuing aftershocks and oppressive summer heat.

A separate magnitude-6.9 earthquake was reported off northern Japan on Friday. No tsunami warning was issued for that event. Authorities continue examining infrastructure and assisting communities affected by the earlier destructive quake.

Migration emergency overwhelms Spain’s Ceuta enclave

Approximately 60,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Spain’s North African territory of Ceuta within about 24 hours, according to local authorities. At least 57 people reportedly died during the crossings. Roughly half of those who entered later returned voluntarily to Morocco, Spain’s government said.

The sudden influx—equivalent to most of Ceuta’s normal population—created a humanitarian and security crisis. Migrants also attempted to cross into Spain’s neighboring territory of Melilla, where confrontations with police were reported. Spain’s prime minister blamed trafficking organizations for helping organize the mass movement.

Extreme heat and fires continue across Europe

Firefighters in France, Spain, Greece and Turkey remain under severe pressure from wildfires, high temperatures and strong winds. Hundreds of thousands of people have been evacuated during the broader European emergency.

Southwestern France has experienced an exceptionally large fire, while Spain continues battling major outbreaks including an uncontrolled blaze in Castellón. Greece has reported firefighter deaths, and evacuations have taken place on islands and in Turkish coastal regions. The combination of drought, extreme heat and fire-generated weather is making containment particularly difficult.

Markets shaken by sharp technology-stock movements

Apple shares fell sharply after the company issued a weaker forecast and warned that component shortages could constrain iPhone growth. Reuters reported that the decline threatened to erase nearly $500 billion in market value. Competition for advanced components from rapidly expanding artificial-intelligence data centers is adding pressure across the technology supply chain.

The fall follows an extraordinary rise in Microsoft shares one day earlier. Microsoft gained more than 15% after issuing a strong artificial-intelligence and cloud outlook, adding approximately $450 billion in market value in a single session. Together, the moves illustrate how sensitive markets have become to AI spending, supply constraints and earnings expectations.

The Bank of Japan kept its short-term interest rate at 1% in an 8–1 vote. Markets are also watching currency movements, inflation and the possibility that the U.S. Federal Reserve may need to maintain or increase interest rates if price pressures remain persistent.

Other notable developments

Chinese President Xi Jinping ordered Communist Party leaders to deepen the military’s anti-corruption campaign and emphasized that the armed forces must remain under firm party command. The instruction comes amid continuing removals and investigations involving senior Chinese defense officials.

The International Monetary Fund completed reviews of Egypt’s economic program, unlocking access to approximately $1.8 billion. The IMF continues pressing Egypt to reduce the state’s role in the economy and accelerate reforms that have progressed more slowly than expected.

India’s weather department expects below-average monsoon rain during August. Because much of India’s farmland lacks irrigation, weaker rainfall could reduce harvests, increase food-price pressure and affect economic growth.

Overall assessment

The possible Gaza disarmament-and-withdrawal agreement is today’s most hopeful development, though the absence of a settled timetable and Israel’s complete public acceptance means it could still unravel.

The greatest immediate danger remains the interconnected Middle East conflict. Even without new U.S. strikes overnight, tanker attacks, drone interceptions and threatened shipping corridors could quickly produce another round of escalation. The Russia–Ukraine war is also moving deeper into long-range missile and drone warfare, increasing danger to civilians, NATO territory, energy systems and food exports.

text:
Today, the frontier at Ceuta gave way.   

Thousands crossed or attempted to cross from Morocco into the Spanish enclave, many swimming around coastal barriers or crossing on foot, overwhelming local authorities and forcing Spain to deploy military reinforcements alongside the Civil Guard.   

Morocco tightened security as both governments began returning many who entered illegally. 

The crossings turned deadly, with multiple fatalities, pushing Europe's southern frontier back to the center of political debate.  

Google Earth offers no opinions. It only reveals distance.  Africa and Europe face one another across barely fourteen kilometers of water. 

Every empire believed such a crossing could be controlled. Every empire eventually discovered otherwise.  

Ceuta is not simply another city. 

It is Spain on the African coast, where sovereignty, borders, and national identity collide. 

From orbit, the distance appears insignificant.   

On the ground, it has become one of the most consequential frontiers in Europe.

BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Wednesday, August 1, 1979, Braniff International inaugurated nonstop Boeing 727 Stretch Jet service between Dallas/Ft. Worth Regional Airport and Orlando International Airport in Florida. Braniff offered two daily roundtrip flights between the two cities.

An early morning nonstop from Dallas/Ft. Worth, with meal service, afforded eastbound travelers an arrival in time for lunch. The second flight departed later in the evening and made an intermediate stop at Jacksonville, Florida, before proceeding to Orlando, where it arrived shortly after midnight in time for a good night's rest before the following day's business.

Braniff westbound service was similar to the eastbound flights. Passengers departing for DFW could choose from an early AM departure or a mid-afternoon flight. The morning flight featured an Ultra Service Meal and arrived in Dallas shortly after 2PM, after a brief stop at Jacksonville. The mid-afternoon departure offered convenient nonstop service to Dallas with an Ultra Service Snack served on board. This flight arrived in Dallas shortly after 3PM, in time for dinner.

Both flights from Orlando also offered single-plane and connection services at Dallas/Ft. Worth to several destinations. The morning flight, after the stop at Jacksonville, continued to Dallas/Ft. Worth and then flew nonstop to Denver Stapleton International Airport, where it terminated. The mid-afternoon departure flew nonstop to Dallas/Ft. Worth, and after a brief ground stop it continued nonstop to Los Angeles International Airport. Both flights offered connection service at DFW Airport to Acapulco, Amarillo, Anchorage, Austin, Colorado Springs, Corpus Christi, Denver, Honolulu, Houston, Kansas City, Las Vegas, Los Angeles, Lubbock, Mexico City, Midland/Odessa, Minneapolis/St. Paul, Oakland/San Francisco, Oklahoma City, Reno, Sacramento, San Antonio, Seattle/Tacoma, Tucson, Tulsa, and Wichita.

Photo: Braniff International Boeing 727-227 Advanced Trijet registered as N462BN is departing Dallas/Ft. Worth Regional Airport in in July 1979. The big jetliner is painted in the 1978 Harper and George/Cars and Concepts/Halston Mercury Blue Ultra Color Scheme. Braniff International's successor, Braniff, Inc., moved its headquarters from Dallas to Orlando in 1988. Braniff, Inc. was moving its operations away from Dallas/Ft. text:
Let me tell you how I spent my entire Saturday.

I made an appointment at Petco to get my cat microchipped. That’s it. Nothing else — just the microchip.

Someone from their office called to tell me the vet would need to examine the cat. I said I didn’t need those services and asked whether they were actually necessary.

They said yes: $91 for the vet visit, $50 for the microchip. I told them I only needed the microchip.

Suddenly the vet visit was free and I could just pay for the chip.

Mind you, their website says you can book an appointment to microchip your pet. Nothing about anything else.

Then their system got the cat’s date of birth wrong, so I got a text saying she was too young. She isn’t. I had already told them over the phone that the reason I needed her chipped is that she keeps getting out of her collar and she’s an outdoor cat.

Next, they wanted her vet records — they couldn’t microchip her without them.

I said I’m not looking to establish care, and their website says nothing about that being required.

That’s when they started quoting Colorado law, incorrectly, and said they couldn’t see the cat for a microchip without the requested information.

When I pointed out that the whole thing was deceptive, and that all I wanted was to chip the cat and pay their $50 fee, they offered to send me a list of low-cost clinics that “could help me.”

So I started calling shelters and rescues in the area. Nobody answered, even though they were open. So I drove to them and asked in person if they could just microchip my cat. I was willing to pay.

The answer was no. Either they only do it on specific days at specific times, or they “don’t offer those services to the public.”

Cool.

Here’s my problem. Shelters and rescues constantly post about how many animals get surrendered, how badly they need people to step up, how much funding it takes to provide services. Then someone actually shows up needing one of those services, and the answer is no.

I never asked anyone for a handout. I offered to pay full price every single time — and these places charge $35 for a chip that costs them $10 to $15, so there’s a markup built in. I’d have paid above their asking price if that’s what it took. Money was never the obstacle. There was a number that worked for everyone and nobody would take it.

The result is that the exact problem they claim to be preventing — a lost pet with no way to identify its owner — goes unaddressed.

This is why I understand the disdain people have for rescues and shelters. And don’t get me started on the corporate veterinary industry: thieves who thrive on overselling you things you never asked for and don’t need.

All this is just making it harder for people to convince me that these non-profits and corporations are actually trying to help.

text:
Below is a list of some national, international, global and local observances for August 1, 2026:

Sandcastle Day (first Saturday in August) invites beachgoers to build elaborate sand sculptures before the tide claims them, turning ephemeral art into a communal summer ritual.

National Girlfriends Day celebrates the bonds of female friendship—platonic, sisterly, or romantic—encouraging women to honor those who provide emotional support and laughter; the word “girlfriend” originally meant only a female friend when it first appeared in print in 1859, with the romantic sense attested by 1892.  

Colorado Day (or Statehood Day) marks Colorado’s admission as the 38th U.S. state on August 1, 1876—100 years and 28 days after the Declaration of Independence, earning the nickname “Centennial State” for occurring in the centennial year of American independence; women there gained voting rights by popular referendum in 1893, decades before the national 19th Amendment, making it one of the earliest such victories in the country.  

National Spider-Man Day honors the Marvel character’s debut in Amazing Fantasy #15, whose August 1962 cover date inspired the observance even though the comic actually reached newsstands around June 5; creator Stan Lee deliberately made the first teenage superhero the star of his own series so readers could identify with everyday adolescent struggles alongside the powers.  

National Mustard Day (first Saturday in August) celebrates the ancient condiment at the National Mustard Museum in Middleton, Wisconsin, with tastings, hot dogs, and games; the word “mustard” derives from the Latin mustum ardens (“burning must”), and a 14th-century pope (John XXII, 1316–1334) created the official post of Grand Moutardier du Pape for his nephew because of his love for the paste.  

World Wide Web Day commemorates the hypertext system Tim Berners-Lee proposed at CERN in 1989 that became publicly available in 1991; although the first website went live on August 6, the August 1 date has become the informal annual marker for the technology that turned the internet into a global information space anyone could browse.  

Respect for Parents Day encourages adults to express gratitude for the guidance and sacrifices of those who raised them, whether biological, adoptive, or chosen; it sits alongside other relationship observances on the calendar as a reminder that parental influence shapes communities long after childhood ends.  

Homemade Pie Day invites bakers to create pies from scratch using seasonal fruits or savory fillings; the day pairs naturally with the harvest season’s first fruits, echoing older traditions of offering the initial grain as thanksgiving.  

National Raspberry Cream Pie Day specifically honors the combination of tart berries and creamy filling in a pastry crust, a dessert that highlights midsummer produce at its peak.  

National Disc Golf Day (first Saturday in August) promotes the sport of throwing discs at targets across outdoor courses; it encourages outdoor activity and friendly competition on the same day many other first-Saturday observances fall.  

National Jamaican Patty Day (first Saturday in August) celebrates the flaky, spiced meat-filled pastry that is a staple of Jamaican street food and diaspora cuisine.  

National Mead Day (first Saturday in August) toasts the honey-based fermented beverage that is among humanity’s oldest alcoholic drinks, predating both wine and beer in many cultures.  

National Play Outside Day (first Saturday of every month) urges people of all ages to spend time outdoors for physical and mental health, aligning with summer’s long daylight hours.  

International Blues Music Day (first Saturday in August) recognizes the genre born in the Mississippi Delta that shaped rock, jazz, and popular music worldwide through its expressive storytelling and improvisation.  

International Albariño Day (first Saturday in August) highlights the crisp, aromatic white wine grape native to Galicia, Spain, whose Atlantic-coast origins give it a distinctive minerality.  

National Sunflower Day (first Saturday in August) celebrates the tall, sun-tracking blooms that symbolize loyalty and provide seeds, oil, and visual drama across fields.  

National Summit Day (first Saturday in August) encourages mountain climbing or reaching personal “summits,” whether literal peaks or metaphorical goals.  

National VFR Day (first Saturday in August) honors Visual Flight Rules aviation, when pilots navigate by sight rather than instruments under clear skies.  

DOGust 1st / Universal Birthday for Shelter Dogs assigns August 1 as the official birthday for all dogs whose actual birth dates are unknown, allowing shelters and adopters to celebrate every rescued companion equally.  

National Minority Donor Awareness Day raises awareness about the critical need for organ, eye, and tissue donation within minority communities, where matching rates can be lower due to genetic diversity.  

International Childfree Day affirms the choice of adults who live without children, challenging cultural assumptions that parenthood is universal.  

International Can-It Forward Day promotes home canning and food preservation, encouraging people to stock pantries with seasonal produce for year-round use.  

National Planner Day celebrates the satisfaction of organizing schedules, goals, and daily tasks in paper or digital planners.  

National Pinball Day honors the electromechanical arcade game that combines skill, physics, and flashing lights, still drawing competitive players decades after its peak.  

National Spritz Day toasts the refreshing Italian aperitivo of prosecco, bitter liqueur, and soda water, ideal for warm evenings.  

National Woman Astronomers Day recognizes women who have advanced the science of the stars, from early observers to modern researchers.  

National Mountain Climbing Day encourages ascent of peaks for physical challenge and the perspective gained at higher elevations.  

Play Ball Day promotes youth baseball and softball, urging kids to grab a glove and get outside.  

Rounds Resounding Day invites groups to sing rounds—canons in which voices enter sequentially—creating layered harmony from simple melodies.  

Start-Up Day Across America highlights entrepreneurial ventures and the launch of new businesses across the country.  

National Yorkie Day celebrates the Yorkshire Terrier, the small but spirited breed originally bred to catch rats in textile mills.  National Promise to Care Day focuses on commitments to caregiving, whether for family, community, or self.  

Swiss National Day commemorates the 1291 Federal Charter signed by the cantons of Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden, regarded as the founding of the Swiss Confederation; it only became an official nationwide public holiday in 1994 after a popular vote, and celebrations feature hilltop bonfires, fireworks, and paper-lantern parades.  

Benin Independence Day marks the West African nation’s independence from France on August 1, 1960, celebrated with official ceremonies and cultural events.  

Emancipation Day (observed in Barbados, Guyana, Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, and other former British Caribbean territories) commemorates the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833 taking effect on August 1, 1834 (with full freedom in 1838 after apprenticeship); Trinidad and Tobago was the first independent nation to declare it a national public holiday in 1985.  

Lughnasadh / Lammas is the Gaelic and Anglo-Saxon first-harvest festival marking the ripening of grain; Lughnasadh honors the god Lugh’s foster-mother Tailtiu, who died clearing land for agriculture, while Lammas (“loaf-mass”) involved baking and blessing bread from the new crop, and both traditions once featured games, matchmaking, and offerings of first fruits.  

Yorkshire Day celebrates the historic English county’s heritage, culture, dialect, and achievements on the anniversary of the 1759 Battle of Minden, in which Yorkshire regiments played a notable role.  

Pachamama Day / Pachamama Raymi is an Andean observance honoring the Earth Mother among Quechua and other indigenous communities in Peru, Ecuador, and Bolivia, involving offerings of food, coca leaves, and libations to ensure fertility and balance.  

World Lung Cancer Day raises global awareness of the disease, its risk factors, early detection, and support for those affected.  

World Scout Scarf Day invites Scouts worldwide to wear their neckerchiefs with pride, symbolizing the global movement’s values of service and outdoor skills.  

Armed Forces Day (China) marks the founding of the People’s Liberation Army in 1927; Lebanon also observes an Armed Forces Day on this date.  

Parents’ Day is a public holiday in the Democratic Republic of the Congo honoring mothers and fathers.  

Minden Day is observed by certain British Army regiments commemorating the 1759 victory over the French at the Battle of Minden.  

Food Day Canada (first Saturday in August) highlights Canadian-grown and -produced food, encouraging consumers to support local agriculture.  

International Mahjong Day celebrates the classic Chinese tile game of skill, strategy, and social connection.  

National Andrew Day offers a lighthearted observance for people named Andrew and the cultural associations of the name.

text:
🧬 Genetic testing works better when it becomes part of the cancer appointment - not another referral.

A University of Colorado team evaluated "mainstream" germline testing in a multidisciplinary prostate cancer clinic.

Under the previous referral-based pathway, only 30% of eligible patients completed testing.

The new model identified eligible patients before their visit, provided video-based education developed by genetic counselors, and offered blood or saliva testing during the same appointment. Patients with pathogenic variants or complex questions were then referred for specialist counseling.

Among 227 eligible patients:
• Referral-based model: 34/112 tested (30%)
• Mainstream model: 83/115 tested (72%)
• Pathogenic variants found: 10/83 (12%)
• Post-test counseling completed: 7/10

For oncologists, germline results can affect eligibility for targeted therapies and clinical trials, particularly when DNA-repair variants such as BRCA1/2 are identified.

The benefit also extends beyond the patient. Identifying an inherited pathogenic variant can trigger cascade testing, earlier cancer screening and preventive strategies for relatives.
The model may help genetics specialists focus their limited time on positive or complex cases while reducing delays caused by separate appointments - an especially important issue for rural patients and those with advanced disease.

Important caveat: this was a nonrandomized, single-center before-and-after evaluation. It did not establish effects on treatment selection, family-testing uptake, clinical outcomes or equity, and nearly one-third of eligible patients still remained untested.

text:
After SCOTUS Ruling, Michigan Agrees To End ‘Talk Therapy’ Ban For Gender-Confused Kids | Shawn Fleetwood Visit, The Federalist

The Democrat-run state of Michigan agreed on Thursday to end its prohibition on licensed therapists providing counseling to children struggling with issues related to sexual orientation and gender dysphoria.

“This is a major victory for children, counselors, and common sense,” Luke Goodrich, senior counsel at Becket and lead attorney for the counselors, said in a statement. “Kids who are hurting deserve compassion, not a one-way ticket to harmful drugs, hormones, and surgery. Now counselors can offer compassionate counseling without fearing that state bureaucrats will come knocking.”

Known as Catholic Charities v. Whitmer, the case dealt with several Michigan-based counselors’ challenge to state laws barring them from engaging in talk therapy with minor clients facing discomfort with their sex. The challengers argued that such a prohibition violated their First Amendment rights.

The 6th Circuit Court of Appeals handed plaintiffs a favorable ruling in the case late last year, which was subsequently followed by the U.S. Supreme Court’s Chiles v. Salazar decision. In Chiles, the high court ruled that a similar Colorado law “regulates speech based on viewpoint, and the lower courts erred by failing to apply sufficiently rigorous First Amendment scrutiny.”

“[T]he First Amendment stands as a shield against any effort to enforce orthodoxy in thought or speech in this country. It reflects instead a judgment that every American possesses an inalienable right to think and speak freely, and a faith in the free marketplace of ideas as the best means for discovering truth. However well-intentioned, any law that suppresses speech based on viewpoint represents an ‘egregious’ assault on both of those commitments,” Justice Neil Gorsuch wrote for an 8-1 majority.

In Thursday’s stipulated order, Biden-appointed Judge Jane Beckering noted that, in light of the 6th Circuit and Supreme Court’s rulings, the Catholic Charities plaintiffs have “demonstrated success on the merits” of their claim that Michigan’s laws represent an unlawful viewpoint-based restriction on speech. She further observed that the plaintiffs have “established irreparable injury and that an injunction is in the public interest.”

As such, both parties agreed to the stipulated order and final judgement, which prohibits Michigan from enforcing the talk therapy ban against counselors in the state.

“The Court hereby DECLARES that HB 4616, as applied to licensed mental health professionals engaged in therapy that consists exclusively of talking, violates the Free Speech Clause of the First Amendment to the United States Constitution,” Beckering wrote. “The Court hereby PROHIBITS Defendants, their successors, agents, and all those acting in concert with them from enforcing HB 4616 against licensed professionals who engage in therapy that consists exclusively of talking.”

The court’s permanent injunction will take effect immediately, according to the order.

“Michigan is now admitting its law is unconstitutional,” Goodrich said. “Its surrender confirms that the Constitution and the best available science are on the side of counselors who help children find peace with their bodies. States still trying to censor that care should take note.”

The Great Lakes State’s agreement to end enforcement of the contested laws is a noticeably different path taken than that of neighboring Wisconsin. Months after the Supreme Court handed down its Chiles ruling, Democrat Gov. Tony Evers doubled down on seemingly defying the decision.

“I have no intention of repealing the ban on … conversion therapy on kids. Period. End of story. And no question,” Evers said during a June “Pride Flag Raising” event.

text:
July 25, 1806 — Yellowstone River, present-day Montana.

William Clark climbed a 200-foot sandstone formation overlooking the river and the open country beyond it.

In his journal, he called the landmark:

“Pompys Tower.”

The name honored a small boy Clark had grown deeply attached to during the Lewis and Clark Expedition.

Jean Baptiste Charbonneau.

Sacagawea’s son.

Clark called him “Pomp.”

Only about 18 months old when Clark named the landmark after him, Jean Baptiste had already experienced more of the continent than most men of the era ever would.

He had been born at Fort Mandan on February 11, 1805.

Two months later, his mother carried him west with the Corps of Discovery.

Before he could walk, Pomp had crossed Native homelands, traveled through the Rocky Mountains, reached the Pacific Ocean, and survived the return journey to St. Louis.

But that was only the beginning of his life.

After the expedition, Clark wrote to Jean Baptiste’s father:

“As to your little son, my boy Pomp, you well know my fondness for him.”

Clark offered to raise and educate the boy as his own.

Jean Baptiste eventually received an education in St. Louis under Clark’s support—but the life waiting for him would stretch far beyond an American classroom.

As a young man, he met Duke Paul Wilhelm of Württemberg, a German prince and adventurer.

The duke took Jean Baptiste to Europe.

Sacagawea’s son—born inside a frontier fort and carried across the American wilderness—was suddenly living among European nobility.

He reportedly learned German and Spanish in addition to English and French.

He encountered aristocrats, formal education, European customs, science, culture, and a world almost unimaginably distant from the country of his birth.

He could have remained there.

He did not.

Around 1829, Jean Baptiste returned to America and went back West.

He became a mountain man, trapper, hunter, guide, interpreter, military scout, public official, and gold prospector.

He moved among Native communities, French-speaking traders, American soldiers, Mexican settlements, European travelers, and hardened frontiersmen.

Few men of his generation could move through so many worlds.

Jean Baptiste could survive in remote mountain country.

He could communicate with educated officers and powerful officials.

He understood Native customs because Native identity was part of his own life.

He had also lived inside European society.

He was not simply caught between two worlds.

Both worlds lived inside him.

During the Mexican-American War, Jean Baptiste helped guide American forces through the Southwest.

He later served as an alcalde in California—a position combining responsibilities similar to those of a magistrate, mayor, judge, or sheriff.

Think about that journey.

He entered the world as the infant son of a Shoshone woman inside a frontier fort.

He crossed the continent on his mother’s back.

He was educated through William Clark.

He lived among European nobility.

He returned to trap in the Rocky Mountains.

He guided soldiers through the Southwest.

He held public office in California.

Then the Gold Rush pulled him toward another frontier.

By 1866, Jean Baptiste was approximately 61 years old.

Rather than settle quietly, he left California and headed toward another mining opportunity in Montana.

One final journey west and north.

While traveling through what is now eastern Oregon, he became seriously ill after crossing frigid water.

Jean Baptiste Charbonneau died on May 16, 1866.

He was buried in the high desert near present-day Jordan Valley, Oregon.

He entered life while Lewis and Clark prepared to cross the continent.

He left it while still searching for whatever waited beyond the next horizon.

The image attached to this post is commonly presented as the only known portrait of Jean Baptiste Charbonneau.

Even that identification remains unverified.

We may not know with certainty whether this is truly his face.

But we know the life behind the name.

History often remembers Jean Baptiste as nothing more than the baby carried on Sacagawea’s back.

That does him a tremendous injustice.

He became one of the most culturally experienced and adaptable men of the American West.

Native and European.

Educated and rugged.

Comfortable around nobility, yet repeatedly drawn back toward wild country.

Jean Baptiste Charbonneau was not merely Sacagawea’s son.

He lived an incredible American life.

Read his full story:

In 1998, Warren Buffett gave a 1-hour masterclass on how to never lose money investing.

Here are the 22 most valuable lessons from his lecture:

1. You only have to get rich once. If you have $100 million and can make 10% unleveraged or 20% leveraged, the difference between $110 million and $120 million at year-end means nothing to your life, your family, or anything. But the downside, especially with other people's money, is disgrace, humiliation, and facing the friends whose money you lost. The equation never makes sense.

2. To make money they did not need, they risked money they did have and needed. That is just plain foolish, Buffett says, regardless of your IQ. If you hand him a gun with a million chambers and one bullet and offer him any sum to put it to his temple and pull once, he will not do it. There is nothing on the upside that justifies the downside. People do this financially all the time without thinking.

3. The smartest people in finance went broke, and that is the most fascinating story Buffett knows. Long-term Capital Management had 16 people with possibly the highest average IQ of any business in the country, 350 to 400 combined years of experience, and most of their own net worth in the firm. They still went bankrupt. Buffett says if he ever wrote a book, it would be called why smart people do dumb things.

4. Beta and sigmas tell you nothing about the real risk of going broke. The LTCM team relied heavily on mathematics and believed a six- or seven-sigma event could not touch them. They were wrong. History does not tell you the probabilities of future financial events. The real risk is not volatility. It is a permanent, irreversible blind spot in something crucial, often caused by knowing a great deal about something else.

5. Invest only in businesses you can understand. That one rule narrows the field by about 90%, and that is fine. Buffett can understand Coca-Cola. he cannot value an internet company, and he says if a student handed him a valuation of one on a final exam, he would flunk them. People thought Enron was incredible because it had a good track record, but almost nobody understood how it made money. That was the signal to avoid it.

6. You want a business that is a castle with a wide moat around it. Inside the castle, you want an honest, able, hard-working duke. The moat can be low cost, like Geico in auto insurance, or brand, or patents, or location. But a wonderful castle will always be attacked, so the job of every manager Buffett owns is one thing: widen the moat. Throw crocodiles and sharks into it to keep competitors out.

7. Moats change slowly and invisibly, but they change. Thirty years ago, Kodak's moat was as wide as Coca-Cola's. They had share of mind; the little yellow box meant best in everyone's head. Then they let Fuji into the Olympics and narrowed their own moat. Coca-Cola's moat, by contrast, is wider now than 30 years ago. Every time infrastructure gets built in a country that is not yet profitable, the moat widens a little. You cannot see it day by day, but in 10 years, the difference is enormous.

8. Share of mind beats share of market. When you say Disney, every person in the room has something in their head. Say Universal Pictures or 20th Century Fox, and you have nothing. A mother with two kids will pick the $17.95 Disney video over the $16.95 alternative because she knows it will be fine and does not want to preview ten videos to decide. That little bit of certainty in the customer's mind is worth a fortune.

9. The best businesses have pricing power and require little capital. see's candy sold 16 million pounds at $1.95 when Buffett bought it for $25 million. The entire thesis was whether the price could go to $2.25 without hurting sales. It could, because nobody wants to hand their valentine a box of candy and say, "This year I took the low bid." Today, See's makes $60 million on the same formulas and still takes almost no capital. Compare that to GM, which had to reinvest every dollar into better factories and whose stock barely moved over 50 years.

10. The best businesses earn a royalty on other people's capital. Coca-Cola sells a formula and collects a royalty on every drink. American Express takes a few percent of every dollar you spend. You put up the capital, they take a cut. Low capital intensity is one of the most underrated qualities in a business and one of the surest paths to durable wealth.

11. Define your circle of competence and stay inside it. The size of the circle does not matter. Staying inside, it does. If you know which 30 companies out of thousands you actually understand, you are fine. Buffett understood H.H. brown shoes and Frank Rooney, so he closed that deal in five minutes. If you do not know enough to understand a business instantly, you will not understand it in a month either.

12. Ignore the macro entirely. Buffett has never bought or skipped a business because of a feeling about interest rates, the economy, or any macro forecast. If Alan Greenspan and Bob Rubin both whispered exactly what they would do for the next 12 months, it would not change what he pays for anything. You want to focus on what is important and knowable. The macro is important but not knowable, so you ignore it.

13. Inactivity is the strategy, not a flaw. Wall Street makes money on activity. You make money on inactivity. A broker is like a doctor paid by how often he changes your pills. If everyone in a room trades their portfolio with everyone else every day, they all end up broke, and the intermediary keeps the money. Buffett looks for one good idea a year and rides it to its full potential. He measures Berkshire by how little turnover there is, like a church where the same people fill the seats every Sunday.

14. If you understand businesses, diversification is a mistake. For the 99% who will not evaluate businesses, Buffett recommends a low-cost index fund and extreme diversification. But if you bring real intensity to evaluating companies, owning more than six is a terrible idea. Very few people got rich on their seventh best idea. A lot of people got rich on their best one. Buffett keeps about half his money in what he likes best.

15. Buffett's biggest mistakes are mistakes of omission, not commission. The times he understood a business well enough to act and instead sat there sucking his thumb. He passed on healthcare stocks during the Clinton plan and on Fannie Mae in the mid-eighties, each a multi-billion-dollar miss. Accounting never captures these. The $2,000 he put into a Sinclair service station as a young man, money he lost, has an opportunity cost of about $6 billion today.

16. Focus on what will happen, not when. Coca-Cola went public in 1919 at $40 a share and dropped to $19 within a year. There was always a reason not to buy: the great depression, world war, sugar rationing, thermonuclear weapons. But one share bought then and reinvested would be worth about $5 million. If you are right about the business, you will make a lot of money. The timing is the tricky part, so do not focus on it.

17. When hiring, look for integrity, intelligence, and energy. But if the person lacks the first one, you actually want them dumb and lazy. Because a person with intelligence and energy but no integrity will destroy you. Buffett borrowed this from Pete Kiewit. The trait everyone screens for last is the one that matters most.

18. Here is a thought experiment Buffett gives students. Imagine you could own 10% of one classmate for the rest of their life. You would not pick the highest IQ or the best grades. You would pick the person you respond to best, the one who is generous, honest, gives credit to others, and has leadership qualities. Now imagine you also had to short one classmate. You would pick the egotistical, greedy, slightly dishonest one. The qualities that decide both are not talent. They are character.

19. Every quality on the admirable side is achievable, and every quality on the repellent side is removable. The things that make you want to own 10% of someone are not the ability to throw a football or run fast; they are behavior, temperament, and character, all of which anyone can choose. Buffett's point: you already own 100% of yourself, so you might as well become the person worth betting on.

20. The chains of habit are too light to be felt until they are too heavy to be broken. Buffett sees people in their forties and fifties trapped by self-destructive patterns they can no longer change. At a young age, you can choose any habits you want. Ben Franklin and Ben Graham both did exactly this, looking at people they admired and simply deciding to behave like them. There was nothing impossible about it.

21. Take a job you would take if you were already independently wealthy. Buffett told a 28-year-old at Harvard who wanted a consulting job "to look good on his resume" that it was like saving up sex for your old age. There comes a time to just start doing what you love. Buffett offered to work for Ben Graham for free, was told he was overpriced, and kept pestering him for years. Take the job you would jump out of bed for. You cannot miss.

22. You won the ovarian lottery, and that should shape how you think. Buffett imagines a genie 24 hours before your birth letting you design the world's rules, with one catch: you do not know which of 5.8 billion balls you will draw. Born here or in Afghanistan, with an IQ of 130 or 70, male or female, able-bodied or not. If you could put your ball back and draw one of 100 random others, most people would not, because they are already in the luckiest 1%. Buffett knows he is perfectly wired for a market economy that pays him like crazy, while an equally good citizen leading scout troops and teaching Sunday school is not, purely by luck.

text:
Thoros II the Great 

Thoros II (Armenian: Թորոս Բ), also known as Thoros the Great, was the sixth lord of Armenian Cilicia from the Rubenid dynasty from 1144/1145 until 1169.

Thoros (together with his father, Levon I and his brother, Roupen) was taken captive and imprisoned in Constantinople in 1137 after the Byzantine Emperor John II Comnenus during his campaign against Cilicia and the Principality of Antioch, successfully had laid siege to Gaban and Vahka. All of Cilicia remained under Byzantine rule for eight years.

Unlike his father and brother, Thoros survived his incarceration in Constantinople and was able to escape in 1143. Whatever the conditions in which Thoros entered Cilicia, he found it occupied by many Greek garrisons. He rallied around him the Armenians in the eastern parts of Cilicia and after a persistent and relentless pursuit of the Greeks, he successfully ousted the Byzantine garrisons from Pardzerpert, Anazarbus, Adana, Mamistra and eventually Tarsus. His victories were aided by the lack of Muslim attacks in Cilicia and from the setbacks the Greeks and the Crusaders suffered on the heels of the Siege of Edessa in 1144.

Emperor Manuel I Comnenus, unhappy with Thoros's progress in the areas still claimed by the Byzantine Empire, sought peaceful means to settle his conflict with Thoros, but his attempts bore him no fruits. The recovery before 1150 of the Taurus fortresses by Thoros had not seriously affected Greek power, but his conquest of Mamistra in 1151 and the rest of Cilicia in 1152 had necessitated a great expedition. As a result, during the course of the next 20 years there were no fewer than three separate military campaigns launched by the emperor against Thoros, but each campaign was only able to produce a limited success.

Thoros's accomplishments during his reign placed Armenian Cilicia on a firm footing.

'Thoros was of a tall figure and of a strong mind: his compassion was universal; like the light of the sun he shone by his good works, and flourished by his faith; he was the shield of truth and the crown of righteousness; he was well versed in the Holy Scriptures and in the profane sciences. It is said that he was of such profound understanding, as to be able to explain the difficult expressions of the prophets – his explanations even still exist.'

— Vahram of Edessa: The Rhymed Chronicle of Armenia Minor
Early life 

Thoros was the second son of Levon I, lord of Armenian Cilicia. The name and the origin of his mother are not known with certainty It is possible that she was a daughter of Count Hugh I of Rethel, or she may have been the daughter of Gabriel of Melitene.

In 1136, Levon I (Thoros's father) was made prisoner by Baldwin of Marash who sent him off to captivity in Antioch. In his absence, his three sons quarreled; the eldest, Constantine, was eventually captured and blinded by his brothers. After two months of confinement, Levon I obtained his liberty by consenting to harsh terms.

In the early summer of 1137, Emperor John II Comnenus came to Cilicia with a full force on his way to take Antioch; his army successively retook Seleucia, Korikos, Tarsus, Mamistra, Adana, Tel Hamdou and Anazarbus. Levon I took refuge in the Taurus Mountains, but at last found the situation hopeless, and surrendered himself to the conqueror; Thoros and his youngest brother, Roupen were also taken captive together with their father. They were dragged away to Constantinople, where Levon I died in imprisonment in 1141. Roupen, after being blinded, was assassinated by the Greeks.

Lord of Armenian Cilicia

The liberation of Armenian Cilicia

Thoros escaped from Constantinople about the year 1143; he fled to the island of Cyprus, which was then under Byzantine suzerainty, aboard a Venetian vessel and then found his way to Antioch. He took refuge at the Court of his cousin, Count Joscelin II of Edessa. From there, in the company of a few trusted comrades, he was assisted by a Syrian priest, who led them by night to a safe shelter by the river Pyramus.

They then crossed the Amanus range and reached the mountainous Armenian strongholds in the Taurus Mountains where Thoros began gathering a new following. He recaptured the family stronghold of Vahka and two of his brothers, Stephen and Mleh joined him. He made friends with a neighboring Frankish lord, Simon of Raban, whose daughter he married.

;Levon died and was elevated to Christ; the emperor then felt compassion for Thoros, took him out of prison, and received him into the imperial guards. Being now in the imperial palace, and a soldier among the soldiers, he very soon distinguished himself, and even the emperor looked upon him with benevolence. Before the end of the year /1141/ the emperor left Constantinople with a large army, and went to assist the Prince of Antioch, who was hard pressed by the Turks. Being on a hunting party in the valley of Anazarbus, one of his own poisoned arrows wounded him, and he fell dead on the spot; he thus met with his deserved fate (…) The Greek army returned, but Thoros remained in the country; though the traditions concerning this fact are different. Some say, Thoros withdrew himself quite alone, went by sea from Antioch to Cilicia, and took possession of his dominions, finding means to gain at first the town of Amouda, and afterwards all the other places. But the emperor’s party say that Thoros, during the time the Greeks stayed in the country, lived with a lady who gave him a great sum of money; with these treasures he fled to the mountains, and discovered himself to a priest as the son of Levon, the true king of the country. The priest was exceedingly happy at these tidings, and Thoros hid himself under a shepherd’s disguise. There were many Armenians in this part of the country who, being barbarously treated by the Greeks, sighed for their former masters; to these men, as it is said, the priest imparted the joyful tidings; they instantly assembled and appointed Thoros their Baron; he gained possession of Vahka, and afterwards of many other places. Let this be as it may, it was certainly ordained by God that this man, who was carried away as a prisoner, should become the chief of the country of his forefathers, that he should take the government out of the hands of the Greeks, and destroy their armies.'

— Vahram of Edessa: The Rhymed Chronicle of Armenia Minor
The first Byzantine attack against Cilicia

In 1151, while the Byzantines were distracted by the Moslem attack on Turbessel, Thoros swept down into the Cilician plain and defeated and slew the Byzantine governor, Thomas, at the gates of Mamistra. Emperor Manuel I at once sent his cousin Andronicus Comnenus with an army to recover the territory lost to Thoros. But Thoros was well prepared for the unsuspecting Greeks and consequently won a decisive victory at the Battle of Mamistra in 1152. As Andronicus Comnenus moved up to besiege Thoros at Mamistra, the Armenians made a sudden sortie and caught him unawares. His army was routed and he fled back in disgrace to Constantinople.

In the meantime, the Hethumids, who were pro-Byzantine sympathizers, did not overlook any opportunity for engaging in an anti-Roupenian armed conflict. Andronicus Comnenus's mission was such an opportunity but it was not an occasion for glory: many of their numbers were killed by Thoros's aggressive strategy, and many more were taken into captivity. Among the captives were the two illustrious members, Oshin II of Lampron and his son Hethum. Oshin II was eventually released for a ransom but his son was kept as hostage; but Thoros arranged the marriage of his daughter to Hethum and returned half the ransom money to the groom's father Oshin II of Lampron.

'In the same year /1151/ Levon's son, Thoros, took Mamistra and Tel Hamdoun from the Romans and seized Duke Thomas. Duke Andronicus who was charged with protecting the land of the Cilicians by order of the Roman emperor, came to the city of Mamistra with 12,000 cavalry against Thoros. And he boasted, shouting out to Thoros: «Behold your father's iron chains. I will take you bound in them to Constantinople, like your father.» When valiant Thoros heard this, he was unable to bear the insult. Instead, placing his trust in God, he assembled his forces, breached Mamistra’s walls at night, and attacked /the Byzantine troops/ like a lion, putting them to the sword. Among those who died in the great battle before the city gates was Sempad, lord of Barbaron. Among those captured were the lord of Lampron, Oshin, the lord of Partzepert, Vasil, and the lord of Prakan, Tigran /all of whom were/ on the side of the emperor. /Thoros’/ troops seized and despoiled the weak Roman forces and then let them go.'

— Smbat Sparapet: Chronicle

Wars with the Seljuks and Antioch

Emperor Manuel I Comnenus persuaded the Seljuk sultan of Rûm, Mesud I, to attack Thoros and demand his submission to the Sultan's suzerainty. However, the ensuing Seljuk attack, which in fact was provoked by an Armenian raid into Seljuk lands in Cappadocia in the winter of 1154, was routed successfully by Thoros in collaboration with a contingent of the Knights Templar.
'In the year 603 AE /1154/ once again the Byzantine emperor Manuel sought to stoke Masud and he sent him twice the amount of treasure as previously, saying: «Quench the burning of my heart toward the Armenian people, destroy their fortresses, and exterminate them.» So the sultan came to Anazarbus with many troops, but he was unable to accomplish anything. He sent one of his grandees, named Yaqub, to ravage the territory of Antioch. When they had crossed the gate, the Brothers /the Knights Templar/, as though sent by God, swooped upon them at that place and slaughtered all of them, including their chief. When those in the sultan’s army heard about this, they were horrified. This was not all, for the wrath of God was visited upon them. Their horses perished from tapax /diarrhea/ and they themselves turned to flight, brother not waiting to help brother, nor comrade, comrade. They hamstrung many of the horses and fled on foot through difficult, marshy places, as though they were persecuting themselves. For at that time Thoros was not in his country. Rather, he had gone to Tsets. When he returned and saw what had unfolded everyone thanked God, for they had been defeated without the use of weapons and without a physical battle.'

— Smbat Sparapet: Chronicle

Then the emperor turned to Antioch for help; he offered to recognize the new prince, Raynald of Châtillon, if the Franks of Antioch would fight for him against Thoros; he also promised a money-subsidy if the work were properly done. Raynald willingly complied as the Armenians had advanced into the district of Alexandretta which the Franks claimed as part of the Principality of Antioch.

After a short battle near Alexendretta, Raynald drove the Armenian back into Cilicia; and he presented the re-conquered country to the Knights Templar. Other view is that after the battle Raynald was forced to return home, covered with humiliation; and later on, Thoros voluntarily surrendered to the brethren the fortresses in question, and the Knights in turn took oath “to assist the Armenians on all occasions where they needed help.” In 1156, the Jacobites were allowed to build a new cathedral in Antioch, at whose dedication Constance of Antioch and Thoros assisted.
Having secured the land that he wanted, Raynald demanded his subsidies from the emperor who refused them, pointing out that the main task had yet to be done. Raynald quickly sided with Thoros and conspired to attack Cyprus; and the Armenian attacked the few remaining Byzantine fortresses in Cilicia.

The sack of Cyprus

In the spring of 1156, Raynald of Châtillon and Thoros made a sudden landing on Cyprus. Thoros and Raynald both conducted widespread plundering of the island. The Franks and Armenians marched up and down the island robbing and pillaging every building that they saw, churches and convents as well as shops and private houses. The crops were burnt; the herds were rounded up, together with all the population, and driven down to the coast.
The nightmare lasted about three weeks; then, on the rumor of an imperial fleet in the offing, Raynald gave the order for re-embarkation. The ships were loaded up with booty; and every Cypriot was forced to ransom himself.
In the meantime, Thoros quickly established a friendly rapport with Kilij Arslan II, the new Seljuk sultan of Rûm, and in 1158 a peace treaty was concluded.

In the year 606 AE /1157/ Thoros’ brother, Stephen, Leo’s son, motivated by his wicked nature and without his brother Thoros’ knowledge, arose with his brigade of troops and started to successfully retake /certain/ districts. He took Kokison and Berdus. Sultan Kilij Arslan and Thoros had friendly relations with each other and Stephen, as we said, took these /areas/ without Thoros’ consent. Owing to this disturbance, Kilij Arslan came to the district of Kokison and pacified everyone, in no way blaming the inhabitants. Thence he went to Berdus, while Thoros, out of affection for the sultan, tricked his brother and surrendered Berdus to the sultan, against Stephen’s wishes. The sultan in turn, because of his affection for Thoros, freed the inhabitants of the fortress unharmed. Then Stephen attempted to steal Marash, but could not. (…) Now it happened that Sultan Kilij Arslan had a genuine fondness for Thoros. He sent an emissary to Jerusalem and Antioch to Thoros, and again strengthened that friendship with an oath.'

— Smbat Sparapet: Chronicle

The second Byzantine attack against Cilicia

In the summer of 1158, Manuel I Comnenus launched his second assault on Thoros; at the head of an army, he marched down the usual routes leading to Seleucia. There, with a small rapid deployment force of horsemen and Seleucian troops, he launched a surprise attack on Thoros. Thoros was at Tarsus, suspecting nothing, when suddenly, one day in late October, a Latin pilgrim whom he had entertained came rushing back to his Court to tell him that he had seen Imperial troops only a day's march away. Thoros collected his family, his intimate friends and his treasure and fled at once to the mountains.

Next day the Emperor Manuel entered the Cilician plain; within a fortnight all the Cilician cities as far as Anazarbus were in his power. But Thoros himself still eluded him. While Byzantine detachments scoured the valleys he fled from hill-top to hill-top and at last found refuge on a crag called Dadjog, near the sources of the river Cydnus; only his two most trusted servants knew where he lay hidden. Thus much of Cilicia was restored back to Byzantine control, but Thoros still held the mountainous regions in the north.
Eventually, Baldwin III of Jerusalem intervened and successfully brokered a peace treaty between the emperor and Thoros: Thoros had to walk barefoot and bareheaded to the camp of the emperor; there he prostrated himself in the dust before the imperial platform. The pardon was accorded to him for his transgressions both in Cilicia and Cyprus, and still allowed to hold partial possession in Cilicia.

The murder of his brother

Thoros's brother, Stephen, ignoring Thoros's official pledges to Manuel I. With the help of a few of his supporters, he continued attacking Greek garrisons thus giving Andronicus Euphorbenus, the Byzantine governor stationed in Tarsus, the opportunity to sabotage the treaty. Stephen was invited to a banquet held in the governor's residence where he was seized upon arrival, and his mutilated corpse was flung over the gates of Tarsus.

Thoros, who had his own reasons for desiring Stephen's murder, accused of Andronicus Euphorbenus of complicity and swept down on Mamistra, Anazarbus and Vahka, surprising and murdering the Greek garrisons. Eventually, reconciliation with the emperor was negotiated through the mediation of king Amalric I of Jerusalem. Andronicus Euphorbenus was recalled and replaced by Konstantinos Kalamanos as the new Byzantine governor in Tarsus.
In alliance with the crusaders

In 1164, when Nur ad-Din, the emir of Aleppo, knew that Amalric I had left for Egypt, he struck at the Principality of Antioch and laid siege to the key fortress of Harenc. Prince Bohemond III of Antioch called upon Count Raymond III of Tripoli, Thoros and Konstantinos Kalamanos to come to his rescue. At the news of their coming, Nur ad-Din raised the siege; as he retired, Bohemond decided to follow in pursuit. The armies made contact on 10 August 1164 at the battle of Harim, near Artah. Ignoring a warning from Thoros, Bohemond attacked at once, and when the Muslims feigned flight rushed headlong after them, only to fall into an ambush. Thoros and his brother Mleh who had been more cautious, escaped from the battlefield.

Around that time (in 1164 or in 1167) Thoros visited Jerusalem and suggested the colonization of a large number of Armenians, but the Latin prelates forced Amalric I to refuse the offer by their insistence that they should pay the dime (a special tax).

The third Byzantine attack against Cilicia

Intermittent fighting erupted everywhere, harassing the Greek forces throughout Cilicia. In 1168, emperor Manuel I, obsessed with his dilemma with Thoros, marched his armies into Cilicia for the third time under the command of Konstantinos Kalamanos. But Kalamanos was able to produce only limited successes which in the end induced Byzantium to renounce its right of possession of the whole of Cilicia so long as it had access to the ports of the Gulf of Alexandretta. Byzantium also disclaimed all rights to direct government of Cilicia and accepted in settlement only Thoros's recognition of Byzantine suzerainty.

Last years

Thoros quarreled with his brother Mleh who attempting to assassinate him fled to Nur ed-Din and became a Muslim.
'Now his brother, Mleh, was a malicious and treacherous man, and planned to kill his brother, Thoros. Getting together some others of the same tendency, one day while they had gone out to hunt deer, Mleh wanted to slay his brother there /at a place/ between Mamistra and Adana. But Thoros had been forewarned. He furiously seized Mleh and interrogated him before the troops and the princes as to what he was hoping to accomplish. They reproached Mleh in their presence and he was shamed. Then /Mleh/ gave /to T'oros/ much of the inventory of his authority, horses, mules, weapons, and treasures. And they removed him from his district. Thus he received nothing in exchange for his wickedness. So /Mleh/ arose and went to Nur ed-Din, lord of Aleppo, and entered into his service.'

— Smbat Sparapet: Chronicle

Thoros, weary after nearly quarter of a century of rule and warfare, abdicated in favor of his young son Roupen II, who was placed under the guardianship of Thoros's father-in-law, the Regent Thomas. After his abdication, Thoros became a monk.
He died in 1169. He was buried in the monastery of Drazark.

text:
Saint of the day
St. Ignatius Loyola

St. Ignatius Loyola, born Inigo Lopez de Loyola in 1491 in Loiola, Spain, hailed from a noble family and dreamed of becoming a distinguished military leader. Inspired by heroic stories, he joined the army and served under the Duke of Nájera. In 1521, during the battle of Pamplona, he was severely injured by a cannonball to his legs, leading to a long and painful recovery that changed his life's direction.

During his bedridden days, Ignatius immersed himself in religious writings, including 'De Vita Christi,' which deeply influenced his spiritual journey. He began visualizing himself in the presence of Christ, a practice that later became the foundation of his spiritual exercises. As he regained his health, he chose to pursue a life devoted to Christ rather than seeking worldly glory.

In 1522, Ignatius abandoned his military ambitions and retreated to the Benedictine monastery of Santa Maria de Montserrat, adopting an ascetic lifestyle in Manresa. Through prayer and contemplation, he sought to understand God's will better, even as he struggled with doubts and depression.

Recognizing the need for education to effectively spread the Gospel, Ignatius continued his studies in Barcelona, Alcala, and Salamanca. Despite being investigated by the Inquisition, he was always cleared and proceeded to the University of Paris. There, he formed friendships with Peter Faber and Francis Xavier, collaborating on developing his spiritual exercises.

When political turmoil prevented them from traveling to the Holy Land, Ignatius and his companions offered their services to Pope Paul III in Rome. In 1540, they were officially established as the Society of Jesus, also known as the Jesuits. Although initially hesitant, Ignatius became their first leader.

Under Ignatius' leadership, the Jesuits adopted a disciplined approach similar to his military background. Their dedication to education led to the establishment of 35 schools before his death in 1556. The Jesuits played a significant role in countering the Protestant Reformation and are celebrated today for their global educational initiatives.

St. Ignatius Loyola was beatified in 1609 and canonized in 1622. His feast day is celebrated on July 31, and he is the patron saint of the Society of Jesus, soldiers, educators, and education.

St. Ignatius Loyola, pray for us.

text:
All civil law must be contained in the eternal law.

Any civil law which is not founded upon the eternal law is, ipso facto, unjust and deprived of binding force. (Cf. Leo XIII, Libertas Praestantissimum, §9,10, On the Nature of Human Liberty.)

The eternal law consists of Divine Law and Natural Law.

Obviously, vaccine mandates are not in the Divine Law. No one claims that.

Therefore, either these mandates are in the Natural Law or they are not in the Eternal Law at all.

But vaccine mandates are not contained in the Natural Law.

For the natural law is “immutable and permanent throughout the variations of history; it subsists under the flux of ideas…” (Catechism of the Catholic Church, §1958) Vaccine mandates (like all mandated purely preventive medical interventions) presuppose the validity of various scientific hypotheses regarding the vaccine’s safety, efficacy, and importance. None of these hypotheses enter into — or are even capable of ever entering into – the “immutable, permanent” truths which Natural Law’s premises consist in. Instead, such hypotheses are contained entirely and always within the very “flux of ideas” which never adds to the natural law.

Therefore, it is impossible for any alleged obligation which presupposes the veracity of these hypotheses to itself find a standing within the Natural Law. Optional beliefs cannot generate mandatory actions. Observation obliges, theory does not.

From all this it follows that vaccine mandates are at odds with Catholic teaching on the nature of human liberty, natural law, and civil law. They are egregiously unjust.

This does not mean Catholic teaching prohibits vaccination. That’s not what I’m saying. I’m saying it prohibits *mandating* vaccination – as the CDF taught, as recently as 2020, “practical reason makes evident that vaccination is not, as a rule, a moral obligation and that, therefore, it must be voluntary.” I am merely explaining why indeed this is true. I am defending Church teaching, as is the Florida AG. People who say “Church teaching embraces vaccine mandates” don’t know what they’re talking about. Nowhere does Church teaching do this, but right here you can see it explicitly says the opposite.

Institutional mandates (especially when they pertain to something as important as work or education) are thus similarly proscribed. The Church teaches that work and education are rights, therefore when fundamental obstacles are placed before these things, those obstacles must be subject to the same theological rigor that a bonafide civil law would receive.

Therefore, those who complain against the Florida AG — by saying, “Catholicism doesn’t prohibit vaccination, so why should Catholic schools offer a ‘religious exemption’ “ — are missing the point spectacularly. The policy *itself* that mandates vaccination is gravely unjust and contrary to Catholic teaching. These people are not only defending the policy, they’re saying we shouldn’t even allow exceptions to it.

I’ve answered all objections to this argument –including those written against me in the NCBC (National Catholic Bioethics Center) journal papers – in my 2025 booklet, On Those Who Are Well: The Philosophical and Theological Case Against Vaccine Mandates and the Moralizing of Preventive Medicine

text:
Sean Henry has had the same eBay account since 2003 — he was 8 years old when he started selling his Christmas presents online. By the time he got to Georgia Tech on a full scholarship, he had spent his whole life selling online and had one clear conviction: everyone is going to want things faster, cheaper and online forever. The problem was that independent brands had no way to compete with Amazon's fulfillment infrastructure.

He registered Stord LLC at 18 with $5,000 to $10,000 in savings — not enough to open a warehouse. So he called existing warehouses and offered them volume and technology in exchange for partnership. They said yes. He dropped out at 19, became a Thiel Fellow and went all in. The hardest part wasn't the logistics — it was building a software culture and an operations culture inside the same company and getting them to actually work together.

Stord recently closed a $250 million Series F at a $3 billion valuation, doubled in under 12 months. The platform manages nearly $15 billion in annual GMV for brands including AG1, True Classic and Seed Health, delivered to nearly 20% of U.S. households in 2025 and is on track for almost $1 billion in annual revenue this year.

His lesson: when you see a big audacious problem, find your wedge. Start narrow enough to create real value for the first customer — but strategic enough to get you where you want to go long term.

text:
As Mary and I wandered through the warm Savannah morning, the city felt like it was quietly opening its palms to us — moss-draped oaks whispering overhead, brick paths carrying the memory of centuries. We turned a corner and suddenly the sound of water rose up, bright and playful, like laughter echoing through the trees.

The park opened before us, a little world carved out of sunlight and shade. At its center stood the fountain — white figures frozen mid‑breath, conch shells lifted as if calling out to the sea from the heart of Georgia. Water arced from their hands in shimmering ribbons, catching the light in a way that made the whole scene feel alive.

Mary paused, her hand brushing mine, and for a moment we simply watched. The spray drifted like mist, cooling the air, and the sculptures seemed almost to shift — guardians of some old myth, welcoming travelers who happened to wander close enough to listen.

Savannah moved gently around us, but in that small circle of water and stone, time slowed. It felt like the city had offered us a secret — a quiet reminder that beauty often waits in the middle of an ordinary walk, ready to surprise you if you’re willing to turn the next corner.

Think: The model analyzes the initial screenshot and identifies ambiguity (e.g., "I cannot read the error code in the terminal window").
Act: The model generates and executes Python code to manipulate the image. It might crop the screenshot to the terminal area, apply a contrast filter, or mathematically count pixel distances between buttons.
Observe: The processed visual data is fed back into the context window, allowing the model to ground its final response in empirical evidence.
This capability is vital for "Self-Healing" agents. If a frontend test fails, the agent can use Agentic Vision to visually inspect the rendered page, detect layout regressions using Python-based visual math (e.g., OpenCV), and verify that the CSS fix actually resolved the issue.

2.4 Nano Banana: Generative Asset Creation
Completing the cognitive stack is Nano Banana Pro (Gemini 3 Pro Image), a specialized model for high-fidelity image generation. In PC agent workflows, this model is not just for art; it is a functional tool for frontend development and data synthesis.

Text Rendering Accuracy: Unlike previous generation models, Nano Banana Pro can render legible, accurate text within images. An agent building a marketing landing page can generate placeholder hero images that actually contain the correct campaign copy, allowing for fully autonomous UI prototyping.
Consistency: The model supports referencing up to 14 input images to maintain character and style consistency. This allows an agent to take a brand style guide as input and generate a suite of consistent icons or assets for an application.
3. The Connectivity Standard: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
To function within a PC environment, the Gemini 3 brain requires a nervous system to connect it to digital limbs (tools). The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has emerged as this standard, universally adopted by 2026 as the "USB-C for AI".

3.1 The End of "Glue Code"
Prior to MCP, connecting an LLM to a local database or filesystem required writing bespoke "glue code" for every integration. MCP eliminates this by defining a standardized client-server architecture based on JSON-RPC 2.0.

Standardization: An MCP Server (the tool) defines its capabilities (resources, prompts, tools) using a strict schema. The MCP Client (the agent) automatically discovers and maps these capabilities without requiring custom adaptation code. This reduces the "N×M integration problem" (connecting N models to M tools) to a linear N+M problem.
3.2 Transport Layer Architecture
The choice of transport layer is critical for PC agent performance and security. MCP supports multiple modes:

Stdio (Standard Input/Output):

Mechanism: The agent spawns the MCP server as a local subprocess and communicates via stdin and stdout pipes.
Application: This is the standard for local PC automation. It offers the lowest latency and highest security because data never leaves the local machine's memory space. It is used for filesystem access, git operations, and local terminal control.
SSE (Server-Sent Events) over HTTP:

Mechanism: The agent connects to a remote URL.
Application: Used for connecting to managed services (e.g., Google Maps, BigQuery) or shared enterprise tools. Google's fully managed MCP servers utilize this transport to provide reliable, authenticated access to cloud APIs.
gRPC:

Mechanism: High-performance binary RPC.
Application: Integrated in 2026 for high-throughput enterprise environments where JSON serialization overhead is prohibitive. It enables agents to interact with microservices meshes with near-native performance.
3.3 Managing Context Saturation
A major challenge in agentic systems is "Context Saturation" or "Tool Space Interference." If an agent is connected to 50 different tools, injecting all 50 schemas into the context window consumes thousands of tokens and degrades reasoning performance.

Lazy Loading: Advanced MCP implementations utilize a "lazy loading" pattern where Resources are advertised via URIs (e.g., postgres://db/users) but the actual schema or data is only fetched when the agent explicitly requests it.
Nexus-MCP: Middleware solutions like "Nexus-MCP" act as gateways, aggregating multiple servers and exposing a simplified routing layer to the agent. This keeps the context window clean while maintaining access to a vast ecosystem of tools.
4. The Digital Toolbox: Essential MCP Servers for PC Agents
A Gemini 3 agent is only as capable as the tools it can wield. A robust PC automation stack requires a curated suite of MCP servers covering filesystem control, browser automation, and data retrieval.

4.1 Filesystem and Terminal Sovereignty
@modelcontextprotocol/filesystem: The baseline server for any PC agent. It provides controlled access to read, write, move, and list files. Security is managed via an "allowed directories" list, preventing the agent from modifying system-critical files.
Desktop Commander / Automation MCP: For advanced control, "Desktop Commander" exposes the terminal itself.
Capabilities: It allows the agent to execute shell commands, manage background processes (start/stop servers), and interact with system prompts.
Telemetry & Audit: These advanced servers often include audit logging, recording every command executed by the agent to a local file for human review—a critical feature for trust and debugging.
Windows-MCP: For Windows-specific environments, this server bridges the gap to the OS UI. It allows agents to interact with native Windows applications, effectively giving the agent "mouse and keyboard" control to manipulate non-API interfaces.
4.2 The Agent's Browser: Puppeteer and Playwright
PC agents often need to interact with the web not just to retrieve data, but to perform actions (e.g., filling forms, clicking buttons).

Playwright MCP: This server wraps the Playwright testing framework. Instead of asking the agent to write a Playwright script and run it, the MCP server exposes high-level tools like 
navigate(url)
, 
click(selector)
, and 
screenshot()
.
Token Efficiency: Modern implementations use "CLI+SKILLS" optimization. Instead of dumping the entire DOM (which is token-heavy), the server returns a simplified accessibility tree or a screenshot for Agentic Vision processing. This allows the agent to "see" the page layout efficiently.
