text:
Isaac Shelby entered the world on December 11, 1750, close to Hagerstown in colonial Maryland as the second son of Evan and Letitia Cox Shelby, who had journeyed from Wales and later joined the Presbyterian faith. After attending nearby schools, he labored on the family farm, took occasional surveying jobs, and by eighteen held the post of deputy sheriff in Frederick County. Economic troubles stemming from Pontiac's uprising forced the household to relocate in late 1770 to the Holston River country near what is now Bristol, Tennessee, where they constructed a fort and opened a trading station. His first taste of combat came during Lord Dunmore's War; as a lieutenant in the Virginia militia he stood second only to his father at the October 10, 1774, clash at Point Pleasant and won notice for courage and competence. When open rebellion against Britain began, he gained a captaincy among the Minutemen in 1776 and spent the next three years gathering supplies for both frontier garrisons and Continental troops while also sitting for Washington County in the Virginia assembly.

News of Charleston's fall in 1780 reached Shelby while he surveyed tracts in Kentucky; he quickly gathered several hundred riflemen and hurried south. He forced the peaceful surrender of Thickety Fort on the Pacolet, seizing ninety-four prisoners, then scored a sharp success at Musgrove's Mill on August 18. There his roughly two hundred men threw up hasty log defenses and drew a Loyalist force twice their size into an ambush, killing or capturing more than a hundred of the enemy. The high point of his wartime record arrived on October 7 at Kings Mountain. Commanding one wing of the Overmountain Men, Shelby directed his troops to creep from tree to tree in the style of frontier skirmishing he called "Indian play." Wave after wave of British bayonet assaults broke against the American line; Major Patrick Ferguson fell, and the remaining Loyalists laid down their arms. The triumph brought Shelby the lasting sobriquet "Old Kings Mountain" together with formal thanks, a sword, and pistols from the North Carolina lawmakers.

In the months that followed Kings Mountain, Shelby offered counsel to General Daniel Morgan and, late in 1781, led six hundred riflemen to the support of Generals Greene and Marion, aiding the seizure of a British outpost near Moncks Corner. Even while campaigning he won election to the North Carolina legislature. By 1783 he had moved permanently to Kentucky, married Susannah Hart, and thrown his energy into the struggle for statehood, attending the successive conventions that produced the new commonwealth and serving as its first governor beginning in 1792. The leadership, logistical talent, and battlefield judgment he displayed throughout the Revolutionary War fixed his reputation as a foremost frontier commander and opened the path to the public honors that marked the remainder of his life until his death on July 18, 1826.

text:
Mallam Nasir El-Rufai has now spent more than 169 days in continuous custody. He faces multiple charges ranging from alleged abuse of office and money laundering to claims of unlawful interception of communications. Yet he has neither been convicted nor subjected to the full, transparent trial process that Nigerian law and international standards of justice demand. 

Bail has been granted in certain proceedings, but the conditions imposed have proven exceptionally stringent, in other matters, applications have been denied or repeatedly adjourned. The result is prolonged pre-trial detention without a final determination of guilt or innocence. This situation warrants careful reflection by those currently entrusted with the instruments of state power. 

The Nigerian Constitution and the Administration of Criminal Justice Act establish clear principles, every citizen is entitled to the presumption of innocence to reasonable bail where offences are bailable and to a speedy trial. Extended detention without conviction, particularly when health concerns and access to medical care have been publicly raised, risks eroding public confidence in the impartiality of institutions. When proceedings appear protracted or conditions for liberty become practically unattainable the distinction between legitimate prosecution and the appearance of selective pressure becomes difficult to ignore. History offers a consistent lesson, Power is never permanent. Those who today exercise authority over the machinery of investigation, prosecution and detention will in time, find themselves subject to the same institutions. The measure of a government’s commitment to the rule of law is not how vigorously it pursues its critics but how scrupulously it upholds due process even when the accused is politically inconvenient. Selective or prolonged restraint of liberty, however strongly justified by the gravity of allegations, ultimately weakens the very foundations of constitutional democracy. A professional and measured approach would therefore prioritise the following:

-Expeditious resolution of all pending charges through open court proceedings.

-Realistic and attainable bail conditions consistent with the constitutional right to liberty pending trial.

-Transparent communication that reassures citizens the process is driven by evidence and law not by electoral calendars or political calculation.

Nigeria’s democratic project is strengthened not diminished, when every citizen regardless of past office or present affiliation receives the full protection of the law. The temporary nature of political power makes this principle not merely idealistic but profoundly practical. Those who remember it while in office leave a more durable legacy than those who forget it.

In a new report, @Heritage’s @DrJayRichards argues that the long-running debate over American identity between “creedalists” and “culturalists” presents a false choice. Creedalists emphasize the nation’s founding principles, such as liberty, equality, and government by consent, as the basis of citizenship and national unity. Culturalists counter that those ideals emerged from a specific historical and cultural tradition rooted in Western, British, and Christian influences and cannot be sustained apart from that heritage.

Richards contends that both perspectives capture important truths but become flawed when treated as mutually exclusive. His report proposes a synthesis summarized as “People, Place, Principles.” According to this framework, American identity rests on three inseparable elements: a people connected by shared history and institutions, a particular geographic homeland that fosters loyalty and stewardship, and enduring principles that provide moral direction and enable self-correction.

Principles require cultural formation to endure, while culture must be guided and judged by universal moral truths. It highlights Abraham Lincoln as an example of integrating national heritage with founding ideals. This synthesis offers a stronger foundation for civic education, patriotism, citizenship, immigration policy, and assimilation, helping preserve American identity while avoiding both abstract ideological nationalism and ethnic nationalism.

text:
House of Cards | why Anthropic cannot fail

FT has just released an interesting (paywalled) piece titled “Inside Google’s $200 bn Wall Street finance machine for Anthropic”

https://t.co/JHnX0KSFfM

The crux of this story is how Anthropic, as a privately-held company without an established credit profile but with large/surging capital spending needs for compute capacity, relies heavily on its ecosystem partners to keep it going

This also means they need to continue ramping their current ARR, generate consistent cash flows to fulfil its lease obligations, and list (IPO) as soon as practically possible – i.e., it absolutely cannot fail, even in the face of competition from open models

The story traces back to when Apollo, together with Blackstone and several global banks, led the initial $35b capital solution for Broadcom’s AI XPV Platform established in June this year

This transaction facilitated Anthropic’s announced capacity expansion of ~1GW of compute infrastructure starting mid-this year

$35b for ~1GW equivalent of TPUs = ~1 mil TPUs (TPU v7) at ~$35,000/unit

This platform is intended to “enable over 20GW in compute capacity for leading frontier AI labs through 2028”, with a scalable capital solution allowing it to access committed capital across a multi-year draw schedule

How things work – 

Google & Broadcom: co-develop and build the TPUs/pods (excluding MediaTek since they are not part of the financing structure)

Broadcom sets up XPV platform, which commits to buy the TPUs using debt (and some equity) anchored by Apollo/Blackstone private credit funds/entities 

The debt structure breaks down into two tiers: 

• Senior A1 (~$6b, offered at 100bps over Treasuries) and A2 notes (~$24b, offered at 5.75%) with residual value backstop provided by Broadcom

• Subordinated first-loss tranche B notes (~$4.5b, offered at 8.5%) 

(Under the residual value support agreement, should Anthropic stop making lease payments and the proceeds from selling the chips prove insufficient to repay what is owed, Broadcom is obligated to cover the full outstanding balance for holders of the A1 and A2 notes)

The TPUs are then leased to Anthropic (over a 5-year term)

The lease rate is not publicly disclosed but recall that Anthropic is said to be paying $1.25b/month to SpaceXAI for access to 300MW of compute on NVIDIA’s GPUs (Hopper+Blackwell) (so perhaps we can assume the monthly stand-alone TPU lease rate to be around $1-1.5 bn/month?)

Besides TPUs/pods, Google needs powered shells (data centers) to house them. This is where the crypto miners-turned-neoclouds fill the gap

TeraWulf was amongst the earliest to partner with Google, and work with Fluidstack as their AI cloud service provider

An example of how the financing structure works is the $3.2b debt financing deal done last October, for the construction of Akela (a 450MW campus) – Google provided a 10-year backstop that covers Fluidstack’s lease obligations/termination payments in the event of payment default/bankruptcy. The deal also came with a lockbox feature with cash flow sweeps prioritizing interest & principal payments (over operating expenses) 

In return for providing the credit backstop, Google received equity warrants exercisable into TeraWulf’s stock (pledge represented ~14% of TeraWulf’s equity as construction collateral)

As the need for powered shells grows – given the 4.5GW of TPU/pods that Google had sold to Anthropic which needed to be installed, they started replicating the TeraWulf’s setup with other crypto miners including Cipher Digital and Hut 8 for data center build-outs in Texas and Louisiana

In Google’s latest SEC filing, they reported the following (as of June 30):

1) Payment obligations related to data centers (accounted for as credit derivatives): $43.8b (this notional amount represents the max potential exposure for its credit backstops with remaining terms of up to 15 years and reduces over time as the underlying parties fulfil their payment obligations)

2) Financial guarantees: $7.6 bn

3) Future capital funding commitments (tied to Anthropic) subject to specified operational/financial milestones through 2030 (accounted for as equity derivatives): $20 bn

4) Future backstops to support build-out of data center & energy supply infrastructure (subject to finalization of terms): $24.1 bn

To round up, Anthropic cannot fail. By extension, this applies to OpenAI too – though with nuanced differences in their setup (i.e., OpenAI hasn’t had an explicit credit backstop yet, which explains why they were exploring that option with NVIDIA)

I guess the widening of hyperscaler/neocloud credit spreads/CDS after the recent launches of Chinese open models (and the looming threats to restrict access to them) were actually credit-negative because of the potential impact on cash flows, not only of the frontier labs but also the hyperscaler/neoclouds

GB News is not a news channel.

On 3 August 2026, GB News published a column by Carole Malone under the headline "Andy Burnham's migrant plan isn't working. What happened in Ceuta is coming to a beach near you." 

Read as a single opinion piece, it is predictable and unremarkable culture-war fare: the new PM is mocked as "Mr Eyelash", the Ceuta crossings are recast as an "invasion", and readers are told that "the majority of Britons" secretly agree with Reform UK's promise to deploy the Royal Navy against small boats.

Read as a product of GB News's ownership structure, it is something else: an instance of a now-familiar house style in which a channel bankrolled by a single billionaire consistently amplifies the policy language of one political party.

Malone's piece works through accumulation rather than argument. Burnham is denied his name for most of the article ("matey", "Man of the People Burnham", "Mr Eyelash") while Farage and Reform's Zia Yusuf are quoted at length and without challenge, their pledge to have "his Majesty's Royal Navy" turn back boats presented as self-evidently the answer the "majority of Britons" are "gagging to hear" - despite it being uncosted, unfeasible, unworkable, and an already failed experiment.

The rhetorical structure is a familiar one in this genre: establish crisis through scale ("60,000... swarmed"), attribute it to institutional cowardice or conspiracy ("because they're 100 per cent in favour of it"), then resolve the crisis with the one policy on offer, borrowed wholesale from Reform's press office.

The migrants who had, by the time of writing, mostly already returned to Morocco go unmentioned, a pattern consistent with the Express, Telegraph, and Mail on Sunday coverage of the same story.

What distinguishes this piece from a newspaper column making the same argument is not its content but its context: it did not appear in a paper competing for readers in an open market, but on a loss-making broadcaster kept alive, year after year, by one man's private fortune.

GB News has never turned a profit. Since its 2021 launch it has run up cumulative losses now exceeding £130 million, a figure covered almost entirely by its two shareholders in holding company All Perspectives: the Dubai-based investment firm Legatum, and Sir Paul Marshall, the co-founder of hedge fund Marshall Wace and a man the Sunday Times Rich List valued at £875 million in 2024. 

Marshall personally injected a further £17.7 million into the channel last year alone, on top of tens of millions in earlier funding rounds.

This is not advertising revenue sustaining a going concern; it is a wealthy individual absorbing eight-figure annual losses indefinitely, on a channel he has openly described in ideological rather than commercial terms.

Marshall is not a passive investor. In February 2024, an investigation by Hope Not Hate found that his private Twitter/@X account had liked and shared posts described as "extreme Islamophobic" and "anti-migrant", including content warning of impending "civil war" in Europe over immigration.

The findings prompted public criticism from figures including Baroness Warsi and led a rival bidder for the Telegraph to call Marshall "unfit to own a newspaper".

The pattern of Marshall's subsequent media acquisitions is not in question: alongside GB News, he founded UnHerd and, in 2024, bought The Spectator for a reported £100 million, consolidating a stable of outlets that share a broadly aligned editorial and ideological politics on immigration, Islam and the culture war.

None of this proves that any individual GB News segment was commissioned to order. What it establishes is structural, not conspiratorial: a channel that has never had to answer to advertisers or subscribers in the way a commercial broadcaster does, because its losses are underwritten by an owner with a documented ideological stake in the subject matter it covers most intensively.
@Ofcom don't appear to care.

THE SURGEON WHO REFUSED TO CUT: A 2024 TESTIMONY 🔻

"I performed over 3,200 surgeries in my career. Tumor removals, organ transplants, spinal reconstructions. I was one of the highest-rated cardiothoracic surgeons in the country. And then I saw what they had in Building 9 — and I never picked up a scalpel again."

⟁

In February 2024, I was recruited for a classified consultation at a military medical research facility in Maryland. They told me it was a "next-generation surgical review." They told me I would be evaluating a new tool for battlefield trauma.

What I walked into was not surgery. It was the end of surgery.

The room was sterile white. No operating table. No anesthesia cart. No instruments. In the center was a pod — matte grey, roughly 7 feet long, with a transparent canopy. Inside was a Marine, 28 years old, who had suffered catastrophic thoracic injuries from an IED blast. His left lung was collapsed. Three ribs were shattered. His aorta had been repaired with a temporary graft that was failing.

They placed him in the pod. A holographic interface appeared above his chest — a real-time, three-dimensional map of every cell in his thoracic cavity. I could see the damage at a molecular level. I could see the graft. I could see the micro-tears forming.

Then they activated it.

⟁

The pod emitted a low-frequency hum. The holographic display showed his cells responding — not chemically, not electrically, but resonantly. The damaged tissue was being rewritten. Not patched. Not sutured. Rewritten at the DNA level.

In 34 minutes, his lung reinflated. His ribs fused. The failing graft dissolved because it was no longer needed — his aorta had rebuilt itself.

I stood there with 22 years of surgical training and watched a machine do in 34 minutes what I could not have done in 14 hours on my best day. And it did it without a single incision. Without pain. Without risk of infection. Without a scar.

⟁

I asked the lead technician how long they had this. He looked at me like I was naive and said: "This unit is a 2019 model. The first prototype was operational in 2003."

2003.

For 21 years, I had been cutting people open — sawing through bone, clamping arteries, stitching organs back together — while this technology sat in a classified facility healing soldiers without a blade.

Every patient I lost on the table. Every family I told "we did everything we could." Every complication, every infection, every scar — all of it was unnecessary. All of it was a choice made by people who decided the public didn't deserve to be healed.

⟁

I resigned from my hospital three weeks later. I couldn't do it anymore. I couldn't stand over a patient with a knife knowing that a painless, scarless, 34-minute cure existed and was being deliberately withheld.

They offered me $2.4 million to consult for the program and sign a lifetime NDA. I refused. Because silence is what kept this technology from the people who needed it most.

The recent declassification orders are real. The facilities are real. The pods are real. I saw them. I watched them work. And now I am telling you — everything you were told about the limits of medicine was a lie.

That's a weak, fluff letter.    
Here's a far better letter:  
Send this letter, and we'll be impressed. =================================  
from: alan@studentloanjustice.org 
to:  alan_garber@harvard.edu 
cc: lawrence_summers@harvard.edu 
date:  Apr 14, 2026, 2:25 PM  
subject:  Offer to pay for the return of bankruptcy rights to student loans.  

Alan,  I am the nation’s first student loan activist, wrote the first published book to be critical of the federal student loan program (The Student Loan Scam, Beacon Press), and have pursued student loan justice for 21 years. My grassroots group now has 1.4 million members across the country.  

Alan: I am disgusted by the collective failure of college presidents in this country to address the unprecedented removal of constitutional bankruptcy rights from student loans. Please don’t pretend to be unaware of this shocking usurpation of the citizens' rights. We both know that all college heads- including you- are very aware of it.   

You may NOT be aware that uniform bankruptcy rights were called for in the Constitution (ahead of every right in the Bill of Rights) as a direct result of a debtor’s rebellion that happened in Western Massachusetts shortly after The Revolutionary War, but it’s true.  Today, 37 of the 43 million federal student loan borrowers are hopelessly underwater on their predatory college debt- It has become a destabilizing, national threat.  

Alan: I urge you strongly to publicly call for the return of standard bankruptcy rights to student loans, and also that the wealthiest colleges in the nation (whose cumulative endowments now approach $1 Trillion in value) pay at least half the cost of the $6 Billion/year in discharges that will result.  This is the solution that will be most beneficial, and least costly to all parties involved.   

It is a very small price to pay considering the alternatives, which could well involve the evaporation of federal loan support for all the colleges, civil unrest, and other horribles one might imagine when the pitchforks and the torches come out.  

These have actually already begun, See the story of Justin Mohn, or the Nelson family of Broken Arrow, Oklahoma for two recent examples (I will paste graphics below).  

Like it or not, Alan.  Fair or unfair, Harvard is the face of the Academy, and the citizens’ rage against this national threatening loan scam will be increasingly- and justly- turned against the colleges who have profited so immensely from it, with Harvard being chief (and most visible) among them.  I know this is the least-cost, most stabilizing solution available. I also see the coming storm. I strongly urge you to take this very good advice. 

Larry Summers has recently called for the return of bankruptcy rights to the loans.  You need to make a similar call while in office, not after you leave. I am cc’ing this letter to him.  

I consider this letter confidential.  Come July, if I hear nothing from you and you take no noticeable, public action toward the end I suggest, I will reconsider that status.  I hope to hear from you in a good-faithed, constructive way.    

I am at your beck and call should you require an expert briefing.  

Godspeed-  Alan Collinge

text:
From a Christmas Eve miracle in 1906 to today’s EV dashboard debates: the story of AM radio is the story of modern mass media.

For over a century, Amplitude Modulation (AM) was the heartbeat of global communication. It broadcasted news during world crises, carried live sports, and introduced the world to rock ’n’ roll.

Here is a look back at the rise, twilight, and enduring legacy of the medium that started it all:

1. The Spark (1906)
Before AM, wireless communication was strictly Morse code. That changed on Christmas Eve 1906, when Reginald Fessenden transmitted human voice and violin music to ships off Massachusetts. Radio operators expecting clicks and dits were stunned to hear "O Holy Night" floating through their headphones.

2. The Golden Era & Technical Leap (1920s–1960s)
The 1920s Boom: Stations like KDKA in the US and 2MT / 2LO in the UK birthed public broadcasting.
The Superhet Revolution: Hardware evolved rapidly from passive crystal sets to Edwin Armstrong’s superheterodyne receiver, allowing precise tuning across crowded airwaves.
Portability & Pop Culture: The arrival of the transistor radio in the late 1950s made music personal and portable. Pirate radio stations in the North Sea beamed rock ’n’ roll to millions across Europe.

3. The Gathering Shadows
By the late 20th century, AM faced hard technical realities:
Interference: Modern electronics, LED lights, and digital adapters generate electrical noise on AM frequencies.
Fidelity & Competition: FM offered crisp, noise-free stereo audio, while digital streaming and podcasts eventually took over.
Tower Shutdowns: Facing massive energy bills to run multi-kilowatt transmitters, broadcasters across Europe have systematically turned off their AM towers.

4. The North American Battleground
While European AM towers fall silent, AM remains vital in the US as the home of news, sports, and talk radio—and an essential public safety network during emergencies.
Its newest hurdle? Electric Vehicles (EVs). 

High-frequency switching in EV powertrains creates heavy interference with AM signals, prompting some automakers to remove AM receivers entirely. This triggered bipartisan efforts like the “AM Radio for Every Vehicle Act” to preserve AM as critical emergency infrastructure.

The Enduring Legacy
AM proved human speech could span continents without wires. It paved the way for television, cellular networks, and digital media.

For anyone who ever turned a smooth vernier dial late at night, watching vacuum tubes warm up while listening to a distant station drift through the static—that warm analog connection was our very first taste of a connected world.

Did you grow up listening to AM radio, or do you still tune in today? What's your favorite memory of the airwaves?

text:
A $30M real estate investment can buy you completely different things depending on where you put the capital.

Monaco.
London.
Miami.
Dubai.

Same money.

Four very different outcomes.

Here's how a global investor should actually think about the decision. 🧵

1/

The first question wealthy investors ask isn't:

"Where is property cheapest?"

It's:

"Where does my capital have the least friction?"

Taxes.
Regulation.
Ownership rules.
Future liquidity.

Because a great asset in the wrong jurisdiction can become an expensive mistake.

2/

Start with taxes.

Dubai has become one of the world's most attractive wealth destinations for a simple reason:

The government has built a system designed to attract capital.

No personal income tax.
No capital gains tax.
No annual property tax.

The main transaction cost is the 4% Dubai Land Department transfer fee.

The capital you make is largely the capital you keep.

3/

Monaco operates on a similar philosophy.

For many residents:

No income tax.
No capital gains tax.
No wealth tax.

But Monaco is a different type of market.

It isn't designed for growth.

It's designed for preservation.

The challenge?

Scarcity.

There is almost nowhere left to build.

That is why Monaco commands some of the highest prices per square metre on earth.

4/

London tells a different story.

For generations, London was the default home for international wealth.

Political stability.
Legal protection.
Global status.

But the equation has changed.

Higher transaction costs, changing tax rules, and uncertainty around future policy have made some international buyers reconsider whether London is still the obvious choice.

5/

Miami sits somewhere in between.

Florida offers major advantages:

No state income tax.
Strong international demand.
A growing business ecosystem.

But unlike Dubai, US buyers and many foreign investors still face federal taxation considerations.

The opportunity is attractive.

The tax structure is simply different.

6/

Then comes the question most investors underestimate:

What does your money actually buy?

This is where the difference becomes dramatic.

A $30M budget in Monaco may buy a rare apartment with an exceptional location.

The same capital in Dubai can buy a waterfront villa, private amenities, more land, and significantly more space.

7/

This isn't because Dubai is "cheap."

The best Dubai properties are not cheap.

Palm Jumeirah villas, Emirates Hills estates, and trophy penthouses command global prices.

The difference is that Dubai still has room to create new ultra-luxury supply.

Monaco doesn't.

8/

That distinction matters.

Monaco's value comes from extreme scarcity.

Dubai's value comes from scarcity plus growth.

One protects wealth.

The other is still attracting new wealth.

Different strategies.

Different investors.

9/

Now look at returns.

Dubai's luxury market has experienced one of the strongest appreciation cycles in the world since 2021, driven by:

• Wealth migration
• Population growth
• Limited prime inventory
• New global demand

Miami has produced strong rental opportunities.

Monaco has historically been a store of wealth.

London remains one of the world's great cities, but international buyers are becoming more selective.

10/

So which city wins?

Wrong question.

The better question:

"What job do I need this capital to perform?"

If the priority is:

Preservation → Monaco
Income → Miami
Global prestige → London
Growth + wealth migration exposure → Dubai

11/

The biggest mistake investors make is comparing properties.

The smartest investors compare ecosystems.

A home is not just a building.

It is a position inside a city.

And cities compete for capital the same way companies compete for customers.

12/

The next decade will likely belong to the places that successfully attract:

Entrepreneurs.
Investors.
Companies.
Families.
Talent.

Because wealth follows opportunity.

And real estate is usually where that movement becomes visible first.

text:
Newcastle United are reportedly continuing to monitor Benfica midfielder Richard Ríos, with the Colombian international remaining a player of interest as the summer transfer window enters its final stages.

According to Portuguese outlet Record, via Sport Witness, Newcastle have tracked the 26-year-old for some time, although their interest has largely stayed out of the public eye. Serie A champions Napoli are also said to be keeping tabs on the midfielder, but Benfica have yet to receive any formal offers.

Ríos only joined the Portuguese club earlier this summer from Brazilian side Palmeiras in a deal worth around €27 million, meaning Benfica are under no immediate pressure to sell one of their newest signings.

The Colombian has made an excellent impression since arriving in Lisbon. Rather than taking an extended break after the World Cup, reports claim Ríos worked with specialist fitness coaches in both Miami and Mallorca to ensure he returned in top physical condition.

That dedication has reportedly caught the attention of Benfica's coaching staff, who have been impressed by his fitness, intensity and all-action style of play. After making a substitute appearance in Benfica's Europa League qualifier against St. Gallen, Ríos is now pushing for a regular place in the starting XI.

Known for his powerful running, ability to carry the ball through midfield and defensive work rate, Ríos has developed a reputation as a dynamic box-to-box midfielder capable of influencing both ends of the pitch.

For Newcastle, he would fit the profile of the athletic, energetic midfielder the club has admired for some time. Following significant changes to the squad this summer, the Magpies continue to assess opportunities to strengthen the midfield with players who can add both quality and depth.

At this stage, there is no indication that Newcastle have made an official approach, and Benfica are not actively looking to sell. However, with both Newcastle and Napoli reportedly keeping a close watch, Richard Ríos is another name to keep an eye on before the transfer window closes. #NUFC

text:
Did Whitmer Push Saline Data Center Without Proper Permits?
State officials warned that the Democrat-backed project was going ahead without required paperwork

By Anna Hoffman @shoesonplease 

Last week, Michiganders learned that the Whitmer administration is considering allowing the Oracle Saline Data Center (“the Barn”) to discharge an average of 15,750 gallons of wastewater into the Saline River every day.

A Freedom of Information Act Request by Michigan Enjoyer shows The Barn’s developer may have known nearly a year prior that it would have a big wastewater problem to deal with.

On Aug. 21, 2025, wastewater engineer Ted Erickson contacted EGLE about the proposed treatment plant. The team was considering underground disposal, but Erickson offered a blunt assessment: “From what I’ve seen–[ground water] is high so not hopeful.”

The day before, EGLE Field Operations Representative (Water Division) Kyle Alexander said in a different conversation with lobbyists that grading on the site could begin in unregulated areas outside the agency’s jurisdiction.

However, because permitting decisions had not been made, he warned that the developer would be “proceeding at their own risk.”

Project representative Patrick Harrington accepted that warning on Aug. 21: “We understand that this grading work will be at our own risk.”

Harrington also resisted combining the temporary stream-crossing permit with the broader wetland review, explaining that work needed to begin in October “to maintain our construction schedule.”

“As referenced above we understand we are doing this at our own risk,” Harrington, a longtime lobbyist in Lansing, added.

Why was the timeline seemingly more important than testing and obtaining permits for critical water infrastructure?

By Oct. 10, a project drawing depicted a wastewater-treatment plant, sanitary sewer and outlet beside the Saline River was submitted.

Five days later, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s Chief Operating Officer Tricia Foster connected Related executives directly with EGLE Director Phil Roos.

Only a few weeks later, Whitmer announced Project Mitten on Oct. 30. Did Whitmer do the developers a special favor by fast-tracking the project despite environmental concerns?

It certainly seems that way.

Included in Related Digital’s Anti Degradation paperwork is an undated, signed letter from Governor Gretchen Whitmer in support of Project Stargate to the Commissioners stating “time is of the essence.”

On Nov. 3, Erickson told EGLE that a surface-water-discharge application would be filed soon and that the owner was “quite concerned with timing and schedule.”

Earlier emails show EGLE officials were already frustrated that the developer’s consultants wanted decisions involving streams, drains, and wetlands without providing a site plan, completed wetland delineation, or Wetland Identification Program application.

One EGLE official wrote internally that the agency’s recommendations had been “generally overridden or ignored to this point.”

EGLE is now considering a draft permit allowing the project’s treated sanitary wastewater to be discharged into the Saline River.

The agency acknowledges that the discharge would increase pollutants and lower existing water quality for certain parameters, although it says the discharge must still comply with applicable water-quality standards.

Ryan Friedrichs—husband of Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, who is supervising her own election for governor—represented Related before Saline City Council on November 10.

One week later, Related formally selected the Saline River alternative.

While the “do it at your own risk” warning applied to early grading, the chronology is clear: Data center construction was advancing while wetland, stream-crossing and wastewater questions remained unsettled.

Would the Barn have received the same interventions from Governor Whitmer and EGLE if Related Digital didn’t have politically connected advocates?

Brock Lesnar Announces Retirement After SummerSlam Loss

The wrestling icon confirmed his retirement following his defeat to rising star Oba Femi at SummerSlam, his final bout inside the unforgiving steel structure. Lesnar expressed simple gratitude for his career highlights, including multiple world titles and UFC crossovers, and said he's ready to enjoy life after spending days recovering in bed. Rival Roman Reigns paid simple tribute with 'Thank you #BrockLesnar,' while fans reflect on unforgettable clashes like those with Undertaker, marking the end of a dominant era and the rise of WWE's next generation.

Bio

Glory to The Conqueror, The Beast Incarnate, The Anomaly or whatever godlike title you choose to bestow upon Brock Lesnar. This monster fit each and every one of them.

Possessing the type of staggering strength and frightening intensity seen only among Superman villains, this 6-foot-3, 266-pound freak of nature from Minneapolis, Minn., forced his way to the top of every major combat sport. He won the NCAA Division I collegiate wrestling championship as a senior at the University of Minnesota, the WWE Championship within six months of his debut and the UFC Heavyweight Title in his fourth professional MMA fight. He also became The One in 21-1.

Plain and simple, the man was built to destroy.

First scouted by WWE officials while smashing his way through the college wrestling ranks, Lesnar debuted on Raw on March 18, 2002, and singlehandedly destroyed a ring full of unfortunate Superstars. From that night on, the domination was unrepentant.

With the sinister Paul Heyman guiding his career, “The Next Big Thing” won the King of the Ring tournament and beat The Rock to win the WWE Title, becoming the youngest WWE Champion in history at that time and the fastest-rising star sports-entertainment had ever seen.

The freight-train momentum of Lesnar didn’t stall one bit after a layoff of nearly 10 years. When The Beast’s sojourn in UFC ended, he returned to WWE in 2012 firing on all cylinders, battling the very best WWE has to offer and achieving the impossible at WrestleMania 30 when he became the first Superstar to defeat The Undertaker on The Grandest Stage of Them All.

Countless monumental wins followed, as Lesnar wrecked John Cena at SummerSlam 2014, decisively defeated Randy Orton via TKO at SummerSlam 2016, Goldberg at WrestleMania 33, Roman Reigns at WrestleMania 34 and longtime rival Cain Velasquez at WWE Crown Jewel.

In a true passing of the torch moment, Lesnar went to war with Oba Femi, culminating in a destructive Hell in a Cell Match that saw The Ruler conquer The Beast. Lesnar has always been quiet and unpredictable, but his embrace of Femi after the match showed his true passion for the future of sports-entertainment.

Brock Lesnar was the man who conquered The Streak. And John Cena. And Randy Orton. And Seth Rollins. And many, many more, becoming one of the greatest forces in WWE history. (WWE)

text:
She was just ten years old when a stranger walked up to her on the street in broad daylight and cut her hair. Her crime was simple: too many strands of hair were slipping out from under her hijab.

When she went to the police for help, they offered no justice. Instead, they told the young girl that it was her own fault.

That little girl was already a chess prodigy in Iran. 

At seven years old, she had won her very first national championship, proudly receiving her trophy while wearing a princess dress and a tiara. As she grew into her teenage years, her incredible talent on the board only shone brighter. 

Dorsa Derakhshani went on to win the Asian Youth Chess Championship three times and earned the prestigious titles of Woman Grandmaster and International Master.

Yet, her brilliant mind could not protect her from a strict system that cared more about enforcing a piece of clothing than celebrating her intellect. Dorsa lived under constant surveillance and suffocating rules, well aware that one small misstep could lead to arrest or worse. Looking back on her childhood, she often reflects, "The blame is always put on the woman."

The turning point came in 2017. Dorsa traveled to Gibraltar to compete in an international tournament, choosing to play without wearing a hijab. 

The reaction from her homeland was swift and harsh. At eighteen years old, the Iranian Chess Federation banned her from the national team. Her career in her home country was stripped away simply because she chose to play the game with her hair uncovered.

Refusing to let this setback destroy her spirit, Dorsa made a life-altering decision. 

At nineteen, she packed everything she owned into six suitcases, took her passport, and left her homeland behind. She landed at Saint Louis University in the United States after earning a full chess scholarship. 

She was completely alone in a foreign country, far from her family and without any safety net.

The pressure was immense, and the fear of failure weighed heavily on her mind. 

"If I fail at university, no one will take care of me," she remembered thinking during those uncertain first months.

She did not fail. 

Instead, she built an extraordinary new chapter for herself. 

Today, Dorsa is pursuing her medical degree at the University of Missouri while continuing to compete on the university chess team. She plans to use the same steady, strategic hands that once moved chess pieces across a board to perform operations and save lives as a surgeon.

The pain of leaving her roots behind remains real, and she misses Iran deeply. However, she understands the dangerous reality of returning under the current government. 

"I have love for my country, but I will not return until the regime has changed," she shares softly. "If I go back, they will put me in prison somewhere, and no one will ever hear from me again."

Dorsa’s journey from a young girl punished for showing her hair to an inspiring future surgeon proves that true strength comes from standing firm in who you are. 

She stepped away from a life of restrictions to create a future defined by freedom, purpose, and unconditional compassion. 

Dorsa once used her mind to win chess matches; now, she is using it to heal people. Though she remains far from the country she loves, she has created a peaceful and meaningful life on her own terms. 

She reminds us that true victory isn't about defeating an opponent—it's about holding onto your freedom, your dignity, and your dreams.

EXCLUSIVE: Nevada rancher Adrienne Snow remembers riding horseback across the high desert as military helicopters thundered overhead.

“You could just bottle up what being an American feels like: to be on a horse with military helicopters flying over you and listening to the national anthem from ‘Top Gun,’” Snow told the Daily Caller. “There’s nothing like it.”

For decades, ranching families in Churchill County raised cattle as military aircraft from Naval Air Station Fallon, home to the Navy’s elite TOPGUN program, trained overhead.

Now, Snow and eight other ranching families say the Navy’s massive expansion of the Fallon Range Training Complex could destroy operations that have survived for generations — while paying them only a fraction of what their losses are worth.

The ranchers are raising a troubling allegation: that federal officials are disregarding agricultural valuation systems created by the federal government itself when determining how much affected families should be paid. The Navy has offered the Snow family $1.48 million for losses projected over 100 years, even though a U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) methodology cited by the family places the annual value of its forage alone at roughly $815,000.

text:
Lift Sanctions on Eritrea in Exchange for Keeping Bab el-Mandeb Open — Enabling a Red Sea Corridor Along Eritrea’s 2,000 km Coastline: A Win-Win for Eritrea, the U.S., and the World​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​ 

The United States must immediately lift the illegal extraterritorial sanctions it has imposed on Eritrea and the Eritrean people. These unilateral measures, added to earlier United Nations sanctions, have isolated the country, inflicted economic hardship on ordinary citizens, and blocked cooperation on critical regional security issues.

United Nations Sanctions on Eritrea

United Nations Security Council Resolution 1907, adopted in December 2009, imposed an arms embargo and targeted sanctions on Eritrea. These measures were fully lifted in November 2018 by Resolution 2444 after improved regional relations.

Illegal Extraterritorial U.S. Sanctions (2021)

Despite this, the United States imposed its own illegal extraterritorial sanctions in November 2021 under Executive Order 14046. These measures targeted the Eritrean Defense Forces, the People’s Front for Democracy and Justice, the Red Sea Trading Corporation, and related entities. Unlike collective UN action, these unilateral American sanctions apply extraterritorially and harm both the Eritrean state and its people.

Violation of the United Nations Charter

Such sanctions violate the spirit of the United Nations Charter. Chapter VII grants the Security Council exclusive authority to impose collective sanctions under Article 41. Unilateral measures undermine this framework and have been criticized in UN human rights mechanisms for their harmful effects on civilians.

The Heavy Cost to Ordinary Eritreans

The sanctions have restricted access to the international financial system, including SWIFT, blocked foreign investment, limited banking, and prevented loans. Imports have grown more expensive, and development in energy, water, and infrastructure has been hindered. Ordinary Eritreans bear the heaviest cost.

Unlocking Red Sea Security Cooperation

Lifting these sanctions would open space for partnership on Red Sea maritime security. Eritrea’s waters remain free from piracy and Houthi attacks. The country can offer a safe corridor for shipping from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to the Suez Canal along its 2,000-kilometer coastline.

Infrastructure and Capacity Needs

To fulfill this role, Eritrea needs reintegration into the global financial system. Access to capital is required for refueling stations, ship repair facilities, LNG terminals, and oil refineries. Modernizing the navy would further strengthen protection of commercial vessels.

Eritrea’s Responsibility: Political Reforms

At the same time, the Eritrean government must act. It should implement the 1997 Constitution, release political prisoners held without charge or trial, and take concrete steps toward openness and accountability. These reforms would strengthen Eritrea’s standing and readiness for cooperation.

A Clear Win-Win Path Forward

Ending the illegal extraterritorial U.S. sanctions is both a legal and practical necessity. It would relieve the suffering of ordinary citizens, restore economic access, and allow Eritrea to contribute to stability in a vital maritime corridor. This outcome is a clear win-win for Eritrea, the United States, and the international community. text:
Happy birthday to former Booker T. Washington, University of Oklahoma and NFL running back Patrick Collins, born on this day in 1966 in Okmulgee.

Collins was the Tulsa World's Metro Player of the Year, Tulsa Tribune All-Metro Offensive Player of the Year and an All-State selection as a senior at Booker T. Washington, rushing for 1,960 yards and 27 touchdowns as the Hornets went through the regular season unbeaten and advanced to the state championship game.

He also earned All-American honors from the National High School Athletic Coaches Association.

A speedster with a 4.4 40 time, Collins was a member of the Hornets' powerful track team. Unfortunately, as a junior, he came down sick prior to the state meet and after finishing second in the 100 meters, he was scratched from the 200 meters and 16-hundred meter relay. 

But, as a senior, he bounced back as the Hornets won the Class 5A track and field championship. He took second in both the 100 and 200 meters and was a member of the team's relay team that took the gold in both the 400 and 1,600 meters.

After high school, he chose to sign with Oklahoma over numerous Division I scholarship offers and was a member of OU's 1985 national championship team, running for an 18 yard gain in the Sooners' victory over Penn State as a sophomore.

His best season came as a senior when he rushed for 626 yards and eight touchdowns and led the Big 12 in yards per carry (7.6), earning honorable mention All-Big 12.

A highlight of his senior season came in the Sooners' 17-7 victory over top-ranked Nebraska. With the score tied 7-7 in the third quarter, Collins took a pitch from Charles Thompson, broke a tackle and raced 65 yards down the left sideline for the go-ahead touchdown. Collins finished with 131 yards on 13 carries.

In four seasons with the Sooners, Collins rushed for 1,369 yards and 20 touchdowns.

An 8th round selection in the 1988 NFL Draft by Green Bay, Collins played in five games for the Packers. He was a member of the Cleveland Browns' practice squad in 1989.

text:
$IONQ 🚨 "Sandia fabricated the ion traps that IonQ's earliest quantum computers were built on."

Rick Muller, SVP and Chief Scientist, IonQ Federal, on yesterday's MOU with Sandia.

He would know. Before IonQ, Muller led Sandia's Quantum Information Science program, ran the DOE's Quantum Systems Accelerator, then directed IARPA.

IonQ spent $1.8B closing SkyWater on July 31 to own the fab. Four days later it signs with the lab that made its first traps. Two co-design areas named:

→ trapped-ion fabrication 
→ silicon photonics

Those set the ceiling on how fast systems scale and how well they link to each other. SkyWater is the capacity. Sandia is a second set of hands on the same two problems.

The release calls New Mexico a new footprint. The people got there first.

At least twelve at IonQ carry Sandia in their career. Three of them are based in Albuquerque.

Muller came that way. So did Jake Douglass, Federal Capture Director, after nearly eight years running quantum business development at Sandia. And Sandia's director, Laura McGill, has sat on SCSP's Commission on U.S. Quantum Primacy next to De Masi since March.

Note who Sandia put next to De Masi in the release. Toby Townsend, Associate Laboratories Director for Deterrence, Science and Energy. Sandia is an NNSA lab. The first word in that title is not decoration.

Then the venue. Sandia's Quantum Demonstration Facility exists to offer impartial third-party verification for pathways to utility-scale quantum computers. It also communicates what it finds to U.S. government stakeholders.

IonQ published its own application-centric benchmarking framework on April 14. Muller's post yesterday devotes a section to "Benchmarking Practical Impact."

Every one of those is someone deciding how quantum gets scored.

You don't sit down at the referee's table unless you like your own numbers.

So here is what actually gets scored.

On the May 6 call, IonQ said tape-out D was complete, that the first fabricated ion trap prototypes were already beyond the critical quality metrics needed for 256-qubit devices, and that it had moved from component-level to system-level testing on the full machine.

At Rosenblatt on June 10, Inder Singh said IonQ had created the first working prototype of the 256-qubit chip, and that the foundry did it in a couple of months instead of nine or ten. IonQ did not own that foundry yet. Singh called it a partner under a commercial agreement.

Seven weeks later it was a subsidiary.

Sandia made the first traps. Oxford Ionics moved gate control off lasers and onto silicon. SkyWater prints it in house, on U.S. soil. Singh's reason for buying it, in June: the supply chain should be onshore, and SkyWater already had the top secret clearances needed to sell to government.

Q2 is tonight. In May IonQ presold its first chip-based 256-qubit system and put a date on it: demonstrate by year-end, customer commissioning by the end of Q2 2027. That was said while SkyWater was still a supplier. In June Singh would only say the deal pulls some of the outer years left, not the whole roadmap.

Tonight is the first earnings call since the fab came in house. The date is the thing to check.

text:
The Fire That Woke The Acoma

Winter 1598. Juan de Oñate’s exhausted expedition finally reaches the Río Grande after months of desert hell. Among the pueblos watching them is Acoma—the Sky City—perched 367 feet up on a sandstone mesa, ancient, proud, and completely sovereign.
Tensions build fast. Spaniards demand food. Acoma offers hospitality but not submission. They’ve seen this before with Coronado and remember the violence. Oñate reads their caution as defiance.

December 4, 1598. Oñate sends his nephew Captain Juan de Zaldívar and a small group up the steep path to demand supplies. A fight explodes. Shouting turns to blades. Eleven Spaniards die, including Zaldívar himself. His blood soaks into the rock of the mesa.

When the news reaches Oñate, something snaps. In the Spanish world of honor, killing a noble relative isn’t just murder—it’s a public challenge to his authority and the Crown. He calls it treachery and rebellion and decides to make an example no pueblo will ever forget.

January 21–23, 1599. Vicente de Zaldívar, brother of the dead captain, marches on Acoma with seventy armored soldiers, harquebuses, swords, and war dogs. The Acoma rain stones and arrows from the heights. The battle lasts three days. When it’s over the Sky City is burning.

The punishment is pure spectacle. Twenty-four men are executed. Seventy warriors die in the fighting. Hundreds of women and children are taken. Every surviving man over twenty-five has one foot cut off. The rest are sentenced to twenty years of slavery.

Even the Spanish Crown later condemned Oñate for the cruelty. He was tried, fined, and banished from New Mexico. But the damage was done.

Acoma rebuilt, as they always do. Stand on that mesa today and the wind still carries the story—resistance, sovereignty, and the day one fight on cold stone ignited a tragedy that still echoes across New Mexico.

text:
MAINE NGOs DISTRIBUTED NEARLY TWICE AS MANY SYRINGES AS THERE ARE PEOPLE IN THE STATE IN 2025: 

According to a 2025 Maine CDC report, Maine non-governmental organizations (NGOs) distributed almost twice as many syringes as there are people in the state. These organizations distributed 2,696,610 syringes in 2025. The U.S. Census Bureau estimated Maine’s population at 1,415,000 that year, equaling 1.91 syringes per person. The 2025 figure is down slightly from 3,188,444 syringes distributed in 2024. Combined, 5,885,054 new syringes were distributed in 2024 and 2025, the Maine CDC reported.  

Among states reporting comparable data, North Carolina was the next closest. The North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services Safer Syringe Initiative reported 8.2 million syringes distributed versus a population of 10.8 million, or 0.76 syringes per person - about 2.5 times lower than Maine’s rate. Maine may lead the nation in syringes distributed relative to population based on these numbers.

The Maine CDC report said the syringes in 2025 went to 11,658 program participants - 2,696,610 syringes for fewer than 12,000 people. Funding for these organizations should be tied to the number of participants they help reduce from the roughly 12,000, rather than the number of syringes distributed.

SYRINGE PIPLINE AND ACCOUNTABILITY BREAKDOWN:

These syringe service programs or SSPs are certified by the Maine CDC and must register with the Department of Environmental Protection as biomedical waste producers to meet biowaste disposal rules. The organizations collect large numbers of used syringes, but once a clean syringe is distributed there is no guarantee it will be safely returned or will not end up in public spaces such as a child’s soccer field.

Once an organization hands out a clean syringe, it is no longer legally responsible if a user discards it improperly. Some programs offer a 1-for-1 exchange, but state law does not require it. An individual with no syringes to return can receive up to 100 per visit. 

After those 100 syringes leave the organization’s possession, they are no longer classified as biomedical waste under Department of Environmental Protection rules. They become “household or home-generated sharps.” Maine’s biomedical waste rules, written more than 35 years ago primarily for responsible home insulin use, have not been updated to reflect widespread drug addiction and the large volume of syringes now in circulation. This needs to change.

WHAT WE CAN DO TO FIX THIS IN THE NEXT LEGISLATIVE SESSION: 

In the next legislative session, lawmakers should work on harm-reduction funding for syringe service programs that track and tie government and grant support to the number of the roughly 12,000 participants who stop using drugs due to the programs requesting funding. Incentivize NGOs to get people off of drugs instead of handing out needles 100 at a time. Funding should only be given to organizations that collect 100% for the used needles that they distribute.

Equally important, a bill updating Maine’s biomedical waste statutes and rules is needed to address used needles so discarded syringes do not become litter in public spaces and can be disposed of safely. Update the rules to classify syringes that are distributed are still legally considered biomedical waste once they are used. This is common sense. If litter is a biohazard, it should still be considered medical waste via statute and rulemaking.

Protecting communities from discarded syringes needs to be a core principle for the 133rd legislature. We must incentivize organizations to reduce drug abuse rather than distribute needles with no downstream accountability for collection of biomedical waste. This should be a priority for all candidates running for office in 2026.

Saint Dominic de Guzman was born in Spain in 1170. As a student, he sold his books to feed the poor during a famine, and offered himself to ransom a slave. At the age of twenty-five, after taking the religious habit he became acting Superior of the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine in Osma, and was soon offered an episcopal chair at Compostella. He answered as afterward he also answered many times: God has not sent me to be a bishop, but to preach. He accompanied his prelate to southern France on a commission for the king of Castille. There his heart was well-nigh broken by the ravages of the Albigensian heresy, a variant of ancient Manicheanism, and the source of devastating wars in southern France. His life from that time on was devoted to the conversion of heretics and the defense of the Faith.
.
In the year 1199, while he was still a Canon Regular of Saint Augustine and was preaching near the Spanish coasts, he was taken captive, with all his audience and a Brother in religion, by a band of pirates. They placed the prisoners in their galleys at the oars. When a furious storm broke, the young Saint exhorted the disciples of Mohammed to think seriously of their souls, to open their eyes to the truth of Christianity, and above all, to invoke the Mother of God. They did not listen until his third exhortation, at a moment when it was clear the ship and passengers could not be saved. They swore to him then that if the God of Christians preserved them by the intercession of His Holy Mother, they would dedicate themselves to their service. Immediately the storm ceased, and the pirates kept their word.
.
When in his 46th year, and with six companions, he began the great Order of Preaching Friars, this Order with that of the Friars Minor, founded by his contemporary friend Saint Francis of Assisi, was the chief means God employed to renew Christian fervor during the Middle Ages. In addition, Saint Dominic founded his Second Order for nuns for the education of Catholic girls, and his Third Order, or Tertiaries, for persons of both sexes living in the world. God abundantly blessed the new Order, and France, Italy, Spain, and England welcomed the Preaching Friars. Our Lady took them under Her special protection. During a debate with the heretics, a book by the Saint, defending Her Immaculate Conception, was thrown into the flames along with one by the heretics, to see whether one might be spared. Saint Dominic's was not injured, and many heretics were converted.
.
It was in 1208, while Saint Dominic knelt in the little chapel of Notre Dame de La Prouille, and implored the great Mother of God to save the Church, that Our Lady appeared to him and gave him the Rosary, bidding him to go forth and preach it. During the famous battles in southern France against the Albigensians, with his rosary in hand he revived the courage of the Catholic armies, led them to victory against overwhelming numbers, and finally subdued the heresy. His nights were spent in prayer; and, though all beheld him as an Angel of purity, before morning broke he would scourge himself to blood. His words rescued countless souls, and three times raised the dead to life. At length, on August 6, 1221, at the age of fifty-one, he gave up his soul to God.
.
Reflection: God has never refused me what I have asked, said Saint Dominic. How could God refuse to respond to the single intention of His Saints, which is His own — the salvation and sanctification of souls? Saint Dominic has left us the Rosary that we may learn, with Mary's help, to ask what pleases God, and then to pray easily and simply with the same trust.
.
Eternal Father, I wish to honor St. Dominic, and I give Thee thanks for all the  graces Thou hast bestowed upon him. I ask Thee to please increase grace in  my soul through the merits of this saint, and I commit the end of my life to him by this special prayer, so that by virtue of Thy goodness and promise, St.  Dominic might be my advocate and provide whatever is needed at that hour. Amen.

text:
Ireland’s €53m Government Jet Delivered Without Israeli-Made Fog-Landing System

Ireland’s new €53 million Dassault Falcon 6X government jet was ordered without a key navigational system designed to assist landings in fog and other low-visibility conditions because the equipment is manufactured by an Israeli company.

The multi-purpose Strategic Reach Aircraft, operated by the Irish Air Corps from Casement Aerodrome in Baldonnell, was delivered in late 2025 and primarily transports the Taoiseach and government ministers. It can also perform long-distance air ambulance and medical evacuation missions.

The jet, which seats up to 14 passengers, replaced the state’s previous Learjet. The missing system is FalconEye, a Combined Vision System developed by Dassault Aviation in partnership with Israel’s Elbit Systems. The equipment, which sits on the aircraft’s nose and feeds enhanced imagery to pilots via a head-up display, uses cameras and sensors to improve situational awareness in poor weather, day or night.

Dassault describes it as providing “unprecedented all-weather situational awareness.”

Multiple sources have confirmed that the system was deliberately excluded. Including it would have required a formal written agreement with Elbit. Irish procurement officials determined this conflicted with government policy and requested that the system not be fitted.

In August 2024, then-Tánaiste and Minister for Defence Micheál Martin directed that Ireland would cease purchases of Israeli military equipment and review existing contracts, citing the ongoing conflict in Gaza.

A former Irish Air Corps pilot, Kevin Phipps, said the system offers “the ability to land in fog when other aircraft would have to divert to another airport.”

The Department of Defence has stated that the aircraft has “no current limits on the operational capability.” The same wording was used in response to a Dáil question from Labour TD Ged Nash in April 2026. 

Sources, however, said the absence of FalconEye restricts the range of options available to pilots in certain weather conditions. The decision contrasts with other recent Air Corps acquisitions. Four new Airbus helicopters for the force include Helionix flight systems jointly manufactured by Airbus and Elbit, which are integral to the aircraft and cannot be omitted. A new maritime patrol CASA C-295 also carries Israeli-made radar.

The Falcon 6X remains fully operational for its intended roles, according to official statements, though the exclusion of the enhanced vision system has drawn attention to the practical implications of Ireland’s procurement policy on Israeli-origin technology.

text:
An American took me to a restaurant and apologized for it in the parking lot.

He said, "It doesn't look like much."

He was underselling. It looked like nothing.

The sign has a phone number on it with no area code. The carpet is a color that no longer exists. There is a case by the door with softball trophies in it and the most recent one is 1998.

The food was the best I have had in this country.

I asked the waitress how long they have been open. She said, "Since '71." She did not look up. She has answered that before.

I asked the man why the owner does not renovate.

He said, "Why would he?"

I have thought about this for some weeks and the law is not what I expected it to be.

A restaurant that renovates is a restaurant that has decided it needs to attract people who have not been there.

The ones who have been there do not require attracting.

So the carpet stays. The sign stays. The menu stays, laminated, with one item crossed out by hand and a new price written beside it in pen, which is the only update the building has accepted in a decade.

New paint is a signal. New paint means the food has stopped being enough.

I said this out loud and a man at the next table turned around in his chair.

His place is in Ohio, forty minutes from where he grew up. The booth is torn. They have never repaired it. He has been going since 1984. The owner died and the son runs it now and the son changed nothing. Not one thing. On purpose.

Then he said, "They put new chairs in one time. Everybody hated it. They took 'em back out."

Took them back out. The chairs were removed for being new.

I go on Thursdays now. I have never seen the owner. The waitress calls me hon and has never asked my name.

I have decided not to offer it.

The accounts of SR-71 Reconnaissance Systems Officer (RSO) Lt. Col. Curt Osterheld and pilot Lt. Col. Gene "Geno" Quist are detailed in Col. Richard H. Graham's book The SR-71 Blackbird: Stories, Tales and Legends. 
In the book, the chapters outline how "terribly" Pentagon politics treated the Blackbird crews and the aircraft itself during the program's shutdown. Reviewers note that their first-hand accounts evoke feelings of disappointment and disgust regarding how the legendary aircraft was prematurely retired.
Key Aspects of Their Pentagon Accounts
Political Sabotage: The crews detailed how Pentagon bureaucrats actively worked to defund and terminate the program despite its unmatched Mach 3 reconnaissance capabilities.
Curt said in the book, and I quote, “probably the bitterest memory of this time came from the personalization of this issue by others in the Pentagon.
Gino Quist and I were both dedicated officers, but we also felt it was our duty to offer a loyal opposition to an action we felt was terribly flawed. 
The careerist sought to portray us as evil and disloyal. (I’m not making this up) for having an opinion other than the Chiefs (Larry Welch)
Some officers within the intelligence community saw this as the next leap forward for satellite reconnaissance’s dominance and their own upward mobility, so they jumped on the kill the SR-71 now bandwagon 
Gino and I were convinced that some took a sadistic delight in the SR-71 struggle for survival. 
I recall a hall meeting with a colonel who was not a flying officer in which he sneered at me and Gino and stated “it serves you pressure breathing Prima Donna‘s right, I hope you all die. 

Curt concludes the paragraph by saying I will leave it up to the reader to decide if an adequate replacement capability has ever been fielded to replace the SR-71?

￼ You can find this on page 202 in the book.￼ I find this kind of behavior, outrageous, and many people do not know about it. That is why I am bringing it out in the open not because I think that telling these stories will make a difference other than letting people know the real reason why the fastest airplane in the world was canceled and it wasn’t because of money.
Linda Sheffield

IREN’s Playbook Is Built for Exactly the Friction Hitting AI Data Centers

The AI data center boom is running into hard local realities. Community pushback and temporary moratoria now span dozens of states. 

Construction jobs spike then largely disappear once facilities go live. Electricity price optics, grid bottlenecks, and demands for conditional approvals that force operators to deliver real local value are becoming the norm.

IREN’s strategy, forged in the renewable Bitcoin mining era and now scaled into AI Cloud, maps unusually cleanly onto these challenges.

The company has assembled roughly 5.8 GW of secured, grid-connected power across North America, with additional capacity in Spain and Australia. Sites are deliberately chosen in renewable-rich or surplus markets such as British Columbia Hydro territory, the Texas Panhandle, and similar regions where power is abundant and the social license is easier to earn. 

Vertical integration, owning the land, high-voltage infrastructure, construction, and operations, lets IREN deliver capacity faster and with more control than pure greenfield hyperscaler projects. Renewable-first designs directly reduce the consumer bill pressure that is fueling political resistance elsewhere.

On the ground, early Canadian sites were located in former industrial communities where power was underutilized after mill closures. The company pairs construction-phase economic activity with ongoing community grants, local supplier relationships, and partnerships with Indigenous groups. This creates the durable tax base and goodwill that short-term construction spikes alone cannot sustain. Large rural and semi-rural campuses in Texas and Oklahoma further distance projects from the densest residential opposition.

Commercially, IREN already operates in the concession environment the market now requires. Multi-year contracts with Microsoft, NVIDIA, and a growing roster of AI developers frequently include substantial prepayments that de-risk capital and lock in long-term utilization. Capacity is heavily contracted, and the platform offers both air- and liquid-cooled options plus managed services. This flexibility makes it easier for customers and localities to say yes.

In short, while the broader industry is still adapting to local politics, power scarcity, and the need for tangible community benefits, IREN’s power-first, renewable-centric, vertically integrated model was designed for precisely these constraints. @DrOz I’ve been a fan of your for a long time! I watch your show Dr.Oz. I see you’re part of the @HHSGov now. Please read my story. I am a wife, mother of three, and small business owner from Oklahoma. I am writing to share my personal experience with kratom and its alkaloids in hopes that my story will be considered before any further restrictions or bans are enacted.

Since the age of 15, I have struggled with social anxiety, depression, ADHD, substance abuse, and opioid dependence. Over the years, I was prescribed antidepressants and other medications in an attempt to manage these conditions, but none of them ever helped me feel like myself. Instead, I spent years searching for something that could quiet the constant feeling that something was wrong.

After becoming dependent on methadone for nearly ten years, my quality of life steadily declined. I was overweight, exhausted, falling asleep throughout the day, and emotionally disconnected. Worst of all, I felt like I was letting my children down. They were the ones who lost the most while I struggled just to get through each day.

Three years ago, I discovered kratom. It became the foundation of a wellness journey that allowed me to move away from pharmaceuticals and reclaim my life. Because of kratom, I was able to successfully stop taking methadone after ten years of dependence. Within the past year, I also discontinued Paxil and later Wellbutrin, which had begun causing significant irritability and anger.

As part of that journey, I have used small doses of kratom alkaloids, including 7-OH & MGM-15. I approach these products cautiously because I am a mother of 3, My goal has never been intoxication—it has always been health, stability, and being present for my family for many years to come.

Today, I no longer struggle with the anxiety &depression that once controlled my life. I no longer drink alcohol or misuse drugs. I am clear-headed, and genuinely joyful. I have been able to build and operate a successful business, & most importantly, I am present for my children.

I understand that kratom and 7-oh have controversial reputation. Like any substance, they can be misused. However, the actions of some should not determine access for everyone. We do not ban alcohol because some abuse it, drive intoxicated, & destroy lives. Instead, we regulate it while allowing responsible adults make their own choices.

It is true that stopping kratom abruptly may produce withdrawal symptoms. However, physical dependence is not unique to kratom. Many legally prescribed meds-including opioids, SSRIs & SNRIs, and other psychiatric medications—can also cause dependence & withdrawal. In my own case, severe Paxil withdrawal contributed to a suicide attempt in 2001. Every medication carries risks, yet we continue researching them, improving them, and making informed decisions rather than banning them outright.

Rather than prohibiting kratom and its alkaloids, I believe more research should be allowed. These compounds may offer safer alternatives for people living with chronic pain, PTSD, OCD, opioid dependence, and other difficult conditions. Many Americans are actively seeking options beyond traditional pharmaceuticals.

I respectfully ask that you consider the experiences of responsible consumers like me before supporting legislation that would remove access to something that has genuinely transformed my life. Policies should be guided by evidence, research, and balanced regulation—not solely by misuse or stigma.

If the goal is to protect public health, I respectfully ask that you consider whether prohibition will truly accomplish that, or whether research, thoughtful regulation, and responsible access would better serve the Americans whose lives have been improved by these products.

Thank you for your time, your consideration, and your commitment to protecting public health while listening to the voices of those whose lives have been positively impacted.

Sincerely,

April Diane

text:
Happy birthday to former Norman, University of Oklahoma and professional linebacker Tyrell Peters, born on this day in 1974 in Oklahoma City.

Peters was a two-time All-State selection at Norman, recording 97 tackles as a junior while also rushing for 703 yards and seven touchdowns.

But that was just an appetizer. As a senior, in addition to All-District 6A-2 and All-State, Peters was named The Oklahoman's Defensive Player of the Year and was named to the AP Super Team after making 143 tackles, 18 for losses while running for 1,312 yards and 21 touchdowns in helping lead Norman to the Class 6A title.

Peters chose the University of Oklahoma over numerous other offers, following in the footsteps of uncles Tony and Terry Peters who played for the Sooners in the 1970s.

As a true freshman, Peters appeared in ten games, but was forced into the starting lineup in OU's bowl game because of an injury to Mario Freeman and not only appeared, but was one of four Sooners to intercept a pass in the 41-10 win over Texas Tech.

As a sophomore, Peters earned second-team All-Big 8 honors after making 101 tackles and first-team as both a junior and senior. He finished his career with 380 tackles, which still ranks eighth on the Sooners' all-time list.

He was invited to the 1997 Hula Bowl and was signed by the Seattle Seahawks as an undrafted free-agent following the NFL Draft, but was waived and quickly picked up by the Baltimore Ravens.

Peters played in 27 games in three seasons with the Ravens, making 10 of his 11 career tackles in his final season in 1999. In 2001, he signed with the New York/New Jersey Hitmen, but played just one game making four tackles before being placed on injured reserve.

https://t.co/bmKbZFEnJZ
Jean Aurel's Manon 70 is a glossy, era-defining update of Abbé Prévost’s 1731 novel Manon Lescaut, relocating the classic tale of passion, betrayal, and material desire from 18th-century France to the jet-set, sexually liberated world of late-1960s Europe. Starring Catherine Deneuve (The Umbrellas of Cherbourg, Repulsion, The Young Girls of Rochefort, Belle de jour, Mississippi Mermaid, Tristana, Donkey Skin, A Cop, Le sauvage, Hustle, The Last Metro, 8 Woman, Le choc, The Convent, Belle Toujours The Hunger, Pola X, A Christmas Tale, Marcel Proust's Time Regained, Dancer in the Dark) at the height of her icy, enigmatic allure, the film functions less as a faithful literary adaptation and more as a stylish lifestyle portrait of swinging-sixties morality, consumer culture, and the tensions between romantic idealism and pragmatic hedonism. At its core, the film examines the conflict between love and luxury in a newly permissive society. Manon is neither pure victim nor simple villain; she is an amoral free spirit who uses sex instrumentally while insisting that the number of men she has slept with is irrelevant compared to those she has loved. This stance both celebrates and undercuts the sexual revolution: liberation is real, but it coexists with transactional relationships, economic dependence, and residual patriarchal violence (François’s physical aggression is met with surprising equanimity). The brother-sister dynamic introduces sly suggestions of incestuous undercurrents and shared opportunism, with Jean-Paul functioning as both pimp and co-conspirator. Today Manon 70 plays as both a period curiosity and a revealing document: a film that captured the optimistic surface of 1960s liberation while revealing its unresolved tensions around money, power, desire, and consent. Its open ending - lovers on the road, still negotiating the same insoluble conflict - feels less like a failure of nerve than an honest acknowledgment that, in a world of abundance and choice, the classic Manon dilemma has no tidy resolution. Kino’s Blu-ray is a solid, no-frills presentation of a stylish and often overlooked Deneuve title. The video and audio transfers respect the film’s original look and sound, the Berger/Woods commentary offers genuine value, and the selection of trailers rounds out a modest but worthwhile supplemental package. Fans of Catherine Deneuve, 1960s French cinema, or Gainsbourg’s film work will find this a notable upgrade over previous home-video edition. Recommended.
