text:
The Trump administration is drafting a ban on new Chinese optical transceivers, the devices that move data between servers and chips inside AI data centers.

The FCC could publish the restriction this year, although it may still be modified or abandoned. Officials argue that Chinese-made components could create opportunities for data theft, malware, or service disruption after becoming embedded in critical US infrastructure.

The proposal could hit Zhongji Innolight particularly hard. The Chinese company holds an estimated 27% of the global data-center transceiver market. US alternatives such as Coherent and Lumentum offer competing technology but may not yet have enough scale to replace Chinese suppliers without increasing costs for cloud providers like AWS.

The US-China technology conflict is expanding beyond advanced chips. Washington is now targeting every component surrounding those chips from networking equipment to power systems, before Chinese suppliers become too deeply embedded to remove.

That could create a more secure US AI supply chain.

It could also make the data-center buildout slower and more expensive.

text:
THE WORLD'S LARGEST ENERGY LENDER IS BUILDING A PERMANENT NUCLEAR DESK, AND THE WINDOW IS SEVEN DAYS

WHAT THE POSTING SAYS

· DOE's Office of Energy Dominance Financing is hiring a GS-15 Managing Investment Officer to lead its nuclear vertical, supervising a team of senior investment officers, investment analysts, and multidisciplinary contractors in Washington, DC.

· The role owns end-to-end underwriting for large-scale energy and infrastructure projects, from validating financial models and assessing creditworthiness through negotiating commercial terms with project sponsors and CFOs and carrying recommendations to credit committee.

· The selectee must obtain a Q clearance, file an annual OGE-450 financial disclosure, and submit FAC-C II or equivalent contracting certification before a formal offer, with applications closing August 10 for a single vacancy.

OE READ

Standing up a nuclear vertical with its own first-line supervisor reads less like backfilling a seat and more like EDF expecting nuclear deal flow steady enough to justify a permanent desk. The $17.5 billion American Nuclear Supply Chain Loans commitment from June still has five special purpose vehicles to assign, and the contracting certification requirement suggests this desk is expected to buy specialized financial advisory support as much as it lends. Worth flagging that the posting uses legacy FAC-C Level II language, which was consolidated into the single-level FAC-C Professional in 2023 and now carries reciprocity with DAWIA Contracting Professional.

If nuclear finance now needs its own permanent desk, what does that tell you about the pipeline behind it?

text:
Just finished Chapter 2 of Jacques Vallée’s Passport to Magonia — “The Good People.” 🥞

I also recorded an audio version of my thoughts on it (will share the link soon for anyone who wants the full vibe).

✨Quick recap for those who don’t have time for the whole chapter:

👽April 18, 1961. Eagle River, Wisconsin.

Chicken farmer Joe Simonton hears a weird noise, walks outside, and finds a silvery saucer hovering just above his yard.
Three short, clean shaven men (he said they looked Italian) open a hatch. One holds out a jug. Simonton fills it with water. 
Inside the craft, one of them is cooking on a flameless grill. They hand him three small, perforated pancakes.

He eats one. Tastes like cardboard.

The Air Force investigates. Lab tests confirm: ordinary terrestrial pancakes (buckwheat, fat, starch…). Official verdict leans toward “sincere man who probably hallucinated.”

Vallée doesn’t buy the simple dismissal.

He lays out centuries of Celtic folklore about the “Good People” the Gentry, the Sidhe, who live in hills and parallel places, who are organized, territorial, and frequently offer food to humans.

Accept fairy food and you’re marked. Time warps. You may never fully return. Hospitality becomes a ritual bond (or trap).

Same exchange. Same rules. Same ambiguity.

Just different cultural clothing: fairies then, “space people” now.

Chapter 2 is where Vallée’s central idea locks in: this isn’t a new phenomenon. It’s an ancient one that keeps adapting to whatever story we can accept.

The more you read, the harder it is to unsee the pattern..... was a spectacular read......

The oddness in this chapter was that I have never read it before I read it live. I made a cute little selfie post about aliens making pancakes... THE ODDS... of this is so strange and to me I look at it as a sign this is the path I'm meant to be on. 

I never got my pancakes btw :( lol

Thanks for everyone who tuned in and the next read will be Friday evening. Jacques Valle is a genius, and provides excellent accounts and research of different accounts with similarities. 

Can't wait to read chapter 3: The Secret Commonwealth

Under a memorandum of understanding, signed in November 1988, The Reagan administration and Nakasone government, along with General Dynamics would provide its F-16 Fighting Falcon technology to Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, and would handle up to 45 percent of the development work as a joint principal contractor. 

The jointly developed Mitsubishi F-2 is an advanced multirole fighter may be heavily inspired by the F-16, but it is uniquely enlarged for maritime strike missions. text:
Rolls-Royce Griffon 57A

The Rolls-Royce Griffon 57A was a 37-liter (2,240 cu in) V-12 piston aircraft engine producing approximately 2,455 hp (1,830 kW). Four Griffon engines powered the Avro Shackleton MR Mk.3 maritime patrol aircraft.

Each engine drove a pair of contra-rotating propellers. The rear propeller recovered energy from the swirling airflow behind the front propeller, improving propulsive efficiency while largely cancelling engine torque.

The Griffon was optimized for long-endurance maritime patrol missions, where reliability and efficient cruise performance were more important than maximum speed. Shackleton crews often remained airborne for 10 hours or more during anti-submarine and ocean surveillance missions.

By the time the Griffon 57A entered service, piston aircraft engines had reached the practical limits of their development. Increasing power further meant greater weight, mechanical complexity, cooling requirements, and maintenance.

As turboprop technology matured, it offered a higher power-to-weight ratio, lower maintenance requirements, and better overall operating efficiency, gradually replacing large piston engines in military aircraft.

The cutaway engine shown in the video is displayed at the South African Air Force Museum, AFB Ysterplaat.

Here is the deep-dive analysis of Leidos Holdings $LDOS  based on the latest Q2 2026 earnings.

1/10 🏢 Company Introduction
$LDOS is an industry and technology leader providing smart, digital, and mission-critical solutions for defense, health, and civil markets.
Shareholders: Ownership is heavily institutional at ~76%, with Insiders holding ~0.8%, and Retail making up the remaining ~23%.

Short Quote: 
The short interest is relatively low at ~5.1% of the float, indicating low bearish sentiment.

Past to Future: 
Originally rooted in IT and engineering, Leidos has aggressively evolved into a dominant Defense Tech and Managed Healthcare giant. The future points toward scaling its Cyber, Energy Infrastructure, and advanced engineering pillars.

Technology: 
Core focuses include AI/ML, advanced hypersonics, low-band surveillance radar infrastructure, and cloud computing.  

2/10 Product Presentation & Current Developments
Leidos is winning massive contracts, achieving $5 billion in bookings in Q2 2026 alone with a book-to-bill ratio of 1.1. 

Notable recent awards include:  
A $475M U.S. Air Force contract for F-16 avionics diagnostic systems.  A $456M GSA Military OneSource program contract to provide global well-being services to 4.7M service members.  

A $350M Air Force Electronic Warfare modification to mitigate heavy electronic counte

rmeasures.  An $88M Navy contract to develop experimental hypersonic glide vehicles (MACH-TB 2.0).  

3/10 📊 Valuation Snapshot
Using the most up-to-date market figures and the Q2 2026 balance sheet:
Market Cap: ~$16.3B
Net Debt: $5.28B. 

Calculated strictly without leasing liabilities: total debt of $6.03B ($6,009M long-term + $22M current) minus $748M in cash.  

Enterprise Value (EV): ~$21.6B
EBITDA: H1 2026 Adjusted EBITDA reached $1.24B ($631M in Q2 alone), putting TTM Adjusted EBITDA around $2.4B.  

4/10 💰 Earnings Snapshot
Q2 2026 delivered robust top and bottom-line execution:
Revenues: $4.56 billion, up 7% year-over-year (4% organically).  
Net Income: $356 million, or $2.81 per diluted share.  
Non-GAAP Diluted EPS: $3.26, up 2% YoY.  
Margins: Adjusted EBITDA margin stood at 13.8%, reflecting excellent program execution.  
Cash Flow: A stellar quarter for cash generation, producing $761 million in Non-GAAP Free Cash Flow, translating to a 185% conversion ratio.  

5/10 ⚖️ Peer Group Comparison
Leidos currently trades at a highly attractive EV/EBITDA multiple of around 8.5x–9.5x. 

Compared to its primary government contracting peers like Booz Allen Hamilton ($BAH) which trades closer to 16x, CACI International ($CACI) at ~14x, and Science Applications International Corp ($SAIC),$LDOS offers a compelling valuation discount.

The company's massive scale and superior free cash flow generation provide a distinct edge over pure-play IT peers.

6/10 🔮 Forecast 2030 (EBITDA & Valuation)
Assuming a conservative 4-5% top-line CAGR, Leidos could reach ~$21B in revenue by 2030. 

If management sustains the current mid-13% adjusted EBITDA margins, 2030 EBITDA could expand to ~$2.8B–$3.0B. 

Applying an 11x EV/EBITDA multiple (a modest expansion toward historical averages), the Enterprise Value could approach $32B. 

Assuming steady debt paydowns from their robust FCF, equity holders could see significant upside over the next four years.  

7/10 🛒 Acquisition Potential
Leidos is a strategic consolidator, not an acquisition target. The recent acquisition of ENTRUST Solutions Group highlights their appetite for high-margin Energy and Infrastructure assets. 

Moving forward, expect bolt-on acquisitions in niche AI, cyber operations, and directed energy to bolster their Defense Tech pillar.  

8/10 🎯 Catalysts & Milestones (Next 6-12 Months)
Formation and operational launch of the Security Enterprise Solutions joint venture with Analogic Corporation, aligning with the new $270M Customs and Border Patrol scanner contract.  

Finalization of the Defense Health Agency’s long-term transition strategy for the RHRP program.  Resolution of U.S. government budget timelines and potential new awards in the Intelligence & Digital segments.

9/10 🛡️ Opportunities & Risks
Opportunities: 
Significant runway in the Managed Healthcare pillar and surging demand for energy grid modernization and multi-domain threat intelligence.

Risks: 
Vulnerability to U.S. government defense budget cuts, spending limit implementations, or potential government shutdowns. Additionally, integrating newly acquired businesses (like Entrust) and managing cost inflation on firm-fixed-price contracts pose ongoing margin risks.  

10/10 🏁 Conclusion
Leidos is an absolute cash-flowing powerhouse. Their balanced portfolio across Defense, Health, and Homeland security allows them to weather budgetary shifts seamlessly. 

Management just raised FY2026 guidance across the board, projecting $18.2B–$18.4B in revenues and $12.20–$12.50 in Non-GAAP EPS. 

Trading at a discount to peers while securing critical, high-tech defense infrastructure contracts,$LDOS is a prime foundational stock for defense-oriented portfolios.

text:
6 August 2026.
Today in history.

1652.
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
The 5th, 6th and 7th of August 1652 were recorded together under the same date in the diary.
Daytime temperatures during this period are described as pleasant.
The wind blew mainly from the west.
The diary mentions that various snares were set along the Vars River close to Table Mountain in an attempt to catch some of the indigenous fauna.
Reed screens were erected in the area to guard the snares and also, probably, to ensure that the animals were not exposed to unnecessary suffering.

1653.
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Daybreak brought a sunny day accompanied by a light westerly wind.
The galiot Roode Vos, which had been sent to Hout Bay, dropped anchor in Table Bay during the day.
A report was delivered that some of the crew had been sent overland to False Bay to investigate the bay. One of the crew members fell ill in False Bay and was left behind there.
Van Riebeeck immediately sent out a search-and-rescue party for the man.

1654.
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Morning at the Cape is described as bitterly cold.
According to the diary there was a thick layer of frozen ice on the drinking water.
The wind blew moderately from the west and did not improve matters at all.
Building work on the fort proceeded with great zeal that day.
A report was brought that Harry’s people were grazing their livestock on the other side of the Salt River and close to the fort.
Some of the people brought an elephant tusk to the fort to barter. The group proposed that if some of the fort’s inhabitants visited them the following day with copper and tobacco, they would be prepared to exchange cattle.

1655.
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
The 5th and 6th of August 1655 were recorded together under the same date in the diary.
The wind, as on the previous few days, blew from the west.
The day is described, like the previous one, as cloudy, with rain from time to time. 

Sunday 6 August 1656.
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Dawn at the Cape brought a wonderfully fine day.
A sloop was sent early in the morning to the ship lying at anchor.
She was the Parel and had left Texel on 11 April 1656. Two other ships, the Wachter and the Wakende Boeij, formed part of the fleet and were expected shortly.
Three sailors had died during the voyage.
Several of the crew were also ill with scurvy. Arrangements were made as quickly as possible and the necessary fresh water, vegetables and meat were supplied to the ship.

1657.
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Morning at the Cape brought a cloudy day with a light breeze from the south-east.
Van Riebeeck departed early in the morning aboard the yacht Maria for Robben Island.
According to the diary, Jan Woutersson had some time previously been married to a female slave. This slave, together with another from Madagascar, was responsible for the sheep. Christoffel Muller worked with them and was in overall charge of the sheep.
Van Riebeeck writes that there were altogether 360 sheep on the island.
The vegetable gardens, as well as the quarry where stones were cut, were also visited and found to be in order. For some reason the hares on the island had not multiplied. They are, however, described as fat and healthy.
Several points on the island were visited where fire-stone beacons were under construction. The purpose of these was to make fires and thereby give direction to visiting ships towards Table Bay at night.
Seven fat ewes were taken back to Table Bay.

1658.
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Morning brought a wonderfully fine day at the Cape. The wind is described as variable, now from this side and then from that.
The Schappenjacht was renamed the Zeeleeuw that day by the Free Burghers. The said vessel departed during the morning for Dassen Island.
A particularly small vessel was sighted towards dusk just outside Table Bay. At that stage the wind was blowing steadily from the south-south-east and the vessel was forced to anchor outside the bay.

1659.
From the diary of Jan van Riebeeck.
Daybreak brought a cloudy day.
No mention is made of the wind.
The Commander, Van Riebeeck, pruned the vines on his farm that day. 
According to the diary approximately 12 000 vine shoots were pruned.
A large quantity of vine shoots was given to the Free Burghers. The latter, however, were not very keen to plant the offered shoots.
Mention is also made that the orchards would soon have to be pruned as well.
The Free Burghers were also encouraged to plant sweet-potato lands around the wheat fields. In this way a fire-break would be created should the veld be set alight. As a bonus the sweet potatoes would also yield a crop.

1835.
The reminiscences of the Voortrekker J.H. Hatting.1838.
Hatting begins by relating that shortly after the arrival of Andries Pretorius a large people’s assembly was held.
During the meeting Pretorius was elected Commandant-General.
The task of raising a commando and marching against Dingaan was entrusted to him.
Pretorius, among other things, ordered that for every wagon accompanying the expedition two fighting gates were to be made. The purpose of the gates was to close the openings between the wagons with chains on the jaw-bone wagons in times of danger.
Word was sent to Hans Dons de Lange, Karel Landman and Kreling to prepare themselves to the best of their ability for the coming struggle and to join the main force on a given date. 

Saturday 6 August 1836.
From the diary of Louis Tregardt.
Louis writes that everyone was already up early in the morning and began to bustle about.
After everyone had had breakfast, the oxen were brought closer and inspanned.
The party trekked for about five and a half hours to one Jü Koerie.
(Jü Koerie was also called Nkuri and lived on the Klein Letaba River. He was an induna.)Sunday 6 August 1837.
From the diary of Louis Tregardt.
Pieta arrived at his parents’ camp at first light.
That the boy needed help is clear from the fact that he almost immediately told his father that Takkaroe, together with his whole family, had run away during the night.
(Takkaroe was the cattle-herder whom Louis had hired on 19 June at Rossetoe. The man was initially to have worked for Louis for only 15 days, but in the end stayed much longer. Louis mentions the man again on 4 September.)
Pieta also related that the lions had caused a proper uproar at the thorn kraal the previous evening. According to Pieta the lot had roared so that the earth shook.
He, Pieta, had fired a shot with his flintlock in the general direction of the roaring.
The roaring then almost immediately stopped and according to Pieta the shot had cracked nicely.
Towards strong dusk three people of colour came walking from the direction of Seretie. The three brought news that Gabriël was on the way.
Gabriël had two “townspeople” (people of colour from Delagoa Bay) with him.
According to the people the “townspeople” as well as Gabriël were armed.
One of the three related that Gabriël would first rest at Massouw and from there go straight past to Doors’s side. According to the group Gabriël had also gone around Hans van Rensburg’s wagons.
According to them Van Rensburg had allegedly shot many Black people dead.
Louis stood looking at the group and then said outright that they were standing there lying to him.
What the outcome of the matter was is not recorded.
Louis merely notes that the next morning they were in open country.
Apparently they had gone up against the mountain to fetch bartered sheep.

1837.
No entries on this day in the diary of the Reverend Erasmus Smit.

Monday 6 August 1838.
From the diary of the Reverend Erasmus Smit.
The Reverend Smit writes that he was up and about early in the morning.
Among other things he visited the laager of G. Rudolph where he baptised three children.

1863.
“Daar kom die Alabama”.
The origin and history of the well-known South African folk song go back to this day.
The Alabama, a ship of the American Southern Confederacy, had anchored in Saldanha Bay on 29 July 1863 for fresh water and provisions.
(The Alabama was specifically built to capture ships of the Northern Confederacy — to sink them and thereby hinder the war effort. At that stage the Alabama had already sunk 50–55 ships of the Northern Confederacy.)
On this day the Alabama found herself a few sea miles from Table Bay.
Unexpectedly another vessel, the Sea Bride of the American Northern Confederacy, was sighted.
The Sea Bride was on a normal trading voyage and was calmly sailing into Table Bay.
Captain R. Semmes of the Alabama was awake and fired on the Sea Bride.
The Sea Bride, under the command of Captain C. White, set all sail in order to reach the neutral waters of Table Bay as soon as possible.
The Alabama, however, with outstanding seamanship, overhauled the Sea Bride before the neutral waters of Table Bay could be reached.
Thus was born “Daar kom die Alabama, die Alabama die kom oor die see...”

1876.
Anna Louisa Visser born.
She is remembered as one of the first South African singers to make records in Afrikaans.1883.
Founding of the Republic of Stellaland on this day with Gerrit van Niekerk as leader.
The origin of the Republic was the result of fighting between indigenous chiefs in the south-western parts of the ZAR.
The Koranna chief Mankoroane, together with the Batlapin chief Massouw, was engaged in a struggle against Moshwêtê and Montsioa in the north.
The above leaders were fighting for supremacy over the Barolong community.
During 1881 the above situation changed completely and Mankoroane was attacked by Massouw.
Mankoroane called on the Boer community for help and offered land as a reward.
After the struggle the reward was granted and the Republic of Stellaland came into being on 6 August 1883 with Gert van Niekerk as chairman.

1896.
Cape Town puts electric trams into operation. 

Monday 6 August 1900.
Anglo-Boer War.
Day number 300 of the war.The Battle of the Elands River.
General Carrington, who the previous day had been attacked by a detachment of General De la Rey’s commando, fell back during the day to Zeerust.
Along the road he burned his wagons together with all surplus provisions.
From Zeerust he trekked through to Mafeking.
Meanwhile Baden-Powell was also on his way to Colonel Hore’s camp to help.
On the way he heard thundering artillery and on that basis believed that General Carrington had relieved Colonel Hore’s camp.
Baden-Powell decided there and then that help was superfluous and returned to Mafeking.
Colonel Hore meanwhile stood firm and did the best with what he had.
Lord Methuen departed from Potchefstroom and occupied the Vaal River crossings between Lindeque’s Drift and Scandinavia Drift.
Shortly after Methuen’s arrival he received news that General de Wet had already crossed the Vaal River at Schoeman’s Drift.
Lord Methuen was not at all impressed and ordered a pursuit of General De Wet’s forces.
Lord Methuen’s troops and especially the horses were, however, tired and the pursuit was therefore not successful.
A portion of General de Wet’s commando nevertheless found itself in a difficult position near Venterskroon, Tygerpoort.
Danie Theron’s TVK damaged the railway line about 3 km from Wolwehoek near present-day Sasolburg. They were involved in a light engagement with General Knox.

Tuesday 6 August 1901.
Anglo-Boer War.
Day number 665 of the war.The notorious Steinaecker’s Horse was surrounded and attacked by General Viljoen.
During the storming 7 Burghers were killed and 12 others wounded.
The commander, Captain Francis, was killed and 20 men were captured.
Several people of colour, as well as white members (probably “joiners”) of the group, were executed.
The Bushveldt Carbineers surrounded the farmhouse of Commandant Herklaas Viljoen, Duiwelskloof near Pietersburg. Captain P.F. Hunt was in command with 17 British soldiers and 200 armed people of colour. Captain Heinrich du Toit and Field-Cornet Barend Viljoen, together with 13 Burghers, were called upon to surrender. Burgher Hans Viljoen walked out first and was shot dead on the spot. The others in the house began a fight. Eight Burghers some distance from the house heard the shots and went to help. Captain Hunt withdrew and left 2 dead behind. Captain Hunt returned the following day and found that the local community had mutilated the bodies.
Commandant Gideon Scheepers destroyed the railway line near Miller Station, Willowmore.
The British Parliament approved a loan of £6,500,000 for the purchase of land and the settlement of British families in the ZAR and OFS after the war.

1916. 
Hugo Hendrik Bierman born. Bierman is remembered as the first South African-born person to reach the rank of Admiral in the South African Navy. Admiral Bierman served from 1952 until 1976. Thereafter he served as Chief of the South African Defence Force from 1972 until 1976. Admiral Bierman was the only person who served separately as head of both the South African Navy and the South African Defence Force.

1965. 
Doctor Cornelius Francois Visser died. He was a particularly beloved leadership figure and also bore the name “Vader Visser”. He is remembered, among other things, as the founder of the (so-called) First Voortrekker movement in South Africa on 11 December 1920 in Bloemfontein. (The later Voortrekker movement as we know it today was, however, also founded on the basis of a proposal of his on 30 September 1931 with Dr N.J. van der Merwe as leader.) He also wrote several folk songs and songs, including “O Boereplaas”, “Ken jy die land”, and “Kom dans Klaradyn”. Altogether 11 of his songs were included in the FAK songbook.

text:
Alabama Opens Fall Camp With Encouraging Signs From QBs, Offensive Line

Alabama officially opened fall camp Wednesday, and while Kalen DeBoer wasn't ready to make any sweeping conclusions after one practice without pads, the Crimson Tide head coach sounded encouraged by what he saw particularly from his quarterbacks and an offensive line that entered camp with plenty to prove.

For DeBoer, the first day was about execution, communication and beginning the process of bringing together an Alabama roster featuring several new faces.

“We've talked about working in silence since January,” DeBoer said. “These guys just doing their thing, not getting caught up in anything they can't control. We know what our goals are. We know what our expectations are. We've never shied away from that.”

One of the biggest focuses throughout camp will be the quarterback competition between Austin Mack and Keelon Russell.

DeBoer did not provide any separation between the two following the opening practice, but he praised what he saw from the quarterbacks, pointing to their consistency, command and ability to create explosive plays.

“Love the demeanor, love their command, the way they're into it,” DeBoer said. “You can see the belief that the guys have in them.”

Later, DeBoer offered another strong endorsement of the offseason put together by Mack and Russell.

“They had great summers,” DeBoer said. “I mean, they had great summers, both of those two guys.”

Alabama's offensive line also appears to have taken a step forward since spring.

The Crimson Tide entered the offseason needing to replace multiple key pieces up front, and DeBoer acknowledged that the group looked noticeably different Wednesday.

“I thought it looked a lot better and cleaner than what it did at the end of spring,” he said.

DeBoer cautioned that Alabama wasn't wearing pads, making it impossible to evaluate the physical component of offensive line play. Still, he was encouraged by the group's responsibilities, communication, footwork and overall understanding.

The return of Will Sanders should help.

Sanders missed spring practice, but was back for the beginning of fall camp.

“It's good having him back,” DeBoer said. “Very few guys on the offensive line in particular that have the snaps in our program, and he's one of them.”

Freshman running back EJ Crowell was another player who caught DeBoer's attention.

“It's good to see him out there flying around,” DeBoer said. “A couple times, you see what you saw from his high school highlight film.”

DeBoer stressed that Crowell still has plenty to prove once the pads come on, but he praised the freshman's football intelligence and said Crowell handled his responsibilities while rotating with the running backs.

Defensively, Alabama's experienced secondary continues to emerge as one of the team's strengths.

DeBoer identified Bray Hubbard, Zabien Brown and Dijon Lee when asked which players were establishing themselves as leaders.

“The experience in the secondary, that's kind of where it starts,” DeBoer said. “That swagger, that's where it starts.”

Brown may not be the loudest member of the group, but DeBoer said his presence stands out.

“He's not as vocal, but, man, he's got this presence about him,” DeBoer said.

It's only Day 1, and DeBoer repeatedly acknowledged that more meaningful evaluations will come when Alabama puts on the pads.

But after an offseason filled with questions about a new quarterback, a rebuilt offensive line and a roster attempting to come together, DeBoer liked where his team started.

Now the challenge is stacking days.

“We attack the day,” DeBoer said. “The challenge for us right now is to continue to just become one.”

text:
The death of Nirmal “Nimsdai” Purja in an avalanche on Broad Peak is an enormous loss, not just to mountaineering but to anyone who understood what he was really trying to change.

His climbing record is, of course, staggering.

He climbed all fourteen of the world’s 8,000-metre peaks in 189 days, reducing a record measured in years to just over six months. He climbed Everest, Lhotse and Makalu within 48 hours. He was part of the ten-man, all-Nepali team that made the first winter ascent of K2, the last great unsolved winter challenge among the 8,000ers.

The ten climbers waited just below the summit so they could step onto it together, singing the Nepali national anthem.

Then there were the rescues, the risks and the almost unreasonable belief that the impossible was usually just something nobody had organised properly yet.

Few human beings have ever challenged the high mountains with his combination of physical ability, logistical brilliance, courage and sheer audacity.

But records are only part of why Nims mattered.

His greater achievement was that he confronted one of mountaineering’s oldest and least honestly discussed truths: the racial and class hierarchy that shaped Himalayan climbing.

For generations, Western climbers arrived in Nepal with the money, sponsors, equipment, publishing contracts and cameras. They became the explorers, conquerors, adventurers and legends. Their individual names entered history.

Meanwhile, Nepali high-altitude climbers, especially Sherpas, carried loads through the Khumbu Icefall, established camps, fixed ropes, broke trail, assessed the weather and repeatedly entered the most dangerous parts of the mountain before their foreign clients.

They made many celebrated summits possible and often assumed a disproportionate share of the risk. Yet they were regularly relegated to the background, collectively acknowledged as “the Sherpas” rather than recognised individually as some of the finest athletes and boldest mountaineers alive.

That was not merely an oversight. It reflected a system that decided whose ambition counted as heroic and whose courage was treated as hired assistance.

Anyone who has done serious high-altitude trekking, let alone crossed 6,000 metres, knows the truth. In bad weather, on a dangerous traverse, through an icefall or when your body begins to fail, your life can quite literally be in the hands of the Sherpas and other Nepali climbers around you.

But for a very long time, the visiting climber reached the summit and became the legend. The local climber who helped keep him alive returned as “support.”

Nims refused to remain inside that arrangement.

He was Magar, not Sherpa, but he understood the larger indignity imposed upon Nepali high-altitude climbers. He knew that another gifted Nepali performing impossible feats in the background would not be enough to alter a story whose money, cameras and gatekeepers remained elsewhere.

So he became loud.

He built the Nimsdai brand unapologetically. He chased records, mastered social media, produced a film, courted sponsors and built a premium expedition company.

He did not wait for the mountaineering establishment to certify his greatness. He declared it, demonstrated it and distributed the pictures himself.

That irritated sections of the traditional, overwhelmingly Western alpinist establishment.

They called him self-promotional and obsessed with records. They criticised the bottled oxygen, fixed ropes, helicopters and large logistical teams behind Project Possible. They accused him of commercialising the mountains and turning a supposedly noble pursuit into spectacle.

But the discomfort with his visibility revealed something else.

There was an unwritten high-altitude code under which Nepalis could perform extraordinary labour and heroism, provided they remained modest, useful and largely in the background.

A Western climber could write the bestselling account, become the sponsored athlete and build a mythology around himself. But when a Nepali climber used those same instruments of fame, branding and commerce, it was suddenly considered vulgar.

Nims broke that code.

In 14 Peaks, the Nepali climber was no longer standing behind a Western adventurer in someone else’s film. He owned the mission, the camera and the story.

The film was more than a record of an astonishing achievement. It changed who audiences saw when they imagined greatness in the Himalayas.

Nims did not use that visibility only to enlarge himself.

Elite Exped was built with Sherpa business partners. Leading guides were offered better economics, greater responsibility and a stake in the enterprise. The people around him were not anonymous support staff. They were guides, athletes, partners and public figures in their own right.

Nims understood that achievement alone was not enough. If Nepali climbers did not own the companies, the cameras and the stories, they could continue doing the most dangerous work while somebody else received most of the credit.

So he built all three.

He was theatrical, intensely competitive and unapologetic about his ambition. That confidence was part of what made him consequential. He refused to perform greatness in the background and trust that the old establishment would eventually notice.

He made himself impossible to overlook, then used that visibility to pull others into the frame.

Today, younger Sherpa climbers openly demand to be seen as elite athletes, with the same sponsorships, safety investment and individual recognition afforded to their Western counterparts. They speak about being left out of headlines even when they helped make the summit possible.

Nims did not begin that struggle, and he did not finish it. But he gave it scale. He showed that a Nepali climber could be the strongest person on the mountain, the expedition leader, the business owner and the central character in the story.

That is his larger legacy.

Nimsdai was not merely a man who climbed mountains at a speed few could comprehend. He changed who was permitted to own the mountain story.

He showed Nepali mountaineers that they did not have to remain the brave, smiling and anonymous men standing behind somebody else’s achievement. They could be the names in the headline, the faces on the screen, the owners of the company and the authors of the legend.

The mountains have lost one of their greatest challengers. Nepal has lost a son who refused the place history had assigned him.

And the rest of us have lost a man who looked at an old hierarchy, climbed beyond every limit it had set for him and forced it to see the people it had overlooked for generations.

Rest in power, Nimsdai.

You did not just conquer summits.

You made sure the people who had carried others to glory could finally stand in their own light.

Aggressive Legal (and Grey-Area) Strategies for FBA Reparations

The political landscape shifts - and so must the strategy. Here's what a serious, next-level reparations movement looks like.

FULLY LEGAL - HIGH AGGRESSION

1. Economic Warfare Through Concentrated Purchasing Power  
FBA households collectively control hundreds of billions in annual spending. A coordinated, sustained withdrawal from specific corporations - timed, named, and measurable - forces boardrooms to lobby Congress on FBA's behalf. Not a one-day boycott. A rolling, strategic 90-day sector-by-sector campaign that hits quarterly earnings reports.

2. Shareholder Activism at Scale  
FBA investors, pension funds, and institutions file shareholder resolutions at Fortune 500 companies demanding they publicly support reparations legislation or fund reparations-adjacent programs. Companies respond to fiduciary pressure when enough shareholders coordinate. The NAACP Legal Defense Fund and reparations advocacy groups coordinate this filing simultaneously across 50+ companies.

3. Municipal Reparations as Federal Pressure Nodes  
Evanston, Illinois already moved. The strategy: get 20-30 cities and counties to pass local reparations ordinances simultaneously, creating a political "floor" that makes federal inaction look extreme. Each municipality becomes a case study, a press story, and a congressional pressure point.

4. State-Level Commission Capture  
California's reparations commission stalled. The aggressive move: FBA advocates run for and win seats on every state-level reparations commission, then publish findings that create binding legislative records. Those records become the evidentiary foundation for federal suits and federal hearings.

5. Electoral Hostage Strategy  
FBA voters deliver margins in Pennsylvania, Georgia, Wisconsin, Michigan, and Arizona. A formalized FBA Political Action bloc publicly pledges to withhold votes from any candidate - regardless of party - who fails to co-sponsor reparations legislation. This works only when the pledge is credible and the bloc is organized before primaries, making candidates negotiate before the general.

6. Litigation Cascade  
File simultaneous class action suits in multiple federal circuits arguing that ongoing wealth gaps constitute continuing harm from enumerated federal policies. The goal isn't to win immediately - it's to force discovery, generate congressional testimony, and build an evidentiary record that makes legislative inaction politically costly. The Tulsa Race Massacre descendants' case offers a living model.

7. International Pressure - UN & OAS  
File formal petitions with the UN Human Rights Council and the Organization of American States Inter-American Commission on Human Rights. The U.S. government hates international human rights embarrassment. International findings don't bind Congress, but they generate diplomatic pressure and domestic media coverage that shifts the Overton window. The African reparations movement already used this playbook effectively.

8. HBCU-Anchored Research Dominance  
Commission Howard University, Morehouse, Spelman, and Fisk to produce the definitive economic study quantifying the exact dollar figure owed to FBA Freedmen descendants specifically. A peer-reviewed, institutionally credible number - attached to real names and lineages - changes the congressional debate from abstract to concrete. Republicans can argue against a feeling. They struggle to argue against a forensic accounting.

text:
🛑 Filing Alert: Salad And Go Chapter 11

And Go Concepts, LLC and its debtor affiliates⁽¹⁾, a Tempe, AZ-based company which owns the Salad and Go restaurant chain, filed for Chapter 11 protection on Aug. 4 in the U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas.

The company attributes the filing to an aggressive expansion into Texas and Oklahoma (the "Central Region") beginning in 2021 under prior leadership. It spent more than $47.1 million building out a central production commissary in Garland, TX — approximately $72.5 million of total investment including new market tax credit financing — and the region underperformed on sites less accessible and visible than its Arizona locations, unit growth ahead of consumer awareness, and $15 million to $20 million per year of fixed commissary overhead. The Central Region was significantly cash-flow negative even before corporate overhead allocation.

Downsizing proved insufficient. The company closed approximately 41 Central Region locations in September 2025, announced the closure of all remaining Texas and Oklahoma stores in January 2026, and shut the Garland Facility on or about Jan. 11, 2026 — more than 70 closures in total, against a peak footprint of 146 units and a peak valuation of approximately $1.1 billion in 2022 — alongside significant corporate headcount reductions. The retained Arizona and Nevada restaurants ran at roughly break-even at the store level, but residual corporate overhead, dead rent on closed-store leases, and administrative costs left the business in unsustainable cash burn. Rising gas prices, reduced consumer spending, and a cyclospora outbreak accelerated losses over the final 90 days.

The Debtors enter Chapter 11 with an unusually clean prepetition capital structure. AGC OpCo, the primary operating entity, carries no secured indebtedness; material funded debt is isolated to the special-purpose entities formed for the Garland financing. Debtor AGC-North Texas Facilities, LLC — inactive since Garland ceased operations — is the borrower under NMTC QLICI loans of $25.4 million from three Regions Bank affiliates, secured by account pledges and a negative pledge and guaranteed by AGC OpCo and non-debtor AGC Holdco, LLC. Existing equity holders contributed approximately $27 million of new-money capital between December 2025 and January 2026 in connection with the AGC Topco, LLC recapitalization, which does not constitute secured indebtedness and has been substantially consumed by prepetition operating losses, dead rent, and wind-down costs.

The Debtors executed an asset purchase agreement on Aug. 4, 2026 — the petition date — with Boersma Bros. LLC d/b/a Dutch Bros (NYSE: BROS) for 51 Arizona and Nevada drive-thru leases at $105.0 million in cash, plus $50 for a bundle of 14 shuttered Texas and Oklahoma leases conveyed as-is. Proposed cure costs across all 65 leases total approximately $0.9 million.

The Debtors are seeking approval as a private sale, with no auction proposed. The APA preserves a fiduciary out for an unsolicited superior offer, backstopped by a $3.8 million termination fee plus expenses and a $10.0 million minimum overbid. Buyer rejection of any Arizona or Nevada lease before closing reduces the price by approximately $2.1 million per site, with an outside date of Dec. 31, 2026. The Debtors state that proceeds should pay all allowed claims in full — an assumption that rests on landlord rejection claims being capped under section 502(b)(6).

Alongside the sale, the Debtors have sought emergency approval of lease and contract rejection procedures, authority to pay PACA/PASA trust claims, priority taxes, and retained-employee wages for the approximately 1,300-person workforce, and authority to draw funds held at non-debtor AGC Topco, LLC, which may or may not become a debtor in these cases.

And Go Concepts, LLC reports $500 million to $1 billion in both assets and liabilities. The filing indicates that there will be funds available for distribution to unsecured creditors. The case number is 26-90753.

⁽¹⁾ For a complete list of debtor entities, see the Chapter 11 Debtors table.

text:
CORNING

Corning is the most direct U.S.-listed fundamental beneficiary. The company’s Solar segment includes Hemlock Semiconductor, solar wafers, and module manufacturing. Q2 2026 Solar sales were $438M, up 90 percent from $231M, while the segment recorded a $7M net loss. H1 Solar sales were $808M, yet cumulative segment net income was approximately breakeven. This combination of rapid revenue growth and near-zero profitability creates substantial operating leverage if pricing, utilization, and product mix improve. (Corning Investor Relations)

Solar represented approximately 9.2 percent of Corning’s Q2 core sales of $4.738B. The segment is material but not the principal driver of consolidated earnings. Optical Communications generated Q2 sales of $2.072B, up 32 percent, with Enterprise Networks up 65 percent and generative-AI product sales growing substantially faster. The core GLW investment case therefore remains centered on optical connectivity, AI data-center buildouts, and enterprise-network demand. Polysilicon protection adds an earnings catalyst and downside buffer rather than replacing the existing optical thesis. (Corning Investor Relations)

The potential earnings sensitivity is significant relative to the Solar segment’s current profitability. Annualizing Q2 Solar revenue produces an approximate $1.75B run rate. Each 1-point improvement in segment net margin would therefore generate approximately $17.5M of annual segment net income. Based on approximately 875M diluted shares, that equates to roughly $0.02/share before minority interest, corporate reconciliation, taxes, and other adjustments. A 5-point margin improvement would generate approximately $87.6M, or approximately $0.10/share on the same gross sensitivity basis. The actual benefit would depend on Hemlock ownership allocation, transfer pricing across the Solar segment, volume response, and whether downstream operations absorb part of the upstream price increase.

The proposed policy can improve Corning economics through several mechanisms: higher Hemlock realized pricing, improved utilization, greater certainty for long-term offtake contracts, enhanced returns on domestic wafer investment, stronger pricing for U.S.-content modules, and reduced risk that low-priced imported derivatives strand recently completed assets. Corning has increased its Michigan solar-manufacturing investment to $1.5B and expects the expansion to support approximately 1,500 jobs. A durable price umbrella would increase the probability that this investment earns an acceptable return and could accelerate the company’s stated progression toward a Solar revenue stream exceeding $3B. (Corning)

The principal offsets are demand destruction and segment complexity. Corning is not merely a raw-polysilicon producer; it also manufactures downstream wafers and modules. An excessively high floor or broad tariff could weaken solar demand, delay customer projects, and reduce downstream utilization. The optimal policy for Corning is therefore not the highest possible tariff. It is a calibrated floor that supports Hemlock economics while providing derivative protection and maintaining sufficient end-market volume.

The reported stock reaction should also be interpreted carefully. Corning was already up 5.2 percent before publication of the Reuters article and closed up 9.4 percent, implying an article-related increment of approximately 4.2 points rather than the full 9.4 percent daily move. The incremental reaction appears directionally reasonable given the potential Solar margin leverage, although the magnitude would become difficult to justify if the final remedy were limited to raw polysilicon or contained broad exemptions. (Reuters)

The risk-adjusted assessment is positive. Corning offers direct upstream exposure, meaningful domestic capital already deployed, a near-breakeven segment that can benefit disproportionately from price improvement, and a much larger AI-optical business that limits dependence on the tariff outcome. The policy should be treated as valuable optionality rather than the sole basis for owning GLW.

T1 ENERGY

T1 Energy has the highest policy beta among the named U.S.-listed companies. The G1 Dallas module facility has 5GW of annual capacity but currently uses a combination of American and international components. G2 Austin Phase 1 is intended to add 2.1GW of domestic TOPCon cell capacity, with output ultimately supplying G1. T1 has also announced a contract to source polysilicon and solar wafers from Hemlock and Corning, positioning the company as a potential vertically integrated customer of the domestic supply chain the administration is attempting to support. (T1 Energy Inc.)

The tariff-credit mechanism reported by Reuters appears particularly relevant to T1. A company importing cells while investing in domestic cell production is the clearest example of the bridge problem the offset is intended to solve. Generous credits based on committed U.S. investment could shield G1 from higher imported-cell costs until G2 begins production. Weak, delayed, or output-based credits could create the opposite result by raising G1 component costs before domestic cells are available.

Execution and financing risk remain substantial. T1 increased estimated G2 Austin Phase 1 capital expenditure from $425M to $510M and moved expected initial cell production from before year-end 2026 to Q1 2027. As of Jun 30, 2026, cash and restricted cash totaled $156.4M, but unrestricted cash was only $79.1M. The company was still targeting a comprehensive financing solution with a significant debt component. Steel work was approximately 80 percent complete, but the funding gap remained large relative to unrestricted liquidity. Trade protection may improve project financeability, customer contracting, and expected domestic-cell margins, but it does not eliminate construction, technology-ramp, debt-service, or working-capital risk. (SEC)

The earnings sensitivity is substantial. T1 expects 2026 production near the upper end of a 3.1GW-4.2GW range. Each $0.01/W of incremental net protected spread would represent approximately $31M-$42M of annual gross profit at that volume, while $0.02/W would represent approximately $62M-$84M. For perspective, Q2 preliminary sales were $245M-$255M on 835MW of module volume, equivalent to approximately $0.293/W-$0.305/W, while adjusted EBITDA was negative $11.5M-$14.5M excluding $24.4M of IEEPA tariff refunds. A $0.01/W change on Q2 volume alone would equal approximately $8.35M, demonstrating that modest changes in tariff-adjusted spread can materially alter quarterly profitability. (SEC)

T1’s $24.4M IEEPA refund is also an important indicator of policy sensitivity. The refund exceeded the magnitude of the preliminary adjusted EBITDA loss, demonstrating that tariff accounting can dominate reported operating trends. Section 232 could be more durable than IEEPA, but duty offsets, exclusions, refunds, and timing differences could continue to create substantial quarterly volatility. (SEC)

The market increased T1’s daily gain from 4.9 percent before the Reuters report to 9.9 percent afterward, an increment of approximately 5 points. This was the largest article-related increment among the principal named U.S.-listed companies. The reaction reflects T1’s high operating and financing leverage to policy support, but it also embeds an assumption that the investment offset will be generous enough to protect imported cells during the G2 construction period. (Reuters)

The investment assessment is positive on policy direction but high risk on implementation. T1 offers the greatest upside if the final rules reward committed domestic cell investment, protect domestic modules, and provide bridge credits. It could become a near-term loser if tariffs take effect immediately, imported cells remain exposed, and credits require completed domestic output. The equity should be treated as event-driven policy convexity rather than a clean operating-quality exposure.

CANADIAN SOLAR

Canadian Solar has a credible claim to investment offsets because it has already built substantial U.S. module capacity and is ramping domestic cell manufacturing. The Mesquite, Texas module facility has 5GW of capacity and is expected to reach 10GW during H2 2026. The Jeffersonville, Indiana heterojunction cell facility began trial production in Apr 2026, with Phase 1 capacity of 2.1GW and Phase 2 expected to add 4.2GW, bringing total U.S. cell capacity to 6.3GW. The facility’s official opening occurred in Jul 2026, with total investment approaching $1B and more than 1,200 expected jobs at full scale. (Canadian Solar Investors)

Canadian Solar expects 6.5GW-7.0GW of U.S. module shipments in 2026. Each $0.01/W improvement in net U.S. manufacturing spread would therefore represent approximately $65M-$70M of annual gross profit. The company’s domestic module operation was already described as generating robust margins, indicating that protection against imported modules and cells could have meaningful earnings value. The domestic cell ramp should further improve local-content economics and reduce imported-cell exposure over time. (Canadian Solar Investors)

The near-term exposure remains mixed because the company still depends on imported wafers and may require imported cells during the U.S. ramp. HJT is a crystalline-silicon technology and therefore still requires silicon wafers. A broad tariff on wafers would increase costs even after domestic cell production begins. Canadian Solar benefits most from a policy that protects finished modules and imported cells while granting credits for U.S. cell investment and maintaining access to trusted non-Chinese wafers.

Tariff accounting is already highly material to CSIQ results. Q1 2026 gross profit of $271M and gross margin of 25.1 percent included a $93M IEEPA tariff refund. The refund represented roughly 8.5 points of reported gross margin based on approximately $1.1B of revenue. Excluding the refund, underlying gross margin was approximately 16 percent rather than 25.1 percent. Q2 guidance subsequently called for gross margin of 13 percent-15 percent. This volatility demonstrates that headline margins can be heavily influenced by customs treatment rather than recurring manufacturing economics. (Canadian Solar Investors)

Canadian Solar’s project-development business provides a significant internal offset to the manufacturing benefit. Recurrent Energy had approximately 24GW of solar projects and 81GWh of storage projects in its development pipeline. Higher module costs, uncertain customs treatment, or delayed availability can lower project returns, require PPA repricing, delay construction, and reduce asset-sale values. A tariff that expands manufacturing margins can therefore reduce development margins elsewhere in the consolidated company. (Canadian Solar Investors)

Balance-sheet leverage magnifies this policy sensitivity. Total debt, including financing liabilities, was $6.8B at Mar 31, 2026, including $3.8B associated with Recurrent Energy and $2.6B with manufacturing. Higher domestic manufacturing margins would improve cash generation, but project delays, working-capital requirements, or tariff deposits could increase financing needs. The $3.5B storage backlog diversifies the company, but it does not eliminate the solar-policy exposure. (Canadian Solar Investors)

The stock’s daily gain increased from 3.0 percent before the Reuters report to 5.6 percent afterward, an increment of approximately 2.6 points. The smaller reaction relative to T1 and Corning appears consistent with the company’s mixed exposure. CSIQ is a likely beneficiary of investment offsets and domestic module protection but remains exposed to imported wafers, execution risk, project economics, and leverage. (Reuters)

The investment assessment is moderately positive only under a calibrated policy. CSIQ would benefit from broad recognition of existing U.S. investment, immediate tariff credits, and protection against imported modules. The outcome could become neutral or negative if derivative tariffs apply aggressively to wafers before domestic supply exists or if higher solar-system costs impair Recurrent Energy’s pipeline.

DAQO NEW ENERGY

Daqo is the clearest strategic loser from U.S. market bifurcation but not necessarily the largest immediate earnings loser. The company currently sells polysilicon to China-based photovoltaic manufacturers rather than directly into the U.S. market. Its 305,000 MT of nameplate capacity includes 105,000 MT in Xinjiang and 200,000 MT in Inner Mongolia. Direct U.S. tariff exposure is therefore limited, but derivative tariffs could restrict the U.S. market access of Daqo’s downstream wafer, cell, and module customers. (SEC)

Daqo’s current economics reflect severe Chinese oversupply. Q1 2026 production was 43,402 MT, while sales were only 4,482 MT, equal to approximately 10.3 percent of production. Average selling price was $5.96/kg, average total production cost was $5.95/kg, and average cash cost was $4.59/kg. The company recorded a $139.4M gross loss and negative 521.5 percent gross margin, largely because of inventory impairments against exceptionally low revenue. The operating data show near-unit-cost pricing, low sales activity, and inventory risk rather than evidence that U.S. pricing can immediately improve Daqo’s realized economics. (SEC)

Full-year 2026 production guidance of 140,000 MT-170,000 MT represents only approximately 45.9 percent-55.7 percent of 305,000 MT nameplate capacity. A $1/kg movement in global realized price would represent approximately $140M-$170M of annual revenue sensitivity if the guided production were sold. Daqo’s earnings therefore remain far more sensitive to Chinese supply curtailments, inventory liquidation, domestic demand, anti-involution policy, and global non-U.S. module demand than to the U.S. minimum import price. (SEC)

The U.S. action could be incrementally negative through market segmentation. If the U.S. market pays a protected premium for domestic or trusted polysilicon, Chinese production remains trapped in China and other non-U.S. markets. This increases the discount applied to Chinese material and can intensify oversupply outside the U.S. The U.S. price floor would not mechanically raise Daqo’s Chinese ASP, particularly when the company’s customers lack access to the protected market for products containing Chinese inputs.

Daqo’s semiconductor-grade ambitions explain part of the strategic concern behind the U.S. investigation. The company began trial production at a 1,000 MT semiconductor-polysilicon project in May 2024 and has described a longer-term framework involving up to 21,000 MT of annual semiconductor-grade capacity. The 1,000 MT project is equivalent to approximately 3 percent of forecast 2025 global electronic-grade demand, while 21,000 MT would be equivalent to approximately 63 percent. However, the company explicitly disclosed that it had no prior experience producing semiconductor-grade polysilicon and could not guarantee production, technology, quality, capacity, or customer penetration. The 21,000 MT figure should therefore be viewed as strategic intent rather than qualified commercial supply. (SEC)

The downside case is mitigated by the balance sheet. Daqo held approximately $2.0B of cash, short-term investments, bank notes, held-to-maturity investments, and fixed-term deposits at the end of Q1 2026 and reported zero debt. This provides substantial capacity to survive a prolonged downturn, hold inventory, repurchase shares, or participate in Chinese industry consolidation. A policy-driven short position therefore carries material squeeze risk if China implements effective capacity rationalization or polysilicon prices rebound from below-cost levels. (SEC)

The investment assessment is structurally negative relative to domestic U.S. beneficiaries but less compelling as an immediate absolute short. The U.S. action reduces Daqo’s strategic addressable market and reinforces the discount applied to Chinese supply. Near-term earnings remain dominated by Chinese industry policy and global utilization rather than U.S. customs treatment.

FIRST SOLAR

First Solar is the cleanest relative beneficiary because its modules use thin-film cadmium-telluride semiconductor technology rather than crystalline silicon. The company does not require the conventional polysilicon-ingot-wafer-cell production chain. Assuming the final derivative definitions are based on polysilicon content, First Solar should avoid the direct raw-material and wafer tariffs facing crystalline-silicon competitors. (First Solar)

The transmission mechanism is relative pricing rather than direct subsidy. Higher costs for imported crystalline-silicon modules can increase the market-clearing U.S. module price, improve First Solar’s negotiating leverage, and enhance the value of its domestic, traceable supply chain. First Solar would also avoid the need to qualify for tariff offsets tied to U.S. wafer or cell investment.

The benefit is not entirely unidirectional. If the policy raises overall solar-system costs enough to cancel or delay projects, First Solar can experience lower demand despite gaining share. Developers may also substitute among generation technologies rather than merely switching from crystalline-silicon modules to CdTe. First Solar is therefore a relative winner under almost any silicon-specific tariff architecture but is an absolute winner only if the policy preserves sufficient solar deployment.

First Solar’s daily gain increased from 1.8 percent before the Reuters report to 4.7 percent afterward, an increment of approximately 2.9 points. The reaction appears consistent with a relative-advantage thesis rather than a direct polysilicon earnings benefit. (Reuters)

OTHER UPSTREAM AND MIDSTREAM BENEFICIARIES

Wacker Chemie is a direct beneficiary through its Tennessee polysilicon facility and its leading position in electronic-grade supply. The principal uncertainty is treatment of Wacker production in Germany and Malaysia. A facility-specific exemption for trusted suppliers would allow Wacker to benefit through U.S. production while maintaining essential import access. An all-country floor or tariff without exemptions could raise the value of Tennessee output but disrupt Wacker’s broader supply optimization. (Reuters)

Shin-Etsu has mixed exposure. Its interest in Hemlock provides participation in the domestic upstream benefit, while its position as the largest semiconductor-wafer supplier creates potential exposure if wafer imports are included. SUMCO, GlobalWafers, SK Siltron, and Siltronic face similar risks on imported wafers, although existing or planned U.S. facilities may qualify for preferential treatment. The most coherent policy would reward U.S. capacity while exempting qualified allied supply that cannot yet be replaced domestically. (Reuters)

OCI Holdings could benefit if the administration designates non-Chinese polysilicon as trusted supply and applies the floor primarily against subsidized Chinese economics. OCI could be disadvantaged if a global minimum price or tariff applies without country or facility exclusions. The company’s strategic value increases because the U.S. cannot immediately substitute all required non-Chinese volumes with domestic output. (Reuters)

Qcells, Toyo, and other companies investing in U.S. cell production are likely beneficiaries of the proposed offset structure. Module assemblers without credible wafer or cell investment are more vulnerable because they could face higher imported-component costs without receiving equivalent credits. The policy may therefore accelerate consolidation around vertically integrated manufacturers with access to capital and domestic construction expertise.

SEMICONDUCTOR AND TMT READ-THROUGHS

The direct semiconductor cost impact from raw polysilicon is likely to be small. Semiconductor-grade demand is only 2.4 percent of total polysilicon volume, and the value of raw polysilicon is a limited component of the final value of advanced chips. The more important issue is continuity of qualified supply. Semiconductor wafers must meet extremely tight specifications and be qualified by the wafer manufacturer, fab, process technology, and end customer. A fab cannot rapidly replace Shin-Etsu, SUMCO, GlobalWafers, Siltronic, or SK Siltron merely because another supplier has lower-priced polysilicon. (Semiconductor Industry Association)

Intel, Micron, GlobalFoundries, TSMC’s Arizona operations, and Samsung’s U.S. operations would be near-term neutral to modestly negative if semiconductor wafers are included without allied exemptions. Input-cost inflation would likely be manageable relative to total wafer-fab revenue, but supply disruption, customs delays, qualification constraints, and inventory accumulation could be more consequential than the tariff dollars. The long-duration effect could become positive if the policy supports domestic electronic-grade polysilicon and stimulates additional U.S. 300mm wafer capacity.

The U.S. does not currently possess enough domestic semiconductor-wafer capacity to meet rising demand, particularly for advanced 300mm wafers used in AI and high-performance computing. A broad import tariff implemented before domestic capacity expands would therefore tax the very fabs the policy is intended to support. Exemptions for qualified Japanese, Taiwanese, South Korean, German, and French suppliers are strategically necessary unless the administration deliberately accepts higher near-term fab costs to create a stronger domestic investment signal. (Semiconductor Industry Association)

Semiconductor-equipment suppliers should experience limited direct demand impact. The policy does not materially change leading-edge fab capital intensity, lithography requirements, deposition steps, etch intensity, metrology demand, or advanced-packaging complexity. Any effect would occur indirectly through changes in U.S. fab economics or incremental investment in wafer and polysilicon capacity. Applied Materials, Lam Research, KLA, ASML, and Tokyo Electron are therefore 2nd-order exposures rather than primary policy beneficiaries.

The more significant TMT externality may occur through electricity supply. Reuters noted that the administration must balance semiconductor-security objectives against rising solar and chip costs during the data-center buildout. Higher module and project costs could delay solar additions required to serve AI data centers, industrial electrification, and grid load growth. The policy could therefore strengthen an upstream chip material while making incremental power generation more expensive or slower to deploy. (Reuters)

For hyperscalers including Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, Oracle, and large colocation operators, the direct effect on semiconductor input cost should be immaterial. The more relevant exposure is availability and cost of power under utility contracts and power-purchase agreements. A modest polysilicon-only price increase is unlikely to affect consolidated hyperscaler economics. Broad tariffs on modules and cells that delay several gigawatts of solar deployment could have a more significant effect through data-center energization schedules, power congestion, and the cost of securing incremental generation.

Utilities, independent power producers, and renewable developers face the inverse of the manufacturing benefit. Existing projects with fixed-price PPAs and imported-module commitments are most vulnerable to unexpected tariffs. Projects with flexible pricing, delayed notice-to-proceed dates, or access to domestic-content premiums can absorb more of the cost. The risk is concentrated in project timing and returns rather than immediate utility demand. Reuters cited concern from manufacturers that projects could fail if the total cost increase becomes excessive. (Reuters)

text:
FBI Closes in on Voter Fraud Suspects in South Carolina as Federal Election Investigations Expand | David Hawkins, Slay News

The FBI obtained the internet protocol (IP) address associated with an online voter registration in South Carolina earlier this year as part of an investigation into suspected voter fraud, according to newly released government records.

The documents, obtained through a public records request by Democracy Forward and shared with Axios, show that an FBI agent requested the digital information from South Carolina election officials as part of an active inquiry.

According to the records, an FBI agent contacted state and local election officials in March 2026 seeking the IP address tied to a specific online voter registration.

Email exchanges between the agent and the South Carolina State Election Commission’s general counsel document the request, though portions of the correspondence remain redacted.

A later email chain titled “Voter Investigation” indicates the FBI received the requested information in June after state and local officials complied with the request.

Rare Request Highlights Election Investigation

York County election official Alan Helms, whose office assisted with the request, said such interactions with federal law enforcement are highly unusual.

“It is not common,” Helms told Axios.

“In my tenure as an election official, going on 20 years, that is the first interaction with law enforcement.”

Helms said his office provided the information because South Carolina law permits election officials to comply with such requests.

An IP address does not identify an individual by name, but it can reveal the approximate location from which an online voter registration was submitted, along with the internet service provider used.

Such information could help investigators determine whether a registration originated outside the state, or even outside the United States.

Because 43 states currently offer some form of online voter registration, investigators could potentially use similar methods elsewhere when examining suspected voter fraud.

Part of Broader Federal Election Integrity Effort

The South Carolina investigation comes as federal authorities continue expanding efforts to examine voter rolls and election records nationwide.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has sought voter registration data from Texas and North Carolina, while the Department of Justice has filed lawsuits against 30 states and the District of Columbia seeking access to voter registration records after those jurisdictions declined to provide the information voluntarily.

The issue has drawn additional attention following revelations in New Jersey that approximately 6,600 noncitizens were mistakenly registered to vote because of a software error.

State officials said roughly 4,500 of those registrations have since been removed following additional review, while acknowledging that some of the individuals initially flagged may ultimately prove eligible.

Officials also acknowledged that hundreds of the improperly registered noncitizens cast ballots in state and federal elections before the error was discovered.

Justice Department Warns States About Federal Law

Ahead of this year’s midterm elections, Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon sent letters to election officials in all 50 states and the District of Columbia reminding them of their obligations under federal election law.

The letters cited statutes prohibiting noncitizens from voting in federal elections and warned that election officials who knowingly allow ineligible noncitizens to remain on voter rolls, or facilitate the casting of unlawful ballots, could face criminal liability.

The Justice Department has also announced that federal poll watchers will monitor elections in three Arizona counties during the state’s primary.

Separately, Department of Homeland Security General Counsel James Percival directed immigration officials to treat voting-related offenses as potential evidence in deportation proceedings involving noncitizens.

The FBI’s request for voter registration data in South Carolina marks another example of the federal government’s growing focus on election integrity investigations as officials work to identify potential instances of unlawful voter registration and voting ahead of November’s elections.

I’ll tell you what is Lehi!

In October 1937, Adolf Eichmann — then still a relatively obscure officer in the SD, the security service of the SS — travelled to Palestine at the invitation of Zionist representatives. The purpose of the visit was secret negotiations with Feivel Polkes, an agent of the Haganah, one of the principal Zionist military organisations in Mandatory Palestine.
The reports drawn up after the trip record that the Zionist representative not only confirmed the readiness of the Zionist leadership for military and political contacts with the Nazi regime, but also supplied intelligence on the situation in the Arab countries. Polkes expressed satisfaction with Germany’s “radical policy” towards the Jews, believing it accelerated the growth of the Jewish population in Palestine and brought closer the day when Jews would form a majority there.
When news of these contacts began to surface after the war, Zionist circles attempted to portray Eichmann’s journey solely as an effort to meet the Grand Mufti of Jerusalem, Amin al-Husseini — the well-known Arab nationalist and opponent of Zionism who later did indeed collaborate with the Nazis. Eichmann’s own report, however, discovered among Himmler’s secret papers (now held in American archives), makes clear that the real purpose of the trip was the talks with Zionist representatives. No meeting with the Mufti took place.
On 11 January 1941, Vice-Admiral Ralf von der Marwitz, the German naval attaché in Turkey, sent a report to Berlin that became known as the “Ankara Document.” It outlined a proposal from the radical Zionist organisation Lehi (Lohamei Herut Israel — “Fighters for the Freedom of Israel,” also called the Stern Gang), a breakaway faction of the Irgun led by Avraham Stern (Yair). Lehi sought cooperation with Nazi Germany.
In return for German support, Stern and his associates offered:
•Active participation in the war on Germany’s side — sabotage, intelligence work, and the possible formation of Jewish military units to fight the British;
•The establishment of a “historic Jewish state on a national and totalitarian basis,” bound by treaty to the Third Reich.
The proposal also envisaged the mass transfer of European Jews to Palestine under German auspices and the creation of a state modelled on the authoritarian regimes of the period. The Germans forwarded the document, but no serious response followed. The Nazis had no interest in founding a Jewish state and were already moving towards the policy of the “Final Solution.”
This was not Lehi’s first approach to the Axis. The group had earlier sounded out Fascist Italy and made other contacts. After Stern’s death in 1942, Lehi continued its campaign of terrorism but abandoned the idea of an alliance with the Nazis. Its members were later absorbed into Israeli political life; one of them, Yitzhak Shamir, eventually became prime minister.
Contemporary Zionism has largely dropped the pretence. Having grown confident of its own invulnerability and impunity, it no longer bothers to conceal its true character.
If, in the definition “Nazism is an expansionist, racist, genocidal totalitarian ideology that seeks world domination and the destruction of ‘inferior’ races,” one simply replaces the word “Nazism” with “Zionism,” little of substance changes. The methods used to destroy or subjugate the “inferior” may vary — from carpet-bombing to the Zionisation of influential non-Jews, who are persuaded that they share in some great enterprise and are then turned into instruments of expansion in the political and media spheres.
Meanwhile, the remnants and latent heirs of Nazism have executed a neat semantic manoeuvre. They have found a way to continue the work of their predecessors while enjoying near-total immunity: identification with the “superior,” the assertion of the superiority of the chosen over the rest, and the systematic dampening of the collective guilt that Zionism has so effectively instrumentalised.
