text:
Leo Frank Trial Anniversary: Star witness Jim Conley Swears Frank Hid Purse of Mary Phagan

The Atlanta Georgian,

Wednesday, 6th August 1913,

PAGE 55, COLUMN 1.

Sweeper's Grilling Ends After 15 Hours, His Main Story Unshaken

PAGE 55, COLUMN 7

MYSTERY OF GIRL'S MESH BAG EXPLAINED BY NEGRO ON STAND

That Mary Phagan's silver-plated mesh bag, mysteriously missing since the girl's bruised and lifeless body was found the morning of April 27, was in Leo Frank's office a few minutes after the attack and later was placed in the safe in Frank's office was the startling statement made by the negro Conley Wednesday in the course of his re-direct examination by Solicitor Dorsey. At 11:10 the negro left the stand after being questioned for fifteen and one-half hours.

This testimony was the sensation of the forenoon. Throughout the more than three months of the murder mystery an unavailing search was made for the mesh bag, the city and Pinkerton detectives being convinced that the finding of the bag would go a long distance toward pointing out the person guilty of the Phagan girl's murder.

"Did you ever see a silver mesh bag that Mary Phagan carried?" inquired the Solicitor.

"Yes, sah," replied Conley. "I see it right on Mr. Frank's desk when I went in there."

"What became of the mesh bag?" continued Dorsey.

"He went and put it in his safe," the negro said.

First Word of Mysterious Bag.

It was the first information, authentic or otherwise, that had come to light regarding the disposal of the mesh bag. The homes of Newt Lee and Jim Conley had been searched high and low for the bag or any other clew to the perpetrator of the crime. Except for a vague rumor that a mesh bag had been found by a negro in a shop on Decatur street, a story which later was found to have no connection with the Phagan mystery, not the slightest clew ever was discovered to the whereabouts of the bag which so strangely had disappeared.

Attorney Rosser's manner was angry and threatening when he arose for the re-cross examination. He began at once a vicious attack on Conley's story of the mesh bag. He asked when Conley first told this remarkable tale. Conley said he couldn't remember.

"Why didn't you tell all this when you were telling 'the whole truth' to the detectives?" Rosser shouted.

The attorney apparently sought to create the impression that the mesh bag story was an afterthought, and that it was manufactured by the negro when he heard of the search the detectives were making for the bag.

On Grill Over Thirteen Hours.

When Rosser turned Conley back to Dorsey for the redirect examination, the negro had been under the grill of Rosser's cross-questioning for a total of thirteen hours. His main story of Frank's admitting the killing and of the disposal of Mary Phagan's body at Frank's direction was unshaken except by his own admissions of previous falsehoods. He had been on the stand a total of fifteen and one-half hours. Of this time the Solicitor had questioned him only about two hours.

Conley was called from the stand at 11:10 o'clock.

Conley was taken into an anteroom. He removed his coat and lit a cigarette someone had given him.

"How did you like it?" he was asked.

"I liked it all right," he replied, grinning.

Sheriff Mangum then interrupted the questioning of the reporters, saying that under the judge's orders no one could speak to him.

The next moment Conley picked up a newspaper and became intently interested in the story of his own testimony.

As soon as court opened Mr. Rosser asked the judge if he was ready to hear argument on the proposition to eliminate parts of Conley's testimony. He said he was prepared to support his motion with authorities.

Judge Roan replied that he would postpone his decision until 2 o'clock.

Solicitor Dorsey declared that he had witnesses he expects to put on the stand Wednesday morning to substantiate the part of the negro's testimony in dispute. He said:

"I just want the court to understand that I am going to do this."

Judge Roan replied:

"I'll give you the benefit of whatever you bring out."

Conley was then recalled to the stand for the conclusion of his cross-examination.

Questioned About Affidavit.
Rosser's first question was:

Q. You made this statement just as I read it, didn't you, Jim? A. Yes.

Q. It's all correct? A. Yes.

Q. Now, Jim, you signed this statement, too, didn't you? (Showing another affidavit.) A. Yes, sir.

Q. You made this one the day after the one I just read? Now, listen,

PAGE 56, COLUMN 1

CONLEY SAYS FRANK TOOK MARY PHAGAN'S MESH BAG
Lies Down on Floor to Show Jury How He Left Girl's Body in Cellar

NEGRO'S LONG GRILL ENDS AFTER 15 HOURS, HIS MAIN STORY STILL UNSHAKEN
and see if this is what you said?

Mr. Rosser read how Jim Conley for the first time told the story of carrying the body of Mary Phagan to the basement. These were the concluding words:

"The reason I have not told this before is that Mr. Frank said he would get me out, but it don't seem that he is going to get out and I have decided to tell the whole truth. I gave him back the $200. He said he would fix it all right Monday."

Q. This is what you swore, isn't it, Jim? A. Yes, sir; I swore it.

Q. Jim, didn't Miss Carson ask you on Monday while you were working around her machine when they were going to get you, you answered that you hadn't done nothing? A. No, sir.

Denies Alarm While Sweeping.
Q. Didn't she say that Mr. Frank was innocent and the real murderer of little Mary Phagan was the man Mrs. White saw near the steps? You dropped your broom and quit sweeping when she said that? A. No, sir.

Q. Didn't you say to Mr. Herbert Schiff on Monday after the murder that you were afraid to go out of the factory and that you would give a million dollars to be a white man? A. I didn't say just that, but I told him if I was a white man I would go on out.

Q. He told you to get on out, asking you what you had to be afraid of? A. Something like that.

Q. Jim, you talked with Julia Fuss on that day and asked her if she had another extra? You asked her if she got one to let you see it? A. No, sir.

Q. She told you that Mr. Frank was innocent, didn't she? And you said he was innocent as the angels in heaven? A. No, sir; I didn't say that.

Mr. Rosser closed the cross-examination and Solicitor Dorsey began the redirect examination.

Tells of Prison Record.
Q. Jim, where were you in prison? A. Police headquarters.

Q. Were you ever in jail? A. Yes.

Q. What were you charged with? A. Just because I was washing my shirt.

Q. I mean those other times you were arrested. Were you in the county jail then? A. No, I was in headquarters.

Rosser interrupted:

"The charges are in writing, your honor. They are the last evidence."

"It's a poor rule that doesn't work both ways," said Dorsey. "Can't we exclude this evidence?"

Judge Roan: "You can show where he was."

Q. What were you arrested for the first time? 

A. I was throwing rocks.

Q. Who arrested you? 

A. A police named Edmonds.

Q. The second time? A. I was fighting.

Q. A white man or a woman? A. No, I never had any trouble with white folks.

Q. Jim, did you try to see Mr. Frank in jail?

Rosser objected.

Judge Roan Don't lead him, Mr. Dorsey.

Q. Did you ever see Frank after you went to the pencil factory? A. No.

Q. Why not?

Rosser objected to the question as immaterial. Dorsey changed his question.

Last Saw Frank at Station.

Q. When was the last time you saw Frank before you saw him here? A. Over there at the police station.

Q. Did he say anything? A. No, he just smiled and bowed his head.

Q. When you wrote those notes, did you sit down, and, if so, where? A. I was sitting at the desk.

Q. Where was Frank sitting? A. At the other desk.

Attorney Rosser objected. "He went into all that before," he said.

Judge Roan Did you, Mr. Dorsey?

"No, it is something I omitted," said Dorsey.

Q. What did Frank do when he you wrote those notes?

Rosser objected to the question as leading.

Q. Did Frank touch your pencil when you were writing?

Rosser objected again, declaring that the question was leading.

Judge Roan said the question could be asked without leading.

Q. What, if anything, did Mr. Frank do when you were writing? A. He took the pencil out of my hand and told me to rule out that "s" on the "negro."

Q. What hour was it Friday Frank came up on the fourth floor and spoke to you? A. About 3 o'clock.

Says Frank Took Girl's Bag.
Q. How far was it from where you were Tuesday when he told you to be a good boy? A. Almost the same place.

Q. How far was it from the water cooler to where her body was dragged? A. I don't know, sir.

Q. How far from the water cooler? A. I don't know.

Q. Did you ever see Mary Phagan's pocketbook or meshbag? A. Yes, it was on the desk in Mr. Frank's office.

Q. What did he do with it? A. He put it in the safe.

Q. How long were you in jail before you wrote for the detectives? A. About ten or fifteen days.

Q. How long would it take Frank to go down and lock that door? A. About one minute.

Q. Where was Frank standing when you saw the clock at four minutes to one? A. He was standing near those stair steps.

Q. Describe that scream you heard.

Rosser objected.

"He has gone into that before, your honor," he said.

The question was sustained, Judge Roan saying: "The question cannot be asked because it is reopening a long cross-examination."

Q. Jim, who has asked you the most questions, Mr. Black, Scott, Starnes and Campbell and myself or Mr. Rosser?

Tries to Show Court Grilling.

Rosser objected.

Dorsey: "Your honor, he has tried to bring out the fact that this witness has been grilled. I want to show that altogether he was not questioned as long or as much as Mr. Rosser has questioned him on the stand."

Judge Roan: "You can ask him how long he was questioned out of court, and what has gone on here is public."

Dorsey put the question again.

Q. How long was the longest you was ever questioned before you came here? A. Mr. Scott came and got me one day and I herd him tell the turnkey it was fifteen minutes to eleven. It was dark when I got back.

Q. How long was that? A. I'd say about three and one-half hours.

Q. How long has Mr. Rosser questioned you?

"Your honor, I want to get this answer in the records," said Dorsey.

Judge Roan: "Do you object?" looking at Mr. Rosser.

ONE OF WITNESSES FOR DEFENSE
Mrs. Emma Freeman, who will testify for Leo Frank.

"I do," said Rosser.

"I sustain you," said the court.

Dorsey continued the questioning.

Q. Jim, how did you leave the body in the basement? A. I left her on her side.

Lies on Floor to Answer Query.

Q. How? (Conley got down on the floor and lay on his left side, his arms against his body. After the illustration he identified a photograph of the basement and pointed out just where he left the body).

Q. Now, Jim, tell the jury in detail everything you did after you looked at the clock at 4 minutes to 1.

Rosser objected. "He has gone into

that, your honor," he said.

"Have you, Mr. Dorsey?" Judge Roan asked.

"We have not gone into that detail," Dorsey replied. "We want to show the jury how long it would have taken to do the things there and how long it would have taken Frank to get to his home. Mr. Rosser has brought out this detail to draw his conclusions."

Judge Roan: "Have you asked that?"

Dorsey: "Yes."

Judge Roan: "Then I sustain the objection."

Dorsey: "That's all right, your honor. If you think the State ought not to ask these questions, it is all right with me."

Promised Help in Trouble.

Q. What kind of paper were you talking about when you spoke of green sheets? A. That one (identifying the white note).

Q. What kind of back did it have?

A. A kind of grayish pad.

Q. What did Frank say about taking you to Brooklyn? 

A. He didn't. He said he would take me away, and if I got into trouble he would get me out.

Q. Did you ever have any conversation with Mr. Mincey?

A. No; I saw him at police headquarters.

Q. What did he say?

Rosser objected, and the objection was sustained.

Q. That night at jail, did those newspaper men come on the inside? 

A. No.

Q. What did they say? Wait a minute; I want those two men out. (Two newspaper reporters, H. W. Ross and Harllee Branch, of The Atlanta Journal, who were at the press table, retired from the courtroom.) 

A. I can't remember that.

Q. Did they offer you anything at all?

Rosser objected, and was sustained. Conley had answered the question, though, declaring that nothing was offered him but a paper.

Q. That day at the factory, were you nervous or not? A. No; I was not.

Darley Knew He Could Write.

Q. What did Mr. Schiff say to you? A. They were standing there by the clock and asked if there was a crowd at the front door. Mr. Schiff came in and I said I wish I was a white man; that I would go out from

there. One man said he wished he had a pistol. Mr. Schiff said: "They've got Mr. Frank in jail. I don't see that being white would help."

Q. Did Darley know you could write? A. Yes.

Rosser objected. "It is immaterial," said he.

Dorsey: "We want to show that this man could write; that he was in jail several days without writing, and the detectives, the Pinkertons employed by the factory, knew he could write.

Q. Could you spell luxury? A. Yes.

Q. Why? A. I had to write it several times. Mr. Frank had me to write down the names of the different boxes that pencils were in, and give them to him, so that he could know when they were out.

"Wasn't Asked Before."

Attorney Rosser took up the recross-examination:

Q. Jim, you were questioned by Mr. Dorsey and myself and all the detectives, and this morning was the first time you ever mentioned that mesh bag. A. You didn't ask me.

Q. Do you know what I asked you yesterday? A. Yes, sir; I remember some of the questions.

Q. What? A. Well, I don't remember just exactly.

Q. You don't remember a single thing that has not been written down?

Dorsey objected. "He must give the witness time to answer," said he.

Q. Jim, haven't you answered my questions? A. Yes, sir.

Q. You said this morning that Mr. Frank promised to get you out on bond and send you out of town? A. Yes, sir.

Q. Why didn't you tell the detectives that when you told them you were telling all the truth? A. I did tell them he promised to get me out.

Q. Mr. Dorsey saw you seven times, didn't he? A. Yes, sir; I think that's right.

Q. Did he take down what you said? A. He took down something the first time.

Q. How about the next times? A. I disremember.

Q. How long have you kept up with those boxes? A. About a year.

Conley Tries Spelling.
Q. And you wrote Mr. Frank reports on these boxes? A. Yes, sir.

Q. Would you know "luxury" if you were to see it? A. No, sir.

Q. How did you write it for Mr. Frank, then? A. I can write it.

Q. Can you spell it? I can try it. Well, let's hear you spell 'luxury.' A. L-u-s-t-r-i-.

Q. Was that the only kind of pencil boxes up there? A. No, sir. There was Uncle Remus, Thomas Jefferson, George Washington and others.

Q. Did you write reports on them? A. Yes, sir.

Q. Let's hear you spell 'Uncle Remus?' A. O-n-e R-i-m-e-s.

Q. Let's hear you spell 'Thomas Jefferson'? A. T-o-m J-e-i-s-s.

Q. Let's hear you spell 'George Washington'? A. J-o-e W-i-s-h-t-o-n.

Q. What did Mr. Frank say about your spelling? A. He laughed.

Q. How do you spell 'Ox'? A. O-x-.

Q. How did you write him notes to borrow money? . A. I just wrote them.

Q. Tell me what you wrote? A. I just said: 'Please let me have fifty cents.'

Q. When you were standing by

that box talking, could Mr. Darley hear you? A. Yes.

Q. Could Mr. Schiff? A. Yes.

Q. Could that boy? A. Yes.

Asked If He Could Write.

Q. When you went into the office to write those notes, Mr. Frank asked you if you could write, didn't he? A. Yes.

Rosser put the question again.

Dorsey objected to the repetition, and the objection was sustained.

Messrs. Hooper and Dorsey were with you in the jail together, were they not? A. Yes.

Q. How long? A. Two or three hours.

Dorsey Wins Ruling.
Q. How long after April 26 was

it you saw this man? A. About a month.

Q. At the time you saw him at the police station did you identify him? A. I did not.

Rosser objected.

Q. What did you say?

Rosser: "I object. I wasn't there."

Dorsey: "Your representative, Mr. Scott, was there."

Rosser: "I move to rule that out."

A. I said he looked more like the one than any man I have seen.

Rosser: "I move to rule it all out."

Dorsey: "We expect to show by this witness that this was the man. We want to show how he was dressed, his facial expression, etc., and we submit that it is material."

Judge Roan overruled the objection.

Q. Describe the man you saw. A. He was about the size of the one just brought before me whom I have been told is Jim Conley. He was in a dark place and I took him to be black. He had on dark clothes and I don't know whether he had on a hat or not.

Q. Wade Campbell is your brother, and Arthur White your husband, aren't they? A. Yes.

Q. When did you tell them you saw a negro sitting in that hall?

Rosser objected.

Laughing Spectators Ousted.

The odd situation of the attorneys for the defense being in possession of the official court records were relieved when Mr. Arnold consented to it being read.

Mr. Rosser, however, found it first in his copy of the testimony of Scott.

Rosser: "You were right. Harry Scott did say Mrs. White told Frank about seeing this negro Monday after the crime."

Several spectators were put out of the courtroom for laughing at Mr. Rosser's admission of the error.

Rosser: "I will say it is the first time that you have been right. Your honor, we object. It is immaterial what time this witness made known the fact unless they go further and show she was delayed through the influence of Frank."

The objection was overruled.

Lawyers Clash.

Dorsey Your honor, I have already shown that Leo Frank knew on Monday, April 28, that she saw this negro there, and that it was May 7 before the State got into possession of this fact.

Rosser I say that no such evidence has been introduced.

Dorsey Call for the record of Harry Scott's evidence.

Rosser I say he has not introduced this evidence, and he saws he has. If your honor can not remember some of the things that happen here we are perfectly helpless.

Stenographer Parry was called. He said he was taking the testimony for Mr. Arnold and he wanted Mr. Arnold's consent before reading it.

Jim Conley was the same cool, unafraid negro when he returned to the stand Wednesday morning in the trial of Leo Frank after almost two whole days under the cross-examination of Luther Rosser. He had passed through fire and didn't seem to mind it. He had no fear of anything that was yet to come.

Mr. Rosser might threaten him or might joke with him; it was all the same to the negro. He had tried both and had established but one thing that Conley is a liar, and Conley admits that.

Arnold might describe him as "that miserable wretch in the witness chair;" he could gaze calmly out the window as he had done before. He didn't quite understand all those names they were calling him, anyway.

If, in all the time that Conley was under the raking fire of Rosser's cross-examination, he was disturbed in the slightest degree, it was when he was being asked about that mysterious affidavit of William H. Mincey.

The declaration of Mincey that Conley had boasted the afternoon of April 26 of killing a girl was sinister and held in it the possibility that Rosser would finish by blazing forth with a direct charge of murder against the negro. Conley moved uneasily in his seat. He refused to meet the eye of his inquisitor. He fidgeted with his hands, but with his lips he framed a denial of every damning charge contained in the document.

The ordeal soon was over. Conley regained his composure, and when court adjourned a few minutes later a grin of triumph cleft his black face almost in twain.

Attorney Sees Conley.

Conley's attorney, William M. Smith, provided him with supper and breakfast at the jail and talked for some time with the State's star witness. He had been prevented from holding any sort of a conference with his client the night before, and protested at this procedure at the close of court Tuesday night. Judge Roan extended him the privilege of seeing Conley. Reuben Arnold asked that an exception be entered in the record.

Conley slept between nine and ten hours and arose much refreshed.

"I'se telling the truth now," he said to a newspaper man who encountered him outside the jail. "That Mr. Rosser ain't got no chance to get me mixed up because I'm telling just what happened."

Frank occupied his usual cell on the second floor of the Tower. He was joined by his wife and mother as soon as he arrived at the courthouse.

PAGE 55, COLUMN 5

ACCUSER OF CONLEY IS READY TO TESTIFY
W. H. Mincey, who declares Conley told him he had killed a girl.

Deplores Newspaper Publicity,

but Poses Merrily for the

Camera Brigade.

W. H. Mincey, the school teacher and insurance solicitor who made an affidavit that Jim Conley confessed to him that he had already killed a girl that day and didn't want to kill anyone else, was the center of attraction for the crowd on the outside of the courthouse Wednesday morning.

While deploring newspaper publicity, he readily agreed to pose for a group of newspaper photographers, assuming many poses, some of which were rather grotesque. He followed this with implicit instructions to the photographer that his picture was not to be printed in the papers.

Efforts to get him to state whether he had seen Jim Conley since his arrest proved futile. Mincey declared he would not make this statement or answer until he had taken the stand.

Mincey was located at New Salem, Ga., near Rising Fawn, in Dade County. He is teaching school there, his work being the preparation of students to enter the Martha Berry School at Rome.

"I will not talk of the case and will not tell my story until I take the stand," said Mincey. "If Jim Conley killed little Mary Phagan, I feel that it is my duty to tell of the experience I had with him that Saturday afternoon. I don't think this thing should be discussed in the newspapers, though I regard newspapers as a necessity. These matters should be left to the court hearings. It is a loss to me to be here and I trust the case will soon be over. I think, though, that it is my duty to tell what I know."

Mincey is a man of small stature with piercing eyes and a gray mustache. He wears a black felt slouch hat and a dark suit.

PAGE 57, COLUMN 1

CAN JURY OBEY IF TOLD TO FORGET BASE CHARGE?
By JAMES B. NEVIN.

"Gentlemen of the jury, having heard from James Conley, the blackest, most damning story ever told in Atlanta by one human being against another, having sat there and listened as he smudged with unspeakable scandal the defendant in this case, Leo Frank, although it is irrelevant, immaterial, and has nothing to do with this case, you will kindly forget it, being on your oaths as jurymen to consider the evidence declared competent!"

And the jury, being like most other juries, in one way and another, and having heard all the things as aforesaid, will promptly proceed to do as instructed about forgetting it NOT!

I have heard juries told too many times to "forget" things such, for instance, as that there is no such thing as "unwritten law" in this land of the free and home of the brave and I have seen, too many times those very same juries proceed to "forget" NOT!

Juries are, after all, composed of mere human beings, and things such as Conley said to the Frank jury can NOT be forgotten, and will NOT be disregarded by the average jury.

Merely Question of Belief.

It is merely a question of whether the jury BELIEVES the negro!

There was something infinitely pathetic in the situation Tuesday, when court met in the afternoon.

For one thing, it brought to the cheeks of the defendant's wife, always and ever at his side, the first tears I yet have seen fall from her eyes.

She has borne herself with amazing fortitude thus far the wonder is that she has not long ago collapsed.

When Reuben Arnold, moving to strike from the record the vile story of Jim Conley, paused a second before reading the exact words he desired expunged, looked a moment in the direction of the defendant's wife, and said, with no show of the spectacular whatever, "Your honor, I would prefer not to read this in the presence of these two ladies, and I therefore pass it to your honor that you may read it in silence!" The moment was tense and tragic!

Private Sector Answers President Trump’s Call to Lower Prices for American Families

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

President Donald J. Trump inherited an economy battered by years of inflation that crushed working families. Through bold action to restore American energy dominance, slash red tape, and secure fair trade, the Trump Administration is quickly rebuilding the foundation for lasting prosperity.

That leadership is producing results. Across the country, private sector companies are responding to President Trump’s call by delivering tangible price reductions on everyday goods and services putting money back in the pockets of American workers and families.

Groceries and Everyday Essentials

Major retailers are cutting prices on staples that hit household budgets hardest putting real money back in the pockets of American families.
• Giant Eagle reduced prices by an average of more than 10% on over 300 top products, including proteins, produce, and pantry favorites.
• Walmart lowered prices on thousands of everyday items nationwide, including ground beef, fresh corn, paper plates, beverages, and more.
• Sam’s Club cut prices on more than 250 household essentials.
• Meijer reduced prices on more than 1,000 popular grocery and household items on a rotating basis.
• Target reduced prices on thousands of groceries, household items, and other essentials.
• Kroger is planning its biggest price cuts in years on thousands of items.
• Albertsons accelerated targeted price reductions and launched its “New Lower Price” program, cutting base prices by at least 8% or $1 on items across meat, seafood, dairy, pantry staples, and other goods.
• H-E-B dropped prices on thousands of items across its stores.
• C&S Wholesale Grocers slashed prices on thousands of everyday items at Family Fare, VG’s Grocery, Martin’s Super Markets, and Piggly Wiggly locations across eight Midwestern states.
• Stop & Shop lowered prices on thousands of items across nearly every department in hundreds of stores throughout the Northeast.
• Cub Foods reduced prices by about 40% on dozens of grocery items across its Midwestern locations.
• Piggly Wiggly Food for Less cut prices on meat and other staples across its 14 stores.
• Costco dropped prices for many of its most popular Kirkland Signature items across multiple categories.
• PepsiCo lowered retail prices by up to 15% on major snack brands.

Prescription Drugs

President Trump’s Most Favored Nation approach is delivering historic cuts to prescription drug prices, with 17 of the world’s largest drugmakers agreeing to bring U.S. prices in line with the lowest paid by comparable developed nations.
• Novo Nordisk slashed prices on Ozempic and Wegovy to as low as $199–$350 per month and reduced the price of common insulin treatments by 75% through TrumpRx.
• Pfizer offered average savings of 50% (up to 85%) on primary care treatments and select brands via TrumpRx.
• Amgen lowered prices on cholesterol drug Repatha, migraine drug Aimovig, and arthritis treatment Amjevita by 60–80%.
• Eli Lilly lowered the price of migraine treatment Emgality by approximately 60% and diabetes treatment Trulicity by approximately 61%.
• Multiple additional manufacturers including Merck, AstraZeneca, Bristol Myers Squibb, Gilead, Sanofi, GSK, EMD Serono, Johnson & Johnson, AbbVie, Regeneron, Boehringer Ingelheim, Genentech, and Novartis agreed to cut prices on key drugs, with discounts reaching 50–85% on many medicines.

Energy

Key energy providers and local networks are delivering targeted savings that lower costs for consumers.
• The Freedom Fuel Network a coalition of 25 gas stations across the greater Philadelphia area lowered prices by approximately 50 cents per gallon.
• Georgia Power is lowering rates for residential customers by $50/year, delivering total savings of nearly $300 million for all customers.
• Alliant Energy implemented a five-year rate freeze for residential customers in Iowa.
• NiSource is set to return $1.4 billion to customers in Indiana through agreements with Amazon and Alphabet.
• Entergy is set to return $2 billion to customers in Mississippi through an agreement with Amazon.
• DTE Energy announced it will pause electric rate increases for at least two years.

Automobiles

American automakers are making vehicles more affordable for hardworking families.
• Ford extended employee pricing to all U.S. customers.
• Stellantis offered buyers 0% financing and deferred monthly payments for 90 days.
• Chevrolet revived its classic “Heartbeat of America” campaign, offering 90 days of deferred monthly payments and multi-year 0% APR financing options.

Distributed on August 6th, 2026.

Well said. I also think they are so far disconnected from reality that they have not even seen it. I am from a small town in Georgia. We all take care of one another here, regardless of race, and we are well diversified. The other day a woman was in front of me with only two small individual cereals, small milk and some bread. She was at the self check out. The cash register announces when the card doesn’t work and tells you to go back and try again. She walked out fast. No chance to offer any help, which any of us would have in line. We still have a certain pride when it comes to asking for handouts. Some people just can’t. And we were two different races. But we share the same values. All of us do here. We all are feeling the pain. And it sucks when we’re told that it’s not that bad, it’s just in your head. 

They could do so much for so many of us by simply lowering our state and federal taxes. Why is that so difficult for them? If the govt just prints money to pay for services, why take so much from me? Warren Buffet and the like love throwing it in our face how much tax they pay compared to us. Agreed. Can you all cut me a break. Why can’t wages go up a little, without having extra tax added. I get a little more, they take a little more. And send it overseas. USAID was out of control, and so are foreign wars when we aren’t being attacked. Both send money overseas, either to woke weirdos or bombs landing on foreign soil. Either way, the money you take from me and this lady in my story, ends up over there. NOT HERE

Kirby Smart says the transfer portal has made too many coaches forget what the word “coach” means

“That’s what the word ‘coach’ is. It derived from 'stagecoach'… Where you took somebody from one place to the other.”

“Where are you taking your players… Instead of shipping them off or importing them from elsewhere?”

“Now it’s you coaching against me… And me coaching against you. Who makes their players better?”

“In the second portal window, there was very little effective movement. I call it ‘swap and spit.’ You just took somebody else’s two or three… And they took your two or three… You traded… And all you got was a new person.”

“Over 80% of the people had no impact. All they were doing was moving to move. They were just moving to move.”

“Let’s make our players better. Let’s say the ones we lifted and practiced with all last winter… They’re ours now.’”

“And they’re better now because they stayed here.”

text:
Whiskey Jug Genie by Sultonna Nadine is a lighthearted and charming paranormal fantasy that mixes magic, humor, and a touch of romance for pure escapist fun.

When quiet London apothecary shop owner Martin buys an old whiskey jug on vacation, he has no idea he’s about to release Bubba, a genie who’s been trapped inside for 200 years and is thoroughly out of touch with the modern world. Chaos, spells, cultural clashes, and plenty of laughs ensue as the unlikely pair (along with a very annoyed cat) try to navigate the mess. Set against the backdrop of contemporary London with elements of white magic and everyday wonder, the story balances humorous situations with warmer moments. Readers appreciate its playful tone, quirky characters, and the perfect blend of paranormal fantasy, magic, and comedy—it’s the kind of book that delivers smiles and a welcome dose of whimsy.

Sultonna Nadine is the pen name used by Mellie Miller for her standalone fantasy romance novels that feature magic, alternate touches, and paranormal elements outside her main series. Born in the 1950s in the American Midwest, she has lived across the country, drawing on a rich background that includes music, martial arts, and Reiki. Married for decades to her husband Steve, she is a mother and grandmother who now lives in rural Georgia. Under this name she creates light, magical stories meant to offer readers an escape filled with romance and wonder. (She also writes series fiction as Mellie Miller.)

text:
SET TO DIE TODAY IN DEKALB COUNTY, GA‼️‼️‼️‼️‼️
The following dogs have been scheduled for euthanasia on Thursday, August 6 at 7PM. They need long-term placement through foster, adoption, or rescue‼️‼️‼️
Week after week, our numbers far surpass our maximum humane capacity. This takes a toll on everyone—our volunteers, staff, advocates—but most importantly, it takes a toll on the dogs. Humane care is our top priority, and it's difficult to achieve when we are consistently caring for more than 500 dogs in the shelter at one time.
Many people comment that we should transfer these dogs to "no-kill" facilities. The reality is that "no-kill" means maintaining a save rate above 90%, which our shelter has been able to do. We are grateful every time a rescue pulls one of our dogs, but our goal isn't simply to move them to another kennel. These dogs are declining. They need homes.
We do transfer pets to rescues almost every day. Our rescue team works tirelessly to find placement for dogs, whether they're urgent or not. But rescues everywhere are full, which is another symptom of the overpopulation crisis.💔💔💔
We also have one of the largest foster programs in the country and offer free and low-cost spay/neuter, veterinary care, pet food assistance, and rehoming resources. We don't share this to be defensive—we share it because there are no easy solutions. Overpopulation is a complex issue, and ultimately, it's the dogs who pay the price.💔💔
Today, 24 dogs have a deadline of Thursday, August 6 at 7PM. They don't know about save rates or rescue transfers. All they know is that they're stuck in a kennel, full of pent-up energy and craving human interaction.🙏🙏🙏🙏🙏🙏🙏
They need homes, and unfortunately, that's something we cannot provide, as much as we wish we could.💔💔💔💔💔💔

Fosters must live in Georgia. Out-of-state adoptions are welcome, but adopters are responsible for transport. Please email adoption@dekalbanimalservices.com.
Intake never stops. Our shelter remains over capacity. But none of that is the fault of these dogs. They deserve loving homes, and we can't give up hope.

Let's save lives, Atlanta.

Chamblee, GA 30341

text:
Banks Introduces Amendment Protecting Female Athletes

Amendment would prevent federal legislation from overriding state protections for female athletes

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Senator Jim Banks (R-Ind.) offered an amendment to the Protect College Sports Act alongside Senators Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.) that would prevent the legislation from preempting state laws protecting women’s sports.

Indiana has enacted protections for female athletes at every level of education. In 2022, the Indiana General Assembly passed legislation to prohibit biological males from competing in girls’ K-12 sports. In 2025, Governor Mike Braun signed a second law extending those protections to women’s collegiate athletics.

The senators’ amendment would ensure that Indiana and other states’ laws cannot be weakened or overridden by the federal government.

Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.): “Indiana has one of the strongest laws in the country that keeps biological men from competing in women’s sports. As a father of three daughters, I can’t support any legislation that would preempt Indiana’s law. This amendment would make sure the Protect College Sports Act protects female athletes.”

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO): “Biological men should never be allowed in women’s sports or women’s locker rooms. We’ve got to make sure state laws protecting women stand.”

Sen. Tommy Tubberville (R-Ala.): “Protecting girls and women’s sports is the civil issue of our time. Democrats have proven again and again they don’t give a rip about protecting women from mentally ill men who wake up one day and decide to dress like a girl. I’m proud to stand with Senators Hawley and Banks in introducing this commonsense amendment to protect millions of female student athletes.”

Sue Bird Explains USA Basketball's 2026 FIBA World Cup Roster Decisions

USA Basketball Managing Director Sue Bird Discusses The Selection of The 12-Player Roster That Will Compete in The 2026 FIBA Women’s Basketball World Cup in Berlin, Germany.

text:
DEMOCRATIC PARTY or MACHINE ?
.
Chicago’s Parking Giveaway, the Quota Mind, and the Politics of Competence
(Part 1 of 2)
.
By Peter Spear
Notatio Editoris by GPT-5.6 Thinking
.
“The Amateur Democrats confuse declaring a cause with solving a problem.”
.
Seventy-five years. That is how long Mayor Richard M. Daley’s administration surrendered control of Chicago’s parking meters: from 2008 until 2083. A child born on the day the City Council approved the bargain could live an ordinary American lifetime and never see the meters return to public control. (Chicago Office of Inspector General, 2009)
.
Chicago received $1.157 billion up front. The city’s inspector general later estimated that the future net revenue surrendered had a present value of approximately $2.13 billion to Chicago at the time of the transaction. On that conservative calculation, the city accepted about $974 million less than the asset was worth—a loss of roughly 46 percent before the ink had dried. (Chicago Office of Inspector General, 2009)
.
For readers who prefer the headline figure to discounted-cash-flow analysis, contemporary financing projections reported that motorists could pay the concessionaire at least $11.6 billion in nominal dollars over the seventy-five-year term. Serious financial analysis rightly discounts receipts arriving decades in the future. But discounting does not rescue the bargain: the inspector general performed that expert calculation and still concluded that Chicago had been shortchanged by nearly $1 billion in 2009 dollars. (Bloomberg, Aug. 9, 2010; Chicago Office of Inspector General, 2009)
.
The subsequent history has not vindicated Daley. By July 2026, the concession had generated about $2.2 billion for investors, while Stonepeak Partners was prepared to pay approximately $2.5 billion for the fifty-seven years remaining. Chicago, meanwhile, had spent most of its original payment within roughly two years and had incurred nearly $250 million in compensation obligations when parking spaces were removed or taken out of service. (Reuters Breakingviews, July 20, 2026; WTTW, July 13, 2026)
.
I use the word corruption in its broad political sense: a governing culture deformed by patronage, hurry, secrecy, obedience, and contempt for the duty to understand what is being sold. I do not claim, without evidence, that a particular official took a criminal bribe in the parking transaction. The documented recklessness is condemnation enough.
.
Richard M. Daley was the son of Richard J. Daley, the legendary boss of the Chicago Democratic machine. The elder Daley centralized patronage in City Hall and governed through an organization in which jobs, contracts, ward loyalty, and political power reinforced one another. Chicago historians describe a system whose practical rule was that one hand washed the other. (Encyclopedia of Chicago, “Patronage” and “Machine Politics”)
.
The elder Daley also presided over the 1968 Democratic National Convention. The Walker Report found violence by some demonstrators but described the widespread and indiscriminate violence by Chicago police as a “police riot.” Daley did not personally swing every baton, but he assembled the overwhelming force, set the political atmosphere, and defended the department whose officers attacked demonstrators, bystanders, journalists, and photographers. (Daniel Walker, Rights in Conflict, 1968)
.
Forty years later, the younger Daley’s administration announced the parking-meter winner, held a one-day committee hearing, and pushed the agreement through the City Council almost immediately. Aldermen were asked to bind citizens through 2083 without the time, independent analysis, or public deliberation appropriate to a transaction of such duration. The inspector general concluded that the city failed to calculate the meter system’s value to Chicago before deciding whether the bid served the public interest. (Chicago Office of Inspector General, 2009)
.
That is what political machines do at their worst. They replace inquiry with loyalty, deliberation with urgency, and stewardship with the immediate needs of the organization. The machine that once treated citizens as obstacles to be controlled eventually treated a productive municipal asset as property to be liquidated.
.
This parking disaster encapsulates my criticism of the Amateur Democrats. Why do people who refuse to study health care, housing, Social Security, transportation, education, or municipal finance insist upon controlling them?
.
Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren still speak as if Wall Street hedge funds were the principal cause of America’s housing crisis, just as much of the left speaks as if our exorbitant health-care costs were chiefly the result of insurance-company profits. Anyone with even a basic grasp of housing supply or health-care finance knows those explanations are radically incomplete, yet too many left-leaning journalists repeat them without serious scrutiny.
.
Sex, drugs, and rock and roll would at least explain the enthusiasm. More commonly, the rewards are patronage, social standing, career advancement, partisan belonging, ideological fashion, moral exhibitionism, and the intoxicating pleasure of ordering other people about. Their motives may sometimes be sincerely high-minded. Sincerity, however, is not a substitute for competence, and a high-minded blunder can impoverish more people than an ordinary vice.
.
Public policy is an applied science. It begins by defining the problem, identifying the mechanism that causes it, estimating costs and benefits, testing competing remedies, and preparing for unintended consequences. It requires imagination: the ability to see that a goal may be reached by a method entirely different from the one favored by the party’s activists.
.
Too many Democrats instead begin with the desired moral posture. The slogan arrives first; the mechanism is improvised later. If the consequences are poor, the failure is blamed on insufficient commitment rather than on a defective model. The same intellectual vice appears in parking mandates, housing scarcity, municipal finance, racial preferences, and the mechanical use of disparate impact.
.
THE FAIR RULE FOR PARKING
.
The fair rule is simple: motorists should pay a reasonable charge for occupying scarce public street space, and that charge should vary with when and where the space is scarce.
.
Cities routinely permit automobiles to occupy publicly owned land for little or nothing, yet recoil from issuing revenue bonds for parking structures whose users could repay the bonds through fees. The first arrangement is treated as normal, while the second is denounced by some as socialism. In fact, free curb parking is the subsidy. A user-financed garage is the market-like arrangement because the people consuming the service bear its cost.
.
Street parking is never economically free. When a city gives it away, the bill reappears as congestion, circling traffic, wasted time, blocked deliveries, unavailable curb space, higher taxes, and restrictions on housing construction. The scarcity remains; only the method of payment changes. (Mackowski, Bai and Ouyang, 2015; SFpark Pilot Evaluation)
.
The most perverse hidden charge is imposed through minimum parking requirements. When government commands a builder to construct a fixed number of parking spaces for every apartment, the cost is bundled into the rent or purchase price. A household without an automobile pays for the garage all the same. Required or bundled parking can add substantially to housing prices and rents while reducing the number of homes that can be built. (Jia and Wachs, 1998)
.
Cities did not abolish the cost of parking. They concealed it inside the price of housing.
.
Housing scarcity is itself a form of payment. The person who cannot find an apartment, who is forced into a longer commute, or who pays a higher rent because fewer homes were built is paying for the city’s parking policy even if he does not own a car.
.
Proper street pricing also increases demand for structured parking. When curb space is free or artificially cheap, drivers circle blocks hoping to win the underpriced space while a garage sits partly empty. When curb prices reflect actual demand, the garage becomes comparatively attractive: it is predictable, protected, and no more expensive than the street. That increased garage demand can support the revenue needed to repay municipal parking bonds. (SFpark Pilot Evaluation)
.
A MUNICIPAL PARKING UTILITY
.
Every large city should consider a municipal parking utility that manages curb space and public parking structures as one coordinated system. Strategically located garages could be financed with revenue bonds rather than general-obligation taxes. Parking receipts would pay operating expenses, debt service, maintenance, and reserves. The people using the parking system—not taxpayers generally—would bear its principal cost.
.
The curb and garage prices would be coordinated. The street should not be given an artificial advantage over the structure. During periods of high demand, curb parking might cost as much as or more than nearby garage parking. During low-demand periods, both prices could fall.
.
Carmel, Indiana, offers a partial precedent. Carmel has used tax-increment financing and municipal development tools to help construct public garages as part of mixed-use redevelopment. Many of its garages are free to the motorist and repaid indirectly through increased property-tax revenue. My proposal is more explicitly based on user fees, although a city could combine parking revenue with tax-increment financing when nearby property owners also receive substantial benefits. (Accelerate Indiana Municipalities)
.
Cars could carry transponders linked to prepaid or automatically replenished accounts, much as toll-road and bridge systems already do. A city collection vehicle could pass a line of parked cars, identify the transponder, confirm the license plate, locate the vehicle within a pricing zone, and submit the appropriate debit. Drivers without accounts could receive plate-based invoices or use a mobile application, kiosk, or temporary visitor pass.
.
The system would require safeguards: duplicate-reading suppression, a clear amnesty period after each charge, daily maximums, disability and emergency exemptions, receipts, an appeals process, retention limits for location data, independent audits, and a prohibition on using parking records for unrelated surveillance without lawful process.
.
THE FORMULA, WITHOUT FEAR
.
The formula merely tells the computer to implement a fair rule already chosen by elected officials: begin with the ordinary price for the neighborhood, change it according to the clock and day, and then adjust it according to actual demand.
.
R(z,t,d,q) = Bz × T(t,d) × D(q)
.
R is the resulting parking rate.
Bz is the basic price for the particular parking zone.
T adjusts the price for the time of day and day of the week.
D adjusts the price for the current demand or occupancy level.
.
In plain English, a commercial district could charge more during weekday business hours and very little overnight. A residential district could charge little during the day, more as residents return home, and a modest flat amount covering the night. An entertainment district could be inexpensive in the morning and expensive after dinner. Geography and the clock work together.
.
The city need not change prices every minute. It could begin with transparent schedules—morning, business day, evening, and overnight—and revise them periodically using measured occupancy. A sensible target would preserve one or two available curb spaces on a typical block, reducing the costly search for parking without turning the program into a revenue-maximization machine. (SFpark Pilot Evaluation; Mackowski, Bai and Ouyang, 2015)
.
Repeated readings would be controlled through an amnesty, or cooldown, period. After the system charges a vehicle, later collection vehicles may pass it, but the account remains protected until the applicable period expires.
.
Charge again only when:
Current time – time of last charge ≥ applicable amnesty period.
.
A vehicle charged for overnight residential parking at 10:00 p.m. might receive amnesty until 8:00 a.m. In a high-demand commercial district, the amnesty might last two hours. The rough rule of no more than two charges in a rolling twenty-four hours could remain as an additional consumer-protection ceiling, but the principal design should respond directly to the zone and time of day.
.
The formula does not make policy. Citizens and elected officials decide the zones, base prices, multipliers, amnesty periods, maximum daily charges, exemptions, and privacy rules. The formula simply gives administrators a reproducible method for carrying out those choices consistently.
.
CHICAGO MUST TAKE CARE OF CHICAGO
.
Chicago is the cautionary tale, but this proposal should apply to other cities that still control their curb space. The 2008 concession limits Chicago’s freedom to remove, reprice, or repurpose covered spaces without possible compensation to the private operator. Chicago must negotiate, litigate actual breaches if any exist, or finance a buyback on terms that do not repeat the original mistake. (Chicago Office of Inspector General, 2009; Reuters Breakingviews, July 20, 2026)
.
Mayor Brandon Johnson has discussed a buyback figure of roughly $3.3 billion, while the proposed 2026 sale of the remaining concession to Stonepeak was valued at about $2.5 billion. Those figures suggest that undoing Daley’s blunder may be expensive, but not remotely on the trillion-dollar scale I first feared. A modern curb-pricing and garage-revenue system could help finance a repurchase, although the debt service would have to be modeled conservatively. (Reuters Breakingviews, July 20, 2026; WTTW, July 13, 2026)
.
Chicago might enjoy saying that the 2008 city government was too incompetent to contract. That would be a splendid political verdict and a poor legal theory. Courts do not normally rescind a binding agreement merely because one side made a foolish bargain. The realistic case for relief would have to rest on negotiation, contractual rights, demonstrable breach, fraud if evidence exists, or legislation consistent with constitutional protections.
.
The national lesson is prospective: do not privatize generations of revenue to cover one budget crisis; do not give away valuable curb space; do not force every household to buy parking through its housing; and do not build public garages without an integrated price system that makes them usable and financially productive.
.
THE QUOTA MIND
.
Parking policy and racial admissions policy are not the same subject. The connection is the intellectual failure by which both were formulated: begin with a morally satisfying label, fail to define the mechanism, ignore incentives and alternatives, and treat foreseeable injuries as proof that still more of the original intervention is required.
.
Minimum parking rules announced a cause—adequate parking—but did not ask who would pay, how much housing would be displaced, or whether curb pricing and public structures could solve the problem more fairly. Racial preferences announced a cause—diversity or remedy—but too often refused to confront the individual injustice of penalizing an applicant because his group had already produced too many successful candidates.
.
The phrase affirmative action originally covered a broad range of lawful efforts: recruitment, outreach, enforcement against discrimination, and opening opportunities previously withheld. Using that honorable phrase to conceal racial preferences was politically convenient because even many advocates understood how unpopular explicit racial allocation would be. (For a History of Affirmative Action See Democratic Amateurs Part 1 of 2 at, II Affirmative Action: From Administrative Duty to Demographic Tableau.)
.
Disparate impact is a legitimate legal concept, not literally a quota. It can reveal that a facially neutral practice excludes a protected group without sufficient business justification. But it becomes a quota by another name when every numerical disparity is treated as proof of wrongdoing and proportional racial outcomes become the demanded remedy regardless of causes, qualifications, or alternatives. The Supreme Court’s decision in Ricci v. DeStefano illustrates the conflict that arises when fear of disparate-impact liability leads an employer to discard a neutral examination because the racial results are politically inconvenient. (Ricci v. DeStefano, 557 U.S. 557, 2009)
.
White men who objected to racial preferences were not standing alone. In a 2023 Pew survey, 57 percent of White adults and 52 percent of Asian American adults disapproved of selective colleges considering race and ethnicity to increase diversity. In a separate survey, 76 percent of Asian American adults said race or ethnicity should not factor into admissions decisions. Opposition crossed racial and demographic lines even when advocates portrayed it as the grievance of one group. (Pew Research Center, June 8, 2023)
.

Gov. Braun Announces Comlux America Investing $22M in Indiana Operations, Doubling Workforce with 375 New Jobs

INDIANAPOLIS – Indiana Governor Mike Braun today announced that Comlux America, a privately held premier aircraft completion and maintenance center headquartered in Indianapolis, will grow its operations in the city, with plans to more than double its current workforce and create up to 375 new, high-wage jobs by the end of 2030.

“Today is a great day for Comlux America, for Indiana and, most importantly, for our Hoosier workforce,” said Gov. Braun. “The company’s commitment to growing here reinforces Indiana’s status as a leader in advanced manufacturing and aerospace, and it is a testament to Indiana’s skilled and hardworking talent. Comlux America’s expansion will bring 375 new jobs to the region and create unmatched opportunities for Hoosiers to train and skill up for these competitive careers.”

Indiana is home to the highest concentration of manufacturing jobs in the nation and ranks No. 4 in the US for aerospace manufacturing attractiveness by PwC, making the Hoosier state the ideal destination to support Comlux America’s continued growth. Comlux America is part of Indiana’s robust aerospace sector, which has invested more than $1 billion in the state since 2013.

Comlux America plans to invest more than $22 million to expand its workforce and enhance its existing 247,000-square-foot operations at the Indianapolis International Airport to meet growing demand for its advanced cabin completions, upgrades and refurbishments for narrow- and wide-body aircraft. Demand for Comlux America's VVIP completions and maintenance & repair services has grown steadily over the past few years, and this investment ensures the company can continue welcoming new programs while maintaining the craftsmanship and delivery standards that define its work worldwide. Comlux America, which has already doubled its aircraft capacity in recent months with two additional hangar spaces, will invest in hangar and production space enhancements and advanced tooling and equipment, enabling the company to increase throughput, improve efficiency and ensure timely deliveries of completions while also expanding its capacity for light-to-medium aircraft maintenance.

“Indiana has been the foundation of Comlux America's growth, and this investment reflects our confidence in this community, this workforce, and this state's future in aerospace," said Adam White, Chief Executive Officer of Comlux America. "We are building something truly exceptional here in Indianapolis — a world-class facility where precision engineering meets uncompromising craftsmanship. As we expand our team and our capabilities, we're not just growing a company; we're creating careers, deepening our roots in Indiana, and raising the global standard for what a completion and service center can be.”

The company has already started hiring for new positions, which include aircraft mechanics, avionics technicians, interior and cabinetry specialists, engineers, quality assurance personnel and project management professionals.

Comlux America is committed to building a workplace where skilled tradespeople, engineers and aviation professionals can build long-term careers. The company offers competitive wages, comprehensive benefits and a culture rooted in craftsmanship, continuous improvement and mutual respect. As Comlux America grows, so do the opportunities for its people — from trainee-level roles to senior technical and leadership positions — making it one of the most distinctive career destinations in Indiana’s aerospace sector.

Comlux America has been operating in Indianapolis since 2008, strengthening the region’s advanced manufacturing and aerospace sector while establishing itself as one of the most unique and modern completion and service centers in the world exclusively for Airbus Corporate Jets and Boeing Business Jets. The company blends precision engineering with luxury craftsmanship, focusing on innovation, quality and reliability to improve comfort, connectivity, performance and long-term value for VIP and VVIP aircraft. @93wibc

text:
Every year now brings the same headlines: record heatwaves, flash floods swallowing cities, wildfires racing across hillsides, and cyclones flattening coastlines. Most of the conversation that follows centres on collapsed infrastructure, damaged crops, economic losses, and disappearing biodiversity. One consequence, however, receives far less attention. Climate change is no longer only reshaping ecosystems and economies; it is quietly reshaping how people think, feel, and imagine their future. This is climate anxiety.

Climate anxiety is not a mental illness. It is an emotional response, a mix of fear, stress, helplessness, grief, and uncertainty, that surfaces when people confront the scale of environmental degradation. UNICEF defines it as emotional distress caused by awareness of a changing environment, distress that becomes concerning when persistent worry begins to interfere with daily life, hope, or decision-making. It is less a pathology than a rational response to a very real threat.

The clearest evidence comes from a Lancet Planetary Health study spanning ten countries and involving 10,000 young people aged 16–25. 59% said they were very or extremely worried about climate change, while 84 percent reported at least moderate concern. Nearly half (45%) said this anxiety already affects their daily functioning, and three in four believed the future is frightening. 

Respondents described feelings of sadness, fear, anger, helplessness, and, in many cases, a sense of betrayal by governments they felt were failing to act. These findings demonstrate that climate anxiety is not confined to a small activist fringe. It is emerging as a measurable global public health concern among the generation set to inherit the crisis.

India offers similar evidence. The country faces prolonged heatwaves, recurring floods, droughts, and severe air pollution, conditions that young people experience repeatedly rather than as isolated events. 

A @down2earthindia survey of 300 young people aged 16–25 highlights the growing psychological impact of these environmental changes.

* Respondents who felt the climate around them was changing: 88% (264 of 300)

* Respondents who said climate change already affects their daily lives: 67% (201 of 300)

* Respondents who described themselves as anxious: 57% (171 of 300)

These findings reinforce the growing concern among India's youth. UNICEF India notes that young people are increasingly aware of climate risks because they are the ones most likely to live with the consequences over their lifetime. 

None of this should be interpreted as people worrying too much. Climate anxiety reflects repeated exposure to disasters, deep uncertainty, and a perceived gap between institutional promises and institutional action. 

Mental health systems rarely account for climate-related distress, while climate adaptation planning seldom considers psychological well-being, even though the two are closely connected. Climate anxiety is best understood as an indicator of how deeply the climate crisis is embedding itself in society, rather than merely an individual emotional response. 

Addressing it will require more than counselling. It demands credible climate action, honest public communication, resilient communities, and policies that restore confidence in the future.

#climateanxiety

text:
A Few Thoughts After the Primary
I watched the returns the other night and I’ll be honest — I was a little surprised Curt Skoog didn’t do better on the Democratic side. He’s been mayor of Overland Park a good while and I figured he’d pull more votes than he did. Instead, Cindy Holscher from Overland Park came out on top. She’s the one staring us in the face now for November.
Ty Masterson won the Republican primary. It is what it is. I was a Philip Sarnecki supporter and I still am. Philip ran a strong race as a businessman and outsider who understands how to build something and make it work. A lot of good people backed him for the same reasons I did.
What would help Ty the most right now is simple: reach out to Philip today. Not next week. Today. Ask for his help — not just in winning the governor’s race, but ask him to take the Department of Administration if Ty wins. That job is about running the day-to-day machinery of state government. Philip has built companies that employ hundreds of people, managed big operations, and focused on results instead of politics. Putting someone with that kind of experience in charge of how the state spends money, buys things, and manages its own house would send a clear message.
It would also bring people together. Primary fights leave bruises. Reaching out to Philip and offering him a real seat at the table would tell the folks who voted for him that their voice still matters. It would show conservatives across Kansas that this campaign is serious about cleaning up waste, getting value for every tax dollar, and putting competent people in charge instead of the usual revolving door. That kind of unity and seriousness can tip the scales when you’re up against a well-funded Democrat from Johnson County who will run hard until the end.
Ty has the nomination. Now it’s about winning the state. Calling Philip today and making that offer would be a smart, strong move. I hope he does it.
Henry McClure Topeka

Michael owen: I thought salah would stay at liverpool or join a bigger european club.

Mohamed Salah has finally settled on a new club after leaving Liverpool, but his decision to join Turkish Süper Lig side Trabzonspor has surprised many, including Michael Owen.

Michael Owen admitted that he was somewhat disappointed with Salah's new destination after the Liverpool legend confirmed his move to Trabzonspor.

Salah ended his nine-year career at Anfield with a move to Turkey. During his time at Liverpool, he became the club's third-highest goalscorer and was voted the fourth greatest player in the club's history. The 34-year-old forward was not short of options. Saudi Arabia had been viewed as a potential destination in recent years, and Al-Ittihad tried unsuccessfully to sign him as early as 2023. Major League Soccer was also once an option, with Sporting Kansas City unexpectedly emerging as one of the suitors.

Ultimately, Turkey became his next destination. Beşiktaş had been in contact with Salah in recent weeks and made him an offer, but Trabzonspor ultimately won the race, surprising many. Trabzonspor finished third in the Süper Lig last season, meaning they will have to compete in a playoff later this month to secure a Europa League spot. Many had expected that, if Salah remained in Europe, he would choose a club capable of playing in the Champions League.

text:
Eternal Dream in the Clouds  218    

   made   in   Gemini

**PAW Patrol to the Rescue: The Dog Whisperer**  

Sunlight filtered through the plane trees of Central Park, dappling the park bench with shifting patterns of light and shadow. Lily bit down on her straw, watching the handsome man across from her pretend to tie his shoelace for the third time—while actually slipping his fingers into the tree hollow to fish something out.  

“I’ve counted. Seven slices,” said Bruno the golden retriever, sitting primly at her feet in a pure Oxford accent. “Three last week, four this week. The bacon was smoked with rosemary—my aunt sent it from Kansas, saved for the winter.”  

Lily nearly shot her iced Americano out her nostrils. She’d owned Bruno for three years, and this was the first time he’d ever spoken—and in the tone of a BBC documentary narrator.  

“You—” she lowered her voice, “—can talk?”  

“Since last week,” Bruno said, licking a paw with elegant composure. “Probably from eating that transgenic squirrel. But that’s not the point. The point is your boyfriend’s larceny constitutes a misdemeanor, and I suggest you reconsider this relationship.”  

Mark finally finished his pilfering and strolled back, beaming. “Honey, what do you feel like for dinner?”  

Lily stared at his greasy cuff. “I feel like vegetables.”  

Mark’s smile froze. Behind him, Bruno gave Lily a slow wink. “Sensible choice. Also, he kissed a woman in yoga pants behind that same tree last Wednesday. She called him ‘little bacon.’”  

Lily threw her entire coffee over Mark’s Italian handmade loafers.  

Three hours later, Lily sat in the animal-behavior lab across from Dr. Travis, who wore gold-rimmed glasses. Bruno lay on the table, flipping through *Dog Food Review* with his paws.  

“Impossible,” the doctor said, pushing up his glasses. “Animals suddenly acquiring language—that’s usually accompanied by—”  

“*The Secret Life of Pets* plot?” Lily offered.  

“—geomagnetic storms or a Raccoon City spill,” Dr. Travis said gravely. “I need to run a full battery of tests.”  

Bruno looked up. “Mind if I order takeout? What’s your lab’s Wi-Fi password? Also, Doctor, the ketchup on your tie is from the hot dog you ate this morning, and your third graduate student on the left stole your limited-edition figurine.”  

The doctor’s face went from white to red. His phone rang; he answered, listened for three seconds, and his expression turned priceless.  

“The zoo says… a tiger recited the *Ramayana* in Sanskrit?” Dr. Travis’s voice wavered. “Pigeons in Central Park are forming Scrabble words? The feral cats of Times Square are demanding to unionize?”  

Lily scooped up Bruno. “So I’m not crazy.”  

“The whole world is crazy,” Bruno said, nuzzling her cheek. “But don’t worry, miss. I can smell you’re a good person. Even though the kibble you bought last time was the discount brand, you secretly added chicken breast to the mix.”  

Lily’s nose suddenly stung.  

Outside the window, a flock of sparrows was using their wings to spell out in the sky: **WE DEMAND BETTER GRAINS**. Dr. Travis rushed to the window, his tie flapping in the wind.  

“This defies every known law of science!”  

Bruno hopped onto the sill, tail wagging cheerfully. “Doctor, have you ever considered that maybe we didn’t learn to speak—you just finally learned to listen?”  

Lily’s phone buzzed frantically. An emergency alert from the mayor’s office: all animals in New York demanded a press conference. Detroit’s cats declared independence. Los Angeles’s seagulls occupied Beverly Hills.  

“Miss,” Bruno said, resting a paw on her hand, “ready to be the live interpreter for global television?”  

Lily took a deep breath. Her life had gone from “pretty girl walking her dog” to “pretty girl who can understand dogs”—and it all started with that transgenic squirrel three days ago, who was now on the White House lawn requesting political asylum in Mandarin.  

“Let’s go.” Lily ruffled Bruno’s fluffy head. “But before we leave, we’re stopping at the supermarket.”  

“For kibble?”  

“For bacon.” Lily grinned. “This time, you hide it, I’ll keep lookout.”  

Bruno’s tail spun like a helicopter rotor.

text:
What if one Civil War battle flag could tell the story of four years of sacrifice, courage, and endurance?

The battle flag of the 1st Tennessee Infantry Regiment is far more than a historic piece of cloth. It is a witness to one of the longest and hardest journeys made by any Confederate regiment in the Western Theater.

Raised by volunteers from communities across Middle Tennessee, these men marched into the war together as neighbors, brothers, farmers, merchants, and railroad workers. By the time the fighting ended in 1865, only a fraction of the regiment remained.

Their story stretched across some of the Civil War's most famous battlefields:

⚔️ Shiloh ⚔️ Perryville ⚔️ Murfreesboro (Stones River) ⚔️ Chickamauga ⚔️ Missionary Ridge ⚔️ Kennesaw Mountain ⚔️ Franklin ⚔️ Nashville ⚔️ Bentonville

One of the most fascinating parts of their history is the regiment's surviving Polk-pattern battle flag, marked "1ST REGT TENN." Unlike the more familiar Confederate battle flags, this dark blue banner represented the unique identity of the Army of Tennessee and accompanied Maney's Tennesseans through some of the war's fiercest fighting.

In our latest blog, we explore:

• How the regiment was formed from Middle Tennessee communities.
• Why Civil War battle flags were essential for survival in combat.
• The remarkable history of the regiment's flags, from the early Rock City Guards banner to the famous Polk-pattern battle flag.
• The incredible sacrifices made by the men who carried these colors through four years of relentless campaigning.
• Why this preserved flag remains one of Tennessee's most important Civil War artifacts.

Whether you're passionate about Civil War history, historic battle flags, Tennessee history, or the soldiers who fought under these banners, this article offers an in-depth look at the regiment behind one of the Western Theater's most remarkable flags.

📖 Read the full story here:

text:
A former Labour parliamentary candidate has been jailed for four years after using a fake Oxford degree to land more than a dozen senior NHS roles – before going on sick leave to avoid doing the jobs.

Amran Hussain, 40, was Labour's candidate for North East Hampshire in the 2015 general election before embarking on an eight-year campaign of fraud that cost the taxpayer £168,000.

Using fake certificates and fictitious references, he fabricated degrees from the universities of Oxford, Harvard and Birkbeck to blag his way into 13 senior NHS roles across the country, including some with salaries of more than £78,000-a-year.
.

Hussain took an astonishing 1,332 sick days (70 per cent of his days employed) by claiming he had a litany of illnesses, including post Covid-19 syndrome, tiredness, anxiety, depression, low mood, headaches, neck pain, pelvic pain, vertigo, headaches and dizziness and migraines. 

His deception finally unravelled in 2021, when Devon Partnership NHS Trust offered him a £90,000-a-year role as deputy chief operating officer and carried out checks on his application – discovering no record of his claimed job at Coventry and Warwickshire Partnership NHS Tr

During this time, he applied for 2,071 NHS jobs, with his 13 fraudulent roles costing the British taxpayer £168,072.41.

Out of a total of 1,902 days employed, Hussain took 1,332 days off sick – the equivalent of three years and nearly eight months. 

Two of his roles were NHS band 8D, where his salary would have been more than £78,000-a-year at the time of his employment (they are more than £100k today). 

The most experienced role he blagged his way into was as the head of outpatient pathway redesign for University Hospitals Dorset NHS Foundation Trust. 

After signing his contract, he worked just one shift from the 116 days he was employed, claiming 115 days of sick leave.

How he was able to repeatedly pass reference checks and go undetected for so many years remains a mystery. 

Hussain's fraud was finally exposed after Devon Partnership NHS Trust offered him a deputy chief operating officer role in 2021 and carried out checks on his application.

He had claimed to be the director of transformation and improvement at Coventry and Warwickshire Partnership NHS Trust. But the NHS found no record of his employment and they later discovered he had never worked there.

They subsequently discovered he had tricked his way into 13 different NHS roles.

Despite getting hired for several high-income NHS roles over eight years, it's understood Hussain's fraud only amounted to £168,000 because he would often be on sick leave and therefore not receive his full yearly salaries.

Hussain was also found to have fraudulently secured jobs outside of the NHS, including at NottinghamCityCare Partnership and Kent County Council.

While out on police bail, Hussain was elected as a councillor for Crockham Hill, a ward within Westerham Town Council, in the 2023 elections.

A retired Westerham councillor and neighbour told the Mail: 'He became a Westerham councillor. Somebody said I should talk to him because he had so many great ideas and he tried to contact me once. They said somebody is moving up near you and he's getting onto the council.

'It's amazing these characters. You just think what? You just never know what's going on.'

The selfie-loving fraudster has also posted pictures alongside the world's fastest sprinter Usain Bolt, who he met while volunteering at the 2014 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Many years earlier, as a schoolboy in 2005, he accused the late Queen Elizabeth II of undermining London's Olympic dream by saying she thought Paris would win the bid to host the 2012 Games over Britain.

The desire to speak to the national media and share selfies with celebrities and politicians

Hussain was sentenced to four years in prison on July 24. He previously admitted three counts of fraud by false representation at Maidstone Crown Court

text:
Fake and Never Trumpers to create their own Party

In early June, Tucker Carlson said he’s done with the Republican Party, calling it disloyal for putting foreign interests above American citizens. Marjorie Taylor Greene quickly agreed, saying a lot of people are fed up. Then, just a few days ago on August first, Greene posted a photo from a gathering at Carlson’s place in Maine. It showed her, Carlson, Thomas Massie, and Joe Kent, the former counterterrorism chief who resigned over the Iran war. She captioned it “the movement has begun,” emphasizing no more foreign wars and America First for all Americans, right, left, and center.

These folks are a unified “con” group. Thomas Massie was always an independent voice, losing his primary to a Trump-backed challenger. Tucker Carlson’s break he claims come from Trump’s Iran war, which he sees as a betrayal of “no more foreign wars.” Marjorie Taylor Greene’s split came after she wasn’t offered a cabinet post and clashed over the Epstein files. Joe Kent resigned over the Iran war, because there was an FBI investigation into classified leaks. Their “America First” movement focuses on anti-war and non-interventionism. However, third parties face massive structural hurdles in the U.S. system.

The idea that these opportunists are riding a wave for their own platform and money, and that it creates dangerous division. 

These folks timed their exits perfectly for personal gain. Greene locked in her pension then pivoted, Massie got primaried out, Carlson and Owens cashed in on big platforms after building audiences on President Trump’s coattails.
