text:
Flip Witte, van hydrologie naar ideologie, de boer als zondebok

Terwijl ik, tijdens m’n ontbijt, de laatste slokken van m’n glas melk drink, lees ik dat volgens ecohydroloog Flip Witte in het @ndnl 'de boer' weer de oorzaak is van een probleem: de droogte. 'Boeren zijn de belangrijkste boosdoener' schrijft hij, maar daar stopt het niet, volgens Flip exporteren wij ook ons schaarse grondwater. Maar Flip zou geen artikel gepubliceerd krijgen in een Nederlands dagblad als daar geen ronkend advies als conclusie op volgt natuurlijk. U raadt het al: de boeren moeten weer inleveren. We ontkomen niet aan een halvering van de veestapel. We moeten, liefst vandaag nog, de keuze maken tussen de natuur en grootschalige export, zegt de man.

Ik kan een smirkende glimlach met moeite onderdrukken. Want zeg eerlijk, hoe voorspelbaar is dit soort academische morele superioriteit inmiddels geworden? Dit soort onheilsprofeten zijn bijna een karikatuur van zichzelf geworden, sterker nog, ik denk dat cabaretier @RKahlmann hier zo een paar rake grappen over uit z’n mouw kan schudden. Ongetwijfeld tot grote hilariteit van het aanwezige publiek, zo van de werkelijkheid losgezongen is het inmiddels.

Maar ik dwaal af, sorry. Terug naar Flip Witte. Flip verdiende ooit bij KWR en de VU zijn sporen en kijkt naar de Nederlandse landbouw en ziet dan vooral een waterverslindende exportmachine die de natuur de nek omdraait, kennelijk heeft hij dan het datacenter in het weiland ernaast gemist, maar okay, dat zie ik nu even door de vingers, da’s onderwerp voor een andere discussie. Flip redeneert dat via zuivel en vlees we ons kostbare grondwater effectief de grens overpompen. De monotone raaigraslanden, de sproeiers, de intensieve veehouderij: allemaal schuldig aan de verdroging van Nederland. Wat mij opvalt is dat Flip daarmee een ingewikkeld hydrologisch vraagstuk terugbrengt tot één beleidsconclusie: minder vee. Alsof grondwaterstanden uitsluitend afhangen van landbouw en niet ook van neerslag, rivierafvoer, waterbeheer, drinkwaterwinning, bodemtype en decennia aan ruimtelijke inrichting.

Wat hier eigenlijk gebeurt is knap omdenken, academisch omdenken zou ik het zelfs willen noemen. Een expert die vanuit zijn model en zijn verheven morele positie de complexiteit van een land dat al eeuwen met water worstelt reduceert tot één schuldige: de boer die het voedsel produceert waar dit land groot mee is geworden. Wat mij vooral opvalt, is hoe moeiteloos een ingewikkeld waterprobleem hiermee wordt teruggebracht tot één morele conclusie. Droogte? Minder koeien. Dalende grondwaterstanden? Minder export. Alsof een land dat al eeuwenlang zijn waterpeil kunstmatig beheert ineens één oorzaak en één oplossing kent. Dat is geen hydrologie meer, dat is politieke simplificatie.

Laten we vooral niet vergeten dat Nederland de tweede landbouwexporteur ter wereld is, dat word je niet zomaar, dat komt per saldo doordat we efficiënt, innovatief en keihard werken op een lapje grond dat eigenlijk te klein is voor onze ambities. Die export voedt niet alleen miljoenen mensen in Nederland, maar ook elders. Die export levert niet alleen miljarden op, die export is een belangrijk onderdeel van onze bestaanszekerheid. Maar van Flip dat mag niet meer. Want de natuur, die volgens ‘experts’ op omvallen staat, die moet voorrang krijgen.

Merkt u hoe makkelijk dit gaat? Hoe complexer het probleem, hoe aantrekkelijker blijkbaar de zoektocht naar één schuldige? De grondwaterstand daalt? De natuur staat op omvallen? Dan is het de schuld van de intensieve landbouw. Nooit een serieus woord over de decennia van beleid dat juist die intensivering heeft gestimuleerd. Nooit een hard woord over de EU-regels, de stikstofwaanzin, de klimaatmodellen die steeds maar weer nieuwe offers eisen van precies dezelfde groep. Nooit de vraag of het soms verstandiger is om water vast te houden, slim te bergen en innovatie te belonen in plaats van weer een sector kapot te reguleren.

Nee, het is altijd dezelfde reflex: de productieve Nederlander moet inleveren. De boer eerst. Daarna de automobilist, de huiseigenaar, de industrie. Alles in naam van een maakbaarheidsgeloof dat ondertussen allang is vastgelopen in zijn eigen rekenmodellen. En het Nederlands Dagblad geeft deze boodschap gewoon een podium. Alsof het een openbaring is. Alsof we niet al jaren horen dat de boer het probleem is, terwijl diezelfde boer tegelijkertijd moet leveren, moet verduurzamen, moet inkrimpen en vooral moet ophouden met zeuren. Je zou potverdorie maar boer zijn in Nederland, dan zakt de moed je toch inmiddels wel in de schoenen?

Ik vraag mij daarom hardop af: wat zou Flip Witte eigenlijk antwoorden als we zijn logica omdraaien? Als we zouden zeggen dat de miljoenen kuubs die drinkwaterbedrijven oppompen voor de industrie, of de Nederlandse dorpen en steden, óók onderdeel van het probleem zijn? Wordt de stadsbewoner dan de boosdoener? Al die zwembadjes die worden volgegooid met kraanwater zodra de thermometer boven de 25-graden uitkomt? De datacenters die er tientallen Olympische zwembaden van datzelfde kraanwater doorheen jagen iedere dag? Nee. Natuurlijk niet. De morele pijlen blijven netjes gericht op degene die letterlijk met laarzen in de modder staat, en al van alle kanten klappen krijgt, da's low-hanging-fruit zoals dat zo mooi heet.

Maar laten we wel wezen, ondanks de lappendeken van Natura2000 gebieden van postzegelformaat is Nederland geen natuurreservaat. Nederland is een land dat moet eten, geld moet verdienen om de economie te laten draaien en dat zwaar leunt op de boeren om te kunnen blijven functioneren. Wie denkt dat we de veestapel kunnen halveren, de export kunnen stoppen en tegelijkertijd onze welvaart, onze voedselzekerheid en onze soevereiniteit kunnen behouden, leeft in een parallelle werkelijkheid. Een werkelijkheid van Excel-sheets, morele superioriteit en de permanente behoefte om de hardwerkende Nederlander als zondebok te gebruiken.

Maar laat ik Flip Witte niet gelijk bij de enkels afzagen, Flip mag blijven rekenen. Flip mag blijven waarschuwen. Maar laten we alsjeblieft stoppen met wat Flip hier doet: complexe problemen reduceren tot één schuldige en één politieke oplossing. Dat is geen hydrologie. Dat is ideologie. Het probleem is een politieke en culturele klasse die liever de productieve basis van dit land kapot reguleert dan onder ogen te zien dat hun eigen maakbaarheidsproject allang is mislukt.

En terwijl ik mijn inmiddels lege glas melk wegzet, vraag ik mij af hoeveel mensen straks nog beseffen dat achter dat glas geen Excel-sheet staat, maar een boer. Misschien moeten we dáár weer eens mee beginnen.

text:
Mitch McConnell has been missing from the Senate floor since mid-June 2026. 

Found unconscious at his home on June 14. First responders performed CPR. For weeks his office offered only the same recycled line: he’s “continuing to improve” and “working closely with staff.” No details. No timeline. No real accountability.

Only after the speculation got loud enough did the official story appear: a fall linked to post-polio complications, a brief loss of consciousness, mild pneumonia, and a move to inpatient rehab. A photo with his wife was released. A second update weeks later confirmed he still was not medically cleared to leave the facility or return to the Senate. As of early August he remains out. No firm return date. He has already missed dozens of votes and key committee work on defense appropriations while claiming he is still “engaged.”

This is not a private citizen’s medical privacy. This is a sitting U.S. Senator from Kentucky who holds one of the most powerful votes in the country. The public is expected to accept vague statements, carefully staged photos, and second-hand claims from allies that they “spoke with him for twenty minutes.” 

The pattern is familiar: delay, minimize, control the narrative, and hope the attention moves on.

The “Weekend at Bernie’s” jokes are crude, but they exist for a reason. When an office spends weeks refusing basic transparency about whether a senator is even capable of serving, people stop trusting the official line. Propping up the appearance of normalcy while the person is sidelined is exactly what that film mocked. 
The difference is that this involves actual legislative power, not a corpse at a party.

McConnell is not unique. 

He is simply the current, high-profile example of a larger habit among career politicians: treat the office like personal property, withhold information when it is inconvenient, and expect the public to accept managed statements instead of straight answers. The same class of people who demand trust while operating in opacity have spent decades perfecting the art of looking busy while the real decisions are made out of view. 

The result is a system that protects the officeholder first and the voters second.

Kentuckians elected a senator, not a figurehead. When the person holding that seat cannot appear, cannot vote, and will not give clear, timely information about capacity, the honest response is not more carefully worded press releases. It is resignation or a clear, public demonstration that the individual is still fit to exercise the power of the office. 

Anything less is just another version of the same old game: keep the title, keep the influence, keep the public in the dark.

The weekend at Bernie’s routine is over the top only if you still believe the people running it have any interest in treating voters like adults. The record says otherwise.

text:
Saint Sixtus II, Pope and Martyr, and Saints Felicissimus and Agapitus, Martyrs: From The Liturgical Year by Dom Prosper Louis Paschal Guéranger, O.S.B., 1904.
.
Red Commemoration.
.
“Xistum in cimiterio animadversum sciatis octaw iduum augustarum die. Know that Sixtus has been beheaded in the cemetery on the 8th of the Ides of August.” These words of St. Cyprian mark the opening of a glorious period both for the cycle and for history. From this day to the feast of St. Cyprian himself, taking in that of the deacon Laurence, how many holocausts in a few weeks does the earth offer to the Most High God! One would think that the Church, on the feast of our Lord’s Transfiguration, was impatient to join her testimony as Bride to that of the Prophets, of the Apostles, and of God himself. Heaven proclaims him well-beloved, the earth also declares its love for him: the testimony of blood and of every sort of heroism is the sublime echo wakened by the Father’s voice through all the valleys of our lowly earth, to be prolonged throughout all ages.
.
Let us, then, today salute this noble Pontiff, the first to go down into the arena opened wide by Valerian to all the soldiers of Christ. Among the brave leaders who, from Peter down to Melchiades, have headed the struggle whereby Rome was both vanquished and saved, none is more illustrious as a martyr. He was seized in the Catacomb lying to the left of the Appian Way, in the very chair wherein, in spite of the recent edicts, he was presiding over the assembly of the brethren; and after the sentence had been pronounced by the judge, he was brought back to the sacred crypt. There in that same chair, in the midst of the martyrs sleeping in the surrounding tombs their sleep of peace, the good and peaceful Pontiff received the stroke of death. Of the seven deacons of the Roman Church, six died with him; Laurence alone was left, inconsolable at having this time missed the palm, but trusting in the invitation given him to be at the heavenly altar in three days’ time.
.
Two of the Pontiff’s deacons were buried in the cemetery of Prætextatus, where the sublime scene had taken place. Sixtus and his blood-stained chair were carried to the other side of the Appian Way into the crypt of the Popes, where they remained for long centuries an object of veneration to pilgrims. When Damasus, in the days of peace, adorned the tombs of the saints with his beautiful inscriptions, the entire cemetery of Callixtus, which includes the burial place of the Popes, received the title “of Cæcelia and of Sixtus,” two glorious names inscribed by Rome upon the venerable diptychs of the Mass. Twice over on this day did the Holy Sacrifice summon the Christian to honor, at each side of the principal Way to the eternal City, the triumphant victims of the 8th of the Ides of August.
.
Xystus Secundus, Atheniensis, ex philosopho Christi discipulus, in persecutione Valeriani accusatus quod publice Christum prædicaret, comprehensus trahitur in templum Martis, proposita ei capitali pœna, nisi illi simulacro sacrificaret. Qua impietate constantissime recusata, cum ad martyrium duceretur, occurrenti sancto Laurentio, et dolenter in hunc modum interroganti: Quo progrederis sine filio pater? quo sacerdos sancte sine ministro properas? Respondit: Non ego te desero fili: majora te manent pro Christi fide certamina: post triduum me sequeris, sacerdotem levita: interea, si quid in thesauris habes, pauperibus distribue. Eodem igitur die interfectus est una cum Felicissimo et Agapito diaconis, Januario, Magno, Vincentio et Stephano subdiaconis, et in cœmeterio Callisti sepultus octavo idus Augusti: cæteri vero in cœmeterio Prætextati. Sedit menses undecim, dies duodecim. Quo tempore habuit ordinationem mense Decembri, creatis presbyteris quatuor, diaconis septem, episcopis duobus.
.
Sixtus II, an Athenian, was first a philosopher, and then a disciple of Christ. In the persecution of Valerian, he was accused of publicly preaching the faith of Christ; and was seized and dragged to the temple of Mars, where he was given his choice between death and offering sacrifice to the idols. As he firmly refused to commit such an impiety, he was led away to martyrdom. As he went, St. Laurence met him, and with great sorrow, spoke to him in this manner: “Whither goest thou, Father, without thy son? Whither art thou hastening, O holy Priest, without thy deacon?” Sixtus answered: “I am not forsaking thee, my son, a greater combat for the faith of Christ awaiteth thee. In three days thou shalt follow me, the Deacon shall follow his Priest. In the meanwhile distribute amongst the poor whatever thou hast in the treasury.” He was put to death that same day, the 8th of the Ides of August, together with the Deacons Filicissimus and Agapitus, and the Subdeacons Januarius, Magnus, Vincent, and Stephen. The Pope was buried in the cemetery of Callixtus, but the other martyrs in the cemetery of Prætextatus. He sat eleven months and twelve days; during whith time he held an ordination in the month of December, and made four priests, seven deacons, and two bishops.
.
The following Preface from the Leonian Sacramentary breathes the freshness of the Church’s triumph over persecution:
.
Preface
.
Vere dignum. Cognoscimus enim, Domine, tuæ pietatis effectus, quibus nos adeo gloriosi Sacerdotis et Martyris tui Xysti semper honoranda solemnia, nec inter præteritas mundi tribulationes, omittere voluisti, et nunc reddita præstas libertate venerari.
.
It is truly just to return thanks to Thee, O Lord. For we know the effects of Thy loving kindness, whereby Thou wouldst not suffer us to omit the ever honorable solemnity of Thy glorious Pontiff and Martyr, Sixtus, during the past tribulations of the world, and dost enable us to celebrate it now that liberty is restored.
.
The Prayer now in use is that found in the Gregorian Sacramentary for Saints Felicissimus and Agapitus, the name of Saint Sixtus having been placed before theirs:
.
Prayer
.
Deus, qui nos concedis sanctorum Martyrum tuorum Xysti, Felicissimi et Agapiti natalitia colere: da nobis in æterna beatitudine de eorum societate gaudere. Per Dominum.
.
O God, Who permittest us to keep the festivals of Thy holy Martyrs, Sixtus, Felicissimus and Agapitus, grant us to rejoice in their society in eternal happiness. Through our Lord, &c.

Codreanu was arguing against the specific liberalism – that being the Parliamentarianism – that was established in his period. In the rest the Legionaries admired the French Revolution especially Emil Cioran & Ion Moța. And Horia Sima included this into his 1980 work "Legionary Doctrine."

From Doctrina Legionară by Horia Sima (p. 43–44):

​"The principles of the French Revolution, considered by contemporaries and later by its commentators as a triumph of free reason, as an apotheosis of the direction inaugurated by the Renaissance, cannot be separated from Christian teaching. The French Revolution offers us an edifying example of the penetrating power of the Christian element in an organization concept of society, even when its authors do not share the Christian point of view, and, moreover, even when they declare themselves enemies of Christianity. The trinitarian formula: liberty, equality, fraternity, which adorns the frontispiece of the French Revolution, has deep affinities with Christian philosophy. If it had such a great power of bearing fruit, the credit must be attributed to the evangelical content within its structure; just as the harmful effects of the same principles are due to the rational element that participated in their shaping. Reason, not being competent to solve great historical problems, disrupted, through its interference, the perfection of the social order established by God."

(p. 44–45):
​"The French Revolution offers us an edifying example... The trinitarian formula: liberty, equality, fraternity, which adorns the frontispiece of the French Revolution, has deep affinities with Christian philosophy. [...] The formula can lead to exceptional results if it remains faithful to the social relationship individual-nation-God, just as it can cause the greatest disasters in the life of peoples if it is removed from this framework and left to function in a vacuum. Therefore, resounding criticisms have been brought against it, while praises have been raised to it at the same time.
'In what consists, or should consist, this work that came to bring a better future to the peoples? The true purpose of the French Revolution was the destruction of medieval feudalism and the introduction of a regime of liberty.'
'This liberty had to manifest itself within the framework of the idea of the National State (examine the spirit of the Marseillaise more than the books of the encyclopedists), meaning the free development of all members of a nation, according to national interests and excluding class privileges.'
'These were the luminous prospects of the great work which was partly realized (such as, for example, the liberation of nations from serfdom and then the founding of National States, as was the case with us), but in large part could not be fulfilled. Indeed, even the realized prospects soon saw themselves altered and completely distorted.'
It would be absurd, as Ion Moța points out, not to recognize the grandiose work of the French Revolution, all the more so since the Romanian people themselves benefited from its fruits. The drama of the revolution consists in the alteration of its initial objectives; it liberated the individual from the shackles of feudalism, but, at the same time, alienated him from the nation and from God. A phenomenon of alienation from its primordial goals occurred with the French Revolution, analogous to what also occurred in the field of the scientific revolution."

(p. 46):
​"The principle of liberty, the most celebrated of the ideological triad of the French Revolution, suffered the greatest degradations in contemporary history. [...] As a result, the principles of liberty, equality, and fraternity were dissociated from the archetype individual-nation-God and took an anti-national and anti-Christian direction of realization."

Thus Legionarism much like Fascism via Giovanni Gentile, aspires to be perfected/correctes form of Liberalism against Liberalism that we know at its current form.

text:
Our freedoms are not guaranteed. Every generation has a responsibility to defend them.

Today, we're seeing democratic socialists and advocates of expanded government power seeking higher office across our country—including here in Wisconsin, where a Democratic Socialist is running for governor. Whether it's Wisconsin, Michigan, New York, or elsewhere, the direction our states take will shape the future our children and grandchildren inherit.

I believe socialism is fundamentally incompatible with the principles that made America exceptional: individual liberty, limited government, free enterprise, private property, personal responsibility, and the constitutional rights guaranteed to every American.

History offers powerful lessons. Communist governments—and many countries that have embraced socialist systems—have concentrated power in the hands of the state, restricted individual freedoms, suppressed political opposition, weakened economic opportunity, and left ordinary people to bear the consequences. Too often, the results have included economic decline, poverty, shortages, and profound human suffering. Those lessons should never be forgotten.

This election is about far more than one office or one candidate. It is about preserving the principles that have made America a beacon of freedom and opportunity for generations. We cannot afford to sit on the sidelines while ideas that move us away from constitutional government and individual liberty gain ground in our communities and our state.

If you believe in the Constitution, free speech, free enterprise, personal responsibility, and the God-given rights of every American, I encourage you to make your voice heard. Vote. Encourage your family, friends, and neighbors to vote. Wisconsin's future—and the future of our republic—depends on citizens who are willing to stand up and defend the freedoms that generations before us fought to secure.

Freedom is never free, and it is never guaranteed. It must be protected by every generation.

Vote Tom Tiffany, Eric Toney, Tony Wied & Barb Bittner to Save WI.

text:
Mexican Army special forces, backed by two armed helicopters, moved into the municipality of Los Reyes, Michoacán, around 2:30 p.m. on Saturday, August 1, and took down Alfonso Fernández Magallón — a man U.S. investigators had spent years trying to reach. Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch confirmed the detention that same evening in a social media post, naming the detainee by his two street names, "Poncho" and "La Quiringua." According to La Jornada's account of the operation, the raid unfolded at multiple points across the town simultaneously.

The Man Behind the Aliases
U.S. Homeland Security Investigations had been building a case against Fernández Magallón for years, ultimately naming him head of the Los Reyes Cartel, a faction embedded inside the broader Cárteles Unidos coalition that controls swaths of western Michoacán. That coalition traces back to 2019, when smaller local factions banded together specifically to keep larger invaders — first the Knights Templar, later the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) — out of their territory.

Two Governments, Two Different Charge Sheets
The legal basis for Saturday's arrest actually comes from Mexican, not American, courts. García Harfuch said the detainee faced a domestic warrant covering unlawful deprivation of liberty and rioting — the closest Mexican equivalent to kidnapping charges — according to an English-language writeup of the operation. Washington's case is built on entirely separate ground: prosecutors accuse him of conspiring for years to manufacture and smuggle methamphetamine, cocaine, and fentanyl into the United States and of using firearms to further that trade. The Treasury Department layered sanctions on top of the criminal case, citing his recruitment of former Colombian soldiers and police to arm the fight against CJNG.

How a $5 Million Price Tag Got Attached to His Name
The bounty tracing back to Fernández Magallón wasn't issued in isolation. On August 14, 2025, the State Department rolled out reward offers covering five Cárteles Unidos figures at once, totaling $26 million: $10 million for Farías, $5 million each for Fernández Magallón and Nicolás Sierra Santana ("El Gordo"), and $3 million apiece for Barragán Chávez and Edgar Orozco Cabadas ("El Kamoni"). That package followed the group's formal designation, effective February 20, 2025, as a Foreign Terrorist Organization and Specially Designated Global Terrorist — part of a wave of similar designations then-Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued that month against cartels across the region.

Beyond drug trafficking, Mexican defense officials linked Fernández Magallón to a specific string of violence against soldiers: an explosive-drone attack on January 19, 2025, in Cotija, and two more on June 15 and July 1, 2026, in Tingüindín and Jacona, respectively. Authorities have not disclosed casualty figures from those strikes.

Michoacán Answers Back With Fire
Word of the capture didn't sit quietly. Within hours, suspected cartel members threw up roadblocks and torched vehicles at multiple points across Los Reyes and the neighboring municipality of Peribán — La Jornada counted at least five separate blockages along roads connecting the two towns and nearby Tocumbo and Uruapan. Civilian and military authorities moved in afterward to reopen the routes.

U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson weighed in that night, crediting the joint security push under Presidents Trump and Sheinbaum and writing that the arrest shows criminals "have nowhere to hide," according to Infobae's coverage of his statement, which notes he specifically thanked Mexico's defense secretariat and security cabinet for the operation.

Why Everyone's Fighting Over This Corner of Michoacán
Michoacán's avocado and lime exports, combined with its Pacific coastline, have turned the state into one of the country's most fought-over pieces of territory for well over a decade. Cárteles Unidos itself was born as a defensive alliance against bigger outside groups, and it remains locked in a grinding conflict with CJNG in and around Apatzingán. Exactly who's allied with whom in that fight keeps shifting: one October 2025 account describes Los Viagras and its armed wing, Los Blancos de Troya, as having drifted toward CJNG's side, while a November 2025 military assessment still lists Los Viagras — along with the smaller Acahuato cartel — as Cárteles Unidos allies. Either way, both camps have converged on the citrus- and avocado-growing municipalities around Apatzingán, extorting the same producers regardless of which banner they fly.

No timeline has been set for a possible extradition, and Mexican officials haven't said whether Fernández Magallón will face his domestic warrant before any transfer to U.S. custody is considered. El Universal has since reported that he was moved to Mexico City following his arrest.

The whole person—fearfully and wonderfully made as an embodied-soul—must remain the priority and target in biblical counseling theological anthropology and methodology as we seek to cultivate whole-person love for God.

Consider Paul’s personal ministry of the Word. In providing biblical counsel about progressive sanctification, Paul does not choose between renewing the mind and presenting the body; he joins them as inseparable dimensions of whole-person living to the glory of God. Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. text:
Criticism is not vilification.

If your religion is oppressive, dangerous, violent, regressive, incompatible, antagonistic, misogynistic, abusive and in other ways contrary to the ordinary way of life - then the fault if yours, as a human being, for choosing to follow it.

Saying something is 'a religion' does not give it immunity to rejection.

Or even condemnation.

That is why we dismissed blasphemy laws.

And why it is so dangerous that our government is restoring them without consent.

Put it this way:

If you set up a temple in the middle of the city and start making sacrifices out of citizens, then yes, your religion should be condemned and banned.

Your religion has become a concern to public health.

The Aztecs were a valid faith for an entire civilisation. The argument is not about how faithfully the views are held, how old the gods are, or the depth of its cultural history. It makes no difference. It has no place in our world. None. We would see no issue with saying so.

There is one religion today that has asserted itself as dangerous to Western Civilisation through its actions, through its teachers, and through the behaviour of its followers.

The things we have seen and heard are simply not acceptable.

They are barbaric.

It takes moral courage to stand up and say - sorry, your faith is below our entry-level standards.

The Christian spirit under which the West was built, and the secular layering that came after, has given far too much accommodation to ideas that cannot live peacefully beside it. 

It is arrogance to assume peace will always manifest and a serious error in judgement to offer almost untouchable protections to those faiths that do not deserve them.

text:
Podcast Summary | The Diary Of A CEO with Steven Bartlett: Man Who Owns 4% Of All Bitcoin: Sell Your Kidney But Keep The Bitcoin, UNLESS… | Michael Saylor

Overview

Michael Saylor presents a comprehensive argument for Bitcoin as the ultimate store of value in an era of inevitable currency debasement and accelerating technological change. He contrasts the 7% annual loss of purchasing power in the US dollar with Bitcoin's historical 33% annual appreciation, positioning it as "digital empowerment" that cannot be seized or inflated away. Saylor pairs his Bitcoin thesis with a disruptive view on AI, arguing that the path to wealth is not outworking machines but asking them for novel, unprecedented solutions. He frames the coming years as a period where abundance in utilitarian goods will coexist with persistent scarcity in status assets, ensuring that capital remains essential. His core advice for individuals and businesses is to avoid fields at the end of their growth curve, embrace long-term compounding, and use AI to create financial instruments and business models that have never existed before.

Key Themes

- Currency debasement is an unavoidable feature of fiat money; the dollar loses roughly 7% of its value annually, making cash a guaranteed losing investment against appreciating capital assets.

- Bitcoin is framed as a superior capital asset and a form of digital property, outperforming gold and the S&P 500, with a projected return of 30% annually for the next two decades.

- The primary use of AI is not to perform existing tasks faster, but to design novel solutions and financial instruments that were previously impossible, creating a massive arbitrage opportunity for early adopters.

- Success comes from focusing energy on a single exceptional strength rather than diluting effort across many mediocre ventures, with long-term compounding serving as the foundation for durable wealth.

- The conventional path to wealth through residential real estate is flawed due to taxes and maintenance, whereas commercial real estate and portable assets like Bitcoin offer better returns without requiring specialized expertise.

- The concept of an "age of abundance" is only half correct; while robots will make basic goods plentiful, scarce luxury items and status symbols will retain immense value, ensuring money still matters.

- Personalized AI algorithms are fragmenting audiences and lowering the ceiling on universal fame, but entities that provide exceptional quality or novel value can still achieve massive scale.

Detailed Summary

Saylor begins by establishing a grim picture of fiat currency, citing the dollar's 7% annual devaluation and the historical tendency of global currencies to collapse within roughly 29 years. He illustrates this with the example of a $10,000 purchase of waterfront Miami Beach land a century ago, now valued at $10-20 million, purely as a reflection of dollar depreciation. This leads to his central claim: wealth must be held in capital assets like gold, which appreciates 12% annually, or Bitcoin, which has appreciated 33% annually over the past six years, outperforming the S&P 500's 15% return. Bitcoin is distinguished from physical assets by its portability and sovereignty; a million dollars can be transferred globally in seconds as a private key or a physical encrypted coin, bypassing the seven intermediaries that a cash transfer might require, including banks and central banks.

He candidly explains why he sold a small portion of his company's Bitcoin holdings despite his famous advice to "sell a kidney but keep the Bitcoin." The sale was strategic, designed to disprove the narrative from short sellers that his company's vast Bitcoin stash was worthless because it could never be liquidated without crashing the market. When the company sold at around $59,000 per coin, the token price actually rose afterward, breaking the "doom loop" theory. He asserts that even if Bitcoin fell to $5,000, his company, which holds 847,000 Bitcoin (about 4% of the total supply), would remain over-collateralized against its debt. The break-even point for the company is a mere 3.2% annual Bitcoin appreciation, which allows it to pay dividends indefinitely by selling a tiny fraction of its holdings.

On the subject of investment strategy, Saylor argues against residential real estate as a store of value, pointing to property taxes and maintenance costs that can financially crush an owner. He concedes it beats holding cash but suggests commercial real estate is superior because tenant rents offset costs while the land itself appreciates. The broader appeal of Bitcoin, he argues, is that it offers the average person a way to invest in an appreciating asset without needing to become a real estate, tax, or business expert. He recommends diversifying for those who are unsure, but insists that long-term capital investors—money not needed for at least four to ten years—are the right candidates for Bitcoin. For a 25-year-old with limited funds, he prioritizes spending on AI subscriptions over investing, suggesting $20 to $200 a month is a smarter bet than a Netflix subscription.

Saylor's analysis of AI is optimistic but demanding. He claims AI generated $15 billion for his company last year by solving a unique problem: they had maxed out traditional equity and convertible bond markets with $30 billion in Bitcoin. Using ChatGPT to validate a novel idea, they designed STRK, a Bitcoin-backed convertible preferred stock with a variable dividend rate that adjusts monthly to maintain a stable price around $100. Lawyers and bankers claimed it was impossible, but the AI confirmed it was legal, leading to a $2.5 billion IPO and an $8 billion shelf registration. He urges entrepreneurs to use AI for the "no-brainer" arbitrage of creating products that are radically cheaper or better, such as delivering "the work of a million accountants for $10 a month." He notes that only 2% of households have an AI subscription, highlighting the untapped potential.

He offers guidance on education and career, advising against studying fields on the downward slope of the growth "S-curve," such as aviation post-1975, which saw only 15% efficiency gains over 50 years after a century of explosive progress. Instead, he points to semiconductors as a field still on the upslope, and encourages learning how to ask AI for things never done before rather than mastering tasks AI can already perform. He dismisses future-proof careers like surgeon, lawyer, accountant, or driver, suggesting that intelligence amplification through technology is the new moat. The next major interface shift, he predicts, will be smart glasses or neural implants, referencing a Meta device shown to him by Mark Zuckerberg that allows the wearer to interact with screens via a wrist strap and peripheral vision.

Saylor warns of a coming "slop tsunami" of AI-generated content that will flood the market against a fixed demand for attention, threatening creators who lack a unique moat. The defense, he argues, is to be exceptionally talented or to understand what humans truly want, citing a 3D animated walkthrough of a 16th-century warship as an example of high-quality content that captivates despite a lack of prior interest. He observes that personalized AI algorithms are lowering the ceiling on universal fame, making it harder for individuals to reach the scale of a Michael Jackson, who benefited from constrained distribution. However, entities like Elon Musk or OpenAI can still achieve massive scale because they offer something genuinely novel.

The conversation shifts to patience and focus as the keys to success. Saylor's company grew from $1 billion to $60 billion by being the first to combine Bitcoin with digital credit, a move that took advantage of a 12-24 month window. He emphasizes that failure is normal, citing a team that ran 60 experiments in a year, five of which met expectations and two of which were game-changing. He cautions against the common failure pattern of diluting focus across ten areas after succeeding in one, advising instead to make one thing twice as good rather than ten things 10% better. He points to long-term examples like Amazon Prime's decade of free shipping losses, which built a moat that eventually produced outsized returns, and Elon Musk's strategy of building businesses on each other, from rockets to Starlink.

Finally, Saylor returns to his personal mission of digital empowerment, framing Bitcoin as a tool that gives economic sovereignty to eight billion people. He views human history as a story of misery caused by lack of clean water, air, food, and sound money. He defends his company's Bitcoin sales as a demonstration of liquidity and a break from the short-seller narrative, and he reiterates that Bitcoin is suited only for long-term investors, not those needing funds in twelve weeks. For self-study, he recommends applied statistics from authors like Nassim Nicholas Taleb and comprehensive history from Will Durant's "The Story of Civilization," arguing that AI cannot provide real-time common sense and that most so-called new ideas are rediscoveries of historical patterns, such as currency debasement, which has occurred in every civilization. He concludes by praising the guest's championing of sovereignty as a winning idea in an era of increasing centralization and censorship.

text:
A 23-year-old guy from Ohio built an AI girl to walk city streets, and earned $6,412 in 17 days.

He built her in Midjourney. Trained a LoRA on 200 faces until one held still, one felt right. Named her Mila. Gave her a walk, a jawline, a wardrobe that doesn’t exist in any closet.

Then he dropped her into cities.
New York. Miami. LA.

Same formula every clip. Wide shot, outfit, four seconds a block, camera trailing like a stranger who can’t stop looking.

Except the comments stopped asking if it was AI.

They started asking where she got the jacket.

TikTok Shop links went under every video. Viewers bought. A boutique in SoHo slid into the DMs, asked for a paid walk-through in their fall line.
He said yes.

Sent an invoice under her name.
Nobody checked.

Then a bigger brand wanted a fitting. Asked for measurements. He typed a number that felt right and sent it back.
The package still arrived. At his apartment. Size medium, tags on, folded in tissue paper for a body that has never worn anything.

He photographed it against a screen with her face on it.

Posted the same night.

$6,412 in 17 days. Affiliate cuts, one paid collab, a licensing offer he hasn’t answered yet.

The boutique still emails her. Asks how the jacket held up in the wind.
He hasn’t told them there was no wind.

🔔 TURN ON NOTIFICATIONS

PROJECT 8 & PROJECT 18 — POST-PRIMARY REPORT
WHAT TUESDAY’S RESULTS MEAN FOR NOVEMBER

Tuesday’s primaries did more than select nominees. They exposed the political fault lines that will shape the battle for Congress this fall.

1. MICHIGAN WILL BE ONE OF THE CENTERPIECES OF THE MIDTERMS

Michigan remains critical to both Project 8 and Project 18.

The open U.S. Senate seat will be one of the most competitive races in the country, with Republican Mike Rogers advancing to the general election. The Democratic contest between Abdul El-Sayed and Haley Stevens was still extremely close Wednesday morning, with major outlets waiting for additional results before making a final projection. (AP News⁠)

That race revealed a deep divide between the Democratic establishment and the party’s progressive wing. Regardless of the final nominee, Republicans now know exactly where the battle lines are drawn.

2. THE HOUSE MAJORITY WILL BE DECIDED DISTRICT BY DISTRICT

Michigan’s competitive congressional races are officially moving into the general-election phase.

In MI-7, Democratic nominee William Lawrence will challenge Republican Rep. Tom Barrett.

In MI-10, Christina Hines won the Democratic nomination and will face Republican nominee Michael Bouchard in another closely watched race. (AP News⁠)

These are the kinds of districts that could determine which party controls the House in January.

3. TRUMP’S ENDORSEMENT REMAINS POWERFUL IN REPUBLICAN PRIMARIES

Trump-supported candidates performed strongly in several of Tuesday’s contests, showing that his endorsement continues to carry significant weight with Republican primary voters.

But winning a primary is only the first step. The focus must now shift toward unifying voters, defining the general-election contrast and building turnout operations in competitive states.

4. DEMOCRATIC VOTERS SENT A MIXED MESSAGE

The progressive movement produced victories in some contests, but it also suffered major defeats.

In Missouri’s 1st Congressional District, Rep. Wesley Bell defeated former Rep. Cori Bush in their rematch, dealing another setback to the progressive wing. Meanwhile, progressive candidates advanced in several Michigan contests. (AP News⁠)

The result was not a complete victory for either the establishment or the socialist-progressive movement. The ideological battle inside the Democratic Party is continuing.

5. TURNOUT WILL DECIDE NOVEMBER

Primary enthusiasm is important, but primary voters represent only part of the November electorate.

Candidates must now persuade independents, unite their parties and turn occasional voters into general-election voters.

The lesson from Tuesday is simple:

Competitive races can be won—but only when voters show up.

text:
Roster turnover is the new normal in the college basketball, and the Richmond Spiders felt it as much as anyone this offseason with ten total players leaving the roster.

However, one rising star decided to run it back for year two with the Spiders.

Aiden Argabright (@AidenArgabright) is back in Richmond for his sophomore season after a stellar freshman campaign. Coming out of high school, he held offers from Mississippi State, Murray State, and several other mid-majors before committing to Chris Mooney and the Spiders.

He hit the ground running. Over his first five games, Argabright averaged 13.2 points and 2.2 steals. He never slowed down, and more importantly, he got better as the season went on. By the end of the year, the 5'11 guard was averaging less than one turnover per game against two assists.

Argabright finished the season averaging 10.8 points, two rebounds, two assists, and 1.2 steals per game while shooting 42.1% overall and 35% from beyond the arc.

He posted a 122.5 offensive rating which was 236th overall, a 60% true shooting percentage, a 15.9 assist rate, and an 8.9 turnover rate that ranked 98th in the country. He drew 6.5 fouls per game and turned that into an 88.4 free throw rate, converting 82.7% from the line on 168 attempts against Division I opponents.

Chris Mooney is entering year 22 at Richmond, and he rebuilt this roster around defense and interior scoring, two areas the Spiders badly needed to address. Argabright is the piece that didn't need addressing.

He's only going to get better as time goes on.

Primary Archetype: Floor General / Pass-First Creator

Sydney Youngblood enters the 2029 evaluation cycle as an advanced lead guard with early national visibility, Nike EYBL experience, and a growing Division I market. Her value is not built on scoring volume alone. The stronger signal is her ability to organize possessions, control pace, and create functional offense without forcing the game.

Youngblood projects as a primary on-ball creator who balances distribution with selective scoring. She plays with poise, changes speeds effectively, and uses the middle of the floor with purpose. Her mid-range pull-up and floater package give her solutions when defenses contain the rim or play conservative ball-screen coverage. She can generate her own offense, but her natural identity remains team-oriented.

The processing profile is the foundation of the projection. Youngblood appears comfortable reading help defenders, advancing the ball early, and keeping teammates involved. She does not need extended isolation sequences to influence the game. Her value comes from creating advantages, extending them, and making the next correct read.

Defensively, the statistical sample remains incomplete, but the competitive infrastructure is significant. Boo Williams and the Nike EYBL environment consistently expose guards to speed, physicality, and pressure. Youngblood’s stated objective of becoming a complete two-way guard aligns with the next stage of her development. Continued growth in point-of-attack defense, screen navigation, and physical strength will shape her eventual collegiate role.

At 5’9”, she possesses functional positional size for either guard spot. The next evaluation phase should focus on three-point consistency, turnover control under increased usage, and how her decision-making holds against older EYBL competition.

The offer sheet reflects meaningful market trust. Mississippi State and Pittsburgh establish high-major recognition, while Old Dominion, Howard, UMBC, William & Mary, Queens, and Hampton demonstrate broad regional and system-level interest.

The Beechum Verdict: Youngblood projects as an early-cycle high-major trajectory guard whose strongest assets are pace, processing, leadership, and connective play. Her ceiling will depend on continued physical development and shooting growth, but the current foundation supports a multi-year collegiate lead-guard projection.

Sitting comfortably at the base of the neck, the round neck creates a clean, closed line when the cardigan is buttoned and an easy open shape when worn unbuttoned. This neckline frames the face gently and pairs well with both simple and statement jewelry. Unlike higher or more structured collars, the round neck keeps the overall impression relaxed and approachable, aligning perfectly with the casual button-down cardigan identity. It also layers smoothly under jackets, coats, or additional knitwear when extra warmth is needed, making the vest-style cardigan a flexible component in multi-layer outfits.

The vest construction supplies structure and modern proportion. Typically sleeveless or featuring minimal sleeve coverage, the vest format keeps the arms free and the overall silhouette light, making it ideal for layering without bulk. The vest shape sits close to the torso, creating a clean line through the body that can be worn alone as a top in warmer conditions or as an open layer over tees, tanks, shirts, or dresses. This dual functionality—wearable as a standalone vest or as a cardigan-style layer—is one of the design’s greatest practical strengths. The vest structure also provides a stable canvas for the striped pattern and the button-down front, ensuring the garment maintains its shape and appearance throughout the day.

Casual identity is expressed through the overall ease of the design. The combination of stripes, a round neck, vest proportions, and a button-down front produces a piece that feels relaxed yet intentional. It avoids overly formal tailoring while still offering enough structure to look polished. This casual character makes the garment suitable for a broad range of everyday situations—running errands, meeting friends, light office environments with flexible dress codes, weekend travel, and relaxed social plans. The button-down feature further supports the casual aesthetic by allowing the wearer to adjust the level of openness and coverage according to preference or temperature.

The button-down front is a key functional and stylistic element. A row of buttons running the length of the front transforms the vest into a true cardigan, enabling it to be worn fully closed, partially buttoned, or completely open. This versatility is central to the piece’s appeal. When buttoned, the garment creates a neat, polished vest-like appearance with a continuous striped surface. When left open, it functions as a light layer that frames whatever is worn underneath, adding depth and interest to simple outfits. The buttons themselves are typically chosen for both durability and visual harmony with the striped fabric, contributing to the overall refined yet casual finish. Easy fastening and unfastening support quick adjustments throughout the day, enhancing the practical comfort of the design.

As a casual button-down cardigan, the piece excels at layering. It can be thrown over a basic tee or tank for instant polish, worn over a dress to add structure and coverage, or layered under a heavier jacket or coat when temperatures drop. The sleeveless or short-sleeve vest construction prevents the bulk that can accumulate with full-sleeve cardigans, making it especially useful for transitional seasons and indoor-outdoor temperature changes. The striped pattern adds visual interest to otherwise simple base layers, while the round neck ensures a smooth transition between garments.

Versatility remains one of the strongest attributes of this new women’s striped round-neck vest and casual button-down cardigan. A single piece can serve multiple roles: as a standalone top on warmer days, as an open layer for casual outings, as a polished addition to smart-casual workwear, or as a travel-friendly layering option that packs easily and coordinates with many other items. The solid structure of the stripes and the clean round neck keep the design adaptable, while the button-down front provides on-the-spot adjustability. This multi-functionality reduces the need for numerous separate layers and supports a more streamlined wardrobe approach.

Comfort is built into the construction. Fabrics chosen for this style of vest-cardigan typically offer a soft hand-feel, light-to-medium weight, and enough structure to hold the striped pattern and button-down shape. The sleeveless or minimal-sleeve cut maximizes airflow and freedom of movement. The round neck sits comfortably without restriction. The button-down front allows the wearer to control coverage and ventilation. Together these elements support all-day wearability across a variety of activities and environments.

Styling possibilities are extensive and straightforward. For a casual everyday look, wear the vest-cardigan buttoned over a simple tee with jeans or trousers and sneakers. For a slightly more polished appearance, leave it open over a collared shirt or blouse and add loafers or low heels. In warmer weather the piece can function as a lightweight top paired with shorts or a skirt. During cooler moments it layers cleanly under a denim jacket, blazer, or coat. The striped pattern coordinates easily with solid bottoms in complementary or contrasting colors, and the round neck provides a clean frame for necklaces or scarves when desired. Accessories can remain minimal to let the stripes take center stage or can be more expressive depending on the overall mood.

The striped design continues to offer both aesthetic and practical benefits. Visually, stripes create rhythm and structure that elevate a simple vest-cardigan silhouette. They have a classic association with casual elegance and work across age groups and personal styles. Practically, the pattern helps camouflage minor wrinkles or wear and maintains a fresh appearance with regular use. Different stripe scales and color combinations produce varied effects—fine stripes feel refined, wider stripes feel bold and graphic—yet all remain versatile within a casual wardrobe.

The round-neck construction supports easy layering and a soft aesthetic. It avoids the formality of collars or the exposure of deeper necklines, striking a comfortable middle ground that suits a wide range of body types and preferences. When the cardigan is buttoned, the round neck creates a neat closed shape; when open, it softens the upper edge of the garment and frames the layers beneath.

Vest proportions keep the piece light and modern. By minimizing sleeve coverage the design reduces bulk and heat retention, making it ideal for spring, summer evenings, early autumn, and indoor environments with variable temperatures. The vest shape also creates a clean vertical line through the torso that many find flattering and that pairs well with both high- and low-waisted bottoms.

Casual button-down functionality is the practical heart of the garment. The ability to button or unbutton according to need transforms the piece from a structured vest into a relaxed open layer in seconds. This adjustability supports changing conditions throughout the day and allows the wearer to modify the level of formality or coverage without changing clothes. The button-down front also makes the cardigan easy to put on and take off, enhancing everyday convenience.

As a new addition to women’s casual wardrobes, the striped round-neck vest and button-down cardigan reflects current preferences for flexible, multi-use pieces that deliver both style and function. It offers the visual interest of stripes, the comfort of a round neck, the light structure of a vest, and the practicality of a button-down cardigan in one cohesive design. This combination supports a wide range of real-life scenarios while maintaining a polished yet relaxed appearance.

Occasion suitability is broad within the casual and smart-casual spectrum. Everyday activities, running errands, casual meet-ups, and weekend plans are easily addressed. Light professional or creative work environments can accommodate the piece when styled with tailored bottoms and appropriate footwear. Travel benefits from its packability, versatility, and ability to serve as both a top and a layer. Relaxed social gatherings and informal evenings are equally well served by the clean stripes and adjustable front.

Layering strategies further expand the usefulness of the design. Over a tank or tee it adds instant structure and pattern. Over a dress it provides coverage and a sporty-chic contrast. Under a blazer or coat it contributes a soft striped layer that peeks out at the neckline and front for added interest. The round neck and vest proportions ensure these combinations remain smooth and intentional rather than bulky.

The overall silhouette created by the striped fabric, round neck, vest shape, and button-down front is balanced and wearable. The stripes supply visual energy. The round neck keeps the upper edge soft. The vest cut maintains a light, modern proportion. The button-down front adds functionality and styling flexibility. Together these elements produce a garment that feels complete and considered while remaining easy to wear and style.

Practical advantages continue to reinforce the appeal. The design is typically easy to care for and maintains its shape and appearance with regular wear. The button-down construction allows for adjustable fit and ventilation. The striped pattern remains versatile across multiple pairings. The vest format supports comfortable movement and temperature regulation. These qualities make the piece a realistic candidate for frequent use rather than occasional wear.

In summary, this New Women’s Striped Round-Neck Vest, Casual Button-Down Cardigan offers a fresh, versatile, and highly practical layering option for contemporary wardrobes. Its new seasonal relevance keeps it feeling current. The striped pattern delivers classic visual interest. The round neck provides soft, flattering comfort. The vest construction ensures a light and modern silhouette. The casual button-down front supplies adjustable functionality and styling range. Together these attributes create a garment that supports everyday wear, casual outings, light professional settings, travel, and relaxed social occasions with equal success. It is a piece designed to be reached for repeatedly because it consistently delivers ease, polish, and adaptable style in a single, well-considered design.

text:
$CTM Q2 2026 earnings: Growth Narrative Masks a Q2 Stall and Profitability Squeeze

Management highlighted a 10% H1 revenue increase, but zeroed in on Q2 alone, the growth story is reversing. Q2 2026 revenue came in at $13.86M, down slightly YoY (-1%) and sequentially vs Q1 ($14.29M). More alarmingly, the bottom line collapsed: Gross margin compressed to 34.0%, and Adjusted EBITDA practically vanished to $26K (down 95% from $500K a year ago). The culprit? A higher mix of low-margin subcontractor work, costs to complete firm-fixed-price contracts, and heavy front-loaded investments in business development and M&A. While a debt-free balance sheet and a $271.7M backlog offer long-term stability, Castellum is currently sacrificing near-term profitability to chase its Phase 3 expansion strategy.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞
• 𝐂𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐧 𝐁𝐚𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐒𝐡𝐞𝐞𝐭 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 — The company fully eliminated its debt in Q1 and funded operations entirely from operating cash flow in H1, growing its cash reserve to $16.9M. This provides a fortress balance sheet to support M&A without dilution.
• 𝐑𝐨𝐛𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐥𝐨𝐠 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐏𝐢𝐩𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 — Total backlog remains healthy at $271.7M, and the qualified pipeline expanded sequentially to $953.5M. Recent wins like the $4.0M Navy ADMACS and a position on the $250M LIIS CMDS MAC validate the company's competitive positioning.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞
• 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐃𝐞𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐒𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐞𝐳𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐁𝐨𝐭𝐭𝐨𝐦 𝐋𝐢𝐧𝐞 — Gross margins are compressing (34% vs 36% YoY) due to an unfavorable mix of lower-margin subcontractor work and cost overruns on remaining firm-fixed-price contracts. Adjusted EBITDA essentially wiped out.
• 𝐓𝐨𝐩-𝐋𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐢𝐬 𝐃𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 — Despite management touting H1 growth, Q2 standalone revenue actually declined YoY by 1% to $13.86M. The ramp-up of new prime contracts was completely offset by the wind-down of legacy work.

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴
Bearish. The PR headlines focus on H1 growth, but Q2 standalone shows flatlining revenue and collapsing margins. Firm-fixed-price contracts and subcontractor mix issues are destroying operating leverage.

𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

🔴 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐇𝐢𝐭 𝐛𝐲 𝐅𝐢𝐫𝐦-𝐅𝐢𝐱𝐞𝐝-𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐬 [NEW]
Gross margin decelerated to 34.0% in Q2 from 36.0% a year ago and 35.4% in Q1. The company explicitly cited the 'cost to complete the remaining work on two firm-fixed-price contracts' alongside a higher mix of subcontractor work. In federal contracting, fixed-price contracts shift inflation and execution risk to the contractor, directly penalizing profitability when costs overrun.

🔴 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐋𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐬 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐒𝐮𝐫𝐠𝐞 [NEW]
Adjusted EBITDA plunged to just $26K (from $500K YoY). This collapse is driven by 'front-loaded' investments in business development, investor relations, and M&A activities. General & Administrative (G&A) expenses climbed to $2.87M, up from $2.73M last year. While management insists these investments will drive multi-year growth, current shareholders are bearing the brunt of the immediate margin destruction.

🔴 𝐐𝟐 𝐓𝐨𝐩-𝐋𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐌𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐮𝐦 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐬
Revenue growth is reversing. Q1 posted a 23% YoY gain, but Q2 came in at $13.86M, representing a 1% YoY decline. Management attributed this to the 'expected wind down of certain contracts' offsetting the ramp-up of the SSI NAWCAD Lakehurst contract. This directly contradicts the overarching 'growth' narrative and places immense pressure on H2 execution to achieve full-year records.

🟢 𝐏𝐌𝐀-𝟐𝟗𝟎 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐍𝐀𝐖𝐂𝐀𝐃 𝐋𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐡𝐮𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐃𝐫𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐁𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐤
The primary drivers for H1's overall 10% revenue growth are the long-term prime contracts won in 2025, specifically the NAVAIR PMA-290 Special Missions program and the NAWCAD Lakehurst MO&I award. The company is leaning heavily on these anchors to generate the base operating cash flow needed to fund its aggressive BD expansion.

🟢🟢 𝐂𝐌𝐌𝐂 𝐋𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐥 𝟐 𝐂𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬 𝐃𝐨𝐨𝐫𝐬 [NEW]
Castellum successfully achieved Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) Level 2. In the DoD contracting macro environment, this is a critical barrier to entry. This validation allows Castellum to aggressively bid on restricted defense programs and serve as a prime contractor on sensitive data networks, directly supporting its $953.5M pipeline.

🟢 𝐅𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐁𝐚𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐒𝐡𝐞𝐞𝐭 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐲 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐌&𝐀
The company's financial footing has stabilized significantly. After eliminating related-party notes in Q1, Castellum ended Q2 entirely debt-free with $16.9M in cash (up from $14.9M at the end of FY25). This liquidity profile allows management to selectively pursue M&A 'through the cycle rather than react to it,' targeting specific contract vehicles and customer access.

𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐞𝐝 𝐏𝐢𝐩𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞: $953.5 million
Accelerating. Up from $938.0M in Q1 2026 and $817M at the end of Q1 2025. This metric reflects the aggressive business development investments the company is currently making at the expense of near-term EBITDA.

𝐎𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐅𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐃𝐲𝐧𝐚𝐦𝐢𝐜𝐬: Debt-free with $16.9M Cash
Stable. The company funded H1 entirely from operations, adding $2.0M to the cash balance since year-end 2025. This signals that despite the GAAP net loss of $(1.38)M for H1, working capital management and non-cash add-backs (like the $1.56M in stock-based compensation) are keeping cash flow positive.

𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: Record Year Expected
Accelerating implicitly. Management reiterated expectations for full-year 2026 to be a record. FY25 total revenue was $52.87M. With H1 2026 at $28.16M, Castellum needs approximately $24.7M in H2 to break the record, requiring roughly $12.35M per quarter—a low bar given the $13.86M Q2 run rate.

𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐥𝐨𝐠 𝐑𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐠𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: 16% Next 12 Months
Stable. The company expects to recognize ~16% of its $271.7M backlog (roughly $43.5M) over the next 12 months, and ~48% over the next 24 months. This implies a steady revenue baseline of ~$10.8M per quarter locked in, meaning BD efforts must convert to fill the gap to the current ~$14M quarterly run rate.

𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐅𝐢𝐫𝐦-𝐅𝐢𝐱𝐞𝐝-𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐞
You noted margin drag from completing two firm-fixed-price contracts. What is the remaining duration and financial liability on these specific contracts, and when will they cleanly roll off the P&L?

𝐒𝐮𝐛𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐫 𝐌𝐢𝐱
The higher mix of lower-margin subcontractor work impacted gross profits this quarter. Is this mix structural to the new NAWCAD Lakehurst and PMA-290 awards, or is it temporary while you hire direct labor?

𝐑𝐞𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐧 𝐨𝐧 𝐁𝐃 𝐈𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬
You are trading near-term EBITDA for front-loaded BD and M&A investments. What are the specific internal KPIs or timeline markers you are using to measure the ROI on these elevated G&A expenses?

text:
The Pawnbroker (1965): the Legion Tottering on the Edge of Its Grave
By the mid-1960s one moral issue after another had been challenged by Hollywood; but the bishops of the U.S. Roman Catholic institution decided to draw a line in the sand when it came to nudity. They ordered Little and Sullivan of the NCOMP (the old Legion) to condemn all movies containing nudity. Hypocritically, the bishops in a statement declared that “nudity is not immoral and has long been recognized as a legitimate subject in painting and sculpture”, but that it was unacceptable in movies!452 Either something is immoral or it is not. Nudity is certainly immoral, biblically, whether in art or in movies. But the Romish bishops have always had their own set of moral standards, which are not those of the Bible, the Word of God.
Usually, if the Legion objected, nude scenes were still removed by the moviemakers. But this changed in 1965, when Sidney Lumet’s The Pawnbroker was released in the USA, and scenes of nudity were deliberately left in the film. The movie was denied a seal by the PCA’s Geoffrey Shurlock, but the producer, Ely LANDAU, appealed to the MPAA board, which eventually gave the seal to the film after LANDAU slightly cut the length of the scenes involving nudity. The film was released, and when the Legion reviewed it a few weeks afterwards its reviewers were divided, some approving of it and others condemning it. Little did not believe the film was obscene, but said it had to be condemned because of the nudity – obeying the instructions from his superiors. Yet this was possibly the mildest condemnation of a film by the Legion in its history, according to Variety magazine.453 The Legion knew that its authority and influence were almost over.
When the film opened, shockingly, a number of “Protestant” reviewers praised it and had no problem with the nudity!454 Roman Catholics were divided over it, and over the Legion’s attitude to it. “There is no place for the ‘Legion’ type of censorship,” stated the editorial of Film Heritage, a Roman Catholic-edited film journal. It called for the Legion to abolish the Condemned rating as it was a
263
“brutalizing form of pressure.”455 Certainly pro-Legion reviewer William Mooring was correct when he wrote that the Code had been reduced to “a mere scrap of paper.”456
The truth of the matter was that the Legion’s condemnation of The Pawnbroker was a further nail in its own coffin. American Roman Catholic audiences, having imbibed the American spirit of “freedom of expression”, no longer wanted the Legion to censor what they could see, and they turned out in large numbers to see the film. Besides, Rome itself was now clearly more broad-minded when it came to scenes previously condemned as “immoral” in movies. This sent conflicting messages to the Papist population. And then too, because the film was about a Jewish Holocaust survivor, and because it was known that the “Church” of Rome had not stood up to Nazi aggression against the Jews and had even, in fact, colluded with Hitler, Rome’s condemnation of the film was seen by many to be yet further evidence of its anti-Semitism. It was plain to see that the Legion was tottering on the edge of its own grave.
Vatican II and Movies
The Second Vatican Council was held from 1962 to 1965, one of its purposes being to “modernise” certain aspects of Roman Catholicism to make it more appealing to the modern age. But in doing so, it actually lost much of its former glory and mystique in the eyes of millions of Romanists. Latin was rejected in favour of the vernacular, priests and nuns became more “user-friendly”, with nuns in particular often casting off their austere dress code and appearing in public as “regular girls”, Papist rituals were downplayed to make Romanism more appealing to Protestants in the ecumenical age, etc. But as a natural consequence, as Romanism in the world lost much of what had made it distinct from other “churches”, it also lost much of its distinctiveness in the movies. Not only that, but now that censorship was virtually dead, moviemakers were free to make movies that attacked Roman Catholic beliefs if they liked. And many of them liked – very much so.
As for priest Little himself, he changed with the changes occurring as a result of Vatican II. As has happened to countless other men through the ages, he told Jack Vizzard that in his younger years things
264
appeared as “stark blacks and whites”, but with age “issues seemed less simple and more complex, and assumed various shades of gray.” After the change of the Legion’s name, he said the Legion had developed a reputation for being a “stubborn, antiquarian, unrealistic defender of Catholic movie goers”, and that this was not how it should function in the aftermath of Vatican II.457 In truth, Roman Catholics had changed, and the Papal institution itself now wanted to “move with the times”. Rome speaks haughtily of “defending eternal morals”, but is ever ready to embrace the shifting sands of the times and adjust its “morality” accordingly. The true moral law of God is eternal, and does not change; and true Christians do not suit their morality to the times they are living in. But Rome will do anything to keep its members.
Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? (1965): Priestly Morals in the Gutter with Everyone Else’s
When it was announced that a film version of the Broadway play, Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? would be made, the Legion once again came out with guns blazing, because it was laced with some of the most filthy language and overt sexual dialogue to which audiences had ever been subjected. When Geoffrey Shurlock read the script in October 1965, he told Warner Brothers that a PCA seal would only be given once all profanity and sexual dialogue had been cut. The reason Warner Brothers wanted a seal and Legion approval as well, even though they knew films were now doing very well commercially without them, was that this particular film had been a big-budget one for the studio, and if Warner wanted to make a profit it was felt that the approval of the PCA and the Legion were still needed. The studio stated that it would make the film an “adults only” one, and that it would submit it to the NCOMP (the Legion) ahead of the MPAA appeal.
The film was shot, however, with the language pretty much intact, and the PCA, after reviewing it in May 1966, did not give it the seal. Shurlock, however, told Warner to appeal his decision to the MPAA board, which was done.
As yet another indication of how much the Legion had changed from the old days, although there was no consensus on the part of the consultors who reviewed it, a sizeable majority voted against condemning the film.
265
Those who favoured it, including some (celibate?) priests, described it as valid adult entertainment, despite its foul language and sexual dialogue! It was clear that the morals of many priests and Papists were no different from those of society around them. Warner gave the assurance that no one under 18 unless accompanied by a parent would be allowed to buy a ticket, and the film was classified “A4” by the Legion (adults only). In June 1966 the MPAA board met to rule on the film, and a seal was granted.
“However, when Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton hit the screen screaming and tearing at each other with a hateful vengeance [in Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?] it was obvious that the movies had been changed forever. No longer were they going to be reigned [sic] in by codes.”458 Quigley’s son, Martin Quigley, Jr., declared in the Motion Picture Herald that the Code was now dead.459 The supreme irony, however, was this: “[Roman Catholic] Church pressure had created the PCA in 1934, and, thirty-two years later, the [Roman Catholic] church played a major role in hastening its demise”, when the Legion granted an “A4” rating to this movie.
“The decision to award Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? an A-IV rating touched off the biggest outpouring of protest letters in the history of the Legion and NCOMP.”460 This just showed that despite the liberalisation within much of the hierarchy of the Roman Catholic institution, there was still a huge bedrock of conservative Roman Catholics who were utterly opposed to the new direction being taken. The NCOMP was referred to as the “NCOMPetents” by one group of angry Romanists. Martin Quigley, Jr. wrote to Spellman, the cardinal, asking him why it was that such things as blasphemy, profanity, and obscenity were now acceptable to the “Church” when displayed in movies. Sullivan the Jesuit was kept busy replying to over a thousand letters about the film. In writing to a bishop, he said that despite the fact the film was controversial it attempted to make “a moral statement about our times consistent with a Christian viewpoint on life.” What an astounding statement! This aptly encapsulated the liberal Romanist notion of “morality”, so far removed from the Word of God. That such a film could be justified, even partially, as being “consistent with a Christian viewpoint of life” speaks volumes about the vile, false “Christianity” of Roman Catholicism. It also shows how the Jesuits
266
had changed course, changed tactics, and swung the “Church” to the left when it came to films.
But then Sullivan went even further, showing how deeply he had himself imbibed liberal Romanism and jettisoned the conservative Romanism of the pre-Vatican II days: he wrote that Pius XII’s encyclical, Miranda Prorsus, had opened the way for a more “tolerant”, open-minded view of movies, and stated that “we cannot intrude upon what is alone their [adult Roman Catholics’] right and obligation, namely, the exercise of individual responsibility in conscience.”461 This may have reflected the general American (and even western) attitude to “freedom of expression” and “freedom of conscience”, but it must be remembered, firstly, that it is not the truly Christian one, for true Christians do not seek to be entertained by filth (thus showing, yet again, the unchristian nature of Romanism); and secondly, it shows the base hypocrisy of Rome, which has always been against liberty of conscience and freedom of expression, and yet – when it suits its purposes – it speaks in favour of the very things it opposes! Vatican II and its aftermath often produced statements like this from the lips of Roman Catholics, so as to attract more people to the “Church” and to hold on to those who had imbibed such notions from the America they lived in.
Darling (1965): the Legion Sinks Still Further
The astounding about-face of the Legion (the NCOMP) was seen again when the 1965 British film, Darling, was shown in America. Although it was about a woman who leaves her husband, has various affairs, participates in an orgy, appears nude, has an abortion, etc., the NCOMP, after getting a few seconds of nudity cut from the film, awarded it Best Picture of 1965, a film of “artistic vision and expression”! The old Legion was clearly nothing like it had once been. And Romish publications reviewed it very positively as well.462 There were protests from many Romanists, however, showing again that the “Church” hierarchy was moving faster than many in the pews.

Audrey Kathleen Hepburn (née Ruston; 4 May 1929 – 20 January 1993) was a British[a] actress and humanitarian. Recognised as a film and fashion icon, she was ranked by the American Film Institute as the third-greatest female screen legend from the Classical Hollywood cinema. She was inducted into the International Best Dressed Hall of Fame and is one of only a few entertainers who have won competitive Academy, Emmy, Grammy and Tony Awards.

Born into an aristocratic family in Ixelles, Brussels, Hepburn spent parts of her childhood in Belgium, the United Kingdom and the Netherlands. She attended boarding school in Kent from 1936 to 1939. Hepburn returned to the Netherlands at the outbreak of the Second World War.[3] She studied ballet at the Arnhem Conservatory during the war. By 1944, Hepburn was performing ballet to raise money to support the resistance.[4] She studied with Sonia Gaskell in Amsterdam from 1945 to 1948 and then with Marie Rambert in London.

Hepburn began performing as a chorus girl in West End musicals and later made minor appearances in several films. She rose to stardom in the romantic comedy Roman Holiday (1953) alongside Gregory Peck, for which she became the first actress to win an Academy Award, a Golden Globe Award and a BAFTA Award for the same performance. The same year, Hepburn won a Tony Award for Best Leading Actress in a Play for her performance in Ondine. She went on to star in a number of successful films, such as Sabrina (1954), with Humphrey Bogart and William Holden; Funny Face (1957), a musical with Fred Astaire in which she sang her own parts; the drama The Nun's Story (1959); the romantic comedy Breakfast at Tiffany's (1961); the thriller-romance Charade (1963), opposite Cary Grant; and the musical My Fair Lady (1964).

In 1967, Hepburn starred in the thriller Wait Until Dark, receiving Academy Award, Golden Globe, and BAFTA nominations. After that role, she only occasionally appeared in films, one being Robin and Marian (1976) with Sean Connery. Her last recorded performances were in Always (1989), an American romantic fantasy film directed and produced by Steven Spielberg, and the 1990 documentary television series Gardens of the World with Audrey Hepburn, for which she won a Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Individual Achievement – Informational Programming. Hepburn won three BAFTA Awards for Best British Actress in a Leading Role and BAFTA's Lifetime Achievement Award. She also won two Golden Globes and the Cecil B. DeMille Award. She was also the recipient of a Screen Actors Guild Life Achievement Award and the Special Tony Award. In 1994, Hepburn's contributions to a spoken-word recording titled Audrey Hepburn's Enchanted Tales earned her a posthumous Grammy Award for Best Spoken Word Album for Children.

Later in life, Hepburn devoted much of her time to charity. She contributed to UNICEF from 1954 onwards. Between 1988 and 1992, she worked in some of the poorest communities of Africa, South America, and Asia. In December 1992, Hepburn received the US Presidential Medal of Freedom in recognition of her work as a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador. One month later, Hepburn died of appendix cancer at her home in Tolochenaz, Switzerland.[5]
