The Farnese Cup or Tazza Farnese is a 2nd-century BC cameo hardstone carving bowl or cup made in Hellenistic Egypt of four-layered sardonyx agate. It is at the Naples National Archaeological Museum.[1] It is about 20 cm (8 in) wide and similar in form to a Greek phiale or Roman patera, with no foot.[2][3] It features relief carvings on both its exterior and interior surfaces.[2][3]

There is no surviving evidence regarding when and why the piece was made, though there is consensus among scholars that it was created in Alexandria, due to the blending of Ancient Egyptian and Ancient Greek or Roman iconography found in its relief carvings. This provides a range of time wherein it may have been created, spanning from approximately 300 BC to 20 BC.[2][4]

The underside has a large Gorgon's head occupying most of the area, probably intended to ward off evil. The upper side has a scene with several figures that has long puzzled scholars. It seems clearly an allegory containing several divine figures and perhaps personifications, but corresponds to no other known representation and has been interpreted in several different ways.

History
The origin of the Tazza Farnese is unknown, leaving archaeologists and art historians to theorize a date and purpose for its creation. While its size and the material used are usually considered, theories of origin are mainly arrived at via individual analysis of the iconography of the piece, and therefore vary from one analysis to the next.[2][3][4]

Many archaeologists and art historians attribute the Tazza to the Hellenistic Period, asserting that its blending of Greek and Egyptian cultural symbols, as well as the funds necessary to commission such a large gemstone cameo, tie it to the Ptolemaic court.[4] Though not a widely held view, more recent analyses of the piece have assigned it a later date in the Augustan Period.[2][3]

After Octavian's conquest of Egypt in 31 BC, the Farnese Cup was possibly acquired by the Treasury of Rome; according to some, it was only made after the Romans took Egypt. It seems it was later taken to Byzantium, then back west after this city was sacked in 1204 during the Fourth Crusade. By 1239 it was in the court of Frederick II,[5] from which it then reached the Persian court of Herat or possibly Samarkand, where a contemporary drawing documents it;[6] thence it found its way to the court of Alfonso of Aragon in Naples, where Angelo Poliziano saw it in 1458. Lorenzo the Magnificent finally purchased the famous "scutella di calcedonio" in Rome, in 1471. From there it came into the possession of the Farnese family through Margaret of Austria and thus into the Naples National Archaeological Museum[1]

The border at Upper Lars is choking again. Over 113,000 Russians bolted through Georgia last week alone. Same script as September 2022. Same panic. Same visa-free escape hatch. Alexei Tabalov from the Conscript School is seeing the surge in legal queries from draft-age men, and the pattern is unmistakable. The Kremlin is laying the groundwork for another wave. This time it is quieter, more surgical. Harder to dodge.

They have already digitized the summons. No more paper that needs your signature. The notice pops up online and your border exit is instantly frozen. Rosgvardia is drilling for exactly this scenario, with fresh orders from Zolotov to guard infrastructure during mobilization, martial law, and wartime. Meanwhile the Defense Ministry quietly pushes quotas on regions: 409,000 contract soldiers by the end of 2026. When the numbers do not come voluntarily, the buses roll up to factory gates. Names are read out. Workers are loaded. Straight to the base. Tabalov calls it busification. In Penza they have graduated to street sweeps, pulling men off tractors, out of apartments, even from fishing spots. Some are beaten. Others are drugged. Signatures are forced. Local cops first tried claiming it was only about migrants who skipped registration. The footage shows otherwise. These are ethnic Russians who look exactly like the demographic Moscow needs to refill the meat grinder.

The student drone corps fiasco tells you everything about how broken their recruitment has become. They targeted fifty top universities, pressured administrations, ran propaganda campaigns, offered cash. The result? Barely 8,000 signed up against an 80,000 target. Turns out men still go to university to avoid the army, not join the suicide squad. So the regime pivots to coercion disguised as contract service, hitting small nations, occupied territories, migrants, and now anyone unlucky enough to be in the wrong Penza neighborhood on the wrong day. Regional quotas roll downhill. Miss your contract target and the difference becomes forced mobilization. Sign the paper and get paid, or wait for the van and get nothing but a rifle and a shallow grave.

The change is permanent. the imperial state project running out of bodies while refusing to admit the war is bleeding it dry. Moscow has already lost the initiative. Ukrainian forces are eliminating around 35,000 Russians per month, more than the Kremlin can sustainably recruit even with all these dirty tricks. Long-range strikes are scaling. Logistics nodes burn weekly. By late 2026 the operational rear will be systematically dismantled. Crimea is being isolated in slow motion. The snail that left Rostov on February 24, 2022, would have crossed Ukraine and entered Poland by now. This conflict’s real tempo is this.

Every Russian fleeing to Georgia, every father hiding in a basement in Bashmakovo, every student dodging the recruiter, proves the regime fears its own manpower problem more than it fears admitting defeat. The hybrid war on the home front, the quiet roundups, the digitized no-exit lists, the regional quotas, all of it exposes the lie that this is still a limited operation. To sustain an unwinnable imperial adventure, it wages total war against the people it governs.

The West should watch this exodus and finally drop the illusion that sanctions or diplomacy alone will change Kremlin calculus. Moscow only understands pressure it cannot escape. Ukraine is doing the heavy lifting on the battlefield, killing invaders faster than replacements arrive, building its own drone and missile industry, and preparing to license Patriots and Tomahawks. Accelerated delivery of long-range systems, full air defense integration, and the political spine to let Ukraine finish the job inside Russian logistics depth are what we need from NATO and the EU. Every Russian fleeing toward the Georgian border is a body Moscow can't send against us. The faster the regime is forced to confront that math openly, the sooner this ends on terms that secure the continent instead of merely pausing the slaughter.

text:
Celsius call read-through: Management sees Q3 as the trough, expects Celsius to return to growth exiting 2026, while Alani and margin initiatives drive the 2027 setup. $CELH 

(1) “Tracked channel dollar growth was approximately 56% in the quarter… We’re bringing new consumers into the brand, and many are repeat purchasers.” — John Fieldly, Chairman & CEO, on Alani Nu (+56% yoy tracked retail sales)

(2) “Given that sequencing, we would expect brand Celsius in the third quarter to look a lot like the second quarter before we exit the year back into growth.” — John Fieldly, Chairman & CEO

(3) “What is most important to stress, the productivity story is intact. Dollars per point in distribution are up approximately 16% in the second quarter versus the first and approximately 7% fewer points of distribution.” — Jarrod Langhans, Chief Financial Officer (+16% qoq productivity)

(4) “We are already seeing green shoots across a number of markets and velocity gains across the board have been significant after the rationalization program we implemented.” — John Fieldly, Chairman & CEO, on Rockstar

(5) “We expect to continue to get Celsius back to growth and category growth in 2027 and beyond.” — John Fieldly, Chairman & CEO

(6) “Our second manufacturing line in North Carolina begins producing in the back half with the full benefit in 2027, and we are advancing vertical integration and direct sourcing beyond that.” — Jarrod Langhans, Chief Financial Officer

(7) “The price pack architecture work we have referenced delivers initial impact in the back half with a much larger opportunity as we look at 2027 and 2028.” — Jarrod Langhans, Chief Financial Officer

(8) “For Alani Nu, we expect our momentum will continue… we have a robust, limited time offer calendar in the back half of this year that we believe will drive not only the brand but also the category.” — Jarrod Langhans, Chief Financial Officer

(9) “Over the next five years, we expect international markets outside of the US to represent more than 15% of our revenue.” — John Fieldly, Chairman & CEO (>15% of revenue within five years)

(10) “Based on what we see today, we would expect the third quarter to be consistent with the second… If fuel or aluminum moderates, you would expect to see improvement.” — Jarrod Langhans, Chief Financial Officer, on gross margin

(11) “The rationalization happened right away. The retail allocation took longer… And innovation, which is one of the biggest growth drivers in the category, was not there to bridge the gaps.” — John Fieldly, Chairman & CEO

(12) “I think… we went too deep on the Celsius rationalization… looking back, I definitely would have not cut as many SKUs within the organization.” — John Fieldly, Chairman & CEO

Verdict: Cautiously bullish

Management openly admitted the SKU rationalization mistake, guided to another soft quarter for core, but consistently framed Q3 as the low point while pointing to 2027 catalysts (innovation, distribution gains, revenue growth management, international expansion, and supply-chain efficiencies) as the basis for reaccelerating growth.

text:
[NEW] Closing Time: Unwinding North Carolina's ABC System

North Carolina's state government holds a near-complete monopoly today on the sale of liquor. Our state's Alcohol Beverage Control system is a relic of the Prohibition Era, almost a century old - and no longer serves North Carolina very well. 

The government does not manage the liquor business very effectively; it carries large costs for taxpayers; and as we've seen quite recently, the ABC is a major target for endemic and nefarious political corruption.

So what should be done?

The reality is that abolishing the ABC overnight would likely cause more problems than it would solve. Instead, we propose a gradual "unwinding" of North Carolina's ABC system: getting the government mostly out of the liquor business itself and loosening consumer-facing restrictions, while maintaining some basic oversight of the industry.

This should include divesting of the state-owned liquor warehouse in Raleigh, regionalizing and privatizing distribution, letting the market decide what products to offer or not, and allowing more independent retailers into the space.

text:
Is Shintō the Japanese Localisation of Sindhu (Hindu) Civilisation?

Shintō is widely regarded as Japan's indigenous religion, distinct from the religious traditions of the Indian subcontinent. Yet this familiar understanding leaves important questions unanswered. Why do Sanskrit, the Siddhaṃscript, sacred syllables (bīja), maṇḍalas, mudrās, and numerous Hindu devatās occupy an enduring place in Japanese religious life? Rather than treating these as isolated borrowings, this article argues that they form a coherent civilisational pattern. Shintō is better understood as the Japanese localisation of Hindu civilisation and, perhaps, even preserves the older civilisational designation Sindhu.

The historical significance of Sindhuextends beyond its original reference to the Indus River. As the civilisation centred on the river developed, the name came to denote not only a geographical region but also the civilisation, its people, and their religious tradition. In this broader sense, Sindhu designated a cultural world united by Sanātana Dharma, Sanskrit learning, sacred literature, ritual practice, and a shared philosophical outlook. Long before the modern terms Hindu and India emerged, Sindhu was the recognised designation of this civilisational order. Through regular phonetic change, it gave rise to forms such as Hindu in the Prakrits of northwestern India and neighbouring Persian, and later India in European languages.

Wherever Hindu civilisation spread, it carried far more than religious belief. It transmitted philosophy, ritual, law, literature, architecture, music, temple culture, and systems of learning as parts of a single civilisational tradition. Sanskrit served as its common sacred and intellectual language, while local languages expressed the same tradition in regional forms.

Unlike the historical expansion of the Abrahamic religions, Hindu civilisation neither sought to replace existing religious traditions nor impose cultural uniformity. Wherever it took root, it was expressed through local cultures while preserving its religious foundations. Indigenous languages, customs, and artistic traditions continued to flourish, giving rise to regional expressions of Sanātana Dharma. The traditions of Bali, Nepal, Cambodia, Java, and Sri Lanka differ in language, architecture, ritual, and artistic expression, yet all remain rooted in Sanātana Dharma, reflecting local historical and cultural conditions rather than independent religious origins. Japan should be understood within this same historical framework.

Japan belongs within this broader history. Conventional scholarship explains the presence of Sanskrit, the Siddhaṃ script, Hindu devatās, sacred symbols, and ritual traditions in Japan as later additions to an otherwise independent indigenous religion. While this interpretation accounts for their presence, it does not explain their coherence or enduring place within Japanese religious life. A civilisational perspective offers a different explanation. Rather than receiving isolated religious elements, Japan participated in the same process through which Hindu civilisation assumed regional forms elsewhere. Shintō is therefore better understood as the Japanese localisation of Sanātana Dharma than as an indigenous religion that later absorbed Hindu traditions.

This civilisational perspective also invites a reconsideration of Buddhism's historical expansion. Buddhism arose within the already established civilisation of Sanātana Dharma and inherited its philosophical vocabulary, sacred geography, cosmology, ritual culture, and religious symbolism. Buddhism did not extend beyond the geographical sphere of Hindu civilisation but spread within it, following the same civilisational, commercial, and religious networks through which Sanskrit, temple traditions, philosophy, and sacred learning had already travelled. The historical spread of Buddhism may therefore be understood not as the creation of a distinct civilisational world beyond the geographical sphere of Hindu civilisation but as the transmission of a reformulated religious tradition within an already existing Hindu civilisation. Japan therefore received Buddhism not as the origin of Hindu civilisation in Japan but as one historical vehicle through which the already established civilisation of Sanātana Dharma was transmitted.

The religious worldview of Shintō closely corresponds to that of Sanātana Dharma. Both regard the universe as permeated by sacred presence rather than divided between the sacred and the secular. Mountains, rivers, forests, waterfalls, rocks, and trees are revered because they manifest a transcendent reality. Human beings participate in this sacred order through reverence, worship, and ethical conduct, maintaining harmony with the natural world rather than exercising dominion over it. Shintō expresses this vision through the kami and Japan's sacred landscapes, while Sanātana Dharma expresses it through its own theological vocabulary. The language differs, but both traditions understand nature as a manifestation of the sacred rather than something separate from it.

This continuity is equally evident in ritual life. Purification precedes worship because communion with the divine requires ritual and moral purity. Ceremonial cleansing, offerings, seasonal festivals, pilgrimage, and the veneration of ancestors all affirm that religious life depends upon maintaining harmony among humanity, the natural world, the ancestors, and the divine. These practices are integral to Shintō, not secondary additions, and they embody principles long established within Sanātana Dharma while expressing them through Japanese ritual forms.

The same historical continuity is reflected in Japan's sacred language and ritual symbolism. Sanskrit acquired enduring religious significance, and the Siddhaṃ script continued in ritual use long after it had ceased to function as an ordinary writing system elsewhere. Sacred syllables (bīja), maṇḍalas, mudrās, and ritual formulae became established elements of Japanese religious practice, preserving not merely their outward forms but their religious significance. Their continued use demonstrates that Sanskrit was received as a sacred language whose ritual efficacy transcended linguistic boundaries.

The transformation of Saraswati into Benzaiten, Ganesa into Kangiten, Indra into Taishakuten, Brahmā into Bonten, Lakshmi into Kisshōten, and Mahakala into Daikokuten exemplifies the historical localisation of Sanātana Dharma in Japan. These devatās assumed Japanese names, artistic forms, and devotional contexts while retaining their religious identity, as they did wherever Hindu civilisation took root.

Taken together, the religious worldview, ritual principles, sacred language, symbolic system, and localised devatāspreserved in Japan form a coherent historical pattern more plausibly explained as the Japanese localisation of Sanātana Dharma than as an independent religion that selectively incorporated foreign practices. Shintō therefore represents not a parallel religious development but the Japanese localisation of the civilisation historically known as Sindhu.

The historical interpretation advanced here also invites a reconsideration of the etymology of Shintō. Conventional scholarship derives the word from the Sino-Japanese reading of Shéndào, usually translated as "the way of the gods." While this explains the later written form of the name, it need not determine its earliest origin. Names transmitted across linguistic boundaries were frequently adapted to the phonological systems of different languages before acquiring new written representations. It therefore remains possible that Shintōpreserves an earlier form that was subsequently interpreted through the Chinese expression Shéndào.

If Shintō represents the Japanese localisation of the civilisation historically known as Sindhu, the name itself may preserve an eastern linguistic development of that older civilisational designation. This hypothesis does not deny the historical significance of the Chinese interpretation but suggests that Shéndàomay constitute a later semantic explanation of an inherited name whose origin lay elsewhere. Such reinterpretation is well attested in historical linguistics, where inherited names often acquire new meanings after entering another linguistic tradition. The close phonetic resemblance between Sindhu and Shintō further warrants investigation.

The proposed relationship between Sindhuand Shintō remains a linguistic hypothesis rather than an established conclusion. It requires further historical and linguistic investigation. Yet if Japan preserved the sacred language, ritual traditions, and localised devatāsof the civilisation historically known as Sindhu, perhaps it also preserved its name.

text:
Drones changed the battlefield. Geography didn’t.

For centuries, armies coming into Korea from the continent tended to use the same northwestern route.

The Sui used it. So did the Tang, the Khitan, the Mongols and the Qing. Chinese forces followed much the same route during the Korean War.

It mostly came down to geography.

The east was too mountainous for large armies and long supply lines. The northwest offered flatter ground and an easier way south.

Modern weapons change how armies fight. They don’t erase the need to move troops and supplies over land.

The same route still matters today.

Bahir Dar is a city in northwestern Ethiopia, the capital of the Amhara Region, and a popular tourist destination known for its location on the southern shore of Lake Tana, the source of the Blue Nile. The city is a hub for historical sites, including medieval monasteries on Lake Tana's islands and the Zege Peninsula, and offers attractions like the Blue Nile Falls and a vibrant fish market.
History & Culture
Founding
The city's origins date back to the 13th century, with the establishment of the Kidanemihret Church.
Name:
The name "Bahir Dar" means "near the sea" and was given during the reign of Emperor Yikuno Amlak.
Tourism
Popular Destination:
Located southeast of the city, these towering waterfalls are a major natural attraction.
Monasteries:
The city and its surrounding area are rich in historical monasteries, offering a glimpse into Ethiopia's religious and cultural heritage.
Fish Market:
Bahir Dar features a lively fish market, providing a cultural experience and a chance to see local life.
Bahir Dar University:
The city is home to a university, contributing to its role as an educational center.

text:
Green Glazed Pottery Tower of the Eastern Han Dynasty: A Millennium-Old Masterpiece of Architectural Aesthetics
Unearthed in 1956 from the Guhe Han Tomb in Gaotang County, Liaocheng, the Green Glazed Pottery Tower of the Eastern Han Dynasty is a national first-class cultural relic now preserved in the National Museum of China. Standing at 144 cm tall, this square four-eaved tower is made of red earthenware with an overall green glaze, representing the pinnacle of ceramic craftsmanship during the Eastern Han Dynasty (25-220 CE).
As one of the few ancient architectural artifacts from Liaocheng to be included in the national museum's collection, the tower holds significant historical and cultural value. Its structure features dougong brackets supporting the eave overhangs and diamond-patterned openwork windows, providing tangible evidence of the wood-frame building techniques that would become a defining feature of traditional Chinese architecture for millennia.

The tower reflects the social and economic changes of the Eastern Han period, when the development of manor economies led to the rise of local powerful families who built fortified towers for defense and surveillance. It also embodies the fusion of Confucian and Taoist influences in architectural design, symbolizing both the pursuit of worldly success and the reverence for celestial harmony.

As an important showcase of Qilu architectural culture and the folk culture of northwestern Shandong, the Green Glazed Pottery Tower offers a unique window into the lives of ancient Chinese people, their beliefs, and their extraordinary craftsmanship.

text:
Republican Accused of Domestic Violence Allegedly Held Daughter’s Favorite Toy Hostage
Republican Congressman Max Miller of Ohio is already fighting for his political life amid allegations that he physically assaulted his ex-wife, Emily Moreno (the daughter of Republican U.S. Senator Bernie Moreno of Ohio), and other women. Now, leaked texts and emails obtained by Mother Jones show Miller has a pattern using their toddler daughter’s favorite toy, a blue bunny she’s had since birth, as leverage in custody disputes.

Senator Moreno told reporters recently that Miller held the bunny “hostage” for 48 hours while his granddaughter cried all night because she couldn’t sleep without it. Miller has denied the allegations and posted screenshots of text conversations trying to prove otherwise.

But this goes back even further than the incident Senator Moreno referenced. Emails from March of 2025 show Emily Moreno begging Miller to give the bunny toy back to their daughter, writing that punishing their daughter over an adult conflict was “just cruel.” A parenting coordinator’s texts describe how Miller repeatedly refused to abide by simple handoff agreements, even when Senator Moreno offered to pick the toy up on his daughter’s behalf.

Miller is still running for reelection, and has August 10th to drop out in order for Ohio Republicans to replace him on the ballot. So far, Miller has refused to abandon his campaign.

Wall Street is building entire neighborhoods that will never be for sale

Not converted rentals. Purpose-built subdivisions where every house is designed from the foundation up to never have an owner

Lennar, the second largest homebuilder in America, sells a large share of new construction directly to institutional landlords. Houses built for American families, sold to Wall Street before the concrete is poured

You will drive past one and think it's a normal street. There is no version of that street where you get to own the house

Put the timeline in order, because nobody ever does

2008. Roughly 7 million American homes go through foreclosure. Families are marched out

2009 to 2012. Those same houses hit the auction block. Blackstone, BlackRock, and Invitation Homes show up with wire transfers and buy in bulk. In some Phoenix zip codes, institutional buyers took roughly 90% of the foreclosed homes in a single quarter. The families who'd just lost them were being denied mortgages by the same financial system that had originated the loans

Today. Houses families lost for $80,000 rent for $2,400 a month. To them

Nobody was prosecuted. Several of those firms are raising fresh acquisition funds for 2026 right now

Then it gets worse, because owning the houses was never the endgame

They also bought the software that sets the price. Landlords feed their private rent data into shared pricing programs and take the number it hands back instead of competing with each other. The DOJ sued over exactly that in 2024. The same software will tell a manager to hold apartments EMPTY rather than lower the rent, because one discounted lease resets the comps for the entire zip code

Read that again. Empty units are more profitable than filled ones, so your city has a housing shortage and a "now leasing" banner on every building at the same time

And your failure to buy is not a side effect. It is the product

Every family that can't scrape a down payment becomes a permanent tenant. A tenant is a better asset than a sale, because a sale pays once and a tenant pays every month for thirty years while the software raises the number every twelve

First time buyers just fell to 24% of all purchases, the lowest in more than forty years of tracking. The average first time buyer is 38. In 1981 she was 29. That is nine years of your life converted into somebody's yield

They are not trying to beat you to a house. They are trying to make sure the concept of your house stops existing

HERE IS THE ONE THING THEY CANNOT TOUCH

There's a category of American house their model structurally cannot buy, and it's the last one available to a normal person:

Anything under about $150,000. Their cost per acquisition makes small deals unprofitable. The overhead doesn't scale down
Anything that needs real work. They buy rent-ready. They cannot underwrite a dead furnace and a gutted bathroom across three thousand houses
Anything outside their target metros. They cluster in about twenty markets for management density. A 1958 ranch in an Ohio county with three employers does not exist on their screen
Anything with a title problem. Probate open, heirs not speaking, code liens attached. Their legal department kills it in an afternoon. You fix it with a title company and $150

That is not a loophole. That is most of the housing stock in this country

The one I bought last quarter: $61,000. I put $28,400 into it. It appraised at $148,000 and rents for $1,275. That house had six offers in 2021. When I called there were zero. No institution will ever want it, and that is precisely why it was sitting there

You cannot outbid Wall Street and you don't need to. You need to want the houses they've already written off as too small to bother with, and there are millions of them

Every one you take off the board is one they never get to rent back to your kids

text:
We  (Ohio Common Ground) give Vivek kudos for putting down on paper  (metaphorically) his position on data centers in Ohio. In it he and his  advisory team make a number of claims. We feel it would be beneficial to  all Ohioans to explore them one-by-one every day until we've covered  them all. Here is today's claim. Please be sure to let us know what YOU think.

CLAIM EXAMINED: The pledge proposes that a data center paired with a power  plant would deliver surplus generation to residential customers within a  legislatively defined "benefit zone," stating that "even 100 MW would  power 75,000–100,000 homes," that residents in the zone would pay  nothing for electricity, and, in the alternative, that data centers  "could also directly reimburse residential customers within the benefit  zone for their electric bills."

Subclaim A — Energy equivalence ("100 MW would power 75,000–100,000 homes").

The  average US household consumes approximately 10,500 kilowatt-hours of  electricity per year (US Energy Information Administration), equivalent  to roughly 1.2 kilowatts of continuous demand. On that basis, 100  megawatts of continuous output corresponds to the average annual  consumption of about 85,000 households. The Congressional Research  Service reports a comparable figure, stating that roughly 100 MW is  sufficient to support the electricity needs of about 80,000 US  households, and that hyperscale data centers ranging from 100 MW to  1,000 MW correspond to approximately the load of 80,000 to 800,000 homes  (CRS Report R48646). The pledge's stated range of 75,000 to 100,000  homes falls within these figures.

This  is an annual-energy equivalence: it compares the total electricity a  100 MW resource would produce over a year against average household  consumption. It does not establish that 100 MW could reliably serve that  number of homes at every hour, because peak residential demand, reserve  requirements, transmission losses, and generation outages require  additional capacity and separate analysis.

OCG ASSESSMENT: Supported as an annual-energy equivalence. Not established  as a guarantee of continuous, reliable retail service.

Subclaim B — Delivery mechanism (benefit-zone credit or direct reimbursement).

The  pledge describes generation located behind the data center's meter,  with surplus output then delivered to the grid and credited to  residential customers within a defined zone. Generation on the  customer's side of the utility meter serves on-site load and does not  supply other grid customers. Output that instead flows onto the grid to  serve residential accounts is grid-connected generation requiring an  approved interconnection. A single block of generation cannot function  at the same time as behind-the-meter supply to the data center and as  exported power serving separate customers. A facility could serve the  data center behind the meter while separately metering and  interconnecting an exportable portion, but those are distinct functions,  and the exported portion would be subject to wholesale-market and  interconnection rules.

Ohio  lies within the PJM Interconnection wholesale market. Power exported  into that market is scheduled and settled under federally approved rules  across the regional pool. It is not physically traced or assigned to  particular residential accounts based on proximity to the plant. Ohio  also maintains retail electric choice under R.C. Chapter 4928, under  which a residential customer may take generation service from a  competitive supplier, a governmental aggregation, or the utility's  standard service offer, and a residential bill comprises separately  billed generation, distribution, transmission, and rider charges. A  universal bill credit would require statutory and administrative design  specifying which charges are eliminated and how a credit follows  customers who change suppliers or move into or out of the zone.

Jurisdiction  determines which version of the mechanism is available to the state.  Under the Federal Power Act (16 U.S.C. § 824), the Federal Energy  Regulatory Commission holds exclusive authority over wholesale  electricity sales and interstate transmission, while states retain  authority over retail sales, generation siting, and taxation. In Hughes  v. Talen Energy Marketing, LLC, 578 U.S. 150 (2016), the U.S. Supreme  Court held a state program preempted because it set an interstate  wholesale rate by conditioning payments to a generator on that  generator's participation in the PJM capacity auction. The Court limited  its holding and stated that states may still encourage generation  through measures such as tax incentives, land grants, direct subsidies,  or re-regulation, provided those measures remain "untethered to a  generator's wholesale market participation."

A  benefit-zone credit tied to the wholesale value of exported power, or  conditioned on wholesale-market participation, would face preemption  questions under that standard. A developer-funded rebate operating  independently of wholesale settlement would fall within the authority  the Court preserved to the states, though it could present separate  questions under state law.

Federal  rules governing large loads co-located with generation are themselves  in development as of today, following a December 2025 FERC directive to PJM to establish such rules.

The  pledge's alternative, under which data centers "directly reimburse  residential customers within the benefit zone," would not depend on  tracing specific electricity to specific homes and would not, by itself,  involve wholesale-market settlement. Its principal open questions  concern eligibility (which customers and property types qualify), scope  (which bill components are covered), continuity (treatment of customers  who change suppliers or relocate), and financial security (guarantees of  payment over the operating life of the facility).

The  quantity of surplus available for either mechanism is not fixed over  time. Data-center facilities commonly increase their power draw across a  multi-year build-out as computing capacity is added, so a facility's  surplus relative to a co-located plant would tend to be largest early in  operation and decline as the facility grows into its allocated load.  The pledge does not specify whether the referenced surplus (illustrated  as 300 MW of a 1,000 MW plant) denotes guaranteed firm capacity,  expected average annual output, or the amount remaining after the data  center's demand is met. These are distinct quantities with different  implications for the benefit delivered.

OCG ASSESSMENT: The mechanism is specified at the level of concept rather  than implementation. Its legal exposure depends on whether the household  benefit is structured as an allocation of wholesale power, which raises  federal wholesale-market and preemption questions, or as a  developer-funded retail rebate, which falls within state authority but  requires enabling legislation, utility and PUCO implementation, and  defined eligibility, covered charges, and funding security.

The  pledge does not identify which architecture it adopts, define "surplus," or specify whether "free" electricity refers to the generation charge alone or to the full residential bill.

text:
MY DATA CENTER POLICY PLEDGE: OHIOANS-FIRST

A top concern I hear from Ohioans across our state – second only to property taxes – is the accelerating pace of data center expansion. Key citizen concerns about data centers include rising electric bills, noise, pollution, and the absence of clearly defined economic benefits for Ohio families. The data center industry has badly failed to earn the trust of millions of everyday Ohioans who are struggling with electric bills and property taxes, wondering why large corporations receive property tax abatements while ordinary homeowners don’t receive the same.

There are hundreds of data centers already across our state, and the pace of construction is accelerating. While I had no part in these past projects, I am committed to ensuring our policies catch up to current realities. Despite my opponents’ claims, I’m not “pro-data center.” I’m pro-Ohio, and I have a plan to fix the problem.

At the same time, I also hear from Ohio's workers about the need to attract high-paying construction jobs to our state, for which the data center boom has been helpful. Preserving economic growth, capital investment, and high-paying jobs in Ohio is also a vital objective.

After traveling all 88 counties and listening to workers, farmers, union leaders, building trades, small business owners, environmental groups, and grassroots activists, I am convinced that the best path forward is neither unrestrained data center growth nor a permanent categorical ban. The right answer is a policy framework that allows Ohio families to prosper economically while protecting local communities.

Today I am announcing my policy pledge to Ohioans on data centers. If a data center is built in your community, then (i) you will no longer have to pay for your home’s electricity, (ii) you will pay lower property taxes, and (iii) the data center will be required to abide by all air and water quality standards without exception, and we will take the necessary steps to protect Ohio’s fertile farmland. If any one of these three conditions is not met, the data center won’t be built. Period. I will work with Ohio’s state legislature to codify these commitments into law immediately after I assume office.

To ensure urgency, I will further issue an executive order on my first day in office to immediately halt the approval of any new data center project announcements in Ohio, until the above-mentioned data center legislation takes effect. These policy objectives are consistent with the principles I have articulated over the first 18 months of my campaign, and today I am making a legislative commitment to codify them into state law.

My Democrat opponent recently announced that data centers must not contribute to higher electric bills for ratepayers, a concept that I advocated for in early 2025 long before she started parroting the same. This is obvious but insufficient. We can and must go further for Ohio families.

Eliminating electricity costs is the right objective. If Ohio’s governor sets this as a clear requirement and negotiates accordingly, I am confident that hyper scalers would be willing to fully cover the cost of power for Ohioans who reside near a data center. That requires the acumen of a businessman, not a bureaucrat, at the top.

This is very practical to implement. Data centers could generate power behind their own meter, and the excess power generated can be credited to the electric charges on a residential customer’s electric bill within a certain radius (the “benefit zone”). This would operate as if customers in the benefit zone had executed a power purchase agreement with the power plant, but at no cost.

For example, if a data center is constructed along with a 1,000 megawatt (MW) natural gas or nuclear power plant, and the data center uses 700MW of that electricity, the remaining 300MW would flow to the power grid. State law would define the benefit zone and credit the 300MW across all residential customers within that zone. Even 100MW would power 75,000-100,000 homes. Given the potential to power so many homes, most of Ohio’s counties would fit entirely within a benefit zone – which means every resident in the county would pay nothing for their electricity if a data center were built there. Alternatively, data centers could also directly reimburse residential customers within the benefit zone for their electric bills.

In addition to providing free electricity for local residents, my plan would also deliver property tax relief to Ohioans within the benefit zone – by prohibiting property tax abatements for future data centers and creating a property tax rebate for Ohio homeowners. That is, data centers would be required to pay 100% of their property taxes without abatements, and these property tax revenues would directly fund property tax rebates for homeowners. This helps deliver major property tax relief for Ohio families without hurting local police, schools, or firemen – and may become essential with a looming ballot initiative to eliminate property taxes expected in 2027.

Finally, my plan ensures that data centers do not receive special exemptions on air and water quality standards and that our farmland is protected. This respects local conservation objectives, while also giving companies a predictable regulatory environment. Simply put: if a data center is going to be built in Ohio, we will require it to minimize its water usage by recycling and reusing its water with the best available technology. We will also require that when the water is released, it comes out just as clean as when the data center took it in. That’s common sense. We will also emphasize the use of vacant and former industrial sites known as brownfields, rather than the use of fertile farmland. Our water and farmland are some of Ohio’s greatest and most precious resources, and my plan ensures that they are protected for all Ohioans.

Ohio requires a governor who is willing to listen and to adopt thoughtful solutions that actually put Ohioans first, by carefully weighing costs and benefits rather than spouting off meaningless proclamations.

That means supporting economic growth for Ohio’s workers, while ensuring that we do it in a way that helps all Ohioans. In sum, my administration will eliminate electricity costs and reduce property taxes for homeowners, while also ensuring that all environmental laws are respected and that farmland is preserved. No data center will be built in Ohio without actualizing these commitments. I look forward to signing legislation in early 2027 to turn this vision into reality.

The Senate Finance Committee sat down Wednesday to fix Social Security and walked away unable to agree on even how to talk about it, the Washington Times reports. The math, however, is not up for debate. The program's main trust fund runs dry in about six years, and current law then forces an 𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐜𝐮𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡𝐥𝐲 𝟐𝟐 𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐝𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐚𝐫 — nearly $500 less a month by 2033 for the one in seven seniors who lean on those checks for most of their income.

The structure was rotten from the start. Sen. Ron Johnson, Wisconsin Republican, noted the system asks today's workers to fund today's retirees and called the promise that your money was saved for you 𝘢 𝘧𝘪𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯. His verdict was blunter still: 𝘚𝘰𝘤𝘪𝘢𝘭 𝘚𝘦𝘤𝘶𝘳𝘪𝘵𝘺 𝘪𝘴 𝘢 𝘭𝘦𝘨𝘢𝘭 𝘗𝘰𝘯𝘻𝘪 𝘴𝘤𝘩𝘦𝘮𝘦. In 1960 there were more than five workers per recipient. Today it is 𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐟𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠.

Republicans want a bipartisan commission to hammer out the tradeoffs and force a vote. Democrats want one thing — tax increases on the rich — and dismiss any commission as cover for cuts. 𝘐𝘧 𝘙𝘦𝘱𝘶𝘣𝘭𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘯𝘴 𝘸𝘢𝘯𝘵 𝘵𝘰 𝘴𝘰𝘭𝘷𝘦 𝘚𝘰𝘤𝘪𝘢𝘭 𝘚𝘦𝘤𝘶𝘳𝘪𝘵𝘺, 𝘱𝘶𝘵 𝘺𝘰𝘶𝘳 𝘱𝘭𝘢𝘯 𝘰𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘵𝘢𝘣𝘭𝘦, said Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, even as his own side offered nothing but higher taxes on a $190 trillion shortfall.

Meanwhile AARP told senators it will not accept 𝐚𝐧𝐲 𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐟𝐮𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐛𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐟𝐢𝐭𝐬 and is running scare ads against the commission idea. Sen. James Lankford, Oklahoma Republican, cut through it: if Congress does nothing, the cuts arrive in six years no matter what. 𝘐𝘵 𝘪𝘴 𝘢 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭 𝘤𝘩𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘦𝘯𝘨𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘣𝘦 𝘢𝘣𝘭𝘦 𝘵𝘰 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘢 𝘨𝘳𝘰𝘸𝘯-𝘶𝘱 𝘤𝘰𝘯𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘴𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯 𝘢𝘣𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘴, he said.

text:
Most Americans don’t actually understand the judicial philosophies they endorse | Eric W. Dolan, PsyPost

A recent study published in Political Research Quarterly suggests that although many Americans express preferences for specific judicial philosophies, most struggle to apply these principles consistently to legal issues. The research indicates that for the general public, judicial philosophy acts more as a symbolic label than a structured framework for evaluating the law. This disconnect provides evidence that the complex legal standards often debated during Supreme Court nominations may hold little practical meaning for the average voter.

During televised Supreme Court confirmation hearings, politicians frequently debate how nominees will interpret the United States Constitution. Two highly discussed approaches are originalism and living constitutionalism. Originalism suggests that judges should interpret the Constitution based on its meaning at the time it was written. Living constitutionalism indicates that constitutional interpretation should adapt to reflect modern views and societal sensibilities.

Judges and legal scholars frequently use these specific concepts to justify their rulings. “Judicial philosophy is one of the most prominent ways that judges, politicians, and the media talk about courts,” said Miles T. Armaly, an associate professor of political science at the University of Mississippi and co-author of the study. “A growing body of research shows that ordinary Americans express preferences for philosophies like originalism and living constitutionalism, and they even evaluate judges and case outcomes through that lens.”

“Because these philosophies tend to align with ideological predispositions at the elite level (i.e., originalism is typical of conservative judges, living constitutionalism of liberal ones), individuals may be able to nominally link a philosophy to their political preferences, but it remains unclear whether they understand what those philosophies actually entail or can apply them consistently across legal questions.”

Recognizing a legal phrase is different from putting those theories into practice. “Recognizing a label is very different from consistently applying the principles that label represents,” Armaly added. “Thus, our motivation was to distinguish between recognizing a judicial philosophy and consistently applying it across different legal questions.”

The authors designed this research to test if the public possesses philosophical constraint. This term describes a cohesive belief system where specific attitudes about legal issues naturally flow from a broader understanding of judicial philosophy. A highly constrained individual would consistently support legal outcomes that match their chosen philosophy.

The authors wanted to see if everyday citizens apply these legal principles as consistently as trained legal professionals do. “Part of our contribution is methodological,” Armaly said. “Rather than assuming legal professionals possess coherent judicial philosophies, we measure them directly and compared them to the mass public. That comparison gives us a much more meaningful benchmark than comparing the public to an abstract ideal of what citizens ‘should’ know.”

To explore this question, the researchers collected data from two separate surveys. First, they gathered responses from a nationally representative sample of 1,000 United States adults using the 2022 Cooperative Election Study. Second, they recruited an online sample of 483 legal professionals in early 2025. This specialized group consisted largely of practicing attorneys, paralegals, and legal assistants.

Participants in both groups answered questions designed to test their understanding and application of judicial philosophy. The scientists first measured basic preference consistency by asking participants to identify their preferred philosophy. The survey asked if respondents believed the Constitution’s meaning is fixed or can change. It also asked if judges should interpret the text as originally understood or according to current modern views.

The authors then measured horizontal constraint, which looks at how consistently individuals apply a philosophy across different scenarios. Participants read five hypothetical cases dealing with constitutional issues like Miranda rights, gun ownership, and political speech. For each case, they chose an outcome that aligned with either an originalist or a living constitutionalist perspective. The survey offered explicit hints in the case descriptions to help respondents match outcomes to specific legal philosophies.

Next, the scientists evaluated vertical constraint to see if participants’ specific case choices matched their originally stated judicial philosophy. For example, if a person claimed to be an originalist, the researchers checked whether that person selected originalist outcomes in the hypothetical cases. The researchers measured this by calculating the proportion of matching responses across fifteen possible combinations.

The results suggest a broad disconnect among the general public regarding judicial philosophy. When asked to pick a preferred legal philosophy, 44.5 percent of the mass public chose “not sure,” while only 23.7 percent of legal professionals selected the unsure option. Only about 30 percent of the general public provided consistent answers across the three basic philosophy questions.

The authors did not anticipate such a high level of uncertainty. “We were a bit surprised by the number of respondents who simply declined to express a preference when given a ‘not sure’ option,” Armaly told PsyPost. “Nearly half of the mass public did not identify with either originalism or living constitutionalism when that option was available. This suggests that earlier research, which didn’t always offer a ‘not sure’ response, may have overstated how many Americans truly have meaningful preferences over judicial philosophy.”

When looking at horizontal constraint, the mass public showed very little consistency in their responses to the specific legal cases. Legal professionals exhibited about 32 percent more consistency across the varying scenarios than the general public. Even with helpful hints provided in the question text, average citizens struggled to pick outcomes that followed a single, cohesive legal framework.

The findings for vertical constraint were similar. Legal professionals achieved a consistency score of about 0.54, meaning they matched their case outcomes to their stated philosophy 54 percent of the time. The mass public scored approximately 0.38, meaning their case outcomes matched their stated philosophy only 38 percent of the time.

According to Armaly, these numerical gaps between experts and the general public reveal a lot about how people process legal information. “The difference we found were not only statistically significant, but also substantively meaningful,” Armaly said. “Legal professionals exhibited roughly one-third more ‘horizontal’ philosophical constraint (i.e., consistency across legal attitudes) and about 45% more ‘vertical’ philosophy constraint (i.e., consistency between stated philosophy and legal positions) relative to the mass public.”

This gap suggests that extensive legal training provides a structure that everyday voters lack. “Those are sizeable differences, suggesting that judicial philosophy functions as an organizing framework for legal professionals, but only weakly for members of the public,” Armaly added.

Despite these low scores among the public, the researchers caution against making broad judgments about voters’ civic abilities. “The main takeaway is not that Americans are uninformed or incapable of thinking about constitutional issues,” Armaly said. “Instead, we find that most people do not appear to organize their views around abstract judicial philosophies in the same way that legal professionals do. Many people can express a preference for, say, originalism, but the label often does not translate into consistent judgments across different legal questions.”

“This is important because individuals offer more institutional support and are more likely to accept outcomes when they perceive courts to employ their preferred policy,” Armaly explained. “However, in the absence of a label describing the decision as ‘originalist’ or ‘living constitutionalist,’ many are infrequently able to spot judicial decisions that employed their preferred philosophy.”

A lack of philosophical constraint does not mean that the public ignores legal interpretation entirely. “One important caveat is that our findings should not be interpreted as saying that judicial philosophy is unimportant, that the public ignores it, or that the public lacks the capacity to use judicial philosophy in a coherent, structured way,” Armaly said. “Previous research shows that people do respond to judges’ stated philosophies when evaluating nominees and court decisions. We do not doubt that these are important factors for individuals assessing institutions.”

Instead, the results provide evidence that the depth of public understanding is often shallow. “Our point is narrower,” Armaly explained. “Many people seem to recognize and use the labels without possessing a deeply structured understanding of what those philosophies consistently imply across cases. Our findings suggest that, for many, judicial philosophy is more of a label than a lens, more akin to a bumper sticker than a belief system.”

One potential limitation is that the online sample of legal professionals might not perfectly represent the entire population of working attorneys and judges in the United States. The data also indicates that even basic ideological consistency does not fully explain the public’s varied responses to specific constitutional cases. Future studies could explore how these patterns translate to other countries with different constitutional frameworks.

The researchers also plan to investigate the origins of the public’s legal opinions. “One natural next step is to better understand how people learn these philosophical labels,” Armaly said. “We know that politicians, confirmation hearings, and the media regularly invoke terms like ‘originalism,’ but it remains an open question whether those discussions increase genuine understanding or simply increase familiarity with the labels.”

“More broadly, we’re interested in how people form attitudes about courts and whether those attitudes are grounded in legal principles, political identities, or something else.”

text:
Just closed out the $COHU swing for a clean 17% and the blowout felt exactly like the setup we tracked. 

Record demand signals in handlers and burn-in plus clear AI test tailwinds.

That got me thinking. What’s the next name in the broader semiconductor equipment and advanced packaging ecosystem reporting soon that could offer a similar or better beat-and-raise setup?

Quick scan of the calendar:

ACMR (ACM Research) → August 7 before the open

This is the pure-play wet cleaning + electrochemical plating specialist with heavy exposure to advanced packaging and ECP tools that are increasingly critical for high-performance AI chips, HBM, and 3D packaging. 

Same secular drivers we just rode in the test/handling space: 

AI compute density, power efficiency, and the packaging bottleneck.

My focus for the next swing / all-in challenge leg: $ACMR.

Why ACMR right now?

Recent quarters show real momentum. Q1 was a clear beat with revenue +34% YoY to $231M (vs ~$216–221M consensus), non-GAAP EPS $0.34 (big beat vs the $0.20–0.26 range). Gross margin recovered nicely to 46.5%. ECP and advanced packaging were the standout growth engines. 

Management reaffirmed the full-year 2026 revenue guide of $1.08–1.175B (midpoint ~25% growth) and noted shipments continuing to outpace revenue recognition. They’re expanding outside China, shipping panel-level tools, ramping Oregon, and winning OSAT/foundry packaging business.

Current Q2 consensus (before they report):

EPS ~$0.30–0.34
Revenue ~$269–275M (+25% YoY)

That’s already solid sequential and YoY growth baked in. The street is pricing continued strength in the high-growth packaging/ECP mix.

Key things I’ll be watching on the August 7 call:

•  AI / advanced packaging / HBM demand commentary and any update on order pipeline or multi-quarter visibility
•  Whether they raise, hold, or add color on the full-year guide and H2 shipment ramp
•  Margin trajectory (mix shift toward higher-value tools), global customer wins outside China, and Oregon progress

This is exactly the kind of setup I like for the all-in challenge: high-conviction sector tailwind (AI packaging & wet process equipment), a name with a track record of beating in this environment, but enough optionality around guidance and new product traction that the reaction can be outsized either way.

Implied move is meaningful (options pricing in a solid single-digit to low-double-digit range historically, with bigger realized swings possible), so it’s not for the faint of heart.

Not financial advice. Just sharing the setup I’m tracking for my own all-in challenge. Earnings are always binary and guidance can surprise in either direction.

While Doué is the player I think Arsenal should try to sign, even at a high cost (or Kvaratskhelia, though I think that’s even harder), the other solutions don't excite me.

At this stage of the transfer window, I think the best solution is to move Eze to the left wing and assemble this attacking squad:

DM: Rice, Zubimendi
RCM: Ødegaard, Nwaneri
LCM: Guimarães, Lewis-Skelly, Merino
RW: Saka, Madueke, Dowman
LW: Eze, Martinelli, Tzolis
ST: Gyökeres, Havertz, (Merino)

Having 15 top-level players for 6 attacking positions seems sufficient for the season, though it is clearly a major regret not to have signed an elite left winger during this window.

Additionally, youngsters like Ife Ibrahim, Harriman-Annous, and O'Neil will feature in cup matches, allowing the others to rest.

Even though Vinicius didn't arrive, Eze can match Saka's creative output on the left flank; Martinelli offers the profile of a runner, and Tzolis that of a finisher.

There is a balance of profiles, and the other options are either too expensive or unconvincing.

Ndiaye is a good winger, but his price tag doesn't reflect his quality.
Nusa isn't quite ready for this challenge yet; there are aspects of his game that need improvement before making the step up.
Barcola is too expensive for what would essentially be a marginal upgrade over Martinelli.
Yildiz is too expensive or simply unavailable.
Nico Williams is expensive and injury-prone.
Álvarez isn't a left winger, and playing with two strikers doesn't make tactical sense.
Gibbs-White is a great option for the left #8/#10 role, but I don't think adding another player there is necessary.

text:
The Arsenal Fit: Bruno Guimaraes

Hello all. Thank you for tuning into my latest analysis on Bruno Guimaraes. I hope you enjoy, and as always, feel free to disagree with any of my points. All feedback is welcomed.

IMO, Bruno G is one of the few midfielders who could genuinely improve us both technically and physically without requiring a major tactical adjustment. I am really excited by the possibility of this signing.

He would restore several qualities we have missed since Granit Xhaka left: aggression, personality, security under pressure and a midfielder who genuinely enjoys contact and competing.

The interesting question I found when researching for this post is not whether Bruno fits in at Arsenal. His qualities clearly do. The real question was how Arteta will/should use him.

Key USPs

Bruno is primarily a pass-first progressor. He constantly scans before receiving, understands where the pressure is from and positions his body well to play forward as early as possible. He is comfortable receiving from the CB, between the lines or with an opponent on his back, using his close control and press resistance to create the separation required for the next action.

His first instinct is rarely to circulate possession without purpose. Bruno looks to punch vertical passes into a forward’s feet, release runners through or over the defensive line and use sharp third-man combinations to get around the opposition midfield. He can also play diags with his low backfoot technique, particularly after regains when the opposition structure is unsettled.

That separates him from several of our current options. MLS is more carry-first, Rice progresses through physicality and vertical running, while Ode controls tempo through shorter combinations. Zubi is also a pass-first line-breaker, but he generally operates from deeper areas and prioritises control. Bruno can carry when required (69th percentile for prog carries), but his instinct is to move the ball forward earlier and with more venom. He ranked in the 93rd percentile for forward passes, 91st for passes into the final third and 89th for progressive passes.

The key translation question is how much of that output survives against our usual opposition. A meaningful share of Bruno’s most dangerous progression came in open or transitional moments, whereas we regularly face compact low blocks with fewer vertical gaps. His percentile rankings still reflect quality, but also role and team context. Bruno should improve the speed and intent of our progression, but consistently creating against settled low blocks will be the real test.

The Likely Tactical Fit: Bruno G in the RHS

Why the RHS makes sense

The most likely structure would have Bruno starting on the right of the pivot, Rice operating from the left and Ode playing ahead while naturally gravitating towards Saka. I understand why people expect that. Bruno has spent most of his recent career occupying the RHS and produced one of the best attacking campaigns of his Newcastle career from there last season (9 goals and 5 assists). His heat map, pass map and final-third actions map all lean towards the right side.

The body orientation is also natural. When Bruno receives in the RHS, his dominant right foot opens towards the centre of the pitch. He can see Saka, Ode and the CF without making a major body adjustment, allowing him to play into feet, find runs through passing lanes or combine with Ode before progressing further.

The technical quality of a Bruno G, Ode and Saka relationship would be ridiculous. Bruno could operate slightly deeper than Ode in the RHS, giving us two different progressive profiles around Saka. Ode controls the tempo through shorter combinations, while Bruno is more willing to break the defensive line early and play that direct pass.

The impact on the Left Winger

The LW would still receive, although often through a more indirect way. The RHS would be loaded, dragging the opposition block across and then Bruno’s can play diagonals to find the LW in isolation.

The concern for me is that the LW may become overly reliant on those diagonals. Even when the switch creates a 1v1, the winger could receive without the close combinations and early vertical service available on the RHS. The effectiveness of the structure would therefore depend heavily on his ability to create independently.

That concern applies most clearly to Martinelli, whose qualities are maximised when he can attack space before the defence resets. Tzolis is also direct, but his stronger carrying and chance-creation profile may make him more comfortable receiving in isolation.

Bruno as the advanced right sided #8

Bruno G could also replace Odegaard as the right #8. In that scenario, Zubi would probably need to start deeper and establish rhythm while Bruno plays more directly around Saka.

Zubi is exceptional at circulating possession safely, controlling the tempo and providing the structural stability that allows others to take more risks. Thus, having Zubi behind Bruno G would allow him to become the more aggressive creator. He would constantly look to release Saka or the CF rather than carrying the responsibility of controlling every phase of possession.

Refer to Image 1

My concern with Bruno G in the RHS

My issue is not whether Bruno can perform in the RHS. It is probably his individually optimal position. My concern is that adding another elite creator to our strongest flank may leave the left side with the same problem from previous seasons: who consistently plays the early vertical pass and creates on that side?

My preferred Tactical Fit: Bruno G in the LHS

Why the LHS needs him

 My personal preference would be to use Bruno as the advanced left sided #8. We have lacked a pass-first progressor in the LHS since Xhaka left. Rice is world class at covering space, winning the ball and exploding vertically, but he does not consistently receive between the lines and play early passes into the winger. MLS is more of a carry-first progressor and can hold on for slightly too long, whilst Eze can sometimes be too casual and slow in progression. Capable but they don’t offer what Bruno does IMO.

I feel Bruno would change the rhythm of that side. Rather than recycling the ball and allowing the opp block to move across, his instinct is to play with intent. He can find the LW into feet, release him through the RB and CB gap or play vertically towards Calafiori or Gyokeres before moving to receive again.

The value he offers is not only the quality of the pass, it is the timing too. Having him on the left would speed up progression, although his right-foot bias could occasionally delay passes towards the touchline. Combinations with Calafiori and selective trivela passes could help offset this limitation.

The difference between receiving early against an unbalanced defender and receiving after three or four circulation passes is obviously massive.

The box midfield structure

The structure I’d imagine would have Rice and Timber forming the deeper line of the box midfield. Rice sits in the deep left channel, Timber inverts from the right and Bruno remains higher in the LHS alongside Ode in the RHS.

Rice protects the centre and transitions, Timber supports circulation, Bruno progresses from the left and Ode continues controlling the RHS around Saka.

Refer to Image 2

Keeping Bruno higher also avoids a potential Rice x Bruno G bottleneck. We don’t need Rice, Ode and Bruno all dropping deep to receive from the CBs. Rice can provide the structural floor in early build-up with Ode dropping deep to receive too, while Bruno receives closer to the opposition midfield.

The Bruno x Calafiori x LW relationship

One of the most exciting parts about Bruno in the LHS is the relationship that it could create between Bruno, Calafiori and the LW. Calafiori naturally moves in the LHS and makes blindside runs beyond the opposition midfield. Bruno can find him vertically, use him as the third man or play around him towards the touchline. The LW could stay wider and be isolated due to Calafiori’s runs and receive during a 1v1 situation or make runs from the outside towards the box.

Another pattern we could see: Gabriel finding Calafiori between the lines. Calafiori lays the ball back to Bruno, who receives facing forward and can curl a pass around the RB (trivela), punch it through the RB and CB gap or shoot towards the far post. This third-man combination would help Bruno avoid receiving with his back completely towards the opposition goal.

We could also see Bruno play directly into the LW before moving around him. If the opposing RB stays attached to the winger, Calafiori can attack inside. If the RB follows Calafiori, the winger receives with more room outside. If the opposing midfielder jumps onto Bruno, Rice can progress into the open space.

Bruno would not need to create every chance with an unbelievable final pass. His quick progression would simply force defenders into decisions they currently do not have to make. Bruno starting on the left would give opposition blocks much less time to recover.

This could also help Martinelli, who is at his best attacking space before the defence resets. Bruno would recognise those runs earlier, although it would not completely solve Martinelli’s difficulties against settled low blocks.

Xhaka comparison and the key trade-offs of Bruno G in the LHS

Any comparison to Xhaka should be positional rather than stylistic. Xhaka’s left foot gave him natural access towards Martinelli and the touchline, while much of his 2022/23 value came through late box arrivals rather than acting as the primary progressor. Bruno could occupy a similar advanced LHS area, but the role would function differently: he would offer more involvement in build-up and more aggressive progression, while providing less natural access towards the LW and probably fewer repeated runs beyond the ball. Depending on Calafiori’s positioning, Bruno may be asked to create from behind the ball more often than Xhaka did in 2022/23.

There are two clear trade-offs with Bruno in the LHS. Firstly, Bruno’s heavy one footedness could occasionally delay passes towards the touchline because his body naturally opens towards the centre rather than the LW. Against an aggressive mid-block, that delay could allow the RB to close the space or pressure to arrive from Bruno’s blind side. His trivela passing can provide an alternative, but it should not be treated as a repeatable replacement for the left footed access Xhaka offered. His ability to win 2.75 fouls per 90 offers some protection under pressure, but it does not completely solve the receiving-angle issue.

The second clear trade-off involves Rice. If Bruno remains advanced and Calafiori pushes forward, Rice would have to stay deeper more often, restricting his dynamic ball-carrying and late box entry. I believe the roles would therefore need to rotate: when Bruno drops, Rice can advance; when Rice runs beyond him, Bruno can hold the deeper left space.

Why the trade-off is worth it for me:
- Earlier service into the LW
- Better combinations around Calafiori
- Symmetrical attacking threat
- A potentially elite rest-defence base, provided Rice and Timber remain disciplined behind the ball.

Attacking Output and Creativity

Bruno scored 9 PL goals from 5.60 xG and recorded 5 assists from 4.98 xA, leading Newcastle in both categories despite missing 63 days last season.

He scored those 9 goals from only 42 shots, producing a 21% goal conversion rate (17.5% non-pen) and a 55% SOT rate (23 on target). His 7 non-pen goals came from 4.02 npxG, while all his attempts produced 8.57 xGOT from 5.60 xG, showing strong shot placement last season, although that level of overperformance may not be fully repeatable.

Bruno isn’t a particularly high volume shooter. He averaged 1.54 shots per 90, but 0.84 of those efforts hit the target. The low volume and high SOT rate (55%) suggest a relatively selective shooting profile.

However, the finishing was not perfect. Bruno scored only 4/8 big chances across all comps and only 2/6 non-pen big chances. He can certainly miss a clear opportunity, particularly in the air, but the overall data still suggests genuine midfield goal threat through late arrivals, second balls and shots from the edge of the area.

Creatively, he recorded 5 assists from 4.98 xA, created 7 big chances and averaged 1.65 key passes per 90. He is not an elite final-action specialist. His creativity often comes one action earlier:
- Line-breaking passes
- Increasing speed of progression
- Creating better receival situations for the player who makes the final pass

That distinction is important. Bruno may not consistently record the assist, but his pass can eliminate the opposition midfield and leave another player attacking the defensive line. His willingness to play forward before the obvious passing lane appears is a major part of his creative value.

Bruno also completed 2.97 accurate long balls per 90 (90th percentile) at 60.4% accuracy. It gives us another midfielder capable of changing the point of attack without needing 5+ circulation passes.

Defensive Profile

The other major reason I love the fit is Bruno’s aggression. He enjoys contact, attacks loose touches with real intent and reacts immediately after turnovers. He won 6.16 duels and made 2.27 tackles per 90 in the Premier League, while winning possession in the final third 0.66 times per 90.

His value is clearest when he regains the ball and immediately looks forward. Bruno can turn a defensive action into a vertical pass or diagonal switch before the opposition block reorganises. However, that instinct is not an automatic fit for us.

Arteta’s mid-block is positionally strict. Bruno’s tendency to leave his zone and attack the receiver can either kill the transition or open space behind him if the pressing trigger is wrong. He may therefore need to channel that aggression more selectively. The key adaptation will be aligning his jumps with our pressing triggers without removing the front footed defending that makes him valuable.

There is also a disciplinary cost. Bruno committed 1.65 fouls per 90 and collected six Premier League yellow cards. He can become emotional and occasionally jump into challenges too early. I would still rather manage that aggression than continue lacking it, but its usefulness will depend on how well his pressing decisions align with the structure around him.

Weaknesses

Despite being excellent under pressure, he is not always secure. He was dispossessed 1.69 times per 90 (19th percentile). He can occasionally hold onto possession for too long, force overly ambitious passes or look for soft fouls that aren’t always given.

Further, his duel volume also looks stronger than his efficiency. Winning 6.16 duels per 90 (79th percentile) is impressive, but his overall success rate was 50.5% (38th percentile). He competes constantly, which increases the number of duels he wins, but he is not completely dominant within those situations.

For me his biggest weakness is his aerial ability. Despite being around 6”0, he won only 0.48 aerial duels per 90 (10th percentile) at a dismal 37.1% win rate (15th percentile). He should not be viewed as a reliable aerial outlet or somebody who consistently dominates direct balls.

Bruno is not an explosive recovery athlete either. Gradient Sports rated him at 16.9/100 for athleticism. His data recorded a top speed of just 31.1 kmph and only 5.15 sprints per 90. His transition defending relies more on anticipation, aggression and elite positioning awareness compared to quick recovery speed. If he jumps out and fails to win the ball, the players behind him may have to cover a large space.

There was also a notable drop in his UCL efficiency. His long-ball accuracy fell from 60.4% in the PL to 39.3%, while his duel success dropped to 41.4%. The seven-game sample and Newcastle’s wider performances provide context, but the decline against stronger opposition is still worth noting.

These are genuine limitations rather than deal-breakers, but they should influence the role he is given and the structure Arteta places around him.

Versatility 

Bruno is primarily an #8, but he can operate across the entire midfield. He is comfortable in either half-space, can drop in as the #6 and has the intelligence to adjust his positioning depending on the structure around him.

His best qualities are still maximised as an #8, where he can progress, create and compete higher up the pitch. However, his ability to cover every midfield role gives Arteta valuable flexibility without requiring a major tactical change.

Leadership Note

Bruno’s leadership is also a cool aspect. As we know, Arteta has consistently targeted players with captaincy experience or prominent roles within leadership groups. Bruno captained Newcastle, Rice captained West Ham, while Odegaard captains both Arsenal and Norway.

That would give us a midfield containing 3 players with major leadership experience. Bruno is vocal, aggressive and willing to take responsibility during difficult moments, which is exactly the kind of personality Arteta values in high pressure situations.

Final Verdict

In summary, Bruno Guimaraes is my ideal signing. He is Premier League proven, experienced and complete enough to contribute across every phase. He provides pass-first progression, attacking output, aggression, leadership and the flexibility to operate across our midfield.

The RHS probably maximises his familiarity and may be his individually optimal position. However, my personal preference remains the LHS because that is where I believe he improves our overall balance the most. The concerns surrounding the adaptation to the LHS and his high-risk playstyle are genuine, but I believe they can be managed within the surrounding structure.

A midfield of Rice, Guimaraes and Odegaard would offer technical security, creativity, aggression and personality. It is a concept that seriously excites me.

I cannot wait to see him link up with that midfield play in red and white.

Thank you so much for reading. This was a long one, but there were too many points I felt were worth including. For context, the first draft was over 4,500 words😬

text:
This graph measures not only whether midfielders resist pressure, but how they respond to it: the X-axis shows passes played under pressure per 90, the Y-axis shows attempts to escape through carries or take-ons, while the colour represents success rate.

Bruno Guimarães is the clear top-right outlier. With roughly 16 pressured passes and 14 escape actions per 90, he offers Arsenal something extremely rare: a midfielder who can both attract pressure and eliminate it. Opponents cannot simply lock his passing lanes because he can turn, protect the ball and carry beyond the first presser; equally, they cannot stand off him because he has the volume and quality to distribute through the block. He would become Arsenal’s main pressure magnet and central progression hub.

Martin Ødegaard also sits comfortably above average in both dimensions, producing around ten pressured passes and ten escape attempts per 90. His slightly lower success colour compared with Guimarães and Rice should not automatically be viewed negatively: Ødegaard often receives higher up, in tighter spaces and with less time, where losing the ball is a greater possibility. His role is more aggressive—manipulating the press in the right half-space, combining quickly and creating the free man after drawing opponents towards him.

Declan Rice provides the balance. He records fewer escape actions than Guimarães or Ødegaard, but remains above average in both categories and combines that volume with an excellent success rate. Rice is the stabiliser: he can power away from pressure when space opens, release the ball securely when it does not, and protect Arsenal’s structure behind the attack.

Together, the three would give Arsenal multiple answers to the same press. Guimarães breaks it centrally, Ødegaard manipulates it between the lines, and Rice carries through it while securing the transition. Press one and another becomes free; close the passing lanes and they can escape by carrying.

Martín Zubimendi offers a different solution from the bench. His passing volume under pressure is above average, but his escape volume is clearly below it. If introduced, Arsenal would become less dependent on individual carries and more focused on positional escapes: short combinations, better angles, bounce passes and third-man movements. That profile could be ideal for calming the game and controlling a lead, but it would not reproduce the same individual press-breaking threat provided by Guimarães.
