text:
Malam Hamza, ca. 1847-1849 (Founder of Ningi Emirate)

The Caliph Aliyu Babba of Sokoto required additional revenue to finance his numerous wars and consequently ordered Sarkin Kano Usman dan Dabo to increase taxation. The order was welcomed by Usman, whose father and predecessor, Ibrahim Dabo, had exhausted much of the treasury through his own military campaigns. Moreover, the inflation of cowrie currency had diminished the purchasing power of the tribute being collected. The new and increased taxes, however, generated considerable dissatisfaction among those required to pay them.

The mallams (Islamic scholars) likewise accused the Emirs and their councillors of neglecting their religious obligations, including the construction and maintenance of mosques, in their pursuit of political power and material wealth.

In Tsakuwa, a town southeast of Kano City, a community of Hausa Islamic scholars became a center of opposition to these policies. The mallams established a flourishing weaving and dyeing industry to support themselves and attracted students from across the region. In the mid-1840s, one of these scholars, Malam Hamza, challenged the legitimacy of al-kharāj, the principal land tax, and led a revolt against the kudin ƙasa imposed by the Kano Emirate.

At the end of 1846, approximately sixteen Hausa scholars and their families, led by Malam Hamza, left the Islamic center of Tsakuwa after refusing to pay the kudin ƙasa. They were pursued by Kano forces, having previously enjoyed exemption from the tax before the establishment of Fulani rule.

Hamza's community, or jamāʿa, eventually established itself in the Ningi Mountains, a frontier region surrounded by the Sokoto Caliphate's vassal states, including Kano, Zazzau, Bauchi, Gombe, Jema'are, Misau, Katagum, and Hadejia.

The local population spoke a variety of Benue-Congo and Plateau languages and consisted largely of stateless pagans organized through segmentary lineage systems. Political and religious authority was generally decentralized, with hilltop shrine priests serving as the principal religious authorities.

Malam Hamza was regarded as a walī, a highly accomplished Sufi saint, and was reputed to possess extraordinary spiritual knowledge. He practiced dhikr and was believed to possess knowledge of hidden mysteries, or sirr. According to tradition, he demonstrated spiritual powers that surpassed those of the local priests, enabling him to win the allegiance of various Ningi pagans and inspire them to revolt. With a Muslim scholar at their head, the people of Ningi became less fearful of the reputed supernatural powers of the Muslims of Kano and Bauchi.

Hamza began preaching among the Ningi communities, calling upon them to fight for their freedom. The millenarian character of his preaching is preserved in an oral tradition collected at Dua, in which Hamza is said to have addressed the mountaineers:

"Some people, red people, will be coming, and they will conquer everyone and stop you from fighting one another. They will take power from you. No one will have the right to enslave anyone, nor the right to fight Kano and Bauchi. After the red people, another group will come. They will be black, and they will fight and defeat all."

At the end of 1848, Hamza and his mallams began the process by which they would ultimately transform the decentralized societies around them into a centralized polity, without relying solely upon military conquest. Hamza constructed a mosque, and word of his presence quickly spread throughout the surrounding mountains. He combined Islamic practices with elements of traditional Ningi religious customs, producing an appealing synthesis in which siḥr (magic) occupied a central place.

In the first major confrontation, the mallams and the Buta defeated a force sent from Bauchi, forcing Dan Daura to flee for his life.

Hamza subsequently turned toward broader political action. His messengers spread among the mountaineers the mystical interpretation of his victory. Communities from Burra, Tiffi, Ari, Guda, Badunga, Rabi, Kuluki, and elsewhere came to Hamza. He distributed the spoils of victory among them and offered their leaders positions of authority within his emerging polity. He reportedly told them:

"You have now succeeded because you have found among yourselves a person like me. Come to my fold, and I will deliver you from your obligations to the Fulani. Follow me, and I will save you from the service of these tyrant Fulanis, who impose upon you many duties and demand things that you cannot pay."

As Hamza continued to call upon the mountaineers to revolt against the authority of the Caliphate, his followers increasingly interpreted his teachings through the framework of siḥr, or supernatural power. Stories of his extraordinary abilities spread throughout the region. He was said to be capable of throwing a piece of paper into the air and causing it to remain suspended, mounting a mat that floated in the air, stretching his tongue around his head like a turban, extending his leg to the length of two spears before returning it to its normal size, and even resurrecting dead ants.

According to tradition, Hamza would have someone kill ants and place their bodies in baskets, after which he would cause them to return to life. He would then tell the people:

"Even if the Fulani kill you, that is how I will return your lives to you. Nobody will ever be able to defeat you as long as I am among you."

text:
Postal Service Rule Could Bar Millions From Voting By Mail

NYT Gift Article link
Listen · 10:04 min
30AUG2026
By Reid J. Epstein
https://t.co/PSZ3jKl9Hk
Reporting from Washington

A judge temporarily blocked the agency from refusing to deliver ballots in noncompliant states, which could disproportionately affect Democrats and many battleground elections.

Voting by mail would become much more difficult, if not impossible, for tens of millions of Americans if the U.S. Postal Service is allowed to implement a restrictive rule governing mail voting that President Trump has demanded.

The effects would likely be greater for Democratic voters, who vote by mail in higher numbers than Republicans, and in states where mail voting is universal or nearly so. 

Mail voting may not happen at all in states that resist the Trump administration’s demands for voter data.

The rule would particularly affect people in rural areas and older voters, who tend to cast ballots by mail in greater numbers.

It could also deeply affect states where some of the most competitive races for House, Senate and governor will determine control of Congress and state governments.

Michigan, where 37 percent of votes were cast by mail in 2022, would be one epicenter, with hard-fought statewide contests and multiple battleground House races. 

California, which mails ballots to all voters, is expected to be central to Democratic efforts to win a majority in the House.

The rule is being challenged in several lawsuits, and it is on hold temporarily following a federal judge’s ruling on Thursday. 

The administration is appealing. 

Even if the Postal Service is permitted to proceed, it is unclear that it would have time to implement the plan ahead of an election that is fewer than 70 days away.

For instance, the rule requires states to upload a list of voters to a federal mail ballot portal that is not yet online. 

Nearly two dozen Democratic-led states and Washington, D.C., have sued to block the proposed rule and said they will not comply with it.

If the agency were to move ahead, state and local officials would shoulder enormous costs in what would need to be a herculean effort to prepare election offices and educate voters in time for the midterm elections in November.

The most dramatic aspect of the proposed rule is a plan to deny services for election mail entirely in states that do not turn over voter data, which federal officials say they want to use to identify noncitizens on state voter rolls. 

The policy would upend mail voting in any state that does not comply, but the effects would be measurably greater in the smaller number of states that rely heavily on mail voting.

More than one in three Democrats voted by mail in 2024, compared with about one in four Republicans, according to estimates by the States United Democracy Center, which examined voting data in 32 states where it was available.

“It’s not that complicated,” said Marc Elias, the Democratic election lawyer, who said the new policy was a blatant effort to disenfranchise Democrats. 

“The administration knows that Democrats are more likely to vote by mail than Republicans. 

Donald Trump has demonized voting by mail and made that differential even greater.”

Election administrators fear chaos
It is far from certain that the rule could be implemented this year, given outstanding legal and logistical challenges with fewer than 10 weeks before Election Day. 

North Carolina, where a highly competitive Senate race could help determine control of the chamber, is set to mail ballots to some voters starting next week. 

More states will soon follow.

President Trump, who voted by mail himself in Florida’s primary this month, created the current uncertainty by signing an executive order in March that called on the Department of Homeland Security to compile state-by-state citizenship lists that could be used to help determine voter eligibility.

Last week, the Supreme Court ruled that the lawsuit was premature because the Postal Service had not yet finalized its rule. 

Now that the agency has done so, though, and a lower court has weighed in, the justices will likely be asked to rule again in the coming weeks, this time on the constitutionality of the plan.

Elections officials from both parties have said that forcing the counties and municipalities that run the nation’s elections to implement new rules in such a short time frame would inject chaos into the nation’s voting processes and could halt mail voting altogether.

Small-town clerks would have to purchase new machines to print the bar codes required under the new rule. 

All mail ballots 

— including some that in the past may have been hand-delivered from a local elections official to the local post office — 

would now have to be routed through a big-city mail sorting center, since only major hubs are able to process the new bar codes.

“People need to understand the changing of an election is somewhat like changing the course of an aircraft carrier. 

You can’t do it on short notice,” said Alan Hays, a supervisor of elections and a Republican in Lake County, Fla., where Mr. Trump received 62 percent of the vote in 2024. 

“Putting such an awesome responsibility on the U.S. Postal Service, with the track record that organization has, on such a short notice is unwise at best.”

The effects would vary across jurisdictions.

In Wisconsin, throwing a wrench into mail voting would cause far more chaos in the state’s rural communities than in its more liberal cities, said Ann Jacobs, a Democratic member of the Wisconsin Elections Commission.

Cities would be able to extend in-person early-voting hours to accommodate a decrease in mail voting, while the state’s far-flung townships would likely have fewer resources and staff to extend voting hours.

“We have clerks who are running the elections out of their homes until Election Day,” Ms. Jacobs said.

Michigan: a case study
No state in the country is home to more critical elections this year or a wider partisan gap in mail voting than Michigan.

The state will administer one of the nation’s most competitive Senate races, a contest that is critical to Democratic hopes of taking back control of the chamber. 

It also has what is expected to be hard-fought, open-seat elections for governor and other statewide offices, along with four battleground House races. 
Majority control of both chambers of the narrowly divided Michigan Legislature is also up for grabs.

Nearly 2 million Michiganders are now on the state’s permanent mail voting list, meaning that each election, officials automatically mail them ballots. 

And while Michigan voters do not register by party, there is a sizable gap between the number of votes for Democratic candidates and those for Republicans that are processed by mail, according to an analysis by the MIT Election Data and Science Lab.

In the last midterm election in 2022, about 57 percent of ballots cast for Democrats arrived by mail, compared with just 37 percent ballots cast for Republicans, MIT found. 

The gap was more pronounced in 2024, when Mr. Trump was on the ballot and regularly denounced mail voting on the campaign trail. 

That year, 60 percent of votes for then-Vice President Kamala Harris arrived by mail, compared with 34 percent of votes for Mr. Trump.

“Anything that obstructs a voter’s ability to vote hurts Democrats in Michigan,” said Lon Johnson, a former chairman of the Michigan Democratic Party. 

“The more complications you have, the more people become suspect, the more they fall into Trump’s line of argument that voting and democracy is a system can be rigged.”

Jim Runestad, a state senator and the chairman of the Michigan Republican Party, said he was not aware of any discussions with Republican campaigns in the state about how they might alter their get-out-the-vote strategy if the rules on mail ballots changed before Election Day.

Mr. Runestad, who said he receives his ballot in the mail and typically returns it to his municipal clerk’s office, said he would prefer that people be required to vote in person on Election Day.

“I know that Republicans are more and more turning to mail-in voting in much larger numbers than they ever have before,” he said. 

“What ought to be of concern across the board for everyone is to make sure that there is no mischief.”

The effects could also be profound in the eight states, as well as Washington, D.C., that mail ballots to all voters. 

Washington State has done away with in-person voting entirely. 

Once voters receive their ballots in the mail, they can either deposit them in a drop box, drop them at a voting center or send them back through the Postal Service.

Even in states that still offer polling locations, Mr. Trump’s rules could foment chaos for election administrators who have built systems around mail balloting. 

Confusion is likely among voters who have not visited a polling place in years.

In Arizona, where about 80 percent of voters received mail ballots in the last midterm election in 2022, Adrian Fontes, the secretary of state, said he was planning for as much as 85 percent this year. 

Mr. Fontes, a Democrat, predicted that restricting mail voting in Arizona would create a backlash from Republican retirees who have long voted by mail.

The MIT analysis found that an estimated 62 percent of Arizona Republicans voted by mail in 2024, compared with 75 percent of Democrats.

“Arizona would no longer be a battleground state,” said Mr. Fontes, who is up for re-election this year. 

“It would turn deep, dark blue.

 Mail voting was created by Republicans, promoted by Republicans, advanced by Republicans and that’s how Republican voters like to vote. 

You think they want that convenience and that security taken away from them? 

Hell no.”

Reid J. Epstein is a Times reporter covering campaigns and elections from Washington.

Reporting from Washington

A judge temporarily blocked the agency from refusing to deliver ballots in noncompliant states, which could disproportionately affect Democrats and many battleground elections.

Voting by mail would become much more difficult, if not impossible, for tens of millions of Americans if the U.S. Postal Service is allowed to implement a restrictive rule governing mail voting that President Trump has demanded.

The effects would likely be greater for Democratic voters, who vote by mail in higher numbers than Republicans, and in states where mail voting is universal or nearly so. 

Mail voting may not happen at all in states that resist the Trump administration’s demands for voter data.

The rule would particularly affect people in rural areas and older voters, who tend to cast ballots by mail in greater numbers.

It could also deeply affect states where some of the most competitive races for House, Senate and governor will determine control of Congress and state governments.

Michigan, where 37 percent of votes were cast by mail in 2022, would be one epicenter, with hard-fought statewide contests and multiple battleground House races. 

California, which mails ballots to all voters, is expected to be central to Democratic efforts to win a majority in the House.

The rule is being challenged in several lawsuits, and it is on hold temporarily following a federal judge’s ruling on Thursday. 

The administration is appealing. 

Even if the Postal Service is permitted to proceed, it is unclear that it would have time to implement the plan ahead of an election that is fewer than 70 days away.

For instance, the rule requires states to upload a list of voters to a federal mail ballot portal that is not yet online. 

Nearly two dozen Democratic-led states and Washington, D.C., have sued to block the proposed rule and said they will not comply with it.

If the agency were to move ahead, state and local officials would shoulder enormous costs in what would need to be a herculean effort to prepare election offices and educate voters in time for the midterm elections in November.

The most dramatic aspect of the proposed rule is a plan to deny services for election mail entirely in states that do not turn over voter data, which federal officials say they want to use to identify noncitizens on state voter rolls. 

The policy would upend mail voting in any state that does not comply, but the effects would be measurably greater in the smaller number of states that rely heavily on mail voting.

More than one in three Democrats voted by mail in 2024, compared with about one in four Republicans, according to estimates by the States United Democracy Center, which examined voting data in 32 states where it was available.

“It’s not that complicated,” said Marc Elias, the Democratic election lawyer, who said the new policy was a blatant effort to disenfranchise Democrats. 

“The administration knows that Democrats are more likely to vote by mail than Republicans. 

Donald Trump has demonized voting by mail and made that differential even greater.”

Election administrators fear chaos
It is far from certain that the rule could be implemented this year, given outstanding legal and logistical challenges with fewer than 10 weeks before Election Day. 

North Carolina, where a highly competitive Senate race could help determine control of the chamber, is set to mail ballots to some voters starting next week. 

More states will soon follow.

President Trump, who voted by mail himself in Florida’s primary this month, created the current uncertainty by signing an executive order in March that called on the Department of Homeland Security to compile state-by-state citizenship lists that could be used to help determine voter eligibility.

Last week, the Supreme Court ruled that the lawsuit was premature because the Postal Service had not yet finalized its rule. 

Now that the agency has done so, though, and a lower court has weighed in, the justices will likely be asked to rule again in the coming weeks, this time on the constitutionality of the plan.

Elections officials from both parties have said that forcing the counties and municipalities that run the nation’s elections to implement new rules in such a short time frame would inject chaos into the nation’s voting processes and could halt mail voting altogether.

Small-town clerks would have to purchase new machines to print the bar codes required under the new rule. 

All mail ballots 

— including some that in the past may have been hand-delivered from a local elections official to the local post office — 

would now have to be routed through a big-city mail sorting center, since only major hubs are able to process the new bar codes.

“People need to understand the changing of an election is somewhat like changing the course of an aircraft carrier. 

You can’t do it on short notice,” said Alan Hays, a supervisor of elections and a Republican in Lake County, Fla., where Mr. Trump received 62 percent of the vote in 2024. 

“Putting such an awesome responsibility on the U.S. Postal Service, with the track record that organization has, on such a short notice is unwise at best.”

The effects would vary across jurisdictions.

In Wisconsin, throwing a wrench into mail voting would cause far more chaos in the state’s rural communities than in its more liberal cities, said Ann Jacobs, a Democratic member of the Wisconsin Elections Commission.

Cities would be able to extend in-person early-voting hours to accommodate a decrease in mail voting, while the state’s far-flung townships would likely have fewer resources and staff to extend voting hours.

“We have clerks who are running the elections out of their homes until Election Day,” Ms. Jacobs said.

Michigan: a case study
No state in the country is home to more critical elections this year or a wider partisan gap in mail voting than Michigan.

The state will administer one of the nation’s most competitive Senate races, a contest that is critical to Democratic hopes of taking back control of the chamber. 

It also has what is expected to be hard-fought, open-seat elections for governor and other statewide offices, along with four battleground House races. 
Majority control of both chambers of the narrowly divided Michigan Legislature is also up for grabs.

Nearly 2 million Michiganders are now on the state’s permanent mail voting list, meaning that each election, officials automatically mail them ballots. 

And while Michigan voters do not register by party, there is a sizable gap between the number of votes for Democratic candidates and those for Republicans that are processed by mail, according to an analysis by the MIT Election Data and Science Lab.

In the last midterm election in 2022, about 57 percent of ballots cast for Democrats arrived by mail, compared with just 37 percent ballots cast for Republicans, MIT found. 

The gap was more pronounced in 2024, when Mr. Trump was on the ballot and regularly denounced mail voting on the campaign trail. 

That year, 60 percent of votes for then-Vice President Kamala Harris arrived by mail, compared with 34 percent of votes for Mr. Trump.

“Anything that obstructs a voter’s ability to vote hurts Democrats in Michigan,” said Lon Johnson, a former chairman of the Michigan Democratic Party. 

“The more complications you have, the more people become suspect, the more they fall into Trump’s line of argument that voting and democracy is a system can be rigged.”

Jim Runestad, a state senator and the chairman of the Michigan Republican Party, said he was not aware of any discussions with Republican campaigns in the state about how they might alter their get-out-the-vote strategy if the rules on mail ballots changed before Election Day.

Mr. Runestad, who said he receives his ballot in the mail and typically returns it to his municipal clerk’s office, said he would prefer that people be required to vote in person on Election Day.

“I know that Republicans are more and more turning to mail-in voting in much larger numbers than they ever have before,” he said. 

“What ought to be of concern across the board for everyone is to make sure that there is no mischief.”

The effects could also be profound in the eight states, as well as Washington, D.C., that mail ballots to all voters. 

Washington State has done away with in-person voting entirely. 

Once voters receive their ballots in the mail, they can either deposit them in a drop box, drop them at a voting center or send them back through the Postal Service.

Even in states that still offer polling locations, Mr. Trump’s rules could foment chaos for election administrators who have built systems around mail balloting. 

Confusion is likely among voters who have not visited a polling place in years.

In Arizona, where about 80 percent of voters received mail ballots in the last midterm election in 2022, Adrian Fontes, the secretary of state, said he was planning for as much as 85 percent this year. 

Mr. Fontes, a Democrat, predicted that restricting mail voting in Arizona would create a backlash from Republican retirees who have long voted by mail.

The MIT analysis found that an estimated 62 percent of Arizona Republicans voted by mail in 2024, compared with 75 percent of Democrats.

“Arizona would no longer be a battleground state,” said Mr. Fontes, who is up for re-election this year. 

“It would turn deep, dark blue.

 Mail voting was created by Republicans, promoted by Republicans, advanced by Republicans and that’s how Republican voters like to vote. 

You think they want that convenience and that security taken away from them? 

Hell no.”

Reid J. Epstein is a Times reporter covering campaigns and elections from Washington.

IN DEPTH

‘Flagrant targeting’

Grandmothers, landscapers, even kids, swept into Florida’s shadowy immigration database

ALICE HERMAN

Suncoast Searchlight

MICHAEL BARFIELD

Florida Trident

YOUN-JOO PARK WGCU

When a Manatee County Sheriff ’s deputy pulled over Jean Gustave in September, the 45-yearold Haitian man had temporary protected status, offering him legal protection from detention and deportation.

An investigation by Matthew Blackwell, the deputy who pulled him over for an alleged tag violation, later found no probable cause. Gustave was not charged or arrested that night.

But authorities kept him on the side of the road in Bradenton as they snapped his photo, took down his personal information and uploaded it to a database run by the Florida Department of Law Enforcement.

Across Florida, law enforcement officers have been asked to gather names, photographs, addresses and other personal information about people they suspect may be in the country without authorization and upload them to a centralized surveillance database during the course of their routine job duties.

The database debuted in August 2025 as Florida created the State Board of Immigration Enforcement and expanded the role of state and local police in immigration enforcement. FDLE developed the reporting system for local agencies to log their “suspected unauthorized alien encounters” into the database, which has since swelled to more than 30,000 entries.

A review of the surveillance database shows officers routinely submitted the names of individuals for whom they could not confirm even basic citizenship details — as well as the names of hundreds of minors.

Because officers are encouraged to report people they merely suspect may be undocumented, attorneys and immigration experts said the system risks sweeping in people with legal status.

The vast majority also had no known criminal background.

• A 36-year-old man from Guatemala who worked for a lawn care service.

• A 35-year-old construction worker from Mexico.

• And a 52-year-old grandmother from Nicaragua who worked for a painting company.

Deputies noted no prior convictions associated with these individuals, who represent just a few examples of the entries in the database.

Florida officials have revealed only fragments of the database publicly and did not return reporters’ questions about how the information is used, how long it is retained and with whom it is shared.

But using web-scraping techniques, reporters were able to pull far more from the state’s own online dashboard than officials had disclosed — providing the most detailed look yet at the reach of Florida’s expanding immigration surveillance system.

Over the course of 10 weeks, Suncoast Searchlight, Florida Trident and WGCU collected and reviewed the data from Florida’s State Board of Immigration Enforcement dashboard, analyzed more than 10,000 consecutive reports from a four-anda- half month period of individual encounters, observed a traffic stop-turned-immigration investigation, spent days on the ground in the most affected communities, obtained and reviewed public records on local immigration enforcement, and interviewed civil rights attorneys and people swept into the system.

Among the findings:

• Florida doesn’t require agencies to vet the data before officers

More IMMIGRATION | A12
zoom-in

Since Florida ramped up its immigration enforcement efforts, routine traffic stops may now lead to ICE detention and deportation. The above stop took place on Palm Beach Boulevard by a Lee County Sheriff’s Office deputy.

PHOTO BY YOUN-JOO PARK, WGCU
zoom-in

SOURCE: DATA FROM THE FLORIDA STATE BOARD OF IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT; ANALYZED BY SUNCOAST SEARCHLIGHT, FLORIDA TRIDENT AND WGCU

Immigration/

from A1

submit it. And agencies have obtained millions of dollars in immigration enforcement grants for broader surveillance technologies like Flock cameras as part of an initiative tied to the reporting effort.

• The dragnet is seemingly indiscriminate. Local and federal authorities have promised their immigration enforcement targets “the worst of the worst.” But in Florida, the vast majority of people who officers encountered and entered into the database were not serious criminals. More than 80% had no known criminal record at all.

• The encounters have targeted working-age Latino men. Florida deportations and detentions have pulled breadwinners away from families — some of whom now struggle to pay for rent, medical bills and even food. Nine out of 10 people listed in the database are men. In many cases, authorities didn’t even verify suspects’ citizenship status with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement before adding their names to the list.

• Only officers trained by the federal government are supposed to conduct immigration enforcement. But records show police agencies have allowed untrained officers to hold people on the side of the road for ICE, a practice attorneys said is illegal.

“The idea that a (local) law enforcement officer could inquire into somebody’s immigration status and then land on some sort of probable cause or reasonable suspicion that the person’s removable from the country is really outlandish,” said Paul Chavez, a civil rights attorney and director of litigation for Americans for Immigrant Justice.

Florida’s immigration enforcement dashboard only offers a glimpse at overall enforcement: it does not include, for example, operations conducted by ICE in the state without local agencies’ involvement. It does not show whether individuals were ultimately deported. And police do not always submit information quickly — like Florida Highway Patrol, which led the state in immigration encounters before June 30, but has not updated its data since.

What the database offers is a glimpse into Florida’s massive street-level immigration enforcement push — and who it has targeted.

In response to an inquiry about the database, ICE directed reporters to FDLE, which also did not return requests for an interview or answer emailed questions about the database.

Months after his encounter with Manatee County sheriff ’s deputies, Gustave’s cellphone was disconnected. A reporter went looking for him at the Bradenton mobile home park where records indicated he lived — a sprawling gravel lot with rows of trailers packed tightly together. No one answered the door.

A neighbor pulled up in his car, and when asked for Gustave’s whereabouts, he said Gustave wasn’t there anymore.

He had been deported.

HOW AN IMMIGRATION SURVEILLANCE DATABASE WAS SPAWNED

One by one, law enforcement officials from across Florida logged into a video conference call on a Thursday afternoon in late August 2025. Nearly 100 were there by the time Melissa Bujeda, an FDLE official coordinating some of the state’s immigration work, began explaining the new task Florida wanted them to take on.

It might be “cumbersome,” she warned.

In addition to their regular workload, she told the members of the Florida Police Chiefs Association that all law enforcement agencies — from campus police to the state Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission — would be required to closely document their immigration enforcement efforts under a Florida law that passed early last year.

Every time an officer encountered an individual they simply suspected of lacking legal status in the United States, they would be required to photograph that person and take down key information about them, including their home address, vehicle make and model, phone number and employer.

At the time of Bujeda’s presentation, a recording of which reporters obtained, law enforcement officers had already reported more than 400 encounters since the database soft launched earlier that month — but FDLE was planning to scale up by getting agencies across the state to submit reports, a prerequisite for them to receive special grant dollars for immigration enforcement.

Bujeda emphasized that the state wanted to make submissions as easy as possible for local officers.

With the click of a button, she said, entries are “immediately sent into our database” — with no supervisory review required.

The submission form states an officer needs only “reasonable suspicion” that someone might be in the country without authorization to place their name, photograph and personal details into the state database without a second set of eyes verifying the information or the basis for including them.

Even when agencies have no encounters, they must submit monthly reports. “You don’t want goose eggs,” said Pinellas Sheriff Bob Gualtieri, who sits on the State Immigration Board, at another statewide presentation to law enforcement agencies across Florida in September 2025. “You don’t want to be that agency that’s dead for months (with) zeros as far as immigration investigations.”

He added that any official who violated the new statute “is subject to action by the governor, including potential suspension from office.”

The reporting system is an extension of Florida’s wide-reaching partnerships between local law enforcement agencies and ICE under ICE’s 287(g) program. Named for a section of federal immigration law, the program allows state and local law enforcement agencies to perform limited immigration functions, like holding people in local jails for ICE. The agency’s “task force” model allows local law officials who have completed federal training to conduct immigration enforcement in the streets.

Under Gov. Ron DeSantis, Florida has embraced the program more aggressively than perhaps any other state in the country, with more than 9,000 “designated immigration officers” credentialed by ICE across the Sunshine State.

But records show the reach of the state’s immigration crackdown extends beyond those federally trained officers — through policies allowing even untrained officers to hold individuals on behalf of ICE and penalties for agencies that do not comply.

In Pinellas County, for example, Gualtieri issued a memo to his deputies in February 2025 stating that if any officer encounters a person during a traffic stop matching an individual with an ICE warrant, they can “request an ICE officer come to the scene to arrest the individual” and wait up to an hour for federal agents to arrive.

Gualtieri forwarded the memo — first reported by Creative Loafing Tampa Bay — to 10 chiefs of police in Pinellas County.

An updated policy issued by Gualtieri’s office seven months later clarifies that ICE or a trained local officer must respond “immediately” when a non-credentialed officer calls.

When reached by a reporter, Gualtieri declined to answer specific questions about the practice.

Similar guidance shared with police across the state by the Florida Police Chiefs Association states that non-immigration officers can hold people they determine have an ICE warrant for a period of time “determined by their respective agency.”

Attorneys and experts in policing told reporters it is illegal for non-federalized officers to extend a traffic stop to hold people for ICE.

“It’s not legal because immigration enforcement is fully within the realm of the federal government,” said Chavez, of Americans for Immigrant Justice.

A non-credentialed officer “holding somebody for immigration purposes is wholly unlawful,” he said. “You can’t pull somebody over and then hold them there past the time they would have otherwise been released.”

‘WORST OF THE WORST’

On Oct. 20, former Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem stood in front of a table in a federal field office in Bradenton piled with guns and bags of white powder. Behind the display stood two photos of men purportedly arrested for homicide and incest.

“I want to speak directly to the American people today, and remind them and recall the fact that we are focused on the worst of the worst,” Noem said. “We’re not going to let individuals terrorize our streets anymore, and we’re not going to let them make victims of families that live in this country.”

But a review of Florida’s immigration enforcement dashboard contradicts those claims.

In the nearly five months of data reporters reviewed, 8 in 10 of local police encounters targeted individuals with no known criminal record.

Even some Florida officials have expressed worry about the impact of immigration arrests on law-abiding community members.

People who are “living the American dream and are being very productive and doing good in this country” should have a clear pathway to legal status, Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said during a meeting of the State Immigration Enforcement Council earlier this year.

Federal agents’ workplace raids and neighborhood sweeps, some members of the council said, could cast too wide a net.

Most people who appear in the Florida database share two things in common: They are of working age. And the vast majority — roughly 90% — are men.

The detention and deportation of working men has become so widespread in Lee County that local volunteers have coalesced specifically around the issue.

Sigfredo Hernandez, a local retiree, has helped mobilize volunteers in Bonita Springs to support women whose partners have been detained or deported — a group he refers to as “ICE widows.” The abrupt loss of a working family member’s income has left many struggling to find the housing — or even food — their families need to survive.

“If they take your breadwinner away,” Hernandez said, “you go from (some) amount of income to zero in a hurry.”

Nancy, a mother of two, moved into a one-bedroom trailer with her children after her husband was detained and deported to Guatemala. She asked reporters to withhold her last name for fear of being targeted herself.

“With this check, I’ll buy diapers and food,” said Nancy, in Spanish. She paused and swung her freezer door open, which was empty, save for two pieces of frozen chicken. “We don’t have anything.”

The grassroots group has begun distributing checks directly to the women through an informal program that Hernandez said has drawn so much interest the volunteers have had to consider who to prioritize first.

“We have to decide how we’re going to ration the money,” Hernandez said. “Some families have greater needs than others, like if they have babies and the mother cannot work.”

EXPERTS RAISE RACIAL PROFILING CONCERNS

Civil rights advocates warn Florida’s immigration operations have opened the door to abuse by allowing officers to upload the information of people they merely suspect of lacking legal status.

Federal authorities previously abandoned the task force model nationwide in 2012 amid allegations of widespread racial profiling — most notably in Maricopa County, Arizona, where former Sheriff Joe Arpaio faced a high-profile lawsuit that found his office had profiled Latinos and violated their Fourth Amendment protections against warrantless search and seizure.

In a 2013 ruling, a federal judge found that Arpaio’s office had used “traffic stops as a pretext,” patrolling Latino neighborhoods to catch people officers thought might lack legal status.

Implementing court-mandated reforms in the wake of that litigation has cost Maricopa County more than $300 million. Observers there say that the widespread resurrection of the task force model under Trump’s second term could prove a liability for local law enforcement agencies across the country that participate.

Amy Godshall, an immigrants’ rights attorney with the American Civil Liberties Union of Florida, said she believes that is already happening in Florida.

A review of the database shows police in Florida are frequently unable to confirm basic details about the individuals they report.

In nearly 330 cases in the last year, police officers indicated that they did not know the country of origin of individuals whose names were uploaded, and in more than 40% of cases reviewed by reporters, officers said they had not confirmed suspects’ citizenship with ICE.

Through a legal observer program, Godshall said the ACLU has received dozens of allegations of profiling by police and sheriffs’ deputies using the 287(g) task force model.

“People are pulled over for pretextual traffic stop reasons, and then the officers ask them immigration questions and call ICE and say, ‘Hey, ICE, do you want this person?’” said Godshall. In some cases, people may be detained on the side of the road for more than an hour while police officers wait for federal agents to get involved.

“People’s rights are being violated in a variety of ways throughout the enactment of these 287(g) agreements,” she said.

DHS did not respond to questions about how the agency safeguards against racial profiling in its 287(g) task force program.

Godshall blamed, in part, the level of training that local officers receive when they become certified to conduct immigration enforcement under the task force model. Compared to federal officers, local police have more limited legal knowledge and experience — and under Trump’s second administration, the Department of Homeland Security has fast-tracked training for local officers.

The task force model “historically required extensive in-person training in Charleston, S.C.,” according to a presentation Gualtieri prepared for Florida’s State Immigration Enforcement Council. Now, it is available through a 40-hour online program.

MORE MONEY, MORE SURVEILLANCE

Among the more than 23 million people who live in Florida, census data suggest that undocumented immigrants make up about 5% or less.

But efforts to crack down on people without legal status in the Sunshine State could have broader- reaching consequences as agencies obtain millions of dollars in immigration grant funding for surveillance technologies like Flock cameras, eyeball scanners and artificial intelligence tools.

During the most recent round of state funding for immigration enforcement in June, 25 local agencies received money to purchase Peregrine software, an AI-driven data analysis tool modeled after the controversial surveillance company Palantir.

In its application for state funding, Marion County officials wrote that Peregrine would allow law enforcement officers to conduct “rapid searches across databases to build profiles on individuals by accessing personal data through public and private sources.”

Peregrine has said it maintains strict security protocols to protect the data agencies collect, but civil liberties advocates warn the technology could erode individuals’ privacy.

The city of Pensacola got funding to train officers on Cellebrite, a company that specializes in extracting data from devices like cellphones. Other agencies received funding for iris scanners, automated license plate readers and mobile surveillance towers.

Lee County, which has reported more encounters than any other local agency, has received more funding, too — netting more than $10 million in state grants.

Lauren Bonds, the executive director of the nonprofit National Police Accountability Project, said that even individuals who have legal status — or aren’t immigrants at all — should pay attention to Florida’s surveillance efforts, including the FDLE database.

“It’s hard,” Bonds said, “with any of these types of surveillance … to really keep it exclusive to immigrants and people who are non-citizens, because it’s just too broad.”

“This kind of flagrant targeting and categorizing of people,” she added, referring to the Florida database. “It’s not something I would have expected to see in America.”

This story was collaboratively reported and produced by Suncoast Searchlight, Florida Trident and WGCU, nonprofit newsrooms serving communities across Florida.

text:
Trump Targets Big Meatpackers, Moves to Expand Ranchers’ Ability to Process Their Own Beef

WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump says his administration is preparing legal action aimed at giving American farmers and ranchers greater ability to process their own livestock and reducing their dependence on the nation’s largest meatpacking companies.

In an Aug. 28 Truth Social post, Trump said farmers and ranchers have faced problems for years with what he called the “Big Processors,” arguing that the highly concentrated industry has put producers at a disadvantage.

“There are, essentially, 4 of them, a very non competitive number,” Trump wrote, before announcing that he was “authorizing legal documents to be drawn” to give farmers and ranchers the right to “PROCESS THEIR OWN FOOD.”

The four companies that dominate U.S. beef processing are JBS USA, Tyson Foods, Cargill and National Beef Packing Co. The four account for roughly 80% to 85% of the nation’s fed-cattle slaughter market, a level of concentration that has drawn scrutiny from ranching organizations, lawmakers and federal regulators for years.

Trump also pointed to foreign ownership within the industry. JBS USA is part of Brazil-based JBS S.A., while National Beef is majority-owned by Brazilian company Marfrig Global Foods. Tyson and Cargill are U.S.-based companies.

The president’s announcement does not mean ranchers can immediately begin slaughtering cattle and selling the meat commercially without inspection. Under existing federal law, livestock producers can process animals for their own household use under certain exemptions, but meat offered for commercial sale generally must be slaughtered and processed under federal inspection or an approved state inspection system.

Exactly how the Trump administration intends to change those requirements remains to be seen. The legal documents referenced by the president have not yet established a new nationwide exemption for commercially sold meat.

Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins indicated the administration is preparing a broader package of changes intended to help independent producers and smaller processors, including efforts to reduce regulatory barriers and expand opportunities for ranchers to sell meat across state lines.

The initiative comes as the U.S. Department of Agriculture is also attempting to increase competition in the beef-processing industry. USDA recently launched the Strengthening Processing for U.S. Ranchers program, known as SPUR, which provides up to $500 million to expand independent meat-processing capacity. The nation’s four dominant beef processors are excluded from receiving funding through the program.

For cattle-producing states such as Arizona, the details of the administration’s proposal could be significant. Smaller and rural producers frequently must transport livestock long distances to federally inspected processing facilities. Increasing access to local processing — particularly if new rules expand direct-to-consumer or interstate sales — could provide ranchers with additional options for getting their beef to market.

Supporters of expanding local processing have long argued that more competition could allow ranchers to retain a greater share of the value of the cattle they raise while strengthening local food systems. Food-safety and industry groups, however, are expected to closely scrutinize any changes to federal inspection requirements.

Trump said he expects the effort to move quickly.

“This should move quickly,” the president wrote.

For ranchers, the most important details are still ahead: who will qualify, what inspection standards will apply, whether meat processed under the new framework can cross state lines, and whether producers will be permitted to sell directly to consumers, restaurants and retailers.

Those answers will determine whether Trump’s announcement represents a limited regulatory change.

text:
Small Town Musings

Jason (my husband)'s hometown is called Wilkes-Barre, located in northeastern Pennsylvania, USA. Across a small river from Wilkes-Barre lies a place called Kingston. When we first moved there from Arizona last year, I set up the warehouse in Kingston.

At the beginning of this year, I moved again, but kept the warehouse in Kingston to cut down on operating costs.

So, I've been staying at home in New Jersey with the kids while remotely monitoring operations. Every couple of weeks, I drive two and a half hours back to Pennsylvania on the weekend. The main purpose: to head back to the warehouse and oversee things.

Jason's whole family is still back in his hometown, and I get along well with them—we all respect each other—and of course, I'd always be happy to see them whenever be back . But if it weren't for work, I definitely wouldn't go back so often. For one thing, I don't enjoy long drives; for another, the small town really doesn't have much to draw me in.

The town is a faded old coal mining area, said to have been bustling and glorious over a hundred years ago. There are classical churches built by early European immigrants, each with distinctive national flavors, plus old mansions and ancient bridges with triumphal arch styles. I remember when I first arrived, I excitedly dubbed the downtown area "some corner of Paris." But starting in the 1950s, with the city's coal mines no longer viable and few businesses or job opportunities left, most of the young, educated folks headed out. The population plummeted and shifted dramatically.

These days, the grand old mansions aren't always inhabited or guarded, the city streets are nearly empty of pedestrians, the roads and infrastructure in every district are outdated and rundown, shabby. Everywhere is perpetually overcast and gray, vast expanses left barren and desolate. All you see scattered around are funeral homes and nursing homes (since so many of the residents are elderly). It's all so desolate and lifeless that it sends a chill down your spine.

Every time I go back, I hope to catch a glimpse of some change or a bit of hustle and bustle. Sadly, what meets my eyes is still just that same gray haze, dullness , silence, and waste.

(I come from a small place myself, not to be too negative, but I'm just stating it like I see it ~)

Yet, for all its decline, the small town draws in many new Latin American immigrants from the New York and New Jersey areas, for its low cost of living and cheap expenses. Those newcomers have become the main force there. So, nearby, you'll find a scattering of restaurants and shops dotted among the little towns.

Next to Kingston, where the warehouse is, there's a town called Edwardsville with a Chinese restaurant named Apple Fusion. The restaurant is not big, very simple and unpretentious, but it's always packed, mostly with takeout. The owner is a kind and affable Chinese fellow.

I remember the first time I met the owner—that warmth and excitement... Just imagine: we'd just moved from the lively Chinese community in Arizona to a place where you hardly see a Chinese face. How disheartening. Being able to chat in Chinese with the owner at the restaurant felt so heartwarming and lucky.

The owner's last name is Li, about my age, from Fujian. He's incredibly kind. When I first moved in and was frustrated at not finding authentic Chinese food, I'd ask every time I went to eat if they could whip up some everyday home-style dishes. Mr. Li always warmly made whatever they ate at home themselves whenever I showed up, often bringing out to table huge bowls of noodles soup and tasty little side dishes.

Mr. Li is also super generous—after every meal, he'd give me a bunch of chives they'd grown in their own yard. He'd pick them fresh from the backyard behind the restaurant, stuff a big bag full, insist I take it, and bade me how to store them properly. His enthusiasm was overwhelming; I couldn't say no.

Our warehouse has high staff turnover and needs constant hiring, and I was griping about how tough recruiting was. One day, when I vented to him, he just offered to post a help-wanted sign in his restaurant. And just like that, the thorny problem was solved.

See, the small town might feel empty and devoid of energy, but it has its warm moments too—and that warmth shows up only in these little things, and in the people and encounters that come out of nowhere.

The world is vast, environments so varied—what we can do is just adapt and blend in, connecting with folks around us as best we can.

Daily life is inherently plain and mundane beyond words, but hold onto gratitude always. Cherish the joy, speak mindfully, act with care.

The photo is from my last visit: stir-fried water spinach and seafood noodles made by Mr. Li :)

Thanks everyone, for continuing to share these little slices of life with you by the Hudson River, as always.

Over the last decade, prior to my dismissal from my tenured faculty position, I applied for the following leadership positions @uarizona:

1. Vice Provost for Faculty Affairs (2018) 
2. Dean of the College of Social and Behavioral Sciences (2022)
3. Dean of the W. Franke Honors College (2023)
4. Associate Dean, College of Social Behavioral Sciences (2023)
5. Associate Graduate Dean of Academic Services (2025)
6. Head of the English Department (2023)
7. Interim Head of the English Department (2022)
8. Director of RCTE x 4 times  (2016, 2018, 2020, and 2023)
9. Associate Head of the English Department (2023) 
10. Interim Director of Undergraduate Studies (2020)
11. Direct of @arizona Writing Program (2020)
12. Interim Director of @uarizona Writing Program (2020)

I lost out on several positions to people who were one full rank below me, or not even on the tenure-track. In one instance, one of these associate professors served as department head when university rules prohibit that absent a higher admin waiver, which was not provided.  

I received the Rhetoric, Composition, and Teaching of English  directorship in 2023, when no one else was available—even then, just barely. Here was one comment about me in the Qualtrics poll for the English Department Associate Head position:

“For several of the same reasons many did not support Matthew becoming the Department Head, I don't believe that he has an inclusive vision for the Department, especially in regard to CT Faculty.”

Wonder what “inclusive vision” means here.

Personality problems  or DEI gone wild?

According to the @uarizona, I had the following issues:

1. “Abraham is difficult to work with. We can produce 10-15 people who will attest to this”;
 
2. “Abraham has targeted and harassed faculty and graduate students in his own program because of their race and gender”;
 
3. “All proper procedures were followed in the hiring process for the admin positions he applied for and sought”;
 
4. “Why didn’t Abraham go to the Office of Equity and Diversify to report his concerns of mistreatment”?
 
5. “Abraham’s leadership philosophy is different than ours and those who have received the positions he vied for. We are happy with our current leaders”;
 
6. “Abraham has a different view of qualifications than we do, it’s not just a matter of rank experience but other ‘factors’”;
 
7. “There are no set guidelines for searches for administrative appointments”;
 
8. “The department head and dean supported Abraham’s bid for full professor in 2016, so how can Abraham allege he has been mistreated?”
 
9. “Chair Sheehan offered to write Abraham a letter for an application to the U of A Leadership Institute, but Abraham was offended by the suggestion.”
 
10. “Abraham ‘leaked’ an admissions document to a graduate student and then accused that student of stealing it off the departmental copier”.

Given @uarizona’s representations, I’m left to wonder why neither Human Resources nor the Office of Diversity and Inclusion ever conducted an investigation into any of my supposed bad conduct. 

My “history of unprofessional emails” was never presented at the November and December CAFT hearings, despite @UAZProvost and @UArizonaSBS claiming such documentation existed.

So, even before you are fired from your tenured position, you are completely marginalized years earlier.

text:
The scientist who taught America how a fertilized egg locks its door was described by a colleague as limited in intelligence, ignorant, incompetent, and conceited, with research that was a nuisance. That assessment, given in 1923, cost Ernest Everett Just the only real laboratory job he was ever in reach of. Eight years earlier the same man had personally secured him the first Spingarn Medal the NAACP ever awarded. Read what one mouth can do in eight years.

Sixty-seven days after Ernest Everett Just died of pancreatic cancer, the most important scientific journal in America printed an admission about what his own country had done to him.

Not to his body. To his work.

It ran in Science on January 2, 1942, volume 95, pages 10 and 11, over the signature of Frank Rattray Lillie, who had run the Marine Biological Laboratory at Woods Hole and the zoology department at the University of Chicago, and who had been Just's teacher, his sponsor, and for more than thirty years the closest thing he had to a protector inside American science.

Lillie wrote this.

"An element of tragedy ran through all Just's scientific career due to the limitations imposed by being a Negro in America, to which he could make no lasting psychological adjustment in spite of earnest efforts on his part."

Then he wrote this.

"The numerous grants for research did not compensate for failure to receive an appointment in one of the large universities or research institutes."

Then he wrote the sentence that should have ended somebody's career and ended nobody's.

"That a man of his ability, scientific devotion, and of such strong personal loyalties as he gave and received, should have been warped in the land of his birth must remain a matter for regret."

Warped. In the land of his birth.

Printed in Science, in 1942, over the signature of a white man who had watched the whole thing from the front row and helped where he could and nowhere near enough.

That is the obituary. Now walk it backward.

He died on October 27, 1941, in Washington, D.C., of pancreatic cancer, at fifty eight years old. He had been back in the country thirteen months.

Go back to September 1940, to a dock in Lisbon, where a Black American scientist and his German wife are waiting to board the S.S. Excambion, which the United States State Department has arranged to carry them off a continent that is burning.

Back up further, to August.

Just was at the Station Biologique in Roscoff, a small marine laboratory on the Brittany coast where the tide goes out for what looks like a mile and comes back over the rocks. He was working in France because he could not get the work he wanted at home.

The Germans came through Brittany that summer. They took him.

The record says only that it was a prisoner camp, and that it was weeks, not months.

His wife was Hedwig Schnetzler, a German philosophy student he had met in Berlin and married on August 11, 1939, and she was several months pregnant when they ran. It was Hedwig's father, a well connected German, who got him out.

Sit with that.

The man was fifty seven years old, he had published roughly seventy scientific papers and two books, and he had been the first American of any color ever invited to work at the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute in Berlin. He came home from Europe alive because his German father in law made a phone call.

Their daughter Elisabeth was born after they reached the United States, and he went straight back to teaching at Howard.

By February 1941 he had severe stomach trouble and kept working through it.

He was trying to finish one last manuscript, a synthesis of biology, history, sociology and anthropology that he was calling Ethics and the Struggle for Existence.

He could not hold his concentration long enough. What survives of it is fragmentary.

In early July he got sick enough that he went up to New York and was admitted to Mount Sinai Hospital, and that is where they found the cancer.

Now go back to 1939, while he was still whole, and understand what the war interrupted.

That year he published two books at once.

One was a manual, Basic Methods for Experiments on Eggs of Marine Animals, which is exactly what it sounds like, and which existed because he had the best hands in the field and other scientists kept asking him how he did it.

The other was called The Biology of the Cell Surface. He finished it in Paris and considered it the summit of his life's work.

The argument of that book was that everybody was looking in the wrong place.

The whole field had its eye on the nucleus, on the chromosomes, on the gene. Just kept saying, in print and out loud, that the outer skin of the cell, the ectoplasm, the surface, was not packaging but the place where the living happened.

He put the question plainly. How could the genes be responsible for a cell becoming one thing rather than another, when every cell has the same genes in it?

He was not entirely right. Nobody has ever said he was entirely right.

He was also not wrong in the way they said he was wrong.

In 2009 the historian of biology Jan Sapp wrote that Just's theorizing on the cell cortex was unsurpassed. Some modern biologists and historians have gone so far as to call him the forgotten father of epigenetics, which is the study of the exact thing he was pointing at, the reason cells carrying identical genes do not become identical things.

His best documented discovery is still standing, and you have never been told its name.

He worked out how an egg slams the door.

In the seconds after one sperm gets in, a wave sweeps across the surface of the egg and shuts every other sperm out. That is the fast block to polyspermy, and a slower structural block follows behind it.

He saw the fast one first, in 1919, watching sand dollar and sea urchin eggs through the summer at Woods Hole.

Thomas Hunt Morgan, who won the Nobel Prize and who Just spent years arguing with, called Just's work on fertilization the fundamental and authoritative study on the subject.

In 1935, at the meeting of the American Society of Zoologists, Just stood up in a room full of white men and told Morgan to his face that his gene centered account of development was insufficient. He called his own counterproposal the theory of genetic restriction.

He lost that argument in his lifetime. He is winning parts of it now, eighty five years after they buried him.

Keep going back.

1928. The Julius Rosenwald Fund gives him eighty thousand dollars over five years, real money in 1928, enough to pay for the European work and prop up Howard's biology department at the same time.

Money he could get. That was never the problem.

Here is the problem, and here is the sentence this whole story is built on.

In 1923 the Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research in New York considered hiring Ernest Everett Just.

It would have meant a laboratory, a salary, no undergraduate teaching, and time. It was the one realistic chance he ever had at the thing every white scientist of his rank in America simply had.

The Institute asked a senior man there for his assessment, and the man was Jacques Loeb, a famous biologist who had known Just since Woods Hole in 1912.

Loeb's answer was that the man is limited in intelligence, ignorant, incompetent, and conceited, and that his so called research work is not only bad but a nuisance.

That was the entire assessment. The job went away.

Now hold that sentence in one hand, because you are going to need the other hand.

Go back eight more years, to February 12, 1915, when Ernest Everett Just, age thirty one, was handed the very first Spingarn Medal the NAACP ever awarded, presented to him by Charles Whitman, the governor of New York.

The first one ever given. Before Du Bois, before Carver, before Marian Anderson, before Rosa Parks.

And the man who secured that medal for him, who pushed his name forward, was Jacques Loeb.

The same man. The same mouth.

In 1915 Loeb wanted the country to see him.

By 1923 Just had begun contradicting Loeb in public, at scientific meetings, about how fertilization actually works, and Loeb wrote him out of a laboratory in a single sentence.

The medal was for being a credit to the race. The job was for being a scientist.

He was allowed exactly one of those.

Loeb was not the only one holding the door. Abraham Flexner, one of the most powerful men in American philanthropy, worried in writing that in supporting Just they were going a little too fast, and that there was more danger of spoiling an exceptional colored worker than an exceptional white one.

Spoiling. Like a child, or like fruit.

Keep walking back.

June 1916, University of Chicago, a doctorate in zoology.

He had been enrolled since 1911 and spent only three academic quarters actually on that campus, because he was carrying a full teaching load at Howard the whole time and doing his research in the summers. His thesis was on fertilization in a marine worm called Platynereis megalops.

1912, his first published paper, in the Biological Bulletin, on the relation of the first cleavage plane to the entrance point of the sperm.

In plain language, he proved that where the sperm goes in determines how the egg first divides. Nobody had shown it.

1909, his first summer at Woods Hole, invited by Frank Lillie. He would come back nearly every summer for two decades.

And here is what those summers actually were.

Picture the dock after dark.

The marine worms he studied swarm at the surface to spawn on a schedule set by the moon, and the window is narrow, so he is out there in the black with the water slapping the pilings, timing it, because the eggs have to be caught at the right minute or the whole night is gone.

He gets them into dishes of seawater, up into the lab, under the glass. And they live.

That was the thing about him.

Other people's eggs died in the dish and his did not, and the men in that building knew it, and they came to him and asked him how.

He worked out indices for judging whether an embryo was developing normally, and he built the technique the field used. In that one room, he was indispensable.

Then the Marine Biological Laboratory built itself a new clubhouse, and there was a party to celebrate it, and Ernest Everett Just was asked not to come.

Not barred by law. Not chased off by a mob.

Asked. By colleagues.

In a New England town, by men who would be back at his bench on Monday asking him to save their eggs.

Twenty summers of that.

In 1929 he went to Naples, to the Stazione Zoologica, and worked on sea urchins. In 1930 Max Hartmann invited him to the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute in Berlin, and he became the first American ever invited there to work.

Then he came back to Woods Hole, and in 1930, in front of the American scientific establishment, he said it out loud.

He said he had received more in the way of fraternity and assistance in his one year at the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute than in all his other years at Woods Hole put together.

Fraternity. That is the word he reached for, not funding, not facilities, not respect.

He made about ten trips to Europe over that decade, and Lillie confirmed in the obituary that over there Just was received with universal kindness and did not experience discrimination on account of his race. The record notes that when he did run into it in Europe, it came from Americans.

Now go back to the word.

November 17, 1911. Washington, D.C., Howard University, the Science Hall they would later rename Thirkield.

It is evening, and three undergraduates named Edgar Amos Love, Oscar James Cooper and Frank Coleman come to the office of a twenty eight year old biology instructor who has been on the faculty four years and is not yet a doctor of anything.

They want to build something that does not exist yet. He gives them the room.

What they founded in that office on that night became Omega Psi Phi, the first national fraternity organized at a historically Black college.

They took their name from the initials of a Greek phrase, and that phrase became the motto. Friendship is essential to the soul.

They set down four cardinal principles. Manhood, Scholarship, Perseverance and Uplift.

Ernest Just was their faculty adviser and their first honorary member. He was not a student founder and he never claimed to be.

Howard would not recognize them, and when the university offered a lesser version of recognition the men refused it, so the fraternity operated with no official standing until that opposition was finally withdrawn in 1914. They incorporated under the laws of the District of Columbia on October 28, 1914.

Sit with the shape of that.

A young Black scientist who would spend the next thirty years being told, politely, in good New England accents, that there was no room for him anywhere, spent one evening in 1911 helping three young Black men build a room.

He gave away the thing he was never given.

Go back four more years, to 1907 and Dartmouth College, where he graduated magna cum laude as the only man in his class to do it.

He was the only Black student in a class of 287.

He had come in on the classics and posted the highest grades in Greek as a freshman, then turned to biology after reading something about fertilization and the development of the egg, and that was that for the rest of his life.

There was a Rufus Choate scholarship, and Phi Beta Kappa, and prizes collected across four years the way other men collect debts.

The faculty did not let him give the commencement address.

Go back to 1903, and Kimball Union Academy in Meriden, New Hampshire, where he had done the four year course in three and finished with the highest grades in the school.

He edited the school paper. He was treasurer and then vice president of the Philadelphian Society.

He played Tom Twist in the class production of She Stoops to Conquer, read the class prophecy on Class Day, and won first prize for extemporaneous speaking at commencement.

And in November of his first term, at seventeen, he published an essay in the school magazine called A Firm Foundation, in which he wrote that we should arm ourselves with the proper equipment so that we shall be able to withstand the test.

Now go back one more year, to the part of this that has nothing to do with science.

1902. He is in his second year in New Hampshire, about eighteen years old.

The school's own archive records that he got a feeling his mother was ill.

He left.

He went south, more than seven hundred miles, from the Connecticut River valley down to Charleston, South Carolina.

He arrived after the funeral.

Her name was Mary Matthews Just, and she had been a widow since 1887, when her husband died and Ernest was four.

She taught Black children in Charleston during the school year, and in the summers she went out to James Island and worked the phosphate.

Understand what that means.

She dug fertilizer rock out of the South Carolina lowcountry in the heat, and with what it paid she founded a school on that island, the Frederick Deming, Jr. Industrial School, and then she ran it.

She also talked Black families into buying up subdivided plantation land on the west bank of the Ashley River and settling it, and in 1886 they incorporated it as a town and named the town after her. Maryville.

For fifty years Maryville was pointed at as a model of Black self government in South Carolina. In 1936 the South Carolina General Assembly revoked its charter.

She died in 1902, and her son got there too late, and went back north, and finished the term.

So here is the debt, and it is not the usual one.

You are not being asked to remember his name, because his name is fine.

It is on a postage stamp the country issued in 1996, on lectures and symposia and scholarships, and on the walls of the fraternity that started in his office. It gets said every November and every August.

You are being asked to say the work with it.

Because the specific method by which this man was buried was that everyone agreed he was a fine Negro scientist and almost nobody repeated what he found.

So when he comes up, say the finding.

Say that he showed where the sperm enters decides how the egg first divides.

Say that he found the fast block to polyspermy, the wave that crosses the surface of a fertilized egg in seconds and shuts every other sperm out, and that it sits in the textbooks now under somebody else's summary.

Say that he spent his life insisting the surface of the cell is alive and doing work, and that the field is coming around to him eighty five years late.

And when you say her name, Mary Matthews Just, say the phosphate and the schoolhouse with it, and say the charter a legislature took back in 1936.

Because nobody ever took his name. They took his laboratory.

Now leave him where he was still winning.

Summer of 1900, seventeen years old, on the deck of a Clyde Line coastal steamer working its way up from Charleston toward New York, going to a school in New Hampshire he has never seen, in a state he has never been to, because his mother taught him this was the way out and then went back to the phosphate fields to pay for it.

She was still alive. He had not yet been told what he was not going to be allowed to have.

He was just a boy on a boat going north, with his mother's whole life folded up in his pocket like fare.

Much of the hardest material here comes from Frank R. Lillie's obituary of Just in Science on January 2, 1942, and from Kenneth R. Manning's biography Black Apollo of Science, published by Oxford University Press in 1983, with the Loeb and Flexner quotations reaching a wide audience through Stephen Jay Gould's review of that book in The New York Review of Books in November 1983. The Omega Psi Phi founding details come from the fraternity's own published history, the Kimball Union material from the academy's archives, the Maryville history from the South Carolina historical marker erected in 1999, and the scientific assessments from the American Society for Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, the Embryo Project at Arizona State University, and Jan Sapp's history of the cell.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter. If you'd like to support the work, here's the link:
https://t.co/AeER0VXKqi
Every coffee helps me keep creating.

ETF แบบ Leveraged ในเกาหลีใต้ที่อิงกับหุ้นผู้ผลิตชิป มีเงินไหลออกเกือบ $1,000 ล้าน ในเดือนนี้ หลังความคึกคักของนักลงทุนต่อการลงทุนในธีม AI เริ่มลดลง พร้อมกับหน่วยงานกำกับดูแลที่เพิ่มมาตรการเพื่อควบคุมมากยิ่งขึ้น ETF ที่อ้างอิง Samsung เงินไหลออกกว่า $381 ล้าน และอ้างอิง SK Hynix มีเงินไหลออกประมาณ $601 ล้าน ถือเป็นครั้งแรกที่ ETF เหล่านี้มีเงินไหลออกสุทธิรายเดือน นับตั้งแต่เปิดตัวในช่วงปลายเดือนพฤษภาคม

*Xi Signals Defiance as US Threatens Sanctions for Iran Support*
รัฐบาลจีนกำลังส่งสัญญาณท้าทายต่อทรัมป์ หลังสหรัฐกดดันจีนเกี่ยวกับความสัมพันธ์ทางเศรษฐกิจกับอิหร่าน ทางโฆษกกระทรวงการต่างประเทศจีนระบุว่าจีนจะใช้มาตรการที่จำเป็นทั้งหมด เพื่อปกป้องผลประโยชน์ของตนเอง หลังจากสหรัฐประกาศคว่ำบาตรหน่วยงานและบริษัทของจีนหลายสิบแห่ง อย่างไรก็ตามตลาดมองจีนมีแนวโน้มที่จะไม่ยอมตัดสัมพันธ์กับอิหร่านโดยมิได้สิ่งใดตอบแทน ซึ่งการที่สหรัฐทำสงครามกับอิหร่านทำให้ทรัพยากรของสหรัฐทุ่มลงมาตรงตะวันออกกลางมาก เปิดทางให้จีนมีพื้นที่ขยับตัวในเอเชียมากขึ้น นักวิเคราะห์มองจีนอาจใช้โอกาสนี้เดินหน้าเรื่องข้อพิพาทดินแดนในทะเลจีนใต้และบริเวณไต้หวัน ล่าสุดสหรัฐพึ่งประกาศยกเลิกการซ้อมรบร่วมกับเกาหลีใต้เพราะขาดทรัพยากร

*Data Centers Use More Water Than California Cities, Study Says*
