text:
Office of the Arizona Attorney General
Criminal Division
October 14, 2022

To whom it may concern:

The Office of the Arizona Attorney General is providing the referenced information to your office for review and potential further action as it relates to potential violations of the Internal Revenue Code by True the Vote, a 501(c)3 organisation. Based out of Texas, True the Vote (TTV) shows Catherine Engelbrecht as the president, with Gregg Phillips being a contracted partner. The executive director is Cole Hughes.

True the Vote's mission according to its website is:

"True the Vote's mission is to train citizens to protect election integrity at the polls, and to help protect all voters' rights."

TTV has alleged wide-spread voter fraud during the 2020 national general election. It purports to have geolocation data that it claims is indicia of ballot stuffing and voting fraud. Specifically, TTV alleges it has in its possession geolocation data from a number of mobile devices showing those mobile devices making several trips in which it is said people are walking to, from, or past ballot drop boxes. Information has not been provided as to the specific location, whether or not there is in fact a drop box at that location, nor is there any information on the person(s) who may be in possession of the mobile device. TTV did not provide any video evidence to support claims of ballot box stuffing. TTV is adamant it has the evidence of ballot stuffing and voting fraud. However, when asked to provide the information, which Ms. Engelbrecht and Mr. Phillips promised to do, TTV never provided the information.

Ms. Engelbrecht and Mr. Phillips met with representatives of our Special Investigations Section on three different occasions (June 3, 2021; April 5, 2022; June 1, 2022). During those meetings, Ms. Engelbrecht and Mr. Phillips stated they obtained the unique individual phone identifier/fingerprint and geolocation data from a private vendor who sells such information for marketing purposes. They report spending $2 million for the information. Prior to each meeting with TTV, Ms. Engelbrecht and Mr. Phillips stated they would provide us with the information to support their allegations. Despite repeated requests, TTV never did provide the information it purported to have in its possession.

In our second meeting, they indicated they had geolocation data that showed there were 243 "mules" in Arizona who were ballot harvesters/stuffing ballot boxes, with the information showing they repeatedly went by and/or to ballot drop box locations. During this meeting, TTV provided us with a document in which they hypothesised as to how the election fraud occurred. Again, we asked for the information and they did not provide it, saying they would. On May 4, we sent an email to TTV requesting the information. On May 6, we received an email from Ms. Engelbrecht in which she stated they had been busy but would send us the information next week. Again, the information never arrived.

TTV then began to publicly assert they had provided us with the information — to include a hard drive — and made that same claim to the Arizona State Senate and the Phoenix Office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). Not only is this patently false, TTV acknowledged via correspondence and during a meeting with them that they had not given us the information but that they would.

In our meeting with TTV on June 1, 2022, they indicated they had given all of the election fraud information to the Phoenix Office of the FBI and we could obtain the information from them. They stated they were working with the FBI as informants and they were not sure they could give the information to our office. This statement reflects TTV's knowledge of having not provided our office with any information that they had previously alleged.

We met with representatives of the Phoenix FBI office on June 8, 2022 and were informed they had met with TTV and TTV provided them an audio recording and video of an interview of a person from San Luis who was alleging ballot harvesting. They did not provide any additional information, only saying that the FBI could contact our office for the information as they had provided all of the information to us. The FBI also informed us that Ms. Engelbrecht and Mr. Phillips were not informants for the FBI. We again requested the information from TTV via electronic and U.S. mail correspondence and leaving voicemail messages. TTV never responded to our email or phone calls, and registered mail was returned having not been signed for.

TTV has stated publicly their geolocation data was instrumental in helping the Atlanta Police Department arrest a suspect wanted for the murder of a young child in that city. In speaking with representatives of that agency, they informed us that they made an arrest in the case two weeks before TTV offered their services and TTV was not a factor in the arrest. TTV has also stated that based upon their information, our office was able to initiate investigations into election fraud in the town of San Luis. This is inaccurate. TTV has not provided us any information/evidence of election fraud in Arizona that has led to us initiating an investigation.

TTV has raised considerable sums of money alleging they had evidence of widespread voter fraud and their efforts would train the public to protect election integrity at the polls and to help protect all voters' rights. They indicate they have provided the information to law enforcement agencies; in our case they have not after promising to do so. Another law enforcement agency has also stated they have not provided them the information, informing them they had given the information to us.

Given TTV's status as a nonprofit organisation, it would appear that further review of its financials may be warranted.

Feel free to contact the undersigned should you need any further information.

Respectfully,

Reginald "Reggie" Grigsby
Chief Special Agent
Special Investigations Section

Office of the Attorney General
Special Investigations Section

text:
At forty-two years old, America’s first Black astronaut candidate had never heard of Harriet Tubman.Somebody said the name to Ed Dwight in a Denver workshop in 1974 and he had to say no, and then no again to Frederick Douglass, and no again to George Washington Carver. Thirteen years of American school, thirteen more in an Air Force uniform, and nobody had ever told him.

What he did about it is standing in public in a dozen states right now.

The man in the Denver studio was forty-two years old and he could not answer the question.

He had a welding torch and a commission and no formal training in any of it. The state's lieutenant governor had come by to sit for a sculpture, and somewhere in the small talk the older man asked whether he had ever heard of Harriet Tubman.

He said no.

Brown tried another. Frederick Douglass, then George Washington Carver, and the answer came back no both times.

Brown kept going down the list, and the man with the torch stood there in his own shop recognizing none of it. He had a degree in aeronautical engineering, nine thousand hours in the air, and thirteen years in the uniform of the United States Air Force, and he was hearing these names for the first time in his life.

Twelve years earlier, his country had chosen him to be the first Black man it sent into space.

His name is Ed Dwight. In 1961 the United States government went looking for a Black astronaut and found him, put him on the cover of Ebony and Jet and Sepia, and sent him around the country to stand in front of Black children as proof of what was possible.

It never sent him anywhere near space. He finally got there in May 2024, at ninety years old, and a charity had to buy the seat.

Everything about that sentence is worse than it sounds. But the studio in 1974 is the part that should make you sit down, so hold it there and go back to the beginning.

Kansas City, Kansas, in the late 1930s. There is a wagon working the scrap rounds, pulled by a horse and a mule, and there is an old man on the bench holding the reins.

The old man is Lobe Dwight, and he and his wife Sarah farm in Kansas City and work the scrap on top of it. His grandson is four or five years old and rides beside him all day, and the boy has one job.

When the old man spots metal in the road, the boy goes over the side.

He jumps down while the wagon is still moving, gets the piece up out of the dirt, hauls it back and throws it onto the load. Then he climbs up and they go another block and he does it again, and again, all morning, in whatever the Kansas weather is doing that day.

Decades later he described the job as being his grandfather's arms and legs. That is the whole arrangement in five words.

The old man could see the metal, and the boy could get to it.

Remember the metal. It comes back.

The boy could also draw. He was tracing cartoons out of the newspaper before he was three, had a library card at four, finished his first oil painting at eight.

His mother, Georgia Baker Dwight, had him in an early learning program at two years old and pushed culture at her children like it was medicine. When it came time for high school she wanted the Catholic education continued at Bishop Ward, and when the school worked out that the applicants were Black the admission was quietly withdrawn.

Georgia Dwight did not appeal to the school, and she did not appeal to the diocese either. "So my mom wrote the Pope," is how her son tells it.

Rome sent word down, and the school opened its doors.

Before they let him walk in, they put him through a course on how to behave around white people. One of the instructions he still repeats is that he was not to look a white girl in the eye.

Eight hundred and fifty students were enrolled the morning he arrived. Three hundred of them were gone soon after.

He graduated in 1951, the first Black male ever to finish there. The Kansas City Art Institute offered him a scholarship, and his father sat him down and told him to be an engineer, because engineers make money.

He gave up the art.

Somewhere in there he saw a photograph that changed the direction of his life. A Black pilot, shot down over Korea, standing on the wing of a jet as a prisoner of war.

Until that picture he had assumed flying was a thing that happened to other people. He joined the Air Force in 1953, took an aeronautical engineering degree from Arizona State in 1957, and started stacking flight hours, more than nine thousand of them eventually, two thousand in high performance jets.

He was told he could not be a squadron leader. The reasoning he was given was that he was short and Black and country boys would not follow him, so they made him the number two man instead.

What he has said about that period is that he refused to let those white guys beat him at anything.

Then, in September 1961, Edward R. Murrow wrote a letter to the head of NASA suggesting the United States train a Black pilot and fly him, so the country could tell that story to the rest of the world. The White House liked it.

Somebody had to be the pilot.

The letter reached Ed Dwight on November 4, 1961. Every commanding officer he showed it to told him to throw it in the trash, that Washington would chew him up and end the career he had already built, that they were going to make hamburger out of him down there.

His mother told him Black people were depending on him.

So he went out to Edwards Air Force Base in the Mojave, into the Aerospace Research Pilot School, the pipeline that fed men to NASA. And then something happened that nobody had planned for.

The mail started.

It came in by the sackful, roughly fifteen hundred pieces a week by his own count, and the base had to store it in containers. Letters from Black families in every state, from church groups, from schoolteachers, from strangers who had seen his face on a magazine cover at a barbershop and wanted him to know somebody was praying.

A great deal of it was addressed to "Astronaut Dwight, Kansas City, Kansas," with no street and no number on it. Just a title the United States never actually gave him, and a town he had left years before.

It reached him anyway.

He would leave the base and go make speeches. There is a photograph from March 1964 of him at Langdon Elementary in Washington, surrounded by children who are looking at him the way children look at somebody who has come down out of the sky.

Then he would drive back to Edwards, where his classmates were furious. They were working themselves into the ground in one of the hardest flight programs in the world, and this man was off giving talks to six-year-olds.

The school's commander was Chuck Yeager, who later wrote in his own memoir about being caught in a fight over a Black student from the very first class. His way of putting it was that he had to prove he was not a bigot.

Here is the piece of it that is on paper. Twenty-six men were competing for eleven places in the second phase of the course.

Dwight did not make the cut.

Then the Air Force chief of staff, Curtis LeMay, telephoned Yeager about the White House's interest in the matter. The list was widened from eleven to fifteen, and Dwight went in, along with three more white pilots who had also missed.

He finished the program in the top half of his class, and the Air Force put his name forward to NASA along with twenty-five others. On October 18, 1963, NASA announced fourteen new astronauts out of a hundred and thirty-six applicants.

Ed Dwight was not one of them.

Yeager's own deputy said years afterward that Dwight was perfectly capable of doing the job. The plain truth, he said, was that it had never been important enough to anybody with the power to make it happen.

Thirty-five days later, John F. Kennedy was killed in Dallas.

Within days Dwight had orders in his hand sending him to Germany. He got on a plane, flew to Washington, sat down in a room with Robert Kennedy, and the Attorney General cancelled them personally.

It bought him a few months. Once the training ended they transferred him anyway, out to Ohio, off the path, and the letters stopped coming.

He resigned in 1966, thirteen years in, still a captain.

The following June the Air Force selected Major Robert Henry Lawrence Jr. for the Manned Orbiting Laboratory, making him the first Black man chosen as an astronaut by any space program on earth. On December 8, 1967, six months later, Lawrence was killed ejecting from an F-104 at Edwards Air Force Base.

He was thirty-two years old. Same base, same aircraft type Dwight had flown out there.

The Air Force did not classify him as an astronaut when he died, so his name was left off the memorial at Kennedy Space Center. It was finally added on December 8, 1997, thirty years to the day.

Dwight, meanwhile, went to work. IBM as a systems engineer, then aviation consulting, then a barbecue chain in Denver called The Rib Cage, then his own land development company, and by the early 1970s he was one of the bigger developers in the city.

Around then he also started walking his own construction sites and picking metal up off the ground.

He took it home. He welded it into shapes for his house, for no reason and no money, doing at forty exactly what he had done at five off the back of his grandfather's wagon.

He has put it more plainly than that. Asked where the art came from, he said "that's how I started my art career, it was doing junk."

Which is how the lieutenant governor of Colorado came to be sitting in his shop in 1974, and how a man who had been America's first Black astronaut candidate came to be standing there saying no to Harriet Tubman. "I was 42 years old and I had never heard of these people," he said later.

Look at what that means. This country had selected him precisely because he was Black, printed his face in every Black magazine in America, sent him out to be looked at by Black children as living evidence of Black achievement, and put him through an American education that ran all the way to a university degree in aeronautical engineering, and in all of that, and in thirteen more years inside its Air Force, nobody ever told him who Harriet Tubman was.

They needed a Black man, and they had no intention of giving him his own history.

Brown, who had flown with the Tuskegee Airmen before he ever became a lieutenant governor, told him nobody was recording any of this. Nobody was building it, and nobody was putting it anywhere people could see it.

Dwight has said the thing he felt was anger.

He shut down the businesses. He enrolled at the University of Denver, learned to run the foundry, and took a Master of Fine Arts in sculpture in 1977 at the age of forty-three.

Since then he has put the names he was never taught into bronze, starting with Frederick Douglass and Harriet Tubman. Duke Ellington, Hank Aaron, Dr. King in Denver's City Park, Underground Railroad memorials standing on both banks of the Detroit River, more than a hundred and twenty public works and a place in the Smithsonian's collection.

What he built was the curriculum nobody had given him, and he put it outdoors, where a person does not have to be admitted to look at it.

Then on December 5, 2014, one of them went to space without him. NASA loaded a Dwight bronze called "Pioneer Woman" onto the first test flight of the Orion capsule.

It climbed to roughly 3,600 miles, circled the earth twice, and came down in the Pacific.

Dwight was eighty-one that day, standing on the ground in Denver. His sculpture cleared the planet ten years before his body did.

The morning finally came on May 19, 2024, at a launch pad in the West Texas desert outside Van Horn.

Nine thirty-six in the morning. He is ninety years old, strapped into a capsule with five people he does not know, a French brewer, a retired accountant, a software engineer, an investor, and a pilot from India.

The booster lights.

By his own account it was the loudest thing he ever heard in his life, and his first thought was that the rocket had exploded and he was dead. He had waited sixty-three years for this and his opening seconds of it were spent believing it had just killed him.

Then the capsule separates and everything goes silent and weightless, and he gets to the window.

There were no dividing lines down there, he said. No borders between countries, nothing marking one state off from another, just water and mountains and the whole thing looking ordered and innocent.

Sixty-five miles up, nine minutes and fifty-three seconds gate to gate, home under two of the three parachutes. At ninety years and two hundred and fifty-three days, Ed Dwight became the oldest human being ever to go to space.

He still is.

He came out of that capsule with both fists in the air. "I thought I really didn't need this in my life," he told the crowd, and then he told them he had been wrong.

Before the launch he had explained who he was doing it for, and it was not himself. It was the people who had wanted it for him for six decades, the ones who had mailed those letters to a town he did not live in, and about them he said, "to them this is justice."

Now the arithmetic.

A seat on that rocket is believed to cost around half a million dollars. Dwight did not pay it, and neither did the government that recruited him, printed him, paraded him and dropped him.

Space for Humanity, a nonprofit, covered it, with help from a family foundation. Strangers bought the ticket, the same way strangers had filled those containers with mail at Edwards in 1963.

The bill to give him a Congressional Gold Medal was introduced in 2023 and died. It was filed again in May 2024 and died again, and filed a third time in February 2025, where it went to committee in both chambers and has been sitting ever since.

So here is what is actually owed, and it is not the medal.

He was forty-two before anybody said the name Harriet Tubman to him. Go and work out how old you were, and how old your children are right now, and then go find one name out of that hundred and twenty and hand it to somebody before they turn forty-two.

Dwight turned ninety-two last September. Illness and failing eyesight mean he does not sculpt anymore, so the hundred and twenty are all there is going to be.

The work is finished. The man is still here.

There is a retrospective of it running right now at the History Colorado Center in Denver, called Casting A Legacy, and it stays up into next year. Ask him which piece in that building means the most and he does not say Douglass and he does not say King.

He says Dirt Farmers. It is a bronze of Lobe and Sarah Dwight, the two people who taught him everything he knew before America got hold of him, standing in the Kansas City dirt they worked, neither of them ever once inside a school.

text:
Two hundred thirty soccer camps. Sixty-three thousand campers.
​
That is the figure buried in the Deseret News piece on Jennifer Rockwood, and it is the one that ought to settle the argument.
​
This summer was her last camp. She had been running them since the nineties, every June and July, on the fields in Provo.
​
Sixty-three thousand kids came through and got coached by her. Some of them came back as her players.
​
Rockwood is the only head coach BYU women's soccer has ever known. She arrived in 1985 as a player on a club team and never left the sideline.
​
Forty-one years. Thirty-one seasons after the program went Division I. Twenty-six NCAA tournaments. Seventeen regular-season titles. A national championship game in 2021.
​
She opened this final season with 470 wins and no active female head coach in the NCAA has more.
​
BYU's athletic director needed six words for it in June. "Jennifer Rockwood is BYU women's soccer."
​
Krysyan Edler reached four of her former players now in the NWSL. Not one of them led with a trophy.
​
Mozingo committed at fourteen, took an offer from UCLA, and called Rockwood to say so. Rockwood told her the spot would still be there. A year later she transferred in, and it was.
​
Hatch, who is from Gilbert, Arizona, described a coach who was intimidating and maternal at the same time and never once had to announce the standard.
​
And Vasconcelos drove back to Provo the day after her interview to watch her daughter get coached at a BYU camp by the woman who had coached her.
​
That is the whole argument in a single image.
​
So here is the case.
​
The field is called South Field. It should carry her name.
​
Jennifer Rockwood Stadium, announced on November 5 at the last home match of the regular season against Arizona State, with the coach standing on the grass and the crowd in front of her.
​
Not in a press release next spring. Not after a naming committee returns its findings sometime later.
​
An institution that waits until someone has gone to honor them has misread the purpose of honoring people.
​
Forty-one years. One sideline. Sixty-three thousand kids.
​
Put her name on it.
​
Commercial autonomous mobility in the Phoenix East Valley will arrive — sooner than most think. For me, it seems like forever...
​
Source: Krysyan Edler writing for the Deseret News, published August 21.

Nick Foles says he turned down more money from Tampa Bay to return to Philadelphia as Carson Wentz’s backup, then says the failures that came before it are what prepared him to become Super Bowl MVP

“Tampa Bay was really interested. Dirk Koetter was there. I had originally committed to him at Arizona State in high school, so I had an opportunity to actually play for him. And they offered me a pretty sweet two-year deal.”

“Then Howie came calling, like, ‘Hey, we’d love to have you back.’ It was a great deal. I was super honored. It was actually less than Tampa. My wife and I talked. We really were like, ‘All right, what is best for our family?’ Yeah, Philly traded me away and that’s tough, but we love Philly. Or do we go to Tampa Bay and just start over?”

“We just sat there and we’re like, ‘You know what? Let’s go back to Philly.’ That just always felt like home. I’m going there to help a young Carson Wentz. I’m not going there to take over. That’s my role. We can focus on being a dad and going to work and being the best teammate I can be.”

“I am here to help this young starter, to help my teammates in the role that they’ve given me. As opposed to a younger me, once you become a starter, like, how do you not be a starter?”

“I had a heart change. And then all of a sudden the year happens the way it did. I was ready because of my year in St. Louis, because of my year in Kansas City. That equipped me and calloused me to prepare me for what was to come in Philadelphia.”

“Without those years, I don’t think I’m ready to handle what came in Philadelphia in ’17. So I’m super grateful for those trials, that prepared me for it.”

“I couldn’t see it until down the road. I’m like, ‘Wow, okay God. I see what you were doing.’ But man, it wasn’t easy when I was in it. But thank you.”

text:
Float through the heart of the Ozarks at Buffalo National River in northern Arkansas. Flowing freely for 135 miles through forested valleys, towering limestone bluffs, quiet pools, and rushing rapids, the Buffalo offers one of the most beautiful river journeys in the country.

Visitors can canoe, kayak, fish, camp, hike more than 100 miles of trails, and explore waterfalls, caves, historic homesteads, and the abandoned zinc-mining community of Rush. The protected corridor also preserves thousands of years of human history, from ancient Indigenous sites to farms and communities established by later settlers.

Little-known fact: Established in 1972, the Buffalo became America’s first national river. The park also contains more than 500 known caves, making it one of the most cave-rich units in the entire National Park System.

Key questions about the PIMS hospital tragedy
#PIMSHospital 

The outcome of the probe into the sad deaths of baby infants at PIMS Hospital in Islamabad have not yet been revealed. How and why did 14 harmless newborns die in a fire? Why were the nursery doors shut? Why were the emergency exits secured? Why were there no adequate fire-safety measures, such as fire extinguishers, present? A key question is whether PIMS Hospital Islamabad had a fire alarm system to warn everyone if there was a fire. If there was a system in place, why wasn’t it used when the fire happened?
In a situation as unfortunate as a fire, what were the roles and obligations of the doctors, nurses, and other workers in the hospital? Once the fire started, should the doctors, nurses, and other workers have hurried to the children's ward, or should they have left the newborns behind to escape for themselves?
Adults in the hospital can ask for help and have the ability to walk or move, but newborns can’t call out for assistance or move on their own. So, why didn’t any doctor or hospital worker consider saving the newborn babies from the flames?
Despite this unfortunate event, there has been no response towards the Executive Director of PIMS because sources suggest he has connections to the current government.
The apex court instructed that Imran Khan, the founder of PTI, should be transferred to Shifa International Hospital within two days to receive a full medical check-up and be evaluated by a team of doctors. However, disregarding the Supreme Court's order, the government transferred him to PIMS Hospital, where it was mentioned that there was no electricity, no ECG machine available, and the CT scan machine reportedly wasn't working properly.
The hospital staff measured Imran Khan's blood pressure, gave him an injection in his eye, and then sent him back to prison. Taking Imran Khan to PIMS Hospital was supposedly a plan to hurt him. Fortunately, people learned about this supposed plan, went to the hospital, and stopped it from happening.
Why was @ImranKhanPTI moved from Shifa International Hospital to PIMS Hospital, and why was he later sent back to Adiala Jail? 
These might seem like simple questions, but shouldn't we think about them more deeply? 
The situation in Kashmir is also important. How did more than 100 Kashmiris reportedly lose their lives due to gunfire at peaceful demonstrations, and why is the Awami Joint Action Committee now being called an agent of India and RAW? Similar claims have also been directed at @PTIofficial and Imran Khan.
Recently, it was said that a reward of Rs. 1 million was offered for each of the nine Baloch women leaders. However, the resolve of the Baloch people is still very strong: 
Oh dear ones, even if a bounty is put on our heads, 
Our message will always be: Keep your heads held high.

A state is meant to act like a mother. Yet, only those nations endure that care for their people just as a mother cares for her kids. A mother would give up her own life to keep her children safe, but sadly, this mindset is missing in our system.
The Pashtun community in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa should consider who set up armed religious schools in their area instead of creating colleges and universities. There were drone strikes in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and military actions were taken under various names claiming to target terrorists.

text:
Logogriph or sentence-completion exercises of this nature tap into what speech-language pathologists and cognitive researchers call a "cloze procedure" or semantic/syntactic priming. When working with older adults or individuals experiencing mild cognitive impairment or age-related hearing loss, these tasks exercise contextual inference—the brain's ability to use surrounding words to predict and fill in missing auditory or textual information.
As hearing acuity declines, the brain often relies more heavily on linguistic context to decode speech. If you are designing a quiz or cognitive exercise format around this, here are a few ways to structure it effectively:
 * **Categorized Difficulty Levels:** Start with high-predictability sentences where the missing word is obvious from strong semantic cues (e.g., "She poured a cup of hot..."), and progress to low-predictability sentences that require deeper contextual memory.
 * **Multi-Modal Delivery:** Since you mentioned hearing loss, design the quiz so participants can toggle between reading text with blanks, listening to an audio clip with background noise (to simulate real-world listening conditions), or both.
 * **Open-Recall vs. Multiple Choice:** Allow older adults to type or say their own words first (semantic flexibility is great for brain health), but offer a multiple-choice option if they get stuck to reduce frustration.
 * **Familiar Idioms and Proverbs:** Use well-known phrases from their generation (e.g., "A stitch in time saves...") which leverage long-term procedural memory even if working memory or hearing is fading.
What specific format or platform are you using to build this quiz? I can help you draft a set of graduated sentences or questions tailored to different cognitive levels.
Observing people on public transport offers a masterclass in micro-expressions and passive engagement. When you pair a cognitive fill-in-the-blank exercise with visual or facial expression reading, you move the activity from pure language processing to social-emotional cognition—something that actively exercises the brain's mirror neurons and empathy networks.
Transport environments like buses and trains naturally evoke distinct behavioral postures and facial expressions:
 * **The Commuter Stare:** Blank, unfocused eyes gazing past the window glass, reflecting a state of low-demand cognitive rest or internal rumination. The jaw is slightly slack, and the brow is neutral.
 * **The Observant Watcher:** Eyebrows raised slightly, head tilted toward the window as they track dynamic movement—like children playing football or the rhythm of passing streetlights. This expression signals active environmental scanning and mild amusement or curiosity.
 * **The Vigilant Listener:** Head cocked, lips slightly parted, eyes narrowed in concentration to filter out the ambient rumble of the engine or catch an upcoming transit stop announcement.
 * **The Private World:** Subtle smiles or micro-frowns triggered by music playing through headphones or a book, showing a disconnect between immediate physical surroundings and internal emotional states.
To weave this into your project, you could present a short sentence about a scene on a bus or train with missing words, accompanied by a description or an image of a passenger's face. The user has to match the missing word in the sentence to the emotional context or focus revealed by that person's expression—bridging language comprehension with social perception.

text:
The Temptation of Being Managed

To be free is not always, in every sense, a pleasant thing.

We often speak of freedom as liberation.
To be able to decide for oneself.
To be able to choose for oneself.
To act according to one’s own will.
All this is indeed of great value for human beings.
And yet at the same time, freedom also means that one must judge for oneself, and bear the consequences of that judgment.

Freedom is therefore not only a joy. It is also a burden.
And when that burden begins to feel too heavy, people often find themselves discovering a strange relief in being managed.
To be managed does not simply mean to be commanded.
It means that what one ought to do has already been decided.
How one should behave has already been indicated.
What counts as acceptable, and what counts as deviation, is made clear.

Procedures are arranged. Standards of evaluation are set.
There is a framework to follow whenever hesitation arises.
From the outside, such a condition may appear to be a limitation of freedom.
But from within, it can be experienced as a state in which one need not hesitate so much, a state in which the burden of judgment has grown lighter.
Here lies the temptation of management.
Human beings do not necessarily wish to decide everything for themselves.

What to eat today. Which road to take. When to rest.
Even small choices, once accumulated, produce fatigue.
And when one must also continue deciding about work, learning, life-planning, relationships, and the shape of one’s future, the burden becomes very great indeed.
For that reason, people sometimes feel reassured by paths that have already been arranged.

It is not that they no longer think at all.
But the reduction in the amount of thinking required can itself feel like a form of rescue.
At that point, management appears not simply as the opposite of freedom, but as a device that lightens the weight of freedom.

This appears even in small and ordinary scenes of life.
If one follows the recommendation, failure becomes less likely.
If one follows the manual, one feels safer.
If procedures are standardized, there is less need to hesitate.
If a system is automated, there is less need to think.
Such convenience is not evil in itself.

Indeed, modern society has reduced many burdens through precisely these technologies of management.
And yet at the same time, the more convenient things become, the more accustomed people grow to conditions in which judgment is no longer required of them.
And the more accustomed they become, the heavier it begins to feel whenever judgment is demanded again.
Management then becomes not merely an external order, but something internalized as comfort.

Part of the reassurance offered by being managed lies in the possibility of avoiding failure.
If one decides for oneself, one may be wrong.
If one chooses for oneself, one must bear responsibility.
If one judges for oneself, one may later be haunted by the thought that some other path would have been better.
In a managed system, by contrast, the mode of decision itself lies outside the self.

So long as one has followed the system, failure no longer seems to belong to oneself alone.
This feeling can bring great comfort, especially in an anxious society.

To be managed narrows freedom of action, but it also appears to diffuse the burden of responsibility.
Management also attracts because it offers predictability.
One knows what one is supposed to do.
One knows how one will be evaluated.
One even knows what will happen if one deviates.
Such predictability gives people a powerful sense of reassurance.

In a freer world, possibilities widen, but what may happen also becomes less certain.
In a managed world, possibilities narrow, but the future becomes easier to anticipate.
And people often prefer the stability of what can be foreseen to the openness of what remains uncertain.
Management is thus welcomed not only as a form of control, but as a technique　for reducing uncertainty.
This temptation becomes especially strong within institutions and organizations.

There are clear rules. Actions are precisely evaluated. Behavior is recorded. Deviation is quickly corrected. From one angle, such an environment appears suffocating.
And yet it also offers the reassurance of knowing exactly what is expected.

One need not construct one’s own standards of value.
One need not test one’s own limits.
One need only fulfill one’s role within an already designed world.
This arrangement makes order appear preferable to freedom, management preferable to autonomy, structure preferable to openness.
And so people are easily led to receive management not as domination, but as rational care.

The temptation of being managed runs deep also because it often feels like care.
It reduces one’s burdens. It saves one from hesitation. It processes complexity on one’s behalf. It arranges things so that one is less likely to fail.
Such forms of management do not appear first as cold domination.

They appear in the face of kindness, assistance, and consideration.
That is precisely why they are difficult to see.
People do not feel that they are being made subordinate. They feel that they are being helped.
At that point, management appears not first as repression, but as support. And this only strengthens the desire for it.
The problem, however, is that this comfort gradually externalizes judgment itself.

What should be chosen is decided by recommendation.
What should be read is arranged by the algorithm.
Which procedure is correct is guided by the system.
Such mechanisms are certainly convenient.
But when one becomes too accustomed to them, one slowly ceases to exercise the capacities to compare, to hesitate, and to interpret for oneself.
As a result, management ceases to be merely an external order. It becomes an internal habit of dependence.
Here lies the danger within the temptation of being managed.

In this sense, the desire to be managed is not simply a psychology of obedience.
It is also a deeply human wish to reduce anxiety, to avoid failure, to escape complexity, to set down, even for a while, the burden of having to go on thinking. That is why the problem is difficult.

To criticize management cannot mean despising the human desire for reassurance itself.
What is required instead is to understand why people experience management as comfort, why they are drawn to a world already arranged, and where the cost of that comfort lies.

A managed environment reduces the burden of judgment.
But it also reduces the occasions on which one judges.
It saves one from hesitation. But it also weakens the power to think through hesitation.

It makes failure less likely. But it also thins out the pathways by which one might try, stray, and think again.
Unless this double character is seen, management will be misunderstood either as pure evil or as pure good.
In truth, it is both a form of domination and a provision of reassurance.

That is why resisting concentration cannot mean simply saying, “Do not be managed.”
What must be asked instead is how people might be given forms of reassurance that do not depend upon concentration.
Can one still have footing while judging for oneself?
Can one still hesitate without being cast out?
Can one have time to face complexity?
Can autonomy exist without becoming a harsh burden of self-responsibility?

Without such conditions, management will always return wearing the face of comfort.
In this sense, the temptation of being managed is an important part of the cultural reproduction of concentration.

People do not submit only because they are forced.
They also move toward managed worlds because within them life seems, for a moment, a little easier.
And that movement strengthens the center still further, which in turn makes autonomy feel heavier still.
Within this cycle, concentration settles in place wearing the face of social rationality itself.

And if we continue this question further, the next thing we must examine is why people wish to escape complexity itself.
Why does a diverse and open world so often feel exhausting?
Why do simple patterns and clear answers hold such power?
That is what we must now consider next.

The Honourable Minister of Information and National Orientation, @HMMohammedIdris’s speech at the celebration of Taraba State at 35, in Jalingo, this week #TarabaAt35

I am delighted to be in Taraba State today, and I bring warm greetings from His Excellency, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, and the Federal Executive Council.

It is a great honour to join the government and people of Taraba in celebrating 35 years of statehood and, importantly, in witnessing the unveiling of a blueprint that looks beyond the achievements of the past to the possibilities of the future.

Thirty-five years is a significant milestone. Since its creation on 27 August 1991, Taraba has developed into a state distinguished by its cultural diversity, agricultural potential, natural resources and remarkable landscapes.

It is not by accident that Taraba's slogan is “Nature's Gift to the Nation.” It reflects the beauty and fertility of the State's terrain and landscape, and the warmth and welcoming nature of its people. It is home to Chappal Waddi, Nigeria's highest mountain, the Gashaka-Gumti National Park and the iconic Mambilla Plateau. 

It is home to nourishing rivers, including the one from which it gets its name. And in its ethnic diversity, Taraba represents a remarkable microcosm of Nigeria, with numerous communities and cultures living together.

Taraba is also one of Nigeria's important agricultural frontiers. Its fertile lowlands support the cultivation of crops such as yam, rice, cassava, millet and maize, while the highlands offer opportunities in crops such as tea and coffee, alongside significant livestock production. Its rivers and water resources also give the state enormous potential for hydropower and other forms of energy development.

What this means is that Taraba's greatest asset is not simply what is beneath the ground or the beauty of its landscape. It is the economic value that can be created from these resources, through agriculture and agro-processing, livestock, energy, tourism, manufacturing and other productive activities.

However, an anniversary is not only about looking back. It is also about asking: What kind of future are we building? That is what makes today's unveiling of the Taraba Regional Development Master Plan so significant.

Development requires vision, planning and consistency. A master plan provides a framework for coordinated growth, responsible investment, infrastructure development and better use of public resources. I commend Governor Agbu Kefas and the Taraba State Government for embracing this long-term approach.

I also acknowledge the progress being made by the Taraba State Government across areas such as education, healthcare, infrastructure, economic development, security and social cohesion. 

The decision to make primary and secondary education free and compulsory is particularly important, given the central role of education in building the human capital that Taraba will require for its next phase of development. 

The State Government has also continued to support students by meeting examination costs, including more than ₦1.8 billion provided in 2026 for NECO, BECE and NABTEB registration for public-school students.

The recent financing secured by Taraba from the ECOWAS Bank for Investment and Development is another significant development. In June this year, EBID and the Taraba State Government signed financing agreements totalling about $268 million for an integrated industrial park, 10,000 hectares of irrigated rice production and processing, and a 50-megawatt solar power plant in Jalingo. These are precisely the kinds of investments that can connect Taraba's natural advantages to jobs, production, value addition and economic growth.

The Federal Government under President Bola Ahmed Tinubu shares this commitment to deliberate and inclusive development. Indeed, Taraba is already benefiting from this vision.

text:
Please take a deep breath before reading what I‘ve written below. And if you choose to respond, please think carefully about what I have said before you write and, if you disagree, please tell me why I am wrong and avoid any personal attacks as I want only what I think is best for BVB. 

Do we not think it says something, even with a squad in as poor a state as it‘s in after getting raided this summer, that Aston Villa has not been trying to bring Jadon Sancho back this window? Especially in the context of their biggest loss having been to their creativity in attack after Morgan Rogers left. 

Villa is a Champions League side fresh off a European title who have a 30% higher wage bill than we do. They have consistently been one of the top performing sides in England for a few years now, having built themselves from being a Championship side not that long ago. Clearly, they are not a stupid club- and I can’t imagine that Sancho would go this far into the window without a club and not be willing to take an offer to return to Villa and play UCL football. Yet despite having more money to spend on wages than us and having had the last year to evaluate the player in his most recent form, Villa have decided it was a better idea to bring in Leon Goretzka than  bring back Sancho. 

This should be a serious red flag. There can only be one of two reasons for why Villa isn’t trying to bring him back. Either there is something about Sancho that they dislike so much that they think it‘s not worth even trying to bring him back, or Sancho is demanding such a high wage and is so insistent on that demand that they think it‘s not worth negotiating with him. We can only speculate about the former, as only Villa would know; but the latter is something we can get a sense of from the market. 

We know that Sancho was at Chelsea in 2025-26 on a loan with obligation to buy from United; and we know that, despite strong numbers in the ECL and a generally reasonable level as a squad player, Chelsea decided to pay the penalty to Untied for not taking up the obligation to pay rather than bringing him back. 

We know that despite Sancho‘s pedigree and his clear talent, he remains without a club near the end of the transfer window despite being a free agent and having being linked with a number of prominent clubs including ours. 

What we can gather from this is that the market simply isn’t willing to pay Sancho what he is demanding in wages. That must mean that he is demanding quite a lot, as there are always clubs who are willing to sign players with Sancho‘s ability. 

We need to avoid nostalgia here. Yes, we had an amazing time with Sancho, but we need to leave the past in the past. We just got out of a summer window in which one of the big achievements was the shedding of lots of big, poor value veteran contracts, and it‘s clearly been established as a priority of Book that we’re going to move away from signing veterans on the market to big wages. This is clearly for the better of the club. 

I know all of us are eager to challenge Bayern and win trophies as soon as possible. But we need to ask ourselves if it‘s more important to chase a trophy now or to lay the foundations for being able to win more trophies more regularly in the future. I would argue it‘s the latter, and the latter requires a process to which we need to commit. Any contract we sign has to be firmly in line with that process and not a reaction to events.

Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov and his wife welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at Manas International Airport on Sunday. Xi arrived in Bishkek to attend the 2026 Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit and pay a state visit to Kyrgyzstan.

At a time when unilateralism and protectionism are straining global cooperation, the SCO offers a practical example of countries with different political systems, development paths and civilizations working together. Over 25 years, guided by the Shanghai Spirit, SCO members have expanded cooperation from security and trade to connectivity, technology, education and green development.

The SCO's experience shows that diversity can be a source of cooperation rather than division. From the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway to cooperation platforms in AI, green industry and digital economy, countries are turning dialogue into tangible development opportunities and creating broader space for people across the Global South to prosper together.

text:
Sjoe! 🇿🇦 The Bureaucratic Swamp Thing That Learned to Send a Monthly Invoice 💸🐊 ~ 🏗️ The Trillion-Rand Question: Investment or Another Layer of Claims? ~ ⏳ Temporary Programme, Permanent Constituency: The Politics of Reversal.
Sjoe. A country can spend more on itself and still feel poorer. That is not a paradox. It is what happens when institutions learn to keep money circulating among the same claimants while the broader economy waits for results that never quite arrive.

Economist Dawie Roodt has stated the core problem with unusual clarity. South Africa faces continuous extraction driven by two interlocking groups: a high-cost civil service and rent-seeking tenderpreneurs. National civil servants—roughly 1.2 million in narrower counts that exclude state-owned enterprises and local government, approaching 2 million in broader definitions—receive average packages of R50 000 to R58 000 a month and absorb between 10.5 and 17 percent of GDP depending on the perimeter used. Years of above-inflation increases have made the wage bill politically difficult to restrain. 

At the same time, procurement systems weighted toward political connection allow tenderpreneurs to capture value without matching efficiency. The combination produces permanent claims on a narrow tax base while service outcomes remain weak.

This is the swamp. Not a single scandal. A recurring pattern of institutional design.

1. The Double Claim

The numbers are not abstract. When a small share of the population draws a large share of national output through salaries, and when a significant portion of remaining public money is allocated through processes that reward access, the residual available for productive investment shrinks. 

Roodt has described the civil-service portion as the real ongoing capture—less dramatic than the high-profile episodes examined by the Zondo Commission, yet more durable because it is written into the monthly payroll and the annual budget cycle.

Political science supplies an additional lens. Public-sector unions and the electoral weight of state employees create powerful veto players. Any attempt at real wage restraint threatens immediate political costs, while the benefits of restraint—higher growth, lower debt service—are diffuse and delayed. 

The result is a classic time-inconsistency problem: short electoral cycles systematically undervalue long-term fiscal sustainability.

A further distortion arises in the labour market itself. When the public sector offers higher average remuneration and greater job security than large parts of the private economy, talent is pulled toward the state rather than toward firms that must compete to survive. Entrepreneurship becomes relatively less attractive. 

The same high public wage premium that protects insiders can therefore suppress the very private-sector dynamism needed to widen the tax base that funds those wages.

Tender systems amplify the effect. Connection-weighted procurement creates a market for intermediaries who specialise in navigating rules rather than delivering at the lowest cost for the highest quality. Economic theory predicts deadweight loss when resources are allocated by political rather than competitive criteria. The loss appears as higher unit costs, delayed projects, and poorer maintenance. 

Taxpayers fund both the elevated fixed labour cost and the less-efficient contracts. Service delivery does not keep pace.

The pattern is self-reinforcing. High wage commitments limit fiscal space. Limited fiscal space increases the political temptation to use procurement for multiple objectives. Those objectives further raise the cost of delivery. The swamp deepens without anyone needing to declare a new crisis.

Sjoe!
It takes a special kind of institutional genius to turn a salary bill into a permanent claim on the future while still calling the arrangement “service.”

Questions Stirring: 
What independent verification exists for the precise share of GDP absorbed by public remuneration across different definitional boundaries? 
How much of the gap between wage cost and service outcome is explained by skills shortages versus incentive structures? 
If the wage bill is politically sticky, what evidence would demonstrate that any future restraint is more than temporary? 

These questions matter together because they test whether the arithmetic is structural or merely cyclical, and because any remedy that ignores the political economy of the payroll will fail.

2. Ambition Meets the Filter

South Africa has announced multi-year infrastructure pipelines of substantial scale. Strategic Integrated Projects have been valued in the hundreds of billions of rand, with identified work approaching R2 trillion in some official presentations. The stated purpose is growth, employment and the repair of energy, logistics and water systems that constrain the economy.

Yet these capital flows must pass through the same institutions already marked by elevated wage costs, capacity constraints at municipal and state-owned enterprise level, and procurement systems sensitive to political connection. 

When large outlays encounter such filters, a material portion converts into higher debt-service obligations, future operating and maintenance claims, and additional contracts available for rent-seeking rather than completed, reliable assets. Historical patterns of underspending and irregular expenditure on infrastructure projects supply the supporting evidence.

Governance research offers a useful distinction between spending and investment. Spending is an outflow. Investment is an outflow that produces a stream of future benefits greater than its cost. When institutional capacity is weak, the conversion rate from the first to the second declines. A bigger budget processed by the same machinery can therefore yield a bigger version of the same incomplete result. 

The recovery intention remains sincere. The institutional filter remains decisive.

Municipalities illustrate the practical consequence most clearly. Many already face unfunded or underfunded mandates while carrying heavy staff costs. New capital projects that arrive without corresponding increases in technical capacity or operating budgets simply add to the list of assets that cannot be properly maintained. 

The result is a familiar cycle: announce, underspend, overspend on salaries, and watch the infrastructure deteriorate faster than it is replaced.

International experience reinforces the point. Several middle-income countries that attempted large public-works programmes without first strengthening project preparation, competitive procurement and maintenance systems discovered that capital budgets became another vehicle for recurrent claims. 

The physical assets, when they appeared at all, deteriorated faster than planned because operating budgets were already committed elsewhere.

Sjoe!
Announcing a trillion-rand pipeline is the easy part. Getting the water to run through the pipes, year after year, is where the real examination begins.

Questions Stirring: 
What measurable improvement in project completion rates, unit costs and subsequent service reliability has accompanied the growth of the infrastructure pipeline? 
How much of announced capital spending is ultimately converted into maintained assets versus recurrent claims? 
If capacity constraints at municipal and SOE level are binding, what evidence shows those constraints are being reduced faster than the spending is increasing? 

These questions matter together because they distinguish between spending and investment, and because the difference determines whether the next decade produces higher growth or higher debt.

3. The Historical Mirror

The United States New Deal of the 1930s economic plans to fix the Great Depression offers a comparative reference point that is frequently invoked and less frequently examined in detail. Temporary work-relief agencies—the Civilian Conservation Corps, the Works Progress Administration and related programmes—employed millions during the Depression years and were largely wound down by the early 1940s as wartime demand absorbed labour.

Simultaneously the New Deal established lasting institutions: Social Security, the Securities and Exchange Commission, the National Labor Relations Board, the Federal Housing Administration and a broader regulatory apparatus. Federal civilian employment rose from roughly 590 000 in 1929 to nearly 900 000 by the late 1930s, peaked near 3.5 million during the war, then settled at a structurally higher postwar baseline around 2.5 million. 

The federal share of total government spending and the scope of federal regulation shifted permanently upward. That administrative state has now operated for approximately ninety years and continued to expand under later legislation.

Path dependence is the key concept. Once organisations are staffed, beneficiary groups form, and administrative routines harden, the political cost of reversal rises sharply. Temporary programmes can be closed when the emergency ends. Permanent programmes generate their own constituencies. The New Deal demonstrates both possibilities in a single historical episode.

Constitutional and legal context matters here as well. South Africa’s Constitution requires that public administration be governed by democratic values and principles that include efficiency, transparency and accountability (section 195). Cadre deployment and connection-weighted procurement sit in tension with those principles. The tension is not merely political; it is constitutional. 

Persistent failure to align practice with constitutional standards weakens the legitimacy of the administrative state itself.

A contrasting international example is instructive. Several East Asian developmental states that achieved rapid infrastructure expansion after the mid-twentieth century kept public employment relatively lean and subject to rigorous performance discipline. Capital budgets were protected from being crowded out by wage claims. 

The difference in institutional design produced markedly different long-term trajectories.

Sjoe!
Ninety years is a long time to keep an emergency temporary.

Questions Stirring: 
Which features of the New Deal’s permanent institutions proved most resistant to later reform, and why? 
How closely do South Africa’s current administrative layers resemble the durable rather than the temporary elements of that earlier expansion? 
What evidence would indicate that South Africa’s present trajectory is more likely to produce reversible programmes than lasting claims? 

These questions matter together because they convert historical analogy into a testable proposition about institutional stickiness.

4. The Formal Layer

Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment was designed to broaden ownership, management control, skills development and supply-chain participation. In operation its scorecard system, third-party verification industry and procurement preferences create strong incentives to optimise for points and access.

Claims associated with William Gumede that roughly R1 trillion has moved among fewer than 100 politically connected individuals since 1994 remain contested. Subsequent commentary has questioned the underlying methodology, data sets and consistency with recorded deal values. What is less disputed is that the compliance apparatus itself functions as a significant transaction-cost and gatekeeping layer, that fronting and repeated empowerment of already-connected players occur, and that broad outcome metrics—unemployment and inequality—have remained weak.

A formal preference regime can add another self-reinforcing administrative stratum. 

The constitutional imperative of redress is not in dispute. The specific institutional form—scorecards, verification industries and procurement weighting—is an empirical question. When the form generates high compliance costs and concentrated benefits, it becomes part of the sticky state rather than a solvent for historical disadvantage.

Political incentives again play a role. Preference regimes create identifiable winners who have every reason to defend the existing rules. Diffused losers—ordinary taxpayers and excluded entrepreneurs—have weaker incentives to organise. 

The result is policy stickiness even when aggregate outcomes disappoint. Foreign investors, observing the same complexity, price higher risk premiums into capital, further raising the cost of the growth the policy is meant to enable.

Sjoe!
A scorecard that needs its own industry of verifiers has already revealed something important about its complexity relative to its purpose.

Questions Stirring: 
What primary data and transparent methodology would be required to settle the concentration debate with greater precision? 
How large is the measurable transaction-cost burden imposed by scorecard compliance relative to the broad-based outcomes achieved? 
If fronting and repeated empowerment of the already-connected are acknowledged problems, what design changes have demonstrably reduced them? 

These questions matter together because they separate the constitutional imperative of redress from the specific institutional form that has evolved, and because form determines whether the policy expands opportunity or entrenches gatekeeping.

5. Compounding and Path Dependence

The cumulative pattern is multi-front. Elevated public wage costs, connection-sensitive tenders, cadre-influenced appointments and formal compliance regimes together raise the fixed cost of the state and the political cost of reform. 

Comparative history indicates that permanent administrative expansions which prioritise internal claims, complexity and protection of incumbents over measurable public-value creation tend to become self-reinforcing.

The New Deal trajectory illustrates durability once structures are staffed and defended. Similar patterns appear where emergency or transformative spending created lasting agencies and beneficiary networks that later proved costly to reverse. 

The result is not that every bureaucracy fails. It is that systems in which extraction and procedural complexity dominate delivery impose ongoing burdens on taxpayers and constrain broader prosperity.

Separate mechanisms interact. The wage bill limits fiscal space. Constrained fiscal space increases reliance on procurement for multiple objectives. Preference regimes add further complexity. Each layer defends itself. 

The swamp compounds. 

Narrow tax bases accelerate the pressure: continuous claims encourage skilled taxpayers to leave, further concentrating the burden on those who remain and making future reform even harder.

Principal-agent problems deepen the difficulty. Officials and politicians face incentives that reward short-term distribution and visible announcements more reliably than long-term maintenance and efficiency. Citizens, as principals, struggle to monitor the multiple layers of agents who control the actual flow of resources. 

Information asymmetry and collective-action problems favour the status quo.

Sjoe!
When every layer has a reason to keep the next layer in place, the system begins to resemble a well-designed trap that no one admits to having designed.

Questions Stirring: 
Which of the overlapping layers has shown the greatest resistance to reform, and what does that reveal about political incentives? 
What evidence would falsify the claim that the current institutional configuration is self-reinforcing? 
If path dependence is real, what sequenced changes have the highest probability of altering the incentive structure rather than merely adding new rules? 

These questions matter together because they move the discussion from diagnosis to the practical problem of reversal, and because reversal is the only test that ultimately matters.

Synthesis

Independent lines of evidence converge. Fiscal arithmetic from the wage bill, delivery shortfalls on infrastructure pipelines, the ninety-year durability of New Deal permanent institutions, the additional transaction costs and gatekeeping of scorecard compliance, and the compounding interaction of these layers form a single coherent pattern. 

Overlapping administrative structures convert recovery spending into lasting claims because the filters through which money must pass already prioritise internal extraction and complexity.

The diagnosis is falsifiable. If wage-bill restraint, competitive procurement, measurable improvement in project completion and maintenance, and broader diffusion of empowerment benefits appear together and persist, the swamp thesis weakens. Until then the pattern holds. 

The stakes are concrete: the difference between a state that enables growth and a state that consumes it.

Objections

One objection holds that high public remuneration is required to attract and retain scarce skills. The data show elevated average packages alongside persistent service shortfalls, suggesting the compensation is not reliably purchasing corresponding performance.

A second objection insists that preference regimes remain constitutionally essential for redress. The constitutional imperative is not in dispute. The specific institutional form is an empirical question open to redesign if outcomes remain weak.

A third objection argues that large infrastructure spending is the only available route to growth. Spending is not the same as investment. When institutional filters convert capital into recurrent claims, the growth dividend remains unrealised.

Conclusion

South Africa’s bureaucratic swamp is the observable outcome of permanent claims that grow more costly and more politically entrenched with each new wave of spending. The wage-and-tender arithmetic, the infrastructure absorption risk, the historical precedent of durable administrative expansion, the additional compliance stratum, and the compounding path dependence answer the central question with cumulative force.

The evidence does not prescribe a single remedy. It establishes the scale and stickiness of the problem that any remedy must confront. The country retains the capacity to choose different institutional filters. Whether it does so will determine whether the next decade produces higher growth or a deeper swamp.

The converging evidence demonstrates that overlapping administrative layers in South Africa convert ambitious recovery spending into lasting fiscal and political claims, with the durability of similar expansions elsewhere underscoring the difficulty of later reversal.

Women will rewtire the worst parts of history, and when it happens they will avoid accountability at all costs.

The trial of Lindsay Clancy, who stands accused of the calculated strangulation of her three young children, Cora, Dawson, and Callan, represents a critical crossroads for the American justice system. 
The defense’s push for a verdict of not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility; seeking psychiatric institutionalization instead of mandatory life imprisonment; opens a horrifyingly dangerous precedent. 
If the court permits severe psychiatric distress or postpartum psychosis to function as a complete shield against penal retribution for the slaughter of innocents, it effectively establishes a legal loophole that privileges the perpetrator over the absolute right to life of her victims.

To fully understand the systemic catastrophe of treating such acts strictly as medical emergencies rather than heinous acts of violence, one must confront the chilling historical parallel of Constance Fisher. In 1954, Fisher drowned her three children in a bathtub during a psychotic episode, was deemed insane, and was committed to a state hospital. 
Five years later, medical professionals confidently pronounced her "cured" and discharged her back into society. Twelve years after her initial horrific act, Fisher suffered another severe breakdown and drowned her three newly born children; who were the exact same ages as her original victims. 
The case of Constance Fisher stands as an indelible, devastating warning about the fallibility of psychiatric evaluations. 
Mental health diagnoses are inherently subjective and fluid; clinicians cannot guarantee future stability, nor can they predict when a "cured" patient might relapse. 

Sparing a child killer from the permanent finality of life in prison under the naive assumption that institutional care offers a permanent cure ignores the lessons of history, creating a catastrophic structural vulnerability wherein a perpetrator could one day be declared rehabilitated and restored to society.

Equally disturbing is the vocal wave of public advocacy and social media coddling that has emerged in support of Clancy. A vocal contingent of supporters has sought to reframe this horrific crime not as an act of murder, but as a collective failure of healthcare providers, overmedication, or maternal mental health support systems. 
This attempt to sanitize filicide under the banner of empathetic activism is profoundly grotesque. By prioritizing the mental comfort and medical distress of the mother over the brutal, violent erasure of three defenseless children, these supporters engage in a dangerous form of moral inversion. 

Public rallies and sympathetic campaigns effectively attempt to dismantle personal accountability, casting the killer as the ultimate victim and reducing the murdered children to mere collateral damage of a medical system failure. 
This public whitewashing minimizes the horrific reality of the crime, insults the memory of the young victims, and signals a terrifying societal willingness to excuse the inexcusable under the guise of misplaced maternal solidarity.

Justice requires absolute proportionality. When three young lives are methodically extinguished, the law must operate without compromise. 
Remanding a perpetrator to a psychiatric facility, where discharge remains a theoretical future possibility based on the shifting sands of medical opinion, fundamentally abdicates the primary responsibility of the justice system: retribution, deterrence, and absolute protection of society. 
The only outcome that honors the sanctity of the young lives taken, guarantees public safety, and resists the absurd narrative pushed by her vocal sympathizers is a sentence of mandatory, permanent life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.

text:
The Honourable Minister of Information and National Orientation, @HMMohammedIdris’s speech at the celebration of Taraba State at 35, in Jalingo, this week #TarabaAt35

I am delighted to be in Taraba State today, and I bring warm greetings from His Excellency, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, GCFR, and the Federal Executive Council.

It is a great honour to join the government and people of Taraba in celebrating 35 years of statehood and, importantly, in witnessing the unveiling of a blueprint that looks beyond the achievements of the past to the possibilities of the future.

Thirty-five years is a significant milestone. Since its creation on 27 August 1991, Taraba has developed into a state distinguished by its cultural diversity, agricultural potential, natural resources and remarkable landscapes.

It is not by accident that Taraba's slogan is “Nature's Gift to the Nation.” It reflects the beauty and fertility of the State's terrain and landscape, and the warmth and welcoming nature of its people. It is home to Chappal Waddi, Nigeria's highest mountain, the Gashaka-Gumti National Park and the iconic Mambilla Plateau. 

It is home to nourishing rivers, including the one from which it gets its name. And in its ethnic diversity, Taraba represents a remarkable microcosm of Nigeria, with numerous communities and cultures living together.

Taraba is also one of Nigeria's important agricultural frontiers. Its fertile lowlands support the cultivation of crops such as yam, rice, cassava, millet and maize, while the highlands offer opportunities in crops such as tea and coffee, alongside significant livestock production. Its rivers and water resources also give the state enormous potential for hydropower and other forms of energy development.

What this means is that Taraba's greatest asset is not simply what is beneath the ground or the beauty of its landscape. It is the economic value that can be created from these resources, through agriculture and agro-processing, livestock, energy, tourism, manufacturing and other productive activities.

However, an anniversary is not only about looking back. It is also about asking: What kind of future are we building? That is what makes today's unveiling of the Taraba Regional Development Master Plan so significant.

Development requires vision, planning and consistency. A master plan provides a framework for coordinated growth, responsible investment, infrastructure development and better use of public resources. I commend Governor Agbu Kefas and the Taraba State Government for embracing this long-term approach.

I also acknowledge the progress being made by the Taraba State Government across areas such as education, healthcare, infrastructure, economic development, security and social cohesion. 

The decision to make primary and secondary education free and compulsory is particularly important, given the central role of education in building the human capital that Taraba will require for its next phase of development. 

The State Government has also continued to support students by meeting examination costs, including more than ₦1.8 billion provided in 2026 for NECO, BECE and NABTEB registration for public-school students.

The recent financing secured by Taraba from the ECOWAS Bank for Investment and Development is another significant development. In June this year, EBID and the Taraba State Government signed financing agreements totalling about $268 million for an integrated industrial park, 10,000 hectares of irrigated rice production and processing, and a 50-megawatt solar power plant in Jalingo. These are precisely the kinds of investments that can connect Taraba's natural advantages to jobs, production, value addition and economic growth.

The Federal Government under President Bola Ahmed Tinubu shares this commitment to deliberate and inclusive development. Indeed, Taraba is already benefiting from this vision.

text:
The Medal Is the Admission

The inquiry reported. Eight officials suspended. Criminal proceedings ordered. One nurse decorated. The file moves on.

Read what the state actually found. The fire crossed the ward in about two minutes. No alarm. No sprinkler. Two of thirteen SOPs mentioned fire at all. No full-time emergency officer — the duty sat with an assistant director as an additional charge. No protocol naming who raises the alarm, who commands, who unlocks the exits, who carries the babies. Exits locked or obstructed. And seven weeks earlier, PIMS had already had a fire in its nursing hostel.

The committee could not establish what started the blaze. It established everything that made the outcome certain before anything started.

Then came the response, and it is entirely political capital and bureaucratic repair. Suspend. Prosecute. Replace. Order audits. Decorate.

Look hardest at the decoration.

A medal for extraordinary courage in that ward is the state conceding, in public, that survival there depended on one human being doing something heroic. It formalises the failure rather than repairing it. It tells every nurse in Pakistan that the system will not hold the line, so be exceptional — and if you are not, expect an OSD order. Two others from the same room received exactly that.

Reward for individual heroism is what a state offers when it has decided not to fix the architecture.

The hole is still open. No published evacuation clock. No named emergency officer. No conversion of the ordered audits into unannounced drills. No answer to the door.

Yesterday I argued the door was locked for a reason, and that the reason is never audited for what it does in an emergency. The report has now documented that in the state’s own hand.

Case closed. Hole unfixed.

The next two minutes are already scheduled.
