text:
The building saved everyone who could walk out of it.

That is not a fire story. It is an institutional design story, and it is the one we are least likely to tell.

The nursery exit was restricted for a reason. The hospital had faced attempted infant abductions. So access was controlled. From the desk where that decision was taken, it was correct — a real risk, met with the only instrument available. Nobody was careless. Nobody was corrupt. The decision would pass any audit.

And it helped kill fourteen children.

Hospitals elsewhere manage the same abduction risk with electronic tagging, matched mother-infant bands, and quarterly drills at unpredictable hours. They solve the problem with capability. We solved it with a lock. When an institution cannot build capability, it manages risk by removing options — and every option you remove is one someone needs on the worst morning of their life.

Then there is the detail that should end the argument. The health minister has confirmed his ministry was issuing fire-safety notices to PIMS for seven years.

The system did not fail to notice. It noticed perfectly. It detected the hazard, wrote to the right office, filed the receipt — every year, for seven years. By every metric we actually measure, that regulatory relationship was functioning.

The notice was the output. Nobody ever specified that a working fire suppression system was the output.

Rescuers found hoses without couplings and no water at the fire point. Somewhere in that building is a file recording their purchase. Three quotations. Competent authority approval. Delivery challan. Inspection certificate. Every rupee accounted for, every rule followed, and no water.

We bought the object. We never bought the function.

Everything announced since is either political — a suspension, compensation, a resolution — or bureaucratic: four parallel inquiries into a single fire. None of it changes what happens at 6:38 tomorrow morning.

And we have run this experiment already. Sahiwal, June 2024: eleven babies dead, extinguishers expired, the medical superintendent and three senior doctors arrested. Punishment happened. Twenty-six months later, fourteen more newborns are dead in the federal capital.

Pakistan does not have an inquiry deficit. It has a conversion deficit.

My new policy note proposes five mechanisms, all running through institutions that already exist:

1.Make licence renewal for any NICU conditional on an unannounced evacuation drill. One exit blocked, power out, clock running — and the result published. Not “fire certificate: yes” but “NICU evacuation: 4 minutes 37 seconds.”
2.Remove the reason for the lock: infant tagging, matched bands, NADRA bedside birth registration.
3.A public register of outstanding safety notices, escalating automatically at day 90 and day 180.
https://t.co/whPt4y7IAJ new health scheme approved without a funded five-year maintenance line.
5.A counter-risk clause on every new control: what failure can this create, and who bears it?

Pakistan does not need another certificate stating that an emergency exit exists. It needs to know whether a nurse can get a baby through it with a corridor full of smoke.

text:
George J. Moses

I have to admit, I’m enjoying watching some of my friends suddenly discover their deep, almost sacred reverence for historic names now that Donald Trump has renamed Lake Ontario “Lake America.”

Where was this passionate defense of tradition when we spent the last decade playing cultural Mad Libs with names?

The Cleveland Indians became the Guardians.
The Washington Redskins became the Commanders.

Aunt Jemima was evicted from the breakfast table and replaced by Pearl Milling Company.

Uncle Ben got demoted to Ben’s Original.

The Native American woman disappeared from Land O’Lakes butter.

Eskimo Pie became Edy’s Pie.

The Dixie Chicks became The Chicks.

Lady Antebellum became Lady A.

Universities and real-estate professionals started replacing “master bedroom” with “primary bedroom.”

Computer programmers began retiring “master/slave” terminology.

Schools, streets, statues and buildings bearing the names of historical figures were renamed by the hundreds.

Then there were the military bases.
Fort Bragg became Fort Liberty.
Fort Hood became Fort Cavazos.
Fort Benning became Fort Moore.
Fort Polk became Fort Johnson.
Fort Lee became Fort Gregg-Adams.
Fort Gordon became Fort Eisenhower.
Fort Rucker became Fort Novosel.
Fort Pickett became Fort Barfoot.
Fort A.P. Hill became Fort Walker.
We even watched Mount McKinley become Denali.

Meanwhile, our vocabulary got its own remodeling job. 

“Mothers” sometimes became birthing people, “pregnant women” became pregnant people, and “breastfeeding” acquired the alternative chestfeeding in some institutional language.

And Columbus Day? Plenty of cities, states and institutions decided Indigenous Peoples’ Day was preferable.

For years the message was: Names matter. Words matter. Language evolves. Old names can be changed when society decides another name better reflects its values. If you're offended by the change, get over it.

Okay.

Apparently there was an asterisk:

This principle remains valid until Donald Trump names something.

Suddenly the people who spent a decade redecorating the dictionary have chained themselves to the furniture.
Personally, I think Lake America is mostly political theater, and pretty funny political theater at that. Canada is perfectly free to keep calling it Lake Ontario. Nobody is confiscating their maps.

But after watching everything from pancake syrup to Army installations get renamed in the name of cultural sensitivity, I simply cannot work up the appropriate level of outrage over a lake.

So to my friends who are losing sleep over Lake America, I offer the same compassionate advice conservatives received during the Great Renaming:

Language changes. Names evolve. Try to keep up. 📷

text:
The Man Who Refused to Leave the Children Behind

Before he became Janusz Korczak, he was Henryk Goldszmit.

A doctor.
A writer.
A broadcaster.
A man who became famous throughout Poland.
But history remembers him for something far more important.
It remembers what he did when he was given the chance to save himself.
Korczak could have escaped.

He was well known. Friends and members of the resistance reportedly offered help. There were opportunities to find safety outside the Warsaw Ghetto.

Yet one problem remained.

The children.

And Janusz Korczak would not abandon them.

For most of his life, he had believed that children deserved dignity.

Not later.

Not when they became adults.

Now.

In 1912, he helped create a Jewish orphanage in Warsaw called Dom Sierot — the Children's Home.

It was a remarkable place.

The children had responsibilities and a voice in the life of the home. They had a children's court, a newspaper, and forms of self-government.

Korczak rejected the idea that children were merely unfinished adults.

To him, childhood was not a waiting room for life.

Childhood was life.

And the children deserved respect while they were living it.

He devoted decades to them.

Then came the German occupation.

In 1940, the Nazis forced hundreds of thousands of Jews into the sealed Warsaw Ghetto.

The orphanage was moved inside.

Korczak went with it.

The conditions became catastrophic.

Food disappeared.

Disease spread.

Everyday survival became a struggle.

But Korczak remained beside the children.

He searched desperately for supplies. He pleaded for help. He did what he could to keep the orphanage functioning while the world around it was being destroyed.

His friends urged him to escape.

He refused.

How could the man who had spent his life teaching children that they mattered suddenly tell them that his own life mattered more?

By the summer of 1942, deportations from the Warsaw Ghetto had begun.

Thousands of people were being taken away.

The destination was Treblinka.

The children were next.

On August 5, 1942, German forces came for the orphanage.

Korczak had a choice.

Again.

Save himself.

Or remain.

He chose the children.

Accounts of the final march differ in some details, but the essential truth has endured.

Korczak left with the children of Dom Sierot.

He did not escape.

He did not step away.

He stayed with them until the end.

Nearly two hundred children and members of the orphanage staff were taken from the ghetto.

They were deported toward Treblinka.

Janusz Korczak went with them.

None returned.

Perhaps that is why his story still hurts.

Korczak was not a soldier with an army.

He had no weapon capable of stopping the machinery surrounding him.

He could not save those children from the fate the Nazis had prepared for them.

But when every chance to escape required him to abandon them, he refused.

He had spent his entire life insisting that children were not less important because they were small.

And when his final test came, he lived by that belief.

Even when it cost him everything.

The Nazis tried to reduce people to numbers.

Janusz Korczak spent his life doing the opposite.

He saw every child as a person.

A person who deserved food.

Safety.

Respect.

A voice.

A future.

And, when there was no future left for him to protect, Korczak refused to let them face their final journey without someone who loved and cared for them.

He died with the children.

That is why we remember his name.

Janusz Korczak.

And beside his name, we must remember the children too.

Not as a number.

Not simply as victims of history.

But as children who once had favorite stories, games, dreams, fears, and lives.

Lives that should have continued.

Remember Janusz Korczak.

And remember the children who never came home.

text:
I have to admit, I’m enjoying watching some of my friends suddenly discover their deep, almost sacred reverence for historic names now that Donald Trump has renamed Lake Ontario “Lake America.”

Where was this passionate defense of tradition when we spent the last decade playing cultural Mad Libs with names?

The Cleveland Indians became the Guardians.

The Washington Redskins became the Commanders.

Aunt Jemima was evicted from the breakfast table and replaced by Pearl Milling Company.

Uncle Ben got demoted to Ben’s Original.

The Native American woman disappeared from Land O’Lakes butter.

Eskimo Pie became Edy’s Pie.

The Dixie Chicks became The Chicks.

Lady Antebellum became Lady A.

Universities and real-estate professionals started replacing “master bedroom” with “primary bedroom.”

Computer programmers began retiring “master/slave” terminology.

Schools, streets, statues and buildings bearing the names of historical figures were renamed by the hundreds.

Then there were the military bases.

Fort Bragg became Fort Liberty.

Fort Hood became Fort Cavazos.

Fort Benning became Fort Moore.

Fort Polk became Fort Johnson.

Fort Lee became Fort Gregg-Adams.

Fort Gordon became Fort Eisenhower.

Fort Rucker became Fort Novosel.

Fort Pickett became Fort Barfoot.

Fort A.P. Hill became Fort Walker.

We even watched Mount McKinley become Denali.

Meanwhile, our vocabulary got its own remodeling job. “Mothers” sometimes became birthing people, “pregnant women” became pregnant people, and “breastfeeding” acquired the alternative chestfeeding in some institutional language.

And Columbus Day? Plenty of cities, states and institutions decided Indigenous Peoples’ Day was preferable.

For years the message was: Names matter. Words matter. Language evolves. Old names can be changed when society decides another name better reflects its values. If you're offended by the change, get over it.

Okay.

Apparently there was an asterisk:

This principle remains valid until Donald Trump names something.

Suddenly the people who spent a decade redecorating the dictionary have chained themselves to the furniture.

Personally, I think Lake America is mostly political theater, and pretty funny political theater at that. Canada is perfectly free to keep calling it Lake Ontario. Nobody is confiscating their maps.

But after watching everything from pancake syrup to Army installations get renamed in the name of cultural sensitivity, I simply cannot work up the appropriate level of outrage over a lake.

So to my friends who are losing sleep over Lake America, I offer the same compassionate advice conservatives received during the Great Renaming:

Language changes. Names evolve. Try to keep up. 😎

text:
THE REBRAND NOBODY HAS TO ADMIT TO
Chapter 1 of 8 — Post 3 of 3
Welcome to the Modern DSA World, Where Right Is Whatever You Want It to Be — Look Under the Big Tent, and You'll Find a Rattlesnake in the Sleeping Bag
This is Part 3 of 3, closing Chapter 1 of an eight-chapter series on the DSA's rebrand, program, and historical parallels. Parts 1 and 2 covered the vocabulary rebrand, DSA's current program, the motte-and-bailey framework, Alinsky's parallel word choice, and the early historical record (Russia, China/Cuba, Hungary, Czechoslovakia).
Did It Ever Start as a Free Democratic Choice? The Historical Record (continued)
The genuine exceptions, and their real limits, are Chile and Venezuela. Salvador Allende won the Chilean presidency in 1970 with a real electoral plurality of 36.6 percent — not a majority — narrowly ahead of conservative candidate Jorge Alessandri. Because no candidate cleared a majority, the Chilean constitution required congressional confirmation, which the centrist Christian Democrats provided only after Allende signed a formal "Statute of Constitutional Guarantees," explicitly promising to respect democratic institutions, press freedom, the rule of law, and the existing constitution. This is the clearest genuine case of a Marxist coalition winning executive power through an authentically free election. Once in office, however, Allende's government pursued rapid economic interventions that included facilitating land expropriations through administrative loopholes, frequently bypassing the legislature rather than working through it. The attempt to force rapid structural transformation on a deeply polarized society, on the strength of only a 36.6 percent mandate, did not produce a stable, consolidated socialist republic. It produced severe constitutional crisis and institutional breakdown, and ultimately the violent military coup of September 1973. Using Allende as proof that "the voters chose communism" skips the plurality, the congressional confirmation bargain, and the fact that the experiment was ended by the army rather than completed at the ballot box. Using the coup as proof that any socialist electoral victory is inherently illegitimate skips the opposite and equally important fact: a freely and fairly elected president was overthrown by force. The honest record is that a plurality government with a socialist program could not consolidate a new constitutional order before it was broken by force from outside the electoral process entirely.
Venezuela under Hugo Chávez is the closest modern parallel to "elections in, authoritarianism out" as a mechanism distinct from either the Bolshevik coup or the Eastern European occupation-and-salami-tactics model. Chávez won repeated, genuine elections, then used that accumulated democratic mandate to rewrite the constitution, pack the courts, and effectively end meaningful rotation of power — electoral authoritarianism carrying socialist branding. If the warning on the table is "movements like this will never win a free vote," Venezuela refutes it directly. If the warning is instead "winning free votes can itself become the method by which the remaining institutional checks get disabled," Venezuela is the clearest supporting exhibit available. Those are two different warnings, and this chapter treats them as such rather than stacking them together as if they were one claim.
Western Europe supplies an important control group often left out of this discussion entirely. Communist parties in France and Italy won large vote shares after 1945 and entered ordinary coalition politics. They did not convert those vote shares into a one-party monopoly state. Eurocommunism, developing later, was in part an explicit doctrinal attempt to make that non-conversion permanent: parliamentary participation, acceptance of political pluralism, and public distance from Moscow's model. The existence of that path does not erase Russia 1917 or Hungary 1945–48. It does demonstrate clearly that "a Marxist party competing in elections" and "a one-party outcome" are not the same variable, and should never be treated as automatically linked.
The Nazis are a partial and genuinely important exception. The National Socialist German Workers' Party used the existing electoral and legal machinery of the Weimar Republic extensively. It did not, at any point, win a free, uncoerced majority for the dictatorship it subsequently built.
The Nazi Party won 37.3 percent of the vote in the July 1932 Reichstag election — its historic high point under genuinely free conditions, and still well short of a majority. Support actually fell to 33.1 percent by the November 1932 election. On January 30, 1933, President Hindenburg appointed Hitler chancellor within a coalition government in which the Nazis held only three of eleven cabinet seats; the conservative politicians who engineered the arrangement believed they could contain and control him. After the Reichstag fire in late February 1933, a further election was held on March 5, 1933, under conditions that included bans on opposition media and organized street violence by Nazi paramilitaries — and even under those explicitly coercive conditions, the party won only 43.9 percent, still short of an outright majority on its own; a governing majority required an alliance with a nationalist coalition partner.
The Enabling Act, which functionally ended German parliamentary democracy, passed on March 23, 1933, only after Communist Party deputies had been excluded from the chamber or arrested outright, and dozens of Social Democratic deputies had been detained or intimidated, with SA and SS paramilitary members physically present inside and around the voting chamber itself, creating an atmosphere of direct, mortal intimidation. It was in this environment that Otto Wels, chairman of the Social Democratic Party, delivered the final speech opposing the Act — facing Hitler directly, over the jeers of the assembled SA men — declaring, "Freedom and life can be taken from us, but not our honor," and adding, "No Enabling Act gives you the power to destroy ideas that are eternal and indestructible." The SPD was the only party to vote no. The legal machinery of a democratic state was used, deliberately and step by step, to terminate that democracy from within.
The Nazi Party's full name did include the word "socialist," and its original 1920 program did contain genuinely worker-facing planks — profit-sharing, nationalization of trusts, an end to what it called "interest slavery" — written deliberately to compete for the same working-class voters that socialist and communist parties were courting. A real anti-capitalist faction inside the early party, associated with Gregor and Otto Strasser, took this language seriously as substance rather than recruitment rhetoric. Hitler eliminated that faction entirely. Otto Strasser was pushed out of the party in 1930; Gregor Strasser was murdered in the Night of the Long Knives in 1934, alongside SA leader Ernst Röhm, in the same purge that simultaneously secured the loyalty of the traditional German military, reassured major industrialists, and definitively crushed what remained of independent labor unions. After that point, the party's organizing principle was race and nation, not class, and "socialist" in its name functioned strictly as residual recruitment bait for a movement that had already killed its own genuinely socialist wing.
The name is therefore a lesson in vocabulary, not proof that Nazism and socialism are the same doctrine wearing different labels. People who treat "National Socialist" as an automatic rhetorical trump card against the modern left are doing, in the opposite direction, exactly what this chapter warns against: letting a single word stand in for an entire program. People who dismiss the Nazi case as irrelevant to any discussion of emergency powers, enabling acts, or the early capture of police and courts are performing the equal and opposite dodge. The genuinely comparable object across these cases is not "left versus right." It is the specific sequence by which a plurality becomes a legal monopoly.
Where the Two Movements Diverge, and Where They Don't
The honest historical conclusion is layered, not simple, and both halves have to be held together or the whole argument breaks. Most twentieth-century communist regimes were born from war, armed coup, or foreign military occupation — not from a free electoral majority freely choosing a communist constitution. Where communist or Marxist parties did compete in genuinely free elections — France, Italy, Chile — the more common outcome was either a large vote share that never converted into a governing majority, or, in Chile's singular case, an election followed by a military coup rather than a consolidated communist state.
The Nazi Party is a distinct case: it used Weimar's legal and electoral machinery extensively, but never received an honest, uncoerced majority mandate for the dictatorship it went on to build. What it received instead was a series of pluralities, a fatal elite miscalculation about controllability, and finally a coerced legislative vote taken with its opposition physically excluded or under arrest. Both movements ended in one-party rule. In neither case did an honest, informed electoral majority choose that specific end-state. Ballots were not what produced either outcome; organized force, and the systematic destruction of every organized political alternative, produced both outcomes — through genuinely different mechanisms, on different timelines, in service of ideological content that was not merely different but actively opposed.
That last distinction matters and should never be flattened for rhetorical convenience. Communism's stated organizing principle was class. Nazism's was race and nation. The regimes that resulted were both totalitarian in structure and method. They were not the same content wearing different labels. Method overlap — treating elections as a tool rather than a limit, exploiting crisis to justify emergency power, neutralizing courts and police early, eliminating rival organized opposition — is a real, documented, comparative-politics observation. Claiming the two movements were ideologically interchangeable because they shared some comparable tactics is a separate, unsupported claim, and this chapter does not make it.
A second distinction is just as important for evaluating 2026. Historical communist parties that actually took the state almost always combined a maximal goal with a disciplined vanguard method — the two came as a package. DSA, in its official materials, explicitly separates those two things: it retains a maximal constitutional goal while explicitly rejecting the vanguard method. That separation is arguably the single most interesting fact about the present document. It can be read generously, as evidence the organization has genuinely absorbed the twentieth century's central lesson about how socialist projects curdle into police states. It can be read skeptically, as evidence that the destination is being carefully preserved while only the most radioactive means are being publicly disavowed. A serious reader has to hold both readings open at once, because the text itself supports both, and the future behavior of a still-comparatively-small organization cannot be reliably inferred from a policy document alone. What cannot honestly be done, if the subject under discussion is the document itself rather than the mood surrounding it, is claim that the destination isn't written down. It is.
What a Fair Opponent Would Say Back
A chapter that only prosecutes will read as a pamphlet rather than an analysis, and the strongest available replies to everything above deserve their own space, stated as forcefully as the case against.
First: platforms are not constitutions. Parties and movement organizations have published maximal documents for decades without ever commanding the votes, state legislatures, or Article V convention support required to enact them. The Socialist Party of America ran Eugene Debs for president repeatedly while the country remained, in every respect, a capitalist constitutional republic. The existence of a text is not the existence of a transition, and treating one as automatically implying the other overstates the case considerably.
Second: parliamentary supremacy is not, by itself, tyranny. The United Kingdom has no separately elected president and no Supreme Court with long-standing American-style power to strike down legislation, and it is not the USSR. Canada, New Zealand, and the Nordic states all combine strong social provision with genuine, durable political pluralism. If the motte offered is "look at Sweden," the fair reply is that Sweden did not abolish an upper chamber as part of an explicit project to end "capitalist oligarchy" and draft a wholly new constitution for a "democratic socialist republic." If the actual bailey is the specific DSA sentence quoted above, Sweden is not the comparison — it's the motte again, wearing a different flag.
Third: the existing American constitutional system already fails straightforward majority-rule tests in ways that predate this program entirely. The Electoral College has installed the popular-vote loser as president more than once. The Senate gives Wyoming and California the same two votes regardless of a population difference in the tens of millions. The Supreme Court is, functionally, a body chosen by a sequence of past presidents and malapportioned Senates rather than by any contemporaneous popular vote. None of those are inventions of DSA — they are among the specific reasons a constitutional-redesign left exists at all in American politics. A critic who treats every one of these veto points as sacred and beyond discussion is not, in that moment, defending "democracy" in the plain majoritarian sense of the word. He is defending one particular eighteenth-century compromise, and should say so plainly rather than invoking "democracy" as if the two were identical.
Fourth: guilt by loose historical association is a genuinely rotten method of argument, in either direction. DSA is not the Bolshevik Party, not East Germany's SED, not Venezuela's PSUV. It is a voluntary membership organization that runs candidates inside the existing Democratic Party's ballot line, holds open conventions, publishes its own internal disagreements in public, and has never come close to the kind of institutional or coercive power any of those historical parties held at the point of their own takeovers. If the twentieth century teaches that socialist projects can curdle into police states under the right conditions, it also teaches that stable liberal democracies have coexisted with organized socialist parties sitting inside their parliaments for well over a century without those parliaments becoming police states.
Those four replies belong in this chapter precisely because they are the replies a serious, good-faith reader will actually raise. They do not erase the Workers Deserve More document or what it plainly says. They bound what that document can fairly be made to prove on its own. A program can be radical, entirely public, and still genuinely far from anything resembling power. It can also be radical, entirely public, and considerably more revealing of the organization's actual long-term aims than its press-conference messaging alone would suggest. Both things are true, at once, of Workers Deserve More — and a fair chapter says so.
Closing the Chapter
The through line here is not that any specific piece of vocabulary automatically implies any specific hidden intention. It is that the gap between a stated method and a stated goal is a real, measurable, and historically recurring feature of movements seeking structural change; that this exact gap is currently visible, in plain English, in a document any American voter can read today; and that the historical record on how such movements have actually taken power — through election, through coup, through occupation, through engineered coalition subversion, or through some combination of all four — is considerably more varied, and more genuinely instructive, than either "they always start with a fair vote" or "they never do" would suggest.
The 2026 program does not require a decoder ring. It says, in its own words, that it wants to abolish the Electoral College and the Senate, replace the presidency and the Supreme Court with officers chosen by and subordinate to Congress, draft a new constitution, and create a democratic socialist republic. It also says that some of its demands can be won right now, under the existing system, and that complete victory requires an entirely new society built from the ground up. It says all of this while the same organization, in its other public materials, explicitly rejects authoritarian socialism and vanguard-party discipline. Holding all of those statements in one head at the same time is harder than simply picking whichever single one flatters a reader's prior view. It is also the minimum honest standard for discussing the organization as it actually is on paper, rather than as either a mascot or a demon.
The next chapter turns from vocabulary and historical origin to method itself: what Saul Alinsky actually wrote, rule by rule, about how power — once a movement has named its goal honestly or otherwise — actually gets taken.

text:
The Maitland Who Received Napoleon’s Surrender

When people think of Clan Maitland, their minds naturally turn toward the Scottish Borders, Thirlestane Castle, the Earls of Lauderdale, and the generations of politicians and statesmen who helped shape Scotland. Yet one of the most extraordinary episodes in Maitland history unfolded far from the family’s ancestral lands and involved one of the most famous men who ever lived. In the summer of 1815, Captain Frederick Lewis Maitland of the Royal Navy found himself face to face with Napoleon Bonaparte at the moment the French emperor’s extraordinary career finally collapsed. The encounter aboard HMS Bellerophon placed a member of the Maitland family at the closing scene of more than two decades of European warfare.

Frederick Lewis Maitland was born in 1777 and belonged to a cadet line of the historic Lauderdale family. He was a grandson of the sixth Earl of Lauderdale, securely connecting his naval career to the wider history of Clan Maitland. Unlike earlier generations who gained influence through Scottish law, government, diplomacy, and landholding, Frederick entered the Royal Navy and made his career during the long wars against Revolutionary and Napoleonic France. His generation represented a changing Maitland world in which members of the extended family increasingly served throughout the British military and the expanding empire.

By 1815, Maitland had risen to the rank of captain and commanded HMS Bellerophon, a seventy-four-gun third-rate ship of the line. Vessels of this type formed an important part of British naval power, combining substantial firepower with the ability to operate as part of the great fleets that had contested control of European waters. Maitland had spent years building the professional experience required to command such a ship during an era when naval service could be demanding, dangerous, and relentless. Nothing in his earlier career, however, could have fully prepared him for the strange responsibility that was about to fall upon him.

The situation changed dramatically after Napoleon’s defeat at the Battle of Waterloo in June 1815. The emperor who had dominated European politics for years was suddenly confronted with the destruction of his restored regime and the disappearance of realistic hopes for another military recovery. Napoleon looked toward escape, and America offered the possibility of leaving Europe behind before the victorious Allied powers could take control of him. Reaching the Atlantic was one thing; getting through the British naval blockade was another. The Royal Navy was watching the French coast, and Captain Maitland’s Bellerophon became one of the obstacles standing between Napoleon and freedom.

The result was one of the most unusual confrontations of the Napoleonic Wars. There would be no tremendous exchange of cannon fire between Napoleon and Maitland, nor would the emperor be dragged aboard after a desperate naval battle. Instead, representatives of the defeated French leader entered negotiations with the British naval command while Napoleon considered the rapidly narrowing choices available to him. The emperor who had marched armies across Europe now found his future being determined partly by ships positioned off the western coast of France. Maitland had suddenly moved from the familiar duties of a naval captain into a delicate situation involving diplomacy, security, international politics, and the custody of the most famous defeated ruler in Europe.

On 15 July 1815, Napoleon Bonaparte came aboard HMS Bellerophon. The significance of the moment would have been difficult to exaggerate for those who witnessed it. A man who had crowned himself emperor, commanded enormous armies, redrawn borders, overthrown governments, and repeatedly defeated the great powers of Europe was now aboard a British warship commanded by a Scottish naval officer from the Maitland family. Napoleon’s arrival represented much more than the surrender of a single individual. It symbolised the end of an era that had dominated European affairs since the French Revolution and the wars that followed it.

For Maitland, the challenge did not end when Napoleon stepped onto his ship. The captain now had responsibility for maintaining security while treating his extraordinary passenger with the formal courtesy expected of a British officer. Napoleon was a defeated enemy, but he was also a former emperor surrounded by followers and accustomed to the rituals of political and military authority. Maitland therefore had to balance firmness with restraint while awaiting instructions from the British government. His conduct during the voyage reflected the discipline of the Royal Navy rather than triumphal humiliation of the fallen French ruler.

One reason the episode remains so valuable to historians is that Maitland later recorded his own account of what happened. His Narrative of the Surrender of Buonaparte and of His Residence on Board H.M.S. Bellerophon, published in 1826, preserved a near-contemporary account of Napoleon’s surrender and his period aboard the ship. Maitland was not writing about an event that had happened centuries before or repeating a piece of family folklore. He had commanded the vessel, participated directly in the negotiations surrounding Napoleon’s arrival, and personally observed the remarkable scenes that unfolded aboard his ship. His narrative gave later generations a Maitland eyewitness to one of the defining moments of nineteenth-century European history.

There is an especially fascinating coincidence in the wider Maitland family story of 1815. While Frederick Lewis Maitland became associated with Napoleon’s surrender at sea, another member of the extended Maitland family, Sir Peregrine Maitland, had been serving with the British Army at Waterloo. Sir Peregrine commanded the First Brigade of Guards during the battle and participated in the struggle that brought Napoleon’s final military campaign to ruin. One Maitland therefore stood within the Allied military force that defeated Napoleon on land, while another soon received the defeated emperor aboard a British ship. Few moments demonstrate more clearly how far the family had travelled from its medieval beginnings in Lauderdale and East Lothian.

The episode also represents a remarkable transformation in Clan Maitland history. Centuries earlier, the family had built its reputation through estates such as Thirlestane and Lethington and through service in Scottish courts, councils, and royal government. Sir Richard Maitland became known as a judge, poet, and collector of Scots literature, while William Maitland of Lethington entered the dangerous political world of Mary, Queen of Scots. John Maitland rose to become Lord Chancellor, and another John Maitland eventually became the powerful Duke of Lauderdale during the reign of Charles II. By Frederick’s time, members of the wider family were serving not merely within Scotland but across the military and political structures of a global British state.

That wider setting makes Frederick Lewis Maitland’s encounter with Napoleon much more than an isolated naval anecdote. It illustrates how Scottish families adapted as their opportunities expanded beyond the institutions that had originally created their power. The descendants and cadet branches of old Lowland houses could enter the army, Royal Navy, colonial administration, commerce, and imperial government, carrying familiar Scottish surnames into events taking place thousands of miles from their ancestral estates. Maitland’s career belongs to that larger transformation. His moment aboard the Bellerophon happened because a family once associated primarily with Scottish law and Border politics had become part of Britain’s international military establishment.

For those interested in genealogy, the story also provides a useful reminder that clan history extends far beyond chiefs, castles, tartans, and medieval battles. The lives of younger sons and cadet branches can lead into some of the most unexpected corners of world history. A researcher beginning with the Maitland surname might expect to encounter Thirlestane Castle, the Earls of Lauderdale, or the political struggles surrounding Mary, Queen of Scots. Few would expect that the same investigation could eventually lead to the deck of a Royal Navy warship and the defeated Napoleon Bonaparte. That unexpected connection is precisely what makes Scottish family history so compelling.

Captain Frederick Lewis Maitland did not defeat Napoleon at Waterloo, nor was he responsible for the political decisions that followed the emperor’s surrender. His historical importance lies instead in where duty placed him at a remarkable instant and in the professionalism with which he handled it. On 15 July 1815, aboard HMS Bellerophon, the long careers of a Scottish naval captain and Europe’s fallen emperor suddenly crossed. For the Maitlands, it created an unforgettable connection between an ancient Scottish family and the final chapter of the Napoleonic age.

The story of Frederick Lewis Maitland is only one episode in the much longer journey explored in The Complete History of Clan Maitland. From the family’s medieval emergence in the Scottish Borders and its great houses at Thirlestane and Lethington to Mary, Queen of Scots, the Duke of Lauderdale, Waterloo, Napoleon, imperial service, migration, heraldry, and the modern clan, the Maitland story stretches across centuries of Scottish and British history. For readers researching Maitland ancestry or simply interested in the families who helped shape Scotland, the book follows that history from its earliest documentary foundations into the modern world. Captain Maitland’s extraordinary meeting with Napoleon demonstrates just how far that journey could lead.

References:
Maitland, F. L. (1826). Narrative of the surrender of Buonaparte and of his residence on board H.M.S. Bellerophon. Henry Colburn.

National Records of Scotland. (1344–20th century). Maitland family, Earls of Lauderdale (NRAS832) [Archival collection].

Paul, J. B. (Ed.). (1908). The Scots peerage: Founded on Wood’s edition of Sir Robert Douglas’s peerage of Scotland (Vol. 5). David Douglas.

Rigby Publishing. (2026). The complete history of Clan Maitland. Rigby Publishing.

NEWSDAILY DEFENCE & GEOPOLITICS

🇰🇷🛬 South Korea has formally stepped into the crowded field of 6th-generation
fighter development. The Defense Acquisition Program Administration issued a Request for Proposal for a Conceptual Study of the Korean Next-Generation Fighter, tasking industry with defining the operational concept, configuration design & technology roadmap for what would become Seoul's 1st indigenous 6th-generation combat aircraft programme. The RFP arrives alongside a parallel, in-house design effort from the Agency for Defense Development that was unveiled publicly in July, giving observers an unusually early look at the shape of South Korea's future fighter thinking is taking.

🇮🇳🛫 In a resounding
endorsement of human ingenuity over autonomous hype, IAF Chief Air Marshal A.P. Singh declared that manned fighter aircraft
will remain indispensable for the foreseeable future, even as drones reshape modern battlefields.
Speaking at the India Defence Canalve organized by BharatShakti here, the IAF supremo dismissed notions of a fully aerial unmanned future, emphasizing the irreplaceable "man in the loop" for decisive strikes & complex operations. "At least in the foreseeable future, manned aircraft are not going anywhere. Look around the world, they are going in for 6th-generation aircraft that have manned &
unmanned teaming. It is manned, so there is a man in the loop", ACM Singh asserted. Yet, he tempered the enthusiasm, portraying drones as potent enablers rather than war-winners. "It (drones) is a new thing
that has come into the market, but they can
only do up to a certain level. They can't really
win you wars; they can aid, create confusion,
A swarm drone system can bring an overload of data, information & an overload of confusion that can be created", he explained. He drove the point home with a stark limitation: "But if you want to hit a place, decimate a place, deep inside the enemy territory, you need to carry a weapon that delivers the punch. A drone cannot really do (that), as of now". On the Atmanirbhar front, ACM Singh struck an optimistic yet urgent tone. India's defense ecosystem is "not groping in the dark,” but must "pace up a little more" through policy tweaks favoring private players & startups.

🇮🇳♻️ The DRDO has floated a tender seeking consultancy services for the development of civil infrastructure dedicated to the Bio-Disposal of Rocket Motors, marking an important step towards environmentally sustainable management of expired & surplus missile propulsion
systems. While the tender focuses on infrastructure planning
rather than disposal
technology itself, it reflects a broader shift in India's defence
manufacturing
ecosystem towards cleaner, safer & globally accepted
methods of
demilitarization. The reference to "Bio-Disposal" in DRDO's latest tender indicates that India is exploring advanced biological & biochemical approaches for neutralising
hazardous rocket
propellant materials.
Rather than destroying energetic materials through combustion alone, bio-disposal
employs carefully
controlled chemical & biological processes to break down hazardous
compounds into
environmentally safer substances. Such technologies are already being researched internationally as viable alternatives for military
demilitarization
programmes.

To the man caught between two worlds, who must choose between duty and heritage before darkness consumes them all — this is for you.

Righteous Allegiance by George Yuhasz

A divided nation. A deadly plot. A man caught between two worlds.

Will Manley is a rising star in the U.S. Government’s clandestine services—an undercover agent tasked with stopping a domestic terror group bent on reshaping America. But as he immerses himself in their radical ideology, he faces a battle more personal than he ever anticipated: a choice between his government career and the legacy of his Native American roots.

At the heart of the struggle is Elias McArdle, a brilliant and ruthless former U.S. Army commander. FBI agent Ron Shortridge works to unravel a web of hate and hidden agendas before an act of terror changes the country forever. Meanwhile, Lenape elder Rebecca Hurney offers a path of healing through ancient wisdom—but time is running out. And a mysterious red fox, secretive and resourceful, may be more than he appears to be.

Filled with suspense, mystery, and political intrigue, *Righteous Allegiance* is a gripping thriller with complex characters that will appeal to fans of Vince Flynn, Lee Child, and Tom Clancy.

text:
In 1942, keeping Britain’s farms working was essential wartime work.

At Clyst Marshes in Devon, Land Girls worked alongside heavy machinery to prepare and drain land so it could be used for growing crops and grazing animals.

Their roles were varied and physically demanding. Across the country, members of the Women’s Land Army learned to use tractors and machinery, worked the land and took on vital agricultural jobs while millions of men were serving away from home.

This photograph captures two Land Girls standing in the doorway of a large drag-line excavator being used to create drainage ditches. In this area, Land Girls were particularly involved in levelling the land after drainage work.

More than eight decades later, it offers a striking glimpse of the contribution women made to Britain’s wartime effort — and the everyday work that kept communities going.

At Veterans’ Foundation, we’re proud to back organisations supporting those who have served, their families and Armed Forces communities across the UK today.

text:
Good morning.

I’ve been ruminating over the post from this past week on authority.  Some struggled with the content, some agreed, some said I misinterpreted the scripture entirely.

I sensed some people are really distraught about the despicable behavior and duplicitous actions of many of our government officials (elected and unelected) over many years; an affront to the will of the American electorate.  In no way do I condone illegal, immoral, unethical conduct by any government official.  We all struggle with the idea of subjecting ourselves to the authority of depraved people.

So I‘d like to take a few moments and examine Jesus’ behavior towards Judas, the betrayer. I’m not equating the Crucifixion of our Lord with the likes of any particular politician or bureaucrat you despise - like (just fill-in the blank). Please just stay with me.

In Matthew 26 we will examine a few selected passages.

Passage 1:  Matthew 26:20-25
"When evening came, Jesus was reclining at the table with the Twelve.  And while they were eating, He said, “Truly I tell you, one of you will betray me.”  They were very sad and began to say to Him one after the other, “Surely you don’t mean me, Lord?  Jesus replied, “The one who has dipped his hand into the bowl with me will betray me.  The Son of Man will go just as it is written about him. But woe to that man who betrays the Son of Man! It would be better for him if he had not been born.”  Then Judas, the one who would betray him, said, “Surely you don’t mean me, Rabbi?”  Jesus answered, “You have said so.”"

Passage 2: Matthew 26:43-54 (Later in Gethsemane)
"When He came back, He again found them sleeping, because their eyes were heavy.   So He left them and went away once more and prayed the third time, saying the same thing.  Then He returned to the disciples and said to them, “Are you still sleeping and resting? Look, the hour has come, and the Son of Man is delivered into the hands of sinners.  Rise! Let us go! Here comes my betrayer!”
While He was still speaking, Judas, one of the Twelve, arrived. With him was a large crowd armed with swords and clubs, sent from the chief priests and the elders of the people.  Now the betrayer had arranged a signal with them: “The one I kiss is the man; arrest Him.”  Going at once to Jesus, Judas said, “Greetings, Rabbi!” and kissed Him.  Jesus replied, “Do what you came for, friend.”  Then the men stepped forward, seized Jesus and arrested Him.  With that, one of Jesus’ companions reached for his sword, drew it out and struck the servant of the high priest, cutting off his ear.  “Put your sword back in its place,”  Jesus said to him, “for all who draw the sword will die by the sword.  Do you think I cannot call on my Father, and He will at once put at My disposal more than twelve legions of angels?  But how then would the Scriptures be fulfilled that say it must happen in this way?”"

Now let’s examine these passages.  The undeniable underlying theme throughout these passages is Jesus never lost control - He didn’t fret, throw a tantrum, or hurl curse words at His enemies.  He knew His Mission because in Matthew 26:39,  Jesus prayed to His Father, "Going a little farther, He fell with His face to the ground and prayed, “My Father, if it is possible, may this cup be taken from Me. Yet not as I will, but as You will.”  Jesus submitted to a horrific unimaginable physical death and a brief spiritual separation from the Father.  Dare I say none us could do what Jesus did.  Jesus knew Judas would betray Him. Jesus exposed Judas’ treachery and at that moment, I believe Judas could have repented but he did not. Judas carried out his plan.

Please pay close attention to Jesus’ declaration, “… Do you not think I cannot call on my Father, and He will at once put at My disposal more than twelve legions of angels? But how then would Scriptures be fulfilled that say it must happen this way?”"  Jesus stood firm and was obedient to the Will of the Father.

I keep replaying in my head some of the comments by very sincere brothers and sisters; how they didn’t think they couldn’t submit to our corrupt governmental authorities.  Please understand I am not here to convince you but to offer hope. The underlying message on authority in my previous post was ultimately that all  authority that is delegated to us in different relationships here on earth is underpinned by God, Himself.  Everyone has some issue or circumstance that is so difficult it makes you momentarily stumble.

So I want to reiterate under no circumstances should you violate your well-formed conscience at the behest of anyone.  If you just can’t do something you find in the Word of God; start with the answer - Jesus (that’s why I examined those passages in Matthew.)  If you are interested, I propose an exercise.

1. Reread Romans 13:1-7 in your Bible (August 26 post). Or if there’s another issue you struggle to do; identify what God expects and what God promises.

2. Start with the promise.  Write it down.  Read it aloud several times.  Quietly, think about what it would look like, how you would feel, etc. Then out loud thank God ahead of time because He always keeps His promises. His Word never fails.

3. Now, ask the Holy Spirit to give you the courage and determination to be obedient to God’s Word.  Ask the Holy Spirit to explain what God is asking of you.  Someone may ask, why should we do something we don’t want to do? Well, to start just because God asked you to do so and for no other reason.

I am going to say something that could offend some and I hope by now you know, my only motivation here is to share what God puts in my heart.  Some of you are afraid “it won’t work this time", or “I really hate these people so much I will never help them win”, or “they have done too much harm already”, etc.  Jesus saw the plan B to have 12 legions of angels at His disposal and He could have defeated any army on planet Earth instead of choosing the Cross.  Thankfully, Jesus obeyed God the Father.  But at the heart of all of this discourse is WE MUST BELIEVE GOD WILL ALWAYS KEEP HIS PROMISES AND FULFILL HIS WORD.

I can’t explain it really but I sense many of us are carrying ghastly scars from fighting the world against injustice, crime, immorality, the list goes on.  We aren’t suppose to do this in our own strength but in our complete trust and faith in our Lord Jesus.

I researched some scriptures I believe that will help to remind us, Who we serve.  I will post those scriptures in a second post today.

What we have is God’s Word.  Hebrews 4:12 says, "For the Word of God is alive and active. Sharper than any double-edged sword, it penetrates even to dividing soul and spirit, joints and marrow; it judges the thoughts and attitudes of the heart.”

Jesus is the King of Kings and Lord of Lords. He will reign forever and ever.  Remember John 16:33, "I have told you these things, so that in Me you may have peace. In this world you will have trouble. But take heart! I have overcome the world.”

I am praying for you and I humbly ask, please pray for me.

Have a blessed day.

Peace and be prepared.

text:
Once again, Iceland isn't going forward with negotiations seeking full EU membership.

Here's an explanation from Chat:
----------------------
Iceland did not vote on EU membership yesterday. It voted on whether to restart negotiations for joining the EU. Had “Yes” won, Iceland would have negotiated an accession agreement and then held another referendum on the actual deal before joining. Instead, “No” is winning roughly 52.5% to 47.5%, and RÚV says the remaining ballots cannot realistically change the outcome. (Reuters)

Why was Iceland considering the EU again?

This goes back to the 2008 financial collapse. Iceland applied for EU membership in 2009, opened negotiations in 2010, and had already opened 27 of the 35 negotiating chapters before a new Eurosceptic government suspended the process in 2013. (Enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood)

The issue came roaring back after Iceland's 2024 election. Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir formed a coalition of the Social Democratic Alliance, Reform Party and People's Party; the government pledged to give Icelanders another say on Europe. Inflation, very high Icelandic interest rates, the volatility of the Icelandic króna and security concerns all helped revive the debate. (Reuters)

The geopolitical part is particularly interesting. Russia's war in Ukraine and increased military activity in the North Atlantic have made Iceland's location much more strategically important. Trump's repeated statements concerning Greenland also caused some Icelanders to question how much they should depend upon the United States. Iceland has no standing army; its defense rests primarily on NATO and its bilateral defense agreement with the U.S. (Reuters)

The really important thing: Iceland is already almost inside the EU economically

This is what makes the vote different from something like Brexit.

Iceland belongs to the European Economic Area (EEA) and EFTA, and is also in Schengen. Consequently Iceland already participates in the EU single market, including free movement of people, goods, services and capital, and incorporates a substantial amount of EU single-market legislation into Icelandic law. (European External Action Service)

But the EEA deliberately leaves several big things outside:

EU Common Fisheries Policy
EU Common Agricultural Policy
EU customs union
common EU trade policy
EU foreign/security policy
monetary union and the euro. (EUR-Lex)

That arrangement is extremely relevant to yesterday's vote.

Fish may have decided it

For Iceland, fishing isn't merely another industry. It is tied deeply to the country's economic independence and national identity.

Iceland fought Britain during the famous Cod Wars to establish control of the fishing grounds surrounding the island. Reuters found that the fisheries issue was the central concern of the referendum campaign. Opponents feared that full EU membership would eventually subject Icelandic waters to the EU's Common Fisheries Policy and reduce Iceland's ability to decide who catches what in its waters. (Reuters)

And there was a conspicuous geographical divide: Reykjavík leaned Yes while rural Iceland leaned strongly No — which makes considerable sense given the importance of fishing and natural resources outside the capital. (Financial Times)

The Yes side essentially argued: we're already following a huge amount of EU law; why not have a seat and a vote where those laws are made? Full membership might eventually also permit Iceland to adopt the euro, potentially eliminating some of the currency volatility and extraordinarily high borrowing costs Icelanders have experienced. (European Parliament)

The No argument was essentially: we already have most of the economic benefits through the EEA without surrendering control of fisheries, agriculture, trade policy and our currency — why give that up?

And the latter argument narrowly won.

So the practical consequence tomorrow morning is actually quite boring: almost nothing changes. Iceland remains in EFTA, the EEA, Schengen and NATO. Icelanders retain free movement within the EEA; trade with Europe continues; tourists won't notice anything different. There is no Brexit-style withdrawal happening.

The political consequence is larger. Frostadóttir explicitly presented this as something of a “now or never” decision and said a No vote would put EU-accession speculation aside. So Iceland's 17-year on-again/off-again EU membership project is effectively going back into the freezer. (Reuters)

And there's an interesting irony here: Iceland's current arrangement may be precisely why membership is so difficult to sell. It already gets an enormous amount of European integration while retaining national control over several things Icelanders value most. Full membership therefore has to offer enough additional benefit to justify giving some of that control up.

That 52.5/47.5 result says Icelanders are almost evenly divided — but for now, “EEA Europe, yes; EU membership, no.”

There is a version of patriotism that would meet this moment. It would put production before process. It would require capacity, housing, doctors, reactors and ports, before jurisdiction expands. It would prefer modern treaties that deliver final title, own-source revenue and one law for every citizen over open-ended claims that multiply vetoes and lawyers. It would treat North American integration as the engine and diversification as something you do from strength, not from stalled corridors and a lecture. It would fund a war of attrition only if it were also prepared to squeeze the industrial pipeline that keeps the other army in ammunition. It would stop asking the maple leaf to do the work of a factory.

That is not the patriotism on offer. The patriotism on offer is elbows up until the invoice arrives lower down the income scale. Carney can ride “orange man” through November if the pain stays abstract. He cannot make process a substitute for production, or make Beijing flexibility costless while the southern bridge still carries the country.

Sovereignty is not a guest-of-honour paragraph. It is the ability to build. The map has not changed. The ledger has.

Production before process. Evidence before narrative. Citizens first. One law for all. The map has not changed. The design bureau has.

Canada first.

Secular Skepticism Toward Joseph Smith’s “Golden Bible”

Just months after the Book of Mormon was published, secular newspapers were already circulating skeptical accounts of Joseph Smith’s claims—angelic visitations, golden plates, and a restored gospel.

text:
Robert John Meehan is an American educator, author, poet, and motivational specialist, widely recognized as “The Voice of the American Teacher” for his insightful, empathetic writings on the realities of teaching—especially in challenging urban and inner-city schools. https://t.co/zf02Z44icy 
Born in 1950 in Clinton, Indiana, raised in Connersville, Indiana, he graduated from Ball State University. He spent more than four decades (with sources often citing over five decades of involvement in education) teaching primarily in difficult urban environments, including Indianapolis Public Schools, focusing on disadvantaged and at-risk youth. He is now retired from classroom teaching and works as an education consultant and motivational specialist based in the Indianapolis area. https://t.co/6j2z4ywEM8 
His writing draws directly from those experiences, capturing the emotional range of teaching—the joys, sorrows, frustrations, and occasional horrors of inner-city classrooms—with poetic insight that resonates with educators. Selections from his work have appeared in educational journals and magazines worldwide. He is noted for encouraging teachers to share their own feelings and experiences and for emphasizing empathy, collaboration, resilience, and the transformative potential of teaching. https://t.co/VBZmiCyu05 
Key Works
•  The Teacher’s Journey: The Road Less Traveled (2011, Tate Publishing) — A collection of poetry reflecting classroom life, with pieces such as “A Bell Too Soon,” “In Memoriam (A Child Missed),” “Field Trip Monitor,” “A Teacher’s Pledge,” and others. https://t.co/NRaI7Gj8Mw 
•  A Teacher’s Treasures: Bounty for All (also referred to as The Teacher’s Treasure) — Further poems and reflections on the human side of education. https://t.co/zf02Z44icy 
He has produced extensive additional material, including essays, aphorisms, musings, blog posts, and hundreds of widely shared quotes (his website features collections of quotes and poems). He advocates open access to his materials for educational use with proper credit. https://t.co/VBZmiCyu05 
Themes and Influence
Meehan’s work stresses that empathy is foundational to teaching (“The roots of all teaching lie in the soil of empathy for the Pupil”), the value of teacher collaboration (“The most valuable resource that all educators have is each other”), high expectations, kindness, and supporting students holistically. He highlights the challenges of under-resourced schools while celebrating the dedication of teachers who work in them. His accessible, emotionally resonant style has made him one of the more frequently quoted education writers among practicing teachers. https://t.co/VBZmiCyu05 
His official site (https://t.co/VBZmiCyu05) serves as a primary hub for his profile, blogs, quotes, and selected poems. He maintains a presence on platforms such as LinkedIn and Facebook under accounts related to his educational writing. https://t.co/VBZmiCyu05 
In short, Meehan is valued in education circles for translating decades of hard-won classroom experience into poetry and reflections that humanize the profession and offer practical inspiration to teachers.

text:
Waco is such an interesting spot for banking. Roots run deep there. Generally agree with your take on megabanks as long as the bottom end of the K (consumers and businesses) remain lazy enough to just take what they are offered without thinking to shop around. Waco is an interesting case with the likes of Alliance and ExtraCo now dominating the local markets. I remember when they got a Chase branch by Baylor, the community banker response was “that’s not going to last very long”. Fascinating because the population isn’t small there at all, at 200k you would think more people would drift to the money centers for tech/accessibility.

I think we as investors underestimate how much the average retail customer is disconnected from the world. From my experience partially growing up in a small town and mainly residing in one for pieces of the year now, we have a LONG way to go until large banks captivate attention and actually make people move.

The people that are constantly preaching that megabanks are “coming” need to look at dinosaur cases like FCBC and Waco in general and the likes with extremely low cost deposit bases that aren’t going away any time soon.

text:
Stanislaw Rajmund Burzynski was born in 1943. In 1967, Burzynski graduated from the Medical Academy in Lublin, Poland. In 1968, he received another degree. Burzynski claims this degree was a Ph.D. in biochemistry, but cancer researcher Saul Green found evidence indicating he received a D.Msc. (Doctor of Medical Science) after a one-year project and passage of a test.

Burzynski moved to the United States in 1970 and worked at Baylor College of Medicine until 1977. That year, he established the Burzynski Research Laboratory, where he began administering so-called antineoplaston therapy. Initially, the protocol was administered to 21 patients, but it was later offered more widely as an "experimental" therapy. This opened him up to "charges of unethical conduct and to the suspicion he had become a merchant of false hope", which led to several instances of media controversy. 

Burzynski incorporated his pharmaceutical company, the Burzynski Research Institute, in 1984. Reviewers of his scientific papers have disputed the design of the trials and scientific validity of the published results.

In February 2017, following lengthy hearings, the Texas Medical Board recommended Burzynski's medical license be revoked, with the revocation suspended, and a fine of $360,000 for billing irregularities and other violations.

text:
Honey Boo Boo just turned 21. She says she has never seen a dollar from the show that made her famous.

Here Comes Honey Boo Boo was a genuine monster. On August 29, 2012, it pulled 2.9 million viewers and beat Fox News coverage of the Republican National Convention in the 18-49 demo. A 6-year-old from rural Georgia out-rated a presidential election.

Then the money.

Her mom, Mama June, admitted on her own show to taking Alana's entire $35,000 Dancing With the Stars fee. She spent it on household bills and manicures. Her words. June has also admitted to a $2,500-a-day drug habit and says she burned close to $1 million in her final year of addiction. Alana was a minor for all of it.

California's Coogan law forces parents to bank 15% of a child performer's earnings. Reality TV mostly slips through because the kids are classed as participants rather than employees. Georgia, where the show filmed, offered no protection at all.

Her older sister Pumpkin took custody of Alana at 14 and opened her the trust account the law never required.

TLC built a franchise on her. Alana got her $35,000 back a decade later, no apology attached.

News Lead Up

Crypto peak!?

The crypto market has broken out of its consolidation

Market Overview

The cryptocurrency market has risen by almost 8% over the past 24 hours to $2.37T, reaching its highest level since early June. The initial momentum came on the back of news that the US Treasury was supporting the debt market. This relatively small but timely move signalled that the government is monitoring the situation in the debt markets, spurring demand for risk assets. The rally was then fuelled by a wave of short-covering, following weeks of extremely narrow trading.

Bitcoin reached $70K, posting a 9% rally over 8 hours during the US trading session. As the new day began, the leading cryptocurrency retreated slightly to $69.6K. On Monday, BTC consolidated above the 50-day moving average, and by Wednesday, it had already tested the 200-day MA. As expected, the market’s long-compressed spring snapped back, catching those who had been range-trading and those who had been building short positions on the rise off guard. If Bitcoin does not quickly lose its recent gains, it will be a significant sign that a bull market has begun, much like in October 2023 or March 2020.

Ethereum recorded an even more impressive breakout, showing an 18% gain over 24 hours at its peak. Having risen to $2.25K, the second-largest cryptocurrency is trading near its April–May highs, having broken above its 200-day moving average and away from a long-term support line that has risen from around $1.75K to $1.9K over the past 8 months. The next significant level where the coin may face resistance to further gains appears to be the $2.5K–$2.8K range. (FxPro)

News Lead Up

Cryptos

August 18, 2026

Crypto: Bears remain in control

Market Overview

The crypto market has lost just over 2% compared to its level seven days ago. However, there were signs of a positive trend on Monday, as the market capitalisation rebounded from a local low of $2.16T to $2.18T. The market continues to hover around its 50-day moving average, consolidating within a very narrow range despite the weakening dollar and a rally in the equity market. Among the top cryptocurrencies over the past 24 hours, the top gainers were Zcash (+4.8%), Dash (+2.4%) and Near Protocol (+1%). Declines affected roughly twice as many coins, with the biggest losses seen in Cosmos (-3.8%), Aptos (-2.7%) and Filecoin (-2%).

Bitcoin has been trading below its 50-day moving average for the fourth day in a row, after an earlier attempt to break above it, followed by a pullback to $63.3K. On weekly timeframes, the leading cryptocurrency remains below the 200-week MA. Thus, the bears are confirming their dominance in both the medium-term and ultra-long-term trends. It will only be possible to speak of a breakout from consolidation and expect increased volatility once the price breaks out of the $62–65K range.

News Background

Claims that the crypto market is dead or nearing its end are appearing with increasing frequency on social media. Santiment believes that this situation, against a backdrop of growing pessimism, may be attractive to long-term buyers.

The crypto market has entered the final phase of the bear cycle. According to estimates by DeFi Report, around 85 per cent of the cycle is already behind us, and how the situation develops from here will depend on global macroeconomic events.

Under a new methodology, the Bitcoin treasuries of Strategy and Metaplanet could be excluded from MSCI indices for holding non-operating assets. No decision has been made yet, and MSCI is gathering feedback until 30 September, promising to publish the results by 16 October. JPMorgan previously estimated a potential outflow from Strategy’s securities under such a scenario at $2.8 billion.

According to estimates from Miner Weekly, public Bitcoin miners have reduced their hash rate by 21 per cent over three quarters due to redeploying capacity to AI infrastructure. The current decline is attributed to a weak mining economy and competition for capital and electricity from the AI sector.

FG Nexus, which held 50,000 ETH, sold off its entire cryptocurrency holdings and wound up its Ethereum strategy less than a year after its launch. The total net loss from holding crypto assets reached $45.2 million. Income from staking amounted to just $144,000.

Hyperscale Data has reduced its Bitcoin reserves to approximately 275 BTC after selling around 685 BTC. The proceeds will be used to develop a data centre in Michigan, service debt and cover other expenses. The company will continue to mine Bitcoin and expects to build up its reserves over time.

Summary: The crypto market remains under pressure: Bitcoin is trading below key moving averages, bears are in control of the trend, and news is fuelling investor caution. (FxPro)

Gold News

Gold seems to have completed its corrective pullback

Last week, gold posted a modest July gain, which has already given buyers a significant boost this week. With prices up 6.5% since the start of the week, gold has confirmed a major technical breakout, bringing to an end the downtrend that began in February. The price rebounded from the key psychological level of $4,000 – where the correction also ended last October – and from the 61.8% retracement of the 2022–2026 rally, reinforcing the significance of the reversal signal.

The bulls also have the strength with which gold broke through the 50-day moving average earlier this week in their favour; this average had served as support for the uptrend since the start of 2025, before turning into local resistance in March. If this is not a false breakout, this line could once again act as support for the medium-term bullish trend.

That said, on weekly timeframes, the bulls still need to do some groundwork. During the latest rally, the price approached but failed to break through the 50-week moving average – an important signal line for the long-term trend. It currently stands near $4,400, whilst at $4,500, there is another potential area of resistance that reversed the trend in December and March.

All things considered, we expect an interesting battle in gold this coming week, with the struggle intensifying following the release of US CPI and PPI data. The path to 4,500 may prove relatively easy, but beyond that, we should brace ourselves for a very significant tug-of-war.

Summary: Gold has emerged from its correction and is heading towards $4,500, but a fierce battle between bulls and bears is likely around the 50-week moving average and following the release of US CPI/PPI data. (FxPro)

Alphabet

Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic expands

The value of Alphabet’s stake in the artificial intelligence start-up Anthropic has soared to around $US124 billion ($178 billion), making it one of the most lucrative bets in the company’s history.The Google parent disclosed in a filing on Thursday (Friday AEST) that the value of its investments in unidentified private companies totalled roughly $US124.3 billion as of June 30. The filing noted that this value is “primarily” driven by one investment, which is a reference to Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public. The company said it recorded about $US77 billion in unrealised gains from its private investments in the second quarter, without providing further details in the filing. Google has emerged as one of Anthropic’s biggest backers over the past several years. The technology giant first invested $US3 billion in the start-up starting in 2023. Earlier this year, it agreed to invest as much as $US40 billion more, consisting of $US10 billion upfront and a potential $US30 billion in additional funding tied to operational and financial milestones through 2030.Alphabet’s filing on Thursday showed the remaining commitment has fallen to $US20 billion as of June 30 from $US30 billion at the end of the first quarter, suggesting that Google invested another $US10 billion in the start-up last quarter. Rio Tinto dodges merger bullet

Rio Tinto has dodged two 'bullets' due to Glencore's rejection of a merger proposal: a possible BHP takeover bid and a dangerous acquisition. BHP looked closely at whether to bid for Rio Tinto if the latter announced a merger with Glencore. The two companies would make excellent merger partners; amongst others things, their staff and senior people have similar cultures, they are co-operating on future Australian iron ore projects and they are copper joint venture partners in Chile and the US. Meanwhile, there are significance cultural differences between Rio Tinto and Glencore; there is little doubt that Rio Tinto's CEO Simon Trott would have had doubts about a merger once he understood these cultural differences. News/Snapshot

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

Workforce Challenges: The Minerals Council of Australia is currently calling for migration reforms to address a significant "skills crunch" in the sector.

text:
Reggie Bush’s White Baby Mama Says He Offered Her Millions to End the Pregnancy — She Had the Baby Anyway, Then Came the Child-Support Battle

The meme is ten years old and still circulating because the story never got a clean public ending.

In late 2016, TMZ and Bossip reported that Miami waitress Monique Exposito was pregnant and named then–Buffalo Bills running back Reggie Bush as the father.

TMZ said there were talks about a large payment tied to ending the pregnancy and staying quiet — and that those talks went nowhere. Bossip later put the figure at $3 million in installments for silence and an abortion.

She stayed pregnant. A son, Preston Alexander Exposito, was born on Super Bowl Sunday 2017.

Bush’s camp, at the time, told TMZ he was aware of the rumors, remained married to Lilit Avagyan, and would meet his obligations if a DNA test showed he was the father.

There was no widely published court order, no public DNA filing, and no official confirmation of a signed $3 million contract. What did appear in gossip coverage was a later claim that payments slowed after the story leaked and that the two sides fought over additional support.

Florida family law is separate from any private adult agreement. A child born after such talks still has a right to support from a legal parent. That is the point the text overlay is making. It is also why the story cannot be written as if a judge already ruled on every dollar.

Bush and Avagyan stayed married and later had another child. Exposito’s then-husband, Alexandre Bastin, filed for divorce and obtained language that he would not be financially responsible for the boy.

Beyond tabloid sourcing, the public record on exact payments remains thin. A private deal between two adults does not erase a child. That much is law.

The $3 million figure is still a media allegation, not a stamped court finding.

What do you see when you look at this?

#ReggieBush
