text:
Trump Delivers America-First Tax Relief, Safer Streets, Job Booms, Drug Price Plunges, and More

President Donald J. Trump and Republicans continue advancing policies that put American workers, seniors, and families first through lower taxes, energy growth, private investment, and fair trade. This progress appears across South Carolina results, Cabinet outreach nationwide, and First Lady Melania Trump’s foster youth scholarships. Auto industry reshoring and record prescription drug price drops add to the victories. However, debt warnings from Congress cannot be ignored, though July unemployment data shows broad improvement. Everyday Americans gain from America-first steps that restore fairness, create opportunities, and address long-standing burdens without relying on foreign free-riding or unchecked spending.  

Historic Tax Relief Reaches South Carolina Workers and Seniors  

President Donald J. Trump’s Working Families Tax Cuts return money to South Carolina households by ending federal income taxes on qualifying overtime for one in four workers and granting a new senior deduction that helps about one million seniors. Average tax refunds hit $3,476 while the Rural Health Transformation Program delivered more than $200 million in first-year funding. These cuts protected 86,000 jobs, $15 billion in state gross domestic product, and $8 billion in wages. The measures strengthen family budgets and local economies under Republican leadership that prioritizes working people over distant interests.  

Private Investment Surges Into South Carolina Manufacturing  

Trump’s America First agenda of tax cuts, energy dominance, and secure borders sparked major company expansions. Eaton committed $340 million in Jonesville for transformers. NorthMark Strategies plans a $2.8 billion high-performance computing center in Spartanburg. TS Conductor invests $134 million in Hardeeville. Rolls-Royce adds $75 million in Aiken. Century Aluminum restores full production with $50 million in Berkeley County. Scout Motors builds a $300 million Supplier Park in Blythewood. Additional projects from Coastal Precast Systems, Georg Utz, Ferrara Candy, Red Metals, AmbioPharm, and Octapharma total billions more and create lasting jobs.  

Cabinet Officials Showcase Nationwide America First Results  

Members of Trump’s Cabinet traveled the country to highlight energy, infrastructure, manufacturing, veterans care, and border gains. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. visited Dubuque to promote community health centers and later joined others on rural health and fitness efforts. Energy Secretary Chris Wright celebrated oil and gas growth in the Permian Basin. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy toured airports and announced port, ferry, rail, and control upgrades. These visits demonstrate measurable wins that reach everyday Americans from coast to coast.  

Additional Cabinet Outreach Advances Key Priorities

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum opened 111 new hunting and fishing opportunities at wildlife refuges. Small Business Administration Administrator Kelly Loeffler pushed higher loan limits with lawmakers and toured manufacturers. Veterans Affairs Secretary Doug Collins focused on women’s and young veterans’ care in Omaha while attending Iowa events. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick discussed farm exports and praised Apple’s Houston expansion. Acting Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling addressed workforce needs and manufacturing growth. 

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin inspected Alaska facilities. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins advanced drone use against pests and defended work requirements. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent linked tax cuts to investment. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth honored troops. Education Secretary Linda McMahon toured university programs. Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner joined criticism of mismanaged homeless agencies. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer examined tire production. These efforts reinforce practical benefits under Republican direction.  

First Lady Expands Foster Youth Education Pathways

Melania Trump’s Fostering the Future initiative received a $2 million donation from IndyCar and Fox Corporation for scholarships at Indiana University and Purdue University. This grows the network to 26 universities that help foster care youth earn degrees, launch careers, and gain financial independence based on merit. An IndyCar race car carrying the branding appeared at the White House and will feature at the Freedom 250 Grand Prix. The program already produced its first doctor and pairs with housing aid plus new savings accounts. It builds long-term opportunity for young people without regard to circumstance.  

Trade Policies Drive Auto Production Back to America

Trump’s trade agenda prompted major reshoring. Ford will bring Lincoln models home from China and create thousands of jobs. Toyota invests $3.6 billion to shift Tacoma production to San Antonio and add 2,000 jobs. Honda keeps Civic output in Indiana. General Motors moves $4 billion worth of production to Tennessee and Kansas. Mercedes-Benz expands Alabama SUVs with $4 billion. Volvo, Stellantis, Nissan, Hyundai, and Rolls-Royce add capacity and jobs across multiple states. Companies respond to fair rules by investing in American workers and supply chains.  

Prescription Drug Prices Record Steepest Drop in Decades  

Trump’s Most Favored Nation agreements with 17 major drugmakers covering 86 percent of the branded market produced the largest annual prescription drug price decline in more than 60 years. Prices fell 3.9 percent since he took office and dropped every month in 2026. The TrumpRx platform already saved $700 million. High-cost medicines including certain diabetes treatments now start as low as $149. The Department of Veterans Affairs locked in more than $10 billion in savings this fiscal year. Patients finally pay rates closer to those in other developed nations.  

Debt Warnings and Job Data Highlight Ongoing Challenges and Gains  

House Budget Chairman Jodey Arrington, Republican of Texas, noted the national debt surpassed $40 trillion and called for an Article V convention of states to pass a balanced budget amendment. Joint Economic Committee Chairman David Schweikert, Republican of Arizona, flagged the new record of $40.047 trillion and more than $2.4 trillion added this fiscal year, describing continued inaction as immoral. July unemployment fell in 29 jurisdictions, held steady in 18, and rose in four, with the national rate at 4.1 percent. Payroll jobs increased in 27 states. These facts show both fiscal pressure that demands attention and labor market resilience under current policies.  

Deeper Fiscal Warnings From Budget and Joint Economic Leaders

Arrington stressed that the national debt topped $40 trillion after nearly 200 years to reach the first $1 trillion, yet now that amount is added in less than five months. The federal government borrows $6 billion each day, with over half going to interest payments that exceed the entire national defense budget. He quoted James Madison that a public debt is a public curse and urged the states to use Article V to pass a balanced budget amendment and reverse the curse. 

David Schweikert noted the debt hit a record $40.047 trillion with more than $2.4 trillion added this fiscal year alone. Interest ranks as the fourth-largest budget item and is nearing the point of consuming most federal spending, which he called an immoral path toward market-unraveling risks if Congress fails to act.

Specific Infrastructure and Manufacturing Gains From Cabinet Visits

Sonderling highlighted a $1 billion Stanley Black and Decker investment in U.S. manufacturing during his Rio Grande Valley stop, including $4.6 million to expand the Mission facility and add 100 jobs to its existing 250 positions. Duffy announced a $16.5 million Federal Transit Administration award for a new passenger ferry linking Tampa and St. Petersburg, a $1 million shipyard grant for Gulf Marine Repair, and a $5 billion multi-phase rail investment to close 30 grade crossings and upgrade 1,000 more. Kennedy unveiled a $102 million investment in rural health care centers at Castle Family Health Centers in Atwater. These targeted commitments expand jobs, training, and local capacity under the administration’s growth agenda.

President Trump’s administration and Republican partners keep delivering concrete results that lower costs, expand opportunity, secure communities, and rebuild industry while confronting debt realities head-on. From state-level wins to Cabinet outreach and targeted reforms, the focus remains on practical gains for families and workers. Continued attention to fair trade, innovation, and fiscal discipline offers the clearest path to sustained strength for the nation.

text:
Ilya Somin is not a serious academic. This essay is embarrassing, and it is no wonder he is taking flak. Somin is blind to the fact that his demand to abolish interior immigration enforcement rests on flimsy and poorly built claims. Blind loyalty to progressive dogma has stopped his brain from working.

Somin builds a radical demand on a handful of contested facts that cannot support the jump. He calls for the complete elimination of the principal federal agency charged with interior immigration enforcement.

In the article he writes that “there is a way out of this dilemma: Abolish ICE and give the money to state and local cops.” He elaborates that the agency should be dismantled and its funds reallocated, perhaps through federal grants, so recipient agencies can target violent and property crime. The facts he offers for this jump belong in a schoolboy’s daydream, not the work of a professor. This analysis should embarrass elite institutions now filled with weak thinkers who produce contemptible foolishness that sounds like the idiotic remarks of children.

Federal immigration power and interior enforcement rest on a clear civil statutory foundation that Congress created in the Immigration and Nationality Act. The Act designates unlawful presence, entry without inspection, and other specified violations as independent grounds of removability that authorize detention and removal. The Secretary of Homeland Security may take any removable alien into custody under the Act and detain that alien pending a final decision on removal. Immigration judges in the Executive Office for Immigration Review hear the case after the agency issues written notice of the charges and affords an opportunity to contest them. These civil administrative proceedings require no proof of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. Immigration and Customs Enforcement simply executes the precise statutory commands that Congress has written into the Act.

Somin’s first elementary mistake is treating the absence of a criminal conviction as equivalent to the absence of legal justification for detention. He writes that “despite administration claims that ICE is protecting the public against dangerous criminals, 65 percent of people detained as of June had no criminal record, and some 90 percent had no convictions for violent or property crime.” He presents these figures as proof that ICE routinely seizes people without legitimate cause. Immigration detention and removal are civil administrative proceedings under the Immigration and Nationality Act. They are not criminal prosecutions. Congress enacted statutes that designate unlawful presence and specified entry violations as independent grounds authorizing the Department of Homeland Security to detain an alien and authorizing the immigration courts to enter a removal order. In these civil proceedings the government need not prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. The statutes require only that the agency furnish written notice of the charges and provide an opportunity to contest those charges before an immigration judge.

By collapsing the civil-criminal distinction, Somin recasts ordinary statutory enforcement as systemic abuse of power. Once that twist is accepted, every interior arrest of a removable alien becomes evidence of cruelty rather than evidence of the agency doing the job Congress assigned it. This basic category error spreads through the rest of his analysis and leaves the demand with no solid ground.

The essay next makes a basic causal mistake to force a charge of racial animus that the facts do not support. Somin writes that “the alarming extent of racial and ethnic profiling by ICE is shown by the fact that the agency’s arrests in Los Angeles County declined by 66 percent after a federal court order barring the use of these and similar tactics.” He treats the racial and ethnic skew in ICE arrests as proof that the agency’s operating rule is racial animus. Unlawful entries are heavily concentrated among nationals of a small number of Latin American countries. Any enforcement effort directed at the actual population of removable non-citizens will therefore generate arrest statistics that are racially and ethnically disproportionate. That disproportion standing alone does not demonstrate that agents stop or detain people because of their race or ethnicity. The essay offers no evidence that race itself functions as a decision criterion in mass arrest and detention decisions. It simply equates the observed disparity with racial motivation without further proof. Somin confuses a later result of enforcing the law against a demographically skewed population with the actual content of the enforcement rule itself.

Finally, the essay converts a contested originalist argument about the limited scope of federal power into the false claim that interior immigration enforcement itself lacks constitutional foundation. Somin asserts that “leaving immigration restrictions more to the states would bring us closer to the Constitution’s original meaning.” He continues that “the Constitution does not explicitly grant immigration authority to the federal government, and Founding Fathers such as James Madison and Thomas Jefferson rightly argued that it did not have any general power to bar migrants.” This argument is severely moronic coming from an elite-institution law professor who should know better.

Although the Constitution contains no explicit general grant of power over immigration, Article I, Section 8, Clause 4 and Article I, Section 9, Clause 1 establish federal power over the admission, exclusion, and removal of non-citizens.

The Naturalization Clause grants Congress authority to create a uniform rule for adopting foreigners into the political community and granting them the rights of native subjects. This authority necessarily includes power to set the conditions under which non-citizens may enter the United States, remain within its borders, or face removal. The Migration or Importation Clause delays any congressional ban on the migration or importation of persons until 1808. That temporary restriction would serve no purpose unless Congress otherwise possessed the power to impose such a ban. Period dictionaries define naturalization as the formal act of admitting a foreigner into a community as a native subject. They define migration and importation as the movement or bringing of persons into a country from abroad. The law of nations in the founding era treated control over the entry of foreigners as an inherent attribute of national sovereignty.

Congress exercised this power near its inception through the Naturalization Act of 1790 and later through statutes governing entry and removal. The Immigration and Nationality Act rests on this same foundation of authority. The Act authorizes the Secretary of Homeland Security to take into custody any alien who is removable and to detain the alien pending a decision on whether the alien is to be removed from the United States. The Act further authorizes the Secretary to order the removal of any alien who falls within the statutory classes of removable aliens. Immigration and Customs Enforcement executes these commands through civil administrative proceedings that apply the existing grounds of removability enacted by Congress. The claim that the Constitution grants the federal government no authority over immigration is therefore incorrect.

That claim confines the Naturalization Clause to formal citizenship procedures alone and strips it of practical force over entry and removal. It reduces the Migration or Importation Clause to a temporary safeguard for the slave trade with no wider effect. The claim ignores the necessary implication of the Naturalization Clause that Congress may regulate the conditions of presence and expulsion. It also ignores the presupposition of power embedded in the Migration or Importation Clause itself. The claim disregards the consistent founding-era understanding that every sovereign nation controls the admission of foreigners. It further conflicts with the concrete commands of the Immigration and Nationality Act that direct the Secretary of Homeland Security to detain and remove removable aliens, and with the early federal statutes that first exercised the power through the Naturalization Act of 1790 and subsequent entry rules. The text of the two clauses, their internal structure, and the contemporaneous meaning of their terms therefore reject the claim outright.

Somin’s analysis collapses at each successive step. The demand to abolish ICE rests on elementary legal errors, causal confusions, and constitutional misreadings. These defects lay bare the thin quality at elite institutions and the weak minds they now hire. And that is why I am so contemptuous towards them. They really don't deserve their positions and they should belong to people with greater merit.

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

On August 30, 1800, a storm broke over Henrico County and Richmond—and Governor James Monroe had only hours to decide whether the capital of Virginia would stand.

Gabriel, an enslaved blacksmith owned by Thomas Prosser, had spent months recruiting men from the plantations north of the city. The plan was no rumor. They meant to gather after dark near Brook Bridge, march on Richmond in three columns, fire the warehouses as a diversion, seize the magazine and armory, and take Monroe himself hostage. Swords had already been forged from scythes and plowshares. Quakers, Methodists, and Frenchmen were to be spared. Most other whites were not. “Death or Liberty” was the language they used.

That morning two enslaved men at Meadow Farm, Tom and Pharaoh, told Mosby Sheppard what was coming. Sheppard got the warning to the Governor’s house. Monroe did not wait for the night to prove it. He called out the militia, posted men on the capitol and the powder, and sent patrols into the flooded roads. Then the sky opened. Bridges washed out. The rendezvous never formed. Gabriel postponed the attack one day. By then the state was awake.

Monroe was thirty-two years from the presidency, but he was already a Revolutionary veteran who had been wounded at Trenton. He treated the plot as what it was: an attempt to storm the seat of government and butcher a city. He offered a reward. Gabriel fled downriver, hid on the schooner Mary, and was taken in Norfolk. He was tried in Richmond on October 6 and hanged on October 10. About twenty-six men went to the gallows. Others were transported. After the first executions, Monroe wrote Thomas Jefferson and asked a hard question—when should the hand of the executioner be stayed? Jefferson answered that there had been hanging enough. Monroe pardoned some. He did not pretend the conspiracy had been a speech.

Virginia kept its capital. The militia held. A planned night of fire and hostage-taking died in the rain and in the speed of a governor who refused to let Richmond be surprised. That is the record of August 1800 in this Commonwealth.

text:
I have to admit, I’m enjoying watching some of my friends suddenly discover their deep, almost sacred reverence for historic names now that Donald Trump has renamed Lake Ontario “Lake America.”
Where was this passionate defense of tradition when we spent the last decade playing cultural Mad Libs with names?
The Cleveland Indians became the Guardians.
The Washington Redskins became the Commanders.
Aunt Jemima was evicted from the breakfast table and replaced by Pearl Milling Company.
Uncle Ben got demoted to Ben’s Original.
The Native American woman disappeared from Land O’Lakes butter.
Eskimo Pie became Edy’s Pie.
The Dixie Chicks became The Chicks.
Lady Antebellum became Lady A.
Universities and real-estate professionals started replacing “master bedroom” with “primary bedroom.”
Computer programmers began retiring “master/slave” terminology.
Schools, streets, statues and buildings bearing the names of historical figures were renamed by the hundreds.
Then there were the military bases.
Fort Bragg became Fort Liberty.
Fort Hood became Fort Cavazos.
Fort Benning became Fort Moore.
Fort Polk became Fort Johnson.
Fort Lee became Fort Gregg-Adams.
Fort Gordon became Fort Eisenhower.
Fort Rucker became Fort Novosel.
Fort Pickett became Fort Barfoot.
Fort A.P. Hill became Fort Walker.
We even watched Mount McKinley become Denali.
Meanwhile, our vocabulary got its own remodeling job. “Mothers” sometimes became birthing people, “pregnant women” became pregnant people, and “breastfeeding” acquired the alternative chestfeeding in some institutional language.
And Columbus Day? Plenty of cities, states and institutions decided Indigenous Peoples’ Day was preferable.
For years the message was: Names matter. Words matter. Language evolves. Old names can be changed when society decides another name better reflects its values. If you're offended by the change, get over it.
Okay.
Apparently there was an asterisk:
This principle remains valid until Donald Trump names something.
Suddenly the people who spent a decade redecorating the dictionary have chained themselves to the furniture.
Personally, I think Lake America is mostly political theater, and pretty funny political theater at that. Canada is perfectly free to keep calling it Lake Ontario. Nobody is confiscating their maps.
But after watching everything from pancake syrup to Army installations get renamed in the name of cultural sensitivity, I simply cannot work up the appropriate level of outrage over a lake.
So to my friends who are losing sleep over Lake America, I offer the same compassionate advice conservatives received during the Great Renaming:
Language changes. Names evolve. Try to keep up.

text:
Ecclesiastes
Chapter 5

“Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. To draw near to listen is better than to offer the sacrifice of fools, for they do not know that they are doing evil. Be not rash with your mouth, nor let your heart be hasty to utter a word before God, for God is in heaven and you are on earth. Therefore let your words be few. For a dream comes with much business, and a fool’s voice with many words. When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it, for he has no pleasure in fools. Pay what you vow. It is better that you should not vow than that you should vow and not pay. Let not your mouth lead you into sin, and do not say before the messenger that it was a mistake. Why should God be angry at your voice and destroy the work of your hands? For when dreams increase and words grow many, there is vanity; but God is the one you must fear. If you see in a province the oppression of the poor and the violation of justice and righteousness, do not be amazed at the matter, for the high official is watched by a higher, and there are yet higher ones over them. But this is gain for a land in every way: a king committed to cultivated fields. He who loves money will not be satisfied with money, nor he who loves wealth with his income; this also is vanity. When goods increase, they increase who eat them, and what advantage has their owner but to see them with his eyes? Sweet is the sleep of a laborer, whether he eats little or much, but the full stomach of the rich will not let him sleep. There is a grievous evil that I have seen under the sun: riches were kept by their owner to his hurt, and those riches were lost in a bad venture. And he is father of a son, but he has nothing in his hand. As he came from his mother’s womb he shall go again, naked as he came, and shall take nothing for his toil that he may carry away in his hand. This also is a grievous evil: just as he came, so shall he go, and what gain is there to him who toils for the wind? Moreover, all his days he eats in darkness in much vexation and sickness and anger. Behold, what I have seen to be good and fitting is to eat and drink and find enjoyment in all the toil with which one toils under the sun the few days of his life that God has given him, for this is his lot. Everyone also to whom God has given wealth and possessions and power to enjoy them, and to accept his lot and rejoice in his toil—this is the gift of God. For he will not much remember the days of his life because God keeps him occupied with joy in his heart.”
Ecclesiastes 5: 1-20 ESV

text:
“No decent person can support Israel” is moral grandstanding, not an argument.

As a libertarian, I don’t need a 3,000-year-old historical claim to defend Israel. Ancient kingdoms, biblical promises and competing narratives cannot establish individual property titles today. Palestinians do not lose their rights because Jews lived there two millennia ago, and Israelis do not lose theirs because Palestinians suffered dispossession.

Start with people alive today.

Israelis have exactly the same individual rights to life, liberty and property as everyone else. They may live where they legitimately own or rent property, build businesses, form communities and defend themselves against aggression. No theory of “decolonisation” gives Hamas or anyone else the right to murder, kidnap or expel them because they are Israeli or Jewish.

That is why October 7 matters. Hamas crossed a border and deliberately attacked civilians, murdered families and took hostages. Israel consequently had every right to use force against those responsible and to prevent them from doing it again.

That right has limits. Palestinian civilians possess exactly the same rights. An Israeli soldier cannot deliberately kill an innocent Palestinian because Hamas murdered Israelis. A settler cannot legitimately seize somebody else’s property. Nor does the Israeli state acquire rights unavailable to ordinary people merely by invoking national security.

But there is an enormous moral and institutional distinction between Israel and Hamas.

Israel is a liberal democracy with competitive elections, opposition parties, private enterprise, religious diversity, a combative press and substantial personal freedom. Arab Israelis vote, organise politically, work throughout Israeli society and sit in parliament. Israelis can call Netanyahu every name imaginable, demonstrate against his government and vote to remove it.

Hamas offers religious authoritarianism, political repression and deliberate violence against civilians.

That distinction matters far more to me than arguments about who controlled Jerusalem in 800 BC.

Judge Israel by what it does. Condemn violations of individual rights, illegal seizures of private property and crimes committed by its soldiers or government. Apply exactly the same standard to Palestinians, Hamas and every other actor.

But calling Israel itself “colonial land-theft and genocide” and declaring every supporter indecent replaces individual responsibility with collective guilt. Israelis become collectively guilty by nationality and Palestinians collectively innocent by nationality.

I reject that framework. I distinguish between aggressors and victims, individuals and governments, legitimate defence and criminal violence.

You don’t need to admire the Israeli state to understand those distinctions.

You just helped close a deal that, if it holds, changes the map of the Western Hemisphere. The risk is not that Caracas said yes. The risk is that the agreement is treated as a one-administration transaction. If it is only barrels and a press cycle, the next opening for Beijing and Moscow is obvious.

I wrote a short piece on that larger problem. The argument is simple: Washington and Bolívar both saw that liberty on this continent fails without scale. The practical work now is not another ideological contest. It is to treat the Americas as one energy, mineral, industrial, and security system — with the United States competent enough at home to be the architect, not just the customer.

The Venezuela agreement is the first material test of that idea. U.S. companies in those fields only matter if the framework outlasts a presidency and outlasts an interim government. That means investment rules, offtake, security against criminal networks, and a path for Venezuelan production to sit inside a hemispheric supply system rather than as a swing supplier for whoever offers the next discount.

I am a naturalized American, born in Caracas. I am not writing to ask you to bless one slate of Venezuelan politicians. I am writing because the deal you negotiated is larger than the argument still being had about who “deserves” to sit at the table.

text:
The great exchange What will you give to God in exchange for freedom and eternal life? Are you ready to part with anything that might keep you from following the Lord Jesus and his perfect plan for your life? Jesus poses these questions to challenge our assumptions about what is most profitable and worthwhile in life. In every decision of life we are making ourselves a certain kind of person. It is possible that some can gain all the things they have set their heart on, only to wake up suddenly and discover that they missed the most important thing of all. Of what value are material things if they don't help you gain what truly lasts for eternity. Neither money nor possessions can buy heaven, mend a broken heart, or cheer a lonely person.   Losing all to gain all with Jesus Christ A true disciple gladly gives up all that he or she has in exchange for an unending life of joy and happiness with God. God gives without measure. The joy he offers no sadness or loss can diminish. The cross of Jesus Christ leads to victory and freedom from sin and death. What is the cross which Jesus Christ commands me to take up each day? When my will crosses with his will, then his will must be done. Are you ready to lose all for Jesus Christ in order to gain all with Jesus Christ? 
"Take, Lord, and receive all my liberty, my memory, my understanding, and all my will, all that I have and possess. You have given them to me; to you, O Lord, I restore them; all things are yours, dispose of them according to your will. Give me your love and your grace, for this is enough for me. (Prayer of Ignatius of Loyola, 1491-1556)

text:
The outrage deserves scrutiny—but the claim needs to be stated accurately.

Los Angeles County created a rent-relief program providing up to $15,000 per qualifying household for financial hardship connected to the 2025 wildfires or federal immigration enforcement. Immigration status is not a requirement.

The county also expanded the program using public funds that included money originally allocated for wildfire-related rental assistance. So there is a legitimate question: Why should wildfire-relief money be redirected to address hardship attributed to ICE enforcement while thousands of wildfire victims remain displaced?

Calling it simply “stealing wildfire funds to give $15,000 checks to noncitizens” is an exaggeration—the assistance is rental relief, not an unrestricted $15,000 check, and recipients must meet eligibility requirements.

But the larger issue is government priorities.

Huey Long offers a historical warning. His administration used government jobs, patronage, public resources and political appointments to build and maintain his political machine. His organization exerted extraordinary control over Louisiana’s government and election machinery.

The lesson isn’t that California is Huey Long’s Louisiana. It’s this:

Government should distribute taxpayer resources according to transparent, neutral criteria—not cultivate or politically favor selected constituencies.

So the questions are:

Why is wildfire assistance being expanded to people whose hardship is attributed to ICE enforcement? What funds were redirected? Under what authority? And why is immigration status irrelevant?

When wildfire victims are still waiting to rebuild, those are legitimate questions about government priorities, fairness and political allocation of public resources.

text:
Mississippi is experiencing a similar moment with the billions being invested in data centers across the state.

I think the opportunity is enormous, but I would add one caution: the announcement itself is not the transformation. It is the opening of a new possibility.

The real test is what happens next. Do suppliers follow? Do universities and community colleges adapt? Do new businesses form? Do wages rise? Do young people who once would have left now have a reason to stay?

Louisiana trained you, but Colorado offered the next decision your career required. Mississippi has lost people for the same reason.

So maybe the measure of success 10 or 20 years from now is not simply how many billions were invested. It is whether those investments created an economic environment where the next generation no longer has to leave home to build the future.

text:
General Heth on Black Participation in Jackson Dedication (10/25/1875)

"The colored volunteers are well uniformed and drilled, and well behaved. Their leading officers and other leading colored men made an application which in substance was about this: “If it is agreeable to the white people, we would like to show our respect and good-will for them and our respect for General Jackson as a great and good man; and we would like to take such place in the ceremonies as the white people may kindly set apart for us.”

This application was made in the most respectful, kind-hearted, and becoming manner. Before it was finally acted on, a great many of the best white people of all classes were consulted about it, and Mrs. General Jackson being consulted has sanctioned the present arrangement. They all agreed that it would be wrong, and have a bad effect, to snub and rebuff this kindly and respectful offer of the colored people to do honor to Jackson. They all agreed that it would have a good effect here and abroad, and it would be a pleasing and significant tribute to Jackson, for the example of the white people, in honoring a Confederate soldier to be followed by the colored people. And they did not come to that conclusion without having good reasons for it, as I now show.

Even in the days of slavery Jackson was for many years a regular teacher of colored Sunday schools. The colored people were very much devoted to him as a man, and when he was buried in 1863 they not only turned out in great numbers, but they were regularly formed as a part of the funeral procession, and marched in it as a portion of the escort of his body to the grave; and all this was done under the orders of Governor John Letcher. Moreover, I am not ashamed of the fact, but am proud of it, that the faithful slaves of my forefathers followed their bodies to the grave, and followed in procession with the white mourners.

For what reason, then, does any man object to the memory of Jackson being now honored by the colored people who desire to honor him? Does it hurt the memory of Jackson if he is honored by all the people of all the races in the world? Does it hurt for him to be now honored by all sorts of people without regard to political distinction and without regard to race or color? Because the colored people honor him, does it make our honors any less? Would any white man refuse to honor Jackson because the colored people do in their hearts and in the most respectful manner pay their honors to his memory also? Is Jackson’s fame so small that everybody cannot do it honor? And are we to back out and let the colored people outdo and eclipse us in honoring our hero?

I want to ask another question. General Joseph E. Johnston and Admiral J. R. Tucker will ride in this procession. The noble sons of General Lee will take part in it. Our Governor and ex-Governors, our judges of the Court of Appeals, our senators and representatives in Congress, and, besides, many others, some of the most distinguished men of other States, will join in it. Thousands of those who have often bared their bosoms to shell and shot and bayonets on the battlefield will join in that procession. Those who followed Stonewall Jackson in the Valley of Virginia, those whom he led in the memorable seven days’ fights around Richmond, who were with him at Sharpsburg and Fredericksburg, who were with him in his last great battle, and were by his side when he fell—all those say that this is right; and I say that those who took no part with him in his grand career, those who did not follow him, and those children whom he and his followers protected, have no right to object. The procession is good enough for all the battle-scarred warriors and veterans I have named, and they are proud to form part of it. Now, I ask, who is it that is too good to join those men in that procession? And who is it that will consider himself contaminated by following where General Joseph E. Johnston leads.

Let there be an end of this talk about the honors to be paid to Jackson on the 26th by the colored people. I do in my soul respect them and applaud them for the way they have behaved themselves in this matter. I am glad to know that not one in a hundred differs with me in these views. I have no word of disrespect or unkindness for those who do so differ. But I am sure they have not reflected maturely. I am confident they will all cheerfully and heartily unite with us. It is all-important that we shall be entirely harmonious. Bad men and enemies of ours would be very glad to see us disagree. They would be especially glad to see any of us—even a single man of us—get angry and quarrel on such an occasion. But that, I am sure, we are too sensible and too patriotic to do.
-H. Heth Acting Marshall

text:
The Denial Machine, Part Two: The Network and Andrew Neil

In Part One, I set out why Chris Packham was right to say the Daily Sceptic is “basically put together by a bunch of professionals with close affiliations to the fossil fuel industry,” tested against the four people the outlet itself names as its climate team, and against Toby Young’s own conduct.

I also introduced Luke Johnson, the businessman who challenged Packham on air without disclosing his own directorships at the outlet under discussion. Part Two follows Johnson’s network further, then turns to Andrew Neil, the one figure in this story whose own public record can be tested independently of any institutional role he’s held.

Johnson’s own network

Johnson’s links run further and deeper than the two undisclosed directorships covered in Part One. In 2013, he co-founded the Centre for Entrepreneurs, a think tank explicitly launched in partnership with the Legatum Foundation, the philanthropic arm of Christopher Chandler’s Dubai-based Legatum Group, and for a period housed within the Legatum Institute itself.

The Legatum Institute is a separate, more overtly political body which openDemocracy has described as becoming “the Brexiteers’ think tank of choice” after 2016, which the Charity Commission found had failed to meet required standards of balance and neutrality in its advocacy, and into whose orbit reporting has traced Koch-linked funding.

Legatum is also the group that, alongside Paul Marshall, backs GB News. None of this means Johnson’s own think tank shares the Institute’s politics, and the two shouldn’t be conflated. But it places Johnson, like Young, Neil and Marshall, inside the same small funding lineage this piece keeps returning to.

The platforms that rushed to Young’s defence after the #bbclaurak broadcast sit inside that same structure at a higher level. The Spectator’s “Steerpike” column ran “When Will the BBC Apologise to Toby Young?” within days. Andrew Neil, then chairman of Press Holdings (the group that owned The Spectator, commonly shorthanded as “Spectator chairman,” a title he held until the September 2024 sale to Paul Marshall) quote-tweeted the piece. But the relationship runs back further than that one defence: Young’s own byline appears on The Spectator’s controversial 11 July 2009 cover, “Relax: Global Warming Is All A Myth,” fifteen years before Packham’s broadcast and under Neil’s own chairmanship.

Marshall’s acquisition, completed five months after the broadcast, is worth dwelling on. His hedge fund, Marshall Wace, held at least $2.2 billion in fossil fuel investments as of June 2023. A later DeSmog/Guardian analysis found that in the first quarter of 2026 its declared fossil holdings nearly tripled over that quarter, reaching $2.8 billion, with Chevron rising from $196 million to $864 million in three months. Marshall Wace called the analysis “a partial and inaccurate picture.” Marshall also owns UnHerd outright and, since a 2022 capital injection, has held a 41 percent stake in GB News’s parent company, alongside the Dubai-based Legatum Group.

Marshall and Legatum turn up together again, further along the same network, and more tightly than a shared founding credit suggests. The Alliance for Responsible Citizenship (ARC), launched in 2023 as a conference and campaigning network with a public brief of civilisational renewal and “responsible citizenship,” presents Marshall, Baroness Stroud and Jordan Peterson as its public founders. Companies House filings reported by DeSmog in 2024 showed the same five people who controlled GB News’s parent company, All Perspectives Ltd, Marshall, Alan McCormick, Richard Douglas, Mark Stoleson and Christopher Chandler, were also the persons with significant control of ARC itself.

That exact overlap has since shifted, not dissolved: McCormick and Stoleson dropped off both companies’ PSC registers on matching dates, Stoleson on 31 December 2024 and McCormick on 12 May 2025, though McCormick remains a director of both. The current PSC list for both ARC and All Perspectives is now an identical four names: Marshall, Chandler, Douglas and Philip Vassiliou, another Legatum figure based, like Chandler and Douglas, at Legatum’s own Dubai address.

Stroud previously served as chief executive of the Legatum Institute, and Legatum’s own charitable foundation gave ARC more than £150,000 in the eighteen months to June 2023, with Marshall separately donating £1 million that year through his Sequoia Trust. Whether the controlling names number five or four at any given moment, it’s the same ownership group already documented behind GB News, controlling a second platform.

The same American climate-sceptic network the GWPF is coupled to has its own UK foothold in this world. The Heartland Institute, which received at least $676,000 from ExxonMobil between 1998 and 2007 and has taken donations from Koch-linked foundations, launched a UK-EU branch in December 2024 at Brooks’s, the Mayfair private members’ club, with Farage attending as “special guest of honour” alongside former Prime Minister Liz Truss and several Conservative MPs. Its UK-EU chief, Lois Perry, later appeared alongside Farage at a panel held at 55 Tufton Street in June 2025; Farage had separately headlined Heartland’s 40th anniversary fundraiser in Chicago in September 2024, telling the audience “let’s get Trump back, let’s drill baby drill.” That places Heartland in the same Tufton Street ecosystem, and the same fossil-fuel-adjacent funding lineage, as the GWPF and the wider network this piece has traced.

It is worth being precise about what that does and doesn’t show. The documented links are between Heartland and Farage, and between Heartland and the GWPF as an institution. Contact with the Daily Sceptic’s own named writers is thinner, but not absent: in August 2026, Heartland UK/Europe’s own account quote-tweeted Young amplifying a claim from Morrison, calling it “spot on.”

That claim was that the Met Office’s 2025 climate report had de-emphasised its long-running wind and storm data. The underlying fact holds up: the Met Office’s own 2024 report says plainly that “observations do not currently suggest that the UK’s climate is becoming windier or stormier.” But that finding is about wind speed and storm frequency specifically. It says nothing about the rainfall those storms produce, and a separate World Weather Attribution study published the same year found that rainfall had already been made about 20 percent heavier by human-caused warming.

What the claim gets wrong is the story wrapped around the wind data: that the Met Office changed its reporting to hide something, or that it had been “duped by activists.” The 2025 report still covers storms at length, including Storm Éowyn as the UK’s most powerful windstorm in over a decade, and the same reports that show wind in decline also show record heat and rising seas, which cuts against any theory of a Net Zero cover-up. A real, publicly available finding, wrapped in an invented story of suppression, travelled from Morrison’s byline to Young’s account to Heartland’s own in a matter of days.

So the allegation under dispute reaches well past the four writers who first tested it. It’s a structure that reproduces the same pattern at every level it’s examined: named bylines, editors, sister organisations, and ownership itself. Marshall, on the evidence above, is the person who most directly embodies that ownership layer. But there’s one figure in this story whose own public record can be tested independently of any institutional role he’s held: Andrew Neil.

Andrew Neil

We’ve already seen his Press Holdings/Spectator chairmanship, and his quote-tweeted defence of The Spectator’s response to Packham. Neil was also GB News’s founding chairman, a channel Marshall personally backed from its very first funding round in January 2021, before it even launched. It’s a channel with its own documented record on this exact subject: a 2023 DeSmog analysis found that one in three GB News presenters, ten of the channel’s 31 hosts, had cast doubt on climate science or policy live on air the previous year, with more than half attacking climate action outright. The pattern is still visible.

In May 2026, @Ofcom opened a formal investigation into GB News over a repeat broadcast of Bev Turner’s autumn 2025 interview with Donald Trump, in which Trump called human-induced climate change “a hoax” and was not challenged once by Turner. Ofcom had initially declined to investigate the original airing at all, on the grounds that a surrounding panel discussion offered alternative perspectives; it changed course only for the unchallenged repeat the following day. At the time of writing, that investigation remains open.

Neil has been an editor, broadcaster and publisher all at once, and has himself a well-documented record of downplaying man-made climate change across more than a decade, independent of the Daily Sceptic entirely. What connects the record, across all three stages below, is the same underlying move: finding a genuine pocket of uncertainty, a cold snap, a revised figure, an unresolved regional finding, and using it to imply the whole scientific consensus is shakier than it is. I’ve broken this down into three loose stages.

Andrew Neil: three stages, one direction

Mockery, from 2009:

Neil was running this pattern before he’d even joined Twitter in 2010. On the BBC’s own website, in a 30 December 2009 blog post titled “It’s going to be a cold 2010,” he seized on a cold snap forecast to question the Met Office’s long-term modelling: “if it can’t get its winter forecast broadly right, why should we believe its forecasts for 2020 or 2050?” Three weeks earlier, on 7 December, he had built an entire post around a single month’s satellite temperature uptick, explicitly conceding “nobody on either side of the debate would put any store by one month’s figures” before doing exactly that.

By March 2013 he was asking “Here’s an existential question to which I don’t know the answer. Is the whole global warming schtick over?” and he’s spent the decade since intermittently repeating the weather-for-climate substitution any first-year science student is taught to avoid: “Damn you global warming!!!!” over a snowy photo, “record Scottish snowfall” cited against a scientist’s prediction. This is not scientific uncertainty. It is the conflation of weather with climate trend.

As recently as 31 May 2026 he posted that London would stay in the late teens with rain all week, “it’s called the British Summer,” and promised “some respite from the London-based media’s climate hysteria.” What followed was England’s warmest June on record for mean temperature, and the first year on record the UK reached 35°C in May, June and July alike, including 36.4°C at Heathrow, London’s hottest June day ever, and 38.1°C at Kew on 13 August. On 11 August, with the season’s mean already at 16.48°C against a 2025 record of 16.12°C, the Met Office said the UK was on course for its hottest summer on record, needing only average conditions for the rest of the month to beat it. A week of ordinary British weather was, once again, treated as a rebuttal of the trend.

Misinformation, 2023:

During a June heatwave, when a coal plant went on standby, Neil tweeted: “Britain burning coal today to generate electricity after heatwave made solar panels too hot to work efficiently... Solar generating only 1.4GW (5%) despite 15GW installed capacity.” That causal claim wasn’t Neil’s own invention, he was echoing a Telegraph report making the identical claim the same day, but it was specifically and directly false. Solar Energy UK’s chief executive, Chris Hewett, called the idea that panels lose effectiveness in heat a “gross and fundamental misapprehension,” noting output “doesn’t fall off a cliff” in hot weather and that identical panels operate fine in the Saudi Arabian desert. Neil’s own number was wrong within minutes on its own terms too: he posted at 09:17 that solar was producing 1.4GW; by 09:35, Gridwatch showed actual output at 6.6GW, nearly five times his figure. Carbon Brief’s own factcheck later named Neil directly, alongside DUP MP Sammy Wilson, as having repeated the same debunked claim. The coal plant had in fact been brought onto standby for an unrelated reason entirely, a tripped interconnector to Norway. This wasn’t scepticism. It was a specific, checkable, false technical claim, refuted by name by the industry body whose subject it was.

Outsourcing, 2024 to 2026:

In a December 2024 post, replying to a user who had shared video of David Attenborough warning about climate tipping points, Neil shifted to conceding the premise while dismissing the consequences: “Climate change is real... but much of it has already been discredited,” with no citation for what or by whom. By February 2026 he was amplifying Wide Awake Media, an account Media Bias/Fact Check rates “Right Conspiracy-Pseudoscience” with “Low” factual reporting, to 885,000 views.

A former @BBC presenter with two decades in senior leadership at Press Holdings and The Spectator, chief executive from 2004 and chairman from 2008 until his September 2024 resignation, was, by this point, no longer making the argument himself. He was pointing his own institutional credibility at a rated-unreliable source and letting it make the argument for him.

The tobacco parallel

The pattern is not new. From the 1950s, the tobacco industry ran a decades-long campaign to manufacture doubt about smoking and cancer, using tactics this piece has already shown recurring here: funding seemingly independent voices through opaque foundations (the CO2 Coalition and GWPF occupy a comparable role to the Council for Tobacco Research, branded-independent research bodies acting as a pass-through for funding whose origin they don’t disclose, not the same organisation, but the same function) and building a network of interlinked think tanks sharing personnel and donors, though not always the same donors by the same route: the IEA and GWPF share an address and a personnel network on Tufton Street, while Spiked’s link runs separately, through the LM Network and a documented Koch Foundation grant to its US arm.

Neil’s own messaging, documented in this piece through his own words, mirrors the rhetorical downplaying pushed by fossil fuel interests once flat denial stopped working: not a claim about who he speaks for, but about which script his own record happens to follow.

The underlying opportunity is the same in both cases too. No science examining a complex system shaped by human behaviour, whether that’s the precise cancer risk from a given smoking history or the precise attribution of a given flood, ever produces uniform, total certainty on every individual case. That residual, honest uncertainty is real, scientists say so themselves, and it is exactly the gap that people with a financial or ideological stake in delay have spent decades widening into “nobody really knows.”

The rhetorical moves match too, and one in particular sits at the very heart of this piece: concealing or disguising the link itself, whether by omission, denial, or narrowing a claim until it no longer covers the thing being asked about. That’s what Johnson did by never disclosing his own directorships on air. It’s what Spiked did in 2016, taking Koch money the same year it attacked the Standing Rock protests without mentioning the Kochs’ financial stake in the pipeline (Spiked says the grants funded a separate US free-speech debate series, a defence its editors have repeated publicly since). It’s what the GWPF has done for over a decade: it has never named its donors, and separate attempts to force disclosure through Freedom of Information and tribunal routes have failed on at least four occasions. And it’s what Young did in writing: opening with an absolute denial of “any affiliations, close or otherwise,” then narrowing to a defensible claim about personal payment, letting the answer to a smaller question stand in for the one actually asked.

Alongside concealment sit the two more familiar moves: downplaying a known problem while formally conceding it exists, which is Neil’s shift from outright mockery to “climate change is real, but this is scare-mongering,” and casting doubt on inconvenient findings, which is Homewood’s output in a sentence and, with a difference worth naming, much of Doshi’s too, though Doshi’s more often takes the form of a competing economic argument for continued fossil fuel use than doubt with nothing put in its place.

Where people sometimes push back on this analogy is to say there’s no tobacco-style smoking gun here, no internal memo proving anyone knew and lied. That’s true of the individuals and organisations named in this piece specifically, but it understates how far the wider parallel actually goes. Big Oil’s own flat denial phase is dated and documented: ExxonMobil ran advertorials into 2004 insisting “scientific uncertainties continue to limit our ability to make objective, quantitative determinations regarding the human role in recent climate change,” and as late as November 2005, then-CEO Lee Raymond told Charlie Rose on air that natural variability, not human activity, better explained the data and that “the science isn’t there” to say otherwise. This came decades after the company’s own scientists had produced accurate internal projections of the warming to come, and years after the IPCC’s 1995 finding of a “discernible human influence.”

That gap between internal knowledge and public denial is the tobacco playbook exactly, and it’s fully proven, just not proven against the specific names in this piece. The underlying interests stayed the same after roughly 2006 to 2007; what changed was the tactic, flat denial gave way to acknowledging the science while emphasising uncertainty, disputing liability, and funding exactly the kind of think tanks and commentators catalogued above. The Daily Sceptic’s climate team and the GWPF sit downstream of that same pivot.

Who pays, who poses

None of what’s catalogued here proves a single coordinated conspiracy running across every issue of the day. What it does show is a repeating structure: concentrated ownership, some of it based outside the UK, as with Legatum’s Dubai headquarters; opaque funding that resists disclosure as a matter of course rather than exception; a strikingly small and densely interconnected cast of people moving between broadcasting chairs, think tank directorships and campaign groups; and a media ecosystem that rewards confident wrongness with reach and engagement, while imposing almost no cost for being repeatedly, demonstrably incorrect.

It is difficult to look at this structure and not notice that the same small set of interests, and often the same individuals, recur whenever the issue at hand would otherwise cost the wealthy more, in tax, in regulation, or in the political consensus needed to act on it. The same ownership and the same think tanks turn up on tax, regulation, and net zero alike. In every case, the beneficiaries of the confusion are rarely the audience being persuaded.

There’s another recurring feature worth naming on its own terms: the men doing the framing overwhelmingly present themselves, and are presented by sympathetic outlets, as ‘anti-establishment outsiders’ taking on a remote, sneering elite.

Luke Johnson warning about the establishment’s “vested interest” while sitting, undisclosed, on the board of the outlet under discussion is a near-perfect miniature of the pattern. 

Multi-millionaire private equity chairmen, hedge fund owners of national magazines, a life peer, and a former BBC presenter with a quarter-century broadcasting career are not, by any ordinary use of the word, outsiders.

They are the establishment, in business, media and increasingly politics simultaneously, and the framing does real work for them: it recasts entrenched concentrated wealth as plucky dissent, and casts anyone defending the mainstream consensus as the establishment figure instead.

Chris Packham was right about the Daily Sceptic’s own climate team, and for three of the four, the evidence of institutional and professional connection is stronger and more direct than Young’s rebuttal acknowledged. Toby Young’s written denial doesn’t survive contact with his own website.

Andrew Neil’s climate record, tracked across more than a decade of his own posts, shows a man playing a specific, recognisable and increasingly threadbare role: taking the real, honest uncertainty that exists at the edges of any science of complex systems, and using it to cast doubt on the whole.

These are wealthy, powerful, well-connected people, downplaying and casting doubt on a warning the oil industry’s own scientists had already delivered decades before most of the public had heard of it. Not every drought, flood or fire happening now carries the same clean scientific fingerprint, and this piece has tried to be honest about that rather than claim otherwise. But the pattern underneath is difficult to ignore: the same small set of interests has repeatedly helped turn legitimate scientific caution into political delay, and delay has a cost that compounds the longer it runs, a cost that keeps being paid by people who had no say in running up that bill.

Some of what’s already been set in motion cannot be undone: sea level rise and ice sheet loss respond to warming on timescales of centuries, and that damage is coming regardless of what happens next. The more alarming popular version of ‘climate lag’ (that even stopping all emissions today would mean decades more of rising temperatures no matter what), isn’t what current climate science actually finds; research on the “zero emissions commitment” suggests genuine net-zero would see global temperature stabilise relatively quickly, rather than continuing to climb for decades afterward.

Current government policies point to roughly 2.6 to 2.7°C of warming by 2100, according to the Climate Action Tracker. About 1.4°C of global warming has already arrived. England and Wales’ May and June heatwaves, the second of which arrived weeks after Neil promised “some respite from the London-based media’s climate hysteria,” were estimated to have killed around 2,700 people combined, 42 percent of those deaths attributable to the warming already here. Bringing the wider trajectory down from here is a matter of political will, not physics.

The tragedy this piece has documented isn’t that it’s already too late. It’s that people with real influence chose delay, and called it caution.

Dr Russell Jackson

From the Book "Thinking & Destiny" by Harold Waldwin Percival https://t.co/DKEWOnm5Wl 1946 by Harold W. Percival Copyright 1974 by The Word Foundation, Inc. All rights reserved, including the right to reproduce this book or portions thereof in any form

The law of thought as destiny works in silence and is unseen. Its course is not perceptible by the senses. Even its results on the physical plane attract no attention unless they are unusual or unexpected. Then by some persons they are called accidents, and are attributed to chance; by others, miracles or the will of God, and an explanation is sought in religions.

It is not generally understood that religion is the relation between doers and the gods they have fashioned out of nature. The God or the gods which men worship are nature gods. This fact is apparent from the symbols by which they demand to be adored. These nature gods, however, are subject to complete Triune Selves: they are created by the embodied doers of Triune Selves.

Triune Selves furnish to the embodied portions of their doers the means of accomplishing the worship due to—and even the worship demanded by—the nature gods. The “divinity” of each human, speaking within, is the thinker of his own Triune Self. Triune Selves educate their doers, and use religions as a means of teaching.

Thus the doer in a human body is allowed to consider a personal God as its creator and source of power, and as the administrator of justice according to a moral code. In so far as the God’s acts or omissions do not fall in with the moral code—the very code which is attributed to the God—the doer believes in the “inscrutable ways of Providence.”

Sometimes small parts of the law of thought are to be found in religions; but then they are colored to fit in with the body of the theology.

When the doer matures sufficiently to see that it is sense-bound in a body which is personalized nature, and to distinguish between the gods or God on the one hand, and, on the other, the Light it receives from its Intelligence, then by that Light will the doer understand the innate idea of justice, the real meanings of the “wrath of God” and of the doctrine of original sin.

Accidents and chance are words used by persons who do not think clearly when they attempt to account for certain happenings. Anyone who thinks must be convinced that in a world as orderly as this there is no room for the words accident and chance.

Every natural science depends upon the recurrence of certain facts in a certain order. A physical law means facts observed and the assurance of their recurrence in orderly sequence. Such physical laws govern all physical actions, from sowing to harvesting, from boiling water to sailing a vessel, from playing a fiddle to the electrical transmission of sound and images by radio.

Can it be that there is no certainty of the orderly sequence of facts and events when we search for moral law, for moral order?

There is such a law, and it accounts for so-called accidents: Everything existing on the physical plane is an exteriorization of a thought which must be adjusted through the one who issued the thought, in accordance with his responsibility and at the conjunction of time, condition and place.

An accident is an exteriorization of a thought. Purpose of an accident. Explanation of an accident. Accidents in history.

An “accident” is an event which happens to one or more persons or things unexpectedly, without being foreseen and without intention. Therefore the accident stands out from the general and foreseen order of events as unusual or separate.

A so-called accident is, like any other event on the physical plane, a thought in a certain part of its course.

A thought is a being created by the Conscious Light and desire; and which, when issued, has in it an aim, a potential design, and a balancing factor—which balancing factor, like the needle of a compass, points to the final balance of the thought as a whole.

The thought endures until the balancing factor has brought about an adjustment through the one who issued the thought. The balancing factor causes exteriorizations as long as the thought endures.

Whenever the thought, moving in its courses, approaches the physical plane, it causes the one who issued it to be in place for an exteriorization of that thought. An exteriorization can happen only when there is a juncture of time, condition and place.

The laws which control the exteriorization do not always fit in with the intention and expectation of the persons concerned; and the exteriorization is then called an accident.

An accident is a perceived physical part of a thought which is proceeding on its otherwise invisible course. The exteriorization makes visible that part of the thought which touches the physical plane and is not yet balanced. The demonstration is made on or through the person who is concerned in the accident.

Accidents such as a personal injury, or a barn being struck by lightning, or an occurrence which prevents one from embarking on a ship that is to be wrecked, come only to those whose thoughts are thereby partially exteriorized to them.

An accident presents to the one to whom it happens something of his past, either distant or recent. The accident is a part of one of his own thoughts that he has not balanced, and which will endure and, from time to time, meet him face to face as a physical event, until he has paid or received payment through the direct exteriorization of the design, learns his lesson from that child of his mind and desire, and has satisfied his conscience.

Often accidents come to injure him, often to help him, and sometimes as protections.

The reasons why events happen to him in the form of accidents, in an exceptional, unforeseen manner, are that a man would not do certain things to himself, like breaking an arm, or that circumstances do not call for a commission of a crime against him, that is, an intentional injury; or finally that the happening accidentally is the easiest and most direct way to bring about the juncture of time, condition and place for the exteriorization.

Further, there is in the happening of an accident a special call for attention. An accident rather than an ordinary event, produces this, because the accident is unlooked for, startling.

An accident is brought about in the ordinary course of the law of thought as destiny. Every man has a vast number of thoughts cycling in his mental atmosphere toward and away from exteriorization on the physical plane. The thoughts live on with a tendency to exteriorize in the events which the balancing factor in each of them requires and projects.

The thoughts begin and continue their cycles from the time a person issues them. Whenever they approach the physical plane, they seek to exteriorize; but they are often held back by the exteriorizations of his present design.

When there is an opportunity, be it ever so slight, the whole nature of the man seizes upon it and uses it to precipitate an event which will bring about one of these exteriorizations. Every thought, once it is issued, endures and appears cyclically, exteriorized as a physical event.

For that purpose, the one who issued the thought calls mentally or psychically on other persons concerned with the thought, through their atmospheres. If a cycle of one of those persons’ thoughts coincides with a cycle of one of his own, this will produce, unintentionally to the first one, the event which is called an accident.

Another manner in which accidents are brought about is by elementals, nature units. They follow and are bound by a man’s thought, and rush with it into his body as an impulse, so that he unexpectedly performs an act which results in an accident to him; he may, for instance, cut himself; or may fall in front of a fast moving car.

Another way in which elementals may act to precipitate a thought, is by producing an occurrence without human intervention, as where fire burns a man, or a cinder gets into his eye, or melting ice drops on him from a roof, or he finds articles of value. In every instance his own thought, seeking exteriorization, is the means of precipitating upon him the event which he calls an accident.

The purpose of an accident is to call one’s attention to the thought of which it is one of the exteriorizations. One to whom an accident happens can always, by searching, find out something about that.

Though the event may not reveal the whole past to him, it may reveal that portion of the past which it is necessary for him to know. If he tries to understand, he will learn, and he will learn more, if he is willing to pay,—he must pay anyway. What he learns will bring him nearer to the adjustment.

Suppose two men are traveling in a mountainous country. By placing his foot on an insecure stone, one of them slips and falls into a ravine. His companion goes to the rescue, finds the mangled body below, among rocks; and close at hand he discovers, cropping out from the side of the ravine, a vein of gold.

The death of the one impoverishes his family and causes failure to some with whom he was in business. Because of that fall, the other discovers an ore deposit which becomes a source of wealth.

Such an occurrence is said to be an accident, bringing death to one, sorrow and poverty to some, failure to others, and “good luck” to the comrade whose wealth is gained by chance.

There is no accident or chance connected with such occurrences. Each of the events is in accordance with the working out of the law as destiny, and is an exteriorization of some thought, issued by the person affected, though beyond the limits of perception.

The one who was killed was a man whose allotted time had run its course, though his death could have occurred a little sooner or might have been postponed for a short time. The manner of his death had been predetermined to be sudden. Further, it was necessary, on account of his family and his business connections, that his relations to them be severed abruptly. Therefore he suffered sudden death.

Whether the poverty awakens self-reliance in those who have been dependent on the deceased and brings out traits which could not be seen while they were dependent on another, or whether they become disheartened, give up to despair or become paupers, rests largely upon the past of those concerned.

Whether the one who discovers the gold improves the opportunity of wealth to be honest, to better the conditions of himself and others, to relieve suffering, or to support educational work; or whether, on the other hand, he does none of these, but uses his wealth and the power which it gives him for the oppression of others; or whether he becomes morally corrupt and urges others to lives of dissipation, is all according to the law of thought, and has been largely determined by previous thoughts of those concerned.

If the deceased had been more careful in the selection of his path, he might not have fallen, though his death, as it was required by the law, would merely have been postponed a short time.

If his companion had not descended the perilous path in the hope of rendering assistance, he would not have found the means by which he acquired his wealth. Yet, even if fear should have kept him from going to the aid of his comrade, he would only have deferred his prosperity, because wealth was to be his as the result of his past thoughts and works.

By not letting pass an opportunity which duty presented, he hastened his prosperity.

It is injurious to speak of accident and chance as events happening without cause and irrespective of law. Such unthinking use of the words fosters in people the belief that they may act or fail to act, and not be held accountable. They come to believe that things may happen to them without cause. So they may dull their moral conceptions.

They limit their views and reasoning to things on the physical plane; they trust to chance, and are liable to become irresponsible.

Events which affect a few or many, or a race or a continent, or the whole world, arrive to those whom they benefit or afflict according to the working of the law of thought as destiny.

To each individual are exteriorized some of his past thoughts. The thoughts press for an opening for exteriorization. If there are many people whose thoughts tend towards a similar event, they are gathered even from the ends of the earth to bring about the so-called accidents. To everyone comes the advantage or loss that exteriorizes some of his past thoughts.

Accidents which happen to a community, like a conflagration, cyclone, inundation or pestilence, are likewise the exteriorizations of thoughts of those affected.

Under this head fall also the destruction of hamlets and cities, and the devastation of countries, like the ruthless razing of Carthage, the sacking of Rome, the plundering of the Spanish settlements by the buccaneers, or the conquest of Peru.

In these cases the “just” suffer with the “unjust.” The “unjust” are the evil ones in the present; the “just” are the unrighteous of the past.

Such destinies have been made by the action and inaction, the participation and indifference, of the inhabitants in times such as those of the persecution of the Huguenots, or of the Netherlands by Alva, or of the Quakers by the Puritans in New England.

They will be brought together in the course of time, and their thoughts will lead them to the place and time of the exteriorization of those past thoughts. That place may be the same locality; or the people may be brought together in another, and there live in prosperity or in trouble, and share in the accidents of the final disaster.

The reckoning may be held up for a long time; but it is sure to come.

The United States of America was set apart by Intelligences to try out self-government by the multitude, and so they have been led to success in their various wars, their political institutions and their economic undertakings, notwithstanding the actions of the people.

In peace and in war, their escape from the natural consequences of their selfishness and indifference is striking. But this protection and universal success, which school histories and orators seem to take as a matter of course, may not last.

There must be an accounting for all that these people did tolerate and do in violation of their great responsibility. The New England bigots, the Massachusetts slave traders, the Southern slave drivers, the oppressors of the Indians, the political and other corruptionists will at some time meet and suffer at the reckoning which is sure to come.

In every life there are numerous events which are generally regarded as accidents.

Such events are, to mention a few: birth at a particular time into a certain country, race, family and religion; birth into favorable or unfavorable conditions; birth into a sound or a diseased body; birth with certain psychic tendencies and mental endowments.

Peoples’ lives are largely made up of events which they cannot choose, and which seem to be determined by accident.

Among these are opportunities offered to enter a trade, a business or a vocation; chance acquaintances who cause, prevent or end associations in work or commerce; and conditions which lead to or hinder marriage and friendship.

People, if they do not look upon events as happenings by chance, explain them as the will of God and seek consolation in their religion.
