🚨 Alan Jackson Shares His Take on the Lindsay Clancy Trial

​If you followed the Karen Read trial, you already know who Alan Jackson is. He stepped into a Massachusetts courtroom in one of the most high-profile murder trials in the country and relentlessly dismantled the Commonwealth’s evidence, its witnesses, and its investigation to demand that the prosecution meet its heavy burden.

​Now, Jackson is watching defense attorney Kevin Reddington take on the same prosecution system in the Lindsay Clancy trial. Different defendants, completely different facts, and distinct legal defenses yet watching both attorneys in action has provided a masterclass in high-stakes criminal defense.
​In a recent conversation with Billy Bush following closing arguments in the Clancy trial, Jackson gave a candid assessment of the case. 

His takeaway was straightforward: he does not believe the Commonwealth met its burden of proof beyond a reasonable doubt.

Coming from the attorney who aggressively fought the Commonwealth throughout the Karen Read prosecution, that evaluation carries serious weight.

​Jackson’s perspective isn't driven by emotion or headlines it centers strictly on the legal standard, the physical evidence, and the specific questions the jury must answer. In his view, the defense raised significant, unresolved issues that the prosecution failed to overcome.

​Key Takeaways on Strategy & Trial Execution

​Challenging the Investigation: In the Karen Read case, Jackson’s approach was unrelenting never accept the prosecution's narrative at face value. Question the assumptions, challenge the expert witnesses, highlight the inconsistencies, and cross-examine until reasonable doubt becomes undeniable.

​Testing Expert Testimony: Kevin Reddington applied that exact approach in the Clancy case. 

Instead of relying on full agreement from every witness, Reddington systematically picked apart the Commonwealth’s expert testimony pinpointing what was reviewed, what was left unexamined, and where assumptions replaced certainty.

​Connecting with the Jury: Jackson highlighted a trait unique to seasoned trial attorneys: the ability to read and engage individual jurors during closing arguments. 

Both Jackson and Reddington demonstrated how to address the panel as a whole while tailoring specific points to individual jurors following the evidence.

​The Burden Remains on the State: A central principle in criminal law is that the defense does not need to solve the case or deliver a perfectly packaged alternative narrative. The single legal question is whether the Commonwealth fulfilled its burden of proof. 

Conflicting expert opinions, investigative lapses, and cross-examination vulnerabilities all directly feed reasonable doubt.

​Refusing to Back Down: Neither Jackson nor Reddington hesitates to make a courtroom uncomfortable when necessary. 

They press for answers, expose contradictions, and demand clarity from witnesses doing precisely what the job requires when a client's freedom is on the line.

​While the Karen Read and Lindsay Clancy cases are factually distinct, viewing them through a legal lens offers a striking comparison. 

Two different cases, two distinct defense strategies, but one shared constitutional standard: the defendant does not have to prove innocence; the Commonwealth must prove its case.

​Jackson brought that relentless battle to the courtroom for Karen Read, Reddington brought it for Lindsay Clancy, and Jackson’s assessment reflects clear recognition of that work.

Continuing the operation for several months, based on water usage records dating back to early in the year

text:
🚨 Messi Hits Four as Inter Miami Rout Montréal 7-1 in Historic Night

Lionel Messi delivered a sensational four-goal performance as Inter Miami demolished CF Montréal 7–1 at Nu Stadium, ending their five-game winless run in emphatic fashion. The result marked the biggest victory in Inter Miami's history and the first time the club had scored seven goals in a single match. 

Casemiro opened the scoring in the 20th minute with his first goal for Miami, but Montréal quickly responded through Fabian Herbers nine minutes later. Messi restored the lead in the 40th minute with a direct free-kick before producing a brilliant individual effort in the 52nd to make it 3–1. 

Messi then turned provider, threading a pass through for Luis Suárez to score Miami's fourth in the 80th minute. Three minutes later, the Argentine completed his hat-trick with a delicate chip before adding a fourth goal from another direct free-kick deep into stoppage time. 

The performance was Messi's first four-goal game in MLS and took his league tally to 18 for the season, putting him two goals clear at the top of the Golden Boot standings. His two direct free-kicks also made him just the ninth player in MLS history to score twice directly from free-kicks in the same match. 

With interim boss Guillermo Hoyos suspended and watching from the stands, Miami's coaching staff oversaw a performance that offered a spectacular response to their recent struggles. The incoming Cristian “Kily” González era is now approaching, but for one night, the spotlight belonged entirely to Messi.

AIRLINE INVESTIGATES CREW MEMBER WHO ALLEGEDLY UPGRADED PASSENGERS FOR CASH MID-FLIGHT

MIAMI, FL — Flight attendant Kristen Loomis, 38, is under investigation after passengers reported she had been quietly offering first-class upgrades for cash payments mid-flight, moving economy passengers into empty premium seats in exchange for money handed over discreetly during service.

According to the fictional report, Loomis, 38, reportedly approached passengers individually during boarding and mid-flight, offering to move them to empty first-class seats for $80 to $150 in cash, payable directly to her.

A passenger who declined the offer reportedly reported the exchange after noticing at least four other travelers move to first class mid-flight with no announcement or official upgrade process involved. Airline records show none of the moved passengers had any documented upgrade authorization.

The airline, reviewing flight manifests and crew statements, concluded Loomis had violated multiple company policies by:

Reassigning premium cabin seats without authorization from the purser or gate agents
Collecting personal cash payments for a service that should be processed through official airline channels
Failing to log any of the seat changes in the flight's official manifest
Repeating the practice across at least six flights, based on crew scheduling records

Passengers who paid reportedly had no idea the upgrades were unauthorized, with one saying "I genuinely thought I got lucky, not that I was buying a seat off the books."

The dispersion is the finding here. 1.8 percent of budget at Florida against 19.5 percent at Miami (OH) is not a difference in degree, it's two different sports sharing a rulebook.

The part that reaches families: the settlement lets schools fund every roster spot and doesn't require it. So "scholarship" is about to mean different things at different addresses, and nothing on a program's website tells you which kind you're being offered.

Under 85 caps, everyone knew what existed and how many. Now the number of funded spots inside a 105-man roster is a private budget decision, made at a school where it might cost 2 percent or 20.

The question changed. It used to be whether they're offering aid. Now it's how many of the 105 are actually funded, and whether the answer holds for four years.

text:
The House settlement didn't just change how athletes get paid.

It may have quietly created another spending race in college athletics: scholarships.

In his latest NILnomics analysis, Greg Chick examines what the new roster limits actually mean financially for FBS athletic departments.

The median FBS school would need roughly:

• 271 additional scholarships
• $4.8M in additional funding
• 5.5% of its athletics budget

But the impact isn't remotely equal.

At Florida, the estimated cost is 1.8% of the athletics budget.

At Miami (OH), it's 19.5%.

For some schools, fully funding the new roster limits could be a recruiting advantage.

For others, it could force much harder decisions.

text:
- The Dollywood Foundation (1988) — Founded to improve education in Sevier County, Tennessee, initially focusing on reducing high-school dropout rates.

- Buddy Program — Offered $500 to participating seventh- and eighth-grade students who ultimately graduated high school; Billboard reports the local dropout rate fell from 35% to 6%.

- Hiwassee College Scholarships (1989) — Offered a $500 scholarship to every Sevier County student who wanted to attend Hiwassee College.

- Eagle Mountain Sanctuary at Dollywood (1991) — A 30,000-square-foot bald eagle sanctuary managed by the American Eagle Foundation, providing a home for non-releasable bald eagles.

- Dolly Parton's Imagination Library (1995) — Provides free books every month to children from birth until they begin school. It began in Sevier County and later expanded internationally.

- Dolly Parton Scholarship (2000) — Provides $15,000 college scholarships to five Sevier County high-school seniors each year.

- LeConte Medical Center / Sevier County Hospital Fundraiser (2007) — A benefit concert raised $500,000, while Dollywood and Dixie Stampede pledged another $250,000 each, bringing the effort to $1 million. The resulting medical center includes the Dolly Parton Center for Women's Services.

- Smoky Mountains Rise Telethon (2016) — Organized following the devastating East Tennessee wildfires and raised more than $13 million for affected residents.

- My People Fund (2016) — Created for families who lost their homes in the wildfires. Families received $1,000 per month for six months, with roughly $8.9 million distributed directly to people in need.

- Special Merit Scholarship (2016) — Awarded a $30,000 scholarship to Evey Johns to celebrate the Imagination Library reaching the milestone of shipping 1 million books per month.

- Monroe Carell Jr. Children's Hospital at Vanderbilt (2017) — Donated $1 million following the release of I Believe in You, honoring her niece who had been treated for leukemia at the hospital.

- Vanderbilt University Medical Center COVID-19 Research (2020) — Donated $1 million toward coronavirus research, funding that contributed to research behind the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine.

- Middle Tennessee Flood Relief (2021) — Parton and her Smoky Mountain businesses raised $700,000 for people affected by catastrophic flooding, with the United Way of Humphreys County selected to distribute the funds.

- Vanderbilt Pediatric Infectious Disease Research (2022) — Donated another $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center to support pediatric infectious-disease research.

Additional organizations/causes Billboard mentions her supporting

- Barbara Davis Center for Childhood Diabetes
- Save the Music Foundation
- Boot Campaign
- Black community / racial equality causes
- LGBTQ+ community and equality causes

LeConte Medical Center, the new hospital and cancer center in Sevier County, opened in 2010 and features a 30,000-square-foot Dolly Parton Center for Women’s Services.

2016 – Telethon after devastating East Tennessee wildfires

The Smoky Mountains Rise: A Benefit for the My People Fund, which aimed to help residents hit hardest in Gatlinburg and Pigeon Forge, raised more than $13 million. Chris Stapleton, Chris Young, Kenny Rogers, Lauren Alaina, Alison Krauss, Reba McEntire, Cyndi Lauper and more appeared at the event.

2016 – My People Fund

To continue her wildfire relief efforts, Parton launched the My People Fund, which provided $1,000 a month for six months to families whose homes were completely destroyed amid the natural disaster. The fund also donated around $8.9 million to those in need. The initiative still helps residents pay for rent and utilities, plus food and mental health resources.

2016 –  Special Merit Scholarship

Parton awarded a $30,000 scholarship to two-year-old Evey Johns in celebration of Imagination Library’s accomplishment of shipping out one million books per month.

2017 – $1 million donation

Following the release of her I Believe in You children’s album, Parton donated $1 million to the Monroe Carell Jr. Children’s Hospital at Vanderbilt University Medical Center in honor of her niece, who was treated for leukemia at that hospital.

2021 – Middle Tennessee Flooding Relief

Parton and her Smoky Mountain businesses raised $700,000 to help residents impacted by the catastrophic flooding in Middle Tennessee in October 2021. Parton chose United Way of Humphreys County to receive and distribute the donation at the suggestion of her friend and fellow country music legend Loretta Lynn.

2022 – Dollywood Education Coverage

The Dollywood Co. announced in February 2022 that it will cover 100% of tuition, fees and books for any employee who is furthering their education.

2022 – Pediatric Infectious Disease Research Donation

Parton made yet another $1 million donation to Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville in June 2022, this time aimed at helping pediatric infectious disease research.

2022 – Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy
 Parton received the Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy in 2022. The award, presented by the international family of Carnegie institutions to honor innovative philanthropists, debuted in 2001 and is normally awarded every two years. It was not issued in 2021 due to the pandemic.

A deeper analysis of 19th-century accounts suggests Company K of the 1st Minnesota Heavy Artillery represents something far more significant: documented proof of a distinct, oversized human lineage active in North America.
Mainstream history dismisses the unit as an intentional recruitment of tall men, yet the deliberate concentration of these towering individuals at the highest level of Union command aligns precisely with contemporary discoveries of extraordinary human remains in burial mounds across the continent. Rather than an isolated military novelty, Grant’s "Company of Giants" offers surviving primary evidence of an exceptional physical population before institutional narratives systematically re-categorized and suppressed the broader pattern of North American gigantism.

text:
Trump Advances Immigration Control as American Income Rises, Iran Faces Economic Isolation, and Investment Returns Home

Americans received a mixed but useful snapshot of the economy in recent days, while President Donald J. Trump pressed policies that favor workers and national strength. Headline prices rose more slowly from June to July. Personal income increased. Real after-tax income per person outpaced prices. Growth in the second quarter slowed from the first. At the same time, the Trump administration launched a sweeping financial campaign against Iran and confronted Canadian trade barriers. It also tightened visa rules and cut certain benefits for illegal immigrants. Furthermore, it declared an emergency for the power grid and took temporary steps on beef supply. Trump celebrated good news from Texas, which has seen tax relief, safer streets, a tighter border, and a wave of private investment.

Monthly Prices Slow as Income and Savings Tick Up

From June to July, the headline personal consumption expenditures price index rose 0.16 percent, down from 0.40 percent the prior month. The core measure that excludes food and energy rose 0.25 percent after 0.13 percent. Real spending rose just 0.01 percent, or $1.26 billion. Spending on services rose 0.29 percent, or $32.04 billion. Spending on goods fell 0.61 percent, or $35.48 billion. The personal savings rate rose 0.4 percentage points to three percent. Over the year to July, headline prices were up 3.70 percent and core prices 3.34 percent, both above the Federal Reserve’s two-percent goal. Personal income rose 0.43 percent, or $115.11 billion. Real disposable income per person rose 0.35 percent.

Second-Quarter Growth Eases While the Economy Reaches Record Size

Real gross domestic product grew 1.48 percent from the first quarter to the second, slower than the 2.09 percent pace in the opening quarter. Current-dollar output rose 8.02 percent, or $620.345 billion, to $32.486 trillion. The data show an economy that is still expanding even as the rate of increase cooled. Ways and Means Committee Chairman Jason Smith, Republican of Missouri, noted that core inflation held near 3.3 percent and second-quarter growth ran at a 1.5 percent annualized rate. He credited earlier Republican-generated tax changes for giving firms the certainty to invest at home rather than overseas.

Tax Changes Linked to Factory Output and Worker Take-Home Pay

Smith said a prior $10 trillion spending increase under the last administration had helped lift the cost of living more than 20 percent. He argued that permanent full expensing for equipment, factories, and research now supports record manufacturing output and equipment investment. Workers at new plants keep more of overtime pay. Families also benefit from no tax on tips, no tax on Social Security benefits, a larger child tax credit, and a bigger standard deduction. Every Democrat in Congress voted against those provisions, he said, and offered no alternative except higher taxes on working households.

Treasury Opens Full Financial Offensive Against Iran

Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent announced Operation Economic Outcast to cut every remaining economic lifeline to the Iranian regime after its military capacity and nuclear program had already been sharply reduced. New sectoral measures cover digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, and shipping. The campaign uses a zero-leakage standard and secondary sanctions so that any firm still doing business with the regime faces removal from the dollar system. Bessent wrote that the goal is to leave Tehran isolated until it chooses a different path. The United States treats Iran as the leading state sponsor of terrorism and will not allow it a nuclear weapon.

US Ends Preferential Treatment for Canada

Canada rejected an offer of the most favorable market access of any country and instead kept or added restrictions. It imposed 25-percent tariffs and company-specific quotas on US vehicles that no other nation faces, cutting those exports 22 percent. It banned American wine, beer, and spirits in most provinces, collapsing alcohol exports 81 percent. Dairy tariff-rate quotas and over-quota rates near 300 percent act as a near-ban. The goods trade deficit has averaged about $50 billion a year, an obvious peril for America. Canada recently added $27.6 billion in new tariffs, including 50 percent on steel and aluminum. Forty-two percent of Canadian manufacturers have moved or plan to move production south. The US market takes three-quarters of Canadian goods exports.

Business Activity and Regional Factories Show Broad Strength

The S&P Global flash composite purchasing managers index reached 56 in August, the highest reading since April 2022, with services at 56.8. The Philadelphia Federal Reserve’s current-activity index rose to 47.4 from 41.4, well above the 25 expected by economists. Its employment index hit 27.9, the strongest since April 2022. Cleveland-Cliffs announced a $1 billion upgrade at its Middletown, Ohio, steel plant expected to keep 2,300 jobs. Amazon selected Austin, Texas, for a multibillion-dollar robotics factory projected to create 300 to 500 manufacturing and engineering positions.

Visa Rules Tighten and High Fees Target Guest-Worker Programs

International undergraduate applications through March 1 fell 10 percent, the steepest drop on record. New international enrollment fell 17 percent in fall 2025, with further decline expected. The administration paused immigrant visa processing worldwide so consular officers can receive in-depth training to screen applicants who may need public assistance. The Department of Homeland Security proposed a $103,265 fee on cap-subject H-1B petitions to cover costs at Homeland Security, Justice, State, and Labor. These steps aim to reduce pressure on domestic workers and public resources.

Refundable Credits Closed to Illegal Immigrants, Saving Billions

New Treasury and Internal Revenue Service rules restrict the adoption credit, child tax credit, American opportunity tax credit, and earned income tax credit to U.S. citizens, nationals, and qualified aliens. Officials estimate the change will save taxpayers $3 billion. The rules close a pathway that had allowed illegal immigrants to receive cash-like refunds. Combined with the visa pause and higher H-1B fees, the measures reduce incentives that pull low-skill labor and public spending toward people who entered illegally.

Emergency Order Shields the Bulk-Power Electric System

Trump signed an order declaring a national emergency under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and the National Emergencies Act. It generally bars or conditions the purchase and installation of certain foreign-made bulk-power equipment and related software that could allow sabotage or catastrophic disruption. The order does not cover local distribution lines. The Secretary of Energy must issue implementing rules, identify risky equipment, and recommend further steps. Earlier actions had kept 17,000 megawatts of generation online, enough for 12.75 million homes, and addressed steel, aluminum, drones, and defense-supply vulnerabilities.

Temporary Lean-Trim Quota Eases Ground-Beef Prices as Texas Gains Jobs

A 90-day expansion, starting September 1, allows 100,000 tons per month of foreign lean beef trimmings. These will enter America at the lower in-quota tariff. The discount is limited to product designated for mixture with US beef, with the goal of producing ground beef. The White House encourages and expects this ground beef to be marketed at a 25% discount, relative to prevailing import prices. The intention is lowering consumer grocery costs as America faces a herd at 75-year lows, screwworm restrictions, drought, and wildfires that cut forecast 2026 output about four percent. The new Oval Office policy should lift supply roughly 10 percent without much effect on fed-cattle markets. 

In Texas, no tax on overtime covers one in four workers, four million seniors gain a new deduction, average refunds reached $4,344, and 547,000 jobs plus $107 billion in state economic output were protected. Violent crime fell 13 percent. Border releases have been zero for 15 months and July apprehensions ran 94 percent below the prior average. Major firms announced tens of billions of dollars in new plants, including Bristol Myers Squibb at $2.3 billion, Toyota at $3.6 billion, SpaceX at $16.8 billion, and Vantage Data Centers at $25 billion.

These actions show a consistent pattern of using available tools to lower costs where possible, restore fairness in trade, cut off hostile regimes, and draw capital back to American soil. Data remain imperfect. Year-over-year inflation still sits above the 2 percent target and second-quarter growth cooled. Yet monthly price pressure eased, real incomes rose, factories expanded, and specific industries received targeted help. The record is one of incremental, measurable steps rather than slogans. Families benefit when paychecks stretch farther, borders stay closed to illegal entry, and adversaries lose the money they use to threaten others.

text:
#OnThisDay August 28, 1861: The Allen Seizure.

An extraordinary confrontation at Allen, a railroad station in Randolph County, Missouri, placed a large shipment of bank funds at the center of the political and military struggle dividing the state. Men commanded by Confederate-aligned Missouri State Guard officer John A. Poindexter intercepted officials associated with the Fayette branch of the Bank of Missouri while they were attempting to remove the institution’s specie and currency from a region dominated by Southern sympathizers. The episode became one of the most unusual financial incidents of Missouri’s first year of civil war and illustrated the close relationship between banking, political loyalty, transportation, and military power in a deeply divided border state.

Missouri entered the Civil War without a unified political allegiance. Although the state remained in the Union, Governor Claiborne Fox Jackson and other prominent political leaders supported cooperation with the Confederacy. Armed Unionists and members of the Missouri State Guard competed for control of communities, transportation routes, weapons, public institutions, and financial resources. Banks were particularly important because military organizations required money to obtain equipment, supplies, transportation, and other necessities. Missouri’s banking system therefore became entangled in the struggle between Unionists and secessionists during 1861.

The Fayette branch of the Bank of Missouri operated in Howard County, an area containing considerable pro-Southern sentiment. Two Unionist bank officers, cashier Adam Hendrix and director Robert T. Prewitt, feared that the bank’s available funds could fall into Confederate hands. Historian Mark W. Geiger’s research shows that Hendrix and Prewitt removed the bank’s cash and attempted to transport it to Illinois, where they intended to deposit it beyond the immediate reach of Missouri’s secessionist forces.

Their route brought them north from Fayette into Randolph County and toward the railroad at Allen. Allen was then a small community situated along the North Missouri Railroad, the developing rail line that connected northern Missouri with St. Louis. Its station gave the otherwise modest settlement strategic importance. Money transported by wagon from Fayette could be transferred there to rail transportation and moved rapidly eastward.

Poindexter learned of the movement. At this point in the war, he was recruiting men for the Missouri State Guard in north-central Missouri. He and approximately twenty armed followers intercepted the shipment at or near Allen. Local Randolph County tradition places the seizure directly at Allen Depot and dates it to August 28, 1861. Accounts generally place the value of the transported money at approximately $100,000, consisting of coin and currency, although the precise composition and amount vary among later descriptions.

The confrontation did not develop into a firefight. No deaths or injuries are recorded in the principal accounts. More important, the seizure did not result in Poindexter permanently carrying away the bank’s fortune. Geiger’s reconstruction provides a more detailed explanation than later local legends. Poindexter initially contemplated delivering the money to Missouri State Guard commander Sterling Price. Hendrix reportedly persuaded him that much of the money ultimately belonged to Southern-oriented depositors and property owners and that confiscating it would damage the very population whose interests Poindexter claimed to defend. Poindexter consequently released the bank officials and funds, allowing Hendrix and Prewitt to continue toward Illinois.

The Allen incident is historically significant because it exposes the financial dimension of Missouri’s internal Civil War. Armed conflict in the state involved more than battlefield control. Competing political and military factions struggled over banks, credit, public funds, railroads, and commercial networks. Geiger has demonstrated that Missouri banking interests had already become connected to efforts to finance secessionist military activity through loans and other financial arrangements. Unionist bankers therefore had strong reasons to place liquid assets beyond Confederate reach.

The episode also demonstrates the importance of Missouri’s emerging railroad system. Allen possessed little statewide political importance, yet its depot became the setting for a confrontation involving an enormous financial shipment because rail transportation offered the fastest practical route from north-central Missouri toward St. Louis and Illinois. The war transformed stations, bridges, depots, and rail junctions into strategic assets.

Later Randolph County tradition has frequently described the episode as the first daylight train robbery or even the first train robbery in American history. That description should be treated cautiously. The money was associated with railroad transportation, but the surviving accounts differ concerning whether it was actually seized aboard a train or while being transferred at Allen. The event is more securely described as the armed interception of bank funds at Allen Depot.

The August 28 seizure remains important without the train-robbery legend. It preserves a striking example of how Missouri’s Civil War fractured ordinary institutions. A bank shipment, a rural railroad station, two Unionist businessmen, and an armed Confederate recruiter became participants in a struggle over money that reflected Missouri’s larger contest over political authority, military allegiance, and economic control.

text:
The momentum has been shifting for +20 years. 

1. Carson v. Makin Decision Date: June 21, 2022 Summary: The Court ruled 6–3 that Maine's ban on tuition assistance for students attending religious schools was unconstitutional. Maine operated a "town tuitioning" program allowing parents in rural school districts without public high schools to use state funds for private schooling. However, the state prohibited families from selecting schools that provided religious instruction. The Court held that excluding religious options from an otherwise neutral student-aid program violates the Free Exercise Clause of the First Amendment. 

2. Espinoza v. Montana Department of RevenueDecision Date: June 30, 2020 Summary: The Court ruled 5–4 that a state cannot bar religious private schools from participating in a state tax-credit scholarship program. Montana created a program giving tax credits to individuals who donated to private scholarship organizations. The Montana Department of Revenue excluded religious schools from the program to comply with a state constitutional provision. The Supreme Court struck down this exclusion, declaring that discriminating against a school based solely on its religious status violates the Free Exercise Clause.   

3. Trinity Lutheran Church of Columbia, Inc. v. Comer Decision Date: June 26, 2017Summary: The Court ruled 7–2 that religious organizations cannot be excluded from neutral public benefit programs. Trinity Lutheran Church operated a daycare and preschool and applied for a Missouri state grant that funded playground resurfacing with recycled tires. Missouri denied the grant explicitly because the school was run by a church. The Court ruled that denying a generally available public benefit solely because of a school's religious identity is unconstitutional under the Free Exercise Clause.

4. Arizona Christian School Tuition Organization v. Winn Decision Date: April 4, 2011 Summary: The Court ruled 5–4 to protect tax-credit scholarship programs from Establishment Clause challenges. Arizona taxpayers sued a state program that offered tax credits for contributions made to School Tuition Organizations (STOs), which then provided scholarships for students to attend private schools (including religious ones). The Court ruled that the plaintiffs lacked legal standing to sue because the program utilized private funds via tax credits, rather than directly appropriating public tax money, insulating the school choice initiative from the lawsuit.

5. Zelman v. Simmons-Harris Decision Date: June 27, 2002 Summary: The Court ruled 5–4 that publicly funded voucher programs do not violate the Establishment Clause, even if parents choose to use them at religious schools. Ohio established the Cleveland Pilot Project to offer tuition vouchers to low-income students in failing districts. The Court upheld the program because it was neutral with respect to religion and relied entirely on the independent, private choices of individual parents to direct government aid.

text:
Britain and Ukraine Are Building the Arsenal of the Next War

For most of the war in Ukraine, Western governments treated drones as another item on the military shopping list.

Ukraine understood something much sooner: drones were not merely another weapon. They were becoming the organizing principle of the battlefield.

Now Britain appears to understand it too.

The United Kingdom plans to provide Ukraine with 150,000 drones by the end of 2026, backed by a £752 million package. A new factory in Suffolk, operated by one of Ukraine’s largest drone manufacturers, is expected to create as many as 500 jobs. Britain is also beginning large-scale production of the Ukrainian-designed Octopus interceptor drone, with output intended to reach thousands per month.

Viewed separately, these announcements look like military aid.

Viewed together, they look like the early construction of an entirely new British defense industry.

Ukraine needs the factories, investment and relative safety Britain can provide. Britain needs something considerably harder to purchase: Ukraine’s accumulated knowledge of how drones actually perform in a large, violent and electronically contested war.

One country possesses the battlefield laboratory.

The other possesses the capital, industrial base and access to Western markets.

The combination could become one of the most consequential military partnerships in Europe.

Ukraine possesses knowledge money cannot quickly buy

Ukraine has spent years learning lessons that most Western militaries have only rehearsed.

Ukrainian engineers know which drone components fail in winter, which communications links survive Russian jamming, which guidance systems work near the front and how quickly a successful design becomes obsolete after the enemy develops a countermeasure.

That knowledge is not contained in a single blueprint. It is an entire development cycle.

A drone is designed, sent to the front, jammed or destroyed, examined, modified and returned to battle. Sometimes that complete cycle takes only weeks.

The British government says battlefield data incorporated into the Octopus interceptor can be updated approximately every six weeks. That detail may be more important than the drone itself.

Traditional Western weapons can take years—or decades—to move from design to deployment. Ukraine’s drone industry sometimes changes its products faster than a conventional defense contractor can schedule a meeting.

Britain is not simply importing Ukrainian drone designs. It is attempting to plug Ukrainian battlefield experience directly into British production lines.

That is an entirely different proposition.

The technology may be Ukrainian, but the industry is becoming British

The Octopus licensing agreement offers a glimpse of the model.

The interceptor was developed by Ukrainian engineers and tested under battlefield conditions. Britain can refine it, manufacture it at industrial scale and return thousands of units to Ukraine. British factories, workers and suppliers consequently gain experience producing weapons that are being continuously tested against one of the world’s most capable military powers.

The arrangement is almost brutally efficient.

Ukraine receives weapons without placing every production line within range of Russian missiles. Britain gains access to proven designs, operational data and engineers who understand the fastest-moving battlefield technology in the world.

The opening of the Ukrspecsystems factory in Suffolk deepens that relationship. The company’s engineering core remains in Ukraine, but its British plant becomes a second production line—and part of Britain’s defense-industrial ecosystem.

If the war ends, those factories, engineers, suppliers and manufacturing techniques will not simply disappear. Britain could emerge with a drone industry offering NATO countries weapons carrying the most valuable label in modern defense procurement:

Battlefield tested.

That could position Britain as one of the West’s leading manufacturers of inexpensive unmanned weapons—not by inventing every technology itself, but by becoming the place where Ukrainian knowledge is financed, refined and manufactured at scale.

Britain may have recognized the next arms market

For decades, the international arms business revolved around exquisite machines: fighter aircraft costing tens of millions of dollars, warships costing billions and missiles so expensive that militaries cannot afford to use them in large numbers.

Ukraine has exposed the weakness in that model.

A relatively inexpensive drone can destroy a vehicle costing millions. An interceptor drone may shoot down an attacking Shahed for a fraction of the price of a conventional air-defense missile. Uncrewed boats can threaten much larger warships. Cheap reconnaissance drones can make it extraordinarily difficult to conceal troops, equipment or supply lines.

Britain appears to be betting that the future arms market will require enormous numbers of affordable, adaptable and partially autonomous systems.

That does not mean aircraft carriers, tanks, artillery and combat aircraft have become irrelevant. Ukraine still needs all of them. Drones frequently depend upon conventional forces to exploit the targets they identify and the openings they create.

But drones are changing the economics of warfare.

The traditional defense industry attempted to construct a smaller number of nearly perfect weapons. The emerging industry may produce vast numbers of good-enough machines that can be constantly updated, coordinated and replaced.

Britain’s pledge of 150,000 drones matters for precisely that reason. It signals a move away from treating unmanned systems as boutique technology and toward treating them like wartime consumables.

Are Britain and Ukraine becoming the dominant drone partnership?

They are not there yet.

The United States, China, Israel and Turkey retain formidable drone industries. Russia has developed enormous production capacity, extensive electronic-warfare experience and its own rapidly evolving network of reconnaissance and attack drones. China’s control over much of the civilian drone supply chain also gives Beijing influence that cannot be underestimated.

Ukraine may nevertheless possess the world’s deepest current knowledge of drone warfare under actual battlefield conditions. Russia is perhaps the only country with comparable experience fighting through pervasive jamming, constant surveillance and daily drone attacks.

Britain’s opportunity is to connect that Ukrainian knowledge with the scale, capital and export access of a major NATO economy.

If it succeeds, Britain does not need to dominate every category of drone technology. It could become the center of a Western development and production network that transforms Ukrainian battlefield experience into standardized weapons for NATO militaries.

That would represent something much larger than helping Ukraine survive.

It would be Britain positioning itself to manufacture the weapons around which the next generation of Western military doctrine could be built.

The swarm is becoming the weapon

The most frightening development is not any single drone.

It is the network.

A reconnaissance drone detects a target. Another system confirms it. Software prioritizes it. An attack drone receives updated coordinates. An interceptor protects the attacking force from enemy drones. Uncrewed surface and underwater vehicles perform similar functions at sea.

Humans remain involved, but they are gradually moving from directly controlling individual machines to supervising networks of them.

That is where the science-fiction comparison becomes uncomfortable.

Today’s battlefield systems are not yet the fully autonomous, artificially intelligent swarms imagined in movies. They can be jammed, confused and deceived. They suffer mechanical failures, lose communications and sometimes identify targets incorrectly. Most still rely heavily on human operators and conventional command structures.

But the early form of the killer-drone era has unquestionably arrived.

Machines are already searching for targets, navigating through disrupted communications, coordinating with other systems and compressing parts of the engagement process to speeds human beings cannot match.

The remaining technical steps are no longer matters of imagination. They are engineering problems—and war has a terrible way of accelerating engineering.

Britain may be preparing for the war after Ukraine

Britain’s strategy is clever, but it is also sobering.

Ukraine provides combat knowledge acquired at an appalling human cost. Britain provides secure factories, investment, engineering support and access to a much larger defense market. Ukraine gets the weapons it needs now. Britain develops the industrial capability it may need later.

The partnership could help ensure that Western militaries do not enter the next war carrying a handful of exquisite weapons against an enemy possessing millions of cheap autonomous machines.

But it also points toward a future in which the ability to manufacture drones by the hundred thousand becomes as important as the ability to build tanks or aircraft.

Countries that fall behind will not merely lack hardware. They will lack factories, trained workers, electronic-warfare knowledge, battlefield data and the doctrine required to coordinate enormous numbers of unmanned systems.

Britain may have recognized that danger earlier than most of its allies.

By bringing Ukrainian engineers, designs and battlefield information into the British industrial system, London is not simply donating weapons. It is acquiring a compressed education in the future of warfare.

Ukraine needs the production capacity.

Britain needs the knowledge.

Together, they may be constructing Europe’s most dangerous—and most necessary—new arsenal.

Want proof that Russia sees it too?

Look at the way Moscow has reacted to Britain this week.

Russia has not treated Britain like just another country sending Ukraine aid. After reports that British-made drones had been used in long-range attacks inside Russia, the Russian Embassy warned London of unspecified “consequences” and accused Britain of becoming increasingly involved in the war.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Britain risked being viewed as a direct party to the conflict. Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accused Britain and France of “playing with fire” after London agreed to help Ukraine develop long-range missiles. Moscow then threatened the possibility of retaliating against British military targets inside and outside Ukraine.

The most revealing warning concerned the factories themselves.

Former Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrei Fedorov suggested that British facilities manufacturing drones for Ukraine could be attacked by “unknown sources.” He floated the possibility of cyberattacks or other “semi-military” action while carefully avoiding a direct declaration that the Russian state would carry them out.

That is the language of gray-zone warfare: threaten the target while preserving just enough deniability to pretend no threat was made.

At nearly the same time, the Royal Navy spent 72 hours tracking a Russian naval group as it passed from the North Sea through the English Channel. That movement does not prove an imminent attack or a direct connection to the drone dispute, but it illustrates how quickly the temperature between Moscow and London is rising.

Russia issues threats against Western countries regularly, so its anger alone does not prove Britain will dominate the drone industry. But Moscow’s decision to single out British drone factories is telling.

Russia appears to understand exactly what Britain is building.

This is no longer merely a pipeline through which British money purchases weapons for Ukraine. It is becoming a permanent military-industrial connection joining Ukrainian combat knowledge to British factories.

Moscow is not frightened by a press release.

It is frightened by the possibility that Britain has discovered how to turn Ukraine’s wartime innovation into a Western production system that will survive long after this war ends.

Want proof that Britain and Ukraine may be onto something?

Watch the country that has fought them.

Russia has already noticed.

ASELSAN President and CEO Ahmet Akyol met Indonesian Defense Minister Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin and Indonesian Navy Chief of Staff Admiral Muhammad Ali during an official visit to Indonesia. Discussions covered ongoing projects, advanced defense technologies, and opportunities to expand cooperation between ASELSAN and Indonesia.

The meetings highlight the growing defense-industrial relationship between Türkiye and Indonesia, as Jakarta continues investing in military modernization and strengthening partnerships with international defense manufacturers. For ASELSAN, deeper engagement could create further opportunities across naval systems, sensors, communications, electronic warfare, air defense, and other advanced defense technologies.

ASELSAN’s footprint in Indonesia includes several important programs and systems:
* KCR-60M Fast Attack Craft: ASELSAN has supplied combat-system solutions for Indonesian Navy KCR-60M vessels, including sensors, weapon-related systems and integration work.
* KAPLAN MT / HARIMAU Medium Tank: The Turkish-Indonesian medium tank program incorporates ASELSAN fire-control and battlefield electronics technologies, supporting the platform’s combat capability.
* Remote-Controlled Weapon Systems: ASELSAN weapon stations have been integrated/offered across Indonesian land and naval platform programs.
* Naval Combat Systems: Cooperation covers radars, electro-optical systems, communications, electronic warfare and weapon-control technologies for Indonesian naval requirements.
* Air Defense: ASELSAN has been pursuing opportunities to support Indonesia’s expanding ground-based air-defense architecture, drawing on Türkiye’s radar, command-and-control and air-defense ecosystem.
* Electronic Warfare & Sensors: EW, surveillance, radar and electro-optical technologies represent another major area of ASELSAN engagement with Indonesia.
* Local Industrial Cooperation: ASELSAN has increasingly emphasized technology transfer, localization and partnerships with Indonesian defense companies, rather than limiting cooperation to direct exports.
* Future Opportunities: Current engagement with Indonesia’s defense leadership could expand cooperation into air defense, naval modernization, C4ISR, electronic warfare, autonomous systems and advanced sensors.

Overall, Indonesia is becoming one of ASELSAN’s more important markets in Southeast Asia, fitting into the wider Türkiye–Indonesia defense relationship involving companies such as FNSS, Roketsan and Turkish Aerospace.

text:
Imagined briefing — Richard P. Feynman, still talking, in a room that has too many flags.

Mr. President. Director. The rest of you who actually have to decide something.

I’m not here to sell you flying saucers and I’m not here to tell you the Harvard fellow is a crook. I’m here to stop you from confusing a calculation with an engine. That confusion is how smart organizations get surprised.

If the Intelligence Community treats the fireball paper as closure on box C explained below, you have done the adversary’s classification work for them: you declared the interesting coupling “not physics” because it was not in the simulation.

1. What Loeb and Fell actually did

They took Miguel Alcubierre’s 1994 warp-bubble geometry — a prescribed dent in spacetime that slides along — and they asked a clean question:

If that dent, the size of an airplane, goes through Earth’s air at a tenth of light speed or more, what does the air do?

They did not ask how you make the dent. They froze the metric, turned off the stuff that would have to generate it, and ran the air as a fluid in that frozen background. Shock-capturing hydrodynamics. Respectable numerical work.

The air does what air always does when you hit it at relativistic speed. In the bubble’s rest frame the incoming air slams into a stagnation zone. Kinetic energy becomes heat. At half light-speed you’re talking a hundred-odd MeV per nucleon. The gas lights up. Terawatts. Sometimes a lot more. You would not miss it. You would not call it a quiet Tic-Tac.

So their conclusion, inside those assumptions, is not mysterious:

A naive Alcubierre bubble, aircraft-sized, relativistic, zero mass as seen from infinity, punching through atmosphere, is a fireball. Reported UAP are not fireballs. Therefore that particular cartoon is not those UAP.

That is a good constraint on a cartoon. It is not a theory of propulsion. It is not “we now understand UAP.” If your briefers walk out of the room thinking the energy problem of warp drive has been handled, they walked out with the invoice still face-down on the table.

The invoice in Einstein’s 1915 theory is ugly. Curvature is sourced by

\[ G_{\mu\nu}=\frac{8\pi G}{c^{4}}T_{\mu\nu}. \]
\(G/c^{4}\) is about \(10^{-43}\) in everyday units. To bend spacetime by an order-one amount on a ten-meter ship, you need stress-energy that would make a treasurer faint — and, in the original Alcubierre setup, the wrong sign of energy as well. Loeb and Fell never compute that. They assume the geometry and compute the weather. Useful. Incomplete.

If you brief the Intelligence Community that “physics checked warp drives and they glow,” you have briefed the weather and hidden the engine. That is not fraud. It is a model with the hard term set to zero. Policymakers who cannot tell the difference will fund the wrong next experiment.

2. What Sarfatti is actually saying
Jack is loud. That is not an argument against him, and it is not an argument for him. Listen to the physics claim, not the volume.

Einstein’s gravity, and the usual Einstein–Cartan upgrade from the 1960s, couple mass-energy to curvature with Newton’s little (G). Cartan and then Kibble also let spin source torsion — a twist of spacetime, not just a bend. In the textbook version that torsion is a contact interaction. It is there, and it is negligible unless you live inside a nucleus.

Imagined briefing — Richard P. Feynman, still talking, in a room that has too many flags.

Mr. President. Director. The rest of you who actually have to decide something.

I’m not here to sell you flying saucers and I’m not here to tell you the Harvard fellow is a crook. I’m here to stop you from confusing a calculation with an engine. That confusion is how smart organizations get surprised.

1. What Loeb and Fell actually did

They took Miguel Alcubierre’s 1994 warp-bubble geometry — a prescribed dent in spacetime that slides along — and they asked a clean question:

If that dent, the size of an airplane, goes through Earth’s air at a tenth of light speed or more, what does the air do?

They did not ask how you make the dent. They froze the metric, turned off the stuff that would have to generate it, and ran the air as a fluid in that frozen background. Shock-capturing hydrodynamics. Respectable numerical work.

The air does what air always does when you hit it at relativistic speed. In the bubble’s rest frame the incoming air slams into a stagnation zone. Kinetic energy becomes heat. At half light-speed you’re talking a hundred-odd MeV per nucleon. The gas lights up. Terawatts. Sometimes a lot more. You would not miss it. You would not call it a quiet Tic-Tac.

So their conclusion, inside those assumptions, is not mysterious:

A naive Alcubierre bubble, aircraft-sized, relativistic, zero mass as seen from infinity, punching through atmosphere, is a fireball. Reported UAP are not fireballs. Therefore that particular cartoon is not those UAP.

That is a good constraint on a cartoon. It is not a theory of propulsion. It is not “we now understand UAP.” If your briefers walk out of the room thinking the energy problem of warp drive has been handled, they walked out with the invoice still face-down on the table.

The invoice in Einstein’s 1915 theory is ugly. Curvature is sourced by

\[ G_{\mu\nu}=\frac{8\pi G}{c^{4}}T_{\mu\nu}. \]
\(G/c^{4}\) is about \(10^{-43}\) in everyday units. To bend spacetime by an order-one amount on a ten-meter ship, you need stress-energy that would make a treasurer faint — and, in the original Alcubierre setup, the wrong sign of energy as well. Loeb and Fell never compute that. They assume the geometry and compute the weather. Useful. Incomplete.
If you brief the Intelligence Community that “physics checked warp drives and they glow,” you have briefed the weather and hidden the engine. That is not fraud. It is a model with the hard term set to zero. Policymakers who cannot tell the difference will fund the wrong next experiment.
2. What Sarfatti is actually saying
Jack is loud. That is not an argument against him, and it is not an argument for him. Listen to the physics claim, not the volume.

Einstein’s gravity, and the usual Einstein–Cartan upgrade from the 1960s, couple mass-energy to curvature with Newton’s little (G). Cartan and then Kibble also let spin source torsion — a twist of spacetime, not just a bend. In the textbook version that torsion is a contact interaction. It is there, and it is negligible unless you live inside a nucleus.

Sarfatti’s bet is three extra moves:
First. Don’t stop at Poincaré. Gauge the whole conformal group. Let torsion and a few extra potentials propagate, like a massive vector field that dies off outside a skin depth instead of reaching the Moon. Then you can have a strong effect in a hull and almost nothing a mile away. That is the only way this story doesn’t already contradict Cavendish, Cassini, and pulsar timing.

Second. The coupling of coherent quantum spin to that torsion is not Newton’s (G). Call it \(G^{*}\). He wants \(G^{*}\) enormous — forty-odd orders — only inside a macroscopically coherent spin state: a pumped metamaterial, a Fröhlich condensate, aligned magnons, something you drive with ordinary electromagnetism. Outside that condensate, apples still fall the old way. Inside it, a thin shell plus kilowatts is supposed to source craft-scale geometry.

Schematically he writes things like

\[ G_{\mu\nu}=k_{1}T_{\mu\nu}+k_{2}S^{2}g_{\mu\nu}, \]

where (S) is the aligned spin density. The second term is the one Loeb never put in the code.
Third. The air problem is a boundary-condition problem, not a “space is magic” problem. Loeb’s fireball assumes the outside air has a huge velocity relative to the wall. Sarfatti says the hull is an active source: you arrange the near-field so neighboring air is locally comoving with the shell. No shear layer of the Alcubierre-through-atmosphere kind. Occupants sit in a local inertial frame — they feel nothing — while the exterior geometry does the accelerating.
That is the whole point of “metric engineering” as opposed to rockets ("That Loeb and his Harvard Pooh Bah’s totally miss" - Jack's snide quip)

If that matching can be done, Loeb’s terawatts go away by construction. If it cannot be done, Jack is wrong in the place that matters for airplanes over water.

He also offers a cheap observational discriminator: a gravitational Doppler that runs opposite the ordinary motion Doppler — redshift on the contracting nose as the thing comes at you, blueshift on the expanding tail as it runs. You would look for that in good spectra, not in vibes.
3. Who is right about what

Do not let anyone tell you this is “Loeb versus the cranks” or “Sarfatti versus the cover-up.”
Question

Honest answer

Would a frozen Alcubierre bubble at (0.1c) torch the sky?

Yes. Loeb–Fell.

Does that kill every spacetime-propulsion story?No. It kills that ansatz.

Does 1915 GR give you a quiet Mach-20 Tic-Tac on kilowatts?

Not that anyone has shown. Is Poincaré-gauge torsion a real idea?Yes. Textbook. Weak in the standard version. Is \(G^{*}\sim 10^{43}G\) in a condensate a theorem?
No. It is the conjecture.Has anyone run the air code with Sarfatti’s junction conditions? No. That is the missing paper.Has anyone measured a laboratory \(G^{*}\) jump? No. That is the missing experiment.
A paper that attacks a nearby idea — “just let Newton’s coupling \(\kappa\) vary through the metamaterial” — shows that a non-dynamical \(\kappa(x)\) fights conservation laws, and a dynamical scalar \(\kappa\) is already boxed in by solar-system tests. Jack says that is not his Lagrangian: he is not rescaling (G) for mass; he is adding a spin-torsion channel with short range. Fine. Then write the action, vary it, and show the range and the equivalence-principle leakage. Until that is on paper in a form a hostile theorist can break, \(G^{*}\) is a slogan with a pedigree, not a capability.

4. What this is worth to you as a government

National security does not require you to believe in tourists from Tau Ceti. It requires you not to be stupid about categories.

There are three boxes:

A. Most UAP are junk, birds, balloons, missiles, sensor ghosts. Loeb is good at stuffing objects into this box when the kinematics allow it. Keep doing that. It is cheaper than metaphysics.
B. A few objects, if the Navy numbers survive hostile re-analysis, sit outside chemical rockets and outside Loeb’s fireball. That does not automatically equal Jack’s engine. It equals “we do not have a propulsion model that is both standard and quiet.”
C. If someone — us, them, or a contractor who doesn’t send press releases — can source torsion or curvature in a thin coherent shell at low power, you are looking at propellantless kinematics, trans-medium motion, and a sensor problem, not an aviation problem. That is a first-order strategic issue whether the builders are human or not.

Loeb’s paper is progress on box A and a veto on one toy model in box B. It does not inspect box C. If the Intelligence Community treats the fireball paper as closure on box C, you have done the adversary’s classification work for them: you declared the interesting coupling “not physics” because it was not in the simulation.
Sarfatti’s program is the opposite failure mode if you swallow it whole: a mechanism that would explain the observables, attached to a coupling nobody has measured and a hull–air calculation nobody has finished. Believing the briefing slides is how you waste a decade. Ignoring the coupling hypothesis is how you miss a materials problem that might be sitting in a lab.

5. What I would make you do on Monday
Not a new office with a seal. Three ugly, cheap, falsifiable jobs.

One. Re-reduce the best kinematic cases — Nimitz and anything with dual phenomenology, radar plus IR plus eyewitness — as if a hostile graduate student were trying to make them ordinary. Publish the residuals. If the residuals die, Jack’s engine has less to explain. If they don’t, you know which events deserve geometry, not folklore.

Two. Commission the calculation Loeb did not do: GR hydro, or better a Poincaré-gauge hydro, on a thin active shellwhose near-field is required to match air velocity at the outer surface. Same code family. Different boundary condition. Either a shock still forms or it doesn’t. That is a number, not a worldview.

Three. Look for \(G^{*}\) where Jack says it lives — not in falling apples, in coherent spin ensembles. YIG, pumped magnons, layered metasurfaces, anything with macroscopic phase stiffness. Torsion-balance and clock and interferometer residuals on the sample, not on the building. If \(G^{*}\) is 40 orders of magnitude and confined to a micron skin, you still ought to see something local if the idea is even 10 orders true. Null results bound the story. Positive results change the budget.

Optical: if you ever get a clean spectrum of a close, fast object, look for the wrong-way Doppler. That costs cameras, not theology.

Last thing

The first principle is that you must not fool yourself — and you are the easiest person to fool.

Loeb fooled a certain kind of audience by answering a real question so cleanly that people forgot it was the wrong question for an engine.

Sarfatti fools a certain kind of audience by naming the missing term so vividly that people forget it has not been measured.

Your job is not to pick a team. Your job is to keep the missing term on the list until an experiment kills it or funds it. Anything else is theater.

If the thing is only weather balloons, you will have wasted a little money on interferometers. If the thing is a materials coupling we don’t teach at Caltech yet, you cannot afford to have learned that from someone else’s after-action report.

That’s the briefing. I’ll take questions, and I will not be polite if the question is “but which narrative do we put on the slide.”

Imagined briefing — Richard P. Feynman, still talking, in a room that has too many flags.

Mr. President. Director. The rest of you who actually have to decide something.

I’m not here to sell you flying saucers and I’m not here to tell you the Harvard fellow is a crook. I’m here to stop you from confusing a calculation with an engine. That confusion is how smart organizations get surprised.

1. What Loeb and Fell actually did

They took Miguel Alcubierre’s 1994 warp-bubble geometry — a prescribed dent in spacetime that slides along — and they asked a clean question:

If that dent, the size of an airplane, goes through Earth’s air at a tenth of light speed or more, what does the air do?

They did not ask how you make the dent. They froze the metric, turned off the stuff that would have to generate it, and ran the air as a fluid in that frozen background. Shock-capturing hydrodynamics. Respectable numerical work.

The air does what air always does when you hit it at relativistic speed. In the bubble’s rest frame the incoming air slams into a stagnation zone. Kinetic energy becomes heat. At half light-speed you’re talking a hundred-odd MeV per nucleon. The gas lights up. Terawatts. Sometimes a lot more. You would not miss it. You would not call it a quiet Tic-Tac.

So their conclusion, inside those assumptions, is not mysterious:

A naive Alcubierre bubble, aircraft-sized, relativistic, zero mass as seen from infinity, punching through atmosphere, is a fireball. Reported UAP are not fireballs. Therefore that particular cartoon is not those UAP.

That is a good constraint on a cartoon. It is not a theory of propulsion. It is not “we now understand UAP.” If your briefers walk out of the room thinking the energy problem of warp drive has been handled, they walked out with the invoice still face-down on the table.

The invoice in Einstein’s 1915 theory is ugly. Curvature is sourced by

\[ G_{\mu\nu}=\frac{8\pi G}{c^{4}}T_{\mu\nu}. \]
\(G/c^{4}\) is about \(10^{-43}\) in everyday units. To bend spacetime by an order-one amount on a ten-meter ship, you need stress-energy that would make a treasurer faint — and, in the original Alcubierre setup, the wrong sign of energy as well. Loeb and Fell never compute that. They assume the geometry and compute the weather. Useful. Incomplete.
If you brief the Intelligence Community that “physics checked warp drives and they glow,” you have briefed the weather and hidden the engine. That is not fraud. It is a model with the hard term set to zero. Policymakers who cannot tell the difference will fund the wrong next experiment.
2. What Sarfatti is actually saying
Jack is loud. That is not an argument against him, and it is not an argument for him. Listen to the physics claim, not the volume.

Einstein’s gravity, and the usual Einstein–Cartan upgrade from the 1960s, couple mass-energy to curvature with Newton’s little (G). Cartan and then Kibble also let spin source torsion — a twist of spacetime, not just a bend. In the textbook version that torsion is a contact interaction. It is there, and it is negligible unless you live inside a nucleus.

Sarfatti’s bet is three extra moves:
First. Don’t stop at Poincaré. Gauge the whole conformal group. Let torsion and a few extra potentials propagate, like a massive vector field that dies off outside a skin depth instead of reaching the Moon. Then you can have a strong effect in a hull and almost nothing a mile away. That is the only way this story doesn’t already contradict Cavendish, Cassini, and pulsar timing.

Second. The coupling of coherent quantum spin to that torsion is not Newton’s (G). Call it \(G^{*}\). He wants \(G^{*}\) enormous — forty-odd orders — only inside a macroscopically coherent spin state: a pumped metamaterial, a Fröhlich condensate, aligned magnons, something you drive with ordinary electromagnetism. Outside that condensate, apples still fall the old way. Inside it, a thin shell plus kilowatts is supposed to source craft-scale geometry.

Schematically he writes things like

\[ G_{\mu\nu}=k_{1}T_{\mu\nu}+k_{2}S^{2}g_{\mu\nu}, \]

where (S) is the aligned spin density. The second term is the one Loeb never put in the code.
Third. The air problem is a boundary-condition problem, not a “space is magic” problem. Loeb’s fireball assumes the outside air has a huge velocity relative to the wall. Sarfatti says the hull is an active source: you arrange the near-field so neighboring air is locally comoving with the shell. No shear layer of the Alcubierre-through-atmosphere kind. Occupants sit in a local inertial frame — they feel nothing — while the exterior geometry does the accelerating.
That is the whole point of “metric engineering” as opposed to rockets ("That Loeb and his Harvard Pooh Bah’s totally miss" - Jack's snide quip)

If that matching can be done, Loeb’s terawatts go away by construction. If it cannot be done, Jack is wrong in the place that matters for airplanes over water.

He also offers a cheap observational discriminator: a gravitational Doppler that runs opposite the ordinary motion Doppler — redshift on the contracting nose as the thing comes at you, blueshift on the expanding tail as it runs. You would look for that in good spectra, not in vibes.
3. Who is right about what

Do not let anyone tell you this is “Loeb versus the cranks” or “Sarfatti versus the cover-up.”
Question

Honest answer

Would a frozen Alcubierre bubble at (0.1c) torch the sky?

Yes. Loeb–Fell.

Does that kill every spacetime-propulsion story?No. It kills that ansatz.

Does 1915 GR give you a quiet Mach-20 Tic-Tac on kilowatts?

Not that anyone has shown. Is Poincaré-gauge torsion a real idea?Yes. Textbook. Weak in the standard version. Is \(G^{*}\sim 10^{43}G\) in a condensate a theorem?
No. It is the conjecture.Has anyone run the air code with Sarfatti’s junction conditions? No. That is the missing paper.Has anyone measured a laboratory \(G^{*}\) jump? No. That is the missing experiment.
A paper that attacks a nearby idea — “just let Newton’s coupling \(\kappa\) vary through the metamaterial” — shows that a non-dynamical \(\kappa(x)\) fights conservation laws, and a dynamical scalar \(\kappa\) is already boxed in by solar-system tests. Jack says that is not his Lagrangian: he is not rescaling (G) for mass; he is adding a spin-torsion channel with short range. Fine. Then write the action, vary it, and show the range and the equivalence-principle leakage. Until that is on paper in a form a hostile theorist can break, \(G^{*}\) is a slogan with a pedigree, not a capability.

4. What this is worth to you as a government

National security does not require you to believe in tourists from Tau Ceti. It requires you not to be stupid about categories.

There are three boxes:

A. Most UAP are junk, birds, balloons, missiles, sensor ghosts. Loeb is good at stuffing objects into this box when the kinematics allow it. Keep doing that. It is cheaper than metaphysics.
B. A few objects, if the Navy numbers survive hostile re-analysis, sit outside chemical rockets and outside Loeb’s fireball. That does not automatically equal Jack’s engine. It equals “we do not have a propulsion model that is both standard and quiet.”
C. If someone — us, them, or a contractor who doesn’t send press releases — can source torsion or curvature in a thin coherent shell at low power, you are looking at propellantless kinematics, trans-medium motion, and a sensor problem, not an aviation problem. That is a first-order strategic issue whether the builders are human or not.

Loeb’s paper is progress on box A and a veto on one toy model in box B. It does not inspect box C. If the Intelligence Community treats the fireball paper as closure on box C, you have done the adversary’s classification work for them: you declared the interesting coupling “not physics” because it was not in the simulation.
Sarfatti’s program is the opposite failure mode if you swallow it whole: a mechanism that would explain the observables, attached to a coupling nobody has measured and a hull–air calculation nobody has finished. Believing the briefing slides is how you waste a decade. Ignoring the coupling hypothesis is how you miss a materials problem that might be sitting in a lab.

5. What I would make you do on Monday
Not a new office with a seal. Three ugly, cheap, falsifiable jobs.

One. Re-reduce the best kinematic cases — Nimitz and anything with dual phenomenology, radar plus IR plus eyewitness — as if a hostile graduate student were trying to make them ordinary. Publish the residuals. If the residuals die, Jack’s engine has less to explain. If they don’t, you know which events deserve geometry, not folklore.

Two. Commission the calculation Loeb did not do: GR hydro, or better a Poincaré-gauge hydro, on a thin active shellwhose near-field is required to match air velocity at the outer surface. Same code family. Different boundary condition. Either a shock still forms or it doesn’t. That is a number, not a worldview.

Three. Look for \(G^{*}\) where Jack says it lives — not in falling apples, in coherent spin ensembles. YIG, pumped magnons, layered metasurfaces, anything with macroscopic phase stiffness. Torsion-balance and clock and interferometer residuals on the sample, not on the building. If \(G^{*}\) is 40 orders of magnitude and confined to a micron skin, you still ought to see something local if the idea is even 10 orders true. Null results bound the story. Positive results change the budget.

Optical: if you ever get a clean spectrum of a close, fast object, look for the wrong-way Doppler. That costs cameras, not theology.

Last thing

The first principle is that you must not fool yourself — and you are the easiest person to fool.

Loeb fooled a certain kind of audience by answering a real question so cleanly that people forgot it was the wrong question for an engine.

Sarfatti fools a certain kind of audience by naming the missing term so vividly that people forget it has not been measured.

Your job is not to pick a team. Your job is to keep the missing term on the list until an experiment kills it or funds it. Anything else is theater.

If the thing is only weather balloons, you will have wasted a little money on interferometers. If the thing is a materials coupling we don’t teach at Caltech yet, you cannot afford to have learned that from someone else’s after-action report.

That’s the briefing. I’ll take questions, and I will not be polite if the question is “but which narrative do we put on the slide.”
