text:
Imagined briefing — Richard P. Feynman, still talking, in a room that has too many flags.

Mr. President. Director. The rest of you who actually have to decide something.

I’m not here to sell you flying saucers and I’m not here to tell you the Harvard fellow is a crook. I’m here to stop you from confusing a calculation with an engine. That confusion is how smart organizations get surprised.

1. What Loeb and Fell actually did

They took Miguel Alcubierre’s 1994 warp-bubble geometry — a prescribed dent in spacetime that slides along — and they asked a clean question:

If that dent, the size of an airplane, goes through Earth’s air at a tenth of light speed or more, what does the air do?

They did not ask how you make the dent. They froze the metric, turned off the stuff that would have to generate it, and ran the air as a fluid in that frozen background. Shock-capturing hydrodynamics. Respectable numerical work.

The air does what air always does when you hit it at relativistic speed. In the bubble’s rest frame the incoming air slams into a stagnation zone. Kinetic energy becomes heat. At half light-speed you’re talking a hundred-odd MeV per nucleon. The gas lights up. Terawatts. Sometimes a lot more. You would not miss it. You would not call it a quiet Tic-Tac.

So their conclusion, inside those assumptions, is not mysterious:

A naive Alcubierre bubble, aircraft-sized, relativistic, zero mass as seen from infinity, punching through atmosphere, is a fireball. Reported UAP are not fireballs. Therefore that particular cartoon is not those UAP.

That is a good constraint on a cartoon. It is not a theory of propulsion. It is not “we now understand UAP.” If your briefers walk out of the room thinking the energy problem of warp drive has been handled, they walked out with the invoice still face-down on the table.

The invoice in Einstein’s 1915 theory is ugly. Curvature is sourced by

\[ G_{\mu\nu}=\frac{8\pi G}{c^{4}}T_{\mu\nu}. \]
\(G/c^{4}\) is about \(10^{-43}\) in everyday units. To bend spacetime by an order-one amount on a ten-meter ship, you need stress-energy that would make a treasurer faint — and, in the original Alcubierre setup, the wrong sign of energy as well. Loeb and Fell never compute that. They assume the geometry and compute the weather. Useful. Incomplete.
If you brief the Intelligence Community that “physics checked warp drives and they glow,” you have briefed the weather and hidden the engine. That is not fraud. It is a model with the hard term set to zero. Policymakers who cannot tell the difference will fund the wrong next experiment.
2. What Sarfatti is actually saying
Jack is loud. That is not an argument against him, and it is not an argument for him. Listen to the physics claim, not the volume.

Einstein’s gravity, and the usual Einstein–Cartan upgrade from the 1960s, couple mass-energy to curvature with Newton’s little (G). Cartan and then Kibble also let spin source torsion — a twist of spacetime, not just a bend. In the textbook version that torsion is a contact interaction. It is there, and it is negligible unless you live inside a nucleus.

Sarfatti’s bet is three extra moves:
First. Don’t stop at Poincaré. Gauge the whole conformal group. Let torsion and a few extra potentials propagate, like a massive vector field that dies off outside a skin depth instead of reaching the Moon. Then you can have a strong effect in a hull and almost nothing a mile away. That is the only way this story doesn’t already contradict Cavendish, Cassini, and pulsar timing.

Second. The coupling of coherent quantum spin to that torsion is not Newton’s (G). Call it \(G^{*}\). He wants \(G^{*}\) enormous — forty-odd orders — only inside a macroscopically coherent spin state: a pumped metamaterial, a Fröhlich condensate, aligned magnons, something you drive with ordinary electromagnetism. Outside that condensate, apples still fall the old way. Inside it, a thin shell plus kilowatts is supposed to source craft-scale geometry.

Schematically he writes things like

\[ G_{\mu\nu}=k_{1}T_{\mu\nu}+k_{2}S^{2}g_{\mu\nu}, \]

where (S) is the aligned spin density. The second term is the one Loeb never put in the code.
Third. The air problem is a boundary-condition problem, not a “space is magic” problem. Loeb’s fireball assumes the outside air has a huge velocity relative to the wall. Sarfatti says the hull is an active source: you arrange the near-field so neighboring air is locally comoving with the shell. No shear layer of the Alcubierre-through-atmosphere kind. Occupants sit in a local inertial frame — they feel nothing — while the exterior geometry does the accelerating.
That is the whole point of “metric engineering” as opposed to rockets ("That Loeb and his Harvard Pooh Bah’s totally miss" - Jack's snide quip)

If that matching can be done, Loeb’s terawatts go away by construction. If it cannot be done, Jack is wrong in the place that matters for airplanes over water.

He also offers a cheap observational discriminator: a gravitational Doppler that runs opposite the ordinary motion Doppler — redshift on the contracting nose as the thing comes at you, blueshift on the expanding tail as it runs. You would look for that in good spectra, not in vibes.
3. Who is right about what

Do not let anyone tell you this is “Loeb versus the cranks” or “Sarfatti versus the cover-up.”
Question

Honest answer

Would a frozen Alcubierre bubble at (0.1c) torch the sky?

Yes. Loeb–Fell.

Does that kill every spacetime-propulsion story?No. It kills that ansatz.

Does 1915 GR give you a quiet Mach-20 Tic-Tac on kilowatts?

Not that anyone has shown. Is Poincaré-gauge torsion a real idea?Yes. Textbook. Weak in the standard version. Is \(G^{*}\sim 10^{43}G\) in a condensate a theorem?
No. It is the conjecture.Has anyone run the air code with Sarfatti’s junction conditions? No. That is the missing paper.Has anyone measured a laboratory \(G^{*}\) jump? No. That is the missing experiment.
A paper that attacks a nearby idea — “just let Newton’s coupling \(\kappa\) vary through the metamaterial” — shows that a non-dynamical \(\kappa(x)\) fights conservation laws, and a dynamical scalar \(\kappa\) is already boxed in by solar-system tests. Jack says that is not his Lagrangian: he is not rescaling (G) for mass; he is adding a spin-torsion channel with short range. Fine. Then write the action, vary it, and show the range and the equivalence-principle leakage. Until that is on paper in a form a hostile theorist can break, \(G^{*}\) is a slogan with a pedigree, not a capability.

4. What this is worth to you as a government

National security does not require you to believe in tourists from Tau Ceti. It requires you not to be stupid about categories.

There are three boxes:

A. Most UAP are junk, birds, balloons, missiles, sensor ghosts. Loeb is good at stuffing objects into this box when the kinematics allow it. Keep doing that. It is cheaper than metaphysics.
B. A few objects, if the Navy numbers survive hostile re-analysis, sit outside chemical rockets and outside Loeb’s fireball. That does not automatically equal Jack’s engine. It equals “we do not have a propulsion model that is both standard and quiet.”
C. If someone — us, them, or a contractor who doesn’t send press releases — can source torsion or curvature in a thin coherent shell at low power, you are looking at propellantless kinematics, trans-medium motion, and a sensor problem, not an aviation problem. That is a first-order strategic issue whether the builders are human or not.

Loeb’s paper is progress on box A and a veto on one toy model in box B. It does not inspect box C. If the Intelligence Community treats the fireball paper as closure on box C, you have done the adversary’s classification work for them: you declared the interesting coupling “not physics” because it was not in the simulation.
Sarfatti’s program is the opposite failure mode if you swallow it whole: a mechanism that would explain the observables, attached to a coupling nobody has measured and a hull–air calculation nobody has finished. Believing the briefing slides is how you waste a decade. Ignoring the coupling hypothesis is how you miss a materials problem that might be sitting in a lab.

5. What I would make you do on Monday
Not a new office with a seal. Three ugly, cheap, falsifiable jobs.

One. Re-reduce the best kinematic cases — Nimitz and anything with dual phenomenology, radar plus IR plus eyewitness — as if a hostile graduate student were trying to make them ordinary. Publish the residuals. If the residuals die, Jack’s engine has less to explain. If they don’t, you know which events deserve geometry, not folklore.

Two. Commission the calculation Loeb did not do: GR hydro, or better a Poincaré-gauge hydro, on a thin active shellwhose near-field is required to match air velocity at the outer surface. Same code family. Different boundary condition. Either a shock still forms or it doesn’t. That is a number, not a worldview.

Three. Look for \(G^{*}\) where Jack says it lives — not in falling apples, in coherent spin ensembles. YIG, pumped magnons, layered metasurfaces, anything with macroscopic phase stiffness. Torsion-balance and clock and interferometer residuals on the sample, not on the building. If \(G^{*}\) is 40 orders of magnitude and confined to a micron skin, you still ought to see something local if the idea is even 10 orders true. Null results bound the story. Positive results change the budget.

Optical: if you ever get a clean spectrum of a close, fast object, look for the wrong-way Doppler. That costs cameras, not theology.

Last thing

The first principle is that you must not fool yourself — and you are the easiest person to fool.

Loeb fooled a certain kind of audience by answering a real question so cleanly that people forgot it was the wrong question for an engine.

Sarfatti fools a certain kind of audience by naming the missing term so vividly that people forget it has not been measured.

Your job is not to pick a team. Your job is to keep the missing term on the list until an experiment kills it or funds it. Anything else is theater.

If the thing is only weather balloons, you will have wasted a little money on interferometers. If the thing is a materials coupling we don’t teach at Caltech yet, you cannot afford to have learned that from someone else’s after-action report.

That’s the briefing. I’ll take questions, and I will not be polite if the question is “but which narrative do we put on the slide.”

Honoring Dr. Karen Trujillo’s Enduring Impact ✨ Dr. Karen M. Trujillo ’92, ’93, ’98 believed education could transform lives, and she dedicated her career to making that belief a reality. 

A proud three-time #NMSU graduate, educator, researcher and superintendent of Las Cruces Public Schools, Trujillo inspired generations of students and championed the teachers who shape the future. She also served as New Mexico’s secretary of education. 

After her passing in 2021, her husband, Ben Trujillo, established the Dr. Karen M. Trujillo Memorial Foundation and created the Dr. Karen M. Trujillo Memorial Endowed Scholarship to support future educators in NMSU’s College of Health, Education and Social Transformation. Since then, seven aspiring teachers have received scholarship support through the fund. “This scholarship allows me to graduate without being in debt. To say ‘thank you’ is not enough,” one recipient shared. 💫 

Over the past five years, the Trujillo Foundation has provided nearly $800,000 in endowed scholarships at NMSU and the six other #NewMexico universities that offer teacher education programs, extending Dr. Trujillo’s impact across the state. Every scholarship recipient reflects Dr. Trujillo’s enduring belief that education creates opportunity, strengthens communities and changes lives. 

This Philanthropy Friday, honor Dr. Trujillo’s remarkable legacy by investing in the next generation of educators. Make a gift to the Dr. Karen M. Trujillo Memorial Endowed Scholarship today.

text:
The Navajo Nation has roughly 400,000 enrolled members and covers more land than West Virginia. Until this April, none of them had ever signed an NFL contract.

The one who finally did played six snaps on Saturday night and got a standing ovation from fans wearing both teams' jerseys.

Shiyazh Pete's first high school didn't have a football team. He transferred to Shiprock, New Mexico, joined the team as a sophomore, and mailed his own highlight tape to colleges during a COVID senior year with almost no recruiting resources on the reservation. The offers came back from Division II and Division III schools. He walked on at New Mexico State instead, redshirted, and spent his first year on the practice squad.

Three seasons later he was a first-team All-Conference USA left tackle, playing with a cast on a dislocated thumb, protecting the quarterback in a 34-10 win at Auburn.

Then Kentucky. Twelve starts in the SEC and a team captaincy. According to the NCAA, five Native Americans played Division I football in 2025. Pete was one of the five and the only one in the SEC.

Draft analysts ranked him somewhere between the 36th and 54th best tackle in the class. Seven rounds went by. Nobody called.

Dallas signed him as an undrafted free agent within days. The team's own rookie minicamp video of him was built around one line he said on camera. He had to earn that star.

Saturday in Glendale, thousands of Navajo Nation members made the trip to a Cardinals preseason game to watch a backup tackle. The Navajo Nation president came. When Pete checked in during the fourth quarter, the Navajo section noticed before anyone else did. Six plays, one touchdown drive, and then a chant of his last name loud enough that his teammates cleared the bench so he could face it alone.

His head coach handed him the locker room afterward. He told a room full of men he'd known for four months that fate brought them there as strangers, and this game, this star, this team would make them brothers.

Every locker room speech ever given is about brotherhood. This one came from the guy who spent his whole career as the only one in the room.

text:
I hope many billionaires will learn from Dolly parton's life. .You don't need to be in politics to make an impact .

There is a lesson in Dolly Parton’s life about what wealth is actually for.

America said goodbye to her this week at the age of 80. The coat of many colours was folded for the final time, but her songs will outlive us all.

Yet that is not the part of her story our children most need to hear.

The part worth repeating is what Dolly did with her wealth once she had it.

She did not wait to hold public office. She did not wait to launch a manifesto. She went home and got to work.

In Sevier County, Tennessee, the high school dropout rate was reportedly around 35 percent. In 1988, Dolly brought seventh and eighth graders together and asked each of them to choose a friend. Then she offered them a simple deal: if both completed high school, each would receive $500. If either dropped out, neither would be paid.

Suddenly, teenagers who might have walked away had someone they did not want to disappoint.

Dolly personally handed out the cheques at graduation. The dropout rate reportedly fell to about 6 percent. A year later, she offered another $500 to every local student who enrolled at the nearby college.

She understood what finishing school meant. She had been the first person in her family to graduate from high school.

When wildfires tore through Gatlinburg in 2016, Dolly did not issue a statement and disappear. Through her My People Fund, she gave roughly 900 affected families $1,000 every month for six months.

In the final month, because more money had been raised than expected, each family received an additional $5,000. The remaining millions went to a local organisation that would continue serving the community long after the cameras had left.

She also helped her home county secure a modern hospital. Proceeds from a 2007 benefit concert, matched by her own businesses, contributed to the opening of LeConte Medical Center in 2010. It included maternity services and a women’s health centre for the same mountain families among whom she had grown up.

Dollywood was never merely a theme park.

Dolly opened it in 1986 partly so that people from her community could find work without having to leave the mountains. It grew into one of the region’s largest employers.

In 2022, she went even further. Dollywood began covering tuition, books and fees for employees pursuing further education: whether they were full-time, part-time or seasonal workers, and beginning from their first day on the job.

In 1991, she helped establish a sanctuary at the park for bald eagles that could no longer survive in the wild. There was no political theatre around it. The birds needed a home, so she helped give them one.

When Hurricane Helene devastated communities across the state line in 2024, she sent help there too. Tennessee was home. North Carolina was a neighbour. That was enough.

But perhaps the work closest to her heart was the Imagination Library.

Her father, Robert Lee Parton, raised twelve children in a small cabin but never learned to read or write. In 1995, Dolly began sending one free book every month to every preschool child in Sevier County. Each book arrived addressed to the child by name.

The idea spread beyond the county, then beyond Tennessee, and eventually beyond the United States. More than 300 million books have now reached children through the programme.

Her father lived long enough to hear local children call his daughter “the Book Lady.” He told her that the Imagination Library was the most important thing she had ever done.

Look at the pattern.

She saw a problem with her own eyes. She put her own money behind a solution. Then she stayed long enough for the work to take shape.

She did not wait for a government study. She did not wait to be elected. She did not announce a “legacy project” and abandon it once the cameras disappeared.

text:
The Next War Elon Didn't Mention: Transformer Capacity Will Decide AI Supremacy in 2027

On August 29, 2026, Elon Musk tweeted a warning that sent ripples through the AI infrastructure world: "Consensus estimate is that ~15GW of AI compute produced in 2027 cannot be turned on in 2027. This is harder than just finding power, as you also need to build out all the transformers, wiring, liquid-cooling, (massive) chillers & complex networking."

This isn't Musk's first time raising the flag. Back in January 2026, he predicted that the limiting factor for AI would shift from chip manufacturing to "turning the chips on" – meaning power delivery, transformer gear, and cooling deployment. He used a sharp analogy: chip production grows exponentially, while energy infrastructure only scales linearly. When those two curves cross, a mountain of high-performance silicon sits idle for lack of the mundane hardware that converts and moves electricity.

Now he's put a number on it: roughly 15 gigawatts of compute hardware produced in 2027 won't be powered up that year.

Why Transformers Are Harder Than GPUs

Musk's list of bottlenecks is long, but the most lethal is the transformer – a century-old device that has suddenly become the biggest stumbling block for the AI boom.

Lead times have spiraled out of control. Before 2020, a large power transformer (100 MVA, 230 kV class) might take 12 to 18 months to deliver. Today? U.S. lead times have stretched beyond 36 months for many projects. In Q1 2026, generator step-up transformers topped 160 weeks – that's over three years, up from 143 weeks in 2024. In the tightest markets, high-capacity units now take four to five years.

The supply-demand mismatch isn't a blip. Analysts at Wood Mackenzie expect the squeeze to last until at least 2030. Siemens Energy's European factories have booked out production for the next four to five years. Data center developers now call suppliers and ask, "Do you have any spare capacity in 2026, 2027, or 2028?" and take it all.

Why can't we just build more transformer factories? Raw materials are constrained – electrical steel for cores comes from a handful of global suppliers, and copper prices have been volatile with mining output lagging. Skilled labor is even scarcer: transformer manufacturing is highly manual, with over 80,000 custom designs, each built to order over three to six months. Training a qualified technician takes years. Manufacturers are also wary of overbuilding after previous boom-bust cycles; a new plant takes four to five years to come online – longer than the typical three-year data center construction timeline.

The real-world consequence: nearly half of U.S. data center projects planned for 2026 are facing delays or cancellations, according to Sightline Climate. About 12 GW of projects were scheduled to go live in 2026, but only a third are actually under construction. Developers are sitting on over $650 billion in planned spending, but the physical gear just isn't there.

What 15GW Actually Means

Fifteen gigawatts of power demand – that's roughly equivalent to the peak electricity load of New York City (about 10 GW) plus another 50% on top. It's the output of about 15 nuclear reactors. Goldman Sachs projects U.S. data center power demand will double from 31 GW today to 66 GW by 2027 – meaning this 15 GW of "dark" compute represents nearly a quarter of that future demand, sitting offline.

Cooling and Networking: The Hidden Siblings

Musk also flagged liquid cooling, massive chillers, and complex networking. None of these are off-the-shelf items. The industry is pivoting from air to liquid cooling – Nvidia's latest systems are all-liquid – but that requires chip-level cold plates, rack-level distribution, and facility-wide 3D pipe networks. Musk himself warned of the risk: "If a liquid cooling pipe bursts – you can lose $1 billion in a single data center."

LG Electronics forecasts the market for data center chillers (air and liquid) will grow from $1.6 billion in 2026 to $12.7 billion by 2030 – a sign that supply is nowhere near demand. And "complex networking" means high-bandwidth, ultra-low-latency interconnects; optical modules, switches, and cables each have their own lead times, often 40+ weeks for top-tier gear.

Who Gets Paid: Mapping the Investment Opportunity

The bottleneck Musk identified isn't just an operational headache – it's a multi-billion-dollar profit pool shifting from semiconductor makers to infrastructure suppliers. Here's how the money flows:

First-order beneficiaries (direct exposure): Transformer manufacturers are the most direct play. U.S. transformer lead times have stretched to 160+ weeks, and data centers' share of the electrical equipment market could hit 40% by 2030, up from under 2% in 2020.

Siemens Energy (ENR): Reported a record €51 billion ($59 billion) order backlog in its Grid Technologies unit in August 2026, driven by transformer demand including data center projects. Total group backlog reached €154 billion with a book-to-bill ratio of 1.72. Expanding transformer manufacturing in North Carolina.

GE Vernova (GEV): Generated over $5 billion in data center orders in H1 2026 alone. Gas-turbine backlog hit 100 GW in Q1 2026. Market cap $279 billion, 67% YTD return.

Hitachi Energy (Hitachi, 6501.T): $300 million investment in China to boost transformer production; India subsidiary committed $210 million to a greenfield facility, ending 2026 with a record backlog of 296 billion rupees.

Hyosung Heavy Industries (South Korea): North American grid equipment orders driving high-margin revenue growth, with operating margin up 4.3 percentage points year-over-year.

Chinese transformer exporters (second-order but faster-cycle): While Western OEMs face 3-5 year lead times, Chinese manufacturers offer delivery in roughly one year.

Jinpan Technology (https://t.co/6ZBT3SSYHh): Data center revenue 1.337 billion yuan, +196.78% YoY; Q1 data center revenue 383 million yuan, +103.77%; 696 million yuan overseas supply contract.

Anker Smartech (https://t.co/QjWkATNma7): First North American data center transformer order Jan 2026; >$100 million tracked orders; 250+ units annual capacity; 30 million yuan SST R&D.

Sieyuan Electric (https://t.co/EpWelEltVG), TBEA (https://t.co/TxwDl1i9lP), China XD Electric (https://t.co/D0a0XuIpJ3): Multiple brokerages highlight as key export beneficiaries.

Cooling and thermal management: As rack densities soar (50kW+ per rack vs. traditional air-cooled limits of ~10-15kW), liquid cooling is becoming mandatory.

Vertiv (VRT): 23.5% global thermal management market share; Q1 2026 net sales ~$2.65B, +30% YoY; backlog >$15B; FY2026 revenue guidance $14B; market cap >$100B.

Schneider Electric (https://t.co/MzSVDXyVdT): Q1 2026 revenue €9.77B, 11.2% organic growth; H1 2026 €21.2B; data center orders triple-digit growth.

Eaton (ETN): Data center orders +85% YoY in Q2 2026.

ABB (ABBN.SIX): Data center orders maintaining triple-digit growth.

Electrical construction & EPC services: The crews that physically install this equipment are equally constrained.

Quanta Services (PWR): Record backlog, visibility to 2027-2028; market cap $94B, 56% YTD.

Comfort Systems (FIX): 55.2% annualized return since 2020 (topped only by Nvidia at 54.9% and Vertiv at 50.5%).

EMCOR (EME): Cheapest P/E (24.5x) in the group.

Revenue → Margin → EPS / FCF:

Transformer OEMs have multi-year revenue visibility with 3-4x book-to-bill ratios. Pricing power is strong – transformer costs could increase 4-10% over the next year. Companies with variable pricing can pass through costs; fixed-price contract holders face compression risk.

Cooling suppliers: Vertiv's shift to liquid cooling (higher ASP and margins) is driving margin expansion.

EPC firms: Backlog provides visibility, but labor cost inflation is a margin headwind.

Expectation / Valuation Gap:

Semiconductor names trade at 30x+ P/E. Infrastructure suppliers trade at lower multiples (Siemens Energy ~15x, Eaton ~20x, GE Vernova 30x). Vertiv is the exception at ~65x P/E. The gap is likely to narrow as investors recognize the physical bottleneck.

Risk / Invalidation:

Accelerated production: New factories or policy support could ease lead times.

Demand destruction: AI capex slowdown would eliminate the bottleneck.

Technological shift: Drastic chip efficiency improvements could reduce GW required.

Geopolitical: Supply chain diversification may increase capacity but takes time.

Valuation risk: Vertiv at 65x P/E is priced for perfection.

Invalidation trigger: If transformer lead times start declining materially, the thesis weakens.

Conclusion: The AI Race Enters the Heavy-Industry Phase

Musk's tweet delivers a clear message: the first half of the AI race was about who bought the most chips. The second half is about who plugs them in first.

Chips can be cranked out around the clock, but transformers, chillers, wiring, and networking – these "heavy" physical components – have immutable build cycles, installation schedules, and skilled-labor requirements. One delayed component stalls the entire data center.

Wood Mackenzie notes that power equipment's share of data center spend has jumped from under 2% in 2020 to 40% today – with roughly $720 billion in planned infrastructure spending now bottlenecked by equipment shortages.

The winners won't be the companies with the largest GPU hoards. They'll be the ones that locked down transformer capacity, secured cooling systems, and reserved grid connection points in 2026. AI has become a heavy industrial race, and the decisive battles may not be fought in Silicon Valley labs – they're being waged on the order books of transformer factories and cooling system backlogs.

This is industry observation and information compilation, not investment advice.

text:
The Arcane Texas Fact of the Day:  Did y'all know there was a "Six Flags" long before there every was a Six Flags?  It's true.   It was called Woodlake Park, and remnants of it still stand.

Woodlake Park, which looks to me like it was approximately halfway between Sherman and Denison, was one of Texas's earliest amusement parks, and it owed its existence to an electric railway. In 1901, the Denison and Sherman Railway opened an interurban line connecting the two cities. To give people another reason to ride, the company developed a wooded area about halfway between them. The area was called Tanyard Springs before the railway folks developed it. A ravine was dammed to create a small lake, and on May 1, 1901, the railway and its new resort, Woodlake, opened to the public.

Woodlake quickly became a major North Texas attraction. Visitors came to swim, boat, fish and picnic, but this was much more than a swimming hole. The park offered amusement rides, a flume, zoo, baseball grounds, penny arcade, roller skating and dancing. Its large two-story "Casino" wasn't primarily a gambling establishment but an entertainment hall used for dances, theatrical performances, vaudeville and public gatherings. Fourth of July celebrations drew particularly large crowds, with interurban cars sometimes packed with standing passengers.  I can only imagine how great it would have been to ride the interurban, disembark, and drink in the sounds and sights and smells. I'm thinking cotton candy, saltwater taffy, a Ferris wheel, boater hats etc ...

The arrangement was wonderfully simple: Woodlake gave people a reason to ride the railway, and the railway delivered customers to Woodlake. As North Texas's interurban system expanded, the park attracted visitors from beyond Sherman and Denison, including southern Oklahoma.

Woodlake's fortunes declined during the 1920s. Automobiles and better roads freed families from the interurban, while movies and radio offered new competition for their leisure time. A series of serious interurban accidents near Woodlake also darkened the park's history. By 1929 the grounds had deteriorated and the amusement park closed.

But Woodlake didn't disappear. The property subsequently became a private retreat and was used for years for Baptist encampments and religious gatherings. Remarkably, much of the old setting survives. Today Woodlake is an approximately 80-acre private preserve containing the seven-acre lake, old stone and brick pathways, the dance hall and ruins associated with the interurban electrical system. Just this year, on May 1, 2026, a Texas historical marker was dedicated there, exactly 125 years after Woodlake opened.

Now don't go searching for it because it's now on private property, but the woods still contain some of the old buildings and railroad paths and whatnot.  Normally I'm all about the whatnot, but private property is private property!

🕊️ Denison Police Share 1992 Parade Photos of Dolly Parton as Nation Mourns Music Icon 🕊️

Denison, TX — As tributes continue across the country following the death of music legend Dolly Parton, the Denison Police Department is remembering a special moment the North Texas community shared with the beloved entertainer more than three decades ago.

The department released archival photographs showing Parton participating in Denison’s Memorial Day Parade in 1992, when local police officers helped escort her through the celebration.

The images show Parton riding through the parade in a convertible, smiling and waving to crowds as Denison police officers walked alongside the vehicle.

Parton died Tuesday, August 25, at age 80 in Nashville, Tennessee. Her career spanned seven decades and extended far beyond country music through film, business and philanthropy.

In its tribute, the Denison Police Department remembered Parton for her kindness, generosity and lasting impact, saying the 1992 parade remains a memory the department is especially proud to hold.

The photographs now offer a glimpse back at the day one of America's most recognizable entertainers shared the streets of Denison with the North Texas community.

📸 Photos: Denison Police Department

Spreadsheet vs. Live Calculator: Why the Tool Matters
The Bigger Problem: Where Do Your Inputs Come From?
When the Numbers Don't Work
FAQs
Most fix-and-flip deals don't fail at the closing table. They fail earlier — when an investor eyeballs rehab costs or nudges an ARV just enough to make a shaky deal look like a winner.
If you're working with $50k to $300k in capital and evaluating flips in the Dallas-Fort Worth market, the math you run before making an offer is the most important work you'll do. Here's every formula you need, a full worked example, and why the tool you use to run that math deserves more attention than most investors give it.
The Core Formulas Every Flip Investor Needs
After Repair Value (ARV)
ARV is what the property will sell for once renovations are done. You build it from comparable sales — ideally homes within a half-mile, similar square footage and bedroom count, sold within the last 90 days, in comparable post-renovation condition.
Overestimating ARV is the most common reason flips underperform. Investors pull comps from a slightly better street, a slightly larger floor plan, or a sale from eight months ago in a different rate environment. The result is an inflated number that makes a bad deal look like a good one.

Rehab Cost Estimate

This is the second place deals go sideways. A rough walkthrough estimate of "$40k" can quietly become $75k once you open walls and find outdated electrical, or discover foundation issues that weren't visible on the first visit.
Rehab estimates need to be line-item specific: demo, framing, roofing, HVAC, plumbing, electrical, flooring, kitchen, baths, paint, landscaping — plus a contingency buffer of at least 10–15%. A round number is not underwriting.
The 70% Rule

The 70% rule is a quick filter. Your maximum offer should be no more than 70% of ARV minus your estimated rehab costs.

Max Offer = (ARV × 0.70) − Rehab Costs
It's a starting point, not a final answer. In competitive DFW submarkets, you may need to tighten to 65%. In slower-moving areas with longer days on market, 72–75% can still work if holding costs are low. The rule tells you whether a deal is worth running deeper math on — nothing more.

Max Allowable Offer (MAO)

MAO is the 70% rule with more precision. You layer in your actual cost structure:
MAO = ARV − Rehab Costs − Holding Costs − Closing Costs (buy + sell) − Desired Profit

Holding costs include financing (hard money or private lending), property taxes, insurance, and utilities across your projected timeline. Closing costs typically run 1–2% to buy and 6–8% to sell when you factor in agent commissions and title. Your desired profit is a number you set based on capital at risk and your minimum acceptable return.

ROI and Cash-on-Cash Return

ROI measures total profit against total project cost.
ROI = Net Profit / Total Project Cost × 100

Cash-on-cash return measures profit against your actual out-of-pocket cash — which matters more when you're using leverage.

Cash-on-Cash = Net Profit / Cash Invested × 100

A deal might show a 20% ROI on total project cost but a 45% cash-on-cash return if you financed 80% of the purchase and rehab. Both numbers matter. Which one you optimize for depends on your strategy and how you're funding the deal.
A Worked Example: DFW Flip Deal

You're looking at a 3/2 in a North Texas suburb. Here are the numbers:

Estimated ARV: $320,000 (based on recent comps in the same subdivision)

Purchase Price Asked: $195,000

Estimated Rehab: $55,000 (line-item estimate with a 12% contingency)

Holding Period: 5 months
Financing: Hard money at 12% interest, 80% LTV

Holding Costs: ~$9,500 (interest, taxes, insurance, utilities)
Buy-side Closing Costs: ~$3,500
Sell-side Closing Costs: ~$22,400 (7% of ARV)
Total Project Cost: $285,400
Total Cash In: ~$68,000 (20% down plus out-of-pocket rehab and closing costs)
Net Profit: $320,000 − $285,400 = $34,600
ROI: $34,600 / $285,400 = 12.1%
Cash-on-Cash: $34,600 / $68,000 = 50.9%
70% Rule Check: (320,000 × 0.70) − 55,000 = $169,000 max offer

At $195,000, this deal fails the 70% rule. That doesn't automatically kill it, but it does mean your margin is thinner than the rule recommends. If rehab runs $10k over or the market softens before you sell, profit compresses fast. That's exactly the conversation the math is supposed to start.

Running the numbers before you make an offer isn't optional — it's the job. Use the formulas, feed them accurate inputs, and pressure-test your assumptions before you're committed. text:
Lee Corso is 91 years old today.

He coached college football for 15 years and finished with a career record of 73 wins and 85 losses.

A losing record. He became the most beloved man in the sport anyway.

Start at the beginning.

His father Alessandro fled Italy at 15 years old during World War I. He had a second grade education and laid terrazzo floors for a living. His mother Irma had a fifth grade education and worked in school cafeterias.

Their son was born in Cicero, Illinois in 1935.

He was good enough at baseball that the Brooklyn Dodgers offered him a $5,000 bonus to sign as a shortstop. He turned it down to go to college.

At Florida State they called him Sunshine Scooter because of how fast he was. He set the school record with 14 career interceptions, a record that stood for more than twenty years.

And his roommate was a guy named Burt Reynolds.

One summer Reynolds came to him and said, "Cors, I'm gonna quit school." Corso asked why. Reynolds told him he was going to Hollywood to be a movie star.

He was serious. He left. He became one of the biggest movie stars on the planet. They stayed close friends until Reynolds died in 2018.

Corso went the other direction and became a coach.

Louisville. Then Indiana. Then Northern Illinois. Then the USFL's Orlando Renegades, where he went 5-13.

He took the hardest jobs in football. At Indiana he went 41-68-2 over ten years.

But in 1979 he took the Hoosiers to the Holiday Bowl and beat an undefeated BYU team, which put Indiana in the top 20 for the first time since 1967.

And in 1976 he did the thing that tells you exactly who he is.

Indiana was playing Woody Hayes and Ohio State. Early in the second quarter, Indiana scored and took a 7-6 lead.

Lee Corso called a timeout.

Not to draw up a play. He gathered his entire team on the field and had them pose for a photograph in front of the scoreboard, because it was the first time in 25 years Indiana had led Ohio State in a football game.

His explanation to Sports Illustrated: "The goal of a lifetime!"

Ohio State then scored 41 unanswered points and won 47-7.

Fans have argued for decades about whether the photo actually exists. Corso never cared. The point was the moment.

He got fired at Indiana. He went to work in business development for a PENCIL COMPANY.

Then in 1987, ESPN launched a show called College GameDay, and hired the coach with the losing record.

He was there from the very first episode.

In October 1996 he tried something new. He put on the Brutus Buckeye mascot head to pick Ohio State to win.

That turned into the single most famous ritual in American sports. Grown men across the country waiting to see which giant mascot head an old man puts on his head.

He made 431 headgear picks and got 287 of them right.

Then on May 16, 2009, Lee Corso had a stroke at his home in Florida.

Partial paralysis. Three days in intensive care. A week in the hospital. He could not speak for a MONTH.

Less than four months later, he was back on College GameDay for the season opener.

He could never ad lib again. Every segment had to be scripted and rehearsed. He'd do the first fifteen minutes, rest for forty five, then come back for the rest of the show. His castmates covered for him for sixteen more years and never once made him feel like a burden.

He kept going until he was 89 years old.

His final show was August 30, 2025, in Columbus. For his 431st and last headgear pick, he chose Ohio State.

The exact same team he picked the very first time in 1996.

Ohio State won.

His statement on the way out was pure Corso. He said he was taking with him a treasure of friends and fond memories.

He's been married to Betsy since 1957. That's 69 years. Four kids. Ten grandchildren.

A guy whose dad laid floors for a living, who never had a winning career as a coach, spent forty years teaching America why Saturdays matter.

Happy 91st, Coach.

text:
On August 27, the President met with the head of the Federal Medical and Biological Agency, Veronika Skvortsova.  Skvortsova is a neurologist and she was Russia's Minister of Health between 2012 and 2020.
She briefed the President on the measures the agency is taking to develop blood services and blood donation in Russia in general, as well as on the agency's activities in industrial, marine, and sports medicine.

***

Pres. Putin: I propose we discuss several topics: the blood service, industrial medicine, and sports medicine—as well as any other matters you deem appropriate and necessary to bring up for discussion today.

Please, go ahead.

Skvortsova: Thank you very much, Vladimir Vladimirovich.

The Federal Medical-Biological Agency serves as the national coordinator for the blood service; it is responsible not only for the collection of blood and blood components and meeting the country's entire demand for them, but also for ensuring safety—including the absence of transfusion-transmitted infections—and for all necessary innovative developments in the field of transfusion medicine.

Given the importance of this area—particularly in recent years—significant attention has been devoted to fostering blood donation as a distinct culture of public service. Working alongside federal executive bodies, civic groups, and youth organizations, we conduct a wide range of initiatives aimed at promoting donation. This has enabled us to increase the number of donors by more than 20 percent since 2020, while also raising the average donation frequency to 2.3 per donor. Consequently, the annual number of donors has risen to over 1.5 million, and the total number of donations has surpassed 3.5 million. This has made it possible to increase whole donor blood collection by 47 percent since 2020. We now collect over 2.7 million liters of whole blood annually; correspondingly, blood plasma collection has also increased by 37 percent over the same period, reaching more than a million liters.

Pres. Putin: How many donors do we have now?

Skvortsova: More than 1.5 million people. However, our database contains a significantly larger number—over 12 million.

Pres. Putin: My father was a donor for many years.

Skvortsova: We are paying special attention to building a strategic reserve of blood and blood components. Compared to 2022, we have managed to increase this strategic reserve more than two-and-a-half-fold, effectively reaching a volume of one million liters across all blood components—including rare blood types and factors. This enables us to release a very large quantity at once should the need arise during an emergency situation.

To ensure the rapid distribution of blood of the necessary types and factors, we are establishing a network of large interregional storage and redistribution centers. This year, hubs in Kursk and Rostov-on-Don are being added to the network. These are large-scale facilities—each with a capacity of over 100,000 liters—that enable the rapid supply of all surrounding regions. A similar facility is also scheduled to open in Mariupol next year.

I would also like to mention that the agency’s hematology research centers developed a unique product in 2023 and 2024: a plastic container that allows for the lyophilization—or freeze-drying—of blood plasma while maintaining complete sterility and preserving all its native properties. This is not a substitute; it is actual plasma, yet it comes in a virtually weightless packet. It has a five-year shelf life and requires no cold chain, meaning it can be used at any temperature. We have established the production of a universal lyophilized plasma that can be transfused in extreme situations or field conditions, where it is difficult to determine the casualty's blood type.

Last year alone, we supplied the Ministry of Defence with over 7,000 units of lyophilized plasma, and in the first half of 2026, we have already delivered more than 13,000 units. In practical terms, this is a product that saves lives on the front line by reversing shock and helping to manage severe bleeding.

But this year, we went a step further. We succeeded in creating a pooled lyophilized cryoprecipitate—effectively concentrating the contents of four plasma bags into a single bag of highly concentrated precipitate. This product contains four times the amount of fibrinogen and blood factors, providing virtually instant relief in the most critical situations.

It is important to note that until 2022, the entire blood service system in the Russian Federation relied on imported equipment; however, between 2022 and 2025, we successfully replicated the full range of seven essential devices required to support the entire blood transfusion chain. These include systems for cytapheresis, sterile tubing connectors, blood component extractors, platelet mixers, freezers, and red blood cell processing units. The final device—developed in 2025—is a virus inactivation system that makes it possible to completely eliminate the risk of transfusion-transmitted infections. FMBA research institutes developed this entire product line together with our business partner as part of the implementation of the import substitution program of the Rostec State Corporation.🏆🇷🇺

In 2021, Vladimir Vladimirovich, you instructed us to sharply increase the collection of blood plasma for manufacturing purposes, given that only 10 percent of blood-derived products were domestically produced, with the rest being imported. Since 2021, we have successfully established six large plasma centers near the facilities that manufacture these blood-derived medicines; consequently, we have increased the collection of plasma for manufacturing 26-fold—from 30 tonnes to a projected 780 tonnes by the end of 2025. This now enables us to fully meet the requirements for producing essential medications, specifically human albumin and immunoglobulins.

Furthermore, we have created and developed standards for all major human immunoglobulins: those against tick-borne encephalitis, hepatitis B, staphylococcus, and tetanus, as well as anti-Rh immunoglobulin. These are products we had previously always purchased, primarily from Western European countries. By the end of last year, we had achieved 100% coverage for all of them except anti-Rh immunoglobulin. Coverage for anti-Rh immunoglobulin stood at 30%, but we have resolved that issue this year as well.

The final two products we were lacking are now effectively in the final stages of development. Thus, we are becoming fully self-sufficient—not only regarding blood and blood components but also, consequently, regarding these derived products.

We can currently state that the country’s needs are being fully met across the board: military and civilian hospitals, as well as clinics under any jurisdiction—whether regional or federal—have all their requirements completely covered.

I would like to say a few words specifically about bone marrow donation. In 2022, you instructed us to create a unified federal registry. Prior to that, 11 local registries had been operating for a decade, accumulating a total of 112,000 potential donors over that period. The registry went live on September 1, 2022. We have managed to increase the number of bone marrow and hematopoietic cell donors nearly fivefold; today, the figure stands at 546,000.🏆

Pres.Putin: What is it called? Hematopoietic?

Skvortsova: Yes, hematopoietic ones. These are the blood-forming stem cells found in bone marrow. Thanks to this, we have already achieved a 97 percent efficiency rate in the registry regarding fully or partially compatible donors. Over this period, the total number of transplants has doubled, while the number of transplants involving unrelated donors—specifically those from our Russian registry—has tripled; they now account for 77 percent of all donors. Things are moving forward, and we are continuing to actively develop all these areas.🏆

The second point I would like to mention, Vladimir Vladimirovich, is, of course, industrial medicine.

Pres.Putin: Industrial and maritime medicine as well, right?

Skvortsova: For nearly 80 years, the agency has been dedicated to safeguarding the health of the workforce—specifically those employed at strategic enterprises involving special working conditions, such as the nuclear and space industries, the defense-industrial complex, and so forth.

Reflecting the shifting paradigm of modern healthcare—specifically the transition from treating the sick to providing medical support for the healthy—we developed a new five-year strategy for industrial medicine (spanning 2023–2027) in 2022. We also established a model comprehensive health center for the workforce that integrates a vast array of services: not only preventive care but also occupational health (including the management of occupational diseases and occupational health assessments), a center for cognitive and psycho-emotional health, psychophysiological laboratories, a rehabilitation center, and a center for reproductive health and family well-being—essentially, a multitude of specialized modules consolidated in a single location.

Most importantly, each center operates a network of digital health stations located directly at production sites, all linked within a unified digital framework. Since 2023, we have rapidly established 60 comprehensive health centers—serving closed administrative-territorial formations, science cities, and satellite towns of nuclear power plants—along with 334 digital health stations. We are on track to meet our target figures next year.

It is worth noting that digital health stations are located directly at the production site; these facilities include a medical unit where workers undergo automated pre- and post-shift check-ups independently. Additionally, a "health point" is set up within the workshop itself, allowing workers to perform self-assessments during breaks—checking around 140 health parameters in just two minutes—and connect via telemedicine with a doctor or a medical assistant; interactive occupational safety kiosks are also available. Options for personal health assistants exist for those with specific risk factors. Thus, individual rehabilitation activities and health monitoring take place during shift changes. 

In effect, we have established a registry of the workforce under this program—including a specialized segment for those exposed to hazardous and dangerous conditions—and created a digital profile for each employee. This registry enables precise risk management and prevention, with a particular focus on critical personnel. In a short span of less than four years, our strategic enterprises have seen a 16 percent drop in overall morbidity and a 15 percent decline in mortality, alongside reductions in temporary disability and the incidence of new disability cases.The duration of active working life increased by 15 percent, and employers' economic costs decreased by 21 percent.

These results were given serious consideration by the social policy division of the Russian Government. At the direction of Tatyana Alekseevna Golikova, we developed these methodological guidelines for employers across the country. They were approved by the Russian Tripartite Commission in September 2025. We are now disseminating this methodology nationwide in collaboration with the RSPP and the Russian Engineering Union; 122 enterprises across 35 regions have already joined this initiative. This work now extends beyond the scope of the Federal Medical-Biological Agency.

And, of course, we are firmly convinced that this is a crucial area, given that the health of the workforce directly impacts the health of both children and older age groups, as well as all economic and other key indicators.

That is why we are actively collaborating with Alexander Nikolayevich Shokhin, Sergey Viktorovich Chemezov, and all other stakeholders.

A vital component of industrial medicine is, of course, maritime medicine. Thirty-six of the Agency’s centers are dedicated to the health of maritime personnel—including seafarers and employees working in maritime and shore-based infrastructure.

At the direction of Nikolai Platonovich Patrushev, Chairman of the Maritime Board, the National Center for Seafarers' Health was established in St. Petersburg in 2025, based at the FMBA’s Northwestern District Center. This center serves as the methodological lead and coordinator for the entire network; modeling the initiative on industrial medicine practices, a registry of seagoing personnel was created. Currently, 45 percent of the country's total seagoing workforce is included in this registry—comprising 45,000 individual records—along with divers and Atomflot personnel. Furthermore, the electronic seafarer health passport and a unified system for medical certification and clearance for duty have already become part of our daily routine.

At the Maritime Board, we discussed how to ensure that sailors who are not served by the FMBA—but rather by a large number of private facilities and so on—are also included in the system...

Pres.Putin: ...and registered here?

Skvortsova: Yes. Because that would make it possible to manage the system comprehensively and simply understand everything happening across all river and maritime basins.

In 2023, a specialized center was established in Murmansk based at our N.I. Pirogov Multidisciplinary Center for Arctic Medicine. Given the importance of the Northern Sea Route and the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor, this center effectively provides medical support to all eight icebreakers, fixed offshore platforms, mobile drilling rigs, and the *Akademik Lomonosov* floating nuclear power plant; it also coordinates with the medical teams—who are essentially the center’s own staff—working on these mobile units, as well as with the round-the-clock psychological support center and the center for radiation, chemical, and biological safety.

In collaboration with the Ministry of Emergency Situations (EMERCOM) and aligned with the Northern Sea Route development plan, we are establishing a comprehensive network of emergency rescue centers. EMERCOM handles its specific areas of responsibility, while we provide emergency medical rescue centers fully equipped with operating rooms, intensive care units, and infectious disease modules—including isolation capabilities where necessary—as well as evacuation facilities. We established the first center in Pevek, Chukotka; it has been operational for a year and a half. A second center was opened this April in Sabetta. Plans are in place to open similar centers over the next two years in Dikson and Khatanga (Krasnoyarsk Krai) and Tiksi (Republic of Sakha/Yakutia). These centers are integrated directly into our network structure and are fully coordinated by the Murmansk Arctic Center.

Thus, the maritime medicine network is developing; it is being coordinated and centrally managed, and we report on this to the Maritime Board.

And, if I may, Vladimir Vladimirovich, a crucial and very rapidly developing area is sports medicine.

In November 2024, at the Council for the Development of Physical Culture and Sport, you issued an instruction to establish a unified methodology for the development of sports medicine and to create—for the first time in our country’s history—a national center for sports medicine. Established by Presidential decree in May 2025, the center has since become fully operational. A dedicated pediatric division was also created, based at the Center for Child and Adolescent Health of the Federal Medical-Biological Agency.

The Center features a unique structure; its core is a major research and analysis complex that has assembled interdisciplinary biomedical research teams for all major sports. These teams collaborate with the Ministry of Sport’s integrated scientific groups. This arrangement has made it possible to shift the focus of their work directly to the Ministry’s training facilities—the ten sites where our national teams train. Consequently, the primary work takes place right at the edge of the field, utilizing wearable digital devices during the actual training sessions.

This work has proven unique and highly significant—we are currently collaborating with 21 sports federations—and has enabled the adoption of cutting-edge methods to dramatically boost athletic performance while safeguarding athletes' health.

For team sports, we have introduced a new methodology for expanding peripheral and stereoscopic vision, enabling the simultaneous tracking of multiple objects. We also developed a methodology to sharply increase starting speed in various track and field disciplines—specifically pre-jump velocity—which has consequently improved performance in high-jump events.

Nutritional science and psychology are topics in their own right. I would like to point out that applying these methods over a two-month period allows our athletes to move from 40th place to first or second in the national rankings. The same approach is applied to children, bearing in mind that minors make up 55 percent of national squads—and over 70 percent in some sports.

Pres. Putin: Is it possible to determine a child’s aptitude for sports?

Skvortsova: On the one hand, there is a predisposition—since we now conduct both molecular-biological and genetic testing on everyone—but given various ethical considerations, we never issue rigid recommendations; instead, we allow the child to develop—as the body is highly adaptable—while providing support and striving to offer guidance very carefully.

The foundation for gathering information on each athlete is the electronic athlete health passport; unlike the system in place prior to 2025, this passport now incorporates all necessary multidisciplinary components and tracks the training process itself dynamically.

Our digital system is integrated with the Ministry of Sports’ "Moy Sport" (My Sport) digital systems and the Ministry of Health’s digital system. In effect, we are creating a "data lake"—as it is currently called—that enables the use of artificial intelligence to predict risk factors and elements limiting each athlete's performance, as well as to overcome them.

In line with your directive to extend this experience to the regions—initially to regional representative teams, which serve as the immediate feeder pool for national squads, and subsequently to a broader scope including school sports leagues, university sports, and essentially all organized sports activities across the constituent entities of the Russian Federation—a federal law was enacted in December 2025. This law amended the legislation "On the Fundamentals of Protecting Citizens' Health in the Russian Federation," authorizing the FMBA to establish unified national methodological guidelines that serve as the foundation for updating and modernizing regional protocols for biomedical support.  This work was completed very quickly, and more than 70 regions are now working with us within a unified methodological framework.

A federal law has been adopted to establish a state information system for the health of Russian athletes, which includes a digital clearance process for their participation in training activities. Under the direction of Dmitry Nikolayevich Chernyshenko, 52 pilot regions have already been integrated into this system; we are working very actively with them, helping them advance their methodological approaches. We hope that this work will be fully completed by July 1 of next year.

Work has now been completed on the Strategy for the Development of Sports Medicine through 2030, with an outlook extending to 2036. You instructed the Government, together with the Federal Medical-Biological Agency, to prepare this strategy back in December 2025. The Government then tasked us with coordinating this effort—involving municipalities, regions, and sports federations—to ensure continuity in athlete development, starting from the school league level.

I would like to conclude, Vladimir Vladimirovich, by noting the significant extent to which sports medicine has contributed to the results we have achieved. We are deeply grateful for the teamwork with the Ministry of Sports and the Olympic and Paralympic Committees. Indeed, starting with the previous Paralympic Games, not a single athlete we worked with personally returned without a medal.🏆🇷🇺

We sincerely hope that, amidst the current changes and our return to the international stage, we can ensure that the contribution of medicine helps maximize the athletes' potential.🏆🇷🇺

Pres.Putin: Thank you very much.

text:
Everybody tells it like she took a leap of faith and quit her railroad job to paint full time. Annie Lee did say that. What she also said, and what almost nobody repeats, is that her son had just been killed in a car accident and she no longer needed the money. She was on bereavement leave when she decided not to go back. Sit with what that means before you share the pretty version again

You already know the painting.

A Black woman sitting on the edge of a bed in a blue room, shoulders down, a lamp and an alarm clock beside her and her slippers still on the floor. She is not sick and she is not sad, she is just tired in the specific way that Monday makes a woman tired.

That picture has been on somebody's wall in your family. Maybe your mother's hallway, maybe your auntie's bedroom, maybe a calendar in a beauty shop.

The woman in it has no face.

None of them do. The woman who painted her left the features off every figure she made, and she was fifty years old before she got her first gallery show.

Her name was Annie Lee. This is what that picture cost.

That cost starts in a front room on the South Side of Chicago in the middle 1940s.

Her mother was a seamstress raising children alone, and she did not believe in raising helpless ones. She taught Annie Lee and her older brother Tony off the same list.

Cook, wash, clean, sew, with nothing set aside as the boy's half or the girl's half.

Sundays were church, then eggnog ice cream at the corner drug store, and sometimes a matinee.

The rest of the week the radio ran while they worked. The Lone Ranger and The Shadow, the serials where a man's whole face arrived as a voice and a footstep and a door closing, and the child on the floor had to build the rest of him out of nothing.

Annie Lee sat in that room learning to knit and crochet with the radio going. She learned to draw in there too, in the same hours, listening to stories that handed her a body with no face on it and dared her to finish the job.

By ten the drawing had turned into painting, and it was immediately obvious. She entered art contests and won them, and the prize for winning was free semesters of lessons at the Art Institute of Chicago.

So there is a Black ten-year-old from the South Side in the 1940s walking through the front doors of the Art Institute, on a pass she took off every other child who entered. Nobody handed her that building, she beat her way into it.

The next building she walked into was Wendell Phillips High School at 39th and Prairie, in Bronzeville, the first majority-Black high school in Chicago and full past bursting. The Great Migration kept arriving, the building kept taking them, and by the mid-1940s the students were running split shifts with portable classrooms parked outside and adults coming in at night for evening school.

Nat King Cole had walked those halls, and so had Gwendolyn Brooks, Dinah Washington, John H. Johnson and the boys who became the Harlem Globetrotters.

Annie Lee cheered for the football team in that building and kept drawing.

The drawing got her an offer that almost never came to a Black girl in Bronzeville in the early 1950s. Northwestern University put four years of art school on the table, free.

She said no.

She married instead. Asked about it decades later, Annie Lee said that at the time it had not been a hard decision to make, and that one line is the only explanation of it she ever gave.

What Northwestern was in those years is a separate question, and the university has answered it.

Black students there were housed off campus under a selective housing system. Black women commuted in from private homes in Chicago or boarded with Black families in the Black section of Evanston.

An experimental interracial residence for women opened in 1947 and closed after a single year. Race stayed on the housing application form until 1962, and restrictive covenants made renting in Evanston a wall of its own.

Whether any of that ever reached a girl on 39th and Prairie is not on any record anybody has produced. It is only what the campus was on the day they offered her the four years.

She never took them, and what came instead was thirty years of a different kind of work.

The husband she married died of cancer. She married again and buried him too, cancer again, and raised a daughter from the first marriage and a son from the second on her own.

Two funerals for two husbands. Children who still needed shoes.

There was no art in those years worth the name. There was work.

The work was the Northwestern Railroad in Chicago, where the record has her as chief clerk in the engineering department, the department responsible for making sure the track was safe to run trains on. She was keeping the paperwork straight on track safety at a company that spent those same years abandoning and selling off branch line across seven states, and every mile of it had to be filed by somebody.

The scholarship she walked away from and the payroll she signed onto carried the same name. None of the biographies stop to notice it.

Being chief clerk of anything means a desk and a fixed hour, and a fixed hour means getting out of bed in the dark.

It is a Monday in winter and it is around five o'clock. Outside it is cold and it is still full dark.

Annie Lee is sitting on the edge of the bed, trying to get herself together. That is her own phrase for it, not mine.

Soon she has to be standing at a stop in the Chicago cold, waiting on public transportation to carry her to a railroad office where she is the chief clerk. It is a serious job with a serious title that still puts her outside in the winter dark like everybody else.

She is fifty years old, or close to it, and she has buried two husbands. She is going to work.

And sitting there in the dark, she has a thought that is not about art at all.

She wonders whether anybody else in the world feels as bad right now as she does.

That is it. That is the entire origin of the most recognized painting in Black American homes.

She did not go hunting for a subject. She was the subject, at five in the morning, on a work day, with a bus to catch.

By that winter Annie Lee had already spent years going back for the thing she gave away. She enrolled at Loop Junior College, then did undergraduate work at Mundelein College and the American Academy of Art.

Then eight years of night classes at Loyola University for a master's in interdisciplinary arts education.

Up before five. Railroad office all day, classroom in the evening, and painting when she got home.

She never intended to teach. She said the master's was the best thing she ever did for herself, that it reopened her mind.

She paid for that degree with eight years of nights in her forties. It was the same education Northwestern had offered her for nothing straight out of high school.

Her body sent the invoice. She developed tendinitis in her arm and problems in her spine from the hours at the easel.

The acrylics were worse. The fumes off the paint made her physically sick in her own apartment, and she kept painting in them because there was nowhere else and no other time.

She had waited her whole life to do this thing, and the thing was poisoning her while she did it.

Annie Lee was still painting in those fumes in 1985, when she got her first gallery show. Fifty years old, one lifetime late.

Everything on the walls sold in four hours.

Four hours. A woman who had been quietly excellent since she was ten stood in a room and watched strangers strip it bare before the afternoon was out, and then had to authorize prints of four paintings just to keep up with what people were asking for.

Then she went back to the railroad. One sold-out room in Chicago was one room, and by her family's account she was not about to give up the security of the day job.

She was still there in December of 1986, when her son was killed in a car accident.

She put in for leave from the railroad to bury him.

That leave is a fifty-one-year-old woman at home in the middle of a Chicago December, in the flat weeks after a funeral. Nothing to do, no reason to move, and a secure job waiting whenever she was ready to go back to it.

Annie Lee was still on that leave when she made the decision.

Every version of her story online calls what happened next a leap of faith. She did use those words, and there is a second half that almost nobody repeats.

She said she had prayed she could make her living painting, and that she felt she was supposed to paint. Then she said that now her son was gone, she did not need such financial resources.

She had stayed at the railroad for the security, and the security was for her children.

That is her own accounting of it, given to an interviewer thirteen years later, and it is the half the inspirational retellings drop. The job was worth less to her in January than it had been in November.

Annie Lee did not go back to the railroad. The leap of faith was real, and it became affordable at a graveside.

What she did with the years she bought was not small.

In 1990 she opened Annie Lee and Friends Gallery in Glenwood, Illinois. She hung forty-nine of her own originals in it and gave the rest of the wall to other artists, which is not what most people do the second they get a room of their own.

From that room she went out on the road with a travelling show that ran for years under the name Eight Men and a Lady, and the men in it rotated. She was the Lady, and by the account of the painter Gilbert Young she was the reason the rest of them kept showing up.

Her paintings kept showing up too, as set dressing on The Cosby Show and on A Different World, and the country met her work without ever meeting her.

Then she did the thing the art world never forgives. She put her designs on figurines, on dolls, on kitchen tiles, on housewares, on anything a family could actually afford to bring home.

That is how she got into your grandmother's house. Not through a museum, through a price a working woman could actually pay.

The fumes finally moved Annie Lee out of Chicago altogether, to Nevada, where she could work outdoors or under an exhaust fan and keep breathing. Through all of it, on every canvas, the same refusal above the neck.

People asked her about the faces constantly and the answer never really changed. You do not need to see a face to understand emotion, she said, and she wanted the movement of the body to carry it so people could use their imaginations.

A girl learned to draw in a room where the radio gave her a voice and no picture and made her supply the face herself. A woman spent forty years painting figures and handing that same job to everybody else.

She told the Chicago Tribune in 1997 that her paintings connected her to women, and that she knew the way she felt was the way a lot of women felt. That was not modesty, she was telling you the source material was her own Monday.

Her grandson Abe Ilo, who holds the rights to her work, has said that Blue Monday was the only painting she ever called a self-portrait. She gave herself the exact same treatment as everybody else she ever painted, which by her own account was the whole point.

The record has handled her about as carefully as it handled the scholarship.

There is a store selling Blue Monday prints right now with a description saying the painting shows a woman hunched over her washing basin. She is sitting on a bed.

The same listing says Annie Lee had no formal art training. She paid eight years of night classes and a master's degree to disprove that sentence.

On December 17, 2022, Lizzo walked out on Saturday Night Live in a white slip dress with her hair in Bantu knots. She sat hunched on the edge of a bed beside a lamp and an alarm clock, blue wall behind her, slippers on the floor, and began to sing.

The set was Blue Monday rebuilt down to the calendar on the wall, with December swapped in for the June in the original. The internet went straight up.

Thousands of people posted the painting beside the performance, and a large share of them were typing Annie Lee's name for the first time in their lives.

Annie Lee had been dead eight years by then.

Two years after that night, a writer put up a short piece about the painting and ended it with three plain questions. Where is the original, is her work in any museum's permanent collection, and did she ever get a retrospective.

Nobody answered.

The one thing the record should have been able to hold is the day she died.

Annie Lee died on a Monday, November 24, 2014, in Henderson, Nevada, seventy-nine years old. The funeral home record says so, and so did every notice published that week.

Several widely circulated biographies still give the date as November 14, The HistoryMakers among them, and the error has copied itself outward from there. It is ten days off and it has sat there more than a decade on pages written to honor her.

The pages cannot get the day right for a woman whose entire body of work is about knowing exactly how somebody feels without being told.

So put the name and the day back on the picture. Annie Lee, born March 3, 1935, in Gadsden, Alabama, died Monday, November 24, 2014.

Next time that blue bedroom comes across your feed with no credit under it, type her name in the comments and fix the date while you are down there. Then tell whoever posted it what the picture cost her, because the woman on that bed is not a mood and she is not a meme.

She is a girl just out of Wendell Phillips who turned down four free years and never explained why. She is a fifty-one-year-old who had already proved she was an artist and could not afford to be one full-time until she buried her son.

She got the rest of her life at fifty-one, with a bad back and paint fumes in her lungs. She used it so completely that a girl not yet born when she left the railroad would one day sit on a network stage in a slip and slippers so the whole country could look at her Monday.

Image Credit: Annie Lee portrait / The Black Art Depot; “Blue Monday” (1985) © Annie Lee, courtesy of Abe Ilo.
