text:
No WHITES Allowed: MI5 Tells Applicants | Steve Watson, Modernity

Britain’s domestic intelligence service is once again telling White university students they are not wanted.

For the 2027 Summer Intelligence Internship, MI5 has confined applications to people from a “black, Asian, mixed heritage or ethnic minority background” who also come from a “socially or economically disadvantaged background.”

White British candidates — including those from the poorest homes — cannot even submit an application. The agency calls this a response to “underrepresentation.” Critics call it what it is: racial exclusion.

The rule sits on the official careers page in plain English. Final and penultimate-year students may apply for the 2026/27 academic year only if they tick the approved ethnic boxes.

MI5’s own wording is blunt: “We’re confining the applications for this internship to those within this demographic due to a current underrepresentation in our workforce.”

This is not a fringe outreach day. The placement is billed as a serious introduction to national security work. Interns are promised “unique insight” into operations and “meaningful contributions to real projects,” not a seat on the sidelines.

The MI5 stint is expected to run from Monday 28 June to Friday 20 August 2027 across sites in Central and West London. Successful candidates are paid £4,849, with accommodation covered if they cannot reasonably commute. GCHQ is running a parallel scheme on similar racial terms.

Applicants must be British nationals, normally resident in the UK for seven of the last ten years, and able to survive the usual vetting. They still face a competitive sift. The racial gate comes first.

The listed groups include Asian or Asian British, Black or Black British, mixed-heritage combinations, “other ethnic minority,” and a narrow “White other” category covering Romany Gypsy, Scottish Travellers or Irish Travellers. White British is not on the list.

The socio-economic test is equally specific. At age 14 the main household earner must have been in technical, craft, routine or semi-routine work, or unemployed and seeking work — or the applicant must have been eligible for free school meals. A White student who meets that poverty test is still barred. An ethnic-minority student who meets it is invited in.

What happened to getting a job on merit?

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp called it “flagrant racism from MI5 & GCHQ.” He wrote: “White applicants for summer 2027 internships – including from disadvantaged backgrounds – can’t apply. The scheme must be scrapped. Applications should be merit-based and colour blind. Working class white boys are among the most disadvantaged – yet are ignored.”

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage put the charge in institutional terms. “Yet again, taxpayer funds are being used to fuel a culture of anti-white prejudice across the public sector. It’s racism. It’s wrong. Only Reform will bring meritocracy back to our institutions. We’ll ensure that nobody is discriminated against based on the colour of their skin.”

This is not a one-off. The Summer Intelligence Internship has been running across MI5, MI6 and GCHQ since 2023. Every cycle has produced the same argument and the same official shrug. The agencies say the programme exists to “increase diversity within our organisations.” Ministers treat the Equality Act 2010 as cover.

In July, Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty asked the Cabinet Office why White candidates were ineligible. Dan Jarvis, minister of state for security, answered that the internships are “designed to provide insight” to people “from demographics and backgrounds under-represented within UKIC,” and that “this is a lawful measure (as set out in the Equality Act 2010) used to encourage people from under-represented demographics to consider national security careers.”

He added that anyone later applying for a proper job would face “fair and open competition, with selection based on merit.”

That last line is doing a lot of work. The paid summer placement is itself the pipeline: mentors, projects, a foot in the door, a chance to apply afterwards with the agency already knowing your name. Excluding the country’s majority from that pipeline is not a neutral “encouragement.” It is a racial filter on the first rung.

The Equality and Human Rights Commission’s own guidance on positive action is narrower than the agencies pretend. Employers may encourage under-represented groups to apply. The Commission says that if they do so, “the advert should clearly state the employer is seeking applications from everyone but wishes to encourage applications from people with a particular protected characteristic.”

Confining applications — telling one racial group not to bother — is a different creature. “Positive action” was sold as outreach. This is a closed shop.

Claire Coutinho has been making that point for years. When the scheme returned in 2025 she said: “Deciding who can do a summer internship scheme based on the colour of their skin is bad enough. To bar patriotic white Britons who want to serve their country, but allow white Irish people, is utterly mad.”

She added: “To make matters worse, the security services will also shut you out if you’re a child of a nurse, a cabbie or your dad ran a corner shop, while the child of an £80,000-a-year train driver is eligible. This is state-sponsored discrimination. We should just choose the best people for the job.”

In the Commons she asked the obvious question: “What message does it send to our young people when they are told there are some job opportunities they cannot apply to solely based on the colour of their skin?” Equality, she said, “must mean equality of opportunity, not putting some people in society on a pedestal above others.”

Jacob Rees-Mogg charged that “MI5 is institutionally, publicly racist against white people.” He noted that the policy “discriminates against 92.6% of my constituents in Somerset.”

Toby Young of the Free Speech Union gave the thought experiment that every defender of these schemes refuses to answer. “Imagine if it was the other way around, and the intelligence services were saying only white people can apply for our summer internships. There would be absolute uproar.”

There would. If the advert had said “no Blacks,” the building would be surrounded by cameras before lunch. Because it says, in effect, no ordinary White British applicants, the official class calls it inclusion.

The security services are not improvising. They are copying a model that British policing has already normalised.

West Yorkshire Police, one of the country’s largest forces, has run a two-track application system for police constable roles. Black, Asian and minority ethnic candidates have been able to apply year-round. White applicants from British, Irish and Eastern European backgrounds have been told to wait for specific recruitment windows.

An internal whistleblower told The Telegraph that minority applicants were treated as “gold” and White candidates as “bronze.” The whistleblower said: “The process restricts progression opportunities for White British candidates, while individuals from other backgrounds are swiftly advanced through recruitment stages.”

Ethnic minority candidates, the same source said, were regularly “shortlisted, sifted, assessed and invited to an interview before White candidates can even apply.”

The force’s own website made the hierarchy official: “We are currently accepting applications for the two police constable entry programmes (uniform and detective) from people from our under-represented groups… If you are not from one of these groups, please keep checking this page for future recruitment opportunities.”

West Yorkshire dressed this up as Positive Action under the Equality Act. A spokesman said ethnic minority representation among officers was around 9 percent against a local minority population of 23 percent, and that early applications were merely “held on file” until a window opened for everyone.

The whistleblower’s account was that the holding file was a fiction: the favoured group moved while everyone else waited outside.

At Thames Valley Police the ideology went further than the application form. Officers were put through mandatory “equity training” on “white privilege,” “micro-aggressions” and the difference between being “non-racist versus anti-racist.”

This followed an employment tribunal finding that the force had positively discriminated against White officers by appointing an Asian detective inspector without considering White candidates who had served 19 to 26 years.

Former assistant chief constable Kerrin Wilson, who led an independent review, recorded “strong feelings of frustration.” “As white males they felt disadvantaged and … they had the perception that unfairness was allowed for minority groups but not for majority populations,” she wrote.

The review warned that the training “can often be seen as demonising white people and therefore building barriers to the learning.” White officers’ response was “very strong, at times bordering on aggressive.” They felt “they have no support within the force.” There was “a tangible feeling of being overlooked.”

Minority staff were not grateful either. Some said they would not seek promotion because “even if they did succeed in securing promotions their efforts would not be accepted by some as genuine.” Some described the force as a “hostile environment.”

Former government adviser and ex-officer Rory Geoghegan said officers “deserve far better from their leaders than to be crudely categorised by skin colour and subjected to reductive, divisive ideologies.” The review, he argued, failed to confront “the unthinking acceptance of critical race theory – a deeply political framework that has no place in an impartial police service.”

That is the culture now being imported into the agencies that handle terrorism, hostile states and domestic subversion. First the police. Then the Bar. Now MI5.

The legal profession built the same wall and called it progress. A paid internship linked to the Bar Council and the 10,000 Interns Foundation offered London Living Wage work experience while restricting eligibility to specified ethnic minority backgrounds. White applicants were excluded outright.

Sophie Corcoran applied anyway. She is now suing. In her own account of the case she wrote that the central issue is simple: “should organisations operating in Britain be permitted to deny opportunities to people purely because they are white? I believe the answer must be no.”

She draws the distinction the agencies keep blurring. Encouraging under-represented people to apply is one thing. “Outright excluding others from opportunities on racial grounds” is another.

She further noted, “The Equality Act was never intended to create a hierarchy of races where some groups are protected from discrimination while others are expected to tolerate it, but this is exactly what these schemes do.”

The schemes also flatten every other kind of hardship into a racial cartoon. “A wealthy privately educated applicant from an affluent background can qualify for some race-based schemes, while a working-class white applicant from a struggling town cannot.”

White working-class pupils have been the lowest-attaining major ethnic group at GCSE level for more than a decade. Corcoran herself grew up with epilepsy, hearing difficulties and dyslexia and attended a failing state school. None of that counted. “Just because someone is black does not automatically mean he or she is disadvantaged. Equally, just because someone is white does not mean he or she is not disadvantaged.”

Rupert Lowe called the Bar scheme “vile, anti-white racism.” Corcoran urged “everyone knows that if the races were reversed, such policies would never be considered acceptable. Equality cannot operate on a double standard.”

The intelligence agencies’ own socio-economic test makes the double standard sharper. They admit class exists. They even try to measure it by the parent’s job when the applicant was 14, and by free school meals. Then they add a racial veto.

National Audit Office internships have run on a similar exclusionary logic, limiting places by sex, “black heritage” or lower socio-economic status and shutting middle-class White men out of a taxpayer-funded programme.

Transport for London has run placements reserved for BAME, disabled or disadvantaged candidates. The pattern is no longer a few over-eager HR departments. It is how the British public sector now allocates opportunity.

Intelligence work is not a diversity seminar. It is judgment, languages, technical skill, nerve and loyalty. The agencies’ public line is that “a diverse organisation is vital to ensure diverse insights.” That sentence has become a mantra. It is used to justify shutting the country’s largest ethnic group out of the training ground.

A security service that filters the next generation by race is telling the public something larger than a recruitment statistic. It is saying the majority population is surplus to the pipeline. It is saying competence will be balanced against a demographic target. It is saying the Equality Act now functions as a permission slip for the one form of racial discrimination institutions are eager to practise.

The other way around remains the test. A Home Office page that read “no Blacks” would end careers by nightfall. A police force that labelled White applicants “gold” and everyone else “bronze” would be in special measures. A Bar scheme that barred African and Asian students would be treated as a national scandal. MI5’s page does the reverse, year after year, with ministerial cover and a press office that talks about underrepresentation.

Merit is not a right-wing hobby. It is the only honest way to staff an intelligence service. Britain’s problem is not that too many White working-class students are bursting through the gates of Thames House. It is that the people who run the gates have decided some citizens are the wrong colour to knock.

text:
Saint Margaret Ward, born around 1550 in Congleton, Cheshire, England, emerged as a beacon of unwavering Catholic faith during one of the darkest periods of religious persecution in English history. Little is known of her early life beyond her origins in a respectable family and her role as a gentlewoman serving as a companion or housekeeper to a prominent Catholic lady named Whitall (or Whittle) in London. This era, under Queen Elizabeth I's reign, saw the brutal enforcement of Protestantism, where practicing Catholicism was outlawed, and aiding priests—considered traitors—could result in imprisonment, torture, and execution. It was in this hostile environment that Ward's courage came to the forefront, leading to her martyrdom and eventual canonization as one of the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales.  

Ward's story is inextricably linked to her bold act of defiance in 1588. Upon learning of the imprisonment of Father William (or Richard) Watson, a Catholic priest held in the notorious Bridewell Prison for his ministry and later writings, Ward felt compelled to assist him. Watson, who had authored theological works like the "Quodlibets," faced inevitable death if he remained captive. Befriending the jailer's wife, Ward gained permission to visit the priest regularly, bringing him food in a basket. Over time, the guards grew lax in their searches, allowing her to smuggle in a length of rope hidden among the provisions. She also arranged for a boat on the River Thames to ferry Watson to safety after his descent from the prison walls.  

The escape unfolded dramatically in the early hours. Watson tied the rope and climbed out, but it proved too short; he jumped the remaining distance, breaking his arm and leg in the fall. In a twist of heroism, Ward enlisted the help of John Roche, a young Irish boatman and her servant, who swapped clothes with the injured priest to facilitate his getaway. The boatmen rowed Watson to a hiding place, but the abandoned rope dangling from the wall—and Roche's suspicious attire—quickly led authorities back to Ward. Both she and Roche were arrested, while Watson evaded capture for a time (though he was later executed for unrelated treasonous activities).  

Imprisoned and interrogated, Ward endured horrific torture designed to break her spirit and extract information about Watson's whereabouts. For eight days, she was flogged, chained, and suspended by her wrists from the ceiling, her toes barely touching the ground—a method so agonizing it left her crippled and paralyzed. Jesuit priest and fellow martyr Robert Southwell later wrote of how these sufferings only fortified her resolve, describing her as strengthened for her "last struggle." At her trial in Newgate, Ward openly admitted her role in the escape, proudly declaring she had saved "an innocent lamb from the hands of those bloody wolves." Offered freedom in exchange for betraying Watson and attending a Protestant service, she refused, stating she had committed no offense against the Queen and could not violate her conscience by abandoning her faith.  

On August 30, 1588—exactly 437 years before the current date—Margaret Ward, then likely in her late 30s, was led to the gallows at Tyburn (near modern-day Marble Arch) and hanged, drawn, and quartered alongside Roche and other Catholic martyrs, including priests Richard Leigh and Edward Shelley. Fearing her words would inspire the crowd, authorities silenced her on the scaffold, but her joyful endurance spoke volumes. Ward's steadfastness exemplified the quiet heroism of lay Catholics who risked everything to preserve their beliefs amid the Reformation's aftermath.  

Pope Pius XI beatified Ward in 1929, recognizing her as a martyr for the faith, and Pope Paul VI canonized her on October 25, 1970, as part of the Forty Martyrs. Known as the "Pearl of Tyburn" for her purity and valor, she is venerated as a patron of those enduring torture and as a model for laypeople defending their convictions.

After 31 years in education, Ohio principal Rob Burnside lost the job he loved after refusing to abandon a homeless student who desperately needed help.

Landerius “DeDe” Hayes was sleeping in a cold car, struggling to eat and without a safe, stable home. When his mother moved outside the school district, he was ordered to withdraw from Lakota East High School.

Burnside refused to simply let him disappear.

He and his wife, Angel, prayed: “God, if this is your will for this young man to be in our home, make it clear.” They then welcomed DeDe into their family, while Burnside allowed him to continue attending school.

The district placed Burnside on leave and eventually gave him a choice: step down or face the termination process.

DeDe even offered to leave the Burnsides’ home to save his principal’s career.

Burnside’s answer was immediate: “No. You’re gonna stay with me.”

“DeDe, you’re part of this family. We’re not gonna turn our back on you.”

Burnside resigned. He and his wife later became DeDe’s legal guardians, and DeDe went on to graduate high school in May 2026.

Burnside says he has no regrets.

“What value can we put on the life of a young person?”

text:
Mannnnnyyyy mannnyyy thoughts on #ToxicTheMovie  (possible spoilers)
_________

What might happen when a woman filmmaker gets the opportunity to make a film about violence and sex? What might happen when she gets access to all the familiar toys of the male-star vehicle: the punch dialogues, the star, the swagger, the slow-motion sequences, the sex, the violence... What might she bring to this cinema that we don't generally get? As it turns out... quite a lot.

First, she refuses to see the protagonist, Raya, as a 'hero'. Quite the opposite, in fact. The film isn't interested in hero-villain demarcations, right-wrong judgments. Raya (Yash) himself says as much at one point. When you are in pain, morality stops seeming important. The film, in fact, has a lot to say about the nature of pain, about what happens when you live with it for so long that you begin to fall in love with it, when it begins to feel more like home than any real home ever could, ever did. There’s a fantastic song in the Tamil version, ‘Vittupogaadha Yen Vali’, that speaks of this dichotomy. "Vittupoiduma en vali, poi vidaadhe en vali..."

You've got Yash, chiselled and ready to kick ass, and usually, that’s reason enough for cinema like this to offer relentless setpieces... There are many here too, and plenty of brutality whose imagination I rather enjoyed (throat dragged on glass shards, ashtray ploughing into someone's mouth, a pressed knee on a sword that decapitates someone...). But Toxic does something interesting with this all-too-familiar image of the arrogant alpha male, besotted with violence and sex. It implores us to see that he is broken... and that is why he's like this.

And that makes sense because what healthy mind would seek power so desperately, relish violence as much, bury itself in dispassionate lust? In another film, these qualities would build Raya’s masculinity. Here, they reveal his damage instead. And so, no, the violence isn’t heroism here. It’s evidence. Severed limbs and broken bones seem to symbolise how Raya feels about himself. He inflicts the kind of pain he feels, and it's still not enough.

The film is similarly interested in lust, and somewhere, through Nadia's (Kiara Advani) words, there's a lovely idea about the difference between using lust to mark territory and actually treasuring the woman you’re with. This film isn't interested in validating lust with the approval of social structures; it's just interested in respectful intimacy. And that's why for perhaps the first time, Nadia is able to create rivulets of emotion in Raya's impossibly barren soul.

One of my favourite moments in Toxic is when Geetu uses Yash's powerful eyes to create two completely different gazes at Nadia. The first time Raya sees her, she is at the circus, at work, performing. His roving eye finds her, the contours of her body specifically, and there’s something predatory, thirsty, about the gaze. He looks at this strange woman like a man eager to possess her, desperate to bed her. Much later, after interactions with her that have softened him, Nadia is at a carnival, laughing and having fun on a ride, and someone is wondering whether Raya is even capable of love. We cut to him watching her. It’s the same pair of eyes, but everything has changed. The gaze is softer. Warmer. There’s something almost protective about it. And you know immediately that this is love. I felt like Toxic is most persuasive in these moments when nobody is explaining these ideas to us.

But it's mostly not the case. I took a while to warm up to Toxic for this reason. Early on, someone asks what language Raya intends to speak with some pirates. We then see him killing them. We understand the answer immediately. But Raya still needs to tell us: “My mother tongue is violence.” And even that isn't sufficient, as he further adds that it is a universal language. Some other contrived dialogue is trying to play around with “root” and “route”. Too often, the conversations in this film are exploited as opportunities to deliver punchlines.

Even that profound, crucial moment just before Ganga (Nayanthara) gets shot suffers from this. Nadia asks, “Kadhala? Arippaa?” and Ganga gives her the straight, simple answer. I found myself wishing Geetu had found a more beautiful, more cinematic way for Ganga to respond than simply having her make it so bluntly clear. There is some repetition in imagery too. Early on, violence is juxtaposed with sex: the breaking of a gate intercut with a potential orgasm inside a car. It's a cool idea, but then, minutes later, people are being murdered while Raya is, you guessed it, making out. This thematic repetition is perhaps an issue with a film that runs for more than three hours.

But there's no taking away from how painstakingly put together this film is. It looks rich and lush with detail, and images and moments rarely feel casually thrown in to fill runtime. There is a wonderful underwater portion, including the gorgeous image of a submerged ferris wheel. Something about a ferris wheel has always seemed tragically haunting to me. Perhaps it’s because of its association with nostalgia: carnivals, childhood, families, happy times. For that reason, an empty ferris wheel is a profoundly sad image, I think. And so, to see one underwater here feels heartbreaking. A monument to happiness has been drowned.

Given how masochistic Raya is, I found it hard not to feel layers of self-harm within this film. Raya isn't just unafraid of death; it feels like he's craving its release. A woman threatens him with a bomb wrapped around her body, and instead of terror, he's almost turned on. Elsewhere, he says, “Death is less cruel than life.” To my surprise, I realised that hurt parts of me were nodding along. While on the subject of self-harm, somewhere in the beginning, Nadia slits her wrist, and I wondered if her apathy towards possible death made her seem particularly attractive to Raya. Later, Raya, I think, says something along the lines of, "Vidudhala kudu, indha kevalamaana vaazhkai lerndhu…” It's all deliberately dark and psychologically distressing. I did feel seen.

All of this subtext is why Raya’s fearlessness seems more disturbing than heroic. It's risky for cinema with blockbuster aspirations, but I loved that Geetu has still done her thing. She seems to ask, is it courage when someone who cannot wait to be ended walks towards their death? The film, which had won me back, began losing me in those indulgent portions involving Raya’s son and his kills. 

Somewhere, I'd begun thinking of Fight Club, considering this too is about an emotionally unstable man who is addicted to fighting, incapable of healthy love... I thought of it more when Raya's son gets punched and seems to relish it (reminded me of Brad Pitt in that basement scene). And then, the clincher: that final twist in Toxic. And yet, here, I thought it didn't quite land with as much force. In fact, it almost seems to undermine what's happened until then.

I think it's strange, and perhaps fitting that Toxic should lose much of its vigour when it loses its women. By the time Rukmini Vasanth’s character recedes, long after Ganga has left us, long after Nadia has perished, the film seems to be dragging along lifelessly, quite like its protagonist. Raya is asked to look around him and confront the fact that he can’t seem to keep a single woman in his life. It’s sad, these cycles of violence. Broken people creating other broken people, who go on to break more people. Raya asks at one point: if peace could do the trick, why have people been fighting wars forever?

Toxic does offer quite a few answers. Pain becomes familiar. Familiarity becomes comfort. Violence becomes language. You hurt somebody because somebody hurt you, and eventually you don’t even remember what another language might sound like. Perhaps you fall in love, perhaps you entertain fantasies about peace and family, but pain, after all, is home, and sooner or later, you find your way back. That idea really moved me.

And this is ultimately why I see value in this film, even if its excess sometimes feels exhausting. Geetu Mohandas gets to play with the machinery of the testosterone-driven star vehicle, and rather than reject its pleasures, she participates in them, but then turns the machinery around to inspect the man, instead of celebrating him. While everyone is cheering, she asks: What happened to a man for him to be like this? 

It's the kind of question rarely asked. I'm glad Geetu did. I hope more women do.

Joe Haden says Cleveland asked him to take a pay cut. He said no, then turned down bigger offers from two other teams and signed a $27,000,000 deal with Pittsburgh.

"They tried to get me to take a pay cut. I'm like, 'No, I'm not. You're tripping. You need to keep me exactly where I'm at.'"

"Then they said, 'No, whatever, let him go.'"

"I got offered by the Dolphins. Dolphins offered me more. And the New Orleans Saints."

"But the only thing I was thinking, I wanted to go play with Coach Tomlin. I want to play with Big Ben. I want to go where they were scoring points. I know over there, them boys gonna be scoring. I don't gotta guard AB. I'm with you. Le'Veon, I'm with you. Coach Tomlin. I loved everything they had going on."

"So I'm like, let me just bring my talents over here."

text:
Harvesting Grace, A Forty-Day Devotional by C.S. McDonald is a warm, reflective Christian devotional that invites readers to slow down and reconnect with God’s grace, especially during the beauty of autumn.

Inspired by the author’s love of the fall season—with its vibrant colors, crisp air, and sense of harvest and gratitude—the book offers forty days of gentle spiritual nourishment. Each entry includes a daily Bible verse, a peaceful and thought-provoking observation, and soft reflections designed to refresh faith and cultivate joy. McDonald encourages readers to pause amid life’s busyness, sit quietly or take a walk, and intentionally harvest God’s steadfast love and boundless grace. It serves as a humble, encouraging guide that can be used in autumn or anytime throughout the year. Readers looking for a calming, faith-centered companion will find it uplifting and accessible.

Buy links
- Amazon (Kindle ebook): https://t.co/342NAD5CIZ

- Also check Amazon and other retailers for paperback or additional formats as they become available.

About the author
C.S. McDonald taught dance and choreographed shows for twenty-six years before turning to writing. She lives with her husband Bill and their dogs on a Thoroughbred farm near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. She is the author of the popular clean Fiona Quinn Mysteries (cozy mysteries featuring a kindergarten teacher turned sleuth) and the Owl’s Nest Mysteries, as well as children’s books inspired by farm life. In recent years she has added devotionals, including *Harvesting Grace*, as part of her spiritual writing. She is a wife, mom, grandma, dog lover, and self-described helpless chocoholic.

SK hynix CEO says the memory shortage runs through the end of 2030

SK hynix CEO Kwak Noh-jung spoke to reporters on Aug 27 (local time) after the groundbreaking ceremony for the company's advanced packaging plant for AI memory in West Lafayette, Indiana. The event was held at Purdue University's Holloway Gymnasium. Asked how long the memory shortage would last, he said:

Nobody knows exactly how long the crunch lasts, but he sees no clear signs of a downturn, and SK hynix expects the shortage to run through the end of 2030.
He thinks the next downturn will look nothing like the cycles the industry has been through over the past several decades.

His reasoning: AI memory is moving away from being 100% standardized product toward partially and fully customized product. Because supply is being built to specific customer demand, an oversupply glut should be far less severe than in past cycles.

Even if a downturn does arrive, he expects demand to soften moderately or simply flatten to planned levels rather than fall off a cliff. Hence, no concern about the post-2030 picture.

On further US fab investment: he said SK hynix is open to building anywhere that offers enough resources. Power, capital, and subsidies.

text:
You do not defend a hospital's clinical standards by describing its gift shop. Brooke Harrington's Economist essay defends sociology by describing her intro syllabus. Here is everything it leaves out, including the one case she was standing too close to see.

The piece from @EBHarrington is a bait and switch. Teaching students about mortgages is useful. Investigating offshore corruption is useful. Neither establishes that sociology is free of ideological bias or that her own research is the neutral toolkit she presents it as.

The criticism came from inside her discipline and she knows it. The Vanderbilt and Washington University report found political criteria displacing scholarly ones in every field examined, and its sociology chapter was written by the sociologist Ashley Rubin. The newspaper coverage quoted Christian Smith, Musa al-Gharbi, Ilana Redstone and Jukka Savolainen. Savolainen said some topics cannot be studied honestly. Redstone said the field treats causation as settled. Harrington converts all of them into "Concerned Pundits on the higher-education beat." That is not an answer. It is a refusal to name who is talking.

Her comparison with economics collapses on inspection. The difference is not what individual researchers find interesting. It is what the professional bodies do. The American Economic Association does not put ceasefire resolutions to its membership. The American Sociological Association does. South Africa in 1987. Iraq in 2003. An amicus brief on same-sex marriage in 2013. Ukraine in 2022. A Gaza ceasefire resolution in 2024 carried by roughly 59 percent of members voting, defending the right to speak against "Zionist occupation." A vote that September to divest from weapons manufacturers. In 2026 the leadership refused to ballot a member resolution on academic boycott despite it clearing the signature threshold, and members demonstrated outside the annual meeting. Harrington picked economics as her comparison. The comparison answers her question and she left it out.

She also left out her own field's account of itself. Michael Burawoy's 2004 presidential address made sociology the mirror and conscience of society in moral and political debate. Mary Romero's 2019 address defended its social justice tradition against detached objectivity. Christian Smith's 'The Sacred Project of American Sociology' (2014) argued the field is organized around a moral project. Nobody outside sociology invented this question.

Lyell Asher supplies the contrast. In 'Why Colleges Are Becoming Cults' he describes a freshman ethics course where students took up abortion, capital punishment and affirmative action, were required to argue against their own convictions, and finished the term without knowing what the professor believed. He changed his mind on capital punishment over three nights of reading. When he described that course to his own students, they were astonished it had ever existed. Set that against Sociology 1, where we know exactly what the professor believes because she told a national magazine, and where the contested questions arrive pre-answered. Asher's point about the word justice lands here: once it names a set of conclusions rather than a dispute, teaching becomes training, which is why people can now be trained in it by a resident adviser. In 'How Ed Schools Became a Menace' he describes research language that assigns guilt before the ambiguity is resolved, so that alternative explanations become defensiveness and objections become evidence against the objector. He traces the habit to its carrier, the education schools that trained the administrative class, whose programs Arthur Levine's four-year study found ranged from inadequate to appalling. Harrington's defense is personal from beginning to end: her syllabus, her research, her consultations with Treasury. The charge is institutional.

The wage gap example fails at the root. "The same work" is a claim about a residual, and a residual measures what has not been measured. Blau and Kahn (2017) show how the gap moves as human capital, occupation and industry enter the model, and they say outright that the leftover can overstate or understate discrimination depending on which controls you use. No observational study controls for everything. The unexplained portion is by construction omitted variables, measurement error and unobserved choice. Nobody has ever isolated a discrimination term by exhausting the alternatives, because observational data does not permit exhausting the alternatives. The convention is to name the leftover and then assign it a cause without saying so. That is an inference from ignorance and it is the load-bearing move in the entire field.

Watch which way the leftover travels as measurement improves. The CONSAD report for the Department of Labor in 2009 found observable factors accounted for 65 to 76 percent of a raw hourly gap of 20.4 percent, leaving 4.8 to 7.1 percent, and CONSAD refused to call any of that remainder discrimination because its own occupational categories were too coarse to support the claim. That makes 4.8 percent a ceiling on what is unexplained, not a floor on bias. Goldin (2014) found what survives concentrates in occupations that pay disproportionately for long and inflexible hours. Bolotnyy and Emanuel (2022) took Boston transit operators working under a union contract that fixes wages, shifts and promotion by seniority for men and women identically, with no managerial discretion anywhere in the system, and the eleven percent gap was entirely accounted for by overtime uptake and unpaid time off. Cook, Diamond, Hall, List and Oyer (2021) took over a million Uber drivers paid by an algorithm that does not negotiate, does not promote and does not know the driver's sex, and the seven percent gap was entirely attributed to platform experience, where drivers chose to work, and driving speed. Two settings built so that employer discrimination is mechanically impossible, and in both the gap survives and is fully explained by something else.

The standard reply is that experimental work catches what regressions miss. It does not. Goldin and Rouse (2000), the orchestra study everyone cites, concedes in its own abstract that the standard errors are large and that one effect runs persistently the other way, then rests on "the weight of the evidence" after acknowledging the results were not statistically significant. Andrew Gelman went through the paper and could not reconstruct the famous fifty percent figure at all. Meanwhile Williams and Ceci (2015) in PNAS ran 873 tenure-track faculty at 371 institutions across all fifty states, evaluating identically rated scholarship counterbalanced by gender, and found a two to one preference for female applicants among faculty of both sexes in every field, with male economists the sole exception showing no preference. The best-powered hiring experiment in the literature runs backwards. Every one of these papers came out of economics, and none of them appear in her lesson.

The lifespan example fails against a case that has been sitting in the literature for thirty years. Harrington says worse medical care, partly. Hispanic Americans have substantially lower household income, less education and far higher uninsurance rates than non-Hispanic whites, and have posted life expectancy roughly three years longer for most of four decades. Both explanations that would let an access model survive this have been tested and both failed. Abraído-Lanza and colleagues (1999) examined the groups for whom return migration is impossible, Cubans barred from returning, Puerto Ricans whose deaths in Puerto Rico appear in US statistics, and US-born Latinos subject to neither selection effect, and every one showed lower mortality than non-Latino whites. Turra and Elo (2008), using Social Security beneficiary records, confirmed salmon bias exists and found it far too small to be the primary explanation. What is left is behavior, diet, smoking and family structure, which is to say the category of explanation the discipline treats as blaming the victim.

This is the pattern and it runs far past two examples. The alternative causes were not tested and rejected. They were treated as disqualifying. Moynihan, a sociologist, argued in 1965 that black family structure was central to black economic outcomes and was called a racist for it. That is not a conservative gloss. Sara McLanahan and Christopher Jencks, writing in 2015, state that for the next two decades few scholars would investigate father absence for fear of being demonized if the findings came out wrong. McLanahan ran the study herself expecting to find no meaningful difference, found the opposite, and published it with Sandefur in 'Growing Up with a Single Parent' (1994). William Julius Wilson reopened the question in 'The Truly Disadvantaged' (1987) and later called Moynihan's report prophetic. Chetty, Hendren, Jones and Porter (2020) found that the fraction of fathers present in low-income black households in a neighborhood is among the strongest predictors of black boys' income, employment and suspension rates, and that it predicts those outcomes whether or not the individual boy's own father is present. Their findings on white racial bias were reported everywhere. The father presence result went in the appendix and stayed there.

The defenses offered against this both fail. Philip Cohen answers the chilling effect by listing family-structure papers published between 1971 and 1985. A chilling effect shifts what gets published and how it is framed; it does not empty the shelf. Cohen's test asks whether the set of publications is empty, which means it returns "no chilling effect" under every possible state of the world, including the one where a chilling effect exists. That is the unfalsifiable design this entire argument is about, run in reverse, by a sociologist defending his own discipline against the charge that it suppressed something, and arguing with a bibliography against the direct testimony of McLanahan, Jencks and Wilson, none of whom are conservatives and all of whom were there. The second defense is that Chetty found individual parental marital status explains little once parental income is held constant. Family structure is a principal determinant of parental income. Conditioning on parental income and then asking what marital status adds is controlling for the mediator, which drives the coefficient toward zero by construction. Chetty's team also cautioned that the neighborhood correlations are not necessarily causal, and they attached the identical caution to the racial bias correlations in the same paper, which were reported as findings on every front page in the country. The caveat is real. Its asymmetric application is the story.

So the field is not incapable of finding these things. It keeps finding them by accident, through researchers who set out to refute them, and then carries forward only the half that fits. That is what Savolainen meant, and it is the direct answer to the Swiss Army knife. A tool that cannot be pointed at certain explanations without professional cost is not general purpose. It has a grain.

Enron is the wrong exhibit. Fastow's roughly three thousand vehicles were domestic special purpose entities exploiting an accounting rule about outside equity, disclosed badly in SEC filings, not assets parked behind offshore secrecy. Fastow and Skilling went to prison. Arthur Andersen was destroyed. Sarbanes-Oxley was signed within nine months. If the thesis is that concealment delivers impunity, Enron is the case where detection, prosecution and legislative correction all worked, onshore, under American law, fast.

The Corporate Transparency Act example understates her own case, which is its own kind of tell. The statute was authored across twelve years by Carolyn Maloney, introduced in the Senate in 2017 by Rubio and Wyden, and enacted inside the fiscal 2021 defense authorization over a veto aimed at the broader bill. What happened since is worse than she says. FinCEN's March 2025 interim rule exempted domestic entities, and on August 11, 2026, thirteen days before her column ran, FinCEN issued a final rule permanently exempting domestic companies and U.S. persons and announced it would delete the beneficial ownership data already collected from U.S. persons. Roughly twenty thousand foreign entities remain covered. She reached for "halted its enforcement" when the fact in front of her was permanent repeal and deletion of the records. And Rubio's vote for ownership transparency does not validate sociology's methods. Agreement on one policy is not a warrant for a discipline.

Langbert (2018) found roughly 44 registered Democrats per Republican among sociology faculty at elite liberal arts colleges. Langbert and Stevens (2021) found about 27 to one at flagship universities against roughly three to one in economics, and also found that more registered Republican faculty gave money to Democratic candidates than to Republican ones. Registration understates the imbalance rather than inflating it. The Moynihan sequence is what a field at those ratios looks like when a disfavored explanation shows up. Asher's account of the hiring expansion between 1965 and 1975, when students and faculty both doubled and the country staffed a second system of higher education in a single political moment, explains how the imbalance formed and why ordinary hiring reproduces it without anyone conspiring. That is a sociological explanation of sociology, and the field will not look at it.

Her own research runs on the same design. 'Capital without Borders' (2016) rests on a two-year training program, a wealth management credential and 65 interviews across 18 countries. The access was remarkable. The sample was not representative of a trade then numbering twenty thousand practitioners, and nothing in the design tries to make it so. Interviews can show how advisers understand their work. They cannot establish how often practices occur, what they produce, or what would happen without them, and they cannot underwrite a worldwide claim about the erosion of democracy. Her sympathetic reviewers said this. Inglis noted her outrage is never in doubt and that it is not clear she ever challenged an informant's base assumptions, because there is no back and forth anywhere in the book. Godechot noted the fieldwork ran through the post-crisis years when practitioners had every incentive to conceal wrongdoing in a short interview, and that the book consequently says almost nothing about illegal evasion. Emmenegger noted the same structures serve charitable giving and family business protection.

Now ask what would have counted against the thesis. Expressed guilt confirms wrongdoing. Absent guilt confirms impunity. An appeal to legality confirms capture. Every answer confirms. 'Turning Vice into Virtue' (Harrington 2019) puts it beyond argument: tax avoidance enters the paper already classified as professional misconduct, and practitioners' appeals to public service and expert neutrality are then modeled as recategorization of that misconduct. The conclusion is in the operationalization. There may be a sound ethical case against the practices. It has to be made somewhere other than in the coding scheme. You cannot prove the sin by parsing the apology.

The quantitative work makes the same move with numbers. Chang, Harrington and Rockmore (2025) in PLOS One use the prevalence of nominees and bearer instruments across a wealth manager's clientele as a proxy for an individual client's association with concealment, which is not observing that client use them. The diversification measure aggregates by country while the interpretation describes individuals spreading assets, and a country's investors can collectively touch twenty jurisdictions with each using one. The blacklist measure counts entities, and counts are not shares of wealth, since nine empty shells hold less than one funded company. The paper states that the individuals named in the Offshore Leaks database are extremely wealthy and have something to hide. That is a verdict on a population delivered as a data description. ICIJ's own documentation says the public database holds only part of the leaked material, that completeness varies by provider, that some entries are ordinary local businesses, and that inclusion establishes nothing improper.

'Offshore' (2024) reads the whole system through colonialism, an analogy her reviewers praise for making an unwieldy subject familiar. Familiarity is not accuracy, and a frame selected for resonance finds itself confirmed. The same applies to professions as institutions whose privileges depend on public service, which she offers readers as ordinary Sociology 1 content while using it in her own work as the instrument of conviction.

She does not only publish what flatters her. Guerra and Harrington (2025) ran two online experiments in Italy, Denmark and the United Kingdom and found no effect of recipients' immigration status on natives' redistribution behavior, a null the authors say challenges prevailing theories of welfare chauvinism. Small samples and a simulated task, but they published it against interest. That is why this is an argument about classification and interpretive overreach and not an accusation of bad faith.

Arday is where the consistency breaks. He resigned on August 5. Her column ran on August 24. She gives it an accusation of plagiarism and a complaint about British commentators. Jack Grove submitted roughly 97 pages to Cambridge and Liverpool John Moores. David Sanders of Purdue reviewed the text comparisons and described extensive plagiarism. Carter-Ruck correspondence kept the Times Higher Education investigation unpublished for ten months. A police complaint led an officer to warn Grove off further contact. Cambridge opened an inquiry into new information about his qualifications and honorary appointments. Asher's diagnosis covers both halves: people shut down discussion either because they cannot defend a position or because they are too certain to bother. The Carter-Ruck letter was the first. Her subordinate clause is the second. Harrington's subject is how the powerful use law and secrecy to escape scrutiny, and the one case in front of her where a lawyer's letter suppressed a journalist for ten months is the case she declined to see.

Pick a lane is a false choice and she knows which lane she is in. Researchers can advise Treasury, write for the public and push policy while keeping findings distinct from commitments. She wrote the political books, coined broligarchy, took it to The Atlantic and to Jon Stewart. All of that is hers to do. The bafflement is the one move not available to her.

Afflicting the comfortable is not a method. An accusation is worth what its evidence is worth, not what its target is worth. The test of a general-purpose analytical toolkit is whether a student can reject the favored explanation for defensible reasons without the disagreement being read as a moral defect. Moynihan failed that test in 1965 and it took thirty years for the field to catch up to him. Mortgages and Weber do not show that anything has changed. Neither does calling an interpretation a framework. Write the critical book and defend its judgments. But stop telling the public that sociology supplies analytical tools rather than predetermined answers while your own signature work is a method built to reach one.

text:
I honestly do not like the way Westernization is gradually taking over our African culture, especially here in Nigeria.

My friend and I visited one of our choir members after church service, and she served us beta jollof rice with assorted proteins.

Her 4 yr old daughter walked up to me, pointed into my plate, and said she wanted my meat. I pretended not to notice. She then made an attempt to pick it up, so I gave her one dangerous, wicked stare and whispered, “Leave here. Go & collect your meat from mummy.”

The girl shrugged her shoulders and tried to fake a frown. I continued eating, and before I could blink, this child had dipped her hand into my food, grabbed the biggest piece of meat, and turned to run.

The way I grabbed her shirt from behind, you would think I had caught a phone snatcher at Oshodi. I slapped her hand and collected my meat immediately. She fell to the ground and started throwing a tantrum.

Her mother rushed out and asked, “Mirabel, what is the matter?” The girl pointed directly at my meat.

Her mother then said, “Oh, you want Aunty’s meat, and Aunty doesn’t want to give you?” She nodded.

Her mother turned to me and said, “Mirabel loves eating meat served to visitors, even after she has eaten her own. She won’t stop crying until she gets some.”

Abasi ooo! Nso ke emi?! 🤦‍♀️

Is this what you people call gentle parenting?

Growing up, I dared not be seen around visitors once food was served. Even if a visitor willingly offered me his food or drink, the look my mother would give me was enough to make me know I was dead if I accepted it.

Parents now seem afraid to discipline or correct their children because they believe it will damage their mental health. Quite sad, African upbringing is gone! 😭

text:
“The Nazi crusade against 'Judeo-Bolshevism'

 finalist for the 75th National Jewish Book Award in nonfiction

A major new history that transforms our understanding of World War II—tracing the conflict and its most infamous crime, the #Holocaust, to #Germany’s implacable hostility toward Soviet #Russia

In the West, World War II is commonly understood as the Allies’ struggle against #Nazism . Often elided, if not simply forgotten, is the Soviet Union’s crucial role in that fight. With this book, acclaimed historian Jochen Hellbeck rectifies this omission by relocating the ideological core of the conflict. It was not the Western powers but Communist Russia that Nazi Germany viewed as an existential threat—in fact, “World Enemy No. 1.” Jewish revolutionaries, the Nazis believed, had seized power in 1917 and were preparing the Soviet state to destroy Germany and the world. And so, on June 22, 1941, a German army of three million attacked the Soviet Union to exterminate “Judeo-Bolshevism,” Hitler’s cardinal obsession. While Europe’s Jews were expelled, exiled, and persecuted by the Nazis, Soviet Jews were immediately slated for elimination. The Soviet lands thus became ground zero for systematic extermination, which was only later extended to all Jews, igniting the Holocaust.

Hellbeck plumbs newly declassified archives and previously undiscovered sources—testimonies, diaries, and dispatches from soldiers and civilians, Soviet and German—to offer a unique history that takes account of both sides. He reconstructs the years leading up to the war when “Europe against Bolshevism” was the Nazis’ most fervid rallying cry, and documents their annihilatory ambitions on the battlegrounds in the East. Widely disseminated accounts of German atrocities mobilized millions of Soviet citizens to join a people’s war against the hated invaders. Hellbeck tracks the desire for revenge that drove the Red Army on its path of reconquest, an advance that further inflamed the belief in a murderous “Bolshevik Jew,” stirring the Germans to fight to the bitter end. Recounted here in vivid detail are the events at Babi Yar, the Battle of Stalingrad, the liberation of the concentration camps, and the arrival of the Red Army in the Nazi capital. Finally, Hellbeck reckons with the West’s persistent disregard of the Soviet Union’s incalculable contribution to winning the war—and its sacrifice of twenty-six million citizens—as anti-communism and the Cold War turned erstwhile allies into mortal enemies.

Hellbeck’s eye-opening work is an astonishing new reading of both the Second World War and how its history has been told.

About the Author
Jochen Hellbeck is Distinguished Professor of History at Rutgers University, specializing in modem Russia, the Soviet Union, and the history of World War II. The recipient of fellowships from the New York Public Library Cullman Center, the Guggenheim Foundation, and the American Academy in Berlin, among others, he is the acclaimed author of Stalingrad: The City That Defeated the Third Reich, Revolution on My Mind: Writing a Diary under Stalin, and the online project Facing Stalingrad. He lives in Brooklyn.

Praise for World Enemy No. 1: Nazi Germany, Soviet Russia, and the Fate of the Jews
“World Ene­my No. 1 is a brac­ing, nec­es­sary cor­rec­tive, chal­leng­ing us to look beyond Allied tri­umphs in the lat­ter stages of the war and the Cold War pol­i­tics that down­played the Sovi­et Union’s role in defeat­ing Nazism. It shifts our gaze instead to the bat­tle grounds and killing fields of the west­ern Sovi­et Union, where the events of eighty years ago con­tin­ue to men­ace Europe." —Jewish Book Council

“A history of World War II closely focused on its true epicenter: the Russian front . . . An essential contribution to the modern literature of what Russians still call the Great Patriotic War.” —Kirkus (starred review)

text:
Part 4 

Lincoln’s election in November 1860 gave the castles a nearer war than Mexico. The 1861 exposé claims the Knights helped shatter the Democratic Party that spring castle speeches against Douglas, pressure at Charleston and Baltimore, the split that handed the presidency to a Republican with under forty percent of the popular vote. 

That causal claim is the pamphlet talking. 

The split itself is not in dispute. 

Neither is what followed in Texas: 

Knights accused of intimidating Unionists at the polls, packing secession meetings, furnishing riders when Ben McCulloch moved on the federal arsenal at San Antonio in February 1861 a column of several hundred men, a substantial fraction identified with six K.G.C. castles, that forced the surrender of United States authority in the city and the seizure of federal property worth more than a million dollars.

After secession, individual Knights melted into Confederate cavalry and state troops. Elkanah Greer would ride as a Confederate colonel. The secret army, such as it was, was absorbed by the open one.

Sam Houston old hero of San Jacinto, still dreaming of a Mexican protectorate even as he fought disunion was reportedly approached and even initiated. He wanted Mexico. He would not take the anti-Union road. He refused the scheme and was broken by the secession machine anyway.

By April 12, 1861, Confederate batteries were firing on Fort Sumter.

And somewhere in that same year, in Indianapolis, a printer named C. O. Perrine copyrighted an 88-page illustrated exposé that claimed to lay the hidden wiring on the table: the growth of the order, the change of ritual, the “inner temple,” the regalia (helmet, silver spear, crescent, mail, sword), the claim that the K.G.C. had helped dissolve the Democracy in 1860, the assertion that secession had been organized long before the first ordinance was passed. The last pages print ritual itself.

The dedication is a political weapon. It is offered to “the uncompromising friends of American freedom,” to those who “prefer death to the destruction of the Union.”

This is not a neutral chronicle.
It is a wartime detonation.

Then comes the turn the title page cannot contain because the title page is still talking about Mexico, and by the winter of 1860–61 some of the men inside the order were no longer talking only about Mexico.

A phrase survives from that season that should stop a reader cold:

“The Knights of the Golden Circle may find its Mexico in the District of Columbia.”

That is the most shocking sentence in the entire file. It means the filibuster had rotated inward. 

The first field of operations was no longer a foreign republic across the Rio Grande. It was the capital of the United States, before Abraham Lincoln could take the oath.

An army informer who penetrated a Texas K.G.C. council of war in November 1860 reported a design “to seize Washington and inaugurate Breckinridge.” 

Directives, the same stream of testimony said, had gone out to seize navy yards and forts while Knights were still sitting as cabinet officers and senators.

Name the offices the exposés and the informer named.

John B. Floyd, Buchanan’s Secretary of War.
Howell Cobb, Secretary of the Treasury.
Vice President John C. Breckinridge, now the Southern Democratic candidate.

Those membership claims are not notarized lodge rolls. Treat them as charged allegations. Then look at what Floyd actually did with the keys he held.

text:
She was born into money.
He was a broke young Army lieutenant.

Her father warned her plainly: marry him, and the family fortune would not support you.

Mamie Doud married Dwight Eisenhower anyway.

Denver, Colorado. July 1, 1916.

Mamie was nineteen.

She had grown up surrounded by comfort, servants, security, and every expectation of an easy life.

Dwight had none of it.

He was twenty-five, a West Point graduate living on a modest Army salary.

Ambition.

Discipline.

Very little else.

They had met only months earlier at Fort Sam Houston in San Antonio.

Mamie noticed him across the lawn at a gathering.

Dwight noticed her too.

He pursued her patiently.

When she went out with other young men, he sometimes waited on her parents' porch until she returned.

Eventually, she chose him.

On Valentine’s Day 1916, Dwight gave her what he could afford: a miniature version of his West Point class ring.

It wasn't expensive.

Mamie treasured it anyway.

When Dwight asked her father for permission, Mr. Doud made his concerns clear.

Army life meant small quarters.

Constant moves.

Limited money.

No servants.

No promise that Dwight's career would become anything remarkable.

Mamie understood.

She said yes.

Their wedding was simple.

After a short honeymoon, she left her comfortable world behind and moved into military housing with her new husband.

The difference was immediate.

Smaller rooms.

Tighter budgets.

Everything carefully managed.

Mamie adapted.

Wherever the Army sent them, she built a home.

She cooked.

Stretched money.

Packed everything.

Made new friends.

Started over.

They jokingly called their home “Club Eisenhower.”

It became known for warmth, not wealth.

Then came heartbreak.

Their first son, Doud Dwight, called Icky, died of scarlet fever at three.

The loss never truly left them.

Years passed.

Posts changed.

Wars came.

Dwight rose from an obscure officer to Supreme Allied Commander during World War II.

Mamie stayed beside him through separations, uncertainty, and military life.

Then, in 1953, thirty-seven years after their modest wedding, Dwight D. Eisenhower became President of the United States.

Mamie became First Lady.

The young woman once warned that marriage meant giving up luxury now lived in the White House.

But that was never the real story.

It was the tiny quarters.

The moving boxes.

The tight budgets.

The grief.

The waiting.

She hadn't chosen him because she knew he'd become president.

She chose him when all he offered was character, ambition, and partnership.

Mamie could have chosen security.

Instead, she chose him.

And together, they built the one thing money could never guarantee:

A beautiful life.

She was born into money.

He was a broke young Army lieutenant.

Her father warned her plainly: marry him, and the family fortune will not support you.

Mamie Doud married Dwight Eisenhower anyway.

Denver, Colorado. July 1, 1916.

Mamie was nineteen years old, raised in comfort as the daughter of a successful businessman. She had grown up with servants, security, and every expectation of an easy life.

Dwight had none of that.

He was twenty-five, a West Point graduate living on a modest Army salary, with ambition, discipline, and little else.

They had met only months earlier at Fort Sam Houston in San Antonio.

Mamie noticed him across the lawn at a gathering.

Dwight noticed her too.

He pursued her with determined patience. When she went out with other young men, he sometimes waited on her parents’ porch until she returned.

Eventually, she chose him.

On Valentine’s Day 1916, Dwight gave her what he could afford: a miniature version of his West Point class ring.

It was not expensive.

Mamie treasured it anyway.

When Dwight asked her father for permission to marry her, Mr. Doud did not hide his concerns.

Army life would mean small quarters.

Constant moves.

Limited money.

No servants.

No guarantee that Dwight’s career would ever become anything remarkable.

And Mamie would have to live on whatever her husband earned.

She understood.

She said yes.

Their wedding was simple.

No enormous ballroom.

No extravagant display.

After a short honeymoon, Mamie left the world she had known and moved into military housing with her new husband.

The difference was immediate.

The rooms were smaller.

The budget mattered.

Everything had to be managed carefully.

Mamie adapted.

Wherever the Army sent them, she created a home.

She learned to cook, stretch money, pack entire households, make new friends quickly, and start over again every time orders changed.

They jokingly called their home “Club Eisenhower.”

It became known for warmth rather than wealth.

Then came heartbreak.

Their first son, Doud Dwight, called Icky, died of scarlet fever at three years old.

The loss never completely left them.

They raised their second son, John, while Dwight’s military career slowly advanced.

Years passed.

Posts changed.

Wars came.

Dwight rose from an obscure officer to Supreme Allied Commander during World War II.

Mamie remained beside him through the long separations, uncertainty, and demands of military life.

Then, in 1953, thirty-seven years after their modest wedding, Dwight D. Eisenhower became President of the United States.

Mamie became First Lady.

The young woman once warned that marrying an Army lieutenant meant giving up luxury now lived in the White House.

But the story was never really about arriving there.

It was about everything before it.

The tiny quarters.

The moving boxes.

The tight budgets.

The grief.

The waiting.

The faith that the person beside you matters more than the comforts surrounding you.

Mamie and Dwight remained married for fifty-two years, until his death in 1969.

She never treated her youthful decision as a sacrifice.

She had chosen the life she wanted.

Not because she knew Dwight would someday become president.

She could not have known.

She chose him when all he offered was character, ambition, and partnership.

Mamie Eisenhower could have chosen security.

Instead, she chose belief.

And together, they built something no inheritance could ever guarantee.

A life.

Carthaginians (Phoenician religion): Worshippers offered young children to deities like Baal Hammon at sacred sites called tophets during times of severe crisis or war.

Canaanites: Communities offered children to local deities such as Moloch and Baal in exchange for fertility, health, and protection.

Pre-Islamic Arabs: Certain tribal groups performed votive sacrifices or buried infants alive as offerings to regional idols to secure divine favor.

Pre-Columbian Mesoamerica (Aztecs and Incas): Major ceremonies and crisis rituals included offering children to rain and weather gods to ensure agricultural success and stability.

text:
These College Football Offenses Will Look DIFFERENT In 2026

The market’s pricing in a new playbook across several key programs. Miami sits at 60% to win the ACC, paying 1.7x—trading like a team with offensive upside baked in. The signal isn’t just optimism; it’s a structural shift. Quarterback Darien Mensah brings a 10-yard average depth of target, three yards deeper than Carson Beck’s seven-yard mark last season. That’s not small—it’s the difference between dinking and dunking versus stretching defenses vertically. Shannon Dawson’s air-raid roots finally have a triggerman who can push the ball downfield. The Hurricanes’ receiver room—Malachi Tony, Cooper Bark, Josh Moore—gets to run free in three- and four-wide sets. Mark Fletcher still pounds the rock, but the identity isn’t lost. In 2024, Miami averaged 1.5 more yards per carry than last year. Aggression feeds the run game too. 

Signals: Mensah’s 10-yard aDOT vs Beck’s 7-yard aDOT; Miami’s 60% ACC win probability; 1.7x payout; receiver depth.

Between the lines: The market isn’t rewarding last year’s game-control approach; it’s betting on Shannon Dawson’s true nature—air raid spacing and tempo. Miami’s playoff run in 2025 came despite conservative playcalling. Now they’re leaning into what got them there in 2024: chaos and points.

Risk: If Mensah can’t process faster or the offensive line struggles in pass pro, the vertical shots die. Then Miami’s back to grinding low-scoring wins, and the ACC market looks overpriced.

Flip: Mensah throws for 300+ yards in Week 1; Miami scores 30+ in two of their first three games; the ACC win probability ticks above 65%.

Trade: Buy Miami ACC win at 60%. Add on any dip below 55% after a slow start. Exit if they lose two conference games by mid-October.

Watch: Mensah’s completion percentage on throws 15+ yards; Miami’s yards per carry early season; opponent third-down conversion rates against the Hurricanes.

Texas is another offense getting a facelift. Steve Sarkisian’s playcalling never dulled—he just lacked tools. Now he’s got a reloaded offensive line, two running backs (Elite Brown, Hollywood Smothers), and Arch Manning entering year two. The key is Manning’s steadiness. In Quinn Ewers’ big wins at Alabama and Michigan, he managed chaos and executed creative schemes. Manning’s mobility adds another layer—defenses must respect his legs, opening up misdirection with two-back sets. Texas moves from predictable to multidimensional. 

Signals: Manning’s year-two progression; revamped O-line; two-back sets; Cam Coleman and Ryan Wingo as WR1 threats.

Between the lines: The market’s undervaluing Sarkisian’s ability to scheme with better pieces. Last year’s struggles were personnel-limited, not philosophical. With Manning’s experience and weapons, Texas returns to 2023–24 form—explosive and unpredictable.

Risk: If the offensive line doesn’t gel early, Manning takes too many hits, and the creativity stalls. Then Texas looks like last year’s stop-start offense.

Flip: Texas hangs 35+ on a quality opponent in the first month; Manning averages 5+ yards per carry through three games.

Trade: Buy Texas to make the playoff at current odds (~45%). Add if they beat Alabama or Michigan early.

Watch: Sacks allowed per game; Manning’s rushing stats; explosive plays (20+ yards) per game.

Nebraska’s makeover is about extending plays. Dylan Raiola’s pressure-to-sack rate was 36%—40% with no blitz. Anthony Colandria cuts that to ~20%. That’s the difference between second-and-15 and second-and-5. Colandria’s legs turn broken pockets into opportunities. Dana Holgorsen should lean on designed QB runs on third down. The receiving corps—Quasi Gilmer, Jakard Barney, Nazir Hunter—benefits from extra time. Nebraska won’t suddenly dominate, but they’ll be competitive in chaos moments against tough defenses like Ohio State and Iowa.

Signals: Colandria’s 20% pressure-to-sack rate vs Raiola’s 36%; Nebraska’s 86% red-zone efficiency last year.

Between the lines: The market’s sleeping on Nebraska’s upside. Colandria’s mobility masks line issues and unlocks playmakers. This isn’t about wins; it’s about staying in games.

Risk: If the offensive line gets overwhelmed anyway, Colandria’s mobility won’t save them. Then Nebraska’s back to last year’s despair.

Flip: Colandria rushes for 50+ yards in a game; Nebraska converts 40%+ of third downs against a top defense.

Trade: Buy Nebraska to win over 6.5 games at ~45%. Exit if they go 0–2 in conference play.

Watch: Sack rate; third-down conversion rate; Colandria’s rushing yards.

South Carolina’s shift is about better life choices—simplifying for LaNorris Sellers. Kendall Briles brings tempo and spacing, attacking defenses before they’re set. Last year, Sellers had no time or space. Now, quick RPOs and formations isolate mismatches. Nicholas Harbor’s speed becomes a weapon in space. The key is whether the line can hold up just enough for the run game to matter. If defenses respect the run, Sellers gets easy throws.

Signals: Briles’ tempo/spacing principles; 80% RPO target; Harbor’s breakout potential.

Between the lines: The market’s overlooking how much scheme can elevate Sellers. It’s not a processing issue—it’s support. Quick reads and spacing fix that.

Risk: If the line can’t block and the run game is ignored, Briles’ scheme collapses. Defenses sit on Harbor and Sellers.

Flip: South Carolina scores 30+ in the first half twice; Sellers’ completion percentage jumps 10% under Briles.

Trade: Buy South Carolina to win over 7.5 games at ~50%. Exit if they lose three straight early.

Watch: Tempo plays per game; RPO success rate; Harbor’s targets and yards.

Auburn’s makeover is explosiveness. Hugh Freeze brings the wide receiver system; Byron Brown brings legs and chemistry from USF. Last year, Auburn ran for 4.5 yards per carry but passed for only 6.2 yards per attempt—two yards less than their run average. Now, Brown’s mobility and deep threat receivers (Ke’Shawn Singleton, Chaz Nimrod) open up the field. The run game sets up play action, and Auburn becomes dangerous downfield.

Signals: Brown’s 1,000 rushing yards, 3,000 passing yards at USF; Singleton’s 17.5 yards per catch; Auburn’s 4.5 YPC last year.

Between the lines: The market’s dismissing Auburn’s upside. Brown’s mobility and receiving corps turn a one-dimensional offense into a threat.

Risk: If Brown can’t handle SEC speed or the line fails, Auburn’s back to last year’s dink-and-dunk.

Flip: Brown throws for 300+ and rushes for 50+ in a game; Auburn averages 7+ yards per pass attempt early.

Trade: Buy Auburn to win over 5.5 games at ~55%. Exit if they go 0–3 in SEC play.

Watch: Brown’s rushing stats; yards per pass attempt; explosive pass plays.

Chaos scenarios loom. LSU-Ole Miss week four sets up a letdown spot. Both play tough games the next week—LSU vs Texas A&M, Ole Miss at Florida. Two losses by October would shake up playoff talks. Nebraska beating Indiana flips Big Ten perceptions—Matt Rhule gets a signature win, and the conference race opens. Clemson’s stretch at Cal and Miami could sink them early if they slip, raising questions about Dabo Swinney’s future. SMU beating Notre Dame would expose the downside of independence for the Irish.

Signals: Week four scheduling pressure; Nebraska’s potential upset path; Clemson’s road-heavy stretch.

Between the lines: The market’s not pricing in early-season chaos. One loss can snowball for teams with tough follow-ups.

Risk: If favorites dominate early, chaos scenarios fade, and markets stay efficient.

Flip: LSU or Ole Miss lose week four; Nebraska beats Indiana; Clemson drops two of three.

Trade: Buy chaos insurance—short favorites in vulnerable spots (e.g., LSU week five, Ole Miss week five).

Watch: Week four outcomes; Nebraska vs Indiana result; Clemson’s road performance.

Bottom line: Miami, Texas, and Auburn offer the best offensive upside with market inefficiencies. Buy Miami ACC at 60%, Texas playoff at 45%, and Auburn over 5.5 wins at 55%. Watch early-season performance for entry points—aggression from Miami, explosiveness from Texas, mobility from Brown. Chaos plays are hedges, not core positions.

SAVANNAH STATE MAKES POWERFUL STATEMENT ABOUT DIRECTION OF PROGRAM IN INSPIRATIONAL 87–0 LOSS

The Thomas Howard era at Savannah State University officially began Saturday night, and the Tigers’ new head coach wasted absolutely no time establishing the direction of the program.

Savannah State was humiliated 87–0.

While traditional football “analysts” remain obsessed with antiquated statistics like “points,” “yards” and “preventing the other team from scoring 87 points,” Howard’s debut offered something considerably more important:

Opportunity.

South Carolina State led 52–0 at halftime and eventually accumulated 627 yards while setting a school scoring record.

But Savannah State never stopped participating.

For four quarters, young Tigers across America watched Savannah State demonstrate that you don’t need touchdowns, red-zone appearances or even a competitive plan to finish a college football game.

That is representation.

Coach Howard inherited a program searching for an identity. After one game, there can be little doubt he has clarified one.

Generations of Savannah children can now look toward the decrepit Ted Wright Stadium and think:

“Someday, that could be my black ass getting beat 87–0.”

SC State Bulldogs may have won the football game.

But Savannah State inspired a generation.

Some victories simply can’t only be measured with numbers.

Fortunately.

text:
THIS 124-KM ROUTE THROUGH CENTRAL ITALY CONNECTS MEDIEVAL TOWNS, GLACIAL LAKES AND SOME OF THE WILDEST LANDSCAPES IN THE APENNINES. 🇮🇹

Between Umbria and Marche, the Monti Sibillini offer a side of Italy that feels completely different from the usual tourist routes.

A journey can begin in Norcia, which is gradually coming back to life almost ten years after the devastating 2016 earthquake. The Civic Theatre, built in 1876, has reopened, following the restoration of the Town Hall and the return of the Basilica of St Benedict to the city.

From there, the landscape changes completely.

The Piani di Castelluccio lead into the mountains, while Lago di Pilato sits in a glacial basin at 1,941 metres above sea level, surrounded by some of the highest peaks of the Sibillini. Its waters are also the only known habitat of Chirocephalus marchesonii, a tiny red crustacean discovered there in 1954.

For hikers, there is the Grande Anello dei Sibillini: a 124-km trail divided into nine stages, crossing forests, mountain ridges, ancient pilgrimage routes, medieval ruins and valleys where golden eagles can still be spotted overhead.

Prefer cycling? The Chienti Valley offers routes through woodland, Romanesque churches and around Lake Polverina, overlooked by the 14th-century Castello di Beldiletto.

Back in Umbria, Vallo di Nera appears almost frozen in the Middle Ages, with double defensive walls, towers, ancient gates and churches filled with medieval frescoes.

And the journey can finish in Spoleto, crossing the spectacular 230-metre Ponte delle Torri before exploring the Rocca Albornoziana and the historic centre.

It’s a journey through two regions, centuries of history and one of Italy’s most underrated mountain landscapes - with medieval villages, local food and nature connecting every stop.

📍 Monti Sibillini - Umbria & Marche, Italy

Source: Il Sole 24 Ore.
