Imagined briefing — Richard P. Feynman, still talking, in a room that has too many flags.

Mr. President. Director. The rest of you who actually have to decide something.

I’m not here to sell you flying saucers and I’m not here to tell you the Harvard fellow is a crook. I’m here to stop you from confusing a calculation with an engine. That confusion is how smart organizations get surprised.

1. What Loeb and Fell actually did

They took Miguel Alcubierre’s 1994 warp-bubble geometry — a prescribed dent in spacetime that slides along — and they asked a clean question:

If that dent, the size of an airplane, goes through Earth’s air at a tenth of light speed or more, what does the air do?

They did not ask how you make the dent. They froze the metric, turned off the stuff that would have to generate it, and ran the air as a fluid in that frozen background. Shock-capturing hydrodynamics. Respectable numerical work.

The air does what air always does when you hit it at relativistic speed. In the bubble’s rest frame the incoming air slams into a stagnation zone. Kinetic energy becomes heat. At half light-speed you’re talking a hundred-odd MeV per nucleon. The gas lights up. Terawatts. Sometimes a lot more. You would not miss it. You would not call it a quiet Tic-Tac.

So their conclusion, inside those assumptions, is not mysterious:

A naive Alcubierre bubble, aircraft-sized, relativistic, zero mass as seen from infinity, punching through atmosphere, is a fireball. Reported UAP are not fireballs. Therefore that particular cartoon is not those UAP.

That is a good constraint on a cartoon. It is not a theory of propulsion. It is not “we now understand UAP.” If your briefers walk out of the room thinking the energy problem of warp drive has been handled, they walked out with the invoice still face-down on the table.

The invoice in Einstein’s 1915 theory is ugly. Curvature is sourced by

\[ G_{\mu\nu}=\frac{8\pi G}{c^{4}}T_{\mu\nu}. \]
\(G/c^{4}\) is about \(10^{-43}\) in everyday units. To bend spacetime by an order-one amount on a ten-meter ship, you need stress-energy that would make a treasurer faint — and, in the original Alcubierre setup, the wrong sign of energy as well. Loeb and Fell never compute that. They assume the geometry and compute the weather. Useful. Incomplete.
If you brief the Intelligence Community that “physics checked warp drives and they glow,” you have briefed the weather and hidden the engine. That is not fraud. It is a model with the hard term set to zero. Policymakers who cannot tell the difference will fund the wrong next experiment.
2. What Sarfatti is actually saying
Jack is loud. That is not an argument against him, and it is not an argument for him. Listen to the physics claim, not the volume.

Einstein’s gravity, and the usual Einstein–Cartan upgrade from the 1960s, couple mass-energy to curvature with Newton’s little (G). Cartan and then Kibble also let spin source torsion — a twist of spacetime, not just a bend. In the textbook version that torsion is a contact interaction. It is there, and it is negligible unless you live inside a nucleus.

Sarfatti’s bet is three extra moves:
First. Don’t stop at Poincaré. Gauge the whole conformal group. Let torsion and a few extra potentials propagate, like a massive vector field that dies off outside a skin depth instead of reaching the Moon. Then you can have a strong effect in a hull and almost nothing a mile away. That is the only way this story doesn’t already contradict Cavendish, Cassini, and pulsar timing.

Second. The coupling of coherent quantum spin to that torsion is not Newton’s (G). Call it \(G^{*}\). He wants \(G^{*}\) enormous — forty-odd orders — only inside a macroscopically coherent spin state: a pumped metamaterial, a Fröhlich condensate, aligned magnons, something you drive with ordinary electromagnetism. Outside that condensate, apples still fall the old way. Inside it, a thin shell plus kilowatts is supposed to source craft-scale geometry.

Schematically he writes things like

\[ G_{\mu\nu}=k_{1}T_{\mu\nu}+k_{2}S^{2}g_{\mu\nu}, \]

where (S) is the aligned spin density. The second term is the one Loeb never put in the code.
Third. The air problem is a boundary-condition problem, not a “space is magic” problem. Loeb’s fireball assumes the outside air has a huge velocity relative to the wall. Sarfatti says the hull is an active source: you arrange the near-field so neighboring air is locally comoving with the shell. No shear layer of the Alcubierre-through-atmosphere kind. Occupants sit in a local inertial frame — they feel nothing — while the exterior geometry does the accelerating.
That is the whole point of “metric engineering” as opposed to rockets ("That Loeb and his Harvard Pooh Bah’s totally miss" - Jack's snide quip)

If that matching can be done, Loeb’s terawatts go away by construction. If it cannot be done, Jack is wrong in the place that matters for airplanes over water.

He also offers a cheap observational discriminator: a gravitational Doppler that runs opposite the ordinary motion Doppler — redshift on the contracting nose as the thing comes at you, blueshift on the expanding tail as it runs. You would look for that in good spectra, not in vibes.
3. Who is right about what

Do not let anyone tell you this is “Loeb versus the cranks” or “Sarfatti versus the cover-up.”
Question

Honest answer

Would a frozen Alcubierre bubble at (0.1c) torch the sky?

Yes. Loeb–Fell.

Does that kill every spacetime-propulsion story?No. It kills that ansatz.

Does 1915 GR give you a quiet Mach-20 Tic-Tac on kilowatts?

Not that anyone has shown. Is Poincaré-gauge torsion a real idea?Yes. Textbook. Weak in the standard version. Is \(G^{*}\sim 10^{43}G\) in a condensate a theorem?
No. It is the conjecture.Has anyone run the air code with Sarfatti’s junction conditions? No. That is the missing paper.Has anyone measured a laboratory \(G^{*}\) jump? No. That is the missing experiment.
A paper that attacks a nearby idea — “just let Newton’s coupling \(\kappa\) vary through the metamaterial” — shows that a non-dynamical \(\kappa(x)\) fights conservation laws, and a dynamical scalar \(\kappa\) is already boxed in by solar-system tests. Jack says that is not his Lagrangian: he is not rescaling (G) for mass; he is adding a spin-torsion channel with short range. Fine. Then write the action, vary it, and show the range and the equivalence-principle leakage. Until that is on paper in a form a hostile theorist can break, \(G^{*}\) is a slogan with a pedigree, not a capability.

4. What this is worth to you as a government

National security does not require you to believe in tourists from Tau Ceti. It requires you not to be stupid about categories.

There are three boxes:

A. Most UAP are junk, birds, balloons, missiles, sensor ghosts. Loeb is good at stuffing objects into this box when the kinematics allow it. Keep doing that. It is cheaper than metaphysics.
B. A few objects, if the Navy numbers survive hostile re-analysis, sit outside chemical rockets and outside Loeb’s fireball. That does not automatically equal Jack’s engine. It equals “we do not have a propulsion model that is both standard and quiet.”
C. If someone — us, them, or a contractor who doesn’t send press releases — can source torsion or curvature in a thin coherent shell at low power, you are looking at propellantless kinematics, trans-medium motion, and a sensor problem, not an aviation problem. That is a first-order strategic issue whether the builders are human or not.

Loeb’s paper is progress on box A and a veto on one toy model in box B. It does not inspect box C. If the Intelligence Community treats the fireball paper as closure on box C, you have done the adversary’s classification work for them: you declared the interesting coupling “not physics” because it was not in the simulation.
Sarfatti’s program is the opposite failure mode if you swallow it whole: a mechanism that would explain the observables, attached to a coupling nobody has measured and a hull–air calculation nobody has finished. Believing the briefing slides is how you waste a decade. Ignoring the coupling hypothesis is how you miss a materials problem that might be sitting in a lab.

5. What I would make you do on Monday
Not a new office with a seal. Three ugly, cheap, falsifiable jobs.

One. Re-reduce the best kinematic cases — Nimitz and anything with dual phenomenology, radar plus IR plus eyewitness — as if a hostile graduate student were trying to make them ordinary. Publish the residuals. If the residuals die, Jack’s engine has less to explain. If they don’t, you know which events deserve geometry, not folklore.

Two. Commission the calculation Loeb did not do: GR hydro, or better a Poincaré-gauge hydro, on a thin active shellwhose near-field is required to match air velocity at the outer surface. Same code family. Different boundary condition. Either a shock still forms or it doesn’t. That is a number, not a worldview.

Three. Look for \(G^{*}\) where Jack says it lives — not in falling apples, in coherent spin ensembles. YIG, pumped magnons, layered metasurfaces, anything with macroscopic phase stiffness. Torsion-balance and clock and interferometer residuals on the sample, not on the building. If \(G^{*}\) is 40 orders of magnitude and confined to a micron skin, you still ought to see something local if the idea is even 10 orders true. Null results bound the story. Positive results change the budget.

Optical: if you ever get a clean spectrum of a close, fast object, look for the wrong-way Doppler. That costs cameras, not theology.

Last thing

The first principle is that you must not fool yourself — and you are the easiest person to fool.

Loeb fooled a certain kind of audience by answering a real question so cleanly that people forgot it was the wrong question for an engine.

Sarfatti fools a certain kind of audience by naming the missing term so vividly that people forget it has not been measured.

Your job is not to pick a team. Your job is to keep the missing term on the list until an experiment kills it or funds it. Anything else is theater.

If the thing is only weather balloons, you will have wasted a little money on interferometers. If the thing is a materials coupling we don’t teach at Caltech yet, you cannot afford to have learned that from someone else’s after-action report.

That’s the briefing. I’ll take questions, and I will not be polite if the question is “but which narrative do we put on the slide.”

Imagined briefing — Richard P. Feynman, still talking, in a room that has too many flags.

Mr. President. Director. The rest of you who actually have to decide something.

I’m not here to sell you flying saucers and I’m not here to tell you the Harvard fellow is a crook. I’m here to stop you from confusing a calculation with an engine. That confusion is how smart organizations get surprised.

1. What Loeb and Fell actually did

They took Miguel Alcubierre’s 1994 warp-bubble geometry — a prescribed dent in spacetime that slides along — and they asked a clean question:

If that dent, the size of an airplane, goes through Earth’s air at a tenth of light speed or more, what does the air do?

They did not ask how you make the dent. They froze the metric, turned off the stuff that would have to generate it, and ran the air as a fluid in that frozen background. Shock-capturing hydrodynamics. Respectable numerical work.

The air does what air always does when you hit it at relativistic speed. In the bubble’s rest frame the incoming air slams into a stagnation zone. Kinetic energy becomes heat. At half light-speed you’re talking a hundred-odd MeV per nucleon. The gas lights up. Terawatts. Sometimes a lot more. You would not miss it. You would not call it a quiet Tic-Tac.

So their conclusion, inside those assumptions, is not mysterious:

A naive Alcubierre bubble, aircraft-sized, relativistic, zero mass as seen from infinity, punching through atmosphere, is a fireball. Reported UAP are not fireballs. Therefore that particular cartoon is not those UAP.

That is a good constraint on a cartoon. It is not a theory of propulsion. It is not “we now understand UAP.” If your briefers walk out of the room thinking the energy problem of warp drive has been handled, they walked out with the invoice still face-down on the table.

The invoice in Einstein’s 1915 theory is ugly. Curvature is sourced by

\[ G_{\mu\nu}=\frac{8\pi G}{c^{4}}T_{\mu\nu}. \]
\(G/c^{4}\) is about \(10^{-43}\) in everyday units. To bend spacetime by an order-one amount on a ten-meter ship, you need stress-energy that would make a treasurer faint — and, in the original Alcubierre setup, the wrong sign of energy as well. Loeb and Fell never compute that. They assume the geometry and compute the weather. Useful. Incomplete.
If you brief the Intelligence Community that “physics checked warp drives and they glow,” you have briefed the weather and hidden the engine. That is not fraud. It is a model with the hard term set to zero. Policymakers who cannot tell the difference will fund the wrong next experiment.
2. What Sarfatti is actually saying
Jack is loud. That is not an argument against him, and it is not an argument for him. Listen to the physics claim, not the volume.

Einstein’s gravity, and the usual Einstein–Cartan upgrade from the 1960s, couple mass-energy to curvature with Newton’s little (G). Cartan and then Kibble also let spin source torsion — a twist of spacetime, not just a bend. In the textbook version that torsion is a contact interaction. It is there, and it is negligible unless you live inside a nucleus.

Sarfatti’s bet is three extra moves:
First. Don’t stop at Poincaré. Gauge the whole conformal group. Let torsion and a few extra potentials propagate, like a massive vector field that dies off outside a skin depth instead of reaching the Moon. Then you can have a strong effect in a hull and almost nothing a mile away. That is the only way this story doesn’t already contradict Cavendish, Cassini, and pulsar timing.

Second. The coupling of coherent quantum spin to that torsion is not Newton’s (G). Call it \(G^{*}\). He wants \(G^{*}\) enormous — forty-odd orders — only inside a macroscopically coherent spin state: a pumped metamaterial, a Fröhlich condensate, aligned magnons, something you drive with ordinary electromagnetism. Outside that condensate, apples still fall the old way. Inside it, a thin shell plus kilowatts is supposed to source craft-scale geometry.

Schematically he writes things like

\[ G_{\mu\nu}=k_{1}T_{\mu\nu}+k_{2}S^{2}g_{\mu\nu}, \]

where (S) is the aligned spin density. The second term is the one Loeb never put in the code.
Third. The air problem is a boundary-condition problem, not a “space is magic” problem. Loeb’s fireball assumes the outside air has a huge velocity relative to the wall. Sarfatti says the hull is an active source: you arrange the near-field so neighboring air is locally comoving with the shell. No shear layer of the Alcubierre-through-atmosphere kind. Occupants sit in a local inertial frame — they feel nothing — while the exterior geometry does the accelerating.
That is the whole point of “metric engineering” as opposed to rockets ("That Loeb and his Harvard Pooh Bah’s totally miss" - Jack's snide quip)

If that matching can be done, Loeb’s terawatts go away by construction. If it cannot be done, Jack is wrong in the place that matters for airplanes over water.

He also offers a cheap observational discriminator: a gravitational Doppler that runs opposite the ordinary motion Doppler — redshift on the contracting nose as the thing comes at you, blueshift on the expanding tail as it runs. You would look for that in good spectra, not in vibes.
3. Who is right about what

Do not let anyone tell you this is “Loeb versus the cranks” or “Sarfatti versus the cover-up.”
Question

Honest answer

Would a frozen Alcubierre bubble at (0.1c) torch the sky?

Yes. Loeb–Fell.

Does that kill every spacetime-propulsion story?No. It kills that ansatz.

Does 1915 GR give you a quiet Mach-20 Tic-Tac on kilowatts?

Not that anyone has shown. Is Poincaré-gauge torsion a real idea?Yes. Textbook. Weak in the standard version. Is \(G^{*}\sim 10^{43}G\) in a condensate a theorem?
No. It is the conjecture.Has anyone run the air code with Sarfatti’s junction conditions? No. That is the missing paper.Has anyone measured a laboratory \(G^{*}\) jump? No. That is the missing experiment.
A paper that attacks a nearby idea — “just let Newton’s coupling \(\kappa\) vary through the metamaterial” — shows that a non-dynamical \(\kappa(x)\) fights conservation laws, and a dynamical scalar \(\kappa\) is already boxed in by solar-system tests. Jack says that is not his Lagrangian: he is not rescaling (G) for mass; he is adding a spin-torsion channel with short range. Fine. Then write the action, vary it, and show the range and the equivalence-principle leakage. Until that is on paper in a form a hostile theorist can break, \(G^{*}\) is a slogan with a pedigree, not a capability.

4. What this is worth to you as a government

National security does not require you to believe in tourists from Tau Ceti. It requires you not to be stupid about categories.

There are three boxes:

A. Most UAP are junk, birds, balloons, missiles, sensor ghosts. Loeb is good at stuffing objects into this box when the kinematics allow it. Keep doing that. It is cheaper than metaphysics.
B. A few objects, if the Navy numbers survive hostile re-analysis, sit outside chemical rockets and outside Loeb’s fireball. That does not automatically equal Jack’s engine. It equals “we do not have a propulsion model that is both standard and quiet.”
C. If someone — us, them, or a contractor who doesn’t send press releases — can source torsion or curvature in a thin coherent shell at low power, you are looking at propellantless kinematics, trans-medium motion, and a sensor problem, not an aviation problem. That is a first-order strategic issue whether the builders are human or not.

Loeb’s paper is progress on box A and a veto on one toy model in box B. It does not inspect box C. If the Intelligence Community treats the fireball paper as closure on box C, you have done the adversary’s classification work for them: you declared the interesting coupling “not physics” because it was not in the simulation.
Sarfatti’s program is the opposite failure mode if you swallow it whole: a mechanism that would explain the observables, attached to a coupling nobody has measured and a hull–air calculation nobody has finished. Believing the briefing slides is how you waste a decade. Ignoring the coupling hypothesis is how you miss a materials problem that might be sitting in a lab.

5. What I would make you do on Monday
Not a new office with a seal. Three ugly, cheap, falsifiable jobs.

One. Re-reduce the best kinematic cases — Nimitz and anything with dual phenomenology, radar plus IR plus eyewitness — as if a hostile graduate student were trying to make them ordinary. Publish the residuals. If the residuals die, Jack’s engine has less to explain. If they don’t, you know which events deserve geometry, not folklore.

Two. Commission the calculation Loeb did not do: GR hydro, or better a Poincaré-gauge hydro, on a thin active shellwhose near-field is required to match air velocity at the outer surface. Same code family. Different boundary condition. Either a shock still forms or it doesn’t. That is a number, not a worldview.

Three. Look for \(G^{*}\) where Jack says it lives — not in falling apples, in coherent spin ensembles. YIG, pumped magnons, layered metasurfaces, anything with macroscopic phase stiffness. Torsion-balance and clock and interferometer residuals on the sample, not on the building. If \(G^{*}\) is 40 orders of magnitude and confined to a micron skin, you still ought to see something local if the idea is even 10 orders true. Null results bound the story. Positive results change the budget.

Optical: if you ever get a clean spectrum of a close, fast object, look for the wrong-way Doppler. That costs cameras, not theology.

Last thing

The first principle is that you must not fool yourself — and you are the easiest person to fool.

Loeb fooled a certain kind of audience by answering a real question so cleanly that people forgot it was the wrong question for an engine.

Sarfatti fools a certain kind of audience by naming the missing term so vividly that people forget it has not been measured.

Your job is not to pick a team. Your job is to keep the missing term on the list until an experiment kills it or funds it. Anything else is theater.

If the thing is only weather balloons, you will have wasted a little money on interferometers. If the thing is a materials coupling we don’t teach at Caltech yet, you cannot afford to have learned that from someone else’s after-action report.

That’s the briefing. I’ll take questions, and I will not be polite if the question is “but which narrative do we put on the slide.”

So this is how I would have proceeded had I been given the chance. text:
New aerial images prove that nature-based solutions safeguard landscapes against severe drought.
Amid a summer of intense heatwaves that have left much of the globe — especially in the Western U.S. and UK — parched and brown, aerial images of the National Trust's Holnicote Estate in Somerset present a stark and hopeful contrast.
 Restored wetlands and river corridors on the estate have remained lush, vibrant green, and teeming with wildlife. Over the past decade, the estate’s conservation team has implemented 'Stage 0' river restoration—an innovative approach originally developed in Oregon—alongside the reintroduction of beavers to return rivers to their natural courses and create 'natural sponges' in the landscape. 
Rather than allowing water to drain away rapidly, these nature-based solutions hold moisture in the soil, protecting the local ecosystem during dry spells.
This visible success directly challenges claims that rewilding land increases wildfire risk, proving instead that re-wetted landscapes serve as natural firebreaks and resilient wildlife refuges. With the UK having lost over 90% of its wetlands in the last century, projects like Holnicote offer a vital blueprint for climate adaptation. Conservationists emphasize that allowing nature to manage water systems not only preserves biodiversity but also buffers downstream communities against both extreme drought and flash flooding. As climate change drives more volatile weather patterns globally, integrating these natural sponges into land management could prove crucial for agricultural and ecological survival.
source: Laville, S. (2026, August 21). Rewilded land remains green amid drought-stricken English countryside, images show. The Guardian.

-Hashem Al-Ghaili

text:
Med students say conventional medicine would benefit by integrating alternative therapies
In the largest national survey of its kind, researchers from UCLA and the University of California, San Diego, measured medical students' attitudes and beliefs about complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) and found that three-quarters of them felt conventional Western medicine would benefit by integrating more CAM therapies and ideas.
The findings appear Jan. 20 in the online edition of the peer-reviewed journal Evidence-based Complementary and Alternative Medicine (eCAM).
"Complementary and alternative medicine, or CAM, is receiving increased attention in light of the global health crisis and the significant role of traditional medicine in meeting public health needs in developing countries," said study author Ryan Abbott, a researcher at the UCLA Center for East-West Medicine. "Integrating CAM into mainstream health care is now a global phenomenon, with policymakers at the highest levels endorsing the importance of a historically marginalized form of health care."
CAM, which includes therapies such as massage, yoga, herbal medicine and acupuncture, is characterized by a holistic and highly individualized approach to patient care. It's emphasis is on maximizing the body's inherent healing ability; getting patients involved as active participants in their own care; addressing the physical, mental and spiritual attributes of a disease; and preventive care. While interest in these fields has increased dramatically in the United States in recent years, information about such therapies has not yet been widely integrated into medical education.
"Even with the high prevalence of CAM use today, most physicians still know little about nonconventional forms of medicine," said study author Michael S. Goldstein, a senior research scientist at the UCLA Center for Health Policy Research and a professor of public health and sociology. "Investigating medical students' attitudes and knowledge will help us assess whether this may change in the future."
While the current results offer valuable insight into medical students' perceptions of CAM, given the low response rate, researchers plan future studies to further refine the tool and see if the findings can be more generalized.
Researchers found that although medical students endorsed the importance of complementary and alternative medicine, obstacles remain that may prevent future doctors from recommending these treatments in their practices. According to the findings:
77 percent of participants agreed to some extent that patients whose doctors know about complementary and alternative medicine in addition to conventional medicine benefit more than those whose doctors are only familiar with Western medicine.
74 percent of participants agreed to some extent that a system that integrates therapies of conventional medicine and complementary and alternative medicine would be more effective than either type of medicine provided independently.
84 percent of participants agreed to some extent that CAM contains beliefs, ideas and therapies from which conventional medicine could benefit.
49 percent of participants indicated that they have used complementary and alternative treatments; however, few would recommend or use these treatments in their practice until more scientific assessment has occurred.
"Our research suggests that persuading doctors to integrate CAM will require investment in the types of clinical research that form the backbone of Western medicine," Abbott said. "Even now, medical schools have the opportunity to train the next generation of medical practitioners in health care systems outside of conventional medicine. Core values of CAM can help students develop a more holistic and individualized approach to patient care."
The study also found that the further along in school the students were, the more likely they were to believe their learning regarding CAM therapies was sufficient. Still, researchers noted that more than 60 percent of participants favored more education related to this field during their time in medical school. Although more than half of all U.S. medical schools currently offer some type of CAM course, researchers say these courses could be augmented or streamlined into more formal, standardized curricula.
Hui added that the importance of integrative medical education is increasingly being realized outside of UCLA. Forty-four highly esteemed academic medical centers are now part of the Consortium of Academic Health Centers for Integrative Medicine, which was established to advance the principles and practices of integrative health care within academic institutions. It provides a community of support for academic missions and a collective voice for influencing change. The consortium also helps disseminate evidence-based information on CAM, informs health care policy and supports medical education

🚨 B-2 STEALTH BOMBERS CONDUCT LIVE-FIRE STRIKE IN NEVADA.

LAS VEGAS, UNITED STATES - U.S. Air Force B-2 Spirit bombers carried out a rare ground-level live-fire demonstration at the Nevada Test and Training Range, dropping precision-guided munitions as part of an advanced strike exercise. The mission involved aircraft from the 325th Weapons Squadron, which flew in from Whiteman Air Force Base to join controllers and instructors based at Nellis.

The training gave aircrews a chance to practice low-visibility targeting and weapons release under conditions designed to mirror combat operations. Joint terminal attack controllers on the range coordinated the strike, using radio and sensor feeds to direct the bombers toward designated impact zones scattered across the desert.

The B-2, one of the most expensive and complex aircraft ever built, is normally seen only at high altitude during long-range missions. Ground-level footage of the bomber releasing live ordnance is uncommon and offers a close look at how the aircraft performs during tactical scenarios. The exercise also allowed weapons school instructors to evaluate crew performance ahead of larger integrated combat drills scheduled later in the year.

The Nevada range, which spans thousands of square miles, is one of the few places where the Air Force can conduct full-scale live-fire events with heavy bombers.

text:
As the restaurant owner noted, he hasn't spoken to anybody with the defense team, nor has the defense team reached out to him.

And in a case like this one, reciprocal discovery is part of the process, especially if it's going to be used as an alibi. While the timeline for this has not been fully triggered yet under the rules of criminal procedure, the defense pulling a "gotcha" is thing of Hollywood movies, not a trial in real life.

Under Utah Code § 77-14-2 any document proffered as an alibi has to file written notice at least 10 days before trial, including witnesses.

More importantly, under Utah Rule of Criminal Procedure 16(b)(3) the defense has to turn over any exhibits (such as a receipt) no later than 14 days before trial.

But here's the true rub. At the preliminary hearing, Judge Graf made it clear he was open to any evidence the defense could offer up - and as it's timely, a defense team would want to introduce things like this early in order to negate probable cause - because if you can overcome probable cause, the case isn't bound over for trial.

If, for example, there's a claim that the text messages were fabricated because he couldn't have sent them based on his location that night, the receipt would be important.

@aburkhartlaw has covered the legal aspects of this case extensively.

https://t.co/cd0w9XQNhP

Basically, if the receipt ever mattered, it would have been used by his defense team back in July.

Applying Occam's razor here, there's one best explanation.

He was never at the steakhouse.

text:
Jimmy, not everyone who disagrees with you is getting paid. That is an embarrassingly stupid argument that shows how intellectually dishonest you are. 

I am not getting paid. In fact, I would make more money if I promoted illogical conspiracies about Charlie’s murder, just as you've gained millions of views promoting Egyptian planes, Fort Huachuca, and other nonsense.

These points are easily debunked.

1. Prosecutors recovered the weapon. There are photographs of it. His father identified it from those photographs. It was found wrapped in a towel in the woods in the direction he fled. That's corroborated by Robinson's texts describing repeated attempts to retrieve “my rifle,” Google Maps data on his phone, Ring footage of his car near the stash point, and an officer who recorded his partial plate all place him there.

2. Bagley found the screwdriver before his body-camera battery died. Batteries die, and the screwdriver’s admission into evidence does not depend on his body-camera footage. The Utah Bureau of Forensic Services photographed, collected, and packaged it before transferring it to the FBI for testing under a documented chain of custody.

3. Same as point one. Tyler is identified through an enormous amount of corroborating evidence, including Candace’s own material. She released a photograph that shows Robinson near campus hours after the shooting, with his face visible, wearing the same maroon shirt and white-logo Hurley hat that he was wearing on campus that morning.

4. It is true that no camera clearly captures Tyler’s finger pulling the trigger. So what? The footage shows him crawl into a prone shooting position overlooking Charlie, remain there until the gunshot, immediately get up, sprint across the roof, jump down, and flee carrying a long concealed object toward the exact area where Tyler’s rifle was recovered. There are a dozen frames in that video where the long object wrapped ina  towel is apparent. A distant camera failing to provide a close-up of him pulling the trigger does not erase that perfectly synchronized sequence of him in the sniper position and the timing of the gunshot or the mountain of corroborating evidence identifying  Tyler Robinson as the killer.

5. Tyler Robinson was the major DNA contributor on the rifle, towel, and screwdriver. The rifle results reached at least one trillion to one. Robinson’s profile was approximately 95% of the DNA mixture on the towel and 89% on the screwdriver. One unusable swab from one exposed section of the roof changes none of that.

6. This skips the part where Lance Twiggs said the last two photographs “definitely do look like” Tyler Robinson. It also skips everything else he said. About a month before the murder, Robinson asked him for a Dremel to engrave ammunition for a family hunting trip. Police later recovered a Dremel and an engraved casing in his house matching the engraved casings at the crime scene. Lance also said Tyler confirmed in person that his confession was true, began crying, and said he wished he hadn't done it.

7. Yes, they can link the rifle to the crime. The comparison between the autopsy fragments and the rifle was inconclusive using a tool mark analysis because the bullet was badly fragmented. That often happens when a bullet is badly fragmented. “Inconclusive” means the rifle could neither be identified as nor excluded as the source. It does not mean the bullet “did not match.” They did confirm that the bullet fragments were consistent with a .30 caliber bullet. Tyler’s operable .30-06 rifle was recovered along the shooter’s escape route with three engraved live rounds and a fired casing inside it. Add the DNA, footage, towel, ammunition, cellphone data, vehicle evidence, Google Maps route, Robinson’s detailed messages about abandoning the rifle, his numerous confessions, his parents identifying him, and turning himself in for the crime.

8. Nobody testified that dust in the barrel indicated the rifle had not been fired recently. When asked what could cause it, the examiner answered, “a plethora of things,” and said she did not know why it was there. She offered no opinion about when the rifle was last fired. Meanwhile, investigators found a fired casing inside the chamber, and the ATF identified it as having been fired in that rifle. Claiming the dust proves the rifle was not fired is inventing a forensic conclusion the examiner never gave.

9. Again, Tyler was the major DNA contributor on the rifle, towel, and screwdriver. People are drawing false conclusions from DNA degradation because they do not understand what it means. DNA degradation does not reveal when DNA was deposited or who touched an object first or last. The experts testified that they could not determine precisely how, why, or when the degradation occurred. It doesn't tell you timing of who touched it first or last.

10. The "bald man with three passengers" is one eyewitness recollection at night. The objective evidence points to Tyler Robinson: the video shows only one person getting out of the car and returning to it; a police officer encountered the vehicle and believed the male driver was Robinson; the partial plate matched Robinson's Challenger; Robinson was simultaneously texting that he was sitting in his car near campus trying to recover his rifle; he even complained about how loud the crickets were, and those loud crickets are heard on the Ring-camera footage of his car; and his cellphone data shows a Google Maps route from that same location, next to the rifle stash point, directly back to his home.

11. Joe Kent ran the NCTC, which is an intelligence analysis and coordination body. It is not an investigative agency and does not have subpoena power. Kent saying the NCTC was prevented from pursuing certain leads does not establish that the FBI stopped investigating those leads, that the leads were credible, or that they implicated a foreign government. At most, it establishes an interagency disagreement about the NCTC’s access to a FBI/Utah State murder investigation. I think there's credible evidence that Kent was leaking nonsense to Candace and if that's the case, he obviously shouldn't have been anywhere near the investigation, but that's a separate conversation.

12. There's no publicly verifiable evidence to support the claim that Tyler Robinson was in Panguich. The restaurant itself stated: “We have no evidence establishing whether Tyler Robinson was at our restaurant around September 10, 2025.” The defense is fighting a death penalty case. If they had a genuine alibi 200 miles away, they would have used it. Candace’s own photograph places Tyler at an Orem Dairy Queen at 6:38 p.m. The restaurant order was reportedly entered in Panguitch, approximately 200 miles away, at 8:55 p.m. He would have had to drive at over 90 mph continously without stopping for 2 hours and 13 minutes to make that. Highly unlikely.

Like I said, Jimmy, this is all embarrassingly stupid.

The only thing dumber would be spending the last ten months viciously attacking Charlie's innocent loved ones, while pretending you were solving his murder because you were parroting Candace's incoherent nonsense about Fort Huachuca and Egyptian planes.

text:
📰Cha Joo-young: The actress who pursued acting despite her parents’ opposition

Before becoming widely recognized as Hye-jeong in The Glory, Cha Joo-young had to fight one of her biggest battles at home.

Her father worked in finance, and her family had expected her to follow a more conventional career path. She studied abroad and eventually graduated from Utah State University with a degree in business administration. Acting was not something her father considered a realistic career for her. 

When Cha decided to become an actress, she deliberately kept it secret from her parents because she knew they would oppose it. She began acting and only told them after she had already started her professional career. Her parents were devastated, stopped speaking to her for a period and asked her to quit and return to the United States. 

Her father was particularly opposed. After she had already debuted, he reportedly even offered to pay her contract-termination fee if she would quit acting. Cha, however, made a deal with him: if she had not succeeded by age 30, she would return to the path he wanted for her. 

Then came The Glory. Her portrayal of Choi Hye-jeong turned her into a much more recognizable actress, but even that success did not immediately make her parents enthusiastic about her career. In 2023, she said they were still not wholehearted supporters, although they were becoming more trusting and attentive. 

And her father’s reaction to The Glory was memorable. Cha warned him beforehand that some scenes might shock him. After watching her controversial scene, he reportedly walked out of the house. 

However, there’s an important update: the situation appears to have changed since then. In 2025, Cha said her father had become more supportive and that he now seemed to like her career, which made her proud. She described breaking through her father’s and family’s resistance as extremely difficult.

Where are the Blueprints?
After contacting the Utah State Archives for original construction records of the Salt Lake City and County Building, the response revealed something shocking, no blueprints, structural drawings, engineering calculations, or detailed ledgers exist to verify its 1891–1894 construction.

 Built in just three years, in a small city and before power tools, the official record offers almost no proof of how it was done. What starts as a simple request quickly exposes a larger pattern: monumental buildings with no verifiable construction records, raising serious questions about the timeline we’ve been told.

No Blueprints
The missing blueprints are the ultimate proof that our official architectural and historical timeline is false. The original blueprints for Big Ben, Cambridge’s New Court, and major cathedrals across England and the U.S. are missing—documents that legally should exist if these buildings were truly constructed in the 1800s. It argues this isn’t lost paperwork but proof that the structures were inherited from an advanced Old World civilization wiped out only a couple centuries ago.

text:
Some bonds go deeper than fame or blood—Dolly Parton didn’t just mentor Miley Cyrus, she stood by her from the day she was born.

In 1992, Billy Ray Cyrus stepped off the road from touring alongside Dolly Parton during the national success of "Achy Breaky Heart" and asked the country music singer to take on a personal role in his life. He asked her to be the godmother to his newborn daughter, Destiny Hope Cyrus. Parton accepted the title.

Years later, when Disney Channel cast the teenager in Hannah Montana, Parton arrived on set to play the recurring television role of "Aunt Dolly." Outside the soundstage, public scrutiny surrounding Cyrus intensified as she entered adulthood. During the 2013 release of Cyrus's album Bangerz, Parton repeatedly spoke to news reporters to offer public support, emphasizing Cyrus's intelligence, vocational work, and songwriting capability.

Their professional lives continued to overlap on live stages and in recording studios. The pair performed Parton's classic 1973 song "Jolene" together across multiple televised broadcasts, and they later recorded the duet track "Rainbowland" for Cyrus's 2017 album Younger Now.

In May 2024, researchers at Ancestry analyzed historical family records from Tennessee. The documents revealed that Dolly Parton and Miley Cyrus shared an 18th-century ancestor named John Vance, establishing that the godmother and goddaughter were also seventh cousins once removed. Upon learning of the documentation, Parton remarked publicly that the connection confirmed what she had felt for decades, noting that they had always been as close as family.

On August 25, 2026, Dolly Parton died at the age of 80 at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center in Nashville, Tennessee, following a brief battle with cancer. Her passing ended a personal connection with Cyrus that spanned thirty-three years, from Cyrus's birth in late 1992 through every stage of her public career.

text:
You do not defend a hospital's clinical standards by describing its gift shop. Brooke Harrington's Economist essay defends sociology by describing her intro syllabus. Here is everything it leaves out, including the one case she was standing too close to see.

The piece from @EBHarrington is a bait and switch. Teaching students about mortgages is useful. Investigating offshore corruption is useful. Neither establishes that sociology is free of ideological bias or that her own research is the neutral toolkit she presents it as.

The criticism came from inside her discipline and she knows it. The Vanderbilt and Washington University report found political criteria displacing scholarly ones in every field examined, and its sociology chapter was written by the sociologist Ashley Rubin. The newspaper coverage quoted Christian Smith, Musa al-Gharbi, Ilana Redstone and Jukka Savolainen. Savolainen said some topics cannot be studied honestly. Redstone said the field treats causation as settled. Harrington converts all of them into "Concerned Pundits on the higher-education beat." That is not an answer. It is a refusal to name who is talking.

Her comparison with economics collapses on inspection. The difference is not what individual researchers find interesting. It is what the professional bodies do. The American Economic Association does not put ceasefire resolutions to its membership. The American Sociological Association does. South Africa in 1987. Iraq in 2003. An amicus brief on same-sex marriage in 2013. Ukraine in 2022. A Gaza ceasefire resolution in 2024 carried by roughly 59 percent of members voting, defending the right to speak against "Zionist occupation." A vote that September to divest from weapons manufacturers. In 2026 the leadership refused to ballot a member resolution on academic boycott despite it clearing the signature threshold, and members demonstrated outside the annual meeting. Harrington picked economics as her comparison. The comparison answers her question and she left it out.

She also left out her own field's account of itself. Michael Burawoy's 2004 presidential address made sociology the mirror and conscience of society in moral and political debate. Mary Romero's 2019 address defended its social justice tradition against detached objectivity. Christian Smith's 'The Sacred Project of American Sociology' (2014) argued the field is organized around a moral project. Nobody outside sociology invented this question.

Lyell Asher supplies the contrast. In 'Why Colleges Are Becoming Cults' he describes a freshman ethics course where students took up abortion, capital punishment and affirmative action, were required to argue against their own convictions, and finished the term without knowing what the professor believed. He changed his mind on capital punishment over three nights of reading. When he described that course to his own students, they were astonished it had ever existed. Set that against Sociology 1, where we know exactly what the professor believes because she told a national magazine, and where the contested questions arrive pre-answered. Asher's point about the word justice lands here: once it names a set of conclusions rather than a dispute, teaching becomes training, which is why people can now be trained in it by a resident adviser. In 'How Ed Schools Became a Menace' he describes research language that assigns guilt before the ambiguity is resolved, so that alternative explanations become defensiveness and objections become evidence against the objector. He traces the habit to its carrier, the education schools that trained the administrative class, whose programs Arthur Levine's four-year study found ranged from inadequate to appalling. Harrington's defense is personal from beginning to end: her syllabus, her research, her consultations with Treasury. The charge is institutional.

The wage gap example fails at the root. "The same work" is a claim about a residual, and a residual measures what has not been measured. Blau and Kahn (2017) show how the gap moves as human capital, occupation and industry enter the model, and they say outright that the leftover can overstate or understate discrimination depending on which controls you use. No observational study controls for everything. The unexplained portion is by construction omitted variables, measurement error and unobserved choice. Nobody has ever isolated a discrimination term by exhausting the alternatives, because observational data does not permit exhausting the alternatives. The convention is to name the leftover and then assign it a cause without saying so. That is an inference from ignorance and it is the load-bearing move in the entire field.

Watch which way the leftover travels as measurement improves. The CONSAD report for the Department of Labor in 2009 found observable factors accounted for 65 to 76 percent of a raw hourly gap of 20.4 percent, leaving 4.8 to 7.1 percent, and CONSAD refused to call any of that remainder discrimination because its own occupational categories were too coarse to support the claim. That makes 4.8 percent a ceiling on what is unexplained, not a floor on bias. Goldin (2014) found what survives concentrates in occupations that pay disproportionately for long and inflexible hours. Bolotnyy and Emanuel (2022) took Boston transit operators working under a union contract that fixes wages, shifts and promotion by seniority for men and women identically, with no managerial discretion anywhere in the system, and the eleven percent gap was entirely accounted for by overtime uptake and unpaid time off. Cook, Diamond, Hall, List and Oyer (2021) took over a million Uber drivers paid by an algorithm that does not negotiate, does not promote and does not know the driver's sex, and the seven percent gap was entirely attributed to platform experience, where drivers chose to work, and driving speed. Two settings built so that employer discrimination is mechanically impossible, and in both the gap survives and is fully explained by something else.

The standard reply is that experimental work catches what regressions miss. It does not. Goldin and Rouse (2000), the orchestra study everyone cites, concedes in its own abstract that the standard errors are large and that one effect runs persistently the other way, then rests on "the weight of the evidence" after acknowledging the results were not statistically significant. Andrew Gelman went through the paper and could not reconstruct the famous fifty percent figure at all. Meanwhile Williams and Ceci (2015) in PNAS ran 873 tenure-track faculty at 371 institutions across all fifty states, evaluating identically rated scholarship counterbalanced by gender, and found a two to one preference for female applicants among faculty of both sexes in every field, with male economists the sole exception showing no preference. The best-powered hiring experiment in the literature runs backwards. Every one of these papers came out of economics, and none of them appear in her lesson.

The lifespan example fails against a case that has been sitting in the literature for thirty years. Harrington says worse medical care, partly. Hispanic Americans have substantially lower household income, less education and far higher uninsurance rates than non-Hispanic whites, and have posted life expectancy roughly three years longer for most of four decades. Both explanations that would let an access model survive this have been tested and both failed. Abraído-Lanza and colleagues (1999) examined the groups for whom return migration is impossible, Cubans barred from returning, Puerto Ricans whose deaths in Puerto Rico appear in US statistics, and US-born Latinos subject to neither selection effect, and every one showed lower mortality than non-Latino whites. Turra and Elo (2008), using Social Security beneficiary records, confirmed salmon bias exists and found it far too small to be the primary explanation. What is left is behavior, diet, smoking and family structure, which is to say the category of explanation the discipline treats as blaming the victim.

This is the pattern and it runs far past two examples. The alternative causes were not tested and rejected. They were treated as disqualifying. Moynihan, a sociologist, argued in 1965 that black family structure was central to black economic outcomes and was called a racist for it. That is not a conservative gloss. Sara McLanahan and Christopher Jencks, writing in 2015, state that for the next two decades few scholars would investigate father absence for fear of being demonized if the findings came out wrong. McLanahan ran the study herself expecting to find no meaningful difference, found the opposite, and published it with Sandefur in 'Growing Up with a Single Parent' (1994). William Julius Wilson reopened the question in 'The Truly Disadvantaged' (1987) and later called Moynihan's report prophetic. Chetty, Hendren, Jones and Porter (2020) found that the fraction of fathers present in low-income black households in a neighborhood is among the strongest predictors of black boys' income, employment and suspension rates, and that it predicts those outcomes whether or not the individual boy's own father is present. Their findings on white racial bias were reported everywhere. The father presence result went in the appendix and stayed there.

The defenses offered against this both fail. Philip Cohen answers the chilling effect by listing family-structure papers published between 1971 and 1985. A chilling effect shifts what gets published and how it is framed; it does not empty the shelf. Cohen's test asks whether the set of publications is empty, which means it returns "no chilling effect" under every possible state of the world, including the one where a chilling effect exists. That is the unfalsifiable design this entire argument is about, run in reverse, by a sociologist defending his own discipline against the charge that it suppressed something, and arguing with a bibliography against the direct testimony of McLanahan, Jencks and Wilson, none of whom are conservatives and all of whom were there. The second defense is that Chetty found individual parental marital status explains little once parental income is held constant. Family structure is a principal determinant of parental income. Conditioning on parental income and then asking what marital status adds is controlling for the mediator, which drives the coefficient toward zero by construction. Chetty's team also cautioned that the neighborhood correlations are not necessarily causal, and they attached the identical caution to the racial bias correlations in the same paper, which were reported as findings on every front page in the country. The caveat is real. Its asymmetric application is the story.

So the field is not incapable of finding these things. It keeps finding them by accident, through researchers who set out to refute them, and then carries forward only the half that fits. That is what Savolainen meant, and it is the direct answer to the Swiss Army knife. A tool that cannot be pointed at certain explanations without professional cost is not general purpose. It has a grain.

Enron is the wrong exhibit. Fastow's roughly three thousand vehicles were domestic special purpose entities exploiting an accounting rule about outside equity, disclosed badly in SEC filings, not assets parked behind offshore secrecy. Fastow and Skilling went to prison. Arthur Andersen was destroyed. Sarbanes-Oxley was signed within nine months. If the thesis is that concealment delivers impunity, Enron is the case where detection, prosecution and legislative correction all worked, onshore, under American law, fast.

The Corporate Transparency Act example understates her own case, which is its own kind of tell. The statute was authored across twelve years by Carolyn Maloney, introduced in the Senate in 2017 by Rubio and Wyden, and enacted inside the fiscal 2021 defense authorization over a veto aimed at the broader bill. What happened since is worse than she says. FinCEN's March 2025 interim rule exempted domestic entities, and on August 11, 2026, thirteen days before her column ran, FinCEN issued a final rule permanently exempting domestic companies and U.S. persons and announced it would delete the beneficial ownership data already collected from U.S. persons. Roughly twenty thousand foreign entities remain covered. She reached for "halted its enforcement" when the fact in front of her was permanent repeal and deletion of the records. And Rubio's vote for ownership transparency does not validate sociology's methods. Agreement on one policy is not a warrant for a discipline.

Langbert (2018) found roughly 44 registered Democrats per Republican among sociology faculty at elite liberal arts colleges. Langbert and Stevens (2021) found about 27 to one at flagship universities against roughly three to one in economics, and also found that more registered Republican faculty gave money to Democratic candidates than to Republican ones. Registration understates the imbalance rather than inflating it. The Moynihan sequence is what a field at those ratios looks like when a disfavored explanation shows up. Asher's account of the hiring expansion between 1965 and 1975, when students and faculty both doubled and the country staffed a second system of higher education in a single political moment, explains how the imbalance formed and why ordinary hiring reproduces it without anyone conspiring. That is a sociological explanation of sociology, and the field will not look at it.

Her own research runs on the same design. 'Capital without Borders' (2016) rests on a two-year training program, a wealth management credential and 65 interviews across 18 countries. The access was remarkable. The sample was not representative of a trade then numbering twenty thousand practitioners, and nothing in the design tries to make it so. Interviews can show how advisers understand their work. They cannot establish how often practices occur, what they produce, or what would happen without them, and they cannot underwrite a worldwide claim about the erosion of democracy. Her sympathetic reviewers said this. Inglis noted her outrage is never in doubt and that it is not clear she ever challenged an informant's base assumptions, because there is no back and forth anywhere in the book. Godechot noted the fieldwork ran through the post-crisis years when practitioners had every incentive to conceal wrongdoing in a short interview, and that the book consequently says almost nothing about illegal evasion. Emmenegger noted the same structures serve charitable giving and family business protection.

Now ask what would have counted against the thesis. Expressed guilt confirms wrongdoing. Absent guilt confirms impunity. An appeal to legality confirms capture. Every answer confirms. 'Turning Vice into Virtue' (Harrington 2019) puts it beyond argument: tax avoidance enters the paper already classified as professional misconduct, and practitioners' appeals to public service and expert neutrality are then modeled as recategorization of that misconduct. The conclusion is in the operationalization. There may be a sound ethical case against the practices. It has to be made somewhere other than in the coding scheme. You cannot prove the sin by parsing the apology.

The quantitative work makes the same move with numbers. Chang, Harrington and Rockmore (2025) in PLOS One use the prevalence of nominees and bearer instruments across a wealth manager's clientele as a proxy for an individual client's association with concealment, which is not observing that client use them. The diversification measure aggregates by country while the interpretation describes individuals spreading assets, and a country's investors can collectively touch twenty jurisdictions with each using one. The blacklist measure counts entities, and counts are not shares of wealth, since nine empty shells hold less than one funded company. The paper states that the individuals named in the Offshore Leaks database are extremely wealthy and have something to hide. That is a verdict on a population delivered as a data description. ICIJ's own documentation says the public database holds only part of the leaked material, that completeness varies by provider, that some entries are ordinary local businesses, and that inclusion establishes nothing improper.

'Offshore' (2024) reads the whole system through colonialism, an analogy her reviewers praise for making an unwieldy subject familiar. Familiarity is not accuracy, and a frame selected for resonance finds itself confirmed. The same applies to professions as institutions whose privileges depend on public service, which she offers readers as ordinary Sociology 1 content while using it in her own work as the instrument of conviction.

She does not only publish what flatters her. Guerra and Harrington (2025) ran two online experiments in Italy, Denmark and the United Kingdom and found no effect of recipients' immigration status on natives' redistribution behavior, a null the authors say challenges prevailing theories of welfare chauvinism. Small samples and a simulated task, but they published it against interest. That is why this is an argument about classification and interpretive overreach and not an accusation of bad faith.

Arday is where the consistency breaks. He resigned on August 5. Her column ran on August 24. She gives it an accusation of plagiarism and a complaint about British commentators. Jack Grove submitted roughly 97 pages to Cambridge and Liverpool John Moores. David Sanders of Purdue reviewed the text comparisons and described extensive plagiarism. Carter-Ruck correspondence kept the Times Higher Education investigation unpublished for ten months. A police complaint led an officer to warn Grove off further contact. Cambridge opened an inquiry into new information about his qualifications and honorary appointments. Asher's diagnosis covers both halves: people shut down discussion either because they cannot defend a position or because they are too certain to bother. The Carter-Ruck letter was the first. Her subordinate clause is the second. Harrington's subject is how the powerful use law and secrecy to escape scrutiny, and the one case in front of her where a lawyer's letter suppressed a journalist for ten months is the case she declined to see.

Pick a lane is a false choice and she knows which lane she is in. Researchers can advise Treasury, write for the public and push policy while keeping findings distinct from commitments. She wrote the political books, coined broligarchy, took it to The Atlantic and to Jon Stewart. All of that is hers to do. The bafflement is the one move not available to her.

Afflicting the comfortable is not a method. An accusation is worth what its evidence is worth, not what its target is worth. The test of a general-purpose analytical toolkit is whether a student can reject the favored explanation for defensible reasons without the disagreement being read as a moral defect. Moynihan failed that test in 1965 and it took thirty years for the field to catch up to him. Mortgages and Weber do not show that anything has changed. Neither does calling an interpretation a framework. Write the critical book and defend its judgments. But stop telling the public that sociology supplies analytical tools rather than predetermined answers while your own signature work is a method built to reach one.

text:
Like everyone else, I have some thoughts on the remarkable life lived by Dolly Parton. One of my earliest memories of my Grandma Stanger is listening to Dolly, Kenny and other larger-than-life country music legends at her side. I’ve remained a huge fan of her music career, the full breadth of it, with her list of collaborators standing as a testament to just how talented she was, and just what a gift it was to perform alongside her. As a student of anthropology, I find her efforts to preserve America’s bluegrass heritage particularly admirable. As an observer of the decay of family values, I can’t help but admire her lifelong commitment to Carl. It has been enlightening to see the way in which people of all walks of life, political persuasions, etc., are mourning her loss. A review of her life makes clear why:

1. She gave away 332 million books. Dolly Parton's Imagination Library, launched in 1995, mails a free, age-appropriate book every month to any child from birth to age five who signs up — no income test, no strings. It started with kids in her home county and now covers all 50 states plus the UK, Canada, Australia and Ireland. Children who got the packages grew up calling her "the Book Lady."

2. She built it because her father couldn't read or write. Robert Lee Parton was, by her account, one of the smartest people she ever knew and deeply ashamed he'd never learned to read. He lived long enough to help hand out books and hear kids use that nickname, and she said that was the proudest moment of her life — bigger than any record.

3. After the 2016 Gatlinburg wildfires, she just handed people cash. The My People Fund sent about 900 displaced families $1,000 a month for six months, with a $5,000 final payment — $12.5 million total, no conditions. University of Tennessee researchers who tracked recipients found nobody quit working, most had housing within a year, and a majority built emergency savings, results that later got cited seriously in guaranteed-income policy debates.

4. She helped fund a COVID vaccine, almost by accident. In April 2020 she gave $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center, having no idea where it would land. It went to the research behind Moderna's vaccine; she found out along with everyone else when her name showed up in the acknowledgments of the New England Journal of Medicine paper.

5. She turned down the Presidential Medal of Freedom — repeatedly. Twice under Trump (once citing COVID, once her husband's health), and again under Biden. Her reasoning was consistent: she didn't want the country's highest civilian honor to read as a political endorsement, and she'd spent 60 years refusing to pick a side.

6. She said no to Elvis, and it may have been the best decision in music-business history. Elvis Presley wanted to record "I Will Always Love You," but Colonel Tom Parker demanded half the publishing. She cried all night and refused. Because she still owned it, Whitney Houston's 1992 version — one of the best-selling singles ever recorded — paid her directly, and she liked to point out she invested a chunk of it in an office property in a predominantly Black neighborhood of Nashville, which she thought was the right way for Whitney's money to work.

7. She gave over $500,000,000 to charity over the court of her lifetime.  Given her net worth at the time of her death, it is easy to determine that, but for her giving heart, she would have died a billionaire.

8. She paid teenagers to stay in school. Her 1991 Buddy Program offered Sevier County seventh and eighth graders $500 if they made it to graduation, pairing each student with a buddy so they'd pull each other through. The county's dropout rate collapsed. She followed it with an ongoing scholarship fund for local students.

9. Dollywood was economic development disguised as a theme park. She deliberately put it in the poor end of her home county, and it became Sevier County's largest employer at roughly 4,000 jobs. In 2022 she started covering 100% of tuition for every employee — part-time and seasonal included — from their first day. The park also hosts the country's largest non-releasable bald eagle sanctuary, and the local hospital's women's center carries her name because she funded it.

10. She kept giving to children's medicine, and kept deflecting credit. After a niece was treated for leukemia at Vanderbilt, she stayed connected to the hospital for decades, including a $1 million gift for pediatric infectious disease research. Asked about her giving, her line was some version of: she wasn't trying to be a saint, she just did what her heart told her and figured money was only worth what it did for somebody.

The world is a better place because Dolly was a part of it, and heaven’s light shines a little brighter because of the newest member of the heavenly choir.

Besides Milton Hershey, a number of other well-known people reserved passage on the RMS Titanic’s maiden voyage (April 1912) but canceled or changed plans and did not sail. “Last-minute” is relative—some cancellations occurred days or weeks beforehand, while others were closer to departure—and reasons varied (business, illness/injury, family advice, superstition, or logistics). Dozens of ordinary passengers also canceled (more than 50 authenticated cases in contemporary reports), but here are the most frequently cited prominent ones:

https://t.co/TzLxjA46hp

J. Pierpont (J.P.) Morgan (financier; his company controlled the White Star Line’s parent firm): Booked a luxurious private suite (reportedly after the Fricks canceled it). He extended his stay in Europe (accounts cite business involving art shipments/customs issues, health/spa time, or both) and did not sail. The suite ultimately went to White Star chairman J. Bruce https://t.co/6RtdhL83iC

Henry Clay Frick (steel magnate and art collector) and his wife Adelaide: Booked a premier suite early in 1912. They canceled after Mrs. Frick sprained her ankle while traveling in Europe/on a cruise; they stayed for treatment. (Their suite was then offered to Morgan, then others.)https://t.co/TzLxjA46hp

Guglielmo Marconi (wireless telegraph pioneer and Nobel laureate): Offered free passage. He sailed earlier on the Lusitania instead, preferring that ship’s stenographer (his own preferred one was seasick, per his daughter’s account) so he could handle https://t.co/o2ieLZLyCl

(His nephew Alfred Gwynne Vanderbilt also reportedly changed plans late and was initially rumored to be aboard; he later died on the Lusitania in 1915.)https://t.co/TzLxjA46hp

text:
Testimonial in praise of the Emerald Alignment. This client self referred with #tinnitus and extreme anxiety.  

" I got tinnitus in October 2023 hours after taking my first dose of Zoloft, a new antidepressant medication that my psychiatrist had prescribed.  In the evening when I was in my bedroom I noticed a high pitched buzz coming from somewhere in my brain.  It was a continuous sound, present 24/7.  I thought the tinnitus was simply a side effect of the medication and that it would go away after I stopped taking them.  Three months later, I weaned off Zoloft and waited for the tinnitus to go away.  However, it did not stop, and in January 2025 it got even louder after getting COVID and an extremely stressful personal event.  I was extremely depressed and distressed.

Growing up I was brought up to believe in things that are "scientific".  Like most people today if I had an ailment I would go to the doctor's and get prescribed medication.  I never gave it a second thought and trusted the medical system completely.  For acne in my teenage years I took antibiotics and birth control.  For depression and severe anxiety throughout my 20s I took antidepressants and benzodiazepines.  I took them because it was "the right thing to do" even though I increasingly felt like they did not help me in the long term.  When you rely heavily on the medical system for your well-being, it can quickly feel hopeless when things are not going well because all your doctor can do is offer is to put you on yet another pill to suppress symptoms.  When I got tinnitus, I got my wake up call from the medical system.  My family doctor whom I had seen since I was a child did not believe me when I said the antidepressant caused tinnitus:  "You must have had tinnitus all along but didn't realize it". Another Ear Nose & Throat nurse practitioner I went to for help with tinnitus asked at the end of the appointment if I wanted her to prescribe any antidepressants or antianxiety medications to help with the tinnitus distress, even though I had told her that the tinnitus was caused by an antidepressant.  I was baffled and soon realized that though they meant well, they had no idea what to do with tinnitus patients and I had to stop relying on them for an answer. 

I found mention of Jennifer's work on the TinnitusTalk forum and got in contact with her.  Thankfully she agreed to help me.  The Emerald Alignment exercise sounded simple to me at first but to my surprise I had trouble doing it consistently (once a day) at first.  The first few weeks I could not be consistent with the practice and I asked myself why.  "Why didn't you do the alignment? It's only 4 minutes a day!  Don't you want to get better?"  The answer came down to lack of self discipline and self-sabotaging tendencies, which ultimately was caused by a lack of self love.  These are traits I've carried around since my teenage years.  I had to completely ignore the voice inside me that told me that this tinnitus situation that I had gotten myself into was completely hopeless. Jennifer gave me a lot of encouragement and allowed me to see this life challenge as an important turning point in my life.  I also had a lot of anger that I had to deal with - at others, at myself, at the medical system. Jennifer also helped me through a lot of that.  There was also the element of not believing in the power of one's belief and intentions and the impact that can have on healing.  I am still working on this area but it is very important to sustain a positive mindset and intention.

After I started doing the alignment consistently and making a habit out of it, I also became disciplined enough to develop other good habits:  I started jogging 5 to 6 times per week (prior to this I've probably jogged a dozen times in my entire life), started waking up early and eating my meals at set times every day. My depression and anxiety have improved to a 1/10 whereas before it was a 9/10 situation.

My tinnitus volume has also gone down, by at least 50% over the past 3 months. In the past 2 weeks there have been hours in a day where I don't hear it at all in my right ear.  Also, my tinnitus used to react to running water, like the kitchen faucet or a video that played the sound of a waterfall.  When the faucet turned on, my tinnitus would increase in volume and after the faucet turned off that increased tinnitus volume would continue for another second until it went back to baseline.  Now it does not react to running water at all.

Another area that has changed tremendously is that my social anxiety is so much better.  I used to feel extremely self conscious almost all the time, especially in public and sometimes even around my own family.  I was always worried about saying the right things or that others were upset at me because I said or did something wrong.  I also had trouble expressing my thoughts when talking to others because I was scared of judgement.  Now I am much more confident and not afraid to say what I am thinking, or even to have conversations with strangers.  This is a big change in my life because in my adult life I have not experienced living without anxiety for such a long period of time.
Throughout this entire process, Jennifer has guided me and supported me, and my husband and I will be forever grateful for that."

A. C (New York)

text:
The way I see it, the deal, as we understand it, was broadly good for the Canadian economy, so-so for steel and aluminum, and bad for autos. That’s a difficult yet reasonable tradeoff in my opinion. 

On the idea of no deal, I accept that that’s a logical position. I just don’t know what the end game is. I can’t imagine a set of economic circumstances or political machinations in Washington that lead to something better than securing tariff-free access for 85-90% of our exports.  

As for autos, there’s no doubt that ongoing tariffs—even relatively low ones—will affect investment and production decisions over the long run. 

That’s of course regrettable for the affected workers and communities. And there’s a role for public policy to support them. 

But that still strikes me as a worthwhile tradeoff. Especially since if we’re being honest, virtually every major auto investment over the past two decades or so has come with significant public money. The EV subsidies took it to a new level.

So if we walked over what amounts to a 7.5% tariff on autos, we’re saying an industry that can’t attract marginal investment without recurring subsidy is worth risking market access for everything else.

I’m not minimizing the costs and tradeoffs here. But protecting the existing auto footprint isn’t the same as protecting the national interest.

It’s not depression,
it’s just tiredness.
No thoughts,
no thinking,
just tiredness in the mind.

It’s not even loneliness;
much alone time is good,
and it can be dangerous—not in a bad way.

In these alone times, there are many realizations,
because there will never be anyone
who will save you—
not from others,
not from yourself.

Your mind is your biggest enemy,
or your worst.
It’s all up to you.
And to just wake up every morning to a new day is a blessed privilege,
even when you have no idea
where this heaviness comes from.

Surviving days is beautiful,
because even when the day offers
sun, rain, smiles, tears,
it’s still beautiful that one can breathe.
Some thoughts are hard to even write, paint, or explain.

These are just feelings—
wordless feelings
with heaviness
and happiness
that I’m here.
We are here,
still.

text:
Venezuela and (negotiated?) spheres of influence

In the wake of the huge oil deal the US closed with Venezuela there is a remarkable quiet internationally given the huge impact this  will have as it greatly increases the Us stength over global energymarkets 

There has not been a word from European capitals, from Beijing, from Moscow, from Brasilia, from anyone.  So what does this point to?;

1 realpolitik in which  the other countries basically see this as a fait compli, a done deal as they see the US is asserting the Monroe doctrine(per NSS) over the American hemisphere. 

2 It could also point to a certain understanding between major worldpowers on spheres of influence which  they unofficially kinda accept of each other, with ofc some red lines due to their strategic importance globally (like Taiwan).

As for the Venezuela deal itself and US Venezuelan relations
The deal is a major win for the Us, less so for Venezuela, sure they are securing  plenty of investments but those investments pale compared to the worth of those oil reserves. It is so lopsided in favor of the USa it reads like a neo colonial deal.

And here lies the long term danger. When the Venezuelan population at large will recognise it  is basically becoming locked in a neo colonial relation with the US that can breed long term resentment and can spawn counter movements. movements that may not   express themselves only politically in time, but possible also violently targeting us interests. 

If the US wants the Monroe doctrine to remain viable long term it needs to form more equal partnerships that provide a fair win win situation for both countries. Or else it can drive countries in the american hemisphere increasingly into the hands of other global players like China who may offer more attractive deals and who have been making active efforts in creating inroads through economic projects.

And in time those projects come with influence, leverage undermining the position of the US. The US needs to understand in today's world countries have more options to whom they can turn. So the partnerships and deals the US offers needs to be more attractive, competitive then the ones from global rivals like China.
