And America’s violent crime rate is its lowest since 1900.  This is what happens when you put the National Guard on the streets in crime-ridden blue cities: fewer victims, safer streets, and better futures for America’s poorest.  Trump Launched an American Industrial Supercycle  

5. He made the 2017 tax cuts permanent…and better. The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the largest tax cut in modern history, including the doubled standard deduction, the expanded Child Tax Credit, and 100 percent expensing for factories and equipment. It also delivered No Tax on Tips, No Tax on Overtime, an abolition of most taxes on Social Security benefits, and major relief for seniors.  Every Democrat voted no. With the 2017 act set to expire in December 2025, that would have resulted in the largest tax hike in American history.  

6. He repealed 129 regulations for every new one. In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions and just five regulatory actions: 129-to-1, and in nearly every case, the “one” was to repeal the others! OIRA says the savings exceeded those of Trump’s entire first term. That is more freedom, lower costs, and less bureaucratic sabotage.  Of these, the crown jewel was the repeal of Obama’s 2009 “Endangerment Finding”, the legal foundation for the Green New Scam’s vehicle mandates. EPA calls it the largest deregulatory action in American history and estimates that by itself, it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. Trump also killed the federal EV mandate, restored Americans’ freedom to buy the cars and trucks they actually want, and even eliminated the incentives behind the almost universally hated start-stop button.  

7. He secured $18 trillion in announced investment commitments. That’s nearly two-thirds the size of the entire American economy, building American factories, chip plants, data centers, energy projects, steel mills, shipyards, and supply chains employing American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, Taiwan Semiconductor, and many corporations and sovereign wealth funds are betting big on Trump’s America.   No President has ever done anything remotely like it. And it’s just getting started. 

 8. He made “reshoring” and “reindustrialization” real, not a slogan. Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is shifting Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. GM, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and others are expanding U.S. production. The capital equipment pouring into the country is the machinery that’s building the growing boom.  

9. He replaced lopsided trade deals with balanced, reciprocal trade. Trump used tariffs as leverage to reverse 80 years of lopsided trade deals that favored everyone but America, and to win new or improved agreements with trading partners accounting for more than half of global GDP. Those agreements open foreign markets, attack non-tariff barriers, defend strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build in America than to export American jobs.  

10. He shifted global energy dominance from the Persian Gulf to the Gulf of America. Once the world’s largest energy importer — “exporting” $700 billion a year to our enemies — America now outproduces Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. The U.S. is also setting new records in oil, natural gas, and LNG exports, becoming the first country ever to export more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a year.  Trump also opened land, accelerated permits, expanded pipelines and export terminals, and made American energy a tool for prosperity and peace.  

11. After four decades of nuclear paralysis, Trump brought five new reactors online in a single year. For more than 40 years, not one new privately developed non-light-water reactor reached criticality in America. Trump ordered at least three by July 4, 2026. DOE delivered four by the deadline, then a fifth just one month later.  Decades of zero. One Trump summer: five. That is a genuine nuclear renaissance.  Trump Made Elections Matter Again  

12. He broke the Deep State’s power to defy the elected branches. In Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court ruled for the first time in 90 years that Article 2, Section 1 is still part of the Constitution: the President may fire subordinate officials in the executive branch, overturning the 1935 precedent that insulated “independent” agencies from voters’ control.  Ever wonder why elections often seem to change nothing? How about one President and 5,000 political appointees vs. 2.8 million unfireable, unaccountable bureaucrats? THAT is the “Deep State”.  Trump then made that victory real. For the first time in a century, all policy-making bureaucrats can now be fired for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful directives. The permanent bureaucracy no longer gets to veto the voters.  

13. He ended nationwide injunction abuse. In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited nationwide injunctions. A single, local, district judge should not be able to block a national policy for everyone, everywhere; and yet that’s exactly what they’ve done, nonstop, ever since Trump (and only Trump) took office in 2017.   In restricting that unconstitutional power, the Court kneecapped the Black Robe Bureaucracy’s favorite tool of unlawful judicial supremacy.  

14. He shut down USAID as a left-wing slush fund and shadow government. USAID had become a taxpayer-funded machine for exporting abortion, gender ideology, censorship, and left-wing politics. It had a bigger budget than the CIA and the State Department combined, absolutely no accountability whatsoever, and a penchant for overthrowing governments.  Trump terminated it — completely — and moved real humanitarian aid under the State Department. Immediately, seven socialist Latin American governments lost re-election. Coincidence?  

15. He shrank Federal employment to its lowest level in 60 years. From a high under Biden, the federal workforce is now its smallest since 1966. Workforce reductions, agency closures, and spending cancellations mean fewer bureaucrats paid to resist the voters.  What’s more, when Biden left office, 94 percent of federal employees “worked” from home. The Trump administration cracked down: as Elon Musk put it, “you can work from the office or you can pretend to work somewhere else.”  

16. He expelled DEI from the federal government. Trump eliminated federal DEI offices and barred race- and sex-based preferences across the executive branch. Government hiring and contracting are returning to merit and equality under the law, ending the grotesque Democrat idea that “fighting discrimination” requires the federal government to discriminate.  He Defended Faith and Family  

17. He delivered sweeping pro-life reform. In his first term, Trump delivered the judges that overturned the abominable Roe v. Wade. Hardly anyone believed it could be done, or that Trump would do it. But he did, and a half-century nightmare finally ended.  Since returning to office, Trump has enforced the Hyde Amendment prohibiting the use of federal funds to pay for abortions, reinstated and expanded the Mexico City Policy prohibiting federal funding of foreign abortions, ended federal fetal-tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, protected Medicaid from funding large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life activists prosecuted by Biden’s weaponized Justice Department.  He’s also done everything within the Executive Branch’s power to defund Planned Parenthood. It would be nice if Congress did likewise.  No President has ever done more to protect life. No one.  

18. He got men out of women’s sports, and restored biological reality to federal policy. The United States government once again officially recognizes two sexes: male and female. Trump ended federal support for the chemical and surgical gender mutilation of children, stopped taxpayer funding of such irreversible abominations, and forced more than three dozen health systems to end or suspend their programs as well.  Trump also enforced Title IX as written: women and girls deserve their own teams, trophies, scholarships, and locker rooms. The NCAA and other athletic organizations changed their rules in response. After years of Democrats doing everything they could to destroy women’s sports and ruin girls’ lives, Trump’s administration protects women and girls again.  

19. He enacted America’s first nationwide school-choice program — and launched Trump Accounts. As part of the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump enacted America’s first-ever nationwide school choice program. The new Education Freedom Tax Credit helps fund scholarships for tuition, books, and other educational costs.  That’s on top of the new Trump Accounts, which give every child a tax-advantaged stake in America’s future, including a $1,000 federal seed for eligible newborns. Parents gain power. Bureaucracies lose it. And children learn first-hand about free markets and future orientation.  

20. He targeted anti-Christian bias and discrimination. Trump created the White House Faith Office, Religious Liberty Commission, and Task Force to Eradicate Anti-Christian Bias. He restored conscience protections and made clear that Christians do not surrender their First Amendment rights merely by entering public life.  He Restored Peace Through Strength and Put America First  

21. He forced NATO to stop freeloading and increase defense spending by 250 percent. For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries, effectively sending America the bill and using American taxpayers to subsidize their bloated welfare states. Trump forced NATO to replace its old two-percent-of-GDP spending target with an enormous five percent by 2035.  Allied spending is rising, American defense orders are soaring, and Europe is becoming a partner instead of a dependent. 

 22. He drove China out of the Caribbean. China spent years building strategic beachheads at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Maduro’s Venezuela. Trump forced Panama out of Belt and Road, expanded American security access around the Canal, and captured Maduro, who now sits in a New York jail cell awaiting trial.  Beijing’s planned encirclement of the United States collapsed. The Monroe Doctrine is back. Call it the Donroe Doctrine.  

23. He brokered eight peace deals in just eight months. In eight months, Trump brokered peace in eight conflicts spanning four continents, including wars that had gone on for as much as 40 years. It’s a record unmatched by any other President.  

24. He launched and funded Golden Dome, the first-ever true missile defense for the U.S. population. Ronald Reagan dreamed of making nuclear missiles obsolete through his Strategic Defense Initiative. Today, Trump is actually building it: a layered homeland shield with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional defenses, and new technologies including microwave systems to destroy drone swarms and directed-energy weapons (yes, lasers) that can replace an $11 million missile with $2 of electricity.  Congress has funded the initial $25 billion, with far more on the way once it passes the NDAA this fall. Better a shield than a sword.  

25. He restored the warrior ethos — and reversed the recruiting crisis. After years of missed targets under Biden, every active military component met or exceeded its 2025 recruiting goal. Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth refocused the newly renamed Department of War on actually winning wars, while pouring resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, missile defense, and America’s atrophied industrial base.  Young Americans once again believe their Commander-in-Chief is worth serving. And they’re showing up en masse.  Now Act Like It Matters  Those are not tweets or campaign promises. They are changes in law, power, investment, sovereignty, culture, and the structure of the Republic itself. And they’re just the top 

26: I could give you hundreds more.  Midterms are turnout elections. We do not need to convince Democrats to love Donald Trump. We need Republicans and friendly independents to understand what is at stake — and to show up.  And let’s be clear. When you say (as some of you will) “the Republicans need to do a good enough job telling this story”, you’re pointing at yourself. You are “the Republicans.” The Democrats don’t rely exclusively on their elected officials to tell their story: everyone from their media lackeys to their lowest-level supporters are constantly spreading their “news”, whatever that “news” happens to be.  

Today’s conservatives have more ability to find whatever you want to know than any group of people in human history, yet half of them couldn’t name any of the accomplishments in this essay, and if they were to read it, they would just complain that something else they wanted hasn’t happened fast enough to suit them. 

 This is called “black-pilling.” It’s a loser mindset, and if you engage in it, you deserve to lose: horribly, painfully, personally. And guess what: you will, unless people who are serious step up to save you. Which is frankly pathetic, but for the rest of our sakes, necessary.  So tell people our story. Donald Trump is delivering great things, whether or not heaven on earth has broken out quite yet. Do the work, send the team he needs to Washington to finish the job, and get ready for 2028 afterward.  Take the time to learn at least five of these victories. text:
The Seattle Times just came out in opposition to giving parents the right to know what’s going on with their kids in school.

While that’s not a big surprise, they made some false claims about I-001, so we wanted to be sure you have the facts you need to help your friends and neighbors understand why voting YES on I-001 is so important.

Below, @letsgowa identified the top false statements from their article. Read through them, then send this email to 10 friends to make sure they have the information they need to talk to voters.

Claim: Most of these parental protections already exist, so I-001 is unnecessary.

Response: Because of the legislature passing HB-1296 in 2025 and stripping rights from parents that were created by I-2081 in 2024, this statement is entirely false. Here are some of the main changes I-001 would make to existing law: •    Current law gives schools up to 45 days to provide education and personal records; I-001 requires records within 10 business days. •    I-001 expressly defines school records to include medical/health records, mental-health counseling records, vocational counseling, discipline, attendance, and other student-specific files maintained by the school. •    I-001 requires notification when schools arrange medical treatment requiring follow-up care outside school hours. •    It requires immediate notification when a child is taken or removed from campus without parental permission, including to a youth shelter or host home. If the rights were already fully protected, the Legislature would not have needed HB 1296 to rewrite the parental-rights law voters enacted through I-2081.
Claim: “The real driver behind this effort” is access to mental-health records.
Response: Giving parents access to information about their students and ensuring they aren’t the last to know about what’s going on in the classroom is the real driver.
Mental-health records are one of eight specifically enumerated categories of school records in I-001. The initiative contains significant provisions that have nothing to do with mental health, including medical notification, law-enforcement notification, removal from campus, sexual-content opt-outs, curriculum access and academic-performance notification.
Keeping kids safe and reinstating parents, not government employees, as the primary stakeholder in their child’s care is the “real driver” behind I-001.
Claim: A child discussing “gender confusion” with a school counselor could have that information disclosed to the parent.
Response: I-001 says parents may inspect records of mental-health counseling maintained by the public school. It does not say that every conversation between a student and counselor must immediately be reported to parents. Counselors and parents will be allowed to work together to come up with the best plan forward for a student, not counselors working on their own and making decisions for a parent. The initiative also contains an explicit abuse/neglect safeguard:

A school is not required to release medical, health or mental-health counseling records during an investigation of child abuse or neglect when the parent is the target, unless the parent obtains a court order.

Students still have access to mental health resources in schools, and counselors remain mandatory reporters who must look out for the best interests of students by allowing parents to be part of the conversation.
Claim: Supporters imply schools can “spirit children off to medical facilities to change genders — without letting parents know.”
Response: While this isn’t the case for everyone, it is the case for many families in Washington State. See an example from an anonymous family who fled the state and a family who still hasn’t heard from or seen their daughter since November.

While this isn’t always the case for every family, I-001 does significantly improve protections for families by:

ensuring prior notification when medical services are being offered to their child, except emergency treatment; guaranteeing notification when medical services or medications could affect insurance payments/copays; providing notification when the school directly or indirectly arranges medical treatment requiring follow-up care beyond school hours. Parents are being left out of the conversation when it comes to care for their children and you don’t have to take our word for it, you can listen directly to the families who have been impacted. I-001 provides protections for parents and students and takes government employees out of the equation.
Claim: I-001 “actually weakens” crime notification.

Response: Current law requires immediate parental notification when a school receives a report that a crime is alleged to have been committed against a child on school property during the school day or during a school-sponsored activity. It also addresses circumstances in which a child is detained based on probable cause for criminal activity at school.

I-001 removes those geographic and time limitations. It requires immediate notification when a criminal action is deemed to have been committed against the child or by the child. HB-1296, current law, limits the right to crimes occurring on campus, during school hours, or during a school-sponsored activity, which means that existing law is narrower than I-001.

I-001 broadens protections for students because it doesn’t restrict the incident occurring to a location, or time and requires immediate notification to parents.

Claim: Students may avoid counseling because parents could obtain their records.

Response: Mental health counselors will not be required to turn over transcripts of their conversations with students. When a public institution creates and maintains mental-health counseling records concerning a minor, I-001 places the parent, not the school, in the position of having access to those records, subject to its abuse/neglect safeguard.
The Editorial Board assumes the conclusion: that confidentiality from parents should take precedence because disclosure might discourage some students from seeking counseling.
The competing concern is that excluding parents from knowledge of a minor child’s significant mental-health issues can itself carry risks, particularly when parents are responsible for obtaining treatment, monitoring behavior and caring for that child outside school.
Here’s the bottom line: The Seattle Times believes parents shouldn’t have the right to more information about their child.
Teachers, parents, doctors, counselors, student-rights advocates, and hundreds of thousands of Washington State signers couldn’t disagree more.

If you believe that parents have the right to know about what’s going on with their students in schools, VOTE YES ON I-001 THIS NOVEMBER.

I’m all for holding Ottawa accountable, but I don’t think “release the failed negotiating text” is nearly as obvious a demand as people are pretending.

Trade negotiations are conducted confidentially for a reason. A failed negotiation today can become the starting point for negotiations tomorrow. Publishing drafts can expose Canada’s red lines, concessions, fallback positions and negotiating strategy while handing Washington information it can use in the next round.

That isn’t transparency. It can become unilateral disarmament.

By all means, bring Charette and LeBlanc before Parliament. Make them explain exactly what changed, when it changed, what Canada offered and why Carney walked away. Compare that testimony with what Washington is claiming. Demand enough disclosure to determine whether Canadians are being misled.

But I’m not interested in automatically accepting Washington’s story either, especially when the two governments are openly disputing what happened at the table.

And the Gordie Howe agreement should be criticized accurately. Canada agreed to put 50% of net bridge revenues for 15 years into a U.S.-controlled economic-development fund. That was a significant concession. But Canada did not hand the United States half the bridge, and the agreement explicitly preserved the existing ownership and governance framework.

There’s a difference between demanding accountability and demanding that Canada publish its negotiating playbook in the middle of an economic confrontation.

I want the first.

I’m not convinced the second is in Canada’s interest.

text:
Study finds media coverage of the 2024 presidential race favored political spectacle over substantive policy debates | Eric W. Dolan, PsyPost

New research provides evidence that mainstream newspaper coverage of the 2024 United States presidential election focused heavily on political strategy and legal controversies rather than policy issues. The findings indicate that while coverage of Donald Trump was persistently negative, Kamala Harris received a temporary positive boost following her sudden nomination. The study was published in the Journal of Political Marketing.

The contemporary political environment in the United States is highly polarized, which shapes both how journalists report the news and how the public interprets it. During election years, readers flock to political news to inform their voting decisions. However, journalists face a choice in how they present this information. A 2011 review of political communication explained that news outlets often frame elections around campaign tactics, momentum, and horse-race polling—focusing on who is winning or losing—rather than substantive policy debates. When this strategy-based framing dominates, the news tends to emphasize political spectacle over practical governance.

Alongside this focus on campaign tactics, political news often carries a heavy dose of negativity. Journalists and readers alike tend to display greater sensitivity to conflict and scandal than to routine achievements. This negativity bias has become particularly pronounced in recent years. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2023 found that negative language use among U.S. politicians surged starting in 2015 alongside Donald Trump’s initial primary campaign and remained elevated throughout his presidency.

The 2024 presidential election presented an unusually chaotic cycle, featuring an assassination attempt, a late-stage withdrawal by Joe Biden, and the rapid nomination of a new candidate, Kamala Harris. The authors of the new study set out to document how these unprecedented political shocks altered the narratives and the emotional tone presented in mainstream print journalism.

The research, led by Ayse D. Lokmanoglu of Boston University, analyzed tens of thousands of articles from five major high-circulation newspapers. The team focused on USA Today, The Washington Post, The New York Times, the Los Angeles Times, and The Boston Globe, collecting articles published between January 1, 2024, and January 31, 2025. After initially gathering over 500,000 articles, the researchers applied keyword filters to identify stories that specifically mentioned Joe Biden, Donald Trump, or Kamala Harris in the headline or opening excerpt. This process resulted in a final dataset of 37,321 full-text articles.

To make sense of this massive amount of text, the scientists used automated computer programs to conduct topic modeling and sentiment analysis. Topic modeling is a technique that identifies clusters of words that frequently appear together, allowing researchers to see what overarching themes are present in a set of documents without having to read each one manually. Sentiment analysis involves using a specialized dictionary to count the number of positive and negative words in an article, providing an overall score for the emotional tone of the text.

The researchers identified five major themes in the news coverage: elections and campaign frames, Trump family legal issues, domestic policy and regulation, foreign policy and ideology, and government and legislation. As the election cycle progressed, the share of articles dedicated to elections and campaign frames surged sharply. This spike was particularly prominent around major political events, such as Biden dropping out of the race and the Democratic National Convention.

Meanwhile, coverage of Trump’s legal issues grew steadily, peaking in late December and early January during developments in his various court cases. In contrast, discussions of domestic policy and regulation steadily declined in volume as the election approached. This pattern indicates a displacement effect, where campaign drama and legal scandals squeezed out substantive discussions of policy.

When looking at the emotional tone of the coverage, the researchers noted that the five newspapers converged on broadly similar patterns. Overall, the median sentiment of the coverage hovered slightly below neutral. However, distinct differences emerged depending on which candidate the article covered. Articles mentioning Trump were consistently negative throughout most of the pre-election period.

Articles mentioning Harris, or both Biden and Harris, trended in a slightly positive direction. Harris received a noticeable positive bump in coverage following the Democratic National Convention and the vice-presidential debate. This temporary boost aligns with the concept of a post-nomination honeymoon effect, where newly introduced or barrier-breaking candidates receive more favorable, optimistic coverage in their early days on the national ticket.

Interestingly, articles that mentioned both Democratic and Republican candidates were persistently negative, suggesting that when journalists write about both sides in the same article, they usually focus on partisan conflict and adversarial attacks.

The findings offer a detailed look at mainstream media narratives, but the researchers noted a few limitations to their work. The analysis focused exclusively on five major newspapers that generally lean toward the political center or center-left. Because the study excluded right-leaning outlets, the results might not capture the full spectrum of the American media diet.

Additionally, the automated tool used to measure sentiment relies on counting specific words, which means it can miss complex rhetorical devices like sarcasm, subtext, or strategic ambiguity. The researchers also filtered their articles by searching for specific candidate names. Articles that discussed broad political platforms or policies without naming Biden, Harris, or Trump directly were excluded, which could have artificially lowered the amount of policy coverage detected in the dataset. Future research could expand on this work by using advanced language models capable of understanding context and nuance, or by linking news publication data with social media metrics to see how readers amplify different types of political stories.

The Seattle Times just came out in opposition to giving parents the right to know what's going on with their students in school.

While that's not a big surprise, they made some false claims about I-001, so we wanted to be sure you have the facts you need to help your friends and neighbors understand why voting YES on I-001 is so important.

You can read the piece from the Times here.
https://t.co/w5oxqbYyOk

Below, we've identified the top false statements from their article. Read through them, then send this email to 10 friends to make sure they have the information they need to talk to voters.

Claim: Most of these parental protections already exist, so I-001 is unnecessary.

Response: Because of the legislature passing HB-1296 this year and stripping rights from parents that were created by I-2081 in 2024, this statement is entirely false.

Here are some of the main changes I-001 would make to existing law:

Current law gives schools up to 45 days to provide education and personal records; I-001 requires records within 10 business days.
I-001 expressly defines school records to include medical/health records, mental-health counseling records, vocational counseling, discipline, attendance, and other student-specific files maintained by the school.
I-001 requires notification when schools arrange medical treatment requiring follow-up care outside school hours.
It requires immediate notification when a child is taken or removed from campus without parental permission, including to a youth shelter or host home.
If the rights were already fully protected, the Legislature would not have needed HB 1296 to rewrite the parental-rights law voters enacted through I-2081.

Claim: "The real driver behind this effort" is access to mental-health records.

Response: Giving parents access to information about their students and ensuring they aren't the last to know about what's going on in the classroom is the real driver.

Mental-health records are one of eight specifically enumerated categories of school records in I-001. The initiative contains significant provisions that have nothing to do with mental health, including medical notification, law-enforcement notification, removal from campus, sexual-content opt-outs, curriculum access and academic-performance notification.

Keeping kids safe and reinstating parents, not government employees, as the primary stakeholder in their child's care is the "real driver" behind I-001.

Claim: A child discussing "gender confusion" with a school counselor could have that information disclosed to the parent.

Response: I-001 says parents may inspect records of mental-health counseling maintained by the public school. It does not say that every conversation between a student and counselor must immediately be reported to parents. Counselors and parents will be allowed to work together to come to up with the best plan forward for a student, not counselors working on their own and making decisions for a parent.

The initiative also contains an explicit abuse/neglect safeguard:

A school is not required to release medical, health or mental-health counseling records during an investigation of child abuse or neglect when the parent is the target, unless the parent obtains a court order.

Students still have access to mental health resources in schools and counselors remain mandatory reporters that must look out for the best interests of students by allowing parents to be part of the conversation.

Response: While this isn't the case for everyone, it is the case for many families in Washington State. See an example from an anonymous family who fled the state and a family who still hasn't heard from or seen their daughter since November.

While this isn't always the case for every family, I-001 does significantly improve protections for families by:

ensuring prior notification when medical services are being offered to their child, except emergency treatment;

Washington Rural Health Transformation Advisory Committee  (RHT-AC)

August 28, 2026

Washington’s Rural Health Transformation Advisory Committee (RHT-AC) is now active. 

RHT-AC supports Washington’s Rural Health Transformation (RHT) Program, a five-year, federally funded program focused on improving health care in rural communities.

Washington received approximately $181 million in first-year RHT funding. RHT-AC will help ensure these investments reflect the priorities and lived experiences of rural communities.

RHT-AC serves as a bridge between communities and state government by providing feedback and recommendations on program implementation. It is not a decision-making body.

The committee held its first meeting in June. RHT-AC will meet quarterly to review progress and provide ongoing guidance.

Who is on the committee

The committee is a cross-sector body. It brings together members from across Washington’s rural health system. This ensures that investments and priorities are informed by the diverse perspectives of people delivering and receiving care in rural Washington.

Members were selected through an open and competitive application process this spring. Tribal delegates were reviewed and selected in consultation with the Governor’s Indian Health Advisory Council and the American Indian Health Commission. Advisory committee members will serve an initial two-year term, with the possibility to extend.

State agencies partnering on the RHT Program also have representatives participating in the advisory committee. They can provide information about work within their agencies and context from broader dialogues with state leaders. Partnering agencies include the Washington State Health Care Authority, Department of Health, and Department of Social and Health Services. The Governor’s Office and Office of Financial Management will also participate.

Learn more about the RHT Program
The RHT Program is part of the H.R.1 budget reconciliation bill. The RHT Program offers $50 billion funding nationwide to improve rural health care. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) administers the program.

In this first year, CMS awarded Washington state about $181 million. These funds will support the hospitals, clinics, and providers that rural communities rely on every day.

Visit the RHT Program page

The King has Died: Norway’s King Harald V Dies at 89 After More Than Three Decades on the Throne

King Harald V of Norway died Friday, August 28, at age 89, ending a reign that began in 1991.

The Norwegian Royal Court said he died peacefully at Oslo University Hospital Rikshospitalet at 6:35 a.m. local time, which was Thursday evening in Washington state. His son, Crown Prince Haakon, succeeds him.

Harald became king following the death of his father, King Olav V. Over the next three decades, he helped bring a more open approach to the monarchy and offered reassurance during national tragedies, including the 2011 terrorist attacks.

Born in 1937, Harald spent part of his childhood in exile in the United States during World War II. He married Sonja Haraldsen, a commoner, in 1968, breaking with royal tradition. They had two children, Princess Märtha Louise and Haakon.

Beyond his royal duties, Harald was an accomplished sailor who represented Norway in the Olympics. His public remarks often reflected a broad understanding of Norwegian identity. In a widely remembered 2016 speech, he described a country that included people of different faiths, backgrounds and sexual orientations.

Despite recurring health problems in his later years, Harald remained committed to serving for life.

“During a crisis, it is often the everyday necessities like diapers, pet food and other basic supplies that families need most,” Spokane Mayor Lisa Brown said. “I am incredibly grateful to the businesses and organizations that have stepped up to offer these items to those impacted by the wildfires. Donations of clothes, shoes, appliances, furniture, toys, and over the counter medications are currently not being accepted.

A primary contact name, email address and phone number

Alaska's state budget teeters on the edge, with officials increasingly raiding the Permanent Fund to cover shortfalls as oil income dwindles. AI data centers offer an unexpected fiscal lifeline, promising tax hauls that could rival petroleum yields if sited wisely. Yet these electronic warehouses draw fierce pushback in populated regions for their industrial footprint and constant hum, leaving Alaska's vast, sparsely settled North Slope as a potential sweet spot.

Proposals vary sharply in merit. An East Coast plan to submerge facilities in Cook Inlet for tidal power and seawater cooling strikes most observers as technically fraught and permitting hell, unworthy of state effort. By contrast, an Alaskan firm's idea for a Prudhoe Bay-adjacent site capitalizes on ready infrastructure like airports, roads, and natural gas supplies in an already industrialized zone free of nearby homes. The scale matches existing oil operations across thousands of square miles of state land.

Loudoun County in Virginia pulls in over a billion dollars yearly from such centers alone, nearly matching Alaska's projected unrestricted oil revenue. With West Virginia courting the industry through long-term incentives, local leaders here could follow suit to stabilize finances without further eroding dividends. The alternative leaves legislators with dwindling options once that fund dries up.

text:
Austin Reed is one of my favorite UFL stories:

In 2022 Reed led ALL of college football with 4,744 yards at Western Kentucky, despite his college success that also included a previous D2 Championship he went undrafted in the 2024 NFL Draft.

Then the Chicago Bears called, and while Reed played quite well during the preseason going 12/16 for 123 yards and a touchdown with a 117.4 passer rating the team simply didn't have room for him, especially considering that same year they drafted Caleb Williams with the first overall pick. 

Austin was released among the final roster cuts and spent the rest of 2024 waiting for a call, but none came... then in January of 2025 the Bears reached back out to offer him a futures contract and things pretty much repeated - great preseason performance, too crowded of a QB room, released and spent all fall sitting around waiting for a call.

Then legendary head coach Bob Stoops retired from coaching leaving the Dallas Renegades without a head coach for the first time in their history. It wasn't until around Christmas that his replacement was announced - former QB and UCLA legend Rick Neuheisel and the former Gunslinger was studying his QB's and had his eye on getting Austin to Dallas.

Reed's family and friends encouraged him to accept an opportunity with the UFL and on January 12th 2026 Austin Reed officially became a Dallas Renegade with both him and his wife Peyton, who were expecting twin girls, moving to DFW for training camp.

A few weeks into training camp though Austin had a 48 hour period that would change his life forever.

His wife Peyton had to have an emergency c-section at 27 weeks, and his twin girls while healthy had to remain in the NICU weighing only 2.5lbs. Despite everything that was going on the UFL season opener was only days away so Austin, a rookie, was still required to attend practice the next morning.

It was at this practice where Austin Reed would be named the Dallas Renegades starting QB, a complete shock to most of the UFL community as the Renegades had a cemented starter with former XFL Championship MVP Luis Perez. 

Coach Neuheisel asks Austin, "You good? Are you going to play well?" and Austin simply replies, "Yes Sir, that's the plan." 

Spending his days at the football facilities and nights at the hospital didn't seem to affect Austin at all, in fact, the opening game of the season Reed set a UFL Record 370 passing yards in a blowout win and he'd eventually lead the entire league in touchdown passes.

Fast forward to today, 7 months to the day since being named a Renegade and Austin has signed a contract with the Baltimore Ravens, an organization that prior to the UFL hadn't even given him a look.

Spring football works.

text:
I don’t think that you understand what’s going on with data centers. data centers are already powered by fuel cells, which serve as both primary base-load power sources and reliable backup systems to address the surging energy demands of AI and cloud infrastructure. 
Current Adoption and Scale Major technology and infrastructure companies are actively deploying fuel cell technology at scale. Notable implementations include:
Equinix has invested over 100 MW in Bloom Energy fuel cells. 
Microsoft has piloted hydrogen fuel cell systems, including a 3 MW prototype and a 48-hour backup demonstration in Wyoming. 
CoreWeave and Intel have deployed significant fuel cell capacities for high-performance computing and AI workloads. 
Apple and Google utilize fuel cells alongside renewable sources for their data center operations. 
Key Advantages for Data Centers Fuel cells, particularly Solid Oxide Fuel Cells (SOFCs) and Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM) types, offer distinct benefits over traditional generators:
Rapid Deployment: Modular fuel cell systems can be deployed in less than a year, whereas gas turbines often have lead times exceeding five years. 
High Efficiency and Density: SOFCs achieve up to 54% electrical efficiency and can deliver up to 100 MW per acre when stacked vertically, making them ideal for space-constrained urban sites. 
Reliability: They provide 99.99% uptime with minimal redundancy and operate quietly without combustion, reducing noise pollution and local emissions. 
Grid Independence: Fuel cells can operate as islanded microgrids, allowing data centers to generate power on-site and bypass congested or slow-to-upgrade electrical grids. 
Market Growth The sector is experiencing rapid expansion, with Rystad Energy projecting fuel cell market revenues to grow tenfold from roughly $2.8 billion in 2025 to $30 billion by 2030.  This growth is driven by the need for scalable, low-carbon power solutions as AI computing demands strain existing electrical infrastructure.

text:
THE PRICE THAT DECIDES SANDISK'S $SNDK NEXT QUARTER IS NOT TRADED ANYWHERE. IT GETS NEGOTIATED - AND THE RAISES JUST SHRANK:

SanDisk SNDK at $1,483.42 (after hours), -$1.53 / -0.10% from Thursday's $1,484.95 close. The regular session finished at $1,485.47, +$0.52 / +0.04%, on 8.1M shares against a 15.8M 30-day average - about half an ordinary day. The Milpitas, California company makes NAND flash memory, the chips inside solid-state drives, memory cards, and the storage that AI data centers are now buying in bulk. David Goeckeler is chairman and chief executive. About 11,100 employees.

First, what is live right now: nothing. It is already Saturday afternoon in Tokyo, Hong Kong and Shanghai, and the weekend everywhere else. US index futures - contracts on where an index will trade at a set date later, and normally the all-night clue to the next opening bell - stopped at 5:00pm ET Friday and do not restart until 6:00pm ET Sunday. Every level below is a settlement, not a market currently trading.

And when all of it does reopen, not one of those markets will quote the number that decides this company's next quarter.

WHERE THE WORLD STOPPED

Asia, which shut hours before New York had its argument:

- Nikkei 225 (Japan): 66,406, +274 pts / +0.41%.
- Hang Seng (Hong Kong): 25,585, +19.05 pts / +0.07%.
- Shanghai Composite (mainland China): 3,952.18, -4.39 pts / -0.11%.

Europe, which heard the first ninety minutes of it and went home green:

- CAC 40 (France): 8,401.18, +81.31 pts / +0.98%.
- DAX (Germany): 26,570, +203 pts / +0.77%.
- FTSE 100 (UK): 10,824, +31.76 pts / +0.29%.

The American contracts, which are your bridge to Monday's opening bell:

- Dow futures: 53,590.00, -31.00 pts / -0.06%.
- S&P 500 futures: 7,724.75, -17.75 pts / -0.23%.
- Nasdaq-100 futures: 29,509.50, -186.00 pts / -0.63%.
- Russell 2000 futures: 2,977.40, -41.60 pts / -1.38%.

The tell is in the last four lines, not the first six. The contract on 30 huge American companies is down six hundredths of a percent. The contract on roughly 2,000 smaller ones is down 1.38%, about twenty-three times as much. That gap is an interest-rate story: smaller companies borrow more and hold less spare cash, so when money is expected to stay expensive they feel it first.

Why it was expected to stay expensive: at 10:00am ET Friday, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh gave his first keynote as chair at the Kansas City Fed's annual symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming. Traders who bet on the Fed's next move went from pricing roughly a 35% chance of a quarter-point increase at the September 15-16 meeting to about 56%. The 2-year Treasury yield - what the US government pays to borrow for two years, and the rate that moves fastest when people rethink the Fed - finished near 4.37% against Thursday's 4.24%.

Asia and Europe are not a second opinion on any of that. They were closed or closing while it happened. Overnight and pre-open moves routinely fade by the time New York actually opens, and this weekend there is not even an overnight session to fade.

THE FACTORIES ARE IN JAPAN. SO IS THE NEWS.

SanDisk does not own a wafer plant by itself. Its flash memory comes out of a joint venture with Kioxia, the Tokyo-listed Japanese memory maker, at two sites: the Yokkaichi plant in Mie Prefecture and the Kitakami plant in Iwate Prefecture. The two have put more than $50B - about 9 trillion yen - into Japan together over 25 years. In January they extended the Yokkaichi venture through December 31, 2034. On July 3 they started producing 10th-generation 3D flash memory at Kitakami.

Then Thursday, August 27, the dated one. The two companies said they plan to invest more than $31B, roughly 5 trillion yen, in those Japanese plants and the technology behind them through 2032, contingent on government support. Hiroo Ota, Kioxia's president and chief executive, called it a commitment "to contributing to the advancement of an AI-driven society." Goeckeler said the spending "will ensure our ability to support customers' increasing demands."

Set $31B against SanDisk's whole market value - share price times every share, about $217B - and you can see it is not a rounding line. It is also not SanDisk's alone; it is the two partners together, and Japan's government is expected to carry part of it.

Note where you would go to price that news. Kioxia trades in Tokyo, which is shut. SanDisk trades in New York, which is also shut.

TWO KINDS OF PRICE

Here is the idea worth keeping past this weekend.

Some prices are set on an exchange. Thousands of people bid and offer, a screen updates, and anyone can watch it. Every figure in the board above works that way.

Other prices are negotiated. NAND flash is sold mostly on contracts, agreed between the chipmaker and a big buyer, repriced on a cycle rather than by the second. There is no ticker. Research firms survey those deals and publish where they landed. No Fed speech moves it, no opening bell touches it, and it will not be any different at 6:01pm Sunday than it is right now.

For a memory company, that negotiated price is not a side detail. It is most of the story.

WHAT IT DID TO THE NUMBERS

SanDisk reported its fiscal fourth quarter on August 5, covering the three months to July.

- Revenue, the money coming in the door: $8.97B, up 51% from the quarter before.
- The split management gave: about one-third of that jump came from selling more chips, about two-thirds from charging more for them.
- Net income: $6.90B, or $43.97 a share on the strict accounting count.
- Adjusted profit per share, earnings with certain one-time items set aside: $39.25, against about $33.38 expected.
- Its own earlier map had been $7.75B-$8.25B of revenue and $30-$33 a share. It came in $720M and $6.25 above the top of both.
- The board added $14B to the buyback, taking the remaining authorization to $15.5B - about 7% of the company, retired from the share count if it is all spent.
- Next quarter is mapped at $10.30B-$10.80B, another 15% to 20% above a record.

Now the ladder those contract prices built, adjusted profit per share by quarter: a loss of $0.30, then $0.29, $1.22, $6.20, $23.41, and $39.25. Five quarters from losing money to earning $39 a share. A year ago today these shares changed hands at $48.56.

THE RAISES ARE SHRINKING

That is the fact the boom half of this note has to survive.

Industry trackers put NAND contract prices up 55% to 60% in the first quarter of 2026 and 70% to 75% in the second - more than doubling across the first half. The third quarter is running at 10% to 15%. The reason given is plain: consumer buyers have reached the limit of what they will absorb, and each new increase is measured against a much bigger base.

The stock market did not wait for that to show up in a report. SanDisk peaked at $2,354.39 on June 22. It is 37.0% below that now.

Micron Technology at $930.80 (after hours), -$4.59 / -0.49% from Thursday's $935.39 close, peaked at $1,255.00 on June 25 and sits 25.8% under it. The Boise, Idaho company, founded in 1978 with about 53,000 employees under chief executive Sanjay Mehrotra, makes the other half of this market: DRAM, the fast working memory a computer thinks in, including the stacked kind bolted next to AI processors. Its May quarter, reported June 24, did $41.46B of revenue against $9.30B a year earlier - more than four times - with $25.11 of adjusted profit a share and its high-bandwidth memory sold out through calendar 2027. Its own map for the quarter just ended is about $50B.

Both now trade near 20 and 21 times the past year's profit. That looks cheap and is the oldest trap in a cycle business: the low multiple comes from a denominator sitting at the top of the cycle, not from a low price.

WHERE THEY SIT

SanDisk is 8th on the Hypergrowth Len5, the style watching fast-growing disruptors. The expansion is unarguable - $8.97B in a quarter, a next-quarter map of $10.30B-$10.80B, and a profit line that went from a loss to $39.25 in five quarters. The half to be honest about is where it came from: two-thirds of last quarter's growth was price, and a price-led expansion is not the same thing as a business getting bigger. A quarter where volume does more of the work than price, landing inside that $10.30B-$10.80B map, would firm it. Contract prices flattening while the buyback quietly does the per-share job would break it.

It is on none of the other five. The two value styles want a fair price beside a durable business, and 20 times peak-cycle earnings is not that - a real markdown, with earnings power that survives a down leg, is what would bring either into range. Income watches cash actually reaching owners, and there is no dividend at all. Momentum watches a name breaking out on its own news; 37% under the June high on half a normal day's volume is the opposite shape, and clearing $2,354.39 on heavy volume would change it.

Micron is 13th on that same Hypergrowth Len5, on the same evidence and the same caveat: $41.46B against $9.30B is extraordinary growth, and a 1978 company with 53,000 employees is neither early nor small. Its September 30 report landing near that $50B map, with the sold-out book stretching further into 2028, would firm it; a map that stops rising would break it. It is on none of the other five - the $0.15 quarterly dividend is about 0.06% of the share price, which is not cash return at a scale the Income Len5 watches, and the value styles hit the same peak-earnings multiple.

THE CALENDAR THAT ACTUALLY MATTERS HERE

Sunday at 6:00pm ET the American contracts resume, and Tokyo opens two hours later. Monday, August 31, London is shut for the UK bank holiday and it is month-end in the US, when funds adjust holdings into the close and prices can move on housekeeping rather than news. Friday, September 4 at 8:30am ET, the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes the August employment report, the government count of jobs added or lost. Micron reports September 30. SanDisk's next report is penciled for November 5 and not yet confirmed by the company.

Every price in this note gets a fresh one over the next 48 hours. The figure that actually sets SanDisk's next quarter will not be among them. It gets written into a contract, on a schedule nobody rings a bell for, and in two quarters it has gone from raises of 55% to raises of 10%.

text:
Corollary:  EVERYONE has SOMETHING to hide.

This is like someone who says they never break the law. Oh really? You never drive 1mph over the speed limit, have had your wheels cross the double yellow line for a moment, or failed to come to a complete stop before the line at a stop sign? Most people have not only committed a crime, they have inadvertently committed a felony. Taking Sudafed into many countries is no different than taking in Cocaine or Meth. When I point that out to people they usually turn pale as they realize they've done it. Kill a mouse and it turns out to be the wrong species of mouse, one that is endangered or threatened, and that's a felony. People who live near Preble's Meadow Jumping Mouse habitat in Colorado and Wyoming, beware. Drive through a gun-free school zone with a gun when you are a state resident with a concealed carry permit and you are ok. Do the same thing with an out-of-state permit which your state recognizes, and so it's legal at the state level, leaves you a felon under federal law as it only has an exception for permits issued by the state the school is in. And so on.

So I'm telling you, everyone has something to hide. Who they want to hide it from may differ. The consequences of it being disclosed may differ. On a grand scale my wife finding out I went into some store to buy her a birthday present doesn't have earth shattering bad consequences, it just ruins a good surprise. So I want that hidden. 

People don't even realize what they should want hidden. If a prosecutor wants to make a case against you for X, let's use drunk driving since I heard this example decades ago from a lawyer friend, they will seek out the cash register receipt for your alcohol purchase. Buy the alcohol with your grocery store discount card and you've made it easy (reading about the case caused the lawyer to use a fake name on her grocery discount card). Pay with a credit card and you've made it easy. They can track the card transaction to the retailer, who has it linked to the detailed receipt showing what you bought. Maybe you weren't intoxicated, but the circumstantial evidence of buying a six-pack earlier in the day may convince the jury you were. Many more examples. Women have often faced hiring discrimination if they are pregnant, so being pregnant or trying to get pregnant may not be something they want an employer to discover until after accepting an offer. In other words, something you want hidden.

I won't weigh in on the privacy risks from various products, just pointing out that everyone has things to hide. That makes privacy concerns about everything from Flock to Alexa to your notebook camera and microphone real. That people overstate specific risks, usually making erroneous claims, doesn't eliminate the valid concerns. And if someone makes the claim its not a problem if you have "nothing to hide", then they are just wrong.

From a scouting perspective, Mark Herzlich was a big, instinctive and highly productive linebacker at @BCFootball whose best tape showed legitimate three-down ability. At roughly 6-foot-4, 244 pounds, he combined size, physicality, range, football IQ and ball production

His best season came in 2008, when he recorded 110 tackles, 13 tackles for loss, six interceptions, eight pass breakups, two forced fumbles and two fumble recoveries, earning ACC Defensive Player of the Year and first-team All-American honors

On film, Herzlich diagnosed quickly, triggered downhill with conviction and played with good physicality against the run. He used his length well to take on blocks, created separation and consistently found the football

What separated him was his ability to impact the passing game. Herzlich showed good awareness in zone coverage, route recognition, anticipation and legitimate ball skills. His six interceptions reflected a linebacker who understood quarterback intentions and could finish plays when the ball came his way. He also offered value as a blitzer because of his timing, size and closing ability

After missing the 2009 season following his diagnosis with Ewing’s sarcoma, Herzlich returned in 2010 and produced 65 tackles, 3.5 tackles for loss, four interceptions, four pass breakups and two forced fumbles

Pre-Draft Measurements:

Height: 6’4”
Weight: 244 lbs
40-Yard Dash: 4.91
10-Yard Split: 1.71
Bench Press: 29 reps
Vertical: 32½”
Broad Jump: 9’4”
20-Yard Shuttle: 4.46
Three-Cone: 7.32

After going undrafted in 2011, he signed with the @Giants and developed into a dependable depth linebacker and core special-teams contributor. He appeared in 88 regular-season games with 17 starts

From a scouting standpoint, Herzlich is a good example of why evaluation cannot be based strictly on testing. His size, instincts, toughness, football intelligence, physicality and versatility translated to the NFL even though his athletic testing limited his ceiling as an every-down defender. His intelligence, toughness and special-teams value became the traits that allowed him to build a lengthy career

See How a Tesla-SpaceX Merger Gives Musk a Shortcut to His $1 Trillion Payday

Deep in a $1 trillion pay package approved by Tesla’s shareholders is an escape clause that could pay off for Elon Musk in several ways if he folds the automaker into his SpaceX empire.
That kind of cars-and-rockets tie-up—the subject of widespread speculation among investors, and hinted at by Musk himself—would likely give him the tighter control he has long sought at Tesla. A hefty-enough price would also, in an instant, wipe away key performance targets standing between Musk and billions of dollars in shares.
“This $1 trillion—that was supposed to be a stretch,” said Mary Ellen Carter, a Boston College accounting professor who studies executive pay. “It turns out it isn’t really that hard. All you have to do is be bought.”
Musk has considerable say over any offer SpaceX makes for Tesla, thanks to his sweeping control over the rocket company. The upshot: Even a stratospheric bid would keep Musk in firm control of the combined company.
Here’s what it could look like if SpaceX were to acquire Tesla
Tesla shareholders voted to adopt the pay package last fall. Under ordinary circumstances, it would deliver to Musk as many as 423.7 million shares if Tesla hits a series of 12 market-value targets and the company also meets just as many cash-flow and operating goals. Among them: delivering Tesla’s 20-millionth vehicle, selling one million robots and putting one million robotaxis on the street.
How the performance targets go away
First a technical note: Musk’s much-ballyhooed potential payout of $1 trillion in stock would now top out around $824 billion. That is because the number of Tesla shares outstanding has risen since shareholders approved the deal. In other words, the same $8.5 trillion market value would be spread across more shares, reducing the value of Musk’s new slug of shares.
The record-setting equity award was “designed to align extraordinary long-term shareholder value with incentives that will drive peak performance from our visionary leader,” Tesla Chair Robyn Denholm told shareholders at the time.
Yet tucked into the bottom of the fifth page of the 16-page 2025 CEO Performance Award Agreement, a single sentence declares half the targets are as good as accomplished if Tesla is acquired or otherwise taken over.
That would leave only market-value targets to determine how many shares Musk gets. The same clause says those targets would be met or missed based on the final deal price—or on Tesla’s market capitalization immediately before any acquisition closed, if that is higher. Musk, SpaceX and Tesla didn’t respond to requests for comment.
“Tesla shareholders could think it’s terrible and the Tesla price drops” ahead of any deal, Carter said. “But it’s whatever SpaceX is willing to offer.”
Every $500 billion added to the deal price would deliver as many shares again, up to $7.5 trillion. An $8.5 trillion acquisition—more than six times Tesla’s recent market value—would deliver the pay package’s full 424 million shares. That is the number of shares that would have clinched the maximum $1 trillion stock award for Musk.
The wild cards
There are few clear constraints on what SpaceX could offer to acquire Tesla. Musk’s holdings of SpaceX Class A shares, with one vote apiece, and Class B, with 10, give him about 86% of any SpaceX vote needed to approve a deal. By controlling most B shares, he also can appoint a majority of the company’s board, which oversees deals.
The company’s legal home of Texas largely protects SpaceX from shareholder lawsuits over any Tesla acquisition, unless plaintiffs own at least 3% of the company. That is a tall order, said Ann Lipton, a University of Colorado law professor specializing in corporate law. “Legally, he has the power to do whatever.”
Shareholders would have to bless any deal at Tesla, where Musk now holds just under 20% of the vote. Although Tesla is also in Texas, disgruntled shareholders there would have a clearer path to suing, raising the importance of getting investors on board, she said. “He needs to persuade the Tesla shareholders.”
There are other possible scenarios. SpaceX has a third, nonvoting class of shares but hasn’t issued any yet. Using those to acquire Tesla could avoid or reduce diluting the votes of existing SpaceX shareholders, albeit at the risk of resistance from Tesla investors.
Potential complications lurk, too. Musk might want to keep acquisition costs down to avoid cutting too deeply into the ownership and voting power, however limited, of existing SpaceX shareholders. Many are longtime supporters who signed on with the company’s initial public offering just weeks ago.

text:
You have to think about the coming Super League through the eyes of an ESPN producer and an advertising executive. Linear television is approaching irrelevance except for live sports and maybe local news in the middle of a snowstorm. The commodity now is not merely football. It is attention. What makes people sit down, turn on a television and remain there for three hours? What will advertisers pay for? 

90K people in Athens, in a sea of red, watching Georgia pummel Tennessee? Check. Clemson running down the Hill into Death Valley at night? Check. Michigan–Ohio State? Alabama–LSU? Texas–Oklahoma? Nobody has to explain those pictures to an advertiser. You can sell those games before you know either team’s record.

Now flip the camera around. An ESPN producer does not want to spend three hours desperately avoiding shots of empty upper decks. Half-full—or worse—stadiums at Pitt, Wake, Boston College, Syracuse and Virginia are not merely attendance problems. They are television problems. Even Miami, for all of its brand value, can produce the bizarre spectacle of a nationally relevant program playing in front of acres of visible green seats. 

And the problem is not merely empty seats. It is the absence of the entire college football tableau: the setting, the tailgating, the entrances, the bands, the traditions, the color, the noise, the sense that an entire campus has been consumed by the game. Outside of Clemson, Florida State, NC State and Virginia Tech, the ACC is strikingly weak at manufacturing that kind of spectacle. Even UNC, for all its ballyhooed “brand,” offers a remarkably anemic gameday experience: tailgating in parking decks, remote lots, and shuttle buses from the Friday Center are hardly the stuff of college football pageantry. TV producers and advertisers know this.

Collectively, this is why I think the ACC gets disproportionately culled if this "Super League" becomes an NFL-sized exercise. Television executives are not distributing merit badges. They are assembling scarce, telegenic inventory, and empty seats and no pageantry are fatal because they communicate something no producer wants communicated: even the people who live there don't care enough to attend.

Where I depart from the 32-team thesis is the endgame. I cannot imagine college football permanently reducing itself to 32 hereditary members while everyone else is condemned to an ornamental second division. Economically elegant, perhaps; politically, institutionally and culturally combustible, definitely. State legislatures alone would make the thing almost impossible.

My guess is that we eventually land much closer to 64 than 32, or we create some genuine avenue for promotion and relegation. There has to be a way onto the dance floor. Otherwise you're asking scores of enormous public universities, endowments, governors, legislators, alumni bases and television markets to acquiesce permanently in their own irrelevance. 

College football may be becoming professional football, but it cannot simply become the NFL. To wit: the NFL never had to tell the Virginia General Assembly that Virginia Tech had been permanently relegated and then wait to see what Richmond did about it. That's why this is different.

OAKLAND DISAPPEARANCES: AMY HILLYARD 

Missing Lost And Trafficked 
Lured Lost And Unsolved 

Oakland, Calif.-The case of Amy Hillyard, a 52-year-old mother and co-owner of the popular Farley's East coffee shops, involves a highly scrutinized timeline surrounding her disappearance on March 25, 2026, from Oakland, California. 

Because she left behind her cell phone, purse, keys, and wallet, investigators have relied entirely on witness accounts and neighborhood surveillance footage.

Timeline of Disappearance: 

March 25, 2026Morning: Amy and her husband, Chris Hillyard, have breakfast together.

Late Morning: Chris drops Amy off at an Oakland BART station so she can travel to a therapy appointment in Walnut Creek.

1:45 PM: Amy sends a final text message to her husband.2:00 PM: Amy returns to her home on the 500 block of Radnor Road near Lake Merritt. Shortly after, neighbors report seeing her outside walking her dog.

3:00 PM: Chris returns home to find the back door open, the dog loose outside of its crate, and Amy's personal belongings left on the kitchen counter. 

There is no note explaining her departure.4:30 PM (Unconfirmed Sighting): Early tracking efforts highlighted grainy surveillance footage showing a woman matching Amy's description walking near East Oakland's Dimond Park. Private investigators later noted that it may not have been her, meaning the 2:00 PM neighborhood sighting remains her last definitively confirmed location.

Search Timeline and Key Events
March 25, 2026: Chris reports Amy missing to the Oakland Police Department. 

Because she suffers from severe 
clinical depression and anxiety, police immediately classify her as an "At-Risk" missing person.

April 22, 2026: The Oakland Police Department publicly announces there is no active evidence suggesting an abduction, kidnapping, or foul play.

May 25, 2026: Community members, friends, and family host a candlelight vigil marking two months since her disappearance. 

Organized volunteer crews continue to canvas local parks, trails, and regional preserves.

June–August 2026: Independent investigators and family members focus digital forensic appeals toward residents in the Cleveland Heights, Lake Merritt, Lakeshore, and Crocker Highlands neighborhoods, urging them to review private security footage around the 2:00 PM timeframe. 

The family has offered a $10,000 reward for information.

🚨 BRIAN STEEL’S CROSS-EXAMINATION OF MR. HESTER GETS INTERESTING

Brian Steel continued questioning Mr. Hester under oath, focusing heavily on his relationship with Slutty, his statements about King Von’s murder, his meetings with the government, and the alleged Atlanta conversation involving Lil Durk.

🔴 HESTER ON SLUTTY

Steel asked Hester who “Slutty” was.

Hester testified that Slutty was T-Roy’s brother and said they were close before Hester went into custody.

Hester also acknowledged that Slutty was killed during the incident involving Dayvon Bennett (King Von).

However, Hester clarified that he personally did not witness the entire incident on video. He said the video was specifically shown to him to demonstrate what happened to DJ Vance.

🔴 STEEL CHALLENGES HESTER’S ACCOUNT OF THE ALLEGED $1 MILLION OFFER

Steel returned to Hester’s testimony about an alleged meeting with Durk in an Atlanta studio, where Hester claimed Durk said words to the effect of:

“Kill Quando Rondo. You will be straight for life.”

Steel pressed Hester on the fact that, without the recorded government interview, the alleged Atlanta conversation would essentially come down to Hester’s word against anyone else’s.

Hester agreed.

Steel then pointed out that the recorded interview actually contains Hester telling investigators that he never discussed Dayvon Bennett’s death with Durk and that the alleged million-dollar/half-million-dollar conversation did not come up.

Hester responded that there was “more to it” and accused Steel of playing only what he wanted to present.

🔴 31 MEETINGS WITH THE GOVERNMENT — ONLY 3 RECORDED

One of the biggest moments came when Steel questioned Hester about his cooperation with authorities.

Hester acknowledged that he has met with prosecutors and agents approximately 31 times.

Steel then established that only three of those meetings were recorded.

Hester said he didn’t know there had been that many meetings and wasn’t keeping count.

Steel emphasized that the jury has no recording of the other meetings — meaning much of what allegedly happened during those conversations comes down to Hester’s recollection and testimony.

🔴 STEEL QUESTIONS THE MISSING CONTEXT

Steel argued that the jury doesn’t know what was said during those earlier meetings because they weren’t recorded.

He repeatedly emphasized the importance of context — particularly regarding Hester’s conversations with investigators about Durk.

Hester acknowledged that the jury does not have recordings showing how those earlier conversations developed.

🔴 AUGUST 18, 2022 — THE CALL BEFORE THE SAN DIEGO FLIGHT

Steel then moved to the morning of August 18, 2022, the day Hester allegedly traveled to California.

Hester testified that he received an unexpected phone call from Antonio Jones, known as Boonie Mo.

According to Hester, Durk’s voice could allegedly be heard through the call.

But Hester acknowledged something important:

There was reportedly no discussion of murder or a specific crime during that call.

According to his testimony, the conversation was essentially about needing Hester to go to California and whether he was available.

🔴 STEEL QUESTIONS THE WIFE & SON AS POTENTIAL WITNESSES

Steel established that Hester said he was in a car with his wife and son when the call came in and that the phone was on speaker.

That means, according to Hester’s testimony, his wife and son could potentially have heard the voice he identified as Durk’s.

Steel asked whether authorities ever contacted Hester’s wife to ask if she heard the call.

Hester said he didn’t know of any such conversation.

Steel then highlighted that Hester had told authorities his wife and son were in the car, yet his wife was apparently never asked to corroborate the alleged call.

The press release lists NASA, the Fed, and the Senate as victims. The disruption is three domains that made two platforms inoperable.

The Justice Department and FBI announced court-authorized domain seizures in the Southern District of California. QTFY, a PRC state-sponsored group employed by Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology Company, built two complementary platforms, QScan and QTRouter.

QScan scans and automatically infects thousands of IoT devices worldwide and adds them to QTRouter. QTRouter is compromised IoT plus commercial proxies plus leased VPS.

The traffic looks like it comes from outside the PRC, maybe local to the target. The seized domains were hard-coded into both malware families for communication and authentication.

The seizures made QScan and QTRouter inoperable.

QTFY offers the work to paying customers, including the Ministry of State Security and the People's Liberation Army.

DOJ's list of "QTFY computer intrusion activity" also names Energy, Justice, HHS, and NIH. ABC News, Alexander Mallin and Luke Barr, puts hundreds of entities on the target side: hospitals, telecom, power, defense contractors.

The group includes former members of China's military. The seizure warrant says that in September 2024, QTFY "conducted computer intrusions" at three Energy Department laboratories, NIH, an HHS agency, and an unnamed US security device manufacturer.

A 2019 NASA attempt is in the file. Court documents do not suggest that effort succeeded.

They also do not state clearly the scale or success against several of the other named agencies.

CyberScoop, working from the affidavit, says the Senate attempt in March was unsuccessful. An attempt on a US election system in June was unsuccessful.

QScan carried more than 200 proof-of-concept exploits. One day in 2024, an FBI agent wrote, it processed over two million scanning and exploit tasks.

The FBI and NSA published an advisory on activity dating back to at least 2018.

I would start with the two platforms.

text:
Did you know a local citrus grower helped make Lake Gregory possible and even put up his own money when the project ran out of funds? 🏞️ 

Lake Gregory, located in Crestline, is a man-made lake in the San Bernardino Mountains. Its story begins with a man named Arthur Gregory, Sr.

Gregory was a Redlands citrus grower who developed the area in the early 1900s when it was known as Houston Flat. He also operated a small sawmill where he made boxes for the oranges he grew in Redlands.

As concerns grew over reliable water sources, Gregory helped establish the Crest Forest Water District. He also donated land for the creation of a new lake and dam.

Construction of the lake and dam began in July 1937 and was scheduled for completion in 1938. During construction, the project ran out of funds. As a result, Gregory stepped in and personally covered the remaining costs. 

In 1938, a major storm brought heavy rain to Southern California. It was estimated that it would take three years to fill the lake. Instead, the rain filled it in just three days.

During that same storm, nearby Big Bear Lake rose several feet in a matter of days.

Today, Lake Gregory Regional Park offers swimming, boating, fishing and more.
