text:
HVAC Sales: A Day In The Life

I left my house at 7am to drive 40 minutes for an 8am meeting. They put everyone’s “numbers” on a big screen on the wall so each consultant could see last month’s metrics: close rate, average ticket, and total revenue. As I mentioned in my Substack article "The Inside Scoop on HVAC," such meetings are required at many companies. The top guy on our team — who I’ll admit was not me — broke the one-month sales record with $803,000.

That’s HVAC in July for you.

I then drove to my first call, a “Marketed Lead,” 25 minutes away. The homeowner had called in requesting a free estimate for the best way to get more cold air upstairs. I’ve worked in many houses like his, sometimes called “California Splits,” and they almost never distribute cold air evenly. His wife was not home — the scenario we call a “one-legger” — and this almost always makes the sale more difficult. I asked about her whereabouts and he said she’d be home soon. One obstacle out of the way.

I asked the client questions about his situation: what he’d been experiencing, what he was looking for, and what he hoped to gain from my appointment. He gave vague, muddled answers about maybe a new system but maybe some mini splits and he didn’t have money for a new system but he wanted a quote anyway and he had no idea when he wanted to proceed. It was clear, early on, that he was either not lucid regarding his situation or was throwing up a number of “smokescreens.”

I explained to him what I always explain these situations: That while there’s always going to be a temperature difference between a top floor and a basement, if it’s really bad then there’s at least one of three problems going on. The equipment is either the wrong size, only one-stage (one speed), or the ductwork is leaking air into the walls and ceilings instead of actually getting delivered to the rooms. In my area the average HVAC system is leaking 20-40% of its airflow into the walls — and this is actually getting worse with new-construction homes — and so even if the system is sized appropriately, you’re only getting a fraction of the airflow anyway.

I use a process of elimination to figure out what the issue is, so I first did what’s called a “Heat Load Calculation.” I went room-by-room measuring windows and counting vents, drawing out a diagram of their home by hand and putting all this information into my Heat Load Calculator. Industry best practices require a Heat Load on every job; if you ever need a new AC or Furnace and your contractor doesn’t do this, he either doesn’t know how or cuts corners. Based on feedback from my clients around town, I would estimate that fewer than 1 in 10 contractors sizes new equipment correctly. It’s not even enough just to measure the windows; you also have to consider the number of panes and which directions the windows are facing.

His system was the correct size, so that wasn’t the problem. It was, however, “one stage.” That’s the bottom tier of equipment (what you might call the “Landlord Special”) and essentially means that the system is either all the way on or all the way off, either 100% or 0% power. It’s the cheapest to install but is also the loudest, the least efficient, and creates the biggest temperature gap between rooms and floors. I mentioned this to the homeowner but, since he’d already told me he did not have enough money for a new system, assumed that replacing this with two-stage or variable-speed equipment was probably not in the works.

As we discussed airflow and possible leakage, he mentioned that the two bedrooms upstairs — where the house was way too hot in summer — had noticeably weaker airflow coming from the vents. So there was the answer: one-stage equipment with leaking ducts, with one solution much more budget-friendly than the other. We were standing in the mechanical room at the time, and as I discussed what I was seeing I noticed something strange: an unopened humidifier box. I asked why he had that, and then all became clear.

He said he planned to install it at some point, as he’d done on a previous home he’d owned, once he was done installing the water softener. That’s the moment I realized what I was actually doing in his house: I wasn’t there to make a sale, I was there to teach him everything he needed to know in order to fix the problem himself. He was knowingly, deliberately wasting my time in order to give himself a great HVAC education.

As an Oblate of St. Benedict, I try to adapt the Rule of St. Benedict to my life “in the world;” some chapters are only relevant in a monastery. The Benedictine ethos emphasizes hospitality and, in a monastic setting, this means treating all guests and visitors as if they are Christ Himself. Since I am going to other peoples’ homes instead of their coming to mine, I reverse the direction and try to treat all homeowners as I would treat Christ Himself. Homeowners like the one in front of me at the time make doing so especially difficult.

For all you know, the contractor you’ve invited out has already been working for 12 straight hours. He hasn’t had time for lunch. His back hurts from the crawlspace job before yours. He drove an hour to your home. He works on commission and cannot feed his family unless he makes a sale. There’s nothing wrong with saying “no” to a pitch, but it’s selfish and unethical to knowingly waste his time.

Once I realized what was happening I decided to leave quickly, but in such cases I still have to act professionally. His wife was home at that point so I sat them down for a few minutes, summarized my findings, and recommended a Duct Sealing. It costs around $5,000 and seals the ductwork from the inside, patching up all the holes it finds throughout the house and massively improving airflow. He told me, as expected, that he “wasn’t making any decisions today.” Understanding the situation, I didn’t bother trying to “overcome objections.” I sent him an email and left.

When I got back to my car, I had — in zoomer lingo — a minor “crash out.” I fell into the passion of anger, ranted about the situation and about how the man had wasted my time, and was upset that I had lost a couple hours of the day when I could have been speaking with a real prospective buyer instead. These things happen, but it gets me every time. After a few minutes of passionate tirade, I re-centered. I always keep an icon of Christ and His Mother on my dashboard, to remind me that God is always watching. It helps keep me calm — especially in moments like this. I took a few deep breaths, repented of my anger, and moved on.

The second job was another “Marketed Lead,” 30 minutes back in the other direction. It was for a man who owned a fourplex and wanted to replace his Swamp Cooler with central AC. I do jobs like this all the time, and as such have learned what to expect. In a perfect world the homeowner already has a spot on his Breaker Panel to add a new 240V circuit; the Swamp Coolers only pull 120V and you can’t just reuse the same breaker. If there’s no 240V spot open, you’re looking at either an upgraded Panel (which costs a couple thousand by itself) or an upgraded Meter outside (which costs twice what the Panel does since the city and power company get involved). You also hope, on jobs like this, that there’s actually room for a Coil above the Furnace; if not, you’re going to spend a day or two just rebuilding or altering the ductwork.

I knocked on his door and heard a voice on the other side. When he opened it he was on the phone, and said “Never mind, he’s right in front of me.” Apparently he’d called the office trying to see when I’d arrive, and he seemed to be in a hurry. He then told me something all consultants hate to hear: that he had to go soon and could only stay long enough for me to get what I needed for the bid. Translated from Clientese, it means no decision will be made that day and at the end he’s going to ask for an email — the kiss of death. (And that’s exactly what happened. After meeting a couple thousand homeowners through the years I’ve become fluent in their elusive language.)

I got probably twice as much time with him as he had intended to give me when I arrived, enough to examine all the ductwork (covered in asbestos tape), the breakers, and plan where the new Condenser outside would go (along with how to get the new lineset and wires there). I showed him the whole scope of the project along with a No Change-Order Guarantee: that the price we agree on is the price he pays, even if the installers find something halfway through the job that requires extra work or parts. He was clearly in a rush and I discerned that if I pushed to close at the table, I would lose the job forever; my only shot was to leave him with information and follow up. Not ideal, but I think it went as well as it was going to.

My third job was a “Tech Lead,” or a lead set by a technician. They had called our technician out to have a look at the system and, after understanding the extent of the required repairs and weighing whether they’d be worth it on a 21-year old system, decided to have me out for a replacement bid instead. Usually (but not always) these are more fruitful than Marketed Leads.

I greeted the homeowner and did my usual introduction, ending up on a comfortable reclining chair in the living room with the husband on a couch to my right and his wife — recovering from a recent knee surgery — on my left. I asked how I could best serve them and they began to tell me the story of the home: they had one system for just the top floor, which they assured me was working great, and a second system in the basement serving said basement and the main floor above it.

The Blower Motor in the Furnace had died, thus preventing airflow of any kind from circulating throughout the home. That motor spins a metal wheel that pulls air in through your intake (or “return”) grills and pushes it out through your supply vents; without the turning of that wheel there is neither AC, nor heat, nor even “Fan Mode.” It’s the heart of your HVAC system.

Given the situation, which could be solved merely by replacing the Furnace and not necessarily getting a new AC, I asked if they were looking to just get the minimum “up and running” package or whether they’d be open to doing both the AC and Furnace together given that both were past their expected lifespan. They wanted to see options for both together.

While the wife stayed upstairs nursing her wounded knee with an ice pack, the husband followed me to the mechanical room (where your Furnace and, usually, Water Heater) are located to ask my thoughts about what I was seeing. Another contractor had told him that the Furnace wasn’t big enough, hence the poor airflow he’d been experiencing in his basement. I did all the measurements; the Furnace size was fine. The problem was actually that his Return Drop — that silver vertical piece of rectangular ductwork that, in most homes, goes from around the ceiling down to the Filter Cabinet on the ground — was nowhere near big enough to circulate the proper amount of air. The Furnace was also sitting flush on the ground, whereas any system serving a 3-tons-or-bigger AC should be raised off the ground on an Air Base. This massively improves airflow and lets the system “inhale” from below as well as the side.

Having begun my career as an Installer and worked my way through the Technician phase, more often than not I have insights into a system and its problems that other consultants are going to miss. I wasn’t selling cars last week and then decided to try HVAC. I paid for my role with blood and sweat.

Thus, I always like when the homeowner is with me in a home so that I can demonstrate my expertise and competence. It doesn’t matter how rich or famous he may be; in that moment, he submits. I have what Oren Klaff calls “local star power.” I am in his home, but he is in my world.

This particular homeowner greatly appreciated my insights, particularly because — as I would learn later in the visit — he was an engineer. A consultant with no eye for detail and design would not have stood even a fraction of a chance. When I was done in the basement I went back upstairs to complete my Heat Load Calculation. Unprompted, the wife began to tell me about all the projects she had done with my company. She “gently” asked if I could offer a 10% discount and then “not gently” suggested that if not, she would call a competitor. My exact words: “I understand and have no doubt we can come to a reasonable arrangement, one that leaves both parties happy.” She nodded.

When I was done with all the measurements I sat down with them both, all in the same living room chairs in which the visit had begun, and I began to discuss my findings. I went over sizing, efficiency, brand, and install (what the project would include and why). They nodded along and asked questions. At the end I put together four packages for them to consider: two which would work with their current setup, an 80%-efficient Furnace and single-stage AC, and two that would require minor construction on the home in order to massively improve the efficiency of their Furnace. Prices ranged from 21 to 28 thousand dollars.

Right at the crucial moment, the doorbell rang. The wife had been expecting a friend, and she happened to show up at exactly what would — in normal circumstances — be the worst possible time in my visit. Thankfully, the wife excused herself from our meeting by saying “I’ll go with whatever he wants” and then left the decision up to her husband. That is a much better scenario, in the sales world, than hearing “we’ll discuss it later” or “send us an email.”

He asked “It’s only 7 thousand from the bottom option to the top?” and I said “correct” while hiding my excitement. This sort of question is what’s called a “buying signal” and shows readiness to move forward with a project. He said “let’s just do the top one” and handed me a credit card. It was a job that could not have gone better — especially in light of the rest of my day. He’s going to love his new system and, I hope, hire me again when the upstairs system breaks too.

Onward.

One more call, 40 minutes away. It’s right by my house and gym. Perfect. Another one-legger, but her husband came home just as I was ready to present options. I restarted more or less the entire presentation, recapping everything I’d discussed with his wife. He nodded and seemed impressed. None of the three contractors before me had been nearly as thorough or communicative. They had no interest at all in the first two guys that came by, as only the one just before me had bothered with the Heat Load. And he was cheaper — probably by a lot. The husband vacillated a bit between wanting to do research and wanting a good deal if it meant moving forward quickly. I prodded and poked a couple times to see if a deal could be made, but he seemed hesitant.

In these situations I do not get aggressive; I back off. It’s more important to me that everyone involved is happy with the project than to get a quick sale that results in “Buyer’s Remorse” for the homeowner. I probably lose sales by not getting more aggressive, but I sleep better at night knowing the clients I do close are happy. In the end, the husband admitted, he already had planned for another guy to come out on Saturday and share his own opinion of the situation. It’s a friend of a friend. I’m not concerned that he’ll be more thorough and competent, but if this couple is just price-shopping I’ll probably lose. I’ll have to follow up with them later.

All in all it wasn’t the easiest day: some ups, some downs, a lot of driving. 40 minutes to the office, 25 minutes to the first job, 30 more to the second one, 15 to call three and then 45 more to end the day. Nearly 3 hours in the car; about average. No time for lunch. An absolutely atrocious 1/4 close rate, but the 1 that sold was hefty and made up for that.

I’ll take it.

text:
On 28 August 1749, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was born in Frankfurt, into a family that contained contradiction that would accompany him throughout life: discipline and imagination. His father, Johann Caspar Goethe, was severe and methodical; his mother, Katharina Elisabeth Textor, only seventeen when she married, was vivacious, musical, a born storyteller. Goethe later condensed the inheritance beautifully: from his father came seriousness, from his mother his cheerful nature and delight in storytelling.
He wanted to know how plants transform, how rocks are formed, how the eye experiences colour, how desire alters judgment and how a life might be lived without dividing experience into convenient departments. The Sorrows of Young Werther made Goethe a European phenomenon; Wilhelm Meister turned self-formation into the substance of the novel; Elective Affinities examined passion with almost chemical coldness; the West-Eastern Divan conversed with Hafez; and Faust, pursued across some six decades, became the vessel into which Goethe poured knowledge, ambition, desire, failure, metaphysics, salvation and the dangerous human refusal ever to say: enough.
Goethe considered his Theory of Colours a serious achievement. Goethe asked not merely what light is physically, but what happens when light becomes human perception. His physics failed where Newton’s prevailed.
Then there was Schiller.
Goethe found Schiller too vehement; Schiller admired Goethe’s mind while remaining suspicious of the man. After a meeting in Jena in 1794 and an argument about plants, opposition became intimacy. Until Schiller’s death in 1805 they exchanged more than a thousand letters, reading, criticising and provoking one another through their work.
When Schiller died, Goethe felt that he had lost part of himself.
Goethe’s biography can no more be written without women than Faust can be written without desire. Friederike Brion, Charlotte Buff, Charlotte von Stein, Christiane Vulpius, his companion and eventually his wife, Marianne von Willemer: women were not footnotes to Goethe’s work. Again and again, experience passed into literature; Goethe possessed the gift of turning life into form.
And age did not cure him of love.
In 1823, at seventy-four, Goethe fell deeply in love with the teenage Ulrike von Levetzow at Marienbad and sought marriage. It came to nothing. Out of the grief came the Marienbad Elegy. The man who had spent a lifetime analysing passion discovered that knowledge offers remarkably poor immunity against it.
There was also Napoleon.
On 2 October 1808, during the Congress of Erfurt, Goethe was summoned before the Emperor. Napoleon had read Werther and discussed it with its author. Goethe’s account records Napoleon saying:

“Vous êtes un homme.”

“You are a man.”

It is difficult to imagine a more compressed meeting between literature and power: the man rearranging the map of Europe confronting the man rearranging its imagination.
Goethe lived another twenty-four years. He kept reading, revising Faust and thinking about Weltliteratur, world literature, the idea that national literatures were entering a larger conversation across borders. He ended not simply as a great writer, but as a mind for whom almost nothing seemed intellectually irrelevant.
He wrote about a young man destroyed by love and fell in love again at seventy-four. He created Faust’s hunger for limitless knowledge and spent his life pursuing plants, bones, colours and clouds. He disagreed with Newton and conversed with Napoleon. He lost Schiller and continued writing. And he reached old age without acquiring that peculiar intellectual disease in which certainty replaces curiosity.
Which brings me to the Goethe sentence I like to leave here on his birthday:

“If you want to get pleasure out of life, you must attach value to the world.”

Perhaps that is the shortest possible synopsis of Goethe.
The world does not owe us its value.
We participate in creating it.

APC HAS FAILED WOEFULLY ON ROAD INFRASTRUCTURE — MAKINDE WILL SALVAGE THE SITUATION!

While Nigerians are being distracted with grandiose promises and the illusion of a coastal highway, commuters across the country continue to groan under the deplorable condition of major federal highways that urgently require rehabilitation.

Nigerians deserve functional roads, safer highways, and infrastructure that works for the people—not endless promises while motorists spend hours battling potholes, failed sections and dangerous road conditions.

It is deeply unfortunate that Nigerians are forced to endure avoidable hardship on our roads while public resources are expended without commensurate results. The situation calls for urgent action, accountability and a complete change in approach.

The Minister of Works, David Nweze Umahi, and the APC-led Federal Government must answer to Nigerians on the state of our federal highways and explain why critical road infrastructure continues to deteriorate despite the enormous resources allocated to the sector.

text:
Start by working strictly through official BLM channels. Wild horses (mustangs) are federally protected under the Wild Free-Roaming Horses and Burros Act. You cannot take them directly from gathers, holding facilities, or public land. Placement happens via the BLM’s adoption program, sales program (for animals offered for adoption at least three times or over ~10–11 years old), or long-term off-range pasture contracts. Nonprofits can participate as organizations.

https://t.co/ZGogbXyoF2

Your 2000 acres backing up to BLM land and 501(c)(3) status are strong foundations for a private sanctuary model (similar to existing Colorado efforts). BLM prioritizes qualified private care to reduce holding costs, but facilities undergo review/inspection, especially for larger numbers.Key BLM Contacts in Colorado

National Wild Horse and Burro Information Center (best first call for program questions, applications, data, or large-scale interest): 866-4MUSTANGS (866-468-7826); wildhorse@blm.gov. Office hours roughly 8 a.m.–4 p.m. https://t.co/9MtKwqyZdt

Colorado primary WH&B contact: Royal Gorge Field Office, 3028 East Main Street, Cañon City, CO 81212; (719) 269-8539 (or main office line 719-269-8500). This office handles much of the state’s adoption/sales activity and the Cañon City holding https://t.co/oANsEC5SVC

Colorado State Office: PO Box 151029 (or Denver Federal Center, Building 40), Lakewood, CO 80225; 303-239-3600; blm_co_info@blm.gov (mailto:_co_info@blm.gov). State Director Doug Vilsack; Deputy State Director for Resources Alan Bittner (involved with wild horse issues).gbp-blm-egis.hub.arcgis.com +1

Contact the nearest field/district office to your property as well (Northwest District in Craig for northern/western areas, Southwest District in Montrose, etc.), since adjacency to BLM land may involve local https://t.co/PjN8p3KJHI

Tell them you are forming a 501(c)(3) sanctuary and want guidance on adopting/purchasing larger groups or applying for off-range pasture contracts. For group sales (5+ animals) or large placements, they often require additional documentation and site verification.

https://t.co/ZGogbXyoF2

Practical Path Forward

Complete 501(c)(3) and prepare facilities — BLM requires adequate corrals initially (minimum ~400 sq ft per ungentled adult horse, 6-ft fencing recommended, access to food/water/shelter), then larger free-roaming pastures once gentled or for long-term care. They may inspect, especially for 25+ animals at one location. Assess your land’s carrying capacity (forage, water, terrain—Colorado arid ranges typically support far fewer horses per acre than humid areas). Perimeter fencing, water development, and a veterinary plan are https://t.co/xk5Qc95TJV +1

Adoption/Sales route — Apply via the Online Corral (https://t.co/OYt2FoKVJw) or local events/facilities. Individuals/organizations generally face a title limit of four animals per 12 months under adoption (more can be held under care agreements), but sales of unadoptable animals and group purchases for sanctuaries have more flexibility. Title transfers after ~1 year of approved care for https://t.co/gWL0N5i4bQ +1

Long-term holding contracts — BLM periodically solicits private landowners for Off-Range Pastures (ORPs) that can hold hundreds to thousands of horses in free-roaming conditions for multi-year terms. Colorado is often eligible. Watch https://t.co/BxIBZZeFft for solicitations (register your entity there first—free Unique Entity ID required). BLM pays a negotiated per-head/day rate; contractors supply land, forage, water, fencing, and care meeting strict welfare standards. Site visits occur. This is the closest match for large-scale, ongoing intake of gathered https://t.co/Re5JBvAA19 +1

Local Colorado context — Colorado has four main herd management areas (Piceance-East Douglas, Sand Wash Basin, Little Book Cliffs, Spring Creek Basin). Gathers occur periodically when numbers exceed Appropriate Management Levels. The state also has a Wild Horse Advisory Committee and Department of Agriculture support program (email CDA_wildhorseprogram@state.co.us (mailto:_wildhorseprogram@state.co.us)).ag.colorado.gov

text:
Fusion info-invest in America

TAE Technologies (via Trump Media & Technology Group, NASDAQ: DJT) is the leading pure-play developer of aneutronic proton-boron (p-B11) fusion. It uses advanced beam-driven field-reversed configurations (FRCs). The company has raised well over $1.3–1.5 billion (investors include Google, Chevron, NEA, Goldman Sachs, and others) and has demonstrated key plasma and fusion milestones, including p-B11 reactions in collaboration with Japan’s NIFS.
In December 2025 it announced an all-stock merger with Trump Media & Technology Group valued at more than $6 billion. TMTG has already transferred significant capital to TAE; the deal remains on track for closing by the end of 2026 (S-4 filing in process). Buying DJT provides direct public-market exposure to TAE’s aneutronic program and its planned commercial path (50 MWe pilot siting and longer-term utility-scale plants).
American Fusion Inc. (OTC: AMFN, formerly Renewal Fuels / RNWF) completed a reverse merger with Kepler Fusion Technologies in early 2026. It is developing the Texatron platform—a compact, pulsed, modular aneutronic system optimized primarily for deuterium–helium-3 (D-He3). The design emphasizes direct electricity conversion, reduced neutron output, and distributed/commercial deployment (data centers, industrial, defense). It trades on the OTC markets and has been expanding its patent portfolio around the Texatron “clam-shell” architecture.
Helion Energy (private) pursues near-aneutronic deuterium–helium-3 fusion in a pulsed field-reversed configuration. It has raised roughly $1.5 billion total, reached a $15.5 billion valuation in its mid-2026 Series G, holds a power-purchase agreement with Microsoft targeting 2028 delivery, and has additional offtake/industrial partnerships (including Nucor). Shares trade on secondary/private markets for accredited investors (e.g., Forge).
Marvel Fusion (Germany, private) is advancing laser-driven inertial-confinement fusion with proton-boron fuel and nanostructured targets. It has raised hundreds of millions of euros in private and public funding (including EQT Ventures, Siemens Energy Ventures, European Innovation Council support) and is building a major laser facility in partnership with Colorado State University.
HB11 Energy (Australia, private) focuses on non-thermal laser-driven hydrogen-boron fusion. It has demonstrated relevant laser-boron reactions and continues R&D and target/laser development with international partners; funding is more modest than the larger players.
Additional private efforts include Blue Laser Fusion (laser p-B11) and various smaller or China-based programs (e.g., ENN’s spherical-torus p-B11 work). Access for most private names is through venture rounds or secondary platforms available to accredited/qualified investors.
The clearest currently liquid public routes to pure or near-aneutronic fusion are DJT (TAE) and AMFN (Kepler/Texatron). Helion offers the highest-profile private near-aneutronic exposure with commercial offtake agreements already in place.

American companies supply many of the specialized parts and systems needed for aneutronic fusion approaches (primarily p-B11 and D-He3 in field-reversed configurations or laser-driven systems). Key needs include high-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets, neutral beam injectors (NBI) and particle accelerators, permanent/rare-earth magnets and assemblies, vacuum/cryogenic systems, precision components, power electronics/capacitors, and related materials.
Magnets and Superconductors
•General Atomics (GA, San Diego, CA) — Designs, engineers, and fabricates large-scale low- and high-temperature superconducting magnets. It completed major pulsed superconducting magnet modules for ITER and has broad fusion magnet capabilities plus experience with related systems.

text:
Books ... How to Quit Cars

By Adam Gopnik
15MAY2023
https://t.co/31IZiM8hA5

They crowd streets, belch carbon, bifurcate communities, and destroy the urban fabric. 

Will we ever overcome our addiction?

“The Honeymooners” (1955-56), the greatest American television comedy, is—to a degree more evident now than then—essentially a series about public transportation in New York. 

Ralph Kramden (Jackie Gleason) is a New York City bus driver, deeply proud to be so and drawing a salary sufficient to support a nonworking wife in a Brooklyn apartment, not to mention a place in a thriving bowling league and membership in the Loyal Order of Raccoon Lodge. 

His employer is the Gotham Bus Company, which seems to be the sort of private-public enterprise that, like the I.R.T., built the subways. 

He and his best friend, Ed Norton (Art Carney), who works in the sewers, make daily use of the subway and bus system, which was designed to whisk the outer-borough working classes into light-industrial Manhattan. 

Neither the Kramdens nor the Nortons seem to own an automobile. 

When Ed and Ralph go to Minneapolis for a Raccoons convention, they take a sleeper car on a train.

What’s striking is that no one watching in the fifties needed to think about any of this. 

Public transportation was the self-evident bedrock of working-class life. 

Yet it was also in the mid-fifties that the hipsters and beatniks and rebels feverishly celebrated the car and the burst of autonomy, even anarchy, it offered to postwar life. 

In Jack Kerouac’s “On the Road,” the car was the vehicle of liberty for the bohemian kids of those working-class Brooklynites. 

Allen Ginsberg’s “Howl” pities those “who chained themselves to subways for the endless ride from Battery to holy Bronx on Benzedrine / until the noise of wheels and children brought them low,” while dreaming wetly of the glories of the open road, which leads to sex, possibly with an idealized version of Neal Cassady, subsequently memorialized as Kerouac’s irresistible Dean Moriarty. 

Cars are for poets and outlaws, the subway for the intimidated and the enslaved.

Kramden and Norton vs. Kerouac and Ginsberg: today, everything has flipped. 

Public transit is now the cause of the reforming classes, and the car their villain. 

The car is the consumer economy on wheels: atomizing, competitive, inhuman

—and implicitly racist, hiving people off to segregated communities—

while the subway and the train are communal zendos. 

Good people ride bicycles and buses; bad people ride in ever-bigger cars. 

Capitalism, not Dean Moriarty, is in the front seat.

The history of transportation will always be social history, writ large. 

Food tastes can change from decade to decade, even from year to year; the history of transportation tends to span half-century intervals, marking whole epochs in consciousness. 

How we move unites us. 

The Paris Métro and the New York subway, built at roughly the same time, undergird two cities where people ate and made love in different ways but remained modern, in large part, because they moved rapidly in units. 

The weary and wary faces of Daumier’s people, in his images of “Les Transports en Commun,” are still familiar. 

Any insular New Yorker instantly “gets” Paris and its Métro; it’s harder for us to “get” Los Angeles.

Perhaps because transportation histories take place on such a big scale, they tend to be highly moralizing: we can be amused by the small gradations in how we eat, but major alterations in how we move must have, we think, some cause or even conspiracy behind them. 

And so the history of roads and what runs on them often ignores the tragedies of good intentions and the comedies of unintended consequences that genuinely got them going. 

People routinely insist, without evidence, that the wide boulevards of Paris were built by Baron Haussmann to prevent revolutionary barricades, even though boulevards were a nearly universal feature of urban development in the later nineteenth century; Philadelphia built them extravagantly, and Kansas City boasted that it had more boulevards than Paris, without any Communards to cannonade. 

People always maintain, similarly, that the big auto manufacturers killed L.A.’s once efficient public-transit system, leaving the city at the mercy of polluting and gridlocked cars. 

That this is, at best, a very partial truth does not weaken its claim on our consciousness. Even our local effort to cast “master builder” Robert Moses as a unique culprit in the story of what went wrong in New York—too many expressways and not enough trains—runs into the fact that Moses was essentially executing ideas that nearly all reformers of his era shared; what happened in New York happened in other big Northern cities at the same time. 

Meanwhile, the preservationist movement that stopped his worst plans is now under fire from the same progressives who used to despise him.

Two new books take up the case against cars, the dominant mode of twentieth-century transportation, from a generally progressive perspective. 

Daniel Knowles’s “Carmageddon” (Abrams), despite its jokey title, is a serious diatribe against cars as agents of social oppression, international inequality, and ecological disaster. 

Henry Grabar’s “Paved Paradise” (Penguin Press) is an anti-parking polemic, with many bits of mordant social history related in a good-natured and at times puckish vein. 

Both books make an argument for alternatives—rapid transit, trains and trolleys, bicycles—but they spend most of their time damning the current conjuncture.

For Knowles, cars are unredeemable instruments of evil. 

He is a writer for The Economist, and his book reads like a series of Economist pieces: briskly written, well researched, and with a knack for landing the significant statistic right after the crisply summarized argument. 

Though he has a few horse-and-buggy narrative mannerisms—he insists on ending a chapter with a paragraph foreshadowing the contents of the next—he is passionate about his subject. 

Cars are dangerous beyond description, their noxiousness beyond the planet’s power to scrub away. 

America has exported its car addiction to the developing world, where congestion, pollution, and destruction of the urban fabric are even worse than they are here. 

The swelling metropolises of emerging nations, such as Brazil’s São Paulo, are bad mock Los Angeleses, their economies stalled along with their traffic: 

“A huge amount of economic growth has been squandered, with the extra income that people are earning being spent sitting in traffic on ever-more polluted roads, instead of on actually living better lives.”

No remedy seems possible. 

The electric car is a chimera, producing more pollution in its construction than its existence justifies, and the dream of a driverless car can never be realized. 

Knowles details the casualties caused by driverless cars, with perhaps too obvious pleasure. 

(Overreacting to accidents is a bad habit when it comes to new kinds of transportation: the disaster of the Hindenburg helped end dirigible travel, a mostly safe, efficient, and by all accounts exceptionally pleasant means of conveyance. 

“Oh, the humanity!” an announcer famously moaned as he watched it burn, but humanity would probably have benefitted from more and better blimps.) 

Still, Knowles is persuasively scathing about the absurdity of Elon Musk’s version of a subway—an underground tunnel that sends individual Tesla cars looping through Las Vegas, common train compartments having evidently been judged crime-prone.

Knowles does ride several slightly dated hobbyhorses, often imputing cupidity as an explanation where stupidity alone would do. 

Jane Jacobs, the enemy of expressways, is given a breathless introduction, and her half-century-old triumph over Robert Moses’s plan to build a highway through SoHo is related yet again. 

But even those of us who think of her as something close to a saint can still recognize that, as with all saints, not everything she believed was true. 

The West Village she loved was a snapshot taken between economic epochs.

Knowles also blames expressways—he focusses on one that goes through Atlanta—for enforcing the segregation of American life, by separating suburbs and inner cities ever more aggressively. 

And yet ascribing general transportation schemes to local American evils risks missing the bigger picture. 

In the postwar period, projects like that were everywhere. 

Paris created its own version with the Pompidou expressway, cutting off the Right Bank from the river, an amputation that ended only last year. 

Philadelphia got the Delaware Expressway, courtesy of Ed Bacon. 

As revisionist urban historians have pointed out, the disagreements among urbanists hardly fall along neat political lines; many of the devils in this story, like Bacon and Edward Logue, were the more consciously progressive figures, while the angels were defending stagnant and immobile arrangements that eventually priced out all but the rich—so that Jacobs’s beloved Hudson Street, left mainly unaltered in its small-scale charm, has few remaining locksmiths and bakers and is a ghetto of the wealthy.

For many Americans, cars are as potent a symbol of freedom as guns are, even if they have similarly destructive consequences.

text:
Books ... How to Quit Cars

By Adam Gopnik
15MAY2023
https://t.co/31IZiM8hA5

They crowd streets, belch carbon, bifurcate communities, and destroy the urban fabric. 

Will we ever overcome our addiction?

“The Honeymooners” (1955-56), the greatest American television comedy, is—to a degree more evident now than then—essentially a series about public transportation in New York. 

Ralph Kramden (Jackie Gleason) is a New York City bus driver, deeply proud to be so and drawing a salary sufficient to support a nonworking wife in a Brooklyn apartment, not to mention a place in a thriving bowling league and membership in the Loyal Order of Raccoon Lodge. 

His employer is the Gotham Bus Company, which seems to be the sort of private-public enterprise that, like the I.R.T., built the subways. 

He and his best friend, Ed Norton (Art Carney), who works in the sewers, make daily use of the subway and bus system, which was designed to whisk the outer-borough working classes into light-industrial Manhattan. 

Neither the Kramdens nor the Nortons seem to own an automobile. 

When Ed and Ralph go to Minneapolis for a Raccoons convention, they take a sleeper car on a train.

What’s striking is that no one watching in the fifties needed to think about any of this. 

Public transportation was the self-evident bedrock of working-class life. 

Yet it was also in the mid-fifties that the hipsters and beatniks and rebels feverishly celebrated the car and the burst of autonomy, even anarchy, it offered to postwar life. 

In Jack Kerouac’s “On the Road,” the car was the vehicle of liberty for the bohemian kids of those working-class Brooklynites. 

Allen Ginsberg’s “Howl” pities those “who chained themselves to subways for the endless ride from Battery to holy Bronx on Benzedrine / until the noise of wheels and children brought them low,” while dreaming wetly of the glories of the open road, which leads to sex, possibly with an idealized version of Neal Cassady, subsequently memorialized as Kerouac’s irresistible Dean Moriarty. 

Cars are for poets and outlaws, the subway for the intimidated and the enslaved.

Kramden and Norton vs. Kerouac and Ginsberg: today, everything has flipped. 

Public transit is now the cause of the reforming classes, and the car their villain. 

The car is the consumer economy on wheels: atomizing, competitive, inhuman

—and implicitly racist, hiving people off to segregated communities—

while the subway and the train are communal zendos. 

Good people ride bicycles and buses; bad people ride in ever-bigger cars. 

Capitalism, not Dean Moriarty, is in the front seat.

The history of transportation will always be social history, writ large. 

Food tastes can change from decade to decade, even from year to year; the history of transportation tends to span half-century intervals, marking whole epochs in consciousness. 

How we move unites us. 

The Paris Métro and the New York subway, built at roughly the same time, undergird two cities where people ate and made love in different ways but remained modern, in large part, because they moved rapidly in units. 

The weary and wary faces of Daumier’s people, in his images of “Les Transports en Commun,” are still familiar. 

Any insular New Yorker instantly “gets” Paris and its Métro; it’s harder for us to “get” Los Angeles.

Perhaps because transportation histories take place on such a big scale, they tend to be highly moralizing: we can be amused by the small gradations in how we eat, but major alterations in how we move must have, we think, some cause or even conspiracy behind them. 

And so the history of roads and what runs on them often ignores the tragedies of good intentions and the comedies of unintended consequences that genuinely got them going. 

People routinely insist, without evidence, that the wide boulevards of Paris were built by Baron Haussmann to prevent revolutionary barricades, even though boulevards were a nearly universal feature of urban development in the later nineteenth century; Philadelphia built them extravagantly, and Kansas City boasted that it had more boulevards than Paris, without any Communards to cannonade. 

People always maintain, similarly, that the big auto manufacturers killed L.A.’s once efficient public-transit system, leaving the city at the mercy of polluting and gridlocked cars. 

That this is, at best, a very partial truth does not weaken its claim on our consciousness. Even our local effort to cast “master builder” Robert Moses as a unique culprit in the story of what went wrong in New York—too many expressways and not enough trains—runs into the fact that Moses was essentially executing ideas that nearly all reformers of his era shared; what happened in New York happened in other big Northern cities at the same time. 

Meanwhile, the preservationist movement that stopped his worst plans is now under fire from the same progressives who used to despise him.

Two new books take up the case against cars, the dominant mode of twentieth-century transportation, from a generally progressive perspective. 

Daniel Knowles’s “Carmageddon” (Abrams), despite its jokey title, is a serious diatribe against cars as agents of social oppression, international inequality, and ecological disaster. 

Henry Grabar’s “Paved Paradise” (Penguin Press) is an anti-parking polemic, with many bits of mordant social history related in a good-natured and at times puckish vein. 

Both books make an argument for alternatives—rapid transit, trains and trolleys, bicycles—but they spend most of their time damning the current conjuncture.

For Knowles, cars are unredeemable instruments of evil. 

He is a writer for The Economist, and his book reads like a series of Economist pieces: briskly written, well researched, and with a knack for landing the significant statistic right after the crisply summarized argument. 

Though he has a few horse-and-buggy narrative mannerisms—he insists on ending a chapter with a paragraph foreshadowing the contents of the next—he is passionate about his subject. 

Cars are dangerous beyond description, their noxiousness beyond the planet’s power to scrub away. 

America has exported its car addiction to the developing world, where congestion, pollution, and destruction of the urban fabric are even worse than they are here. 

The swelling metropolises of emerging nations, such as Brazil’s São Paulo, are bad mock Los Angeleses, their economies stalled along with their traffic: 

“A huge amount of economic growth has been squandered, with the extra income that people are earning being spent sitting in traffic on ever-more polluted roads, instead of on actually living better lives.”

No remedy seems possible. 

The electric car is a chimera, producing more pollution in its construction than its existence justifies, and the dream of a driverless car can never be realized. 

Knowles details the casualties caused by driverless cars, with perhaps too obvious pleasure. 

(Overreacting to accidents is a bad habit when it comes to new kinds of transportation: the disaster of the Hindenburg helped end dirigible travel, a mostly safe, efficient, and by all accounts exceptionally pleasant means of conveyance. 

“Oh, the humanity!” an announcer famously moaned as he watched it burn, but humanity would probably have benefitted from more and better blimps.)

text:
PAYPAL $PYPL LOST $8.2 BILLION OVERNIGHT. S&P 500 FUTURES ARE DOWN 2.75 POINTS:

PayPal PYPL at $51.86 (premarket), -$9.61 / -15.6% from Thursday's $61.47 close. The San Jose company runs the payment button at online checkouts, plus Venmo and Braintree. Bloomberg News reported that the group trying to buy the entire company - the private-equity firm Advent International and the privately held payments company Stripe - has dropped the pursuit. PayPal, Stripe and Advent each declined to comment. So a 15.6% fall is happening this morning on a news report that none of the three companies involved has confirmed.

Multiply that $9.61 by the 855.5M PayPal shares in existence and about $8.2B of market value - one share's price times every share, the whole company's price tag - went missing between Thursday's closing bell and this sentence.

Now look at what the American futures board did with it. Index futures are contracts on where an index will trade at a set date later on. They run all night, which makes them the earliest and least reliable clue about where the 9:30am ET opening bell lands.

- Dow futures: 53,637.00, +16.00 pts / +0.03%.
- S&P 500 futures: 7,739.75, -2.75 pts / -0.04%.
- Nasdaq-100 futures: 29,611.50, -84.25 pts / -0.28%.
- Russell 2000 futures: 3,014.70, -4.30 pts / -0.14%.

WHY $8.2 BILLION BARELY REGISTERS

An index is an average, and an average is a machine for making one loud number quiet. The S&P 500 tracks 500 companies. PayPal was worth $52.6B at Thursday's close - real money, and a modest slice of that crowd. Spread one company's worst night of the year across 499 others having an ordinary one and you get 2.75 points.

The funds that hold those baskets say the same thing. SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust, ticker SPY, at $771.06 (premarket), -$0.04 / -0.01% from Thursday's $771.10 close. Four cents. Invesco QQQ Trust, ticker QQQ, at $719.07 (premarket), -$2.04 / -0.28% from $721.11 - it tracks the Nasdaq-100, a much shorter list, and PayPal is on it.

That is most of the split on the board above. The Dow contract is the green one because the Dow holds 30 companies, and neither of this morning's two big fallers is among them.

THE OTHER FALLER IS THE BIGGER INDEX EVENT

Marvell Technology at $221.24 (premarket), -$20.21 / -8.4% from Thursday's $241.45 close. The Wilmington, Delaware company designs the chips that shuttle data around inside a data center - the plumbing of the AI build-out rather than the processors that get the headlines.

It reported its fiscal second quarter Thursday after the close: record revenue - money coming in the door - of $2.739B, +37% from a year earlier and +13% from the previous three months; adjusted profit per share, meaning earnings with certain one-time items set aside, of $0.94. Both cleared what analysts expected. Management then raised its own map twice over, to about $12B of revenue this fiscal year from about $11.5B, and to about $18B next year from about $16.5B.

The stock is down 8.4% anyway, and the reason is the price it was already carrying. Marvell has climbed roughly 28% in a month and sits 260% above the $61.44 it traded at last September 4. A beat of about 1% does not pay for a run like that.

Here is why it matters more than PayPal to the board above. Marvell is worth about $211.5B, four times PayPal's size, so an 8.4% fall is roughly $17.7B - more than twice the money that came off PayPal - and Marvell sits on that same short Nasdaq-100 list. Two names, one index, and the technology-heavy contract being the reddest thing on the screen stops being a mystery.

EUROPE IS GREEN AND NONE OF IT IS CROSSING

- CAC 40 (France): 8,401, +81.03 pts / +0.97%.
- DAX (Germany): 26,495, +127.46 pts / +0.48%.
- FTSE 100 (UK): 10,810, +17.00 pts / +0.16%.

Paris is leading the continent on a morning its own inflation reading got hotter. INSEE, France's national statistics agency, put its first estimate of August consumer prices at 2.7% above a year earlier on the harmonised measure - the version built so euro-area countries can be compared like for like - up from 2.4% in July, with energy prices running 16.7% above a year ago. Separately, Fitch Ratings, one of the three big agencies that grade how likely a government is to repay what it borrows, reviews France today; it cut that grade from AA- to A+ on September 13, 2025. A market up nearly a percent into both of those is not one braced for either. Europe still has three and a half hours of its own session left to change its mind.

THE EMPTY 8:30 AND THE CROWDED 10:00

Most mornings a government data release lands at 8:30am ET and futures reprice on it in the hour before the bell. Today that slot is empty. Nothing scheduled arrives between now and the open, which is a large part of why those four contracts have barely moved since dawn.

Then 10:00am ET, half an hour after the bell, two things land together.

- The University of Michigan's Surveys of Consumers publishes its final August reading - a monthly survey asking American households how they feel about their own money and the wider economy, scored as an index. The preliminary reading was 51.0 against about 54.5 expected, -7.6% from July, with households penciling in 4.3% price rises over the coming year.
- Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh gives his first keynote as chair at the Kansas City Fed's annual symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming. He speaks two days after the Bureau of Economic Analysis put the personal consumption expenditures price index for July - the inflation gauge the Fed watches most closely, because it follows what people actually buy - at 3.7% above a year earlier, unchanged from June and hotter than the 3.6% economists expected.

New York is coming off a strong Thursday, which is worth holding beside all of the above: the S&P 500 closed at 7,730.99, +55.29 pts / +0.72%, and the Nasdaq-100 at 29,641.56, +417.04 pts / +1.43%. Hold every overnight figure loosely, though. Pre-dawn trading is thin, so a move made by few participants gets undone by few, and nothing printed before sunrise owes anybody a promise it survives to 9:30am.

Two dates ahead of that: Monday is month-end, when funds adjust holdings into the close and prices can move on housekeeping rather than news, and next Friday, September 4, the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes the August jobs report at 8:30am ET. That slot will not be empty.

WHERE THESE TWO SIT

PayPal is 40th of 46 on the Quality-Value Len5, the style that wants a durable business at a fair price. The fair-price half is loud this morning: at $51.86 the shares cost about 9.9 times the last year of profit, and the company keeps buying back its own stock, which quietly raises every remaining owner's slice. The durable half is the open question, and it has nothing to do with the deal. It comes from the July 28 report, where the total spent through PayPal's systems rose 10% while transaction margin dollars - the money PayPal keeps from each payment after the cost of moving it - rose 1%. Volume growing ten times faster than the money kept is the thing to watch; that gap closing settles the read, and another year of it widening breaks it.

PayPal is on none of the other five. Deep-Value and Special-Situations hunts the genuinely cheap or a business carrying a dated event - there was an event, and this morning it evaporated, which is exactly why an unsigned offer is not something to lean on; a signed agreement with a closing date would change that. Momentum watches names already breaking out on news of their own, and a 15.6% fall on a stock 34.5% under the $79.215 it reached last October 28 is the opposite shape. Both growth styles want expansion you are not overpaying for, and mid-single-digit revenue growth with profit per share going backwards is not expansion. Income watches cash genuinely reaching owners, and what leaves here goes out through buybacks rather than a payout worth a real share of the price - a dividend that mattered against the share price is the change.

Marvell is on none of the six. Both value styles want a fair price standing beside a durable business, and at about 84 times the last year of profit the price half is missing; a real markdown with data-center demand still growing would bring either into range. Both growth styles want expansion you are not overpaying for - the expansion is genuine at 37%, and the price is again the half that fails. Momentum watches names already breaking out on a live event of their own, and a company that posts a record quarter, raises two years of guidance and falls 8.4% anyway is the exact opposite shape; clearing the $329.88 it reached on June 18 on heavy volume would be the change. Income is settled on size, at $0.06 a quarter against a $221 share.

Thursday's closing price of $61.47 was a bet that somebody would eventually pay more than the $60.50 a share on the table. This morning there is no offer, no statement from any of the three companies, and a stock 15.6% lower than it was at the bell. At 10:00am the newest Fed chair gives his first keynote at a symposium whose subject this year is what payments become next - and one of the country's largest payment companies will spend that hour finding out what it is worth standing on its own.

Not investment advice.

EARNINGS PREVIEW - MARVELL $MRVL PROMISED GOOGLE 7% OF ITSELF FOR $120B OF CHIPS:

Marvell Technology $MRVL at $240.01, -$0.37 / -0.15% today. The Wilmington, Delaware chip designer builds the custom processors, optical parts and storage controllers that wire AI data centers together. Second-quarter fiscal 2027 results, for the three months ended August 1, land after Thursday's close, August 27, with the call at 1:45pm PT / 4:45pm ET - a date the company set itself.

Eight days ago the setup changed. An August 19 filing disclosed a custom-chip agreement signed July 29 with Alphabet $GOOGL at $343.19, -$3.77 / -1.09% today, the Mountain View owner of Google. Attached to it: a warrant - a contract letting the holder buy stock later at a price fixed today - for 58,970,907 Marvell shares at $206.58, good until August 18, 2033. That is roughly $12.2B of stock and close to 7% of the company.

Read the vesting before the headline. Only 1,360,867 of those shares unlock on a calendar. The other 57.6M unlock in 240 slices, one for every $500M of custom product Google actually buys - roughly $120B of purchases through fiscal 2033. Google is not being handed 7% of Marvell. It is being offered 7% at $206.58 if it spends $ 120B.

The bar for Thursday is Marvell's own. In May, for the quarter ended May 2: revenue $2,417.8M, +28% year over year, with data center at $1,832.7M, +27% - 76% of the whole company. Non-GAAP earnings - profit per share with some one-time items stripped - $0.80. Operating cash flow $638.8M, a record. Management then mapped this quarter at $2.700B +/- 5%, about +35% on last year's $2,006.1M, with non-GAAP EPS of $0.93 +/- $0.05.

Three questions going in, not predictions.

- Does revenue land inside that $2.700B band, and is data center still roughly three of every four sales dollars?
- Does gross margin - what is left of each sales dollar after making the product - hold the guided 58.25% to 59.25%? The trend is the real question: 61.9% two years ago, 59.4% a year ago, 58.9% last quarter. Chips built to one buyer's design earn less per dollar than parts sold to everyone. Growing into Google is not free.
- What gets written for next quarter, and does the roughly $11.5B fiscal 2027 and $16.5B fiscal 2028 revenue map management laid out in May still stand? An investor day follows October 6 in New York.

Published analyst models sit near $2.71B and $0.93 adjusted - expectations on the record, not a forecast from here.

The stock got here violently. From the June 18 close of $310.58 it fell to $163.40 on July 29, -47.4% in six weeks. It has added +$76.61 / +46.9% since. Two sessions did most of that: August 4, +12.8% on a new AI memory product line, and August 19, +9.85% on the Google filing. It still sits 27.2% under the June 18 intraday high of $329.88.

Len5 fit: Marvell is on none of the six. Hypergrowth is the right shape - early, fast-growing disruptors - and roughly 40% guided growth qualifies, but a $210B company is past early; a growth break, not more growth, settles that. Quality-Value and Growth both want a fair price, and 82x trailing earnings against 11.6x book value - assets minus liabilities - is the half that fails; a deep drawdown with earnings power unchanged changes it. Income is the loudest no: $0.06 a quarter is a 0.10% yield. Alphabet is the top-ranked name on Quality-Value - a durable search and cloud franchise at a real discount - and sits 44th on Deep-Value and Special-Situations; the price climbing back toward the rest of megacap tech takes it off both.

One number in that agreement is already settled: $206.58. Everything else has to be earned $500 million at a time, and Thursday is the first quarter that counts toward it.

text:
The AI Upside #59

What if finding information about disability services was as simple as asking a question?

For people with disabilities and their caregivers, getting help can sometimes mean navigating dense government documents, complicated benefit information, and lengthy PDFs just to figure out where to start.

Researchers at the University of Delaware tested whether AI could make that process easier.

They created a closed-system generative AI chatbot trained specifically on public disability-services documents.

Then they put it to the test.

In a study involving 334 participants, half used the AI chatbot to answer common questions about benefits and services, while the other half searched the original PDF documents.

The results were encouraging.

People using the chatbot answered the questions more accurately.

They also reported significantly lower administrative burden than participants searching through the PDFs.

That matters because accessibility isn't only about ramps, screen readers, or physical accommodations.

Information itself needs to be accessible.

When important answers are buried inside complicated documents, finding the right service can become another obstacle for people already navigating complex systems.

AI offers an interesting way to reduce some of that friction by helping people find and understand information that already exists.

There are important limitations.

This was a research-tested prototype in a controlled setting. The chatbot did not determine eligibility, approve benefits, or replace human caseworkers. The university's public summary also does not provide the exact effect sizes for the improvements.

But the idea demonstrated here is powerful:

Sometimes making a system more accessible doesn't require changing the services themselves.

It starts by making those services easier to understand and navigate.

Real stories. Real impact.

Scale: 334 participants, with approximately half using the chatbot and half searching the original documents.

Key findings:

• Participants using the AI chatbot answered disability-services questions more accurately than participants searching PDFs.

• Chatbot users reported significantly lower administrative burden.

Important limitation: The university's public summary does not provide effect sizes, exact group counts, or detailed statistical results. The study evaluated information navigation in a research setting, not actual benefits eligibility or service approval.

text:
Atiku; the leader Nigeria needs

By Haruna Lawal

Nigeria finds itself at a crossroads. The current administration's policies, have left the average citizen grappling with a cost-of-living crisis, while insecurity continues to blight agricultural heartlands. As the 2027 elections loom, the question on every mind is this: who possesses the requisite experience, the national coalition, and the bold vision to steer the nation back to prosperity? For a growing number of Nigerians, the answer lies in former Vice President Atiku Abubakar.

Atiku is not a newcomer to the political scene; he is a reformer with the scars of leadership. His tenure as Vice President from 1999 to 2007 remains a benchmark for economic liberalisation. As chairman of the National Economic Council, he oversaw the deregulation of the telecommunications sector, a move that unleashed millions of jobs and billions in private investment, transforming how Nigerians live and work. This track record suggests a man who understands the levers of economic policy, not merely as theory, but as a practical tool for national development.

His latest policy proposals demonstrate a nuanced understanding of fiscal reality. While the current government removed the fuel subsidy, Atiku has proposed a targeted alternative. His Atiku Economic Recovery Plan does not suggest a return to the opaque import-subsidy regime but a shift toward a "production subsidy" that would incentivise domestic refining. The principle is sound: subsidise the barrel of oil produced in Nigeria, not the one imported. By making the process capped, transparent, and independently audited, he aims to lower energy costs while preventing the fraud that characterised the old system. This is not a return to the past, but a carefully calibrated instrument for industrial growth.

Beyond economics, Atiku offers a coherent plan for national cohesion. The endless cycle of farmer-herder clashes, particularly in states like Benue, has destroyed lives and livelihoods. Atiku has pledged to end this violence by resurrecting the peace accord model he successfully deployed in 2001 to broker peace between Fulani and Tiv communities. He understands that without security, the nation cannot feed itself, and he has promised the investment needed to reopen railway lines and roads to connect the food basket states to the rest of the country.

However, a leader must also be a unifier. Nigeria's diversity is its strength, but it demands a president capable of building bridges. Atiku's political career demonstrates an ability to build national coalitions across regional, religious, and party lines. He has long been one of the most consistent advocates for "True Federalism," arguing that empowering states to control their resources and establish their own police forces is essential for accountability and development.

Ultimately, the argument for Atiku rests on the premise that Nigeria cannot afford another experiment. The nation needs steady hands to guide it through turbulent waters. With his experience, his detailed economic blueprints, and his commitment to restructuring, Atiku Abubakar presents himself as the leader equipped to rebuild trust in governance and unite the country around a shared vision of prosperity.

Haruna Lawal writes from Kaduna.

text:
Home Depot $HD today announced its new "Express Delivery" service

Express Delivery offers rapid delivery of many SKUs direct to homes and job sites in 3 hours or less 

The service utilizes Home Depot's ~2,350 retail stores as neighborhood fulfillment "hubs"

The strategy makes sense

Especially since ~90% of the U.S. population lives within 10 miles of a Home Depot store

But it also begs the question:

Will Home Depot need to enlarge its stores to better accommodate express delivery and online fulfillment?

After all many other retailers are also embracing the "stores-as-a-delivery hub" model 

But they are adding new stores in larger real estate: 

▪️ ~1/2 of new AutoZone $AZO store openings are in Big Box "Mega Hubs" that are 5x the size of a standard store and geared to provide rapid delivery to its collision center customers

▪️ Advance Auto $AAP and O'Reilly $ORLY are also opening dozens of Big Box hub stores that support store fulfillment--and delivery 

▪️ Many recently-opened Tractor Supply $TSCO stores are in spaces of ~40-50K sq ft--or nearly 3x the size of its standard real estate prototype--in part to fulfill online orders and provide "Final Mile" delivery services

Even Costco $COST is increasing the size of some new of its clubs to provide facilitate store-based delivery:

The new club that Costco is building in Fresno, CA will be ~219K sq ft, or ~50% larger than a standard club

One reason why the new club is so much larger?

It will include a ~47K sq ft "Market Delivery Operation" distribution space where large and heavy items like appliances and furniture will be loaded onto box trucks for last mile delivery to Costco members

text:
Blessed Victor Chumillas Fernandez was a Spanish Franciscan priest and martyr of the Catholic Church who died during the religious persecution that accompanied the Spanish Civil War. Born on 28 July 1902 in the small town of Olmeda del Rey in the province of Cuenca, he grew up in a humble and devout family of six children. After the early death of his father he helped support his mother by working while still attending school and catechism classes. From childhood he showed a strong attraction to the religious life and was especially moved by stories of the martyrs of Japan.

In 1914 he entered the Franciscan minor seminary at Belmonte. He took the Franciscan habit in 1917 at Pastrana, made his first profession the following year, professed solemn vows in 1923, and was ordained a priest in Toledo in 1925. Over the next decade he served in various houses of the Order of Friars Minor as teacher, rector of students, guardian, preacher, catechist, and spiritual director. He also edited Franciscan magazines, founded a journal of essays on science, art and religion, directed choirs, played the organ, wrote poetry and composed music. In the autumn of 1935 he was appointed guardian and rector of the Franciscan convent and theologate at Consuegra in the province of Toledo, where he guided a community that included several priests and a large group of young theology students.

When the Civil War broke out in July 1936 the friars were expelled from their convent. A few weeks later they were arrested and confined first in the local jail and then in the parish church. Throughout their captivity Father Victor strengthened his brothers with prayer, confession, renewal of vows, and words of encouragement, openly expressing his own desire for martyrdom. In the early hours of 16 August 1936 twenty members of the community, led by their guardian, were taken by truck to a lonely spot called Boca de Balondillo near Fuente el Fresno in the province of Ciudad Real. There they were shot. Before dying they prayed the Our Father and forgave their executioners. Father Victor urged them to lift their eyes to heaven and to offer their lives joyfully for Christ.

Two other Franciscans of the same province, killed in September and October of the same year, completed the group of twenty-two. The Church later recognized that they had died in hatred of the faith. On 28 October 2007 Pope Benedict XVI declared Victor Chumillas Fernandez and his twenty-one companions blessed. Their liturgical memorial is kept on 6 November. Their remains now rest in the Franciscan church of San Juan de los Reyes in Toledo, a quiet witness to a community that chose fidelity to Christ even unto death.

text:
Dr. Samuel Caldwell Benedict: The State Board of Health President Who Defended Dr. Roy F. Harris

Dr. Samuel Caldwell Benedict, M.D. (1855–1914), was one of Georgia’s senior physicians, medical educators, and public-health officials when he entered the Leo Frank trial as a prosecution rebuttal witness on Tuesday, August 19, 1913. The following morning, The Atlanta Constitution featured his photograph on page 3 beneath the heading “Defends Dr. Harris.” The portrait was credited to Francis E. Price, staff photographer, and identified him simply as “DR. SAMUEL BENEDICT” (AC, 1).

Benedict was far more than an ordinary local physician. His full name was Samuel Caldwell Benedict, and by 1913 he was dean of the University of Georgia School of Pharmacy and professor of materia medica. The University of Georgia’s 1913–1915 catalogue lists him in precisely those positions (UGA, 3). Georgia Archives also identifies Benedict as the first dean of the University of Georgia School of Pharmacy, which had been established in 1903, and records that he died in 1914 (DLG, 4).

His medical career stretched back decades. In 1894, Benedict was identified as professor of medical jurisprudence at the University of Georgia and vice president of the National Association of Railway Surgeons. An address he delivered before the Medical Association of Georgia that year was subsequently published in the medical literature. By the time of the Frank trial, the Atlanta Georgian described Benedict as having served on the University of Georgia faculty for thirty-two years (PMC, 5; AG, 2).

Benedict’s importance at the Frank trial arose from the defense attack upon Dr. H. F. “Roy” Harris, secretary of the Georgia State Board of Health. Harris had examined Mary Phagan’s remains and offered medical testimony concerning the condition of her stomach, the digestion of her last meal, the injuries to her body, and his estimate of the time of death. The defense devoted several medical witnesses to challenging his conclusions and professional methods.

One of those witnesses was Dr. Willis F. Westmoreland, a former president of the State Board of Health. On August 11, Westmoreland attacked Harris’s scientific conclusions and testified that he had previously brought charges of “scientific dishonesty” against Harris. Westmoreland claimed that the board had found Harris guilty but refused to remove him, causing Westmoreland to resign. Contemporary reporting, however, stated that the board had instead given Harris a “clean bill” after Westmoreland brought the accusation (AC, 6).

Solicitor General Hugh M. Dorsey therefore called Benedict during the State’s rebuttal on the afternoon of Tuesday, August 19, 1913. Benedict was especially valuable because he was then president of the Georgia State Board of Health and could speak directly about the board proceedings that Westmoreland had described.

Dorsey asked Benedict whether he had been present when Westmoreland preferred the charges against Harris. Benedict answered that he had. The official minute book was then produced in court. Benedict identified the entry on page 128 as the correct record of the meeting. When asked about the board’s vote, he replied, “I think it was unanimous.” He explained that the charges themselves and Harris’s defense were not recorded in the minutes. The minutes recorded the board’s official action (AG, 2).

The critical exchange followed when the lawyers clarified exactly what Westmoreland had previously claimed. Attorney Reuben Arnold stated that Westmoreland’s position was that the board had found Harris guilty but refused to dismiss him, after which Westmoreland resigned.

Benedict answered directly:

“That is not true.”

The Constitution summarized the effect of the testimony by reporting that Benedict had been introduced by the State to answer the accusation of scientific dishonesty against Harris and that the minutes of the State Board of Health were at variance with Westmoreland’s statement (AC, 1).

Benedict’s testimony had a narrow but important purpose. He did not perform Mary Phagan’s autopsy and did not independently calculate the time of her death. His role was to address the defense’s attempt to damage Harris’s professional credibility. Westmoreland had presented the jury with the impression that Harris had previously been formally condemned by his own State Board of Health for scientific dishonesty. Benedict, the board’s sitting president, appeared with the official minutes and directly contradicted that account.

The episode became important enough for Dorsey to return to it during his closing argument. Dorsey reminded the jury that Westmoreland had claimed Harris had been found guilty of scientific dishonesty and argued that the minutes of the board disproved Westmoreland’s version. Dorsey used the episode to argue that the defense’s medical attack upon Harris had gone beyond disagreement over digestion experiments and had attempted to undermine the personal and professional standing of the State’s principal medical witness (AJ, 7).

The photograph in The Atlanta Constitution therefore represents a man who occupied a significant position in Georgia medicine in 1913. Samuel Caldwell Benedict was the president of the Georgia State Board of Health, the first dean of the University of Georgia School of Pharmacy, a longtime university professor, and a physician whose professional career extended for more than three decades. His appearance in the Frank trial was brief, but it supplied the State with an authoritative answer to one of the defense’s strongest personal attacks upon Dr. Roy Harris.

The placement of Benedict’s portrait beneath the newspaper heading “Defends Dr. Harris” accurately captures why he was there. He was called to place the official record of Georgia’s State Board of Health before the jury and to answer, in his own words, Westmoreland’s assertion about Harris: “That is not true.”

References

AC. The Atlanta Constitution. (1913, August 20). “State Is Hard Hit by Judge Ruling Barring Evidence Attacking Frank,” p. 3. Photograph of Dr. Samuel Benedict credited to Francis E. Price, staff photographer. Transcription and source information

AG. The Atlanta Georgian. (1913, August 20). “State Closes Frank Case Near Jury; Defense Begins Its Sur-Rebuttal.” Account of Dr. Benedict’s August 19 testimony. Atlanta Georgian transcription

UGA. University of Georgia. (1913–1915). General Catalogue, 1913–1915. Samuel Caldwell Benedict listed as dean of the School of Pharmacy and professor of materia medica.

DLG. Digital Library of Georgia. (ca. 1910). Phar. Dean’s Office, 1903–1938. Georgia Archives, Vanishing Georgia Collection. Identifies Samuel Benedict as the first dean of the University of Georgia School of Pharmacy and records his death in 1914. Digital Library of Georgia record

PMC. Benedict, S. C. (1894). “Suggestion and Its Therapeutic Uses.” The Medical and Surgical Reporter, 11(5), 257–268. Identifies Benedict as professor of medical jurisprudence at the University of Georgia and vice president of the National Association of Railway Surgeons. National Library of Medicine text

AC. The Atlanta Constitution. (1913, August 12). “As the Very Wildest of Guessing Dr. Westmoreland Characterizes Testimony Given by Dr. Harris,” p. 3. Contemporary article transcription

AJ. The Atlanta Journal. (1913, August 25). “Leo M. Frank’s Fate Is Now in Hands of the Jury.” Dorsey closing argument concerning Harris, Westmoreland, and the State Board of Health minutes. Atlanta Journal transcription
