🚨 NFL CAMP BUZZ  - August 19th  RAPID FIRE 🚨

🌵 Arizona Cardinals

– Kendrick Bourne firmly positioned as WR3
Bourne was described as comfortably Arizona’s third receiver after consistently getting open and avoiding drops throughout camp and the preseason. (Donnie Druin)

🌉 San Francisco 49ers

– Christian McCaffrey expected to play Week 1
Kyle Shanahan expects McCaffrey to be ready for the opener, and Adam Schefter said he should play against the Rams barring a setback. (Matt Maiocco, Adam Schefter)

– Kaelon Black operates as lead back
Black handled the lead role with McCaffrey sidelined by tightness and Jordan James injured. (Matt Barrows)

– DeMarcus Robinson could challenge for starting Z role
Deebo Samuel has been deployed throughout the formation, while Robinson has frequently worked with Brock Purdy and drawn strong praise from the quarterback. Robinson could join the first team when the starters play in the preseason. (Matt Maiocco)

☠️ Las Vegas Raiders

– Mike Washington emerging as Ashton Jeanty’s handcuff
Washington followed a strong preseason opener with a productive joint practice against Houston’s defense, and Klint Kubiak offered positive comments about him. He appears to be Jeanty’s clearest current handcuff and could carve out an additional role. (Levi Edwards)

🏹 Kansas City Chiefs

– Cyrus Allen continues making his case
Allen beat first-round pick Mansoor Delane deep and made an impressive one-handed catch. WR coach Chad O’Shea praised Allen’s work ethic and response to coaching, adding to the rookie’s mounting camp buzz. (Nick Jacobs)

– Rashee Rice’s movement bears watching
Rice reportedly has not looked like himself. Any decline in his agility would be concerning given his reliance on yards after the catch, while Allen’s repeated flashes could make the receiver competition more interesting. (Pete Sweeney)

– Emmett Johnson increasingly looks like RB2
Johnson received the second running-back carry with the starters on multiple consecutive days, increasingly pointing toward him as Kansas City’s No. 2 back. (Pete Sweeney)

– Tyquan Thornton returns after cart departure
Thornton practiced Wednesday after leaving the previous day’s session on a cart with a hamstring issue.

⚡ Los Angeles Chargers

– Tyler Biadasz out indefinitely
Biadasz suffered ACL damage and additional injuries to his left knee. He will seek more medical opinions, and his absence could extend through the season. (Adam Schefter, Ian Rapoport)

– Chargers’ offensive line increasingly unsettled
Rashawn Slater has missed eight consecutive practices with a knee injury, Biadasz could miss the season and the starting left-guard job remains undecided.

– Omarion Hampton dominates joint-practice work
Reports from the 49ers joint practice consistently described the Chargers offense scoring frequently and Hampton running through defenders like a man among boys.

– Quentin Johnston trending in the right direction
Johnston appears to have avoided a significant issue and is expected to be okay after leaving practice earlier this week.

– Tre Harris now dealing with an undisclosed injury
Harris did not practice Wednesday because of an undisclosed injury. His status is worth monitoring with Johnston also recently banged up.

🧀 Green Bay Packers

– Matthew Golden’s hands and acceleration stand out
Andy Herman called Golden the most natural hands-catcher he has covered in Green Bay and praised his ability to accelerate through the catch.

🐴 Denver Broncos

– Bo Nix starts hot with Waddle and Engram
Nix opened practice on fire, hitting Jaylen Waddle for a 60-yard touchdown over Pat Surtain II before connecting with Evan Engram on back-to-back gains of roughly 25 and 15 yards. Waddle and Engram both continue to generate encouraging signs in Denver’s passing game.

🦁 Detroit Lions

– Jameson Williams returns on limited basis
Williams resumed practicing after missing time with a shoulder injury.

– Sam LaPorta sits with undisclosed issue
LaPorta missed Wednesday’s practice for an undisclosed reason. Jeff Mueller, PT, DPT said the absence would not be particularly concerning unless it is related to LaPorta’s back following lumbar microdiscectomy or to his hamstring; neither connection has been reported.

🟣 Minnesota Vikings

– Kyler Murray connects deep with Justin Jefferson
Murray escaped pressure and found Jefferson for an approximately 30-yard touchdown against Baltimore’s defense. (Will Ragatz)

⚔️ Tennessee Titans

– Wan’Dale Robinson seeing heavy volume
Robinson caught at least five passes Wednesday and received even more targets, reinforcing expectations that he could command substantial receiving volume. (Easton Freeze)

– Tony Pollard returns to practice
Pollard returned Wednesday after missing time with a foot injury.

– Michael Carter projected outside the 53-man roster
A Titans roster projection had Carter missing the final roster. Detroit and Green Bay could make sense as potential destinations with coaching connections; Carter might not become fantasy-relevant himself but could disrupt an established handcuff role if signed elsewhere. (Austin Stanley)

– Carnell Tate dealing with stiffness after collision
Tate’s issue following his practice collision was described as stiffness rather than concussion-related. The expectation is that he could return to the field within the next few days.

🐎 Indianapolis Colts

– Tyler Warren suffers groin injury
Shane Steichen confirmed Warren injured his groin and left practice. Jeff Mueller, PT, DPT said a mild strain averages roughly two to three weeks, while a more significant strain could threaten regular-season games; the severity has not been reported.

– DJ Giddens aggravates hamstring concern
Giddens left after individual work with an apparent recurrence of the hamstring problem that had sidelined him for weeks. Already viewed as a roster-bubble candidate, the setback could make Seth McGowan the leading in-house RB2 option, though a veteran addition remains possible. (Joel Erickson)

– Josh Downs expected in two-receiver sets
Indianapolis reportedly plans to keep Downs involved in two-receiver personnel and use him creatively rather than limiting him to obvious passing situations.

– Keenan Allen signing becomes official
The Colts officially signed Allen after agreeing to terms earlier in the week.

🐂 Houston Texans

– Jayden Higgins suffers season-ending torn ACL
Higgins tore his ACL during the Raiders joint practice and will miss the 2026 season. He had produced an excellent offseason and was being counted on as Houston’s No. 2 receiver. (Ian Rapoport, Aaron Wilson)

– Higgins injury could reshape Houston’s offense
Houston could lean more heavily on 12 and 13 personnel while rotating Jaylin Noel, Tank Dell and Xavier Hutchinson behind Nico Collins. The loss may create additional opportunity for Dalton Schultz, and Brandin Cooks could be a veteran option because of his relationship with Nick Caserio.

– Tank Dell remains limited during recovery
Dell attended practice but had not dressed for several consecutive days. There is concern about his ability to tolerate back-to-back days of knee loading, and Houston appears to be treating any meaningful 2026 contribution as a bonus. (Aaron Wilson)

– Texans could explore veteran WR help With Jayden Higgins lost for the season and Tank Dell still working his way back, veteran free agents Brandin Cooks, DeAndre Hopkins, Tyler Lockett, Sterling Shepard, Josh Reynolds, Gabe Davis and Zay Jones were identified as potential options Houston could consider. No signing or reported interest in those players has been established.

– Nico Collins’ health becomes even more important Houston’s WR depth is suddenly thin behind Collins, who has dealt with soft-tissue injuries in the past. If Collins were to miss time, the current options include Jaylin Noel, a still-recovering Tank Dell, Xavier Hutchinson and Justin Watson, making his availability particularly important following Higgins’ ACL tear.

– David Montgomery and Woody Marks split responsibilities
Montgomery was the primary rusher during the Raiders joint practice, while Marks ran most of the running-back routes. Houston has limited Montgomery’s camp touches to preserve his health, leaving the overall distribution unsettled.

🐆 Jacksonville Jaguars

– Bhayshul Tuten delivers his best practice
Tuten excelled during the Panthers joint session after some uneven work since the pads came on. Chris Rodriguez Jr. previously received his heaviest camp workload relative to Tuten, and the backfield still appears headed toward a committee. (John Shipley)

– LeQuint Allen injury could expand Tuten’s opportunity
Tuten could receive additional playing time with Allen sidelined, while Ameer Abdullah may now have a clearer path to the roster.

– Travis Hunter plays only two offensive snaps
Hunter logged two offensive snaps during the Panthers joint practice, notable usage in one of the closest game simulations available before Week 1. (Michael DiRocco)

– Brian Thomas Jr. and Nate Boerkircher flash
Thomas produced a strong joint-practice performance, while Boerkircher scored a touchdown and drew a comparison to Tucker Kraft. (John Shipley)

– Parker Washington remains a high-conviction fantasy target
Washington was singled out as a ride-or-die fantasy selection despite his rising draft cost.

🐾 Carolina Panthers

– Tetairoa McMillan torches Jacksonville’s coverage
McMillan repeatedly beat the Jaguars during the teams’ joint practice. (John Shipley)

⚜️ New Orleans Saints

– Alvin Kamara expected out at least one month
Kamara avoided a major knee injury but suffered a sprained MCL and is expected to miss at least the next month. (Nick Underhill, Adam Schefter)

– Kamara injury involves same knee as 2025 MCL sprain
Jeff Mueller, PT, DPT noted that initial contact appeared to come from the side of Alvin Kamara’s right knee, potentially stressing the same MCL that was injured last season and contributed to him missing the final six games. Kamara has 3.5 weeks until Week 1, while his current MCL sprain is expected to sideline him for at least a month.

– Travis Etienne could be headed for a major Week 1 workload

– Devaughn Vele positioned as WR3
Vele appears firmly established as New Orleans’ third receiver and is expected to play in two-receiver sets, making him the preferred Saints receiver flier. (Matthew Paras)

– Bryce Lance produces with first team
With Vele and Jordyn Tyson sidelined, Lance worked opposite Chris Olave and caught three of four targets, including a third-down conversion. Barrion Brown also received first-team opportunities. (Nick Underhill, Matthew Paras)

🏴‍☠️ Tampa Bay Buccaneers
– Bucky Irving remains the clear lead back
Baker Mayfield praised Kenneth Gainwell but described him as a spark who spells Irving. The wording further supports Irving as Tampa Bay’s lead back, with the size of his workload remaining the primary question. (Brianna Dix)

🍑 Atlanta Falcons

– Quarterback uncertainty adds risk to Drake London’s cost
London made a contested catch during practice, but Kevin Bowen described Tua Tagovailoa’s joint-practice performance against Indianapolis as poor following a difficult preseason opener, while Michael Penix Jr. continues recovering from an ACL injury. 

– Trey Sermon placed on injured reserve

– Kenyon Sadiq getting closer to returning
Aaron Glenn said Sadiq is nearing a return. Missed offseason and camp work, an established tight end ahead of him and Omar Cooper’s slot role could delay Sadiq’s fantasy impact, though his falling price creates late-round appeal.

🐬 Miami Dolphins

– Chris Bell could return for preseason finale
Bell will miss this week’s game, while beat writers view his availability for the finale as roughly 50-50. Getting one preseason appearance could help his season-long outlook, making him a potential late flier. (Alain Poupart)

🇺🇸 New England Patriots

– A.J. Brown dominates team drills
Brown caught all seven of his team-drill targets against Philadelphia in what was described as his best practice of camp. (Mark Daniels)

– Demario Douglas creates sharp separation
Douglas left Cooper DeJean behind during a joint-practice route. (Conor Ryan)

🦅 Philadelphia Eagles

– Dontayvion Wicks creates immediate separation Wicks won cleanly off the line during practice and remains essentially free in many fantasy drafts. (Brian Kubena)

– Makai Lemon returns on limited basis
Lemon was upgraded to limited participation following a hamstring injury. Two soft-tissue setbacks, missed time, his fit with Jalen Hurts and uncertainty over earning an outside role in frequent two-receiver sets could contribute to a slow start. (EJ Smith)

– Lane Johnson expects Saquon Barkley rebound
Johnson said the new offensive system should produce the version of Barkley seen two years ago. (John Clark)

🗽 New York Giants

– Najee Harris joined Giants for playing-time opportunity
Harris said the chance to earn playing time was a major reason he signed. New York’s desire for a physical running game could create work for Harris alongside Cam Skattebo. (Jordan Raanan)

🪖 Washington Commanders

– Rachaad White misses second consecutive practice
White has missed two straight sessions. Jeff Mueller, PT, DPT raised the possibility of a right-groin strain based on the timing of the absence, but no injury or diagnosis has been confirmed.

– Jacory Croskey-Merritt and White lead backfield

It's a parable and a joke.
~~~~~~
This guy in Kansas is at home when his town starts flooding.

Soon its a few inches in his house and rising. There is a knock on the door and its his neighbor, theyre driving out of town and offer him a lift. 

"No thanks. The lord will see me through this".

They leave and in an hour he is on the roof, surrounded by water when a fire department boat floats up and the men inside tell him to get in.

"No thanks. The lord will see me through this".

They leave and it isn't long until he is clinging to his chimney. Its pretty dire but just then a helicopter floats overhead and drops a rope. Over the loudspeaker they tell him to grab it. 

"No thanks. The lord will see me through this".

Finally the waters win and claim the mans life. Entering heaven he does ask St. Peter about that.

"I was a good Christian in life. You're letting me in to heaven. Why wouldn't God send help?"

Incredulous, St. Peter twists his nose and says " SIR, We sent a car, a boat and a helicopter. You said "no" everytime!"

text:
Nobody writes about the Ford 300 that never went in a truck. But thousands of Ford 300 inline-sixes spent their entire lives bolted to a steel skid on a concrete pad, never connected to a transmission, never attached to a driveshaft, never installed in a vehicle of any kind. Ford sold the 300 as an industrial power unit a bare long block with a bell housing adapter for a PTO (power take-off) connection to generators, water pumps, air compressors, welding machines, and hydraulic power packs. The same engine that Ford installed in F-150s and Broncos was available as a standalone stationary power source for farms, ranches, oil field service companies, and construction sites. The 300 didn't care whether it was moving a truck or spinning a generator shaft. It made torque at low RPM either way.

The agricultural connection is where the 300's reputation was actually built not on highways but on dirt roads between fields. A grain farmer in Kansas or Nebraska in the 1970s needed a truck engine that started at five AM in January, pulled a loaded grain trailer to the elevator twenty miles away, and came home to run an irrigation pump or a grain auger until dark. The 300 did all three jobs on the same tank of fuel. The V8 F-250 option the 360 or 390 FE — made more power but burned 30 to 40 percent more fuel doing the same work. On a farm where fuel was a line item on a balance sheet that determined whether the operation survived another year, the 300's fuel economy wasn't a convenience. It was a financial survival tool. Farmers didn't choose the 300 because they didn't want a V8. They chose the 300 because the V8's fuel bill threatened their margins.

The marine application proved the 300's thermal endurance. Ford and aftermarket marinizers — companies like Crusader, Pleasure Craft, and Perkins adapted the 300 for inboard boat use with raw-water or closed-loop cooling systems, marine exhaust manifolds, and corrosion-resistant coatings. A marine engine operates differently from a truck engine: sustained high-load RPM for hours without the cooling airflow that highway driving provides. An engine that overheats after thirty minutes at wide-open throttle is useless in a boat. The 300's cast-iron block and head with thick water jackets designed for air-cooled highway operation in desert climates had enough thermal mass and coolant capacity to survive sustained marine loads that lighter aluminum engines couldn't handle. The 300 in a workboat ran at 3,000 RPM for eight hours a day, six days a week, pushing commercial fishing vessels, towboats, and utility craft along America's rivers and coastlines. The gear-driven camshaft that never needed replacement in a truck never needed replacement in a boat either. Same engine. Different element. Same reliability.

The 300 was the last engine Ford offered that could legitimately claim to be a universal power source. A V8 is too wide for many industrial frames. A four-cylinder doesn't make enough torque for heavy loads. A diesel requires fuel infrastructure that not every job site has. The 300 inline-six was narrow enough to fit on a standard industrial skid, powerful enough to run a 25-kilowatt generator or a six-inch irrigation pump, simple enough to be maintained by a ranch hand with a socket set, and fueled by gasoline available at every gas station and farm co-op in America. It was the mechanical Swiss Army knife of American industry from 1965 to 1996. When Ford discontinued it, no replacement filled every role the 300 had occupied. The 4.9-liter hole in Ford's lineup was filled by the 4.6-liter Modular V8 in trucks and by nothing in industrial and marine applications. Some industrial users stockpiled 300 cores in the late 1990s buying used engines from salvage yards and storing them against the day their running 300 finally needed a replacement. The engine was worth hoarding because nothing else could do every job it did.

text:
You call it a well earned chunk out of Reform, and then spend a thousand words explaining why the right needs to unite. That is the contradiction you never really resolve, because the Dover result makes it impossible to avoid.

You stood in Dover and took 284 votes. The Greens beat Reform by just 34. You then told Kent Online that the result was exactly what we wanted and that you would take it quite happily. So let’s be honest about what happened. You didn’t just stand aside and offer voters another choice. You were pleased with a result in which the Green candidate beat Reform because the right vote was divided.

Perhaps you think that is a price worth paying. If so, say that. But you cannot celebrate the result as a success for Restore and then turn around and lecture Reform about the need for unity.

The other problem is the constantly shifting description of what happened. When the result is inconvenient, Dover is one seat, ten villages, no consequence. Yet when Restore needs to demonstrate that it is becoming a national force, the same sort of result becomes seismic. You cannot minimise a result when defending it and magnify it when promoting yourselves. At some point, you have to decide what the result actually means.

You also say that voters deserve a choice. Of course they do. Nobody is arguing that Restore should not exist or that people should not be free to vote for it. But there is a very big difference between offering voters a choice and deliberately building a strategy around taking enough votes from Reform that Reform cannot win without addressing us. The first is democracy. The second is political leverage.

And that matters because you are not simply competing for the same voters while pursuing completely separate objectives. You are competing for voters who broadly want the same thing a government on the right. If the consequence of that competition is to split the vote and hand seats to the Greens, Conservatives or Labour, then eventually someone has to take responsibility for the outcome.

That is why the egos must be put aside argument rings rather hollow. Restore was founded by Rupert Lowe following his very public break with Nigel Farage and Reform. You now say the answer is for Reform to take your offer seriously, while your strategy is to keep standing candidates and attritting Reform’s vote until it does. That is not really putting egos aside. It is trying to win a negotiating battle by making the alternative more painful.

There is nothing wrong with having principles. There is nothing wrong with demanding changes from Reform. There is nothing wrong with standing candidates. But if your strategy knowingly makes it harder for the right to win, you cannot then present yourselves as the people saving the right from itself.

So which is it? If Dover was genuinely insignificant, then stop celebrating it as a major success for Restore. If it was important, then acknowledge what actually happened Reform lost by 34 votes while Restore took 284, and the Greens won.

That is not an argument against anyone having the right to vote Restore. It is an argument about consequences. Politics is not just about the purity of the choice you offer voters. It is also about what happens after they make that choice.

And in Dover, the result was Green first, Reform second and Restore fifth.

You can call that a well earned chunk out of Reform if you want. I think it tells voters something much more important if the right divides, the Greens win.

That is why i stand with @reformparty_uk.

text:
Now that the dust has settled, mostly, following the Guston, St. Margaret’s and Kingsdown by-election, we can start to take stock. 

A lot has come out of this, arguably, relatively minor political exercise. One seat (out of 32) on Dover District Council. 

For such a seemingly insignificant election, in the grand scheme, it has has had seismic impact and a disproportionate level of media interest. Because it says a great deal about the current state of our national political picture. 

So, I stood for Restore Britain in the Guston, St Margaret’s and Kingsdown by-election on Thursday. Restore Britain gained 10.64% of the vote share. That almost certainly caused Reform to lose to the Green Party. Let me be clear, that was a Reform lose. They lost that to the Greens and they lost votes to Restore Britain. 

So what?

Well….

The Right needs to start having an intelligent conversation about collaboration if we are to ensure that this country doesn’t succumb to the madness and destruction of the Left.

But people also deserve a choice. I’m sure most of us agree with that.

And what I can tell you, after delivering circa 15,000 leaflets with my fantastic team and knocking on almost 2,000 doors, is that all is not well within the legacy Reform support base.

They are disillusioned. Big time.

Many are ready to jump ship. I had that conversation time and time again. What is stopping them is almost universally the fear of splitting the vote on the Right. Many are holding their noses as they continue to vote Reform.

The principal reason? Nigel Farage.

I have the doorstep data. The receipts, if you like.

We live in a democracy. Still, just. And people need options, particularly if the dish being served is limited and not really to their taste.

Restore Britain has an absolute duty to its members and supporters to continue pushing forward. Of course we do. Especially in light of the burgeoning dissatisfaction among hitherto Reform voters.

Restore Britain has made the offer to work with Reform. . It has been rejected. By Nigel Farage. Repeatedly. But the offer remains on the table. I have that from the highest authority.

The Guston by-election was a microcosm of British politics. From our side of the fence, it isn’t a pretty picture. Unless something changes, the outlook is bleak. I think we all agree on that.

Restore Britain is not going away.

The Conservative and Unionist Party is not going away.

The ONLY sensible way forward is to find a way of working together for the future of our beautiful country.

The Guston by-election was a necessary demonstration of Restore Britain’s ascendancy and intent. In reality, the collateral damage of a Green win is minor at this level. Ten villages. One district council seat. No national or geopolitical consequence.

In many ways, therefore, it was probably a necessary wake-up call to all of us.

We must push for a grand collaboration on the Right. We must. It is essential.

I have nailed my colours firmly to the Restore Britain mast. My loyalty is not in question. But I also understand the stakes, and that is precisely why I say we must find a way to work together.

I will continue to fight for Restore Britain because, frankly, I believe we have the best suite of policies and the most credible and capable leadership. By far.

But I’m not merely open to collaboration. I am actively pushing for it.

Egos must be put aside. Great minds must come together. At the moment there is resistance, and we all know where much of it is coming from.

If Restore Britain needs to keep demonstrating that it can shape the battlefield until minds are changed, then that is exactly what we must do.

And in Dover, the result was Green first, Reform second and Restore fifth.

You can call that a well earned chunk out of Reform if you want. I think it tells voters something much more important if the right divides, the Greens win.

That is why i stand with @reformparty_uk.

text:
succeeds by borrowing the appearance of something valuable. Darkness painted black advertises itself. Darkness painted like light must be tested.

That principle reaches far beyond dramatic visions. Satan can counterfeit holiness with self-righteousness, unity with doctrinal surrender, charity with indifference to truth, scholarship with unbelief, tradition with human authority, liberty with lawlessness, zeal with fanaticism, and spirituality with emotional intoxication. None of those counterfeits begins by announcing the substitution. The replacement happens quietly. Soon “love” means refusing to rebuke error, “grace” means refusing to preach against sin, “scholarship” means correcting the Bible, “unity” means pretending doctrine does not matter, and “spirituality” means trusting whatever happened during the music. The words still shine, but somebody has changed the bulb behind them. One of Satan’s oldest tricks is to steal God’s vocabulary and quietly change the definitions.

This is why appearance can never carry final authority. A beautiful sanctuary can contain bad doctrine. An ugly building can contain sound doctrine. A preacher may be polished and faithful, or polished and false; another may be plain and faithful, or plain and ignorant. Godliness is not authenticated by architecture, robes, stage production, antiquity, popularity, academic titles, emotional atmosphere, or outward solemnity. Second Timothy 3:5 warns about “Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof.” A form can be impressive because forms are visible. Truth requires something harder: open the Book, identify the doctrine, and see whether the shining thing standing before you agrees with what God already said.

2. Eden Proves That False Light Usually Begins By Editing God’s Words

The first satanic attack recorded in Scripture is an attack upon words. Genesis 3:1 begins with, “Yea, hath God said?” Satan did not first attack Adam’s marriage, Eve’s emotions, or the geography of Eden; he attacked divine revelation. He questioned whether God had really said what Eve had been told. Then in verse 4 he moved from questioning to contradiction: “Ye shall not surely die.” Once the authority of the word had been loosened, Satan could offer a new interpretation of reality. God had said death; Satan said advancement. God had established a boundary; Satan presented the boundary as intellectual oppression. Every counterfeit light eventually has to make room for itself by moving something God already said out of the way.

That pattern survives wherever religious men claim an illumination superior to the written word. “The Bible says that, but God showed me something deeper.” “Paul taught that, but the Spirit is doing a new thing.” “The text says one thing, but modern scholarship has discovered what the church could not know until now.” “Christ said this, but our tradition interprets it through a higher authority.” The costumes differ while the serpent’s question remains remarkably recognizable: “Yea, hath God said?” New light that requires old Scripture to become uncertain is not progress. God does not need to contradict yesterday’s inspiration in order to illuminate today’s believer. The Holy Ghost who moved holy men of God to speak does not return centuries later to apologize for what He had them write.

text:
Who’s afraid of the Amish data?

Daniel Horowitz
August 21, 2026

Completely unvaccinated children are increasingly rare. The Amish offer a natural comparison population — and a test public health should welcome.

Nothing scares the vaccine establishment more than a meaningful control group. Some vaccine trials do use inert placebos, but most compare a new product with an existing vaccine or another formulation. What we almost never get is long-term randomized evidence comparing children who receive the full schedule with children who receive none of it.

Thanks to ubiquitous mandates, cultural taboos, and pressure from pediatricians, truly unvaccinated children are also increasingly difficult to find in large numbers. That is why the Amish data are so revealing — and why they should be studied rather than waved away.

Completely unvaccinated children are increasingly rare. The Amish offer a natural comparison population — and a test public health should welcome.

Nothing scares the vaccine establishment more than a meaningful control group. Some vaccine trials do use inert placebos, but most compare a new product with an existing vaccine or another formulation. What we almost never get is long-term randomized evidence comparing children who receive the full schedule with children who receive none of it.

Thanks to ubiquitous mandates, cultural taboos, and pressure from pediatricians, truly unvaccinated children are also increasingly difficult to find in large numbers. That is why the Amish data are so revealing — and why they should be studied rather than waved away.

Why treat a naturally occurring unvaccinated cohort as an inconvenience rather than an opportunity?

Last year, the Supreme Court vacated a shocking Second Circuit decision siding with the state of New York against Amish parents who declined to vaccinate their children. In Miller v. McDonald, the parents argued that forcing the Amish to violate their religious beliefs in their own private schools violates the First Amendment. Yet after the Supreme Court sent the case back for reconsideration in light of its recent religious-liberty precedent, the Second Circuit last month again ruled for New York.

The legal fight continues and so does the coercion.

Putting aside the legal and moral issues at stake, the facts presented during discovery about the health of the unvaccinated Amish should be newsworthy across the world, especially as we debate both the new mRNA flu shot and the discovery that Anthony Fauci was aware of COVID vaccine injuries from the beginning.

Siri & Glimstad LLP, which represents the Amish families, provided the federal district court in New York with sworn expert medical evidence about the health status of 168 students in the three Amish schools targeted by the state for financial penalties.

The doctor’s declaration states: “I am advised that there are 26 families across the three Amish schools at issue, which have a total of 168 unvaccinated children (meaning they have received no vaccines) and that none of them have any health issue that arose after birth.”

The declaration then compares those 168 children with national background rates for allergies, autism, asthma, and ADHD. Using those rates, a random sample of 168 U.S. children would be expected to include several cases of each condition. According to the declaration, however, there were no documented cases of autism, ADHD, asthma, or food allergies among the 168 Amish children.

No, that does not magically turn 168 Amish children into a randomized clinical trial. The Amish differ from the broader population in diet, lifestyle, environment, genetics, health care use, and countless other ways. But it does make them a rare, naturally occurring cohort of completely unvaccinated children — exactly the kind of population serious researchers should want to examine.

And the court filing does not rely only on the Amish. It also presents records from 99 unvaccinated children who had religious exemptions in four contiguous school districts in Ulster County, New York. Those records were drawn from state school health examination forms completed by physicians. 

The numbers are striking. The filing reports zero cases of autism and diabetes in the Ulster County group, lower rates of ADHD and allergies, and a much lower asthma rate than the cited background figures.

Those differences do not prove vaccination caused the higher general population rates. They do raise an obvious question: Why not study the difference rigorously?

The court-filed evidence also notes that the expansion of the childhood vaccine schedule has occurred during the same decades in which autoimmune, developmental, and neurological diagnoses have risen sharply. Correlation is not causation, and anyone pretending otherwise is doing bad science. But correlation can be a reason to investigate— especially when government is mandating the products in question.

These retrospective comparisons do not prove that vaccines cause autism, asthma, allergies, ADHD, or any other condition. They cannot control for all the differences between vaccinated and unvaccinated populations. But when government mandates a growing schedule of products for healthy children, shouldn't the burden be on public health authorities to pursue the strongest possible long-term safety evidence?

Why treat a naturally occurring unvaccinated cohort as an inconvenience rather than an opportunity?

That problem remains with the latest mRNA flu vaccine, which is being compared against another flu vaccine rather than an unvaccinated cohort. If officials want to mandate these products, why not demand the strongest possible evidence about their long-term effects? And why did the New York Department of Health decline to engage the data the Amish families placed before the court rather than explain why the comparisons are misleading?

What is self-evident is that vaccine mandates make these questions harder to answer by shrinking the pool of children who remain completely unvaccinated. New York is willing to coerce Amish families in the name of public health? Then public health officials should be willing to confront the data those families have put before them and show their work.

Religious liberty demands no less. Neither does science.

text:
If you’re using MetaMask and a transaction is stuck on PulseChain, you can usually clear it by replacing the stuck transaction with a cancellation transaction using the same nonce.

How to cancel a stuck transaction in MetaMask

Find the stuck transaction
Open MetaMask → Activity.
Tap the pending/stuck transaction.
Find and note its nonce.
Enable nonce editing
Go to Settings → Advanced.
Enable Customize transaction nonce (wording may vary by MetaMask version).
Create a cancellation transaction
Start a new transaction to your own wallet address.
Send 0 PLS (or the minimum allowed by the wallet).
Manually enter the same nonce as the stuck transaction.
Use a higher gas fee
Set the gas fee higher than the stuck transaction.
The replacement needs to offer a sufficiently higher fee for validators to prefer it.
Confirm the transaction
Once the replacement transaction is confirmed, the original transaction with that nonce can no longer be included.
Your next transactions should then proceed normally.

Important: The nonce must be exactly the same as the stuck transaction. Don’t randomly increase the nonce, or you can create additional pending transactions.

text:
🚨🚨 BREAKING! 🧵

SpaceX says it’s building its largest spaceport yet, committing $100 billion for a Louisiana site—adding to its list of billion-dollar expansion plans

Rather apparent in SpaceX’s IPO filings is the ever-constant named goal of reaching Mars to build compute infrastructure and even human settlements on the red planet. 

In Elon Musk’s first earnings call, he reiterated those goals, the very ones that led him to create the company over two decades ago. Now he’s expanding his lofty space travel aspirations with a new real-estate and infrastructure investment.

SpaceX is committing $100 billion to build a massive new spaceport in coastal Louisiana, giving the rocket company another multibillion-dollar expansion project as it races to scale Starship, satellite manufacturing and AI infrastructure. 

The facility, called Starbase Louisiana, will occupy roughly 125,000 acres on Pecan Island in Vermilion Parish and is expected to become the fourth and largest of SpaceX’s launch complexes.

Construction is scheduled to begin in 2027, with the first launch targeted for as early as 2029. At full buildout, the site is expected to contain five launch facilties—each with two launch pads—along with propellant farms, a propellant-production facility, power generation, vehicle-processing facilities and housing for employees and their families.

“Starbase Louisiana will ultimately have over a dozen launch towers, enabling more than 30 Starship flights per day and making it the biggest launch site on Earth,” Musk posted on X. “SpaceX makes sci-fi real.”

“Potentially the world’s largest spaceport”
Louisiana Economic Development describes the project as potentially the world’s largest spaceport, with the capacity to support thousands of launches a year.

That claim is about launch capacity, not land. By physical footprint, the current record holder is Russia’s Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan, sprawling across roughly 6,717 square kilometers—more than 13 times the size of SpaceX’s planned Louisiana site. 

What Musk and Louisiana officials mean by “biggest launch site on Earth” is cadence: Starbase Louisiana is designed for more than a dozen launch towers and over 30 Starship flights a day, a pace no existing spaceport, including Baikonur, comes close to matching.

Louisiana Economic Development estimates SpaceX will create more than 3,000 direct jobs over the next decade, with an average annual salary of $92,600, as well as roughly 8,100 indirect jobs—leading to more than 11,100 new job opportunities in Acadiana.

“Today is a pivotal moment for Louisiana. This announcement pushes our state beyond $250 billion in new investment and puts us at the center of the next great frontier,” Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry said in the news release. “We have the people and talent to build what the world once thought impossible, creating jobs on land, across the Gulf and through space. Our job creation knows no bounds.”

The Louisiana site is intended to become a major part of SpaceX’s push to make Starship a high-frequency launch system. 

The company says the Gulf Coast location provides access to a wide range of launch trajectories, while the availability of natural gas can support the facility’s fuel and power requirements. SpaceX also envisions the site supporting missions beyond conventional satellite launches, including lunar and Mars missions and the deployment of satellites for its emerging orbital data center business.

The project is also projected to be a major economic-development bet for the state. Louisiana offered SpaceX an incentive package tied to the capital investment, job creation and other commitments. 

Under a local payment-in-lieu-of-taxes agreement, SpaceX will make a $20 million upfront payment and at least $25 million annually for 25 years, with the state estimating more than $820 million in direct local payments under the agreement.

News Flashback

Early 2026

Jan-March

Streaming Wars

The "Streaming Wars" refers to the intense competition among digital media platforms to dominate the subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) market by capturing and retaining global audiences.

As of early 2026, the landscape has shifted from a period of rapid expansion into a phase of major consolidation and a focus on profitability over subscriber volume.

The "Winner" and Current State (2026)

Netflix Dominance: Industry analysts increasingly cite Netflix as the victor. In January 2026, Netflix reported 18% year-over-year revenue growth and is currently pursuing a high-stakes $83 billion all-cash acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studio and streaming assets (including HBO/Max).

The "Big 3": Despite fierce competition, the market is primarily dominated by Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and Disney+.

YouTube's Rise: Some experts argue YouTube is the true winner of the broader attention economy, surpassing traditional streaming services in total viewership by pivoting back to user-generated content.

Key Strategies in 2026

Consolidation: Smaller or struggling services are being shuttered or merged. For example, Disney recently shut down Hulu as a standalone service.

Monetization Shifts: Platforms have moved away from "growth at all costs" to strategies like password-sharing crackdowns, ad-supported tiers, and price hikes.

Live Sports & Events: Services are increasingly bidding on live sports rights (e.g., Netflix hosting WWE's Raw starting in 2025) to differentiate their offerings.

Bundling: To combat "subscription fatigue," platforms are forming strategic partnerships with telecommunications companies and banks to offer bundled service hubs.

Consumer Impact

Price Hikes: Many consumers are canceling services due to rising costs; over 40% of Americans cited price as their primary reason for unsubscribing in late 2025.

Resurgence of Piracy: Fragmented content and high costs have led to a significant comeback for pirate sites, which some users now find more comprehensive than paid services.

"South Park: The Streaming Wars": The term was popularized in mainstream culture by a 2-part South Park special released on Paramount+ in 2022, which satirized the industry's aggressive competition.

Gold (1974)

Gold is a 1974 British action-thriller directed by Peter R. Hunt, starring Roger Moore and Susannah York. Based on the 1970 novel Gold Mine by Wilbur Smith, the film is set in the South African goldfields and follows a conspiracy by a global syndicate to manipulate the price of gold by sabotaging a rich mine.

Plot: Rod Slater (Moore), a newly appointed general manager, is manipulated by his boss, Manfred Steyner (Bradford Dillman), into drilling through a protective barrier into a subterranean lake. This is intended to flood the mine, causing a global gold shortage and driving up prices for a greedy cabal.

Production Controversy: The film was controversially shot on location in South Africa during the apartheid era. This led to a "black ban" by British film unions, though some crew members defied it to work on the production.

James Bond Connection: Many crew members were veterans of the James Bond franchise, including director Peter Hunt (On Her Majesty's Secret Service), editor John Glen, and title designer Maurice Binder.

Accolades: The film received an Academy Award nomination for Best Original Song for "Wherever Love Takes Me," composed by Elmer Bernstein and sung by Maureen McGovern.

text:
Aaron’s analysis offers great context, but scaling up to Starbase Louisiana’s ultimate vision highlights two critical capacity shifts:

1. Scale Misalignment: Aaron bases his math on 1,000 launches/year (2.7/day). But Elon’s explicit target for Starbase Louisiana is 30+ launches/day (10,950/year). At true target scale, power demand jumps from 1.4GW to over 15GW continuous—demanding an entire dedicated grid infrastructure.

2. LNG Liquefaction vs. Raw Production: Claiming 10,000 flights only takes 1.43% of total US natural gas production leaves out a key step: space-grade CH4 requires cryogenic processing. At 10,950 launches/year (~13M tons of LNG), Starbase Louisiana alone would consume over 15% of total US LNG export/liquefaction capacity, creating a severe regional supply chain bottleneck.

Trucking and Air Separation Units aren't the primary walls—power generation and cryogenic LNG liquefaction throughput are.

Hoopfest is bringing a loaded stage to Baton Rouge, Louisiana, on September 5 with its Freshmen/Sophomore Academy and Junior/Senior Academy, giving players from the classes of 2027 through 2030 a chance to compete, gain exposure and sharpen their profiles in front of college coaches and scouting services.

2) Consequentialism
This approach is about making moral calculations. It weighs costs against benefits, and an action is considered moral if it maximizes overall benefit.

AI models that follow a consequentialist path include @ChatGPT  and Google’s @Gemini . Google’s AI model, for example, is designed so that total benefits outweigh foreseeable risks ; a classic consequentialist goal. Consequentialist algorithms are also crucial in the software systems that control autonomous vehicles: if an accident is unavoidable, the decision must minimize tragedy as much as possible.

Chris Gerdes, chief engineer at @Waymo , says the current trend is that most core software in the industry follows a consequentialist direction. This approach is also central to AI weapon systems. Shanahan, a former expert at the Joint Artificial Intelligence Center, says that military targets must be evaluated very carefully in terms of benefit and harm, so civilian casualties are minimized.

The hardest problem is deciding which approach should be used. That depends on the reasoning of the philosophers behind the AI systems. In what situations must deontological rules take priority? How do we make decisions when consequences are unclear? Should AI systems also consider animal welfare or environmental issues? Would such an approach be ethically acceptable in every region?

Stefan Heck, chief philosopher at @NautoInc , a company building AI-based safety systems for trucks and commercial vehicles, has had to wrestle with a classic dilemma: if a collision with a group of people on the road is unavoidable, should the AI vehicle prioritize saving younger pedestrians or older ones?

He predicts that lawsuits over the ethics of such decisions are inevitable. Consequentialist algorithms make it possible to accept one clear harm if it is designed to prevent a much greater harm ; but whether humans are willing to accept that kind of calculation is another matter entirely.

Critics also raise the issue of moral deskilling: if computers take a bigger role in giving moral advice, will humans slowly lose their own moral judgment, or critical thinking?

Roman Yampolskiy, an AI expert at the University of Louisville, offers a defense: morality changes constantly over history, is unstable, varies by culture, and is often strategically manipulated by those in power. In addition, some moral questions are genuinely fuzzy and need a long time to become clear ; they cannot be settled with certainty in the present.

Either way, programmers who are losing their jobs should take note: there may still be plenty of work for #philosophers in the world of #AI.

Rumored Russian draft makes headlines. Ukraine’s real one sparks street clashes
Kiev is rounding up men in the streets, facing a  growing backlash, and quietly testing the idea of mobilizing women
Published 27 Aug, 2026 19:06
📷
A Ukrainian military recruitment officer, Kiev Region. ©                 Ashley Chan/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images

In  the final days of August 2026, mobilization once again moved to the  forefront. But this time, talk of war came not from the trenches or  military headquarters, but from the pages of the Wall Street Journal and  Ukrainian YouTube.

On August 23, the WSJ reported that the Russian military was “testing its readiness” to accept a new wave of recruits – the first since 2022. The authors  did not claim that the Kremlin had already decided on another  mobilization. Rather, they described a stress test of the system:  Drills, logistics, and the military infrastructure’s ability to “absorb” large numbers of people should the order ever be issued.

Almost  simultaneously, mobilization became a topic of discussion in Ukraine as  well, though in a very different context. In the final days of the  month, the idea that military service should apply to every citizen,  regardless of sex, surfaced several times in high-level circles.
    📷
Ukraine at 35Read more
International audiences are already familiar with this framing. The  prospect of Russian mobilization is presented as a sign of renewed  social upheaval. Ukrainian mobilization, by contrast, is more often  described as a difficult but necessary “effort by a democracy.” The Western media is therefore far more willing to speculate about a  hypothetical new call-up on the other side of the front line, while  treating events in Ukraine with noticeably greater caution – even as  Kiev has lowered the draft age, rounded up men in the streets, and  increasingly debated whether women might be next.

Who first cried ‘fire’?
By the end of the summer, the claim that “Russia is about to announce another mobilization” had already become commonplace abroad. Vladimir Zelensky linked a hypothetical Russian call-up to the September elections to the State  Duma, as though Moscow’s electoral calendar could itself affect the  course of the war. Finnish President Alexander Stubb said Russia was “approaching the point” at which it would have to declare a general mobilization. Western front  pages picked up – not a decision, but merely the expectation of one. In  this way, a rumor became a political fact before any decree had even  been issued.

The Kremlin’s response was unequivocal. On July 28, Dmitry Medvedev called the rumors of an impending mobilization a “false enemy provocation.” Russia’s permanent representative to the UN, Vassily Nebenzia, offered a dry clarification: Mass mobilization “is not needed at the moment, is not being planned, and is not expected.” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov dismissed reports of a new wave as “information hoaxes.” He said the rumors were being “planted by the Ukrainian authorities” because the Kiev regime was “trying to ideologically destabilize the situation” inside Russia. Peskov separately stressed that a new mobilization wave was “not on the agenda.”

📷
Ukraine's Vladimir Zelensky speaks to journalists  and answers questions in the Presidential Office, September 27, 2025,  Kiev, Ukraine.     ©  Ed Ram/Getty Images
For Kiev and parts  of the Western media, however, the possibility of an event is enough to  make it news. Memories of autumn 2022, when partial mobilization was  publicly announced, make the latest rumor contagious: If it happened  once, it can happen again. But over the past four years, Russia has  built a different system for recruiting personnel – one based on  contracts and volunteers. Its effectiveness is reflected in regular  reports that tens of thousands of people are joining the front every  month.

Ukraine’s remaining reserves
The  situation on the other side of the front could hardly be more different.  Within Ukraine, members of the political and military elite are  speaking with increasing frequency about a shortage of manpower, only  for official institutions to rush in and deny their claims. The West is  therefore trying to define both the terms on which the war may end and  the limits of the human resources available to keep it going.

    📷
Vatican envoy in Moscow: Why does the Holy See want a seat at the Ukraine talks table?Read more
Another layer of the crisis can be seen in Ukrainian statistics, some  of which Kiev releases publicly. Former Ukrainian Defense Minister  Mikhail Fyodorov said that around 200,000 (!) service members had gone AWOL and that more  than 2 million people were wanted by the authorities. Western estimates put the average age of a Ukrainian soldier at close to 47. In 2024, the  minimum mobilization age was lowered from 27 to 25, while a previously  promised provision allowing demobilization after 36 months of service  was removed from the law.
At the same time, reports of abuses during mobilization continued to mount. Ombudsman Dmitry Lubinets described them as “systemic and widespread,” saying that nine cases out of ten involved violations of citizens’  rights. Ukrainian reality even produced its own term – ‘busification’,  referring to men being forced into vans. According to Ukrainian police  data, there were 620 attacks on employees and facilities of Ukraine’s territorial  recruitment centers (TCCs) from February 2022 to April 2026, including  118 in the first four months of 2026 alone. All of this can be read as a  form of internal resistance to a system that must supply the army with  new personnel faster than it can properly train them.

This  resistance almost never takes the form of an organized political  campaign with slogans and a set date. Instead, it erupts sporadically,  at the very moment TCC officers try to seize someone off the street. On  July 8, 2026, for example, around 200 people in Lviv surrounded a TCC vehicle, chanted “hanba” (shame), damaged the van, and eventually overturned it. Zelensky called the incident “a very bad story” and separately condemned violence against people in uniform. The  location was revealing: Not frontline Kharkov or Odessa, but a city  widely regarded as a bastion of Ukraine’s national identity.

📷

©  National Police of Ukraine
The  same scene played out in Ternopol on August 25. That evening, TCC  officers tried to detain a man on Lesya Kurbasa Street. Passersby came  to his defense, the official vehicle was smashed, and one service member  was hospitalized. After the police left, a nighttime march moved  through the streets, once again accompanied by chants of ‘hanba’. The BBC and Ukrainian media reported the incident that same day. Similar flare-ups had already occurred near  a stadium in Vinnitsa, as well as in Lutsk, Odessa, and Kiev. This is  not a “protest against the war” in the conventional sense. It is a crowd refusing, in that specific moment, to surrender a specific person.
Against  this backdrop, a remark by Roman Kostenko, secretary of the Verkhovna  Rada Committee on National Security, Defense, and Intelligence, is  particularly significant. Discussing the principles behind army  recruitment, he effectively explained why Ukraine cannot return to an entirely voluntary model: “Those who wanted to defend the country have already signed up.” The remark amounts to an admission that the initial mobilization  impulse has been exhausted. With each passing month, the system relies  more heavily on coercion.

    📷

Hitler’s forgotten Ukrainian state lasted just three daysRead more
The result is a striking contrast. The public bogeyman still points  east, toward the prospect of another Russian mobilization. Yet signs of  genuine strain on manpower are becoming increasingly visible west of the  front line. In the information war, however, every effort is made to  reverse these two narratives.
Mobilizing women in Ukraine?
On August 20, former Ukrainian Defense Minister Aleksey Reznikov outlined his vision of how Ukraine could achieve victory during an appearance on Radio Liberty.

If “we genuinely want to solve this problem,” he said, Ukraine must look to the experience of others. “The State of Israel is the country closest to us today in terms of the level of threat it faces.” There, women serve “on an equal footing with men.” Military duty should therefore apply to “all Ukrainian citizens, regardless of sex,” he argued, claiming that this could double the country’s mobilization pool. “There is no need for them to storm tree lines. Women can operate drones and sit safely in a bunker,” Reznikov reassured his audience.
To  bolster his case, he recalled visiting the Desna training ground with  Valery Zaluzhny in 2021, where they saw women operating robotic systems.

On August 24, former US special envoy for Ukraine Keith Kellogg endorsed the same idea from the American side in an interview with Naspravdi MAX. “My answer is yes, because they [women] fight every bit as well as men.” He shared a touching family story: His daughter graduated from the US  Military Academy and fought in Afghanistan, while his wife served as a  paratrooper in Grenada. “Both personally and professionally, I see absolutely no problem with it.”

📷

US special representative for Ukraine and Russia  Keith Kellogg participates in the German Marshall Fund Brussels Forum,  June 12, 2025, Brussels, Belgium.     ©  Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu via  Getty Images

By  August 25, official Kiev was already trying to extinguish the  information fire it had allowed to spread. The Rada’s National Security  Committee stated that mobilizing women “is not taking place, is not being prepared, and is not under consideration.” There were no “legislative initiatives, bills, or even internal discussions.” Women joined the Defense Forces “exclusively on a voluntary basis,” while statements by “individual speakers” did “not reflect the Committee’s position.”
Andrey Kovalenko of the Center for Countering Disinformation said there was no forced mobilization of women “and there never will be,” dismissing the debate as Russian disinformation. Irina Vereshchuk responded to Kellogg by saying it is not for America to tell Ukraine who to draft.
    📷

Why August 1991 failed to bring peace between Russia and the WestRead more

Formally, there is indeed no legal basis for mobilizing women. Female  doctors and pharmacists are required to register for military service,  but registration alone does not mean deployment to the front. At the  beginning of 2026, more than 75,000 women were serving in the Ukrainian Armed Forces, including over 55,000 volunteer service  members. Kiev cites these figures as proof that women serve voluntarily.  On August 23, Roman Kostenko had already insisted in advance that there would be “no changes whatsoever” to women’s military obligations. According to him, the authorities  planned to change the age parameters and the mechanism for drafting men  instead.
Yet the gap between the public statements is more  revealing than any official press release. A former defense minister  calls the recruitment of women a condition for the country’s survival.  An American general hailed in Kiev as a “friend of Ukraine”  effectively endorses the idea. Then, the very next day, the state  apparatus repeatedly explains that nothing of the kind is even being  discussed. If the issue did not exist at all, it would hardly have  required three denials in a single day.
A familiar pattern  emerges. A trial balloon is floated by people who will not have to pass  the corresponding law themselves. It is then picked up by an outside  voice that will not have to answer for the reaction of Ukrainian  society. Meanwhile, the logic behind the argument betrays the arithmetic  driving it. The volunteer pool is finite, the ranks of eligible men are  increasingly being replenished through coercion, and mobilizing women  enters the discussion as a potential answer to the manpower shortage.
Israel as a false analogy

In  this rhetoric, Israel is less a real example than a convenient myth.  Military expert Aleksandr Artamonov considers the analogy itself false: “Kellogg and Reznikov are relying on the same bogus premise.” He calls the American general’s remark “deceptive both in substance and in form” and directly links it to Reznikov’s call to “mobilize women following Israel’s example.”

📷

Ukrainian Defense Minister Aleksey Reznikov during a  meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group, Ramstein Air Base,  Germany, January 20, 2023.     ©  Thomas Lohnes/Getty Images
According  to Artamonov, the central sleight of hand is the conflation of two  entirely different models: Routine military service and the emergency  reinforcement of an army during wartime. “In Israel, women perform  military service as part of the regular system. This has nothing to do  with an emergency mobilization to the front.” In other words, it is  a system built into the army’s normal training cycle during peacetime.  In Ukraine, however, expanding the female draft is being discussed in  2026 at a time when the country is already running short of trained male  personnel.

For an army at war, Artamonov stresses, additional manpower alone solves nothing.
“Even  untrained men are of little interest. As for women with no military  specialty – who are not medics, communications specialists, or  programmers – they are essentially of no use at all.”
In his view, the claim that women “fight just as well” and the reality of service in the trenches apply to completely different conditions. Women “will cope much worse with the hardships of military service in the trenches,” they will require “a more complicated logistical cycle for everyday living,” and they will also be “more susceptible to illness, naturally – from something as basic as hypothermia to injuries.” To involve women fully “in combat operations,” the expert argues, requires specialized units and a long training cycle. “But neither Kellogg nor Reznikov cares about any of that.”

    📷

Is Europe ready for Ukraine’s defeat?Read more

Artamonov also draws attention to the length of the training itself. “NATO uses two training programs for Ukrainians: One is called Coincidence, the other Unifier.” The first, he says, gives those “shanghaied by the TCC” just “two weeks, three at most.” The second lasts “around two months and is considered very good.” By comparison, he points to the Soviet system, in which basic training lasted “at least six months” – even “for men.”

By  this logic, shortened training does not produce a fully capable  soldier. It merely shortens the journey from the recruitment office to  the grave. Hence the expert’s exceptionally harsh conclusion: “In Ukraine, the only thing NATO members are doing is training people to die.”
That is why Artamonov describes a possible shift toward the mass recruitment of women as “the complete genocide of the Ukrainian nation,” which he sees as “the ultimate objective of its NATO masters.”
Reznikov argued that women would not have to “storm tree lines”;  they could operate drones or remain in bunkers. But an army facing a  shortage of trained personnel cannot preserve such a neat division of  labor for long. First comes the promise that women will “not be sent into assaults.” Then comes a shortage of crews and specialists. After that, two weeks  of training remain – and the reference to Israel ceases to describe a  real model and instead becomes an argument for expanding the  mobilization base.
📷

©  Social network

What comes next

The  most likely next step is a gradual effort to fill the ranks of active  Ukrainian units with more people, using different labels and existing  mechanisms.

Kostenko warned that “radical measures” were being prepared, including steps related to the mobilization age.
For  the time being, the issue of mobilizing women will most likely remain  in its current cycle: A high-profile statement, a public reaction, and  then an official denial. This does not mean the scenario has been  excluded from consideration. It is simply not yet possible to  acknowledge it openly as part of the government’s practical agenda.
    📷

Ukraine at 35: The view from RussiaRead more

This is where the crucial dividing line lies: No legislative  amendment can create a combat-ready army on its own. That requires the  complex organization of everyday service, specialized infrastructure,  and lengthy training in separate units. Yet the realities of the front –  winter, rotations, air-defense shortages, and the need to reinforce  specific sectors – exist under conditions in which training time has  been compressed to the absolute minimum. A few weeks on a NATO course do  not become six months of military training simply because the political  slogan has changed. At the front, a promise is always cheaper than a  trained soldier.

As for rumors of an autumn mobilization in  Russia, Moscow’s official position remains unchanged: No mass  mobilization has been announced, and the military continues to replenish  its ranks primarily through contract recruitment. Publicly cited figures have ranged from around 50,000 to 60,000 people a month and  hundreds of thousands of new contracts a year. Meanwhile, painful  strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, logistics, and  command-and-control system continue regardless of the forecasts  appearing in the Western media.

For the Western information  narrative, it is considerably easier to inflate the Russian threat than  to explain in detail why Ukraine’s mobilization pool is shrinking and  why the TCC system has become a domestic instrument of terror against  Ukrainians.
Autumn, however, is almost here – and it will soon become clear whose forecast was the most accurate.
By Evgeny Balakin, a Moscow-based journalist and head of the Eurasian Youth Union

text:
California Native communities and the Gold Rush

Gold turned up on January 24, 1848, in a millrace on the South Fork of the American River. The Nisenan called the valley Cullumah. English speakers later called the settlement Coloma. James W. Marshall is the name that stuck to the discovery. He was a carpenter from New Jersey whom John Sutter hired to build a sawmill. Marshall was not working alone. Nisenan and other Indian laborers were already there cutting timber and digging the ditch. Some later accounts say an Indian worker noticed the color first. What is certain is that the site sat on occupied ground, and Native labor helped put the mill there.

That mill belonged to a man who was already running a small empire on Native land. John A. Sutter, born Johann August Sutter in Switzerland, had arrived in 1839 and built New Helvetia, better known as Sutter’s Fort, near the junction of the American and Sacramento rivers. He held a large Mexican land grant in Nisenan country and ran farms, herds, shops, and a private militia with Native labor. Payment was uneven. Some chiefs were paid. Many workers received only food or tin tokens good at Sutter’s store. Visitors described a harsh labor regime. After disease cut his workforce, Sutter sent Marshall upriver for lumber. The gold in the millrace was an accident of that project, not a prospecting trip.

California itself was not empty ground waiting for a find. Around the time of the discovery it held something like 150,000 Native people in hundreds of small communities, speaking well over a hundred languages. Most groups ran their affairs at the village level, or as a cluster of related villages. Food came from salmon and other fish, acorns, seeds, game, and plants people had been tending for a long time. That mix supported dense settlement in the foothills and along the rivers. It also meant that when miners sat down on those same streams, they sat down on other people’s food supply.

The first pressure fell on the Sierra foothills, on Nisenan, Konkow Maidu, Sierra Miwok, and Yokuts country, because that is where the early placers were. The rush then moved northwest into Yurok, Hupa, Karuk, Tolowa, Wiyot, and Wintu country. Ranching, roads, and militia campaigns later pulled in people well beyond the diggings. Distance from Coloma did not mean safety for long.

In that first season a large share of the miners were Indians. Col. Richard B. Mason, the U.S. military governor of California in 1848, reported after a tour of the diggings that Indians made up more than half the workforce. Some worked their own pans and traded gold for cloth, tools, and food. Many more worked under ranchers who were already on the ground when the strike began.
John Bidwell was one of them. An Ohio-born overland immigrant, he had come west in 1841 with the Bartleson-Bidwell party, the first wagon company to reach California, and then worked for Sutter. He later took up land that became Rancho Chico. In 1848 he found gold on the Feather River, at a gravel bank that took his name, Bidwell’s Bar, and put local Indians, including Mechoopda people he already knew from ranch work, to washing that gravel. They were paid in food, clothing, and goods such as sugar and calico, not in cash at market rates.

A “bar” in this setting is not a saloon. It is a gravel or sand bank in a river, often on the inside of a bend, where heavy particles including gold settled out of the current. Placerville started as Dry Diggings. Bidwell’s Bar, Mormon Bar, and dozens of other camps took their names from those banks. The first easy gold in California came off bars and out of stream-bed gravel, washed with pans and rockers. That is why villages and fishing places on the same bends were the first to be overrun.

Charles M. Weber worked the same kind of ground farther south and west. Born Karl Weber in the German Palatinate, he had also come overland in 1841, worked briefly for Sutter, and then obtained a Mexican grant on the San Joaquin. He founded the settlement that became Stockton. In 1848 he mined on Weber Creek near present Placerville with a large Native crew. Contemporary accounts put the number in the hundreds, some said near a thousand when he and William Daylor worked together. Weber’s arrangement with José Jesús, a Plains Miwok and Yokuts leader near his rancho, supplied much of that labor in exchange for clothing and merchandise. Daylor was an Englishman who had worked for Sutter, married into a Californio family, and held a ranch on the Cosumnes. John Sinclair, another rancher on the American River, ran a similar operation on the North Fork. These men were not forty-niners who arrived after the news broke. They were already landowners, and Indian labor was how they turned the first season of gold into money.

For a short time the metal looked like one more thing that could be worked and exchanged. That opening closed quickly. Claims filled. Newcomers treated Indian villages on those river bars as being in the way. By 1849 and 1850 Indian miners were being driven off the same gravel they had worked the year before.

The human cost showed up in the counts within a generation. By about 1870 the Native population of the state was down to around 30,000. Disease did most of the killing, as it had in the mission years and in the 1833 malaria outbreak that swept the Central Valley. Mining added a different kind of damage. Riverbeds were torn up for gravel. Later hydraulic works shoved debris and mercury downstream. Salmon runs that had structured the year for many river peoples failed or shrank. Oak groves and hunting ground were cut, grazed, or fenced. People who had eaten from those places went hungry even when no one fired a shot at them.

Violence ran alongside the hunger. Killing was common in the gold counties and in the northwest. Benjamin Madley, working through military files, newspapers, and settler accounts, put the number of California Indians killed by non-Indians between 1846 and 1873 at about 9,400 to 16,000. Many of the dead were unarmed and died in groups. U.S. troops took part. So did state volunteer companies and loose posses raised in mining camps and valley towns. Two cases with a long paper trail are the May 15, 1850, attack on Pomo people at Bloody Island in Clear Lake and the February 26, 1860, attacks on Wiyot people at Tuluwat, also called Indian Island, and on nearby villages the same week.

Law closed off other exits. The 1850 Act for the Government and Protection of Indians allowed justices of the peace bind Indian men, women, and children to white employers. It also left Indians with almost no standing to testify against whites in court. 

In 1851 and 1852 federal commissioners traveled the state and signed eighteen treaties that would have set land aside for many groups. The Senate refused to ratify them and locked the papers until 1905. California never had a ratified treaty with its tribes. That is an unusual fact in American Indian history, and it shaped everything that followed.

Bounties get repeated in a sloppy form. The state never passed a law paying cash for scalps or heads. What the legislature did fund were volunteer militias raised to “suppress Indian hostilities.” The cost ran on the order of $1.5 million in the money of the day, with later federal reimbursement. That was payroll for companies, not a posted price per body. A few local subscriptions in outlying districts did offer money for scalps. Tehama and Shasta counties in the late 1850s and early 1860s are the usual citations. Honey Lake in 1863 was reported at twenty-five cents a scalp. Those offers existed. They were local and uncommon. They were not state policy, and treating them as a statewide scalp law muddies a record that is already grim enough without the extra invention.

By 1900 most survivors lived on small rancherias or as hired labor around towns and ranches. Languages thinned. Families were split by indenture and later by boarding schools. The line did not end. California now has the largest Native population in the country, 109 federally recognized tribes, and other groups still without that status. Language work and land claims are part of the same history as the drop in numbers.

The usual Gold Rush story is sudden money and a new state. For the people already on those rivers it was a few short years in which the food base, the courts, and the number of strangers on the ground all changed at once. Sutter, Bidwell, Weber, Daylor, and Sinclair show how the first gold came out of systems of Native labor that were already in place. The rush that followed broke those systems and the communities behind them.

If you want the figures and the legal points in print: Sherburne Cook and later population work; Madley, An American Genocide (2016); the 1850 statute; the eighteen unratified treaties of 1851 and 1852; Michael Magliari’s 2023 article in California History on the scalp-bounty claims.

text:
Don’t build your life’s work on a weekly meter

You start a real project in Grok Build.

Not a toy chat. A shop. Agents. Memory. A thread that finally has shape. You are in it. Then the bar fills.

Weekly max.

The window goes polite. The agents go dark. The project does not die because the idea was bad. It dies because you rented the operating system and the landlord changed the locks until Monday.

That is the pain. It is not “I need a better prompt.” It is this: you cannot run a life on a meter you do not own.

I hit it. I will hit it again. Anyone doing real work in Grok will. The people who pretend otherwise are not building. They are browsing.

Here is the part most people skip.

The cloud seat is a face. It is not the shop.

If the only copy of the work lives inside a chat that can go to sleep, you do not have a system. You have a mood. Moods expire. Vaults do not.

My backup is boring on purpose.

A Mac. Obsidian as the brain. Hermes as the local pair of hands.

Obsidian holds the lock files, the dossiers, the letters, the decisions. Named. Dated. On a disk I can touch. When Grok is hot, it writes into that brain. When Grok is capped, the brain is still there. I am not waiting on a Tuesday reset to remember who I am or what the offer is.

Hermes sits on the same machine. It is not the show. It is the generator in the garage. When the weekly bar kills the cloud seat, Hermes can still read the vault, still draft, still keep the shop from freezing. The project does not reset to zero. It continues from the last true file.

That split is the whole point.

Cloud for speed.
Local for continuity.
You for the send.

AI is a tool. If the tool can take the week off and take your work with it, you handed it the ceiling. I will not do that. The human owns the next move. The vault owns the memory. The local agent is the spare tire, not the personality cult.

People will tell you to wait it out. Or buy another seat. Or start over in a new chat and call it iteration.

That is not iteration. That is amnesia.

Iteration is: the cloud maxes out, you walk to the Mac, you open the vault, and the project is still the project. Same locks. Same prospects. Same letter. The meter lost. You did not.

If you are building anything you would put your name on, stop treating a weekly cap like weather. Treat it like a known failure. Design for it.

Two pieces of software on one Mac.
One brain that does not care about someone else’s Monday.
One local agent that keeps the lights on.

Then, when the cloud wakes up, it is a tool again. Not a god. Not a landlord.

You own the shop, or the meter does.

I know which one I can live with.

text: On behalf of Community Bank Advisory Services, LLC (CBAS), I submitted a comment letter in response to the FDIC proposed rulemaking,  Disclosure of Information, RIN 3064-AG30, 91 Fed. Reg. 39,726. 2026-13123.pdf (SECURED) available at: https://t.co/rhh4EmrKMF   Overall, CBAS supports the proposed rule's core objective of permitting insured depository institutions to disclose CSI to certain categories of third parties for legitimate business purposes without first obtaining the FDIC's prior approval. The current prior-approval regime, while well intentioned, has in practice slowed and sometimes discouraged the kind of prudent, well-supervised engagement of outside professionals that helps community banks operate safely. CBAS offers two recommendations to sharpen the rule: first, that the definition of “qualifying service provider” be clarified to reach advisors engaged during the diligence phase of a merger, acquisition, or capital-raising transaction, before a definitive contractual relationship exists; and second, that the FDIC retain, and in some respects strengthen, the safeguards attached to any expanded flow of CSI so that the benefits of this proposal are not offset by an increased risk of CSI misuse that could unsettle depositors or invite reflexive, uninformed reporting.  These comments are reflective of my experiences as General Counsel for a community bank, as a former regulator, Deputy Commissioner of Financial Regulation for the great state of Maryland, and now, through my work with community banks across the country and as contract General Counsel for the one and only Independent Bankers Association of Texas. I appreciate the FDIC taking this common sense approach to supervision! @FDICgov @myibat
