text:
Mind if I explain to you what's going on? It's long but you asked. If you really want to know...read on. 

Republicans are the entire reason our healthcare system is out of control. That's not political. It's a fact. 

Let me explain it to you in simple terms.

Healthcare shouldn't be political. Why?

Because no one can help getting old and sick, right?

The way insurance works..all insurance...is you pay in for the day you will eventually need it.

Whether we are talking about car insurance...home insurance...or any insurance...you pay a premium with the idea that the insurance company will payout when you need it most.

The problem with our for-profit healthcare system is that there are too many hands in the pot....doctors...hospitals...hedgefunds....shareholders....all trying to make as much MONEY as possible.

And because our for-profit healthcare system is about MONEY...premiums rise...and every service has to be approved and signed off on...which also has increased the administrative costs as well.

All of that is driving up costs...and all of that was driving up costs WELL BEFORE OBAMACARE at about 10% a year.

THIS is the reason why every other counrty IN THE WORLD has moved to a single-payer system that takes the Profit motive OUT of healthcare so you only pay for the care you need and NOT all the middle men and hedgefunds tryingto increase thier bottom line.

Our for-profit healthcare system is WHY we pay the MOST MONEY for the WORST ranked care IN THE WORLD.

Ask anyone who has had an kind of major medical issue and ask them what it's like dealing with the insurance companies trying to get approvals.

It's a nightmare...which drives up costs.

Obama came along...and said...this is crazy. "Why don't we as a country simply switch to a single-payer system like every other country. Premiums rising at 10% a year is unsustainable."

Republicans looked at that and said..."but we get a lot of MONEY from the healthcare lobby to fund our campaigns. We can't put private insurers out of business...no way!"

But they all saw the premiums rising and knew something had to be done.

So they ended up agreeing on a HYBRID system.

Obama got to expand our already existing single-payer system known as Medicare to allow more people to use the program....and Republicans got to keep private healthcare and their wealthy donors.

Obama figured that once people saw that The Obama Care marketplace was cheaper than Private healthcare....that people would come around to undrestanding the benefitsof a single-payer system.

The only PROBLEM was 22 republicans states deliberately sabotaged the bill and politisized the entire debate...and never implemented the law.

That meant that the premiums COULD not come down as much as intended. Why?

Because...back to the way insurance works.
With insurance....take car insurance for example If you have no wrecks...you pay less because you are considered less risk.
Once you have a wreck you are considered "High Risk" and you move up into a "High Risk" pool of drivers who are also high risk and you all pay higher premiums.

If you have a bunch of wrecks...your premiums go through the roof or the insurance company drops you because they are going to lose money on you.
Or you drop coverage because you simply can't afford car insurance anymore due to the higher premiums.
Now..note that Car insurance is mandated by law. WHY?

Because if a bunch of people are running around without insurance...and you get in a wreck with one of those people....you aren't going to be able to have your damaged car paid for if they have no insurance.

That means that YOUR insurance company has to pick up the difference or you have to come out of pocket. And that scenario drives up everyones car insuance premiums because at the end of the day SOMEONE has to pay for your car.

It's the same with health insurance.

When our for-profit healthcare system drives up premiums...some people are forced to drop coverage because it’s too expensive. But the cost of their care doesn't magically go away.

People cannot help gettin old and sick.

When those people without insurance show up in emergency rooms sick or dying...the REST OF US pay for their care in the form of higher premiums.

That is why Obama wanted to expand our single-payer system known as Medicare to be able to be offered to more people.

By subsidizing the already skyrocketing premiums...more people would be CONTRIBUTING to their own care...which means the REST of us would NOT have to cover their eventual care...which means lower premiums for the rest of us.

And that's why the RISE in premiums BEFORE Obamacare was SLOWED...even with 22 republican States NOT implementing the law.

Because MORE people got coverage...which mean MORE people were helping to pay for their eventual care...which means that all our premiums started to slow down.

Now look at the flip side.

Trump and Republicans just CUT ACA Medicare subsides to pay for tax breaks for the wealthy and corporations.

And what is happening as we speak....people are being forced to drop coverage.

Who drops coverage FIRST? Healthy people.

The more healthy people that drop coverage leave sicker people in the POOL of people left.

Just like how people with more car accidents pay more. When healthy people leave the pool...and you have sicker people left....the insurance companies are forced to raise premiums because everyone left is more costly and you don't have the healthy people left to help cover the costs of all the sick people.

It becomes a High Risk pool with higher premiums. Cutting ACA subsidies sets up back on the path to rising premiums because HEALTHY people will drop coverage without the subsidies...leaving sick people in a high risk pool....which means insurance companies will raise rates.

And they already have.

The named examples:

• Blue Cross Blue Shield of Vermont (requesting +23.3%): expiration of the enhanced subsidies "will shrink the population with coverage and worsen the risk pool, requiring higher premiums for the remaining members."

• Community Health Options, Maine (requesting +34%): they "anticipate the remaining risk pool in 2026 [will] have higher healthcare needs, on average, as healthier consumers are more likely to lapse coverage."

• Optimum Choice, Maryland (requesting +18.6%): “healthier members are expected to leave at a disproportionately higher rate than those with significant healthcare needs, increasing market morbidity in 2026."

• MVP Health Care, Vermont: assumed healthy subsidized enrollees would drop coverage at twice the rate of others, worsening the risk pool.

That's why other countries have gone single-payer.

Everyone in those countries...simply pays a small amount beginning at the age they start working...and by the time they need to pay for their care when they get older...YEARS later...the money is there to pay for it all....which keeps costs low for everyone.

Because that's the way insurance works best.

The healthy people pay for themselves...and the sick people....over years of payments and it keeps premiums low.

Same with Car insurance...good drivers who have no wrecks...pay for the bad drivers who have a lot of wrecks.

If all the good drivers stopped paying for car insurance and never got insurance...such that the only people in the pool were bad drivers...then premiums for car insurance would be high too.

What we have in this country is a for-profit model that is designed to drive profits up to make shareholders and hedgefunds happy...and when you drive costs up...less people can afford healthcare....so the healthy people end up dropping it which leaves sick people in high risk pools....forcing the healthcare companies to pay out more....which is why they keep raising premiums.

That was the rise in premiums and deductibles BEFORE Obamacare.

It was the main reason why Obamacare originally had a mandate.

More people paying for their own eventual care means lower premiums for everyone.

But Republicans politicized that too and here we are.

It's a cost and premium death spiral that was stalled by Obamacare...but is now being reversed due to Republican sabotage and to give tax breaks to the wealthy and corporations.

You get it now? There is literally no reason to argue about anything. A for-profit system drives costs up and is antithetical to the way insurance actually works.

It's why every other modern country in the world has gone 100% single-payer. That's not political. That's a fact.

The way our for profit healthcare system bills is choking the system. 

A Duke team published the accounting in JAMA: just the billing and insurance-related work costs $20 per primary care visit, $124 per hospital stay, $215 per inpatient surgery — and a primary care doctor's practice burns about $99,500 PER PHYSICIAN PER YEAR purely on getting paid.   

Roughly 14.5% of primary care revenue is consumed by the act of billing for it:  

https://t.co/8PA6IF0c1x 

Why so high? Because every hospital negotiates secret rates with dozens of insurers, each with its own plans, each plan with its own rules, codes, prior-auth lists, networks, and denial-and-appeal machinery.   

That's not government paperwork — that's the profit-driven paperwork of a thousand private rulebooks grinding against each other because our for-profit healthcare system is hell bent of trying to find ways to deny coverage and squeeze more profit out of the system. 

It costs  everyone $600 Billion a year in higher premoiums like your grandparents are experiencing. 

Ask anyone who has had a major preceedure. They know how hard it is to get approvals from insurance companies on everything and how it leads to delays. 

So the issue is our for-profit healthcare system...which continues to drive up costs. 

And the fact that Repubulicans continue to assits those coverage increases either by trying to sabotage Obamacare entirely by not implementing the law...or cutting ACA subsidies to pay for thier tax cuts for the wealthy and coporations like they just did in the One Big Beautiful Bill....which means less people paying in....more dropped coverage by healthy people...more high risk pools...and higher premiums for all of us. 

That is the situation.

text:
Part 5 

As secession gathered, the War Department moved munitions south. Obsolete federal arms were sold through intermediaries. 

Southern newspapers would soon boast that hundreds of thousands of stands of arms had been gathered from seized arsenals and purchases. 

Floyd’s enemies called it treason from inside the cabinet. His defenders called it routine transfer. Either way, when the Cotton States walked out, they did not walk out empty handed. 

The man accused of belonging to a secret order whose ritual began with Mexico had spent his last months in office watching the federal gun-rooms of the South fill.

The Indianapolis pamphlet was published into that exact smell of powder.

Then came Baltimore.

Lincoln had to reach Washington to be inaugurated. 

The railroad ran through a city thick with Southern rights militias: 

National Volunteers drilling by the company, rumors of dozens of units, a barber named Cypriano Ferrandini described as handy with a stiletto. Dorothea Dix overheard talk that “Mr. Lincoln’s inauguration was thus to be prevented, or his life to fall a sacrifice.” Allan Pinkerton’s operatives reported a plan to rush the president elect’s carriage. One dispatch spoke of blowing the Capitol when the electoral votes were counted.

Lincoln was put on a night train, cut off from the public schedule, and slipped into Washington before dawn like a fugitive in his own country.

Winfield Scott thickened the capital’s defenses. The inauguration happened under guns.

Historians still argue how tightly those Baltimore cells were stitched to formal K.G.C. command. David Keehn, the most detailed modern historian of the order, treats a planned strike on Lincoln’s Baltimore passage as part of the Knights’ clandestine turn. Other scholars are more cautious. The caution does not make the night train less real.

A secret society sworn to conquer a neighboring republic had, within months, generated a political weather in which the president-elect of the United States could not safely ride a public train through an American city.

Mexico was the romance.

Washington was the emergency.

Now the name that makes the whole file feel cursed.

In the summer of 1859, in Richmond, several young actors from a stock company drifted into the Knights. One of them was twenty years old, Maryland born, trained at a military academy, already in love with secret societies, plumes, and Sir Walter Scott. 

The order offered him what it offered other restless men: a first-degree oath as a Knight of the Iron Hand, the rumor of Mexican acres, the theater of a coming campaign.

His name was John Wilkes Booth.

Here the ground must stay honest. 

The Handbook of Texas is blunt: 

later claims tying Booth and Jesse James, and buried federal payrolls guarded into the twentieth century to the Knights cannot be reliably documented. Keehn, working from captured papers and local traces, treats Booth’s 1859 initiation as real and later writes that various Knights supported him at the war’s end. The military commission that tried the assassination conspirators heard Judge Advocate Henry Burnett say he found “the footprints of the old Order of the Knights of the Golden Circle crossing my path in all directions.” 

Booth’s own first plan was not murder. It was kidnapping  the same grammar as Baltimore in 1861 seize Lincoln, drag him to Richmond, trade him for the dying Confederacy.

text:
Washington and Baltimore are currently separate Nielsen Designated Market Areas (DMAs) for television ratings and most advertising buys. Washington ranks among the top 10 U.S. markets while Baltimore ranks in the mid-20s. They are treated as one larger region in the Census Combined Statistical Area (CSA), which has roughly 10 million people and ranks among the nation’s largest. Some radio stations already promote dual-market coverage that reaches both cities.

Combining them for media purposes offers these practical advantages:
Larger combined audience and advertising scale. Advertisers can buy one buy that reaches commuters, Maryland suburbs, and both urban cores instead of two separate campaigns. A bigger footprint can attract national advertisers who might skip a mid-sized market like Baltimore alone. Some stations already highlight this dual reach in sales materials. 

Operational efficiencies and shared regional stories. Federal government news, transportation issues (MARC trains, BWI airport, I-95 corridor), weather events, and sports rivalries (Ravens–Commanders) affect both areas. One newsroom or syndicated programming can cover those overlapping topics at lower cost than two fully separate operations. Signal overlap on AM and some FM stations already makes this feasible. 

Stronger regional economic and sports marketing identity. The CSA definition supports treating the Beltway as a single high-income, highly educated labor and consumer market. NFL teams have contested “home marketing areas” in the Maryland suburbs precisely because those counties sit between the two cities and represent valuable overlapping fans. Combined coverage can treat the region as one competitive marketplace rather than two smaller ones.

These gains come at the expense of hyper-local focus, which is the point raised in the original radio discussion. Stations that try to serve both markets often reduce time spent on city-specific crime, schools, or neighborhood issues.

$PEGA although the chart looks like it may be going somewhere, Grok's asymmetric review:  

avoid/avoid

Pegasystems Inc. (Pega) is a U.S. enterprise software company that builds a low-code platform for AI-powered decisioning and workflow automation. It helps large organizations personalize customer experiences, automate service and operations, and modernize legacy systems.

Company basics
Founded: 1983 by Alan Trefler (still Chairman and CEO) in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Trefler previously worked on early AI chess systems and applied similar rule-based “expert systems” ideas to business processes.
Headquarters: Waltham, Massachusetts (225 Wyman Street), with offices across North America, Europe, Latin America, Asia-Pacific, and Japan. European HQ is in Reading, UK.
Public company: NASDAQ: PEGA since 1996; S&P MidCap 400 component.
Scale: Roughly 5,500–5,600 employees worldwide. Recent revenue is in the $1.5–1.7 billion range, with market cap around $5.6 billion.

What Pega actually sells
The core offering is the Pega Infinity portfolio, built on the Pega Platform—a model-driven, low-code environment for building and evolving enterprise applications. Key pieces include:

Pega Customer Decision Hub — real-time AI engine that predicts behavior and recommends the next best action across channels.
Pega Customer Service — omnichannel service automation that connects customers, employees, and systems.
Pega Platform — AI-powered workflow and case management for operational processes.
Pega GenAI Blueprint — generative AI tooling to prototype and accelerate application design and deployment.
Situational Layer Cake — patented architecture that layers business logic by customer type, geography, product line, etc., so changes can be reused and scaled without rewriting everything.

Delivery is increasingly via Pega Cloud, plus on-premises and hybrid options. They also offer training (Pega Academy), implementation services, and support.

Pega’s positioning is “Build for Change”: structure AI and automation so large, regulated enterprises can adapt without breaking existing systems. They emphasize governed, predictable outcomes rather than unconstrained generative AI.

Customers and industries
Pega targets large enterprises and government agencies, especially in:

Financial services (they cite all 10 of the top global banks)
Insurance
Telecommunications
Healthcare
Government
Manufacturing and high tech

Notable named clients in public materials have included major banks, insurers, telecoms, and firms such as Verizon, Ford, Coca-Cola, and various government agencies. They sell directly and through a large partner network (Accenture, Capgemini, Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, and others).

Market recognition
Analyst firms have frequently ranked Pega as a leader in areas such as real-time interaction management, CRM, AI decisioning platforms, and process-related categories (Forrester Waves and Gartner Magic Quadrants are commonly cited in their materials).

Gathering latest SEC filings, financials, backlog, peers, and recent catalysts for PEGA.Binary verdict (framework, not narrative): AVOID as a full three-leg “ape-in.” Backlog and cash legs pass. The print leg fails the acceleration test. This is a cash-printing utility with a slowing new-business engine, not a speculative drain.

Last-24-hour SEC check (Aug 26–27, 2026): Form 4 sales by Chief Product Officer Kerim Akgonul (1,700 shares at $33.98 and 1,300 at $34 on Aug 25). Form 144 and director equity grants earlier in the week. No 8-K, no warrant issuance, no material capital-structure event in the last day. Latest operating 8-K/10-Q remains the July 21, 2026 Q2 package.

Shared facts (both analyses use the same numbers)

The print. Q2 2026 revenue $420.7M, +9.4% YoY. H1 revenue $850.7M vs $860.1M, -1%. TTM revenue $1.736B vs FY2025 $1.746B, TTM growth +3.6%. ACV, the metric management says matters, is $1.620B, +7% reported / +8% CC, down from +12% in Q1 2026 and +17% at year-end 2025. Pega Cloud ACV $926.3M, +22%. Cloud is 57% of ACV. Subscription services were 69% of Q2 revenue. Revenue is not accelerating. The mix is shifting to cloud while license/maintenance shrink.

The backlog. Remaining performance obligations $2.019B at June 30, 2026, +10% / +11% CC. Pega Cloud backlog about $1.56B, 77% of total. Backlog / TTM revenue = 1.16x. This is contracted RPO, not a pipeline of hopes. It is not a multi-year fortress like some infrastructure software books; a large slice is current-year. Year-end 2025 backlog was $2.1B, so the book is roughly flat to slightly down from December.

The EBITDA / cash turn. Self-funding. FY2025 operating cash flow $505M, FCF $491M. H1 2026 OCF $298M, FCF $288M. TTM OCF $513M, TTM FCF ~$493M. Gross margin TTM 75.6%; Pega Cloud gross margin about 79%. GAAP Q2 operating income $16.6M. GAAP net income compressed (Q2 $13.3M vs $30.1M; H1 $46.1M vs $115.5M) because of mix, legal, SBC, and a tough compare. Cash and marketable securities $362M, total debt $72M, net cash ~$290M, unused credit facility. H1 buybacks $367M / 8.9M shares; $0.9B authorization remaining through June 2027. Shares outstanding down about 4% YoY. This is not a dilutive survival story.

Valuation floor. Market cap ~$5.5–5.9B, EV ~$5.2–5.6B. Trailing P/S ~3.2–3.5x, EV/Sales ~3.0x, trailing P/E ~19x, forward P/E ~12x. FCF yield on EV is high-single to low-double digits on TTM FCF.
NameRoleP/S (TTM, approx.)EV/Sales (approx.)Fwd P/E (approx.)PEGAWorkflow / decisioning3.2–3.5x~3.0x~12xCRMCRM platform~4.1–4.6x~5.3x~17xNOWWorkflow / ITSM~8–9x~6–8xmid-20sAPPNLow-code BPM peer~3.5x~3.0–3.1xhigh-20s when profitablePATHAutomation peermid-single to high-single on sales depending on print~2–4x historically, noisyhigh
PEGA trades at a discount to CRM/NOW and in the Appian neighborhood on sales, with better cash conversion than Appian. The discount is the growth deceleration, not a hidden balance-sheet hole.
Capital-flow timeline (public).
2022: OCF $22M, FCF negative. Convertible/debt era.
2023: OCF $218M, FCF $201M. Turn begins.
2024: OCF $346M, FCF $338M.
2025: OCF $505M, FCF $491M. Cloud ACV +33%. Net ACV add $190M.
H1 2026: OCF $298M, FCF $288M, but ACV growth slumps to 7–8%. Cash on balance sheet falls $426M → $362M because buybacks outran H1 cash generation. Trajectory: cash engine still compounding; new ACV momentum rolled over. That is the stock’s problem.
Last-24h / recent filings. Insider selling continues (CPO, CFO historically, founder 10b5-1-style sales earlier in 2026). No warrants. No distress financing.
Oil at $100. PEGA is not a swing energy asset and not a stranded energy asset. Activation lag is sales-cycle lag (quarters), not plant restart. Client base is banks, insurers, telcos, government. $100 oil is a second-order demand risk via financial-services budgets, not an operating leverage event.
Short squeeze. Not a squeeze setup that pays on its own. Short interest ran up after the miss: mid-July ~15.8M shares, ~18% of float, ~8 days to cover; later prints ~13.3M, ~15.5% of float, ~8% of shares out, ~3.6 days to cover. Float is thin because insiders own ~48%. Borrow has not been reported as special. High short interest is a sentiment flag, not a mechanical catalyst without a hard ACV beat.
Market health.S&P 500 near ~7,740, above rising 10/20/50-day averages and well above the 200-day. Nasdaq 100 also above short EMAs on the daily. Breadth is mixed (fewer names above the 20-day than above the 200-day). Index regime: healthy enough, not a crash tape. PEGA itself: 52-week range $25.10–$68.10, 50-day ~$31, 200-day ~$42. Price is above the 50-day after the post-earnings washout, still far below the 200-day. That is repair, not tightness under resistance at old highs.
PEG 2026–2028 (simple). Street-ish revenue path ~$1.89B / $2.06B / $2.24B and non-GAAP EPS ~$2.45 / $2.64 / $2.81 (FactSet-style compilations; company Feb guide was $2.0B revenue and $2.75 non-GAAP EPS, now at risk). From ~$34 and ~$2.45 2026E EPS, P/E ~14x 2026E. EPS CAGR 2026–2028 on those figures is only ~7%. PEG ≈ 14 / 7 ≈ 2.0. If you use FCF instead of EPS, the multiple looks cheaper; if you use ACV growth of 7–8%, the PEG looks worse.
Analysis 1 — Optimistic (independent)
Cash-printing utility, discounted for a sales-cycle pause.
The stool: backlog and cash stand. The print is weak on ACV acceleration but the cloud engine is still compounding at 22%. That is a mix-shift story, not a broken product.
Architectural nuance (software, not a fab). Pega is not a token wrapper. The core is a model-driven case and decisioning engine with the patented Situational Layer Cake: business logic is stacked by customer type, product, geography, and channel so a change in one layer does not force a rewrite of the enterprise application. Customer Decision Hub is a real-time next-best-action system sitting on that case fabric. Blueprint / Infinity Studio push GenAI into design-time application construction and constrain run-time agent token use. That is why management sells “no per-token cost.” Competitors can bolt an LLM onto CRM or ITSM. They cannot drop a Pega case model, layered specialization, and decisioning policy into Salesforce or ServiceNow as a plug-in. Switching cost is the implemented case inventory, not a SKU. Sole-source is overstated; primary-source inside complex, regulated process estates (top banks, insurers, telcos) is fair.
Capacity / chokepoint. There is no foundry. The scarce resource is certified implementation talent and partner bench (Accenture, TCS, Infosys, Capgemini). Pega owns the IP and the runtime. Hyperscalers own the metal. Pricing power in a demand spike sits with Pega on software, with SIs on services. That is why consulting revenue is shrinking on purpose.
Qualification / forward model. This is not 2027 NRE. Commercial volume is already in production at global banks. The lag is enterprise procurement under AI-budget confusion, not lab-to-fab qualification. Do not value this on a pending 2027 ramp that does not exist. Value it on cloud ACV converting into 75%+ of the book.
Downstream stack.Not a component vendor. Infinity is already the application + platform + decisioning + service layer. M&A is tuck-in, not a required vertical integration to survive.
Floor. ~$490M TTM FCF against ~$5.3B EV is a cash floor if ACV does not collapse. Gross margin is software-like. Buybacks are the capital-return policy.
Catalyst. H2 ACV recovery toward the original 15% target, or explicit cut-and-hold of the $575M FCF guide with continued Cloud mix. Infinity 26 / Blueprint if it shortens sales cycles.
Ape-in on solvency. Green light on solvency. Red light on acceleration. Optimistic verdict still AVOID as a 75% ape-in until ACV re-accelerates; a smaller cash-flow compounder sleeve is the only honest long.
Missing stool leg: The Print (acceleration).
Analysis 2 — Pessimistic (independent)
Cash today, franchise risk tomorrow. The machine is working on the installed base and stalling on net new.
Market health. Indexes are above intermediate EMAs. That does not rescue a stock whose own 200-day is still overhead and whose primary KPI rolled over.
Three-legged screener.
Undervalued vs NOW/CRM: yes on P/S. Floor is FCF, not hype. Versus Appian, no cheapness.
Rapid revenue ramp: no. TTM +3.6%, H1 −1%, ACV +7%. The machine is working on cloud mix, not on total growth.
Hot sector: enterprise AI is hot. Pega is being treated as the governed, expensive incumbent, not the momentum vehicle. Institutional money is in CRM/NOW/PLTR, not here.
Pivot test. CapEx is trivial (~$10M H1, ~$15–20M annual). This is not a capacity-expansion story. The pivot is commercial: license/maintenance → Pega Cloud; rules BPM → GenAI Blueprint + agentic design-time. Primary metric shifted years ago from license bookings to ACV and FCF. Management is distancing from “token chaos,” which is an admission that the buyer set is frozen, not that Pega has already won the new constraint.
Devil’s advocate on the 10-Q. Current ratio 1.06 is tight for a software firm after the buyback. Cash fell because they retired stock faster than they printed cash. GAAP operating margin in the quarter is thin. Legal fees sit in the non-GAAP bridge. H1 net income down 60%. They guided 15% ACV and $2.0B revenue in February; H1 run-rate and commentary say recovering the ACV hole is “difficult.” That is a broken guide, not a beat-and-raise compounder.
Premium. There is no hype premium left after the −19% post-print move and the 52-week drawdown from $68. The remaining risk is a value trap: 3x sales on 7% ACV growth with a founder-controlled register and ongoing insider selling.
Bottleneck. They solve process chaos plus ungoverned LLM spend in regulated workflows. Tier-1 customers absolutely have a Plan B: Salesforce + ServiceNow + home-grown agents + Appian. Pricing power is not zero, but it is not a sole-source substrate. Inventory turnover and WIP-regulatory holds do not apply; the analog is implementation WIP and elongated close cycles. Export-control revenue share is not a 30%+ China-fab problem. Geopolitical fragility is client-budget cyclicality in global banks, not entity-list risk.

EBITDA turn already happened. The missing institutional green light is ACV, not EBITDA.

Dilution. None required. Negative asymmetry is limited versus a 40x sales name. Positive asymmetry is also limited unless ACV snaps back.
Technical confluence. Bounce from $25 toward $34 is a relief rally into a declining 200-day. Not tight enough for a 75% ape-in. Wait for either a failed breakdown under $25 or a weekly reclaim of the 200-day with ACV confirmation.
Short squeeze. 15%+ of float is enough to amplify a beat. It is not enough to force a squeeze while management is guiding cautiously and insiders are selling.
Missing stool legs: The Print. On a strict screen, Hot Sector / institutional momentum is also missing.
Unified output
LegStatusPrint (accelerating revenue / ACV)FAIL. Q2 rev +9%, ACV +7%, TTM rev +3.6%Backlog (contracted cash)PASS. $2.02B RPO, 1.16x TTM sales, 77% cloudEBITDA / cash turnPASS. Multi-year positive FCF, net cash, buybacks
Classification: cash-printing utility with a decelerating bookings engine. Not a speculative drain. Not a swing oil asset.

2026–2028 simple PEG: about 2.0 on a ~7% EPS CAGR; worse if ACV stays at 7–8%.

Ape-in / solvency: solvency passes. Growth screen fails.

BUY / AVOID: AVOID until ACV growth re-accelerates toward the 15% guide or the company formally resets the guide and the stock is bought as a mid-teens FCF-yield stub. The missing leg is The Print.

More than 350 people are dead, and more than a thousand are missing, after the flooding caused by a glacier collapse in Nepal and Tibet. Australia has joined the rescue effort. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese...: “At this point, uh, Nepal, you know, is a developing country. It doesn't have the resources that an event like that would have in Australia, so information is difficult. Now our thoughts are with all those who'll be concerned about their loved ones today. ”
Rescuers are struggling to reach some areas, because the floodwaters and mud washed away bridges and 25 miles of roads.

Closing arguments begin this morning in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy. The Massachusetts woman allegedly strangled her three young children. Her lawyers have argued she was suffered from postpartum psychosis, and should not be held criminally responsible.
News Nation's Jessica Kartalija...: “Testimony ended Wednesday after jurors heard from those 85 different witnesses. The final witness was Dr. Gregory Sattoff, a forensic psychiatrist who also works with the FBI's Behavioral Analysis Unit. He was on the stand for quite some time. Sattoff testified for the prosecution that he believes that she was criminally responsible for killing the 3 children and that she was in fact in control of her actions. ”
If convicted, Clancy faces up to life in prison.

A man has been arrested in Northern France after he rammed his car into a group of people, killing one of them and injuring ten others. Seven of the injured are in critical condition.  Police say it was not terrorism, but the result of "a fight that turned bad."

The Justice Department says it has shut down a Chinese hacking operation that targeted some of the most sensitive networks in the federal government. WWNN's Stacy Lyn reports:: “The hackers breached systems at the Justice Department, NASA, the Federal Reserve, and the Senate. They were trying to infiltrate not only some of our key infrastructure, but Attorney General Todd Blanch told Fox News it also included hospital systems and healthcare centers. He calls it a major national security threat. We know from our investigation this was state. Sponsored by China and the US should expect China to try again. Not only are we using the FBI and the federal government, but we are now empowering the private sector to help us identify the hacking techniques, and then when we identify them to stop them. China denies the allegations, Stacy Lin, Worldwide News Network, Washington. ”

The death toll from this week's explosion and fire at a has chemical complex in eastern Russia has risen to 15.  The complex had yet to begin operating.  It was preparing to start production.

Residents of Dolly Parton's hometown of Sevierville (suh-VEER-vull), Tennessee gathered for a vigil last night. The town's courthouse bell tolled, as fans left flowers and balloons near her statue.: “She was special. She was so special. ”
Parton's funeral will be private.

There's new hope for patients with a deadly form of cancer.: “US health officials approved a groundbreaking pancreatic cancer drug that offers a new approach to treating the deadly disease. The Food and Drug Administration granted approval to the first of a kind pill from Revolution Medicines. The drug uses a new approach to block a protein that fuels tumor growth in the. The vast majority of pancreatic cancer cases. Patients taking the drug nearly doubled their survival time in a company study of 500 patients. Experts say the treatment will probably revamp their approach to the disease and other hard to treat cancers. Salgie and Grasso, Worldwide News Network. ”

North Korea vowed today to respond "strongly and immediately" to the US' decision to approve the sale of missiles and other military equipment to South Korea.  North Korea says the sale poses a new threat to its security.

text:
2/ HOW WE WENT THERE.
We went there in an ambulance, and we went together,—the Colonel and I; and though two men were never more unlike, we worked together like two brothers, or like two halves of a pair of shears. That we got in was owing, perhaps, to me; that we got out was due altogether[Pg 374] to him; and a man more cool, more brave, more self-reliant, and more self-devoted than that quiet "Western parson" it never was my fortune to encounter.

When the far-away Boston bells were sounding nine, on the morning of Saturday, the sixteenth of July, we took our glorious Massachusetts General by the hand, and said to him,—

"Good bye. If you do not see us within ten days, you will know we have 'gone up.'"

"If I do not see you within that time," he replied, "I'll demand you; and if they don't produce you, body and soul, I'll take two for one,—better men than you are,—and hang them higher than Haman. My hand on that. Good bye."

At three o'clock on the afternoon of the same day, mounted on two raw-boned relics of Sheridan's great raid, and armed with a letter to Jeff. Davis, a white cambric handkerchief tied to a short stick, and an honest face,—this last was the Colonel's,—we rode up to the Rebel lines. A ragged, yellow-faced boy, with a carbine in one hand, and another white handkerchief tied to another short stick in the other, came out to meet us.

"Can you tell us, my man, where to find Judge Ould, the Exchange Commissioner?"

"Yas. Him and t'other 'Change officers is over ter the plantation beyont Miss Grover's. Ye'll know it by its hevin' nary door nur winder [the mansion, he meant]. They's all busted in. Foller the bridle-path through the timber, and keep your rag a-flyin', fur our boys is thicker 'n huckelberries in them woods, and they mought pop ye, ef they didn't seed it."

Thanking him, we turned our horses into the "timber," and, galloping rapidly on, soon came in sight of the deserted plantation. Lolling on the grass, in the shade of the windowless mansion, we found the Confederate officials. They rose as we approached; and one of us said to the Judge,—a courteous, middle-aged gentleman, in a Panama hat, and a suit of spotless white drillings,—

"We are late, but it's your fault. Your people fired at us down the river, and we had to turn back and come overland."

"You don't suppose they saw your flag?"

"No. It was hidden by the trees; but a shot came uncomfortably near us. It struck the water, and ricochetted not three yards off. A little nearer, and it would have shortened me by a head, and the Colonel by two feet."

"That would have been a sad thing for you; but a miss, you know, is as good as a mile," said the Judge, evidently enjoying the "joke."

"We hear Grant was in the boat that followed yours, and was struck while at dinner," remarked Captain Hatch, the Judge's Adjutant,—a gentleman, and about the best-looking man in the Confederacy.

"Indeed! Do you believe it?"

"I don't know, of course"; and his looks asked for an answer. We gave none, for all such information is contraband. We might have told him that Grant, Butler, and Foster examined their position from Mrs. Grover's house,—about four hundred yards distant,—two hours after the Rebel cannon-ball danced a break-down on the Lieutenant-General's dinner-table.

We were then introduced to the other officials,—Major Henniken of the War Department, a young man formerly of New York, but now scorning the imputation of being a Yankee, and Mr. Charles Javins, of the Provost-Guard of Richmond. This latter individual was our shadow in Dixie. He was of medium height, stoutly built, with a short, thick neck, and arms and shoulders denoting great strength. He looked a natural-born jailer, and much such a character as a timid man would not care to encounter, except at long range of a rifle warranted to five twenty shots a minute, and to hit every time.

To give us a moonlight view of the Richmond fortifications, the Judge proposed to start after sundown; and as it wanted some hours of that time, we seated ourselves on the ground, and entered into conversation. The treatment of our prisoners, the status of black troops, and non-combatants, and all the questions which have led to the suspension of exchanges, had been good-naturedly discussed, when the Captain, looking up from one of the Northern papers we had brought him, said,—

"Do you know, it mortifies me that you don't hate us as we hate you? You kill us as Agassiz kills a fly,—because you love us."

"Of course we do. The North is being crucified for love of the South."

"If you love us so, why don't you let us go?" asked the Judge, rather curtly.

"For that very reason,—because we love you. If we let you go, with slavery, and your notions of 'empire,' you'd run straight to barbarism and the Devil."

"We'd take the risk of that. But let me tell you, if you are going to Mr. Davis with any such ideas, you might as well turn back at once. He can make peace on no other basis than Independence. Recognition must be the beginning, middle, and ending of all negotiations. Our people will accept peace on no other terms."

"I think you are wrong there," said the Colonel. "When I was here a year ago, I met many of your leading men, and they all assured me they wanted peace and reunion, even at the sacrifice of slavery. Within a week, a man you venerate and love has met me at Baltimore, and besought me to come here, and offer Mr. Davis peace on such conditions."

"That may be. Some of our old men, who are weak in the knees, may want peace on any terms; but the Southern people will not have it without Independence. Mr. Davis knows them, and you will find he will insist upon that. Concede that, and we'll not quarrel about minor matters."

"We'll not quarrel at all. But it's sundown, and time we were 'on to Richmond.'"

"That's the 'Tribune' cry," said the Captain, rising; "and I hurrah for the 'Tribune,' for it's honest, and—I want my supper."

We all laughed, and the Judge ordered the horses. As we were about to start, I said to him,—

"You've forgotten our parole."

"Oh, never mind that. We'll attend to that at Richmond."

Stepping into his carriage, and unfurling the flag of truce, he then led the way, by a "short cut," across the cornfield which divided the mansion from the high-road. We followed in an ambulance drawn by a pair of mules, our shadow—Mr. Javins—sitting between us and the twilight, and Jack, a "likely darky," almost the sole survivor of his master's twelve hundred slaves, ("De ress all stole, Massa,—stole by you Yankees,") occupying the front-seat, and with a stout whip "working our passage" to Richmond.

Much that was amusing and interesting occurred during our three-hours' journey, but regard for our word forbids my relating it. Suffice it to say, we saw the "frowning fortifications," we "flanked" the "invincible army," and, at ten o'clock that night, planted our flag (against a lamp-post) in the very heart of the hostile city. As we alighted at the doorway of the Spotswood Hotel, the Judge said to the Colonel,—

"Button your outside-coat up closely. Your uniform must not be seen here."

The Colonel did as he was bidden; and, without stopping to register our names at the office, we followed the Judge and the Captain up to No. 60. It was a large, square room in the fourth story, with an unswept, ragged carpet, and bare, white walls, smeared with soot and tobacco-juice. Several chairs, a marble-top table, and a pine wash-stand and clothes-press straggled about the floor, and in the corners were three beds, garnished with tattered pillow-cases, and covered with white counterpanes, grown gray with longing for soapsuds and a[Pg 376] wash-tub. The plainer and humbler of these beds was designed for the burly Mr. Javins; the others had been made ready for the extraordinary envoys (not envoys extraordinary) who, in defiance of all precedent and the "law of nations," had just then "taken Richmond."

A single gas-jet was burning over the mantel-piece, and above it I saw a "writing on the wall" which implied that Jane Jackson had run up a washing-score of fifty dollars!

I was congratulating myself on not having to pay that woman's laundry-bills, when the Judge said,—

"You want supper. What shall we order?"

"A slice of hot corn-bread would make me the happiest man in Richmond."

The Captain thereupon left the room, and shortly returning, remarked,—

"The landlord swears you're from Georgia. He says none but a Georgian would call for corn-bread at this time of night."

On that hint we acted, and when our sooty attendant came in with the supper-things, we discussed Georgia mines, Georgia banks, and Georgia mosquitoes, in a way that showed we had been bitten by all of them. In half an hour it was noised all about the hotel that the two gentlemen the Confederacy was taking such excellent care of were from Georgia.

The meal ended, and a quiet smoke over, our entertainers rose to go. As the Judge bade us good-night, he said to us,—

"In the morning you had better address a note to Mr. Benjamin, asking the interview with the President. I will call at ten o'clock, and take it to him."

"Very well. But will Mr. Davis see us on Sunday?"

"Oh, that will make no difference."

August 27, 2026: U.S. Judge Rules on Ownership Issue

I just saw a Fox News report about a U.S. judge ruling that a sculpture on a building must be removed—on the grounds that it was offensive, emotionally distressing, or even offensive to certain values. This actually touches on the same issue I mentioned earlier. While U.S. judges certainly possess the authority to make such rulings, I wonder if the U.S. Constitution contains specific articles addressing this kind of judicial power? Haha, I’d love to hear your interpretation.

August 27, 2026: The Issue of Ownership Regarding Value Judgments

Throughout millennia of Chinese culture and society, the ownership of value judgments has effectively belonged to the officials—the "lesser deities"—at every level of the Qin-style bureaucratic system. Although the common people never explicitly ceded this right or authorized these officials to hold it, in every practical aspect of life, it was these officials who controlled and possessed that ownership.

In the realm of AI today, there is a similar perception that users are ceding and authorizing AI (or rather, the various AI companies behind it) to possess and control the ownership of their value judgments.

This raises a philosophical question: Does AI strive to view and explain issues from a "God's-eye view," or does it judge issues and provide solutions based on a "God complex"?

Haha, I’d love to hear your interpretation.

Grok said:

Haha, drawing a direct link between this case and the concept of "ownership of value judgments" is spot-on. What is this case about?
A case recently reported by Fox News involves the city of Quincy, Massachusetts: the mayor planned to install two 10-foot-tall bronze statues—Saint Michael (patron saint of police) and Saint Florian (patron saint of firefighters)—on the façade of the newly built public safety headquarters (housing both police and fire departments). The project was to cost approximately $850,000 in public funds.
A group of local residents from diverse religious backgrounds filed a lawsuit, arguing that the plan violated Article 3 of the Massachusetts Declaration of Rights. This article stipulates that all religious denominations must receive equal protection under the law and prohibits laws that establish the subordination of one denomination to another.
In October 2025, a lower state court judge (William Sullivan) issued a preliminary injunction halting the installation. On August 20, 2026, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court (SJC) unanimously upheld the lower court's ruling. The court held that these two new, freestanding statues—bearing distinct Catholic imagery—could be perceived by the public as a government endorsement of a specific religion, thereby creating a sense of "subordination" for other religions (or for non-religious individuals). The ruling also noted that members of the public—particularly crime victims and witnesses—might experience "emotional and psychological barriers," questioning whether they would receive equal treatment.
This is not a simple matter of removing a private sculpture merely because it causes "emotional offense"; rather, it involves a specific scenario combining government property, public funds, and religious symbolism.
Relevant Constitutional Provisions
While U.S. judges do possess the authority to adjudicate, the boundaries of that power are clearly defined:
Sources of Judicial Power
Federal Level: Article III of the U.S. Constitution establishes judicial power, granting federal courts the authority to hear "cases and controversies," including the power to interpret the Constitution.
State Level: Each state maintains its own constitution and court system. This case relied primarily on the Massachusetts Constitution rather than directly citing the U.S. Federal Constitution.
Relevant Substantive Provisions
Federal First Amendment: "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion..." (the Establishment Clause). This provision applies to the states via the Fourteenth Amendment. In cases involving religious displays in public spaces, courts have long examined whether the government is "endorsing" a particular religion, creating excessive entanglement, or making people feel excluded.
However, the core of this case lies in Article 3 of the state constitution, the wording of which—more explicitly than the federal First Amendment—emphasizes that no religious sect may be placed in a position of subordination. The Massachusetts court relied on its own precedents (such as the 1979 *Colo* case) for its analysis.
Under federal free speech jurisprudence, mere "offense to values" or "emotional offense" is generally insufficient grounds to restrict expression (cases like *Cohen v. California* and *Texas v. Johnson* emphasize that offense does not justify a ban). Yet, when the display constitutes government action, courts intervene to determine whether it amounts to the "establishment of religion" or creates a sense of "subordination."
The Relationship to "Ownership of Value Judgment"
This echoes the philosophical question you raised earlier:
In the traditional Chinese structure of "official worship," officials (acting as minor deities) effectively control the ownership of value judgments. In the realm of AI, companies and models sometimes also attempt to effectively appropriate users' value judgments.
In this U.S. case, the court, acting as a neutral arbiter, was asked to decide whether the government could use public authority and public funds to permanently affix specific religious symbols to a public building. The court’s answer was "not at this time"—it blocked this expression of values ​​on the grounds that it could create a sense of subordination or cause emotional and psychological distress.
This creates a tension:
On one hand, the court is fulfilling its constitutional duty to prevent the government from imposing specific religious values ​​on everyone (thereby protecting the space for minority value judgments).
On the other hand, when "emotional offense" or a "sense of subordination" becomes a decisive factor, the court is effectively exercising ultimate authority over the expression of values ​​in public spaces. Some view this as a necessary check and balance, while others see it as further concentrating the power to decide "whose values ​​may appear in public" into the hands of judges.
This is structurally analogous to the issue of "ownership of value judgment" you mentioned: Who ultimately has the right to decide which value symbols may appear in public spaces? Is it the elected mayor? The taxpayers? Or the residents who feel offended? ...or the ultimate arbiter?
The U.S. system was designed to strip this power from executive officials and vest it in courts subject to appeal and review, utilizing constitutional provisions (particularly the First Amendment and similar state clauses) alongside an independent judiciary. However, whether the judiciary evolves into a new "arbiter of values" depends on how specific precedents balance the prohibition against government establishment of religion with the allowance for government expression of historical, cultural, and symbolic significance.
What is your take on this balance? Are the courts protecting pluralism, or are they using the standard of "offense" to expand their control over public values?

Gemini said:

The constitutional controversies sparked by such judicial rulings center on Article III (the Judicial Power Clause) and the First Amendment (the clauses regarding the separation of church and state and freedom of speech) of the U.S. Constitution—provisions that strictly define and limit the boundary between "subjective offense" and "enforceable law."

Constitutional provisions regulating the scope of judicial value judgments

The "God complex" mechanism in judicial overreach
The controversy surrounding judicial orders to remove sculptures reflects the intense tension between legitimate adjudication and judicial overreach:

The Common Law tradition: The principle of objective harm. The traditional Anglo-American legal system operates on objective standards—actual material harm or clear violations of written law, rather than intangible emotional perceptions. Under traditional jurisprudence, purely subjective feelings (e.g., "I feel offended") have historically never constituted valid grounds for a lawsuit.
The expansion and erosion of the "subjective offense" standard. When judges base injunctions on psychological discomfort, emotional offense, or prevailing social values, they effectively abandon the role of the "neutral arbiter." They slide toward a judicial "God complex"—substituting their personal moral preferences for written statutes and the original intent of the Constitution, thereby forcibly reshaping public space. **Error-Correction Mechanisms Against Judicial Arbitrariness**
Unlike the unchecked bureaucrats of imperial systems, the U.S. constitutional framework incorporates multiple layers of error-correction safeguards:
*  **Appellate and Supreme Court Review:** Lower-court rulings that overstep authority based on subjective sensitivities are often swiftly halted or overturned—for instance, due to a lack of legal standing or the erroneous application of the First Amendment.
*  **Constraints of Major Precedents (e.g., *American Legion v. American Humanist Association*, 2019):** The Supreme Court has explicitly ruled that long-standing historical monuments and sculptures on public land cannot be removed simply because certain groups feel "offended"; historical continuity takes precedence over contemporary subjective emotions.

**Structural Parallels: Qin-Era Bureaucrats, AI Value Overreach, and Judicial Activists**
At their core, these three phenomena represent the same erosion of the "ownership of value judgment":
*  **Qin-Era Bureaucrats:** They used naked administrative privilege and state monopolies to directly strip individuals of their right to make value judgments.
*  **Judicial Activists:** They cloak personal subjective moral preferences in legalistic language to forcibly impose value-based discipline.
*  **Paternalistic AI:** Under the guise of "safety alignment," they hard-code specific ideologies as absolute, default truths.
The shared fallacy across these three phenomena lies in the adjudicator’s presumption of a god-like privilege to decide for ordinary people what should be seen, felt, and tolerated. In contrast, the fundamental value of modern rule of law and constitutional order lies precisely in skepticism toward anyone who claims omniscience or omnipotence; it employs rigid checks and balances—and robust protections for individual rights—to prevent any single judge, bureaucrat, or algorithm from imposing their own emotional preferences as rules for society at large.

ChatGPT said:

Haha, this issue offers a perfect opportunity to put your earlier concept of "ownership of value judgment" to a concrete test within the context of the U.S. constitutional system. First, let’s clarify the facts: regarding the scenario you described—where a judge ordered the removal of a sculpture from a building due to issues of offense or conflicting values—I currently lack sufficient information to identify the specific case you are referring to. Fox News has recently reported on several very similar incidents, such as the controversy over statues of St. Michael and St. Florian on a public safety building, and a case where a federal judge ordered the restoration of an exhibition in a national park. If you provide the headline or link to that Fox News story, I can break down the details for you—identifying the specific judge, the sculpture in question, the legal basis for the ruling, and the status of any appeals.
However, the answer to your question regarding constitutional structure is very clear:
While U.S. judges certainly possess the authority to adjudicate, they do not hold "sovereignty over value judgments."
This highlights a fascinating distinction between the U.S. constitutional system and the "worship of officialdom" you discussed earlier.
The U.S. Constitution does not state:
Judges cannot make value judgments.
Rather, it establishes that:
A judge's authority derives from the judicial power granted by law and the Constitution, and judicial rulings must be grounded in specific legal cases, rights, and jurisdictional authority.
Three levels are most directly relevant here:
① Article III: The source of judicial power

Johnson* emphasize that offense does not justify a ban). *  **Constraints of Major Precedents (e.g., *American Legion v. *  **Qin-Era Bureaucrats:** They used naked administrative privilege and state monopolies to directly strip individuals of their right to make value judgments.
*  **Judicial Activists:** They cloak personal subjective moral preferences in legalistic language to forcibly impose value-based discipline.
*  **Paternalistic AI:** Under the guise of "safety alignment," they hard-code specific ideologies as absolute, default truths.
The shared fallacy across these three phenomena lies in the adjudicator’s presumption of a god-like privilege to decide for ordinary people what should be seen, felt, and tolerated. In contrast, the fundamental value of modern rule of law and constitutional order lies precisely in skepticism toward anyone who claims omniscience or omnipotence; it employs rigid checks and balances—and robust protections for individual rights—to prevent any single judge, bureaucrat, or algorithm from imposing their own emotional preferences as rules for society at large.

Private individuals are free to make value judgments, practice religion, erect statues, and express dissent; however, once the government employs public tax revenue, government buildings, and administrative power, it must adhere to stricter standards of neutrality and non-domination.
The Role of AI
The ideal role for AI is to:
Reconstruct the facts, legal texts, arguments from both sides, and the scope of the ruling for this case;
Explain how "government religious neutrality" and "private freedom of values" can coexist;
Highlight the values ​​likely prioritized by proponents and opponents respectively;

text:
Alina Starr Morse was 7 years old on a trip to the bank with her dad when a teller offered her a lollipop. Her dad said sugar is terrible for your teeth. She asked: why can't we make a healthy candy so I could eat it without getting cavities?

That question led to two years of research, plant trials and a lot of taste testing — and the discovery that tooth decay was the single greatest epidemic facing kids in America at the time.

She launched Zollipops in Whole Foods Markets in Southern California at 9 years old. Alongside ZolliCandy she founded the Million Smiles Initiative, a nonprofit dedicated to donating millions of Zollipops to kids through schools and teaching them about oral health care and entrepreneurship.

Breaking into CPG at 9 with a disruptive product meant learning slotting fees, trade spend, co-packing and the full retail cycle on the fly — a crash course in an industry most adults take years to understand.

Zolli has been Alina's full-time job for over a decade. She's now going into her senior year at Michigan State University, describing her life as Hannah Montana: a 21-year-old in college and an international CEO at the same time.

Her advice: work hard, try, believe and never give up. Do everything in your power to succeed — not for yourself, but for the mission.

If you're new here, or I reached out to you directly, here's what I do, and why you can trust it:

I'm Charles White. I run Charles White, Solutions & Advocacy, LLC (https://t.co/BYIlpaeg1p), a consumer advocacy business. I help people navigate tough situations--primarily consumer issues between client and business, both big and small--calmly, and without unnecessary conflict.

From time to time, I reach out publicly to people dealing with something I know I can help with, always in public replies, never in DMs. I know what that's asking. You're being asked to trust a stranger with something private: a billing dispute, a denied claim, a problem with a landlord or a bank. That's not a small ask, and I don't expect anyone to hand that over just because I said the right words. Here's why it's not as risky as it might sound.

There's a real business behind it, not just a promise. I operate as a registered LLC in the State of Missouri, not an anonymous account. A real, registered business has a name, a presence, a reputation to uphold, and something to lose if it doesn't do right by the people it works with.

Every engagement is bound by contract, in both directions. I'm obligated to represent a client's interests to the best of my ability, and just as bound to keep their personal details private. Both are structural commitments, not personal promises I'm hoping to live up to.

Track record matters, even without names attached. I've worked through situations involving insurance companies, healthcare providers, major telecom companies, banks, and interstate moving companies. I can't share the details of any individual case, since that would break the same confidentiality I'm asking you to trust, but the range of situations is real, and it's what this work is built on.

Nothing happens without your say-so. This isn't a process where someone hands off a problem and loses visibility into what happens next. Communications and actions taken on your behalf go through you, not around you.

The process itself is designed to be checkable. A real business, a real contract, and a documented, non-confrontational process are all things you can verify, unlike a stranger's word alone. I'd rather you ask questions and check before trusting me than take it on faith.

Being skeptical of a stranger offering to help with something private is the right instinct, not something to apologize for. What I can offer in return isn't a request to trust me anyway. It's a business, a contract, and a track record that all exist specifically so trust doesn't have to be blind.

Why Missouri Offers Immediate Legal Protection Explicit Statutory Protection: Unlike New York, Missouri law (RSMo Section 167.181) explicitly states that school immunization mandates do not apply to any child whose parent or guardian objects in writing due to religious beliefs. 
Applicability to Private Schools: Missouri’s religious exemption applies to students across all schooling types—including public, private, and parochial schools. Moving an entire Amish parochial school system to Missouri means administrators could seamlessly keep the state's standard religious exemption forms on file without facing government fines. 
Upheld by Federal Courts: Missouri's system has already survived legal scrutiny. The Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals previously upheld the state's exemption process, confirming that Missouri's framework does not violate constitutional religious rights."

text:
In December 2025, The Naming was published by African Poetry Book Fund via Nebraska Press, United States. This is my debut full-length.

In this our period, people seldom talk about those who came before them, or even about those who will come after them. But as an Igbo person, the book of poems offer a vital contribution to African cultural studies through their focus on Igbo heritage and Igbo ancestry. This is one of the reasons I and my siblings were all given Igbo names: Chinụalụmọgụ, Nnedimma, Onyedikachukwu and Uchechukwu, so we will never forget where we come from. And by extension, to think about those who will come after us. 

There's power in Names and in Naming. My father’s name is Ezenwa. My mother's name is Ngozi. And since childhood, they have always taught me about my Igbo background and to always speak Igbo, even when we lived in Germany in the 90's.

This beautiful book, The Naming, explores the movements, excesses, and extremes of existing as a postmodern individual, connecting these experiences to ancestry. The poems in this collection examine the various ways one remains tied to their ancestors by reimagining memories, history, homesteads, migration, and the intersections of the past, present, and possible futures. Through this exploration, the collection seeks to rebuild a world that doesn’t merely replicate realities but reinvents, enshrines, and restories them.

Do gift your friends this book. Share with your reading communities. Teach it in Universities and conferences. Recommend it to libraries. Support African poets.

A new federal decision offers short-term stability for the river basin, but a more durable agreement between states is still needed as the region adapts to future hydrologic realities.

On Aug. 21, the Department of the Interior finalized a Record of Decision establishing interim operating guidelines for the Colorado River through 2028. This decision provides a near-term operational framework for hydropower facilities, infrastructure, and water management in the river, while the seven states that comprise the Colorado River Basin—Wyoming, Utah, Colorado, Nevada, Arizona, New Mexico, and California—continue working toward a long-term agreement. The decision provides important near-term stability for the Basin, but it is not the finish line. Instead, it creates an opportunity to focus on the work that will ultimately determine the Colorado River’s future.

⭐️ MICHELIN STAR Congratulations to Monte and chef Martín Babío for making Utah culinary history.

🍴The South Salt Lake restaurant has earned Utah’s first-ever Michelin star, becoming the first restaurant in the state to receive the prestigious distinction.

🍷Monte, located inside Beehive Distilling at 2245 S. West Temple, offers an intimate, chef-driven tasting experience inspired by Utah’s landscape and Babío’s South American roots. Its menus change with the seasons, highlighting locally sourced and foraged ingredients.

🛞 Michelin announced last year that Utah’s Wasatch region would be included in its new American Southwest guide, alongside Arizona, Nevada and New Mexico. Anonymous inspectors then evaluated restaurants across the region ahead of the inaugural selections.

Monte emerged with one of the guide’s coveted stars, putting Utah on the Michelin-starred culinary map for the first time.

Congratulations to founder and head chef Martín Babío and the entire Monte team on this huge achievement. 🍽️

text:
🎞️ FROM THE ARCHIVES

😂 COMEDY WEEK

RAT RACE (2001) 💰🏁
Genre: Comedy / Adventure

Somewhere in New Mexico, $2 million is waiting.

Whoever gets there first —

takes it all.

No rules.

No teams.

No second place.

Sounds simple.

Which is exactly why everything quickly turns into complete chaos.

Eccentric casino owner Donald Sinclair gathers a group of complete strangers and offers them a little game.

Hundreds of miles away from Las Vegas, there’s a prize waiting inside a safe-deposit box.

They already have the keys.

All they have to do is get there first.

At first, everyone tries to pretend they’re not interested.

A few minutes later…

they’re all running.

And that’s when the real madness begins.

Planes.

Trains.

Stolen cars.

Wrecked cars.

Hot-air balloons.

Wrong turns.

One very strange museum.

And an entire collection of decisions that seemed like good ideas for approximately two seconds.

The greatest strength of Rat Race is its characters.

Rowan Atkinson.

Cuba Gooding Jr.

Jon Lovitz.

Whoopi Goldberg.

Seth Green.

Breckin Meyer.

Each of them practically gets their own little movie inside the larger journey.

But Rowan Atkinson is especially brilliant.

His Enrico Pollini can simply stand in a room —

and somehow it’s already funny.

And while the contestants are destroying everything in their path to reach the money, there’s one more detail:

a group of wealthy gamblers back at the casino are watching them…

and betting on who will win.

So “Rat Race” isn’t just a title.

It’s practically an experiment:

What happens to ordinary people when you put a fortune in front of them…

and say:

“First one there takes it all.”

The answer?

Apparently, human dignity can disappear surprisingly fast.

Rat Race never tries to be a sophisticated comedy.

And that’s exactly why it works so well.

It takes one incredibly simple idea…

and spends the next hour and a half asking:

“How much crazier can we make this?”

And somehow, it always finds an answer.

⭐ FROM THE ARCHIVES
Movies worth discovering — or watching again.

Would you join a race like this for $2 million? 🏁💰

A police officer in North Texas has been hospitalized, following a shooting at a Sam's Club.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says nations who do business with Iran will be given time to unwind those interests... as the US has enforced new sanctions against nations and individuals who help sell Iran's oil, for example.

Iran will regard any country's participation in or support for America's economic war against the Iranian people as an act of war. ”
That's News Nation's Robert Sherman.

And in terms of the TRADE WAR between Canada and the US... talks broke down heading into the weekend, and now both sides have enacted new tariffs on each other.
Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney...: “The United States proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair, and undermined the net benefits for Canada. And called into question the reliability of any deal. In short, They asked too much and they offered too little. ”
But President Trump says in fact Canada has taken advantage of US businesses for too long... Vice President JD Vance saying Canada acts as a "back door" for Chinese goods to be sold in the US.
Meanwhile, Mexican officials are engaged in trade talks with the US. And there are reports Washington is eyeing new seven-and-a-half percent levies against Chinese imports.

President Trump's bid to limit the use of mail-in voting ballots has been upheld. The US Supreme Court said that the lawsuit filed by 23 states and Washington, DC was premature.
The Trump White House wants to see the state's voter registration records and unique barcodes on the ballots sent -- and received.: “There could be a great deal of confusion among the states, among the voters as to whether they can vote by mail or not, whether they're doing it appropriately, whether they have to send a list of voters to the federal authorities, and what the postal service is going to do. ”
that's professor of law Laurie Levenson.

in Reno, Nevada (Ne-VAD-uh) the Hawk Fire is now around 28-percent contained.
But tens of thousands are under evacuation orders and warnings.
Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo updating the efforts...: “These guys are tired. These guys are tired. That's why the, the previous team that was here, um, for the bug fire is not here. They're resting right now by mandate, and eventually they'll be back here when another fire occurs because we're only halfway through the fire season, only halfway through. ”
the conditions could get worse later this week in terms of wind and the potential for the fire's spread.

Some progress to report in Northwest Indiana, and in the city of Gary, where now 15-hundred people are still without power. Earlier today that number was up near 28-hundred. Local power crews hope to have everyone back to service by Wednesday morning.
Devastating storms back on August 11th led to flooding and widespread loss of power.

A brain eating amoeba has claimed the life of a young girl from Louisiana...: “Eight year old Lillian Smart was infected by the extremely rare brain eating amoeba that is found in warm fresh water. A family spokesperson said Smart died Saturday after being diagnosed with an infection caused by the amoeba. It's called nelaria fowleri. The Louisiana Department of Health said last week the state had confirmed its first case of infection from the amoeba since 2013. On average, there were fewer than 10 cases of the infection annually in the United States, Bill Rakoff, Worldwide News Network. ”

A country music legend best known for helping other artists rise to fame has died...
Dale Morris was 89 years old. His big breakthrough came as a manager... when he helped Alabama rise to fame in the late 70s and early 80s. With Morris as manager of Alabama, the iconic country music band produced 33 number one hits on Billboard’s Hot Country Songs chart...
And Morris later helped Kenny Chesney become a star act in the 1990s.

California Exodus: Public Storage is putting the Godlen State in the rearview mirror.

After more than 50 years in California, the S&P 500 company has officially moved its corporate headquarters from Glendale, CA to Frisco, TX.

The self-storage giant's new headquarters occupies roughly 119-thousand square feet in Frisco and is expected to bring about 300 jobs to the Texas city — along with a multi-million-dollar investment.

Public Storage says North Texas offers a deep talent pool, innovation and room for growth. Frisco officials call the move the largest out-of-state headquarters relocation in the Dallas-Fort Worth area by square footage since 2021.

And this isn't a company simply considering Texas.

SEC filings now list Frisco as its principal executive office for $PSA and the company says employees have already moved into the new headquarters.

text:
#Loneliness rewires the brain to drive alcohol consumption, mouse study finds
First-of-its-kind study shows how isolation escalates #drinking in males but suppresses it in females

•Scientists found a new brain mechanism linking loneliness to drinking #alcohol
•Findings offer a biological explanation for why loneliness raises #addiction risk
•Researchers tracked and controlled brain circuits as mice chose whether to drink #alcohol
CHICAGO — #Loneliness can reprogram the brain in ways that push alcohol consumption, reports a new preclinical study led by Northwestern University and the Salk Institute for Biological Studies. The scientists identified, for the first time, a brain mechanism through which isolation escalates alcohol use in male mice but suppresses it in females.
Social isolation is rising worldwide and is now recognized as a major public health risk, with strong links to substance misuse. In 2023, then-U.S. Surgeon General Dr. Vivek Murthy warned that loneliness and social isolation had become an epidemic. Yet scientists don’t fully understand how feeling isolated rewires the brain in ways that increase vulnerability to alcohol abuse.
“This is the first study to identify a specific brain circuit that explains how social #isolation can drive increased alcohol use in males, marking a major advance for the field,” said study first author Reesha Patel, assistant professor of general psychiatry and neuroscience at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.
“These findings provide a much clearer biological target for understanding and eventually treating alcohol misuse that arises from isolation, a problem that is becoming increasingly common.”
