text:
Well, it was one of those late-summer evenings in the high country of northwestern Colorado, up in the Yampa River Valley near Steamboat Springs, when the light turns the ridges the color of an old brass lantern that’s been polished by a thousand thumbs, and the wind comes down off the Park Range and the Flat Tops like it has a few private thoughts it isn’t ready to share out loud. The town itself sits at about sixty-seven hundred feet, a real Western place where the streets were laid out wide enough for cattle drives and where you can still see ranchers in boots and Stetsons going about their business as if the ski mountain and the fancy coffee shops never quite arrived. All around it the land opens up into hay meadows and pine-and-aspen hills, with the Yampa River running through the middle of things and the big wilderness areas—Routt National Forest, the Mount Zirkel country, the strange flat-topped volcanic cliffs of the Flat Tops—standing off in the distance like patient relatives who have seen everything and decided not to comment. Even in summer the mornings up there drop into the forties without apology. The air has a sharpness that makes your breath hang white and your fingers slow on a tin cup. That is the country this story comes from.

There was an old fellow named Harold—though when they were young nobody used last names much and first names only when they had to. He and four other boys used to camp on a little rise of ground on a rancher’s place in those hills back when their knees still worked and a good dirty joke could keep you warm half the night. They would hike in with packs that felt light no matter what they carried, cut a few poles for a lean-to if the weather looked mean, and build a fire that cracked and spat as if it had its own stories to tell. The rancher was a quiet man who didn’t talk any more than he had to. He let them use the spot year after year as long as they left it cleaner than they found it and kept the fires small. He has been gone nearly twenty years now. But his son is still there. The son was only five or six the first summer those five boys showed up with their noise and their fire and their endless talk. A little kid in boots two sizes too big, hanging around the edge of the firelight among the lodgepoles and the aspens, trying not to laugh too loud at the parts he wasn’t supposed to understand. That kid grew up and took over the ranch—the hay meadows, the cattle, the ditches, the whole works—and every spring he would walk up to that rise and clear the deadfall off the old fire ring. When people asked him why he bothered with a patch of ground that wasn’t good for much of anything, he would just shrug and say, “In case the Boys ever come back one last time.”

They never did come back all together.

One of them went off to the war—the long one they called the Global War on Terror—and came home under a flag. Harold stood at the graveside in a suit that didn’t fit right and watched them fold that flag into a tight triangle the way men who have practiced the gesture too many times can do it without thinking. He took the triangle home and put it in a drawer. It is still there, far as he knows. Another, the loud one who always had a scruffy dog named after a brand of cheap whiskey following him around like a second shadow, jumped into a freezing river one winter to pull the animal out of the current. The dog made it to shore, shaking and looking faintly embarrassed. The man did not. His heart gave out in the cold water, and they found him the next morning with his arms still stretched forward as if the effort had frozen him in the act of saving. Harold went to that funeral too and stood in the back watching the old dog sit beside the widow like it was still waiting for the next command. The third one simply got angry about something no one ever quite understood. One day the letters stopped and the phone calls went unanswered and the silence settled in for good, thicker than any argument. Harold tried once—sent a short note that said nothing more than the hill was still there if he ever wanted to see it. The note came back unopened. The fourth lived longest but left the slow way. Nursing home. Dementia. The last time Harold visited, the man looked at him with polite confusion and asked if he was the new orderly come to change the sheets.

So one clear morning Harold decided he wanted to see the old spot again. Not for any grand reason. Not to settle accounts or rewrite the past. He simply wanted to sit once more where the five of them had sat, to feel the same ground under him, and to let the memories rise the way smoke rises from a fire that has been tended right. He packed light—a bedroll, a small stove, the old coffee pot that had traveled many miles and seen better days—and he drove over Rabbit Ears Pass and down into the Yampa Valley until the pavement quit and the pines took over. Then he walked the last stretch under the trees, the air growing cooler with every step, the elevation reminding his knees that he was no longer the boy who used to make that hike without thinking about it.

When he reached the edge of the ranch the son was working near the barn, a man in his fifties now, broad-shouldered and quiet in the same way his father had been. Harold said who he was and half expected to be turned around. Instead the son looked at him a long minute and then smiled that slow smile of a man recognizing something he had been waiting for without quite knowing it.

“You’re one of the Boys,” he said. It was not a question. He wiped his hands on his jeans and nodded toward the hill. “I left that spot alone all these years. Figured you might come back one last time.”

He told Harold to take the old track up through the meadows, and when Harold tried to thank him the son just shrugged. “Dad would’ve wanted it that way. He always said you five were the only ones who ever treated the place like it had a memory of its own.”

The hill was still there. Of course it was. Hills don’t go anywhere. It was a modest rise among the lodgepole pines and the aspens, with a view that opened west and north across the valley toward the distant blue folds of the mountains—the Park Range, the edges of the Flat Tops, the long ridges that turn the color of brass in the late light. The old fire ring was half-buried in needles, but the ground around it was clear of heavy brush, as if someone had quietly kept it open against the slow push of the forest. Harold cleared the stones with his hands, feeling the familiar roughness, and built a small fire. Nothing fancy. Just enough flame to push the evening chill back a little and give the memories a place to gather.

He sat with his back against a log that might have been a younger version of itself the last time he was here, and he let the light fade the way it always had up in this country—blue to rose to that deep violet the high elevations keep for their private hours. The air had that same sharp cold that used to make them huddle closer, the kind that comes easy at sixty-seven hundred feet even in late summer when the days have been warm. He could almost hear the old jokes rising with the sparks, the slap of a knee, the easy silence that followed when the laughing had run its course. He thought of the quiet one who had gone to war—the one who listened more than he talked and looked at the fire as if it might answer questions no one else could hear. They had stayed up later than the others one night, passing a bottle back and forth, talking about what they might become. That friend had said he thought he might try the service for a while, just to see a wider piece of the world. Harold had nodded and said it sounded fine. Neither of them had known how wide that world would turn out to be, or how final. At the funeral the flag had been folded with the precision of men who had practiced the gesture too many times. Harold had taken the triangle of cloth home and kept it in a drawer for years, unable to look at it and unable to throw it away. Sitting now by the new fire he imagined the quiet friend walking up the hill out of the dusk, still carrying that listening look, and taking his old place in the circle without a word.

Then there was the loud one with the dog. First to laugh, last to let a joke die. He had named the mutt after a brand of cheap whiskey and claimed the animal understood every word of the dirty stories. One night the dog had stolen a whole package of hot dogs from the cooler and eaten them right there in the open, looking proud the entire time. They had laughed until they could not breathe. The river accident happened years later, long after the camping trips had become memory. Harold had heard about it over the phone from a mutual acquaintance, the voice on the other end careful and distant. He had driven to the funeral and stood in the back watching the old dog—gray around the muzzle by then—sit obediently beside the widow. The animal had looked up every time someone approached, as if still expecting its owner to come around the corner with a stick or a scrap of food. Harold had wanted to say something about the river and the cold and the reaching arms, but the words would not come. Now, by the fire, he could almost see that friend again, the dog at his feet, both of them steaming a little from the heat of the flames, the man already launching into another story that would end with everyone wiping their eyes.

The angry one was harder. Harold turned the memory over carefully, the way a man turns a stone that might hide something sharp underneath. They had been close once. They had shared a tent through three days of rain that turned the ground to soup and made every sock in the pack smell of mildew. They had argued about politics and women and the proper way to pack a mule, arguments that ended in laughter more often than not. Then something shifted. A letter went unanswered. A phone call was not returned. The silence grew its own gravity. Harold had tried once, years later, sending that short note about the hill. It came back unopened. Sitting in the dark now he wondered if the anger had been about something small that had looked large at the time, or something large that had looked small. He imagined the man walking up the trail anyway, older, slower, carrying the years like an extra pack, and sitting down without apology. The fire would not care about the silence. The fire only knew how to burn.

And the careful one, the one who double-checked the knots and wrote the names of birds and the dates of first frost in a little notebook he kept in his shirt pocket. In the nursing home the notebook was gone. The careful hands had grown uncertain. The last visit had been short. Harold had sat beside the bed and talked about the campsite, about the cold mornings and the dirty jokes, about the way the light looked at dusk over the Yampa Valley. The man had smiled politely and asked again if Harold was the new orderly. When Harold left he had stood in the parking lot for a long time watching the sun go down behind a row of identical brick buildings, and he had understood that some goodbyes happen while the person is still breathing.

The fire settled into a bed of coals. A night bird called once from somewhere down the slope and then fell quiet. Harold fed the flames a few more sticks and watched the sparks climb toward the first stars. He thought about the five of them as they had been—young, certain that the future was a wide-open trail and that friendship was a thing that could not be broken by distance or time or the ordinary accidents of living. He remembered one particular morning when the cold had been so sharp it made their teeth ache. They had built the fire higher than usual and stood around it in a tight circle, shoulders touching, the steam from their coffee rising between them. Somebody started a joke about a preacher who tried to baptize a mule. By the time the story ended they were all laughing so hard they had to lean on one another to stay upright. The sun had cleared the ridge while they were still wiping their eyes. That was the morning Harold kept coming back to. Not the funerals or the silences or the nursing-home hallways. Just that circle of warmth and the sound of five voices tangled together in laughter under a sky that seemed big enough to hold all of them forever.

He stayed through the long middle of the night. The cold deepened the way it always does in the high country when the wind settles and the sky goes hard with stars. He wrapped the bedroll around his shoulders and kept the fire alive with small, careful additions of wood. He spoke a few of the old jokes aloud just to hear a human voice in the silence, and the sound of them was both familiar and strange, like hearing a song you once knew by heart after many years of not singing it. He told the one about the mule again, and the one about the traveling salesman who mistook a rancher’s daughter for a hired hand, and the one about the three hunters and the talking bear. Each joke opened a door onto another memory—the time the quiet friend burned the bacon so thoroughly they had to scrape the pan with a rock, the time the dog chased a squirrel up a tree and refused to come down until full dark, the time they all swore they heard a mountain lion only to discover it was the angry one snoring in the lean-to.

Sometime after midnight the rancher’s son walked up the hill carrying a thermos of coffee and two tin cups. He did not say much. He simply sat down on the far side of the fire and poured. They drank in the kind of quiet men keep when the important things are already understood. The son looked at the fire ring and said, “Dad used to check this spot every spring. He’d clear the deadfall and make sure the stones were still in place. Said it was the least he could do for the only visitors who ever treated the land like it had a memory of its own.” Harold nodded. He told the son a few of the old stories—the dog and the hot dogs, the three-day rain, the night they thought they heard a mountain lion. The son listened the way his father had once listened, with the patience of a man who knows that stories are the only real fences that last.

They sat like that for a long time. The son talked a little about the ranch—how the hay meadows still needed the ditches cleaned every spring, how the cattle still found the same draws in winter, how the view from the hill had not changed much even though almost everything else had. Harold talked about the way the light used to look at dusk when they were young, how the ridges would go from blue to rose to violet and the first stars would prick through like quiet promises. Neither of them said anything about the friends who were gone. They did not need to. The fire and the hill and the cold air said it for them.

Toward morning the sky began to pale in the east. The stars faded one by one, the way conversations fade when the important things have already been said. Harold let the fire burn down to a soft glow and watched the first light touch the farthest ridges—the ones that roll away toward the Flat Tops and the Park Range and the long empty country that still feels like it belongs to itself. He thought about how the hill had waited all these years without complaint, how the stones of the fire ring had held their places through snow and thaw and the slow drift of pine needles, how a boy who had once been five years old had grown into a man who kept a promise no one had asked him to keep. He thought about the friends in their different absences—one beneath a military headstone, one claimed by cold water, one sealed behind a wall of anger, one lost inside his own mind—and he understood that the circle they had made around the fire had never really broken. It had only changed its shape. The living carry the dead the way these mountains carry the light: quietly, without ceremony, and for longer than anyone expects.

When the sun finally cleared the ridge he kicked dirt over the last of the coals until the final thin thread of smoke disappeared. He shouldered his pack, took one more look at the view that had outlasted all of them, and started down the track through the pines and the aspens. The rancher’s son walked with him as far as the barn, then stopped and offered his hand.

“You come back anytime,” he said. “The spot’ll still be here.”

Harold shook the hand and nodded, feeling the weight of the years and the lightness of something that had been carried carefully for a long time. He did not look back as he walked. Some places are best left the way you found them—holding what they hold, saying what they say without words.

He drove back over Rabbit Ears Pass in the early light, the valley falling away behind him, the mountains standing the way they always have. The coffee in the old pot had gone cold. The bedroll smelled of woodsmoke. In the glove box, under a pile of maps that were no longer needed, the folded triangle of flag waited the way it had waited for years. Harold did not take it out. He simply drove, and the road unspooled beneath him the way roads do when a man has nowhere particular he needs to be in a hurry.

The old man sat in the corner booth of the diner just off Highway 40, the one with the cracked vinyl seats and the coffee that tasted like it had been brewed sometime around the last cattle drive. He wrapped both hands around his mug like it might try to get away and looked out the window toward the dark shape of the mountains. Then he started talking, soft enough that you had to lean in a little.

“You ever been up around Steamboat?” he said. “Yampa Valley country. Hills looking out toward the Flat Tops and the Park Range. Mornings still cold enough up there to make a man grateful for company that ain’t around anymore. Old jokes still hanging in the lodgepoles and the aspens if you listen right. And a little fire on a familiar hill… that can hold more warmth than all the years a man’s given, I swear it can.

“Friends are gone different ways—war took one, a river took another, silence took the third, and forgetting took the last. Old rancher’s gone too. But that little boy who used to sit at the edge of the firelight? He grew up and kept a promise nobody ever asked him to keep. Left the spot open all those years just in case.

“Hill’s still there. Light still moves across those ridges the same way it did when five young fools believed the world was wide and friendship was permanent. And somewhere in the quiet that follows a man down the trail and over the pass… well, you can almost believe the circle never really broke. Laughter’s only resting. Next joke’s already waiting under a sky big enough to hold the living and the gone… for as long as those mountains decide to stand.”

He took a slow sip of coffee, set the mug down careful, and didn’t say anything else for a long while. The neon sign outside buzzed. A truck went by on the highway. And that was all.

text:
Everybody tells it like she took a leap of faith and quit her railroad job to paint full time. Annie Lee did say that. What she also said, and what almost nobody repeats, is that her son had just been killed in a car accident and she no longer needed the money. She was on bereavement leave when she decided not to go back. Sit with what that means before you share the pretty version again

You already know the painting.

A Black woman sitting on the edge of a bed in a blue room, shoulders down, a lamp and an alarm clock beside her and her slippers still on the floor. She is not sick and she is not sad, she is just tired in the specific way that Monday makes a woman tired.

That picture has been on somebody's wall in your family. Maybe your mother's hallway, maybe your auntie's bedroom, maybe a calendar in a beauty shop.

The woman in it has no face.

None of them do. The woman who painted her left the features off every figure she made, and she was fifty years old before she got her first gallery show.

Her name was Annie Lee. This is what that picture cost.

That cost starts in a front room on the South Side of Chicago in the middle 1940s.

Her mother was a seamstress raising children alone, and she did not believe in raising helpless ones. She taught Annie Lee and her older brother Tony off the same list.

Cook, wash, clean, sew, with nothing set aside as the boy's half or the girl's half.

Sundays were church, then eggnog ice cream at the corner drug store, and sometimes a matinee.

The rest of the week the radio ran while they worked. The Lone Ranger and The Shadow, the serials where a man's whole face arrived as a voice and a footstep and a door closing, and the child on the floor had to build the rest of him out of nothing.

Annie Lee sat in that room learning to knit and crochet with the radio going. She learned to draw in there too, in the same hours, listening to stories that handed her a body with no face on it and dared her to finish the job.

By ten the drawing had turned into painting, and it was immediately obvious. She entered art contests and won them, and the prize for winning was free semesters of lessons at the Art Institute of Chicago.

So there is a Black ten-year-old from the South Side in the 1940s walking through the front doors of the Art Institute, on a pass she took off every other child who entered. Nobody handed her that building, she beat her way into it.

The next building she walked into was Wendell Phillips High School at 39th and Prairie, in Bronzeville, the first majority-Black high school in Chicago and full past bursting. The Great Migration kept arriving, the building kept taking them, and by the mid-1940s the students were running split shifts with portable classrooms parked outside and adults coming in at night for evening school.

Nat King Cole had walked those halls, and so had Gwendolyn Brooks, Dinah Washington, John H. Johnson and the boys who became the Harlem Globetrotters.

Annie Lee cheered for the football team in that building and kept drawing.

The drawing got her an offer that almost never came to a Black girl in Bronzeville in the early 1950s. Northwestern University put four years of art school on the table, free.

She said no.

She married instead. Asked about it decades later, Annie Lee said that at the time it had not been a hard decision to make, and that one line is the only explanation of it she ever gave.

What Northwestern was in those years is a separate question, and the university has answered it.

Black students there were housed off campus under a selective housing system. Black women commuted in from private homes in Chicago or boarded with Black families in the Black section of Evanston.

An experimental interracial residence for women opened in 1947 and closed after a single year. Race stayed on the housing application form until 1962, and restrictive covenants made renting in Evanston a wall of its own.

Whether any of that ever reached a girl on 39th and Prairie is not on any record anybody has produced. It is only what the campus was on the day they offered her the four years.

She never took them, and what came instead was thirty years of a different kind of work.

The husband she married died of cancer. She married again and buried him too, cancer again, and raised a daughter from the first marriage and a son from the second on her own.

Two funerals for two husbands. Children who still needed shoes.

There was no art in those years worth the name. There was work.

The work was the Northwestern Railroad in Chicago, where the record has her as chief clerk in the engineering department, the department responsible for making sure the track was safe to run trains on. She was keeping the paperwork straight on track safety at a company that spent those same years abandoning and selling off branch line across seven states, and every mile of it had to be filed by somebody.

The scholarship she walked away from and the payroll she signed onto carried the same name. None of the biographies stop to notice it.

Being chief clerk of anything means a desk and a fixed hour, and a fixed hour means getting out of bed in the dark.

It is a Monday in winter and it is around five o'clock. Outside it is cold and it is still full dark.

Annie Lee is sitting on the edge of the bed, trying to get herself together. That is her own phrase for it, not mine.

Soon she has to be standing at a stop in the Chicago cold, waiting on public transportation to carry her to a railroad office where she is the chief clerk. It is a serious job with a serious title that still puts her outside in the winter dark like everybody else.

She is fifty years old, or close to it, and she has buried two husbands. She is going to work.

And sitting there in the dark, she has a thought that is not about art at all.

She wonders whether anybody else in the world feels as bad right now as she does.

That is it. That is the entire origin of the most recognized painting in Black American homes.

She did not go hunting for a subject. She was the subject, at five in the morning, on a work day, with a bus to catch.

By that winter Annie Lee had already spent years going back for the thing she gave away. She enrolled at Loop Junior College, then did undergraduate work at Mundelein College and the American Academy of Art.

Then eight years of night classes at Loyola University for a master's in interdisciplinary arts education.

Up before five. Railroad office all day, classroom in the evening, and painting when she got home.

She never intended to teach. She said the master's was the best thing she ever did for herself, that it reopened her mind.

She paid for that degree with eight years of nights in her forties. It was the same education Northwestern had offered her for nothing straight out of high school.

Her body sent the invoice. She developed tendinitis in her arm and problems in her spine from the hours at the easel.

The acrylics were worse. The fumes off the paint made her physically sick in her own apartment, and she kept painting in them because there was nowhere else and no other time.

She had waited her whole life to do this thing, and the thing was poisoning her while she did it.

Annie Lee was still painting in those fumes in 1985, when she got her first gallery show. Fifty years old, one lifetime late.

Everything on the walls sold in four hours.

Four hours. A woman who had been quietly excellent since she was ten stood in a room and watched strangers strip it bare before the afternoon was out, and then had to authorize prints of four paintings just to keep up with what people were asking for.

Then she went back to the railroad. One sold-out room in Chicago was one room, and by her family's account she was not about to give up the security of the day job.

She was still there in December of 1986, when her son was killed in a car accident.

She put in for leave from the railroad to bury him.

That leave is a fifty-one-year-old woman at home in the middle of a Chicago December, in the flat weeks after a funeral. Nothing to do, no reason to move, and a secure job waiting whenever she was ready to go back to it.

Annie Lee was still on that leave when she made the decision.

Every version of her story online calls what happened next a leap of faith. She did use those words, and there is a second half that almost nobody repeats.

She said she had prayed she could make her living painting, and that she felt she was supposed to paint. Then she said that now her son was gone, she did not need such financial resources.

She had stayed at the railroad for the security, and the security was for her children.

That is her own accounting of it, given to an interviewer thirteen years later, and it is the half the inspirational retellings drop. The job was worth less to her in January than it had been in November.

Annie Lee did not go back to the railroad. The leap of faith was real, and it became affordable at a graveside.

What she did with the years she bought was not small.

In 1990 she opened Annie Lee and Friends Gallery in Glenwood, Illinois. She hung forty-nine of her own originals in it and gave the rest of the wall to other artists, which is not what most people do the second they get a room of their own.

From that room she went out on the road with a travelling show that ran for years under the name Eight Men and a Lady, and the men in it rotated. She was the Lady, and by the account of the painter Gilbert Young she was the reason the rest of them kept showing up.

Her paintings kept showing up too, as set dressing on The Cosby Show and on A Different World, and the country met her work without ever meeting her.

Then she did the thing the art world never forgives. She put her designs on figurines, on dolls, on kitchen tiles, on housewares, on anything a family could actually afford to bring home.

That is how she got into your grandmother's house. Not through a museum, through a price a working woman could actually pay.

The fumes finally moved Annie Lee out of Chicago altogether, to Nevada, where she could work outdoors or under an exhaust fan and keep breathing. Through all of it, on every canvas, the same refusal above the neck.

People asked her about the faces constantly and the answer never really changed. You do not need to see a face to understand emotion, she said, and she wanted the movement of the body to carry it so people could use their imaginations.

A girl learned to draw in a room where the radio gave her a voice and no picture and made her supply the face herself. A woman spent forty years painting figures and handing that same job to everybody else.

She told the Chicago Tribune in 1997 that her paintings connected her to women, and that she knew the way she felt was the way a lot of women felt. That was not modesty, she was telling you the source material was her own Monday.

Her grandson Abe Ilo, who holds the rights to her work, has said that Blue Monday was the only painting she ever called a self-portrait. She gave herself the exact same treatment as everybody else she ever painted, which by her own account was the whole point.

The record has handled her about as carefully as it handled the scholarship.

There is a store selling Blue Monday prints right now with a description saying the painting shows a woman hunched over her washing basin. She is sitting on a bed.

The same listing says Annie Lee had no formal art training. She paid eight years of night classes and a master's degree to disprove that sentence.

On December 17, 2022, Lizzo walked out on Saturday Night Live in a white slip dress with her hair in Bantu knots. She sat hunched on the edge of a bed beside a lamp and an alarm clock, blue wall behind her, slippers on the floor, and began to sing.

The set was Blue Monday rebuilt down to the calendar on the wall, with December swapped in for the June in the original. The internet went straight up.

Thousands of people posted the painting beside the performance, and a large share of them were typing Annie Lee's name for the first time in their lives.

Annie Lee had been dead eight years by then.

Two years after that night, a writer put up a short piece about the painting and ended it with three plain questions. Where is the original, is her work in any museum's permanent collection, and did she ever get a retrospective.

Nobody answered.

The one thing the record should have been able to hold is the day she died.

Annie Lee died on a Monday, November 24, 2014, in Henderson, Nevada, seventy-nine years old. The funeral home record says so, and so did every notice published that week.

Several widely circulated biographies still give the date as November 14, The HistoryMakers among them, and the error has copied itself outward from there. It is ten days off and it has sat there more than a decade on pages written to honor her.

The pages cannot get the day right for a woman whose entire body of work is about knowing exactly how somebody feels without being told.

So put the name and the day back on the picture. Annie Lee, born March 3, 1935, in Gadsden, Alabama, died Monday, November 24, 2014.

Next time that blue bedroom comes across your feed with no credit under it, type her name in the comments and fix the date while you are down there. Then tell whoever posted it what the picture cost her, because the woman on that bed is not a mood and she is not a meme.

She is a girl just out of Wendell Phillips who turned down four free years and never explained why. She is a fifty-one-year-old who had already proved she was an artist and could not afford to be one full-time until she buried her son.

She got the rest of her life at fifty-one, with a bad back and paint fumes in her lungs. She used it so completely that a girl not yet born when she left the railroad would one day sit on a network stage in a slip and slippers so the whole country could look at her Monday.

text:
GARIBALDI PROVINCIAL PARK, spanning 1946.5 km, presents a pristine wilderness characterized by volcanic mountains, sub-alpine meadows, and glacial lakes, situated 65 km north of Vancouver. Mount Garibaldi, with an elevation of 2,678 m, was designated in 1860 by British naval officer G.H. Richards during his survey of Howe Sound, honoring the 19th-century Italian patriot Giuseppe Garibaldi. The Squamish Nation historically referred to this peak as Chuckigh (Cheekye), signifying "dirty snow." Its inaugural ascent occurred in 1907, subsequently attracting mountaineering enthusiasts whose advocacy led to the establishment of the provincial park. Founded in 1920, the park showcases remarkable volcanic formations, including the eroded Black Tusk cone and the natural lava dam known as the Barrier, which resulted from Mount Price's eruption approximately 12,000 years ago. Garibaldi Lake subsequently formed behind this dam. The Garibaldi Chalet, notable as the park's inaugural lodge and British Columbia's first private ski lodge, commenced operations at Diamond Head in 1946 and continued until the 1970s. The park offers convenient access via Highway 99, located between Squamish and Pemberton. The Whistler and Blackcomb ski resorts are situated adjacent to the park's northwestern boundary.

text:
Archaeologists have uncovered new evidence from the Qurayyah Oasis in northwestern Saudi Arabia, revealing a major Bronze Age centre known for producing distinctive painted pottery around 3,200 years ago. Recent research published in PLOS One found that the pottery featured recognizable black-and-red geometric patterns along with stylized animal and human figures.

Researchers say the pottery was produced through organized manufacturing and appears to have been distributed beyond the local area. Similar Qurayyah Painted Ware has been found across parts of northwestern Arabia and the southern Levant, providing evidence of long-distance trade and cultural connections during the Bronze Age.

The discovery offers fresh insight into the craftsmanship, commercial networks and cultural exchanges of ancient Arabian societies. UNESCO also identifies Qurayyah as an important ancient oasis that developed agriculture, irrigation, copper production and sophisticated pottery manufacturing.

Cardinal Sako born when?
Louis Raphaël I Cardinal Sako, Patriarch of Baghdad (Chaldean), Iraq, revealed in an interview that his parents re-used the birth certificate of his older brother (who had died). His actual birth date is 1 year later than previously thought (thus 4 July 1949).

The interview can be found here.

Here is the relevant section, in the original language and with a translation (provided by Google Translate):

KNA: Sie haben unlängst Ihren 75. Geburtstag gefeiert.

Sako: Das stimmt nicht. Ich wurde 1949 geboren. Aber ich hatte einen älteren Bruder selben Namens, der gestorben ist. Meine Eltern haben mir seine Geburtsurkunde gegeben. Ich werde also erst nächstes Jahr am 4. Juli 75 Jahre alt.

KNA: You recently celebrated your 75th birthday.

Sako: That's not true. I was born in 1949. But I had an older brother with the same name who died. My parents gave me his birth certificate. So I won't be 75 until July 4th next year.
The correct date is not reflected in any of the usual sources (yet).

Because that Constitution belongs to the people, its champion — as George Washington perceived — should be a monarch whose obligation is not to politics or religion but to the sovereign nation. Through the natural system of heredity (being born and bred to the task), such a Constitutional guardian would provide an ‘ongoing continuity’ of public representation through successive governments. In this regard both monarchs and ministers would be servants of the Constitution on behalf of the Community of the Realm. Such a concept of moral government lies at the very heart of the Grail Code, and it remains within the bounds of possibility for every civilized Nation State. A leading British politician recently claimed that it was not his job to be popular! Class structure is always decided from above, never from below. It is therefore for those on self-made pedestals to be seen to kick them aside in the interests of harmony and unity. The University of Notre Dame provides a variety of official student organizations, ministry resources, and support networks for LGBTQ+ students, while balancing its identity rooted in Catholic tradition.

Student Organizations & Support

PrismND: The first and official LGBTQ+ undergraduate student organization on campus, providing weekly hangouts, peer support, and social events.

GradientND: An official student group supporting LGBTQ+ graduate students.

Campus Ministry: Offers pastoral care, an annual student LGBTQ retreat, and specialized Masses through Campus Ministry's LGBTQ Ministry.

University Counseling Center (UCC): Offers LGBTQ-affirming therapists and dedicated therapy groups for students.

Alumni & Employee Networks

ARC ND: The Alumni Rainbow Community connects LGBTQ+ alumni and allies with the university.

SpectrumND: An employee resource group for faculty and staff that engages in regional events like the South Bend Pride Festival

LGBTQ Ministry
All Are Welcome
“You are the body of Christ. Each one of you is a part of it.” -St. Paul to the Corinthians
Welcome to Notre Dame, where every student is valued, respected, and supported. We warmly welcome our LGBTQ students as vital members of our rich and vibrant community. Rooted in the Catholic tradition of human dignity, compassion, and love for all people, we are committed to fostering an inclusive environment where each individual can grow academically, spiritually, and personally. We recognize that we are all in different places on our journeys and we welcome you wherever that may be. Your presence enriches our campus, and we are dedicated to walking with you in your journey with openness, understanding, and care.

Please be on the lookout for more information about our annual LGBTQ Retreat coming up in the spring semester!

For more information about our LGBTQ ministry or to get involved, please contact Tami Schmitz, Director of Pastoral Care, tschmitz@nd.edu.

text:
UK
Moment cops chase VW during pursuit before seven including two police officers die in horror A66 crash - as top cop pays heartbreaking tribute

This is the moment police are seen pursuing a car down a narrow road just minutes before seven people were killed in a head-on smash, including two officers who lost their lives.  

Footage exclusively obtained by SWR shows a Volkswagen Passat speeding past homes on Lime Road, Teesville, at 3.36am on Saturday morning. 

In the video captured by a home security camera, two police cars follow just seconds later, both with their lights flashing and sirens sounding. 

The dramatic pursuit began about a mile away from where the Volkswagen smashed into a police car while travelling in the wrong direction down the A66 in Teesside. 

The vehicles collided at around 3.40am in South Bank, near Middlesbrough. 

The marked police car was heading the correct way down the A66 before the crash and was not involved in the initial pursuit, it is understood. 

Cleveland Police Chief Constable Victoria Fuller paid tribute to the two 'brave' police officers killed, and named them as PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, during a police press conference.

She said on Saturday: 'This is an incredibly sad day for Cleveland. The loss has been felt across our communities, by our police family and by our partner agencies.

'These were brave officers protecting our communities and serving our residents who didn't return home to their families at the end of their shift. 

'My thoughts and thoughts of everybody here at Cleveland Police are with their family, friends, colleagues and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time.

'Early today the Deputy Chief Constable and I visited Matthew and Tom's families to offer our condolences, support one another and begin to come to terms with this unimaginable loss.'

On Saturday evening, the flags outside Cleveland Police headquarters had been lowered to half-mast in remembrance of the two officers.

The crash comes just days after five young men were also killed in a head-on smash on an Irish motorway. The youngsters, who were in a stolen BMW travelling the wrong way down the M9, died at the scene in Co Kildare in the early hours of Sunday. 

Teesville resident Neil Hutchinson, 47, said: 'There were police cars tearing down the street at 3.30am with lights flashing and their sirens going, it woke me up.

'You could tell from the noise that they were travelling at high speed. Two cars went down the street and then a few seconds later there was a third, they were obviously going after another vehicle. 

'It's a narrow street with cars parked on either side so it must have been a serious situation to be going at that speed down this road.

'We woke up this morning to the news that people have been killed. They were travelling in the direction of the A66 so it must have been part of the same incident.'

Libertarian Party of Ohio State Central Committee Announces 2026 Candidate Endorsements

COLUMBUS, OHIO - August 25, 2026 The Libertarian Party of Ohio State Central Committee formally endorsed a slate of Libertarian candidates seeking federal, statewide, state legislative, and county offices across Ohio during its previous meeting.

These endorsements represent candidates from communities throughout the state who are stepping forward to offer Ohio voters a Libertarian choice and advance the principles of individual liberty, limited government, fiscal responsibility, personal freedom, and accountable representation.

The Libertarian Party of Ohio State Central Committee endorsed the following candidates:

Bill Redpath - U.S. Senate
Nathan Weise - U.S. House, District 1
Michael Veloff - U.S. House, District 5
Thomas McMasters - U.S. House, District 10
Brennan Barrington - U.S. House, District 15

Tom Pruss - Ohio Secretary of State
Josh Umbaugh - House District 40

Jason Purviance - House District 47
Philip Pirdy - House District 55
Ron Grethel - House District 62
Justin Peroli - House District 66

Timothy Godwin - House District 97
Ken Sharp - Senate District 11
Cassaundra Fryman - Huron County Commissioner
Katherine Bowles - Warren County Commissioner
Eric Terford - Franklin County Commissioner

“Ohio voters deserve meaningful choices at every level of government. I am proud that our State Central Committee has endorsed Libertarian candidates from the top of the ticket to county government who are willing to put their names on the ballot, take our message directly to voters, and challenge the political status quo.

“Our work does not end with an endorsement. The Libertarian Party of Ohio must continue building the organization and infrastructure necessary to support our candidates, strengthen our county parties, and establish a lasting Libertarian presence throughout Ohio.

“I want to thank every one of these candidates for stepping forward to represent the Libertarian Party and the principles of liberty. Running for public office requires an enormous commitment, and I look forward to seeing our candidates take that message to Ohioans throughout the remainder of the 2026 election.”

State Central Committee
Libertarian Party of Ohio

The Libertarian Party of Ohio State Central Committee congratulates each endorsed candidate and encourages Ohioans to learn more about the Libertarian candidates appearing on their ballots in the November 2026 General Election.

Consciousness_and_the_Universe__Quantum_Ph_-_Roger_Penrose.pdf

Consciousness and the Universe

Quantum Physics, Evolution, Brain & Mind

Editors

Sir Roger Penrose
University of Oxford, Oxford, United Kingdom

Stuart Hameroff, M.D.
University of Arizona, Arizona,

Subhash Kak, Ph.D.
Oklahoma State University, Oklahoma 

pg. 139-142

Chapter 5. How Consciousness Becomes the Physical Universe 

Menas Kafatos, Ph.D.1, Rudolph E. Tanzi, Ph.D.2, and Deepak Chopra, M.D.3 (Cont.)

4. Bridging the Gap: A Consciousness Model

Our purpose here is not to settle these technical issues – or the many others that have arisen as theorists attempt to link quantum processes to the field of biology – but to propose that technical considerations are secondary. What is primary is to have a reliable model against which experiments can offer challenges. Such a model isn’t available as long as we fail to account for the disappearance of the material universe implied by quantum theory. This disappearance is real. There is, at bottom, no strictly mechanistic, physical foundation for the cosmos. The situation is far more radical than most practicing scientists suppose. Whatever is the fundamental source of creation, it itself must be uncreated. Otherwise, there is a hidden creator lying in the background, and then we must ask who or what created that.

What does it mean to be uncreated? The source of reality must be self-sufficient, capable of engendering complex systems on the micro and macro scale, self-regulating, and holistic. Nothing can exist outside its influence. Ultimately, the uncreated source must also turn into the physical universe, not simply oversee it as God or the gods do in conventional religion. We feel that only consciousness fits the bill, for as a prima facie truth, no experience takes place outside consciousness, which means that if there is a reality existing beyond our awareness (counting mathematics and the laws of physics as 1 part of our conscious experience), we will never be able to know it. The fact that consciousness is inseparable from cognition, perception, observation and measurement, is undeniable; therefore, this is the starting point for new insights into the nature of reality.

What is the nature of consciousness in our model? We take it as a field phenomenon, analogous to but preceding the quantum field. This field is characterized by generalized principles already described by quantum physics: complementarity, non-locality, scale-invariance and undivided wholeness. But there is a radical difference between this field and all others: we cannot define it from the outside. To extend Wheeler’s reasoning, consciousness includes us human observers. We are part of a feedback loop that links our conscious acts to the conscious response of the field. In keeping with Heisenberg’s implication, the universe presents the face that the observer is looking for, and when she looks for a different face, the universe changes its mask.

Consciousness includes human mental processes, but it is not just a human attribute. Existing outside space and time, it was “there” “before” those two words had any meaning. In essence, space and time are conceptual artifacts that sprang from primordial consciousness. The reason that the human mind meshes with nature, mathematics, and the fundamental forces described by physics, is no accident: we mesh because we are a product of the same conceptual expansion by which primordial consciousness turned into the physical world. The difficulty with using basic terms like “concept” and “physical” is that we are accustomed to setting mind apart from matter; therefore, thinking about an atom isn’t the same as an atom. Ideas are not substances. But if elementary particles and all matter made of them aren’t substances either, the playing field has been leveled. Quantum theory gives us a model that applies everywhere, not just at the micro level.

I’m asking Northeast Mississippi CC to please grant my release and not make me sit out a year. Harvesting Grace, A Forty-Day Devotional by C.S. McDonald is a warm, reflective Christian devotional that invites readers to slow down and reconnect with God’s grace, especially during the beauty of autumn.

Inspired by the author’s love of the fall season—with its vibrant colors, crisp air, and sense of harvest and gratitude—the book offers forty days of gentle spiritual nourishment. Each entry includes a daily Bible verse, a peaceful and thought-provoking observation, and soft reflections designed to refresh faith and cultivate joy. McDonald encourages readers to pause amid life’s busyness, sit quietly or take a walk, and intentionally harvest God’s steadfast love and boundless grace. It serves as a humble, encouraging guide that can be used in autumn or anytime throughout the year. Readers looking for a calming, faith-centered companion will find it uplifting and accessible.

text:
INDIANA ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION 

There’s a pretty interesting connection when you start following the money around SK Hynix, the new semiconductor factory at the Purdue campus in West Lafayette Indiana.

SK hynix has had a major manufacturing presence in Wuxi, China, for years. It also established HITECH Semiconductor (Wuxi) in 2009 with Wuxi Taiji Industry. SK hynix owns 45% of HITECH, and Wuxi Taiji has been identified as a state-owned company tied to the Wuxi government.

So, no, that doesn’t mean China owns SK hynix. But it does mean SK hynix has had long-standing business and manufacturing relationships involving Chinese government-linked companies.

And this isn’t a small operation. CSIS has estimated that SK hynix’s China operations represent around $20 billion in investment and roughly half of its DRAM production.

The U.S. government awarded SK hynix up to **$458 million in CHIPS funding**, with another **$500 million and potential federal Investment Tax Credit** for its roughly **$3.87 billion** advanced HBM packaging and R&D project at Purdue Research Park.

Then there’s Indiana.

The Indiana Economic Development Corporation offered SK hynix up to **$554.7 million in tax rebates** and up to **$45 million for infrastructure** around the project.

Purdue and the Purdue Research Foundation also provided incentives and in-kind support valued at about **$60 million**, including discounted land for roughly 90 acres.

So we’re talking about a very large package of U.S. federal, Indiana and Purdue support.

And here’s where the questions start getting interesting.

The whole point of the CHIPS Act was to strengthen America’s semiconductor supply chain and reduce dependence on countries considered national security concerns, including China. The CHIPS rules also put restrictions on recipients expanding certain semiconductor manufacturing capacity in countries of concern.

How does the U.S. government’s investment in SK hynix’s Indiana operation fit with SK hynix’s continued, large-scale manufacturing presence in China?

text:
British scientist David Morens plotted with senior US health official to shut down Covid lab leak theory, court documents allege | Daily Mail

A British scientist involved in animal experiments at the Chinese lab suspected of being behind the Covid-19 outbreak has been accused of plotting with a US health official to muzzle the theory.

US court documents allege zoologist Dr Peter Daszak conspired with David Morens to disrupt suspicions that the research may have caused the global pandemic.

They claim the former president of US-based non-governmental organisation EcoHealth Alliance sent bottles of wine to Morens, then a senior figure at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, to thank him for ‘behind the scenes shenanigans’.

Other gifts supposedly offered to the official, who offered to get Dr Daszak’s work ‘re-funded’, included dinners at Michelin-starred restaurants.

Morens, 78 - a former advisor to Dr Anthony Fauci, who led the US pandemic response – is facing up to five years in jail after pleading guilty on Tuesday to conspiring to evade public records laws and conceal government documents connected to research funding and the Covid-19 outbreak.

Molecular biologist Professor Richard Ebright, who is based at Rutgers University in New Jersey and has campaigned for a full investigation into the lab leak theory, told the Telegraph: ‘Morens' guilty plea is an important step in holding accountable US officials who funded the reckless research in Wuhan.’

Covid-19 was first detected a few miles from the Wuhan Institute, where work on genetic changes to bat coronaviruses and how their mutations could transfer into humans was being conducted by scientists including Dr Daszak – who has no charges against him at present.

A US Attorney’s Office for the District of Maryland press release states Morens and other conspirators were working to ‘counter the narrative that Covid-19 leaked from a lab’.

Evidence considered included a June 2020 email in which Morens spoke of writing a ‘scientific commentary’ about Dr Daszak’s work that would appear independent.

He wrote: ‘Let’s win this anti-science battle, get you re-funded… then settle some scores and kick some ass.’

A fortnight later, Dr Daszak is said to have sent two bottles of wine to Morens and described it as starting ‘a continued series of expressions of gratitude for your advice, support and behind-the-scenes shenanigans in my battle against your bosses’ boss, his boss and the ultimate boss on the hill (ie Donald Trump).’

Morens then published an article, The Origins of Covid-19 and Why It Matters, which argued the virus was ‘natural’ and had come from animals, as well as calling for funding for work like Dr Daszak’s to help prevent another pandemic.

Dr Daszak would go on in 2021 to visit the Wuhan Institute as part of a World Health Organisation team investigating the source of the pandemic.

The subsequent report – dismissed as a ‘whitewash’ – concluded a lab leak was an unlikely cause.

In 2024, emails released by the US House oversight committee suggested Dr Daszak and Morens had discussed concealing their shared correspondence.

One, in June 2020 from Morens, bemoaned ‘paranoia-inducing’ freedom of information requests but spoke of deleting evidence, adding: ‘We are all smart enough to know to never have smoking guns.’

US court documents state the conspirators ‘concealed their communications’ in order to publish articles that didn’t directly mention Dr Daszak ‘to generate the appearance of disinterested scientific consensus’.

Viscount Ridley, co-author of Viral: The Search for the Origin of Covid-19, claimed it was ‘time [Dr Daszak] was held to account’.

‘And then, when the pandemic broke out in Wuhan… did his utmost to kill any investigation into the possibility that a laboratory accident killed millions of people.’

Morens’ plea deal with the US District Court in Maryland means he could still face a $250,000 fine when he is sentenced in November.

Dr Fauci recently exercised his right to avoid implicating himself by invoking the Fifth Amendment at a Senate hearing where he was questioned about his relationship with Morens.

Dr Daszak was approached for a comment.

He has previously vehemently denied that Covid leaked from a lab, while an EcoHealth spokesman said there is no way the experiments conducted by themselves and the Wuhan Institute could have started the pandemic.

In 2023, Dr Daszak retweeted a post by fellow virologist Dr Angela Rasmussen which said: 'By demonizing and alienating colleagues in China instead of building collaborative trust, this is what the relentlessly toxic lab leak conspiracy machine has yielded: The complete and total disintegration of any meaningful further investigation into the origins of SARS-CoV-2.'

The following year, Dr Daszak said: 'In South and South East Asia there is a very dynamic interface, with as many as 60,000-plus people a year being infected by bat coronaviruses, so that’s a high risk for future pandemic emergence.'

text:
THE CLAY MATHEMATICS INSTITUTE HAS OFFERED A MILLION DOLLARS SINCE THE YEAR 2000 FOR ONE PROOF - THE SAME PROOF HILBERT LISTED AS THE MOST IMPORTANT PROBLEM ON EARTH IN 1900 - AND THIS LECTURE IS THE CLEAREST EXPLANATION OF WHY NOBODY HAS COLLECTED YET

This is Alex Kontorovich, Rutgers and Yale, public lecture on the Riemann Hypothesis. He opens with one claim - Riemann was the first human being to hear the music of the primes. The goal of the next hour is to make you hear it too.

He starts with Euclid's proof that primes are infinite. No computer, no list, no experiment. You assume there are finitely many, multiply them all together, add one, and the number you get cannot be divisible by any prime on your list. So it must be prime itself. Contradiction. The entire argument is a conversation between two ideas with no numbers needed. That proof is 2,300 years old and has never been wrong.

Then the Möbius function. Every number gets a spin - up, down, or zero - depending on how its prime factors are arranged. Two primes give a down. Four primes give an up. A repeated prime factor gives nothing. You add up those spins out to a thousand, then ten thousand, then twenty thousand. The graph looks exactly like a coin flip. Up, down, nowhere near where it started, hugging the curve of the square root. The primes are producing something indistinguishable from randomness.

Then the Von Mangoldt function. It assigns log values to prime powers and zero to everything else. You add those up, subtract the straight line, and watch the remainder wiggle. Same coin flip. Same square root boundary. Two completely different functions built from primes, both behaving randomly in exactly the same way.

Then Fourier. Any wave - a saxophone, a heartbeat, a square pulse - can be decomposed into pure sine waves with specific frequencies and amplitudes. Riemann did the same thing for primes. He found the waves hidden inside the prime counting function. Wave after wave added on top of each other, each one sharpening the step function that tracks where primes live. By wave 100, the match is almost exact.

Watch the moment he shows all of Riemann's waves lined up by frequency and amplitude. Every single wave plays at exactly the same volume - one half. Not approximately. Not on average. Exactly one half. That is the Riemann Hypothesis. All the music the primes are playing comes from instruments tuned to the same loudness. One line on a graph, and nobody has proved it in 165 years.

A number theorist I know showed this lecture to a graduate student the week before their qualifying exam. Said it was the first time the million-dollar problem felt like a question about harmony rather than a formula on a page.

Free on YouTube, recorded at a public science talk, no prerequisites.

bookmark this and watch later - after this lecture every time you hear music you will wonder if the primes already knew the chord

text:
This is not Kawhi Leonard.

I’ve watched virtually every Kawhi interview since 2010, from a quiet kid at San Diego State to one of the NBA’s most private superstars.

This ain't that dude. 

Between 2008 and 2024, I’d describe Kawhi as publicly reserved and privately awkward.

His teammates always said the media didn’t know the real Kawhi. But the two versions weren’t actually that different. He wasn’t putting on an awkward persona. He genuinely seemed like someone who lived a lot of his life inside his own head.

Quiet. Deliberate. Sometimes uncomfortable. Sometimes unintentionally hilarious.

There was a hitch in his communication. Long pauses. A certain guardedness. Almost like a filter between what Kawhi was thinking and what eventually came out.

But slowly, over the past year, and especially this offseason, I’ve noticed something change.

He sounds different.

There’s less hesitation. Less of that communication “hitch.” He seems more comfortable taking up space.

He jokes without seeming to realize he’s being funny.

Most importantly, he doesn’t seem like he’s trying to figure out how he’s supposed to be perceived.

He just seems… present.

For years, people said Kawhi’s personality held him back from becoming a bigger marketing star. He was described as camera-shy, awkward, boring, robotic, monotonous.

And this is where I want to offer a theory that I know will get me flamed.

But there is some science behind the broader idea.

Trauma doesn't just live in your memories.

The nervous system is involved in how you breathe, move, speak, react to stress and regulate muscle tension. Research has found associations between psychological trauma, autonomic nervous-system dysregulation, chronic pain and other physical symptoms.

That doesn't mean trauma gets “stored in your muscles.” And it certainly doesn't mean I can diagnose Kawhi from watching interviews.

But it does mean the mind and body are considerably less separate than we sometimes pretend.

Your psychological state can influence your physiology, including how you breathe, hold tension, move and use your voice.

Think about someone experiencing profound grief. You can see it in their face, but sometimes you can see it in everything else: their posture, their walk, their voice, the way they gesture, the way they brace themselves.

And this isn't just theoretical.

Aaron Gordon has spoken about experiencing this mind-body connection following the death of his brother Drew, who died in a car accident in 2024.

Since then, Aaron has dealt with a string of soft-tissue injuries, particularly involving his hamstrings.

In a 2026 interview, Gordon connected those injuries to the tension he was carrying, saying his body was “holding everything in” and that, for him, the tension manifested in his hamstrings.

It's not proof that grief caused his injuries. But Aaron believes it. 

Enter Kawhi. 

Because Kawhi experienced something unimaginably traumatic when he was 16.

His father, Mark Leonard, was shot and killed at the car wash he owned in Compton in January 2008. 

Kawhi has never publicly said, “This trauma changed the way I move or communicate.”

I would never pretend he has.

But I do wonder whether we've spent 15 years watching the behavioral consequences of someone learning, very young, to keep an enormous amount of emotion inside.

Maybe I'm completely wrong.

Maybe this is simply what happens when a person gets older.

Maybe becoming a father changes you. Maybe 15 years of fame changes you. Maybe he's simply happier, healthier, or more comfortable with who he is.

Maybe it's all of those things.

Whatever the explanation, something is different.

And it's not just that Kawhi seems happier.

His entire physical and verbal presence feels different.

I feel like I'm watching Kawhi Leonard just exist.

Maybe Kawhi hasn't become a different person.

Maybe he's simply becoming more of himself.

For the first time since 2008...

Kawhi Leonard looks free.

text:
Periodic reminder that the Spanish inquisition was good and only reason people have a negative view of it is because of movies and Dutch, French, and British propaganda that survived the test of time

In the 300 years of the Inquisition, only 27 witches were executed, many of whom had committed more serious unaffiliated crimes. Movies have greatly overblown how many people the Inquisition actually killed, as well as the fact that it actively hunted weapon smugglers, pedophiles, criminals, and murderers. Overall, the Inquisition is known to have executed around 1,000 people across those 300 years (a number the Aztecs could average in a year)

In fact, many people would voluntarily hand themselves over to inquisitors because the alternatives were far worse and offered far less justice. People often claim torture was widespread, yet the actual rate was about 2%. Sessions never lasted more than 15 minutes a day, a doctor was present, and the goal was never to cause permanent injury (it was still bad, of course, but for its time it was very humane)

Yes, the Inquisition did kill SOME innocents mostly people of the Jewish faith who refused to convert or move out. 

But most of the lies about it were created by the Dutch, French, and British at the time, and later repeated by Protestants after the Reformation. The claim that the Inquisition was simply a genocidal body that did nothing for the good of the people and randomly seized and executed victims is false. The accused were provided with lawyers, most were acquitted, and those found guilty usually received only minor punishments (depending on the crime, of course)

text:
Human sacrifice is where the biggest differences and the biggest misconceptions show up.
Both cultures practiced it. Neither invented it. The scale, style, frequency, and purpose diverged sharply.

Among the Maya, sacrifice was real but generally smaller in scale and more episodic. It occurred in specific contexts: dedication of temples or monuments, responses to drought or crisis, victory in war, or calendrical rites. Methods varied — heart extraction, decapitation, arrow sacrifice, and throwing victims into cenotes (sacred sinkholes). Child sacrifice happened, sometimes in pairs or groups of related boys, and recent DNA work at Chichén Itzá shows many of the victims in one major deposit were local male children, including twins, possibly linked to Hero Twin mythology in the Popol Vuh. Elite bloodletting (nobles piercing their own tongues, ears, or genitals) was also important and often more common than killing others. There is no evidence of the massive, ongoing, state-organized annual harvest of victims that characterized the Aztecs. 

Archaeological finds confirm sacrifice, including skulls that may have been displayed, but the numbers are far lower and the practice was not the central engine of a large imperial system. Traditional older views that the Maya were peaceful while the Aztecs were uniquely brutal have been corrected — the Maya did sacrifice people — but the quantitative and political difference remains large.

The Aztecs took the practice further than any other known Mesoamerican society. It was frequent, public, and institutionalized. The core belief was that the current world (the Fifth Sun) existed because the gods had sacrificed themselves to set the sun in motion. Humans owed a blood debt. The sun, rain, and continued existence of the cosmos required human hearts and blood. Major festivals on the ritual calendar involved public sacrifice. War captives were preferred because they were obtained through battle, which itself carried religious meaning. The “flower wars” with certain neighboring states helped supply live prisoners. Priests cut open the chest with an obsidian knife, removed the heart, and offered it. Bodies were often rolled down the temple stairs. Skulls went onto large wooden racks (tzompantli). Archaeology at the Templo Mayor has recovered hundreds of skulls (including men, women, and children) and confirmed the existence of the racks and towers the Spanish described. Most victims appear to have been outsiders — war captives or people sent as tribute — rather than random local citizens.

Spanish accounts exaggerated the numbers, sometimes wildly. Claims of 80,000 sacrificed in four days for the 1487 rededication of the Templo Mayor are logistically impossible and not supported by archaeology. More careful modern estimates based on the physical evidence and the ritual calendar still put the annual figure across the empire in the low thousands at its height (some older scholarly estimates ran higher, into the tens of thousands, but recent work with the skull towers points lower). Even the more moderate numbers represent a significant ongoing practice. The Spanish had propaganda reasons to inflate the horror, but Indigenous allies of Cortés (especially the Tlaxcalans) confirmed the practice and resented the constant demand for victims. Sacrifice served both religion and politics: it maintained the cosmic order in Aztec eyes and functioned as state terror that reinforced domination over subject peoples.

So the distinction is real. Maya sacrifice was present, varied, and often tied to local rulership, crisis, or specific mythology, but limited in scale. Aztec sacrifice was larger, more systematic, more public, and tightly bound to imperial expansion and the ideology of feeding the sun. Both were religious. The Aztec version was also a tool of empire.
