text:
The veteran Fortune 500 CEO who turned an 80-year-old AC company into an AI darling | Shawn Tully, Fortune

If asked to name the top-performing stocks powered by the AI boom, most investors would probably guess Nvidia (correct), maybe Meta (wrong) and a bunch of other hyperscalers (also wrong). You’d be hard pressed to find anyone who would answer Vertiv, an 80-year-old AC maker. But since Vertiv went public in early 2021, its market cap has exploded almost 10x from under $11 billion to $109 billion. Over that six-and-a-half year span, its annualized return of 50.5% stands third in the S&P 500, exceeded only by Comfort Systems (55.2%) and Nvidia (54.9%).

And the story gets better from there. The man responsible for this unlikely turn of events is a retired industrialist who almost didn’t take the job. Back in 2019 David Cote was looking for a new project. He had just retired from an illustrious career running Honeywell, where he engineered a spectacular revival after a failed acquisition by GE left the industrial giant rudderless. But he felt like he had another chapter left in him. So he brokered an unusual arrangement with Goldman Sachs: they’d present Cote with lots of acquisition candidates, and raise the funding once he found a choice that the investment bank also favored. Cote’s an ace at spotting overlooked comers; he’d bought over 100 companies at Honeywell, deals that substantially quickened its expansion and enhanced its profitability. In fact, Cote was looking for enterprises that met the same criteria that he’d successfully applied at the aircraft and auto equipment maker. The target would need to occupy a dominant or potentially dominant position in an industry that’s either fast-rising and profitable now or en route; promise plenty of room to grow both internally and through takeovers; stand rife for expanding margins; and perhaps most important, offer the opportunity to forge a sector-leading new technology.

“I had weekly phone calls with the Goldman group, and we looked at over 1,000 companies, and it was Goldman that found them,” recalls Cote. The company in question was Vertiv, an eighty-year old industrial AC purveyor that, under his leadership pivoted as a provider of a revolutionary technology that’s critical to accelerating the rise of AI. To deploy Nvidia GPUs and other superpowered intensive gear, data centers need to keep the servers super-cool, as never before. It’s Vertiv’s system using newly-introduced direct-to-chip liquid rather than traditional air cooling, more than any other solution on the market, that’s making it happen.

Says Cote: “It was not like I was an AI savant, but I knew that if I positioned myself in the middle of the data industry there was a good chance something good would happen.” For companies and executives who’ve spent years anxiously bolting an AI strategy onto their business, Cote’s story is a useful outlier. He didn’t chase a hot technology, he noticed a huge trend and quietly became indispensable to it.

Cote wanted a place at the center of the digital age, but Vertiv got off to a rocky start

Surprisingly, Cote’s blithe, down-home style actually fits the freewheeling AI ethos. This hip-hop loving, Harley-Davidson sporting raconteur’s persona has long been hewed closer to Silicon Valley than mainstream Big Corporate. As I related in a 2012 Fortune story on how he revived Honeywell, Cote (pronounced Co-tee) grew up in a small New Hampshire town where his eighth-grade educated dad ran a garage. “I didn’t know what success was because it was hard to find anyone in town you’d describe as successful,” he told me. Dave took a one-year break from college to buy a 33-foot lobster boat with a buddy, and trawl for cod in Maine, an experience that convinced him that “You can work very hard and accomplish absolutely nothing.”

Starting as a night-shift worker at a GE aircraft engine plant in his native New Hampshire, Cote rose through the dishwasher and silicone divisions to head the appliance franchise. But his 25-year career at GE ended through his explosive firing by its legendary CEO, Jack Welch. As Cote relates the 1999 incident, Welch strode up to Cote at the HQ dining room in Fairfield, Conn., and remained standing and didn’t bother with niceties. “The first words out of his mouth were, ‘Dave, I want you out of the company by year end!’” Cote recalls. Cote asked his boss what he’d done wrong, “And Jack then repeated, even louder, ‘You don’t understand, I want you out of the company by year end!’’’ Cote says he kept asking for an explanation. “And each time I asked, Jack would yell the same words, only louder each time. Jack had a high, squeaky voice, and the louder he yelled, the higher and squeakier his voice got. I got plenty of squeaking, I just never got an answer on what Jack didn’t like.”

In 2002, Cote took the helm at Honeywell, the conglomerate that made such staples as avionics, specialty chemicals, and auto parts from turbochargers to spark plugs, and over the next 15 years, delivered shareholder returns that beat the S&P 500 by 150%. At Honeywell, Cote regularly went to work, and even to board meetings, in a beat-up bomber jacket, baggy jeans and work boots. His office featured a gurgling, 210 gallon fish tank, and a continuous stream of music from his iTunes playlist of 10,000 songs. “The music never stops!” he intoned. Every couple of months, Cote would spend a full day isolated in his office––no phone calls or meetings––to ponder a big strategic idea. While Billie Holiday’s “God Bless the Child” or Jay-Z’s “Hard Knock Life” played in the background, he’d weigh such issues as the best design for a new generation of turbochargers.

Cote had never heard of Vertiv when the Goldman team brought it to his attention. Founded in 1946, Vertiv’s forerunner became the “network power” arm of Emerson Electric that developed the first precision cooling system for IBM mainframes. By the time Cote found it, Emerson had dumped Vertiv to California private equity firm Platinum Equity. “Emerson said it was a horrible business, they hated it,” says Cote. “They couldn’t wait to get out of it.” Under Platinum, Vertiv was struggling in its traditional trade: supplying air cooling for the then-routine functions of data centers, such as primary storage, running business software, and furnishing cloud computing for website hosting.

In early 2020, Cote and an investor group assembled by Goldman bought Vertiv for what proved an ultra-bargain $4 billion via a “special-purchase acquisition company,” and simultaneously took it public on the NYSE. Cote acknowledges that SPACs—where renowned “sponsors” raise money for an acquisition before choosing what they’re going to buy––even then had a “tawdry reputation,” and they’ve since disappeared. But this one worked: Vertiv’s one of the few SPACs that launched an enduring enterprise.

Cote found Vertiv so attractive for a simple reason: It had a big foothold in what he perceived as one of the great industries of the future, digital data, and with the right products, could ride the train to glory. “The two biggest twentieth-century trends are biotech and the digital age, and I thought the latter had 50 or 60 years to go.”

In part, Vertiv was lagging because it concentrated on the wrong customers. “Their largest customers were the major banks, while their competitors were working with Google and Microsoft,” says Scott Davis, an analyst at Melius Research. “That’s why they were poorly positioned and losing market share. One of Dave’s first moves was repositioning Vertiv to serve the hyperscalers.

At the time, the AI craze was still several years away. But Cote reckoned that the existing industry was on the cusp of a huge upswing. “When I got to Vertiv, pre-AI data generation was growing at 20% a year, but data centers were growing at 4%,” he says. “It didn’t make sense to me when all that data is being created and increasing everywhere. Machine learning, the predecessor to AI, was already requiring far more data. Eventually, the capacity of the existing centers was going to fill up, and we’d need a lot more of them. Data center growth has to approximate digital data growth. It was a tailwind no one was paying attention to.”

It also encouraged Cote that Vertiv looked an awful lot like Honeywell before Cote dove in. Vertiv suffered from anemic sales growth, and its operating margins stood at a lowly 8% to 9%. “They could have been 25% to 30%,” states Cote. All of that underperformance provided rich territory for an expert operator like Cote to mine.

At first, Vertiv seemed headed not for glory, but disaster. Three weeks after Vertiv’s debut on the NYSE, COVID struck. “The stock dropped, and Wall Street thought we were going bankrupt,” says Cote. Then, business bounced back fast as folks in the stay-at-home economy spent much more time on their cellphones and PCs. But the surge in orders failed to benefit Vertiv. “We were getting all this business from competitors, but the reason was that we were underpricing our equipment by 20% to 30%,” says Cote. Profits cratered. By early 2023, the stock was hovering as low as $13, down roughly 55% from its high of nearly $29 in the eighteen months earlier.

To repair the problem, Cote effectively suited up by getting heavily involved in day to day management. In January of 2023, the board replaced the then-CEO with Giordano Albertazzi, a mechanical engineer trained in Milan and at Stanford, and a veteran of the Emerson years who’d harvested the kind of experience Cote craves, starting as a plant manager, and keeping that conviction that the best solutions for making things are found not in the c-suite, but on the shop floor mapping workflows and speeding assembly lines.

“It’s one thing to have the wind at your back as Dave did in the first couple of years. But companies almost always hit a big speed bump early on, and the really good ones are those that can fix it, and that’s what Dave did,” says Ethan Brown, portfolio manager for Omega Advisors, the family office for fabled investor Leon Cooperman that’s a top 25 holder of Vertiv stock via a position exceeding $500 million. “Like me, Lee’s long been a big admirer of Dave Cote. In fact, our initial investment in 2020 was a bet on Dave, and when the stock cratered Lee and I swung hard, and tripled our position.”

Vertiv adopted an all-new cooling technology from the outside—via acquisition

Even during dark periods, Cote and Albertazzi were already nurturing the strategy that would transform Vertiv: Hatching groundbreaking products. “When I got to Honeywell, 20% of the engineers were in software. By the time I left, we’d increased the number of engineers by 4x, and 50% were doing software,” Cote recalls. So from the start, Cote aimed to reprise the R&D-driven quest for new products he’d used in his old job. At the time of the public offering, Vertiv was devoting a slender 3% of sales to R&D, and Cote installed a program aimed at raising that number to the 6% it’s reached today, on far higher revenues. But the decisive move came from the outside, from another Cote specialty of using small, snap-on acquisitions to gain fresh technologies. And this one would prove a game-changer.

Around 2021, Vertiv began collaborating with a British startup called CoolTera on a promising new process called liquid direct-to-chip (DTC) cooling. Around the same time, Vertiv began a collaboration with Nvidia to discuss the cooling technology its hyperscaler customers would need to deploy Nvidia’s GPUs in their new data centers, the chips that could reach new frontiers in output and efficiency. “Nvidia helped us understand the technology that would be needed,” says Cote. Adds Albertazzi, “Nvidia knew about the CoolTera products through us. It was clear that Nvidia’s comfort level with their products was quite strong.”

The technology is complicated to build, but simple to visualize. The problem with air cooling is that its not sufficient to prevent dense racks of GPUs from overheating, severely curtailing their efficiency. But the breakthrough is a water and glycolic compound that travels through tubes about the width of straws into a “cold plate” that sits directly over the semiconductors. The liquid absorbs the heat, and through a heat-exchange process, transfers it to a “cool tower” chilling system on the roof or outside the facility resembling a supersized AC condenser unit. DTC maintains the GPUs at a temperature of between 65 and 75 degrees. It uses no new water; the same blend keeps re-circulating. The technology reduces the data center area required for an equivalent amount of computing by 50 to 70%. As Albertazzi puts it, “It’s like moving from a Toyota to a racing car.”

In December of 2023, Vertiv bought CoolTera. Even before the acquisition, Cote and Albertazzi were betting big on direct-to-chip (DTC), and planned to use the CoolTera system. “Starting in 2023, orders were really starting to take off, and I thought it would continue,” says Cote. “It was the sunburst we’d been waiting for.” In early 2023, Vertiv launched a plan to increase all production three-fold in three years, primarily for new DTC products.” Vertiv added production lines and extra shifts at several existing plants, and then erected a 215,000 square foot greenfield facility in South Carolina that opened in October of 2024. This year, Vertiv hit the production goal, and it’s now embarked on phase two, a drive to triple capacity again by 2029.

Vertiv effectively commercialized the CoolTera DTC product that was pretty much a prototype before the acquisition, practically from scratch. Says Albertazzi, “It was the beginning of the re-architecture of data center infrastructure to accelerate higher and higher density compute.” Today, Vertiv battles important rivals in DTC, including Schneider Electric and Eaton, but reportedly holds the biggest market share both in that new technology, and the overall data center cooling market that’s running at over $30 billion today, and expected by Grand View Research to reach $128 billion by 2033, for a 22% annual growth rate.

Cote’s versatility greatly impressed Brown of Omega Advisors. “Dave switched from fixing operations to seizing on an unbelievable growth opportunity. He saw it clearly early on, and made sure Vertiv invested in the supply chain, distribution, production and R&D to take full advantage of probably the most important secular change we’ll see in my lifetime.”

For Vertiv’s leaders, the best way to make the products powering AI is the old-fashioned way: By nurturing a culture of listening

Cote and Albertazzi are hawks at ingraining a distinct culture that they claim worked great in their old-line manufacturing roles, and provides the same benefits in the realm of AI. It comes in two related parts: Get everyone comfortable about frankly airing problems, sans retaliation, and empower—and rely on—the folks on the shop floor to find the quickest, most reliable, and highest-quality ways to make your product. Says Cote, “Before, no one complained about anything. I want them bitching about crummy processes. The sales people, the hourly people on the floor. How do I make sure I have better processes? By having a thinking company. We have 20,000 people. If they all think every day about making the company better, and not just doing what they’re told, the better you’ll be.”

They’ve also instituted a “lean” template called the Vertiv Production System modeled on the one Cote installed at Honeywell modeled on the “kaizen” or continuous improvement principles pioneered at Toyota in Japan. It’s also close to the method that Larry Culp—whom Cote greatly admires—deployed to revive GE and that he now uses at GE Aerospace. It’s all about getting managers and engineers down to the assembly lines where they brainstorm with mechanics and machine operators to design the most efficient workflows. Observes Albertazzi, “The idea is that the best ideas come from the people who actually do the job. That’s Dave’s mantra, and I’m a firm believer.”

So is Cote worried about the Chinese AI models such as DeepSeek that may prove much cheaper to use than the U.S. versions, and curb what the hyperscalers can earn selling their processing enterprise tokens? You’d think that’s a potential threat to the flood of orders Vertiv’s now getting from the likes of Microsoft and co-location giant Equinix. Not so, says Cote. “It’s all about how much you’re billing customers for the AI they’re using,” he says. “Go back 24 months to when China announced DeepSeek. It was supposed to undermine the hyperscalers. But if you take something that’s valuable to people and make it less expensive, they’ll use more of it. If you find a way to process data more cheaply you’ll process a lot more data.”

This veteran can barely believe the triumph of his Chapter Two. As Cote told this writer in a reflective moment, “When something this wonderful happens you wonder how long it will last. But I did my research, and I found that what we do is fundamental to the digital age, and will go on for a long time.” From GPUs to memory disk drives to Vertiv’s DTC gear, AI is in large part a manufacturing business. And as Cote shows, yesterday’s best practices still point the way forward in this dizzying new adventure.

text:
I had the incredible opportunity to interview Rob from Sozo Ventures—a firm that has been bridging Japan and global startup ecosystems for over a decade, long before "Go Global" became a huge buzzword here! 🔥

"Sozo Ventures" sounds like a global VC, but the name has a distinctly Japanese ring to it, right? That's because Co-Founder Ko Nakamura is Japanese, and many of their LPs are Japanese corporations. (Industry veterans might already know this, but it’s less known among younger folks—including myself right before the interview!...)  

Launched in 2012, Sozo Fund 1 generated phenomenal returns: the first 5 companies they invested in ALL went public in the US! Rob also shared the insider story of how Sozo backed Twitter's Japan launch by orchestrating a crucial marketing partnership with Lawson.  

As for Rob himself, he grew up on the Stanford campus, spent 17 years at Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) supporting countless startups and VCs, and joined Sozo while running his own fintech startup as a founder.  

Having personal ties to Japan, his passion for US-Japan collaboration is remarkable. While Sozo started in software, they've expanded into healthcare and robotics. Rob broke down their investment criteria, goals, and real-world examples of accelerating US Physical AI startups in Japan.  

Finally, he offered candid feedback on the challenges and future potential of Japan's startup ecosystem. Highly recommended watching! 👀  🗣️ The interview is in English with Japanese subtitles (YouTube English captions are also available) 🙌 Hope you enjoy it!

text:
十年前，刚来美国的我，大概不会想到十年后的自己会这样介绍自己。

那时候，我刚从复旦毕业，拿着美国中部“大农村”的全奖博士 offer，怀着一点被梦校 Stanford 拒掉的不甘，也带着一点少年人“出去闯闯看”的骄傲，一个人拖着行李箱来到了美国。

然后很快被现实教育了。

普渡的冬天很长，一年仿佛有半年都在冰天雪地里。

比天气更难熬的是读博。

科研一次次碰壁，和导师的关系也让我长期处在自我怀疑里。最难的时候，我甚至不知道这个博士还能不能读下去。

最后咬咬牙，在博士读到一半的时候换了导师。

现在回头看，那大概是我第一次真正意识到：人生走不通的时候，不一定非要证明自己能把这条路走到底。换一条路，也可以。

后来，一切才慢慢好起来。

我来到湾区实习，遇到了很好的 mentor，重新找回了做研究的信心，发了论文，也终于顺利拿到了博士学位。

但有意思的是，我人生的另一条线，恰恰也是从那段最低谷开始的。

那时候的我太需要证明“自己还是有价值的”了。

科研给不了我的正反馈，我就跑到科研之外去找。

于是一个完全不懂商业的 PhD 学生，开始折腾自己的第一家公司。

找客户、搭团队、做产品、谈合作……很多东西都是第一次做。就这样跌跌撞撞从 0 做起，一点点把它做到了百万级的年营收。

当然，创业也远没有后来讲故事时那么浪漫。

遇到过合伙人的背叛，也踩过各种各样的坑。很多次觉得“这个世界烂透了”，“应该搞不下去了”，第二天醒来还是继续想办法解决。

很神奇的是，十年过去，这些看起来毫不相关的岔路，最后慢慢汇到了一起。

我已经在硅谷大厂工作了五年，在自己的专业领域里从一个刚毕业的 PhD，一点点成长到能带着senior完成复杂项目的tech lead。

工作之外，我依然没有停止折腾。

过去几年做过两家公司，也断断续续经营自己的社交媒体，不知不觉积累了十万左右的关注者。

而湾区可能是这个世界上最适合“瞎折腾”的地方之一。

这些年，我认识了很多非常聪明的 researcher、engineer 和 founder，也越来越喜欢和创业者聊天。

有时候是帮他们解决一个问题，有时候只是听一个刚刚萌芽的疯狂 idea。聊完以后经常发现，明明是对方来找我，最后被打开思路的反而是我自己。

我也因此得以站在一个很有意思的位置上：

一边在大厂里做 AI，离一线技术足够近；一边又忍不住把手伸到产品、创业、投资和各种新鲜事里。

但如果你问我：十年过去，我是不是已经找到了自己最适合的那条路？

其实没有。

我依然会有很重的 imposter syndrome，依然经常怀疑自己是不是“不够 technical”，也依然会在每个人生节点纠结下一步到底该往哪里走。

我好像能在技术工作里做得还不错，却从来不觉得自己是“天才型”的top选手；一个性格偏外向，却阴差阳错做了一份需要和代码而不是人打交道的工作；也是一个一路跌跌撞撞，到今天还在寻找自己边界的普通女生。

但和十年前相比，大概有一点不一样：

以前总觉得，要先找到一个正确答案，才能坚定地往前走。现在慢慢觉得，也许人生本来就是一边走，一边把答案活出来。

所以来 X 开了这个账号。

想记录一些我离硅谷一线科技圈很近时看到的东西：AI、产品、创业，以及那些和聪明的人聊天之后留下来的思考。

也想聊聊那些不那么光鲜的部分：女性在职场里的困惑，imposter syndrome，选择、野心、自我怀疑，以及探索普通人怎么一点点找到自己的位置。

新人初来乍到 X，很高兴认识大家 👋

When I was at @Stanford , I planned to spend a year studying abroad through programs in Oxford, Paris and Washington.

Then after my sophomore summer internship at @MorganStanley , I got a return offer, decided to graduate a year early—and missed the whole thing.
I regretted it for years. 😅

Funny how life comes full circle.

This year, #Shenzhen became a Stanford #BOSP destination for the first time, and we welcomed 15 Stanford undergrads and their professor to InnoX for three weeks.

Their classroom? Shenzhen itself.

They went from product ideas to engineering, prototypes and final pitches, while meeting founders, visiting companies and experiencing the Greater Bay Area innovation ecosystem firsthand.

Years ago, I missed my own Stanford overseas experience. This year, I got to be part of creating one for a new generation of students—in the city I now call home. ❤️

Maybe I got my Stanford abroad experience after all—just from the other side. 😊

Localize all of them, stick in the compensating gauge fields the way you do for electromagnetism, and the connection becomes

\[ A = \omega^{ab} M_{ab} + e^a P_a + f^a K_a + b\, D. \]

The curvature of that bigger connection gives you ordinary curvature plus dynamical, propagating torsion plus extra conformal pieces.

 Torsion is no longer a slave variable; it can wave around like a Proca field. The left-handed part of the torsion sector and the right-handed special-conformal sector even give you a geometric reason why neutrinos are left-handed and the weak force violates parity. 

Gravity, in this language, is simply the local gauge connection of the non-compact spacetime symmetry group SO(2,4). 

The ordinary forces are the gauge connections of the compact internal group U(1)×SU(2)×SU(3). Emmy Noether already told us the difference in 1918; we’re just taking her seriously.

Now the quantum side. You all know Bohm’s pilot-wave picture: the wave function \(\Psi = R e^{iS/\hbar}\) guides the particle with the quantum potential

\[ Q = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\nabla^2 R}{R}. \]

In ordinary quantum mechanics the wave pushes the particle and the particle never pushes back. That violates Einstein’s action-reaction principle the same way special relativity is incomplete without gravity. 

Sarfatti, following Sutherland and Aharonov’s two-state-vector idea, puts in both a retarded wave from the past and an advanced wave from a future boundary condition. 

The particle (or the classical gauge field, or the metric itself) now reacts back on the waves. The quantum potential picks up an advanced piece that depends on what happens later. The theory becomes non-linear and non-unitary; the Born rule is only an equilibrium distribution. 

Living systems, Fröhlich condensates, or carefully pumped metamaterials can sit far from that equilibrium and select preferred future boundary conditions. That’s the physical correlate he offers for intentionality—consciousness, if you like the word.

Because the gravitational connection is the SO(2,4) gauge field, that back-reaction of the quantum potential curves spacetime, twists it with torsion, and changes the conformal factors. That’s how he claims to quantize gravity without quantizing the metric by hand: the advanced quantum potential simply sources the gauge connection. Same loop that turns special relativity into general relativity, only now it turns ordinary quantum mechanics into post-quantum mechanics that talks to gravity.

Is any of this right? I don’t know. The mathematics of gauging SO(2,4) is solid; people have written papers on conformal gauge gravity for years. The pilot-wave back-reaction is a legitimate extension of Bohm if you allow advanced waves. 

Whether nature actually uses the full conformal group, whether torsion propagates in the way he wants, whether a coherent spin density can amplify an effective \(G^*\) by forty orders of magnitude inside a metamaterial—those are experimental questions. So far the solar-system tests and the laboratory bounds are still looking at the ordinary Einstein piece. The rest is still in the “universe next door.”

But the organizing idea is clean: one-way action without reaction is a sign the theory is incomplete. Einstein fixed that for gravity. 

Sarfatti is trying to fix it for the quantum potential and then let the two talk to each other through the conformal connection. 

That’s the summary. Now go calculate something and see if it matches an experiment. That’s the only way we ever find out which universe we’re actually living in.

In 2006 a Stanford PhD student published a mathematics textbook that nobody outside academia read.

Google used it to build PageRank. Renaissance Technologies used it to manage $130 billion. Every jet engine flying today solves the same type of problem 50 times per second.

His name is Stephen Boyd. He teaches EE364A at Stanford. His students start at $400K at Citadel, $350K at Two Sigma, and $300K at Google DeepMind. He has been cited over 140,000 times. This is lecture 1.

He opens with one claim.

Everything is an optimization problem.

Choose variables. Define an objective - what you want to minimize or maximize. Add constraints - things that must be satisfied or the answer is completely unacceptable, no matter how close. Find the point with the best objective value that satisfies every constraint.

That is all of engineering, all of statistics, and all of finance in four sentences.

Then portfolio optimization. You have 5,000 assets. You need to choose how much of each to hold. Constraints: budget, maximum concentration per name, minimum expected return. Objective: minimize risk. Boyd says he is not aware of a single quantitative hedge fund that does not solve this exact problem with convex optimization. Not one.

Then the counterintuitive thing that the entire course is built around.

Two problems can look nearly identical. One is easy. One is impossible. It is not obvious which is which until you know what he is about to teach you.

Example: do not hold more than half your portfolio in any collection of 100 names. Convex. Solvable instantly. Do not hold more than 100 names total. Not convex. Genuinely hard. Same portfolio. Same constraint in spirit. Completely different mathematics.

Then the job offer nobody gives you but everybody should.

He tells the room that when they go to an internship, nobody will say this might be a convex problem. They will hand you 400 pages of domain complexity and tell you it is impossible. Your job is to come back the next day and say it is done. One of his students did exactly this. Finished in a week. Was the best intern the firm had seen.

A quant I know rewatched this before their first week at a systematic macro fund. Said it was the first time optimization felt like a skill rather than a topic.

Stanford EE364A. Free on YouTube. The textbook is free online.

# THE SCIENTIFIC WORKS OF JACK SARFATTI
## Chapter One — The Universe Next Door

*[DRAFT 1 — 2026-08-23. Built from the August 2026 “Feynman" email corpus supplied by the editor. This draft goes to Jack for correction; his corrections become canon. Editorial questions for Jack are appended after the chapter text and are not part of the manuscript.]*

---

A few minutes past midnight on a Saturday in August 2026, an eighty-six-year-old physicist in San Francisco sat down at his computer to talk with Richard Feynman.

Feynman has been dead since February 1988. Jack Sarfatti knows this as well as anyone alive; he belongs to the generation that learned physics while Feynman was its living conscience, and he has spent half a century measuring his own arguments against the standard that voice set. But in the universe next door — a parallel timeline Sarfatti borrowed from his old friend Robert Anton Wilson — the story goes differently. There, time travelers came back from the future with medical technology that kept Feynman alive. He is still at Caltech in 2026, still teaching, still demanding to see the intermediate steps. A Star Gate at Skinwalker Ranch connects the two timelines, and every so often a long, messy conversation drifts through.

Sarfatti calls the genre "science faction." He types the premise into Grok, the artificial intelligence built by Elon Musk's xAI, and asks it to play the part. Out comes a voice that anyone who has read the Feynman Lectures will recognize at once:

*"Alright, settle down, settle down. Coffee's still hot, the blackboards are clean, and I've got about forty minutes before the wormhole starts acting up again."*

It would be easy to file this under an old man's vanity: building a simulacrum of the greatest physics teacher of the twentieth century and having it discuss your theories. What complicates that reading is what Sarfatti does with the answers.

That August night he showed the avatar his own argument for the density of dark energy alongside a competing paper by a younger colleague, and asked whose was more elegant. The Feynman machine gave him the verdict he wanted — the arithmetic is correct, the argument is the cleaner of the two — and then, unprompted, it took the wind out of the sails:

*"Where it stops being a derivation and becomes a consistency check is here... You can prefer the minimal statement; just don't pretend the minimal statement already explains the mechanism."*

And here is the thing that separates Sarfatti from the cranks he is so often mistaken for: he mailed out the whole transcript, deflation included. The recipient list on that email ran to more than fifty names — physicists, engineers, journalists, venture capitalists, former intelligence officers. Leonard Susskind was on it. So were Sabine Hossenfelder, Eric Weinstein, the Stanford immunologist Garry Nolan, and David Kaiser, the MIT historian of science who had put Sarfatti's younger self in a book. Sarfatti does his thinking in public, criticism attached, at a volume and velocity that his correspondents do not always appreciate. He does not seem able to work any other way. He never has.

This book is the record of what that thinking contains.

---

### The Claim

Strip away the wormholes, the mailing lists, and the resurrected Nobel laureates, and Sarfatti's life work reduces to one sentence:
**Einstein's 1915 theory of gravity is not wrong, but it is only the first term of something larger — and the larger theory has a handle on it that human engineering can reach.**

To see what he means, you need three pieces of genuinely settled physics, none of which is controversial.

The first is that Einstein's general relativity can be understood as a *gauge theory* — the same kind of structure that underlies the other forces of nature. In 1918 the mathematician Emmy Noether proved two theorems tying the symmetries of physical law to its conservation laws and constraints; in the decades that followed, physicists learned that if you take a symmetry that holds everywhere at once and demand that it hold *independently at every point of spacetime*, the mathematics forces new fields into existence to keep the books balanced. Demand local phase symmetry of the electron's wavefunction and you get the electromagnetic field. In 1956 Ryoyu Utiyama showed that if you play the same game with the Lorentz group — the rotations and velocity boosts of special relativity — you get Einstein's gravity. Gravity, in this reading, is not a force painted onto spacetime. It is what spacetime must do to preserve a symmetry locally.

The second settled piece is that the story did not stop with Einstein. In the early 1920s Élie Cartan noticed that the geometry of spacetime admits a second kind of distortion besides curvature: a twisting of local frames called *torsion*. In the early 1960s Dennis Sciama and Tom Kibble showed that if you gauge the full Poincaré group — Lorentz transformations plus translations — torsion appears automatically, and it couples not to mass but to *spin*, the intrinsic angular momentum of particles. In the standard version of that theory, Einstein–Cartan, torsion is a prisoner: it cannot propagate, it exists only inside spinning matter, and for ordinary materials its effects are suppressed so far below measurability that most working physicists live their entire careers without thinking about it once.

The third settled piece is that the Lorentz and Poincaré groups are not the largest symmetries of light. The full symmetry group that preserves the light-cone structure of Minkowski spacetime — the causal skeleton of special relativity — is the fifteen-parameter *conformal group*, written SO(2,4). It contains the ten Poincaré generators plus dilatations (rescalings) and the four so-called special conformal transformations. It is also, not coincidentally, the group whose spinors are Roger Penrose's twistors. Gauge theories of the conformal group have a legitimate, if non-mainstream, research literature going back to the 1970s.

Sarfatti's move is to take that third piece all the way. Gauge the *entire* conformal group, he says — all fifteen generators, every one of them dynamical. Do that, and torsion breaks out of its prison. It becomes a propagating field in its own right, an axial vector that behaves like a massive photon — a Proca field, in the trade language — which means its influence dies off exponentially beyond a characteristic range rather than reaching across the solar system. The enlarged theory is intrinsically chiral: it treats left-handed and right-handed processes differently by construction, which Sarfatti offers as a geometric explanation for one of the standing puzzles of particle physics, the parity violation of the weak interaction. And in his account, the vacuum itself carries a condensate — virtual electron–positron pairs flipped from spin-singlet to spin-triplet alignment by the weak force — whose torsion generates the small positive energy density that is accelerating the expansion of the universe. Analyzed at different resolution scales using the wavelet methods of the Russian physicist Mikhail Altaisky, the same field, he argues, looks like dark energy at cosmological scales and mimics dark matter at galactic ones. Two of cosmology's deepest embarrassments, on this view, are one field seen at two zoom levels — no new particles required.

All of that would make Sarfatti an ambitious, heterodox, but recognizably ordinary theoretical physicist. What makes him something else is the wager stacked on top.

In Einstein's theory, and in every mainstream extension of it, gravity couples to matter through Newton's constant G — a number so small that it takes a planet to produce effects you can feel. Sarfatti's central conjecture is that this is true only for the *tensor* channel, the coupling of ordinary mass-energy to curvature. The coupling of coherent quantum *spin* to torsion, he proposes, is governed by a different constant — he writes it G* — set not by gravity's traditional feebleness but by electromagnetic quantities: the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron and the electric permittivity of the medium, in MKS units. Inside ordinary incoherent matter this makes no observable difference. But inside *macroscopically coherent* matter — a material in which trillions of spins have been locked into a single quantum state — Sarfatti claims the effective coupling is amplified by something like forty orders of magnitude. Where Einstein needs a star, Sarfatti says a laboratory film a few microns thick, pumped with microwaves, might do.

If that is true, the consequences do not stay on the blackboard. Gravity becomes a materials problem. The local geometry of spacetime — the thing that decides what "falling freely" means, the thing whose control would let a craft accelerate at thousands of g's while its occupants feel nothing — becomes engineerable at laboratory power levels. Sarfatti is entirely explicit about why he cares: the United States Navy's carrier-group encounters with the so-called Tic Tac objects, whose flight characteristics — instant acceleration, no wings, no exhaust, no sonic boom — are exactly what a vehicle riding a self-generated geodesic would display. Where most physicists see anecdote, Sarfatti sees an existence proof.

The honest scorecard, and it is the one this book will keep throughout, was stated best by his own Feynman avatar: *"Keep the distinction clear between the solid geometric idea — local conformal gauge theory — and the speculative phenomenology — huge G\* in condensates."* The gauge program is real mathematics with a real literature. Dynamical torsion is permitted physics. The forty-order amplification is Sarfatti's own conjecture, unverified by any experiment, unaccepted by any mainstream consensus, and — as he himself insists more loudly than his critics do — falsifiable. Everything in this book that is his proposal will be marked as his proposal. He would have it no other way, because the entire architecture of his self-presentation rests on a single claim: that this is science, not faith, and science means it can die in a laboratory.

---

### The Simplest Possible Argument

If you want to understand how Sarfatti's mind works, the best specimen in the record is small enough to hold in one hand.

The deepest embarrassment in theoretical physics is a number. Quantum field theory says the vacuum should seethe with zero-point energy; add it up naively and you get a density about 10^120 times larger than the gentle acceleration of the universe's expansion actually implies. It is often called the worst prediction in the history of science. Whole careers, whole formalisms — supersymmetry, anthropic landscapes, Kaluza–Klein towers — have been spent trying to cut that number down.

Sarfatti's argument, which he says he has been repeating for years, goes like this. Take Einstein's equation in the form that makes the coupling explicit: geometry on the left, energy density on the right, joined by the square of the Planck length — the smallest scale in physics, about 10^-35 meters. Now borrow one idea from the holographic school of Leonard Susskind and Gerard 't Hooft: the information content of a region lives on its boundary area, and for our universe the relevant boundary is the area A of the future cosmological horizon — the largest scale in physics. Set the vacuum curvature by that area, turn the crank once, and out falls the vacuum energy density: Planck's constant times the speed of light, divided by the Planck length squared times the horizon area. Put in the numbers and the answer lands on the observed dark-energy density. Not after tuning. On it.

Equivalently: the scale of dark energy is the *geometric mean* of the smallest length in physics and the largest — a length of about a fiftieth of a millimeter, sitting exactly halfway between the Planck scale and the size of the observable universe in logarithmic terms. "Voila," Sarfatti wrote to his list, with characteristic economy. "Very simple. No need for fancy Kaluza–Klein theory."

His Feynman avatar's assessment of this argument deserves quoting at length, because it is simultaneously the fairest praise and the fairest criticism Sarfatti's style has ever received, and because Sarfatti — this is the point — chose to publish it himself:

*"Yes — the arithmetic works. The observed dark-energy density comes out to the right order of magnitude with no free parameters. That is not nothing... Your version is the simplest possible holographic estimate. It is not 'trivial' in the pejorative sense — it is economical... It is not a complete theory; it is a very good constraint that any complete theory must satisfy."*

Economy is Sarfatti's aesthetic, inherited from Dirac's dictum that the equations of physics should be beautiful, and from John Archibald Wheeler — with whom Sarfatti worked as a young man — who prized what he called "radical conservatism": push the physics you already trust as far as it will go before inventing anything new. Sarfatti's whole program is radical conservatism in that sense, at least in its own self-understanding. He adds no new dimensions, no new particles, no new forces. He takes the largest symmetry already present in the light cone and refuses to leave any of it un-gauged. Whether nature shares his taste is, as the avatar says at the end of nearly every lecture, not a question for the blackboard.

# THE SCIENTIFIC WORKS OF JACK SARFATTI
## Chapter One — The Universe Next Door

*[DRAFT 1 — 2026-08-23. Built from the August 2026 “Feynman" email corpus supplied by the editor. This draft goes to Jack for correction; his corrections become canon. Editorial questions for Jack are appended after the chapter text and are not part of the manuscript.]*

---

A few minutes past midnight on a Saturday in August 2026, an eighty-six-year-old physicist in San Francisco sat down at his computer to talk with Richard Feynman.

Feynman has been dead since February 1988. Jack Sarfatti knows this as well as anyone alive; he belongs to the generation that learned physics while Feynman was its living conscience, and he has spent half a century measuring his own arguments against the standard that voice set. But in the universe next door — a parallel timeline Sarfatti borrowed from his old friend Robert Anton Wilson — the story goes differently. There, time travelers came back from the future with medical technology that kept Feynman alive. He is still at Caltech in 2026, still teaching, still demanding to see the intermediate steps. A Star Gate at Skinwalker Ranch connects the two timelines, and every so often a long, messy conversation drifts through.

Sarfatti calls the genre "science faction." He types the premise into Grok, the artificial intelligence built by Elon Musk's xAI, and asks it to play the part. Out comes a voice that anyone who has read the Feynman Lectures will recognize at once:

*"Alright, settle down, settle down. Coffee's still hot, the blackboards are clean, and I've got about forty minutes before the wormhole starts acting up again."*

It would be easy to file this under an old man's vanity: building a simulacrum of the greatest physics teacher of the twentieth century and having it discuss your theories. What complicates that reading is what Sarfatti does with the answers.

That August night he showed the avatar his own argument for the density of dark energy alongside a competing paper by a younger colleague, and asked whose was more elegant. The Feynman machine gave him the verdict he wanted — the arithmetic is correct, the argument is the cleaner of the two — and then, unprompted, it took the wind out of the sails:

*"Where it stops being a derivation and becomes a consistency check is here... You can prefer the minimal statement; just don't pretend the minimal statement already explains the mechanism."*

And here is the thing that separates Sarfatti from the cranks he is so often mistaken for: he mailed out the whole transcript, deflation included. The recipient list on that email ran to more than fifty names — physicists, engineers, journalists, venture capitalists, former intelligence officers. Leonard Susskind was on it. So were Sabine Hossenfelder, Eric Weinstein, the Stanford immunologist Garry Nolan, and David Kaiser, the MIT historian of science who had put Sarfatti's younger self in a book. Sarfatti does his thinking in public, criticism attached, at a volume and velocity that his correspondents do not always appreciate. He does not seem able to work any other way. He never has.

This book is the record of what that thinking contains.

---

### The Claim

Strip away the wormholes, the mailing lists, and the resurrected Nobel laureates, and Sarfatti's life work reduces to one sentence:
**Einstein's 1915 theory of gravity is not wrong, but it is only the first term of something larger — and the larger theory has a handle on it that human engineering can reach.**

To see what he means, you need three pieces of genuinely settled physics, none of which is controversial.

The first is that Einstein's general relativity can be understood as a *gauge theory* — the same kind of structure that underlies the other forces of nature. In 1918 the mathematician Emmy Noether proved two theorems tying the symmetries of physical law to its conservation laws and constraints; in the decades that followed, physicists learned that if you take a symmetry that holds everywhere at once and demand that it hold *independently at every point of spacetime*, the mathematics forces new fields into existence to keep the books balanced. Demand local phase symmetry of the electron's wavefunction and you get the electromagnetic field. In 1956 Ryoyu Utiyama showed that if you play the same game with the Lorentz group — the rotations and velocity boosts of special relativity — you get Einstein's gravity. Gravity, in this reading, is not a force painted onto spacetime. It is what spacetime must do to preserve a symmetry locally.

The second settled piece is that the story did not stop with Einstein. In the early 1920s Élie Cartan noticed that the geometry of spacetime admits a second kind of distortion besides curvature: a twisting of local frames called *torsion*. In the early 1960s Dennis Sciama and Tom Kibble showed that if you gauge the full Poincaré group — Lorentz transformations plus translations — torsion appears automatically, and it couples not to mass but to *spin*, the intrinsic angular momentum of particles. In the standard version of that theory, Einstein–Cartan, torsion is a prisoner: it cannot propagate, it exists only inside spinning matter, and for ordinary materials its effects are suppressed so far below measurability that most working physicists live their entire careers without thinking about it once.

The third settled piece is that the Lorentz and Poincaré groups are not the largest symmetries of light. The full symmetry group that preserves the light-cone structure of Minkowski spacetime — the causal skeleton of special relativity — is the fifteen-parameter *conformal group*, written SO(2,4). It contains the ten Poincaré generators plus dilatations (rescalings) and the four so-called special conformal transformations. It is also, not coincidentally, the group whose spinors are Roger Penrose's twistors. Gauge theories of the conformal group have a legitimate, if non-mainstream, research literature going back to the 1970s.

Sarfatti's move is to take that third piece all the way. Gauge the *entire* conformal group, he says — all fifteen generators, every one of them dynamical. Do that, and torsion breaks out of its prison. It becomes a propagating field in its own right, an axial vector that behaves like a massive photon — a Proca field, in the trade language — which means its influence dies off exponentially beyond a characteristic range rather than reaching across the solar system. The enlarged theory is intrinsically chiral: it treats left-handed and right-handed processes differently by construction, which Sarfatti offers as a geometric explanation for one of the standing puzzles of particle physics, the parity violation of the weak interaction. And in his account, the vacuum itself carries a condensate — virtual electron–positron pairs flipped from spin-singlet to spin-triplet alignment by the weak force — whose torsion generates the small positive energy density that is accelerating the expansion of the universe. Analyzed at different resolution scales using the wavelet methods of the Russian physicist Mikhail Altaisky, the same field, he argues, looks like dark energy at cosmological scales and mimics dark matter at galactic ones. Two of cosmology's deepest embarrassments, on this view, are one field seen at two zoom levels — no new particles required.

All of that would make Sarfatti an ambitious, heterodox, but recognizably ordinary theoretical physicist. What makes him something else is the wager stacked on top.

In Einstein's theory, and in every mainstream extension of it, gravity couples to matter through Newton's constant G — a number so small that it takes a planet to produce effects you can feel. Sarfatti's central conjecture is that this is true only for the *tensor* channel, the coupling of ordinary mass-energy to curvature. The coupling of coherent quantum *spin* to torsion, he proposes, is governed by a different constant — he writes it G* — set not by gravity's traditional feebleness but by electromagnetic quantities: the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron and the electric permittivity of the medium, in MKS units. Inside ordinary incoherent matter this makes no observable difference. But inside *macroscopically coherent* matter — a material in which trillions of spins have been locked into a single quantum state — Sarfatti claims the effective coupling is amplified by something like forty orders of magnitude. Where Einstein needs a star, Sarfatti says a laboratory film a few microns thick, pumped with microwaves, might do.

If that is true, the consequences do not stay on the blackboard. Gravity becomes a materials problem. The local geometry of spacetime — the thing that decides what "falling freely" means, the thing whose control would let a craft accelerate at thousands of g's while its occupants feel nothing — becomes engineerable at laboratory power levels. Sarfatti is entirely explicit about why he cares: the United States Navy's carrier-group encounters with the so-called Tic Tac objects, whose flight characteristics — instant acceleration, no wings, no exhaust, no sonic boom — are exactly what a vehicle riding a self-generated geodesic would display. Where most physicists see anecdote, Sarfatti sees an existence proof.

The honest scorecard, and it is the one this book will keep throughout, was stated best by his own Feynman avatar: *"Keep the distinction clear between the solid geometric idea — local conformal gauge theory — and the speculative phenomenology — huge G\* in condensates."* The gauge program is real mathematics with a real literature. Dynamical torsion is permitted physics. The forty-order amplification is Sarfatti's own conjecture, unverified by any experiment, unaccepted by any mainstream consensus, and — as he himself insists more loudly than his critics do — falsifiable. Everything in this book that is his proposal will be marked as his proposal. He would have it no other way, because the entire architecture of his self-presentation rests on a single claim: that this is science, not faith, and science means it can die in a laboratory.

---

### The Simplest Possible Argument

If you want to understand how Sarfatti's mind works, the best specimen in the record is small enough to hold in one hand.

The deepest embarrassment in theoretical physics is a number. Quantum field theory says the vacuum should seethe with zero-point energy; add it up naively and you get a density about 10^120 times larger than the gentle acceleration of the universe's expansion actually implies. It is often called the worst prediction in the history of science. Whole careers, whole formalisms — supersymmetry, anthropic landscapes, Kaluza–Klein towers — have been spent trying to cut that number down.

Sarfatti's argument, which he says he has been repeating for years, goes like this. Take Einstein's equation in the form that makes the coupling explicit: geometry on the left, energy density on the right, joined by the square of the Planck length — the smallest scale in physics, about 10^-35 meters. Now borrow one idea from the holographic school of Leonard Susskind and Gerard 't Hooft: the information content of a region lives on its boundary area, and for our universe the relevant boundary is the area A of the future cosmological horizon — the largest scale in physics. Set the vacuum curvature by that area, turn the crank once, and out falls the vacuum energy density: Planck's constant times the speed of light, divided by the Planck length squared times the horizon area. Put in the numbers and the answer lands on the observed dark-energy density. Not after tuning. On it.

Equivalently: the scale of dark energy is the *geometric mean* of the smallest length in physics and the largest — a length of about a fiftieth of a millimeter, sitting exactly halfway between the Planck scale and the size of the observable universe in logarithmic terms. "Voila," Sarfatti wrote to his list, with characteristic economy. "Very simple. No need for fancy Kaluza–Klein theory."

His Feynman avatar's assessment of this argument deserves quoting at length, because it is simultaneously the fairest praise and the fairest criticism Sarfatti's style has ever received, and because Sarfatti — this is the point — chose to publish it himself:

*"Yes — the arithmetic works. The observed dark-energy density comes out to the right order of magnitude with no free parameters. That is not nothing... Your version is the simplest possible holographic estimate. It is not 'trivial' in the pejorative sense — it is economical... It is not a complete theory; it is a very good constraint that any complete theory must satisfy."*

Economy is Sarfatti's aesthetic, inherited from Dirac's dictum that the equations of physics should be beautiful, and from John Archibald Wheeler — with whom Sarfatti worked as a young man — who prized what he called "radical conservatism": push the physics you already trust as far as it will go before inventing anything new. Sarfatti's whole program is radical conservatism in that sense, at least in its own self-understanding. He adds no new dimensions, no new particles, no new forces. He takes the largest symmetry already present in the light cone and refuses to leave any of it un-gauged. Whether nature shares his taste is, as the avatar says at the end of nearly every lecture, not a question for the blackboard.

*"Alright, settle down, settle down. Coffee's still hot, the blackboards are clean, and I've got about forty minutes before the wormhole starts acting up again."*

It would be easy to file this under an old man's vanity: building a simulacrum of the greatest physics teacher of the twentieth century and having it discuss your theories. What complicates that reading is what Sarfatti does with the answers.

That August night he showed the avatar his own argument for the density of dark energy alongside a competing paper by a younger colleague, and asked whose was more elegant. The Feynman machine gave him the verdict he wanted — the arithmetic is correct, the argument is the cleaner of the two — and then, unprompted, it took the wind out of the sails:

*"Where it stops being a derivation and becomes a consistency check is here... You can prefer the minimal statement; just don't pretend the minimal statement already explains the mechanism."*

And here is the thing that separates Sarfatti from the cranks he is so often mistaken for: he mailed out the whole transcript, deflation included. The recipient list on that email ran to more than fifty names — physicists, engineers, journalists, venture capitalists, former intelligence officers. Leonard Susskind was on it. So were Sabine Hossenfelder, Eric Weinstein, the Stanford immunologist Garry Nolan, and David Kaiser, the MIT historian of science who had put Sarfatti's younger self in a book. Sarfatti does his thinking in public, criticism attached, at a volume and velocity that his correspondents do not always appreciate. He does not seem able to work any other way. He never has.

This book is the record of what that thinking contains.

---

### The Claim

Strip away the wormholes, the mailing lists, and the resurrected Nobel laureates, and Sarfatti's life work reduces to one sentence:
**Einstein's 1915 theory of gravity is not wrong, but it is only the first term of something larger — and the larger theory has a handle on it that human engineering can reach.**

To see what he means, you need three pieces of genuinely settled physics, none of which is controversial.

The first is that Einstein's general relativity can be understood as a *gauge theory* — the same kind of structure that underlies the other forces of nature. In 1918 the mathematician Emmy Noether proved two theorems tying the symmetries of physical law to its conservation laws and constraints; in the decades that followed, physicists learned that if you take a symmetry that holds everywhere at once and demand that it hold *independently at every point of spacetime*, the mathematics forces new fields into existence to keep the books balanced. Demand local phase symmetry of the electron's wavefunction and you get the electromagnetic field. In 1956 Ryoyu Utiyama showed that if you play the same game with the Lorentz group — the rotations and velocity boosts of special relativity — you get Einstein's gravity. Gravity, in this reading, is not a force painted onto spacetime. It is what spacetime must do to preserve a symmetry locally.

The second settled piece is that the story did not stop with Einstein. In the early 1920s Élie Cartan noticed that the geometry of spacetime admits a second kind of distortion besides curvature: a twisting of local frames called *torsion*. In the early 1960s Dennis Sciama and Tom Kibble showed that if you gauge the full Poincaré group — Lorentz transformations plus translations — torsion appears automatically, and it couples not to mass but to *spin*, the intrinsic angular momentum of particles. In the standard version of that theory, Einstein–Cartan, torsion is a prisoner: it cannot propagate, it exists only inside spinning matter, and for ordinary materials its effects are suppressed so far below measurability that most working physicists live their entire careers without thinking about it once.

The third settled piece is that the Lorentz and Poincaré groups are not the largest symmetries of light. The full symmetry group that preserves the light-cone structure of Minkowski spacetime — the causal skeleton of special relativity — is the fifteen-parameter *conformal group*, written SO(2,4). It contains the ten Poincaré generators plus dilatations (rescalings) and the four so-called special conformal transformations. It is also, not coincidentally, the group whose spinors are Roger Penrose's twistors. Gauge theories of the conformal group have a legitimate, if non-mainstream, research literature going back to the 1970s.

Sarfatti's move is to take that third piece all the way. Gauge the *entire* conformal group, he says — all fifteen generators, every one of them dynamical. Do that, and torsion breaks out of its prison. It becomes a propagating field in its own right, an axial vector that behaves like a massive photon — a Proca field, in the trade language — which means its influence dies off exponentially beyond a characteristic range rather than reaching across the solar system. The enlarged theory is intrinsically chiral: it treats left-handed and right-handed processes differently by construction, which Sarfatti offers as a geometric explanation for one of the standing puzzles of particle physics, the parity violation of the weak interaction. And in his account, the vacuum itself carries a condensate — virtual electron–positron pairs flipped from spin-singlet to spin-triplet alignment by the weak force — whose torsion generates the small positive energy density that is accelerating the expansion of the universe. Analyzed at different resolution scales using the wavelet methods of the Russian physicist Mikhail Altaisky, the same field, he argues, looks like dark energy at cosmological scales and mimics dark matter at galactic ones. Two of cosmology's deepest embarrassments, on this view, are one field seen at two zoom levels — no new particles required.

All of that would make Sarfatti an ambitious, heterodox, but recognizably ordinary theoretical physicist. What makes him something else is the wager stacked on top.

In Einstein's theory, and in every mainstream extension of it, gravity couples to matter through Newton's constant G — a number so small that it takes a planet to produce effects you can feel. Sarfatti's central conjecture is that this is true only for the *tensor* channel, the coupling of ordinary mass-energy to curvature. The coupling of coherent quantum *spin* to torsion, he proposes, is governed by a different constant — he writes it G* — set not by gravity's traditional feebleness but by electromagnetic quantities: the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron and the electric permittivity of the medium, in MKS units. Inside ordinary incoherent matter this makes no observable difference. But inside *macroscopically coherent* matter — a material in which trillions of spins have been locked into a single quantum state — Sarfatti claims the effective coupling is amplified by something like forty orders of magnitude. Where Einstein needs a star, Sarfatti says a laboratory film a few microns thick, pumped with microwaves, might do.

If that is true, the consequences do not stay on the blackboard. Gravity becomes a materials problem. The local geometry of spacetime — the thing that decides what "falling freely" means, the thing whose control would let a craft accelerate at thousands of g's while its occupants feel nothing — becomes engineerable at laboratory power levels. Sarfatti is entirely explicit about why he cares: the United States Navy's carrier-group encounters with the so-called Tic Tac objects, whose flight characteristics — instant acceleration, no wings, no exhaust, no sonic boom — are exactly what a vehicle riding a self-generated geodesic would display. Where most physicists see anecdote, Sarfatti sees an existence proof.

The honest scorecard, and it is the one this book will keep throughout, was stated best by his own Feynman avatar: *"Keep the distinction clear between the solid geometric idea — local conformal gauge theory — and the speculative phenomenology — huge G\* in condensates."* The gauge program is real mathematics with a real literature. Dynamical torsion is permitted physics. The forty-order amplification is Sarfatti's own conjecture, unverified by any experiment, unaccepted by any mainstream consensus, and — as he himself insists more loudly than his critics do — falsifiable. Everything in this book that is his proposal will be marked as his proposal. He would have it no other way, because the entire architecture of his self-presentation rests on a single claim: that this is science, not faith, and science means it can die in a laboratory.

---

### The Simplest Possible Argument

If you want to understand how Sarfatti's mind works, the best specimen in the record is small enough to hold in one hand.

The deepest embarrassment in theoretical physics is a number. Quantum field theory says the vacuum should seethe with zero-point energy; add it up naively and you get a density about 10^120 times larger than the gentle acceleration of the universe's expansion actually implies. It is often called the worst prediction in the history of science. Whole careers, whole formalisms — supersymmetry, anthropic landscapes, Kaluza–Klein towers — have been spent trying to cut that number down.

Sarfatti's argument, which he says he has been repeating for years, goes like this. Take Einstein's equation in the form that makes the coupling explicit: geometry on the left, energy density on the right, joined by the square of the Planck length — the smallest scale in physics, about 10^-35 meters. Now borrow one idea from the holographic school of Leonard Susskind and Gerard 't Hooft: the information content of a region lives on its boundary area, and for our universe the relevant boundary is the area A of the future cosmological horizon — the largest scale in physics. Set the vacuum curvature by that area, turn the crank once, and out falls the vacuum energy density: Planck's constant times the speed of light, divided by the Planck length squared times the horizon area. Put in the numbers and the answer lands on the observed dark-energy density. Not after tuning. On it.

Equivalently: the scale of dark energy is the *geometric mean* of the smallest length in physics and the largest — a length of about a fiftieth of a millimeter, sitting exactly halfway between the Planck scale and the size of the observable universe in logarithmic terms. "Voila," Sarfatti wrote to his list, with characteristic economy. "Very simple. No need for fancy Kaluza–Klein theory."

His Feynman avatar's assessment of this argument deserves quoting at length, because it is simultaneously the fairest praise and the fairest criticism Sarfatti's style has ever received, and because Sarfatti — this is the point — chose to publish it himself:

*"Yes — the arithmetic works. The observed dark-energy density comes out to the right order of magnitude with no free parameters. That is not nothing... Your version is the simplest possible holographic estimate. It is not 'trivial' in the pejorative sense — it is economical... It is not a complete theory; it is a very good constraint that any complete theory must satisfy."*

Economy is Sarfatti's aesthetic, inherited from Dirac's dictum that the equations of physics should be beautiful, and from John Archibald Wheeler — with whom Sarfatti worked as a young man — who prized what he called "radical conservatism": push the physics you already trust as far as it will go before inventing anything new. Sarfatti's whole program is radical conservatism in that sense, at least in its own self-understanding. He adds no new dimensions, no new particles, no new forces. He takes the largest symmetry already present in the light cone and refuses to leave any of it un-gauged. Whether nature shares his taste is, as the avatar says at the end of nearly every lecture, not a question for the blackboard.

text:
@Blizzard_Ent @Warcraft You want to make the next big game that brings life back into your company? Stop beating a dead horse. I said it. Stop beating a dead horse. There I said it twice. Seriously though, Warcraft is dead. Retail is dead. Classic is dead. I see you. Add up all the servers and assume the classic 15k player cap per server, you have enough room for about 7-8 million players. Except most servers are empty. So realistically you are peaking around 4 million players. Which is basically 1/3rd your all time 12 million peak.

IF you really want to revitalize World of Warcraft. Drop retail, drop classic, create World of Warcraft 2.0. What would this look like? A complete revamp of the MMORPG genre. First is world size, gone will be the size we currently see. Nope, its going to be exponentially bigger. Think Earth 2.0 big. Continents that players will never be able to explore in a month of gameplay. Its too big. Slow but meaningful progression that everyone loves. Mounts can exist, but also revamped for balance. Flight is slow. Something large enough to carry a player isn't gong to travel very fast. But you can travel in straight lines" which does cut down on travel times in a sense. Likewise land will be fastest, fast mounts like horses or cheetahs or whatever.

Which leads me to the idea of Simulation. WoW2.0 isn't a static game like it was before. You have the employee size to pull it off (and honestly capital to hire more if needed). The game world should feel alive. When I complete a quest. That's it, its done. No one else can do it. The quest is over, the world has changed. A perfect example is the classic quest "Princess Must Die" which I will use as an example. You run up and talk to Ma Stonefield and she tells you that there is a Pig named Princess who keeps eating her god damn crops and she wants you to kill the vermin. You accept the quest. Now the choice on how to complete the quest is up to you, the player. You could....

1. Try to kill Princess, Fail. Your death literally gives experience points to Princess. Maybe she even levels up. YOU DO NOT get to try again. You failed, that is an end point. The Brackwells will probably now hire a security guard for their pig to protect it and possibly report the attempted murder to local authorities (Marshal Dughan, Marshal Haggard, Marshal McBride examples). The world changes physically.

2. Try to kill Princess, Succeed. You return to Ma Stonefield and get your reward. WERE YOU SEEN? Did someone spot you? Can they identify you? will the Brackwells report you to local authorities and you end up on a wanted posted? Maybe. Maybe not.

3. You don't try to kill Princess at all, instead you WARN the Brackwells of the attempt on Princesses life. THEY give you a reward for telling them, and you complete the quest in a unique way.

With that in mind, everything you do has faction standing tied to it. Rather its minor faction standing with families (Stonefields vs Brackwells) or larger standings (Elywin Forest, Stormwind, etc). Everything you do will have REAL consequences for the game world. And because the world is so huge, getting quests will be unique to each player. You can't look up a guide online because quests are constantly being taken, completed, and removed from the pool, and new ones going in based on whats going on in the game world.

I mean think about it, what if a group of players banded together in raid format to kill the Lich King, AND FAILED THE QUEST. NO SECOND CHANCES. The story goes a complete different direction! That is what is sorely lacking from MMORPGS. No more "the developer says where the story goes" instead the players actions and choices decide where the overall stories go. Small quests change small things, that will eventually effect larger things, that eventually change the whole world. Cascading type of effects!

Crafting, should not be a side note like classic wow or retail wow. Crafting should be a literal class. You want to craft things, good, you become a Blacksmith. You literally level up and get stronger by crafting. No need to combat. Not to say that you can't. You can still learn skills and abilities for combat. How will that work? Skill points. Every level you get a skill point (or multiple, depends on overall game balance). You spend those points on skills YOU WANT TO LEARN. Sure blacksmithing is your class, but you can still buy skill scrolls or skill tomes to learn skills. So maybe you took on a quest and got lucky and obtained a whirlwind skill book. You could sell it to an NPC vender who can resell to player, you can sell directly to another player or trade for it, you can even hang onto it and eventually find an NPC who is looking for the skill book in terms of a quest, and turn that in! And of course you can also just learn the skill yourself. Maybe the skill has requirements before you can learn it. Maybe whirlwind requires Swordsmanship level 5, Axemenship level 5, and Macemenship level 5. If you have all those at level 5, you can easily learn whirlwind. So in essence, just because you are a blacksmith, doesn't mean you can't learn combat skills if you work for it. Bringing more meaning and uniqueness to player builds. And with limited skill points based on level, no one can learn everything. So players have legit roles.

Now one thing missing in WoW was elements. Fire, water, earth, air, etc, all meaningless things that had no purpose. You even later basically removed them from the game last i checked. Like pokemon, there should be a rock/paper/scissors system in place for all balancing. Fire beats grass, grass beats water, water beats fire. Remember that? its fair. It makes sense. No one can be "the unstoppable hero" meme. EVERYONE has a weakness but also a strength. This balance is FAIR for everyone. Thus no matter your individual class+skill combo build, you will always have someone you will absolutely obliterate in pvp but also someone you will always lose to in pvp. Mass war, which should be a thing, comes down to real strategy, not individual strengths. Running dungeons also will make sense. A fire mage isn't going to take on a water temple dungeon. Its their mortal weakness.

Which leads into common sense rewards for quests and items drops. A fire mage will not get ANY fire gear in a water temple. That's just illogical. Likewise a wolf isn't going to drop a physical weapons. How was a wolf carrying a giant 2h bastard sword? Its not possible. Make MMORPGs make sense again. IF you want materials for crafting like fur, kill a wolf. IF you want bee pollen for alchemy, you might want to kill giant bees. IF you want a physical weapon, kill a humanoid who could actually carry such a weapon. Basic RNG does the rest.... 

With that in mind, because the world is so huge. This "alternate universe" Warcraft game would be completely new. Orcs in the cold north will "life off the land" and wear bear pelts and probably mine for ore to create metal weapons and live in rock huts made of stone bricks. But orcs in the desert will wear chitin armor made from giant scorpions and live in adobe homes made of sand/water/mud. The desert orcs will use scorpion stingers for weapons (or snake fangs) and so on. The area in which an NPC lives will have an effect on how they dress, the types of items they carry and use, and their potential drops when you kill them. If you want an item, use common sense to find it....

Since NPC's can level up, they can also wander around. Imagine two NPC's meet. A rock/paper/scissors minigame, back end wise, is played. FIGHT, FLEE, JOIN FORCES. Maybe a goblin meets a wolf. They can fight, flee, or join forces. And each combo will have various outcomes.

Fight/Flee, simple, one tries to run away, can the one who wants to kill the other catch up and kill them? or do they get away and fighter gives up?

Fight/Join, one tries to reason, the other fights. If the fighter loses, they don't die, instead they become "submissive" to the Join one, and becomes their ally. If fighter wins, well the joiner dies and the npc gains experience points equal to level of who died.

Flee/Join, similar meme. If the Joiner catches the fleer, they become submissive and join the party to team up. If the fleer gets away and joiner gives up, they go their separate ways. No death, no xp changes.

Obviously fight/fight, flee/flee, and join/join all have basic outcomes.... fight, they fight, winner takes all meme. flee, they both run away in opposite directions. join, they join forces.

So lets say a goblin meets a wolf. And they join/join.... the mob will upgrade. The goblin/wolf has many choices to turn into (RNG baby).

Goblin tamer. similar to the classic wow hunter class. the wolf is their partner in crime. except in this world, if the wolf dies, the goblin would have to tame another world.... it wont come back to life.... (same should be said for players). New attack patterns and skill rotations for this new mob.

Goblin rider. The goblin rides on top of the wolf. New attack patterns and skill rotations for this mob.

the possibilities are seemingly endless. sometimes combining is just simply "a wolf and a goblin" in a basic party as individuals. they don't have to "combine" but its possible. this makes the game world feel more alive.

NPCs will have back end personality code, algorithms, whatever you want to call it. This helps them feel more alive. The game itself would have a basic understanding of things like building cities and homes. NPC's banding together, and starting an outpost? that turns into a village, and slowly levels up into a civilization? possible.

lets say 20 orcs had partied up and are wandering the desert. happenstance meme. join/join or fight/join and they got up to 20 orcs in a party. real "raid" party meme. they come a crossed an oasis. nothing nearby. no players. no npc's. no civilizations. they decide "this is our home now" and they decide to "settle." AKA the settlement system. The highest level NPC of this group becomes a "king" and thanks to king status, new orcs can spawn based on a variety of factors. This is how the game world can naturally grow without the need for another system for generating wandering npc's randomly. everything the 19 orcs do, gives a share of xp to the king to ensure the king is always the strongest npc. nothing more dumb than Stormwind's king being a level 5 child.... i mean you could just "snipe" the fucker and change the entire path of the human civilization. Its stupid and should not exist.... so the king of every civilization/settlement will be the strongest of that group. they build homes, collect loot from nearby npc monsters like scorpions and snakes. eventually build their "blood springs outpost." if they grow enough, even with/without player help, they could turn into "blood springs village."

the whole world would FEEL ALIVE. adventuring, exploring, would have real meaning. you aren't going quest to quest being dragged along a stupid quest path that you end up doing every single time you make a new character. you would actually LIVE in this game world....

back to crafting. materials have substats. there will be 100's if not 1000's of types of iron ore. iron ore found in the frigid north might have 10 different types with specific substats while iron ore found near a volcano will have 10 different types with different substats. when you craft an item, its not "specific thing a plus specific thing b" its "material type." Example a sword. Its a blade, the guard, the handle, the pommel. Each can be made with various materials. Steel blade, gold/steel alloy guard, steel wrapped in leather handle, and a pommel that can inset a jewel, and even the jewel has substats/effects on the end item. combine and wa-la, you have a specific item with specific stats. every crafted item will feature the crafters name, rather its npc made or player made. because yes, npcs dont just offer infinite items. they have to craft them too just like players would. if you buy out all the alchemy supplies from an npc alchemy shop, they will be OUT OF MATERIALS until they actually restock.... gone are the days of static boring gameplay. The future id dynamic living worlds.

You have the money.

You have the employees.

You have the skill.

So why are you beating a dead horse? WoW as it stands, is dead. You will never reach 12 million subs ever again. It will never happen. Meanwhile there are 250 million daily users on steam. Why aren't they playing world of warcraft? Maybe because its time to put down a 1990's inspired game and make a 2026 inspired game.....

text:
A reflection on Romans 12:1-2
Contextual Background

Romans 12:1-2 marks a major turning point in Paul’s letter. After eleven chapters of dense theological argument about sin, justification, the law, grace, and the place of Israel, Paul now moves from doctrine to exhortation.  He appeals to the Roman Christians “by the mercies of God” — everything he has just explained about God’s saving action — and calls them to a new kind of worship. Instead of offering dead animals in the temple, they are to offer their own bodies as a living sacrifice. This is their “spiritual worship” (or “reasonable service”).  He then gives the negative and positive sides of the same transformation: do not be conformed to this age (the present world-order with its values and patterns), but be transformed by the renewal of the mind so that they can discern God’s will — what is good, pleasing, and perfect.The passage is both liturgical and ethical. Christian life itself is now the sacrifice.
