text:
China Is Starting a Runaway Nuclear Arms Race. Golden Dome Can Make It Irrelevant.

Beijing’s massive nuclear buildup has broken the old arms-control balance. America can try to outbuild Russia and China combined — or it can use new technology to completely change the equation.

Deep in the Xinjiang desert, China is building a nuclear fortress.

Reuters recently identified more than 80 new pads near China’s Hami missile fields, possible launch positions for mobile missiles and air-defense batteries. They are surrounded by bunkers and facilities analysts believe may support electronic warfare, satellite communications, command and control, maintenance, and storage. Nearby airfields and railheads knit it all together.

No one outside Beijing knows how every pad will be used. But they know exactly what it means. China has tripled its strategic nuclear force — the weapons that would target and destroy American cities — in just four years. Nor are they slowing down: the construction continues, fast.

That would be alarming all by itself. But when combined with Russia’s nuclear forces, it complicates arms control calculus almost impossibly, and threatens to force a costly global arms race of ruinous proportions.

The uncertainty is a big part of the point. The Chinese are dispersing, hardening, concealing, and multiplying the forces around Hami, one of three vast new ICBM silo fields. The Pentagon believes they have likely already loaded more than 100 DF-31-class missiles into silos across those three fields. China’s nuclear stockpile has reached the low 600s and is on track to exceed 1,000 warheads by 2030.

This is not China’s historical “minimum deterrence.” It’s the construction of a survivable, rapidly expanding strategic force designed to complicate every American calculation and give China real first-strike capabilities. It’s also sufficiently concentrated so as to make it readily defensible by antiballistic missiles (ABMs).

Does China want to fight a nuclear war with the United States? Doesn’t matter. It absolutely wants nuclear cover for conventional aggression: a force frightening enough to keep America out of a Taiwan invasion or other adventure while Beijing changes the map.

This is exactly the danger Donald Trump has sought to pre-empt in Iran. But China is a tougher nut to crack. And the danger is not limited to China’s fast-growing arsenal.

For half a century, nuclear strategy has rested on bilateral arithmetic. Washington counted Moscow’s launchers and warheads. Moscow counted ours. Each side knew roughly what the other could destroy, what would survive, and what would come back.

China has turned that equation into a nearly unsolvable triangle, in which any two powers could gang up on the third. Traditional equal arms-control limits become almost meaningless when any two parties can combine twice the firepower permitted to the third.

That makes the world very dangerous very fast. And since China and Russia don’t trust each other either, all three countries have to try to outbuild the others, not individually but combined. That rapidly spirals to numbers of weapons far in excess of the Cold War peak, with staggering economic costs and vastly higher risk of miscalculation and conflict.

This is why President Trump’s Golden Dome is the most important defense project in the world.

Arms control can’t solve this problem. And China has never participated in any arms control agreement anyway. They’re pretty clear on the point that they don’t mean to start.

So if the old ways won’t work, we need a new one. And it just so happens that American technology can solve the problem…if we use it.

Why Arms Control Is No Longer a Solution

I have long asserted the utter uselessness and counterproductivity of arms control. There are really only two significant exceptions.

The first was Ronald Reagan’s Zero Option. Reagan proposed eliminating an entire class of weapons: Soviet and American intermediate-range nuclear missiles in Europe. The Soviets mocked him until his military buildup and Strategic Defense Initiative left them no better alternative. Then, in 1987, they signed Reagan’s Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces (INF) Treaty. For the first and only time, an entire class of nuclear weapons was banned, and thousands of missiles were destroyed.

The second was another Reagan idea, the Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, or START, and its successor treaties.

What was so special? The START treaties did something truly innovative. Remarkable, really. And hardly anyone understands it. They actually reduced total deployed nuclear weapons on each side below the number of must-kill targets.

People talk about “Mutual Assured Destruction” (MAD) as though it’s assured. But what if it isn’t? What if a surprise attack (like Pearl Harbor) caught the other side napping? What if it hesitated? The right strike package might well leave the victim with no retaliatory force. And that’s not the worst of it: if an enemy achieved a large enough margin of superiority, the victim might feel the need to surrender before the first shot was even fired. But the requirements are the same either way.

A successful disarming strike would require far more than just destroying the victim’s missile silos, which would be tough enough. It would also need to eliminate his submarines and their bases, his bombers and airfields, his mobile launchers, command centers, communications, leadership, warning systems, and every other force capable of ordering or delivering unsurvivable retaliation.

Many of these targets would require multiple warheads. Some warheads would inevitably turn out to be duds. Some would miss. Some targets would move. Some bombers and submarines would escape. So the attacker would have to hit each target with more firepower than needed to leave the victim entirely or largely naked.

New START’s limits — just 1,550 deployed strategic warheads and 700 deployed delivery vehicles, versus a combined Cold War stockpile that once exceeded 70,000 — made that problem insoluble. Under the treaty, there was a 100 percent certainty that your enemy was going to hit you back, hard. Neither side could possibly destroy everything it needed to eliminate in a first strike. Thus, first strikes became implausible at best, and MAD was actually assured.

That’s why the system worked. It did not make nuclear weapons humane. Mutual Assured Destruction is and always has been grossly immoral. It held hundreds of millions of innocent civilians hostage to the promise of national suicide. But by making a successful first strike impossible, START made one irrational.

So what’s the catch?

China is not and never has been subject to any of these treaties.

New START expired on February 5. Even before that, China had no interest in joining it, publicly refusing the trilateral negotiations any real agreement now requires.

Such a three-way deal might be theoretically possible, but the key word is “theoretical.” In practice, it would require extraordinarily deep reductions, intrusive verification, and confidence that nobody maintains clandestine forces. For the numbers to go low enough for the system to work, even a very small degree of cheating would destabilize the whole scheme. No one’s intelligence is that good. Nor will it ever be.

And such a treaty remains a promise, one in which everyone is incentivized to lie.

Iran is an object lesson. Tehran claimed it had kept the range of its ballistic missiles below 2,000 kilometers. Then on March 20, it fired two Intermediate Range Ballistic Missiles (IRBMs) at Diego Garcia, roughly 4,000 kilometers away. One failed in flight; an American interceptor engaged the other. But while neither hit Diego Garcia, their range put London, Paris, and Berlin within reach.

That puts Iran about a half-step away from an ICBM that could hit New York or Los Angeles. It’s no big leap for a country that can already orbit satellites. It puts the entire world at risk. And Iran lied about it for years, a lie that Western intelligence agencies foolishly accepted at face value.

Who do you think is more competent: the (dead) Ayatollah or Xi Jinping?

American and Israeli forces have demolished Iran’s nuclear infrastructure and most of Iran’s missile stocks and factories. But attempting the analogous operation against Russia or China would almost certainly start a nuclear war. That’s the difference between preventing a bomb and trying to disarm a nuclear superpower. The latter ain’t never gonna happen.

So if arms control is now obsolete, the only way to avoid three countries (at least) spiraling up to hundreds of thousands of nukes on a hair trigger is to make those weapons obsolete too.

That’s where missile defense comes in. It’s advanced just a bit since the Reagan or Nixon years. It’s about to become unlimited and impenetrable.

Better a Shield Than a Sword

But well before that, Donald Trump’s Golden Dome can add so much risk to a first strike — by leaving enemies wondering whether enough of their warheads will get through — that a first strike becomes impossible.

That’s the play: technologically leapfrogging out of the age of any-minute nuclear armageddon and into one in which defense is stronger than offense.

Ronald Reagan understood the obscenity of the “Mutual Assured Destruction” arrangement; he also knew that under the right circumstances, the Russians wouldn’t believe in it. He asked why we should avenge Americans after they died when we might protect them instead. As a result, he launched the Strategic Defense Initiative, transforming the strategic contest and helping drive the Soviet Union beyond its economic limits.

Edward Teller — the father of the hydrogen bomb — personally gave me a copy of his book Better a Shield Than a Sword. The title captured the choice Reagan understood: America did not have to remain forever dependent on the threat of nuclear vengeance. It could build defenses strong enough to make the weapons themselves obsolete, and in the process, end the global hostage taking of the world’s civilian populations.

Washington never finished the job. It was unwilling to spend the money required by the technological limits of the time (how would we build bridges to nowhere and “Learing Centers” if we did?), and in the meantime, the Cold War ended. This froze the immoral MAD hostage-taking in place, but without the intense, permeating fear of the previous four decades.

God bless him, George W. Bush finally withdrew from the ABM Treaty. America built limited defenses against limited attacks. It also prioritized tactical missile defense for U.S. forces and allies throughout the world. But it still didn’t build a comprehensive shield for the American people. And what does “defense” even mean if you don’t defend your civilian population?

Now, President Trump is changing all that.

Golden Dome Is Reagan’s Vision Fulfilled

Golden Dome is no longer a campaign promise or a Pentagon PowerPoint.

The Department of War completed its initial architecture blueprint in April. It has established a command-and-control consortium and awarded active contracts for critical components. The design links persistent space-based sensing, ground and space interceptors, existing air- and missile-defense systems, and machine-speed command and control into a single layered shield.

The point is to attack the attack, and at every stage: disrupt it before launch when possible; destroy boosters while they are still rising; kill missiles, glide vehicles, and warheads in space; then catch whatever remains with terminal defenses. No layer has to carry the entire burden. Each reduces the problem for the next.

Congress has already committed nearly $38 billion to Golden Dome and the missile-defense and space systems being integrated into it: $24.4 billion through the 2025 reconciliation law and another $13.4 billion through the fiscal 2026 defense appropriations act. The administration’s 2027 request includes another $17.9 billion in direct Golden Dome funding, while House appropriators count more than $25 billion in total investments supporting the shield. The separate supplemental seeks still more for the munitions and space-data backbone Golden Dome will require.

Nor is this money being spent on a system that might appear sometime in the 2030s. Gen. Mike Guetlein says the War Department will deliver an operational capability by summer 2028 — before Trump leaves office — and then continue expanding toward an ever-larger architecture costing approximately $185 billion through 2035.

That is a very large number. But for a system designed to prevent the destruction of the United States, it is a bargain.

The space layer is moving first because everything else depends on seeing the attack. The Space Force has issued 20 prototype agreements to 12 companies for space-based interceptors, with an initial capability demonstration planned for 2028. The Space Development Agency has awarded roughly $1.75 billion for 36 additional missile-warning, tracking, and defense sensor satellites expected to be ready for launch by the end of that year.

Those satellites are not yet in orbit. The interceptors are prototypes, not an operational constellation. But they are also not studies waiting for another study. They are hardware under contract, tied to an architecture and a delivery schedule.

The same transformation is happening on the ground.

The Army increased its PAC-3 MSE acquisition objective from 3,376 interceptors to 13,773. Its 2027 request supports 2,798 PAC-3 MSEs and 857 THAAD interceptors. A seven-year production framework aims to more than triple annual PAC-3 capacity, from roughly 600 to 2,000, while THAAD capacity is slated to rise from 96 to 400.

Such long-term commitments let manufacturers build plants, buy machine tools, qualify second sources, stock long-lead materials, create new jobs, and train skilled workers. They convert appropriations into a real industrial base: American jobs protecting the American people.

Just as important, the shield is being designed around cost-matching. It makes no sense to fire a multimillion-dollar ballistic-missile interceptor at a cheap drone. PAC-3 MSE must be reserved for targets that require it. Lockheed’s new PAC-3 ACE is intended to perform roughly two-thirds of the MSE mission set for about half the cost. 

Against lower, slower threats, Lockheed and companies like Epirus are adapting cheaper missiles, high-power microwave systems, and lasers. Lockheed CEO Jim Taiclet says its MORFIUS system can disable as many as 50 drones on a single battery charge. Epirus’s Leonidas can take out 100 drones per shot.

Expensive weapons for hard targets. Cheap weapons for cheap targets. Electricity wherever possible. And a technological revolution coming right behind.

The Laser Endgame

Kinetic interceptors are the immediate answer. They are not the ultimate one.

Every missile magazine is finite. An attacker can keep adding rockets, drones, cruise missiles, hypersonics, and decoys until the defender runs out of interceptors — or goes broke trying to buy enough.

Decoys make that arithmetic even worse. An enemy can release thousands of fake warheads, each requiring no nuclear material and little sophisticated machinery. They may be nothing more than metalized balloons or radar reflectors costing thousands of dollars apiece. But the defender has to treat every one of them as real — potentially firing thousands of $35 million interceptors, perhaps multiple interceptors per target, to destroy them. The enemy spends millions. We spend ourselves into oblivion.

Directed Energy Weapons — yes, lasers — change all of that. And the first generation is already here.

Israel’s Iron Beam laser system became fully operational in December. It is a 100-kilowatt-class weapon designed to destroy rockets, mortars, and drones at a marginal cost of roughly $2 per shot. Compare that to a $4 million Arrow-3, a $6 million SM-6, or a $35 million SM-3. Can the defender possibly keep up in a real arms race? In the long run, not a chance.

Lockheed has already destroyed drones and cruise missiles with lasers in live-fire testing. It has a 300-kilowatt-class system and is developing a transportable 500-kilowatt weapon. Neither can stop an ICBM. Yet.

Lasers collapse the cost curve. They also hit their targets at the speed of light. The enemy must manufacture, fuel, move, hide, launch, and guide another missile. The defender instantly generates another shot with electricity. The attacker’s magazine empties. The defender’s recharges.

Power is the key. On land, small modular nuclear reactors can supply fixed defensive complexes. At sea, nuclear-powered ships such as aircraft carriers or the new Trump-class battleships can become mobile defensive nodes.

In space, the economics and range of the defender’s platforms get even better. Nuclear power can ultimately support persistent platforms above clouds and most atmospheric interference. Starship-scale reusable lift makes it practical to orbit the reactors, radiators, large apertures, replacement hardware, and sheer mass such a shield will require.

Golden Dome does not depend on lasers magically arriving tomorrow. Trump is building the kinetic shield right now — by the thousands — while driving down interceptor costs and developing the directed-energy layers that can ultimately make magazine depth unlimited.

Once that layered energy defense can reliably destroy boosters, glide vehicles, and warheads across multiple phases of flight, nuclear weapons effectively become obsolete. Building them just adds expensive targets, sure to be shot down, by virtually any delivery system short of a Star Trek transporter.

No adversary can coerce or blackmail a nation that cannot be successfully attacked. Which is exactly why Ronald Reagan offered America’s SDI technology to the Soviets: to ensure that everyone was defended and no one could attack. The Communists wanted to attack and declined the offer.

All of which brings us back to modern Russia and China. Perhaps they will cooperate; perhaps not. But Trump hasn’t made Reagan’s offer. A virtually invulnerable America leaves the two enemies warily eyeing each other. That’s better. But it’s not as good as eliminating nuclear weapons as a viable threat.

And that’s why Golden Dome is the most important program on Earth.

The Nuclear Balance of Terror Has an Off-Ramp

America can win another offensive arms race: indeed, it’s the only country that could. Its economy is significantly larger than Russia’s and China’s combined. Its technology is far superior. Its allies multiply its strength. If forced, America can outbuild them both.

But the cost would be immense. There was a limit in the two-way race in the Cold War era. The logic of a three-way race requires that the weapons count spiral ever upward, with economic ruin being preferable to destruction. And that’s assuming that no one slips, no one miscalculates, no one gambles. Those things are highly unlikely under the New START limits. In this new normal, they will grow more dangerous with every passing year until the world is an impoverished powder keg.

That’s not a world you, or I, would want to live in.

Golden Dome offers an equally dramatic alternative: a kinetic shield now, an effectively bottomless energy shield later, and the final destruction of the Sword of Damocles dangling above the world for lo these past eight decades.

We can end the decades of nuclear terror. We can raise Teller’s shield against his sword.

That’s not a military breakthrough. It’s a civilizational one.

BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Friday, August 26, 1966, the world’s largest jetliner arrived at Dallas Love Field for a visit with Braniff International officials. The massive airliner, the Douglas DC-8-61 Intercontinental Jet flew to Dallas for a technical review and demonstration in hopes that it might interest Braniff in the new aircraft for its long-range routes between the US Mainland and Latin America.

Braniff management attending the special event were Braniff Airways Chairman of the Board and primary shareholder Troy Victor Post. Mr. Post was accompanied by President Harding L. Lawrence and Board Member Mr. E. Grant Fitts. Chief Pilot A. G. Heimerdinger flew the big jet to Dallas and along with Douglas Regional Sales Manager Mr. D. B. Talmage acted as tour guides for the new airliner, which was parked at Braniff’s Operations and Maintenance Base on the east side of Love Field.

The big airliner was on the last leg of an 11-day tour that covered half of the world, which would end with the jet departing Dallas for the flight back to the Douglas plant at Long Beach, California, where it was produced. The tour first departed Long Beach and headed west to Tokyo, Japan, which was flown in a record 11 hours and 32 minutes and 49 seconds. The 5630 mile flight arrived at TYO with sufficient fuel to fly on for another 1000 miles, if necessary.

The luxurious stretched Series -61 could carry up to 251 passengers, the highest number of any airliner offered in 1966. Douglas’s new jet was stretched 37 feet longer than the current DC-8. A remarkable 240 inches were added in front of the wing to the Douglas 61 and 200 inches aft of the wings, which provided the greater carrying capacity as well as increased range.

Braniff had on order 26 new Boeing jets that cost $171 million USD and it would soon acquire five new DC-8 Super 62 Intercontinental Jets from Douglas Aircraft Company as a result of its pending merger with Pan American Grace Airways, which occurred a few months later on February 1, 1967. The new Super 62 was 157.4 feet in length compared to the impressive 187.4 feet of the DC-8-61. However, Braniff’s Super 62 featured an even greater range, which coupled with its lower capacity made it more perfectly suited to the long but sometimes lower density "thin" South American routes.

The world’s largest jetliner was scheduled to go into service by the end of 1966. It received its provisional Federal Aviation Agency certification in July 1966 and had completed its first flight a few months earlier on March 14, 1966. The DC-8-61 could operate with a flight crew of 3 to 5 plus cabin attendants and could fly 7,430 statute miles nonstop with zero payload and full fuel. At maximum takeoff weight of 325,000 pounds the FAA Takeoff Field length was 10,560 feet and landing was 6140 feet.

Photo: Braniff International McDonnell Douglas DC-8-62 Intercontinental Jet registered as N1803 is parked on the ramp at the Braniff Terminal of the Future at Dallas Love Field on September 24, 1971. The plush Braniff airliner is painted in the 1967 Alexander Girard/Harper and George Panagra Green Solid Color Scheme. Braniff decided that the lower capacity but longer range Super 62 over the massive DC-8-61 was a better choice for its needs. While Braniff’s Latin America Division had become truly profitable in 1965, the density of the routes were better suited to a smaller capacity aircraft. Braniff shrewdly measured this in the early 1970s and decided against the McDonnell-Douglas DC-10-30 for the same reasons. In 1977, Braniff placed deposits for new Boeing 767 and Boeing 757 aircraft. The Boeing 767 would have replaced the Super 62 in Latin America.

In 2015, this @YCombinator founder had $100 left in the bank. He turned down a $500k acquisition offer. Today his company is worth $1.25 billion.

The story of Jake Loosararian:

> electrical engineering at Grove City College
> as a college student, hear that a worker died inspecting a boiler
> that day, start building a robot that climbs walls and carries ultrasonic sensors
> spend months inside a dirty, hot boiler getting the prototype to work

> 𝟮𝟬𝟭𝟯: graduate. cofound @geckorobotics with Orion Correa and later Troy Demmer, your old dorm roommate
> name it after a gecko you watched grip a shower wall in a Costa Rica rainforest
> pour your $40k life savings into the company
> don't know how to raise money yet. just build
> work 100hrs/week on Gecko

> 𝟮𝟬𝟭𝟱: get a $500k acquisition offer from a large energy company
> turn it down even though you have $100 left in the bank
> sleep on the floor at your best friend’s place for 2.5 years

> 𝟮𝟬𝟭𝟲: get into YC, one of the first robotics companies in the batch
> achieve the robotics sensor unlock: ~3k manual data points vs. 8M+ from your robots
> expand robotic repair fleet from power plants to Fortune 100 energy, oil and gas, manufacturing, bridges, large-scale built infrastructure
> sign a $100M+ energy deal with NAES, with an option to grow beyond $250M
> cut nuclear reactor-vessel inspection from 300 hrs → 6 hrs (~98% faster)

> 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟱: close a $125M Series D, bringing total funding to ~$347M
> hit $1.25B valuation
> march 2026: land the US Navy’s largest robotics contract yet ($71M)

Software alone can't inspect a nuclear missile silo. It takes robots, sensors, and a founder obsessed enough to sleep inside power plants until it works.

This is why we back the AI + hardware + software intersection at @MVP_Ventures

Jake, you’re a legend. Proud to have you by our side.

The visualization sells the moment. The scrolling text underneath is what's actually doing the work.

text:
The debt Jesus paid was the infinite debt of humanity’s sin: our rebellion, our guilt, the moral bankruptcy that separated every soul from a holy God.

It was not a commercial invoice. It was the cosmic ledger of righteousness broken. Scripture declares: “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). That shortfall is the debt. It is owed not to Satan, not to the law as an impersonal force, but to the justice of the living God Himself, the One whose pure holiness cannot simply overlook evil without ceasing to be just. “The wages of sin is death” (Romans 6:23). Death: spiritual, judicial, eternal, was the just penalty.

Why blood? Because life is in the blood (Leviticus 17:11), and from the first pages of Scripture God revealed that sin’s wage could only be paid by a life given in place of another. The sacrificial system of the Old Covenant was the shadow… every lamb pointed forward. Then came the reality: “Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins” (Hebrews 9:22). 

God did not require blood because He is bloodthirsty. He required it because justice is not optional to His nature. Love without justice is sentimentality; justice without love is cruelty. At the cross both met in perfect harmony.

Jesus never uttered the exact phrase “I paid your debt,” yet He declared the substance with thunderous clarity. He said, “The Son of Man came… to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). He said, “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:28). He cried from the cross, “It is finished” (John 19:30) tetelestai—the word stamped on ancient receipts meaning “paid in full.”  Paul later unfolded it: God made Him “who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). Peter wrote that we were ransomed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19).

The awe is this: the Creditor became the payment. The Judge stepped down from the bench, took off His robes of glory, and climbed onto the cross as the condemned. The debt was real. The blood was real. The payment was complete. And now, by grace through faith, the ledger is closed for all who trust Him.

As for the Muslim practice of animal sacrifice (Qurbani or Udhiyah): it is performed primarily during Eid al-Adha in remembrance of the willingness of Ibrahim (Abraham) to sacrifice his son in obedience to God, and God’s provision of a ram in the son’s place (a narrative shared, with differences, in the Qur’an and the Bible). The meat is shared with family, friends, and the poor. It is an act of obedience, gratitude, and charity, not an atonement that cancels the eternal debt of sin. In Islamic theology, sacrifice does not function as substitutionary payment for moral guilt before a holy God in the way the cross does in the New Testament. It commemorates submission and provides for the needy.

The Christian confession is that the final, once-for-all sacrifice has already been offered. No further blood of bulls or goats or lambs is needed. The Lamb of God has taken away the sin of the world. The debt is paid. The books are closed. And every knee will one day bow before the One who settled the account with His own life.

text:
MPC Friday Report — August 28, 2026
Milk Producers Council 

Chicago blocks: $1.4825, −4.50¢ on the week; weekly average $1.5085 (−5.35¢). Chicago AA butter: $1.4625, unchanged on the week; weekly average $1.4625 (+1.15¢). CME spot NDM: $1.8650, +6.50¢. National plant average week ending Aug. 22: $1.6221 on 17.89 million pounds vs. $1.5800 on 19.35 million the prior week. Dry whey: Dairy Market News $0.7000 (week ending Aug. 28); national plants $0.6672 (week ending Aug. 22).

California FMMO projections (Aug. 27 estimate vs. last week): Class I no change (last week $20.96–$21.56, location-based). Class II $18.72 (was $18.77). Class III $16.67 (was $16.63). Class IV $17.39 (was $17.29).

Milk and dairy: Class III stuck, Class IV firmer, powders tight in the middle of the country

Class III futures are holding around $17. Class IV gained: September +34¢ to $19.20/cwt; October +66¢ to $19.55.

Summer heat plus pull from bottlers, Class II, and cheese plants has tightened Midwestern and Southwestern milk. National output is still massive, but little is left for Central dryers — powder production there has slowed to a trickle. Western dryers are full. The seasonal lull across the U.S., Europe, and Oceania has lifted powder prices. CME spot NDM at $1.865 is well above the international market, so exports will suffer, but domestic and Mexican demand look adequate to clear the smaller U.S. supply.

Whey broke a five-month range: spot powder +3.5¢ to 73.75¢, highest since February. Manufacturers keep pushing high-protein whey, which restrains dry whey output. DMN called the market “quiet” — steady production, unchanged demand.

Butter held at $1.4625. Cold Storage confirms stocks are still below a year ago, but the deficit is closing fast: −16% YoY in February, −10% March, −8% May, −7% June, −3% July. Demand and exports are strong, but butterfat output is heavy and inventories could soon exceed year-ago levels.

Cheese is already there. July 31 cheese stocks: 1.433 billion pounds, +0.4% vs. July 2025. Exports are large but not large enough to offset rising cheese output and soft domestic use. One processor called domestic demand “meh.” Blocks dropped 4.5¢ to $1.4825.

Grains: bulls in charge, feed costs heading higher
December wheat jumped 85¢ to $7.84/bu, a three-year high. Plains drought cut the U.S. wheat crop to its smallest harvest since 1970 and tightened Western forage, lifting hay. Europe’s grain harvest is 8% below last year’s bumper crop. Russia–Ukraine attacks on ports and ships continue to throttle Black Sea exports. Tighter, less accessible global wheat points to even stronger U.S. corn export demand on top of an already fast pace.

ProFarmer’s crop tour raised doubts that this year’s corn crop will hit trendline yields. December corn added another 28¢ to $5.3625/bu — also a three-year high, and $1 above two months ago.

Soybeans: traders still expect yields near last year’s good crop after timely August rain, and exports have been unimpressive. Crush is running hard for soybean oil into biofuels, and meal demand (domestic and export) is firm. December soybean meal rallied $23 to $348.80/ton.

Net for dairies: higher feed costs are arriving just as beef income is rolling off its peak.

Producer margins: Class III dairies are taking the cheese setback on top of rising feed costs. Summer checks were already small; futures only offer a modest lift versus June–July. Beef still pads the bottom line, even if calf and cull checks are smaller than a couple of months ago. Class I, II, and IV producers still have decent fall/winter futures. Margins are shrinking, but widespread red ink is not here yet. U.S. milk output growth is expected to continue.

text:
Hebrews 10:1-18 TS2009

For the Torah, having a shadow of the good matters to come, and not the image itself of the matters, was never able to make perfect those who draw near with the same slaughter offerings which they offer continually year by year. Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered? Because those who served, once cleansed, would have had no more consciousness of sins. 

But in those offerings is a reminder of sins year by year. For it is impossible for blood of bulls and goats to take away sins. Therefore, coming into the world, He says, “Slaughtering and meal offering You did not desire, but a body You have prepared for Me. “In ascending offerings and offerings for sin You did not delight. “Then I said, ‘See, I come – in the roll of the book it has been written concerning Me – to do Your desire, O Elohim.’ ” 

Saying above, “Slaughter and meal offering, and ascending offerings, and offerings for sin You did not desire, nor delighted in,” which are offered according to the Torah, then He said, “See, I come to do Your desire, O Elohim.” He takes away the first to establish the second. By that desire we have been set apart through the offering of the body of יהושע Messiah once for all. 

And indeed every priest stands day by day doing service, and repeatedly offering the same slaughter offerings which are never able to take away sins. But He, having offered one slaughter offering for sins for all time, sat down at the right hand of Elohim, waiting from that time onward until His enemies are made a footstool for His feet. For by one offering He has perfected for all time those who are being set apart. 

And the Set-apart Spirit also witnesses to us, for after having said before, “This is the covenant that I shall make with them after those days, says יהוה, giving My laws into their hearts, and in their minds I shall write them,” 

and, “Their sins and their lawlessnesses I shall remember no more.” 

Now where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer a slaughter offering for sin.

News Lead Up

Crypto peak!?

The crypto market has broken out of its consolidation

Market Overview

The cryptocurrency market has risen by almost 8% over the past 24 hours to $2.37T, reaching its highest level since early June. The initial momentum came on the back of news that the US Treasury was supporting the debt market. This relatively small but timely move signalled that the government is monitoring the situation in the debt markets, spurring demand for risk assets. The rally was then fuelled by a wave of short-covering, following weeks of extremely narrow trading.

Bitcoin reached $70K, posting a 9% rally over 8 hours during the US trading session. As the new day began, the leading cryptocurrency retreated slightly to $69.6K. On Monday, BTC consolidated above the 50-day moving average, and by Wednesday, it had already tested the 200-day MA. As expected, the market’s long-compressed spring snapped back, catching those who had been range-trading and those who had been building short positions on the rise off guard. If Bitcoin does not quickly lose its recent gains, it will be a significant sign that a bull market has begun, much like in October 2023 or March 2020.

Ethereum recorded an even more impressive breakout, showing an 18% gain over 24 hours at its peak. Having risen to $2.25K, the second-largest cryptocurrency is trading near its April–May highs, having broken above its 200-day moving average and away from a long-term support line that has risen from around $1.75K to $1.9K over the past 8 months. The next significant level where the coin may face resistance to further gains appears to be the $2.5K–$2.8K range. (FxPro)

News Lead Up

Cryptos

August

Crypto has reached May’s max, aiming higher

Market Overview

The cryptocurrency market has risen by 0.75% over the past 24 hours to $2.68T, trading close to this week’s highs. Judging by intraday movements, the market is poised for further growth, as investors actively buy up local price dips. While the major cryptocurrencies have stabilised near their highs of recent months, buyer interest has shifted towards altcoins. Over the past day, the top gainers were Official Trump (+27%), Uniswap (+6.7%) and Solana (+6.3%). The biggest fallers were SushiSwap and IOTA (both down 2.3%) and Immutable (down 1.8%).

The sentiment index continues to hover just below the extreme-greed threshold, a level we last saw consistently from May to August last year. Spikes in the indicator in January and May were short-lived or failed to sustain levels above the 50-mark. We are therefore observing an important confirmatory signal of a shift in sentiment from bearish to bullish.

At the time of writing, Bitcoin is trading just below $80K, but during a period of reduced liquidity ahead of the start of the Asian session, the price spiked to near $81.5K, setting a new high over the past three and a half months. It was near these levels in May that the leading cryptocurrency formed a local rebound peak, so it is logical to expect consolidation at this level for 5–10 days, though it may take longer. The next stage of growth is expected to be the $90K region, where BTC has held steady for two months since the end of November last year.

News Background

Inflows into US spot Bitcoin ETFs have continued for eight consecutive trading sessions. During this period, investors have poured $2.8 billion into the funds, bringing the total inflow to $54.7 billion.

Concerns over US government debt are driving investors towards alternative savings options such as Bitcoin and gold, according to BlackRock. The recent rise in BTC is consistent with the cryptocurrency's cyclical nature.

The US authorities have transferred 24,408 BTC, worth approximately $1.91 billion, from a wallet containing assets confiscated from the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX. The transfer of assets does not necessarily indicate an impending sell-off, though Arkham does not rule it out.

The UK has announced plans for the Bank of England to facilitate the development of payment systems and new forms of digital money, including stablecoins. The regulator’s primary focus will remain on financial stability.

A survey by the National Institute on Retirement Security found that 53% of Americans oppose employers offering cryptocurrency as a means of saving for retirement. Only 6% of those surveyed fully support using such an asset to build up retirement savings.

Summary: The crypto market is at $2.68T (+0.75%), with BTC at $80K and altcoins rising. ETF inflows hit $2.8 billion over 8 sessions, while BlackRock views BTC as a hedge against US debt risks. (FxPro)

Gold seems to have completed its corrective pullback

Last week, gold posted a modest July gain, which has already given buyers a significant boost this week. With prices up 6.5% since the start of the week, gold has confirmed a major technical breakout, bringing to an end the downtrend that began in February. The price rebounded from the key psychological level of $4,000 – where the correction also ended last October – and from the 61.8% retracement of the 2022–2026 rally, reinforcing the significance of the reversal signal.

The bulls also have the strength with which gold broke through the 50-day moving average earlier this week in their favour; this average had served as support for the uptrend since the start of 2025, before turning into local resistance in March. If this is not a false breakout, this line could once again act as support for the medium-term bullish trend.

That said, on weekly timeframes, the bulls still need to do some groundwork. During the latest rally, the price approached but failed to break through the 50-week moving average – an important signal line for the long-term trend. It currently stands near $4,400, whilst at $4,500, there is another potential area of resistance that reversed the trend in December and March.

All things considered, we expect an interesting battle in gold this coming week, with the struggle intensifying following the release of US CPI and PPI data. The path to 4,500 may prove relatively easy, but beyond that, we should brace ourselves for a very significant tug-of-war.

Summary: Gold has emerged from its correction and is heading towards $4,500, but a fierce battle between bulls and bears is likely around the 50-week moving average and following the release of US CPI/PPI data. (FxPro)

Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic expands

The value of Alphabet’s stake in the artificial intelligence start-up Anthropic has soared to around $US124 billion ($178 billion), making it one of the most lucrative bets in the company’s history.The Google parent disclosed in a filing on Thursday (Friday AEST) that the value of its investments in unidentified private companies totalled roughly $US124.3 billion as of June 30. The filing noted that this value is “primarily” driven by one investment, which is a reference to Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public. The company said it recorded about $US77 billion in unrealised gains from its private investments in the second quarter, without providing further details in the filing. Google has emerged as one of Anthropic’s biggest backers over the past several years. The technology giant first invested $US3 billion in the start-up starting in 2023. Earlier this year, it agreed to invest as much as $US40 billion more, consisting of $US10 billion upfront and a potential $US30 billion in additional funding tied to operational and financial milestones through 2030.Alphabet’s filing on Thursday showed the remaining commitment has fallen to $US20 billion as of June 30 from $US30 billion at the end of the first quarter, suggesting that Google invested another $US10 billion in the start-up last quarter. Rio Tinto dodges merger bullet

Rio Tinto has dodged two 'bullets' due to Glencore's rejection of a merger proposal: a possible BHP takeover bid and a dangerous acquisition. BHP looked closely at whether to bid for Rio Tinto if the latter announced a merger with Glencore. News/Snapshot

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.
Workforce Challenges: The Minerals Council of Australia is currently calling for migration reforms to address a significant "skills crunch" in the sector.

@DollyParton made a positive impact on me that has lasted decades ~ and will ultimately last forever for me. THAT was Dolly. To meet her, to know her, was to L💖VE her…and all she did was BE HER ANGELIC, KIND & GENEROUS SELF and make me a Cup of Coffee…☕️ 

The unforgettable encounter with Dolly happened while I was at  🎶 Ocean Way Recording Studios 🎶 in Hollywood, California directing segments for a music video featuring my friends Michael McDonald, James Ingram, David Pack and Patti Austin. 

During a break in filming I went to the lounge / kitchen to get a cup of coffee. There wasn’t any left, however this absolutely GORGEOUS and KIND lady offered to make me a cup and bring it into the studio. She asked who I was working with, and got excited to know that some of her friends were in the studio with me.  This blonde, 5 foot tall POWERHOUSE of a BEING was one of the ✨ BRIGHTEST LIGHTS ✨ I had ever met in my Life (including to this post). She had a smile 😁 that warmed your heart and a sparkle in her eyes that mesmerized you!😍She radiated JOY and COMPASSION. She had a Servant’s Heart for others.

I walked back into the recording Studio (without coffee) and my friend Michael McDonald asked, “Where’s your coffee?” I told him about the LOVELY Lady I had just met in the kitchen and he said, “That’s Dolly!”

😳🤩”DOLLY!!?” I said, “Dolly Parton!?” Michael said, “Yes” as he chuckled, obviously surprised that I didn’t realize who it was. I didn’t, because she wasn’t wearing one of her big performance wigs. She was wearing blue jeans and an angora sweater (not Rhinestones and Glitter!). She also didn’t act like a conceited Celebrity. She was… just, well… She was “DOLLY!” 🦋💖🎶 How blessed the Planet 🌎 has been for her to have shared her 💫 One of a Kind LIGHT and TALENT with us all. 

Rest in Peace in Heaven Dolly.

🇺🇸 California Moves Closer to Banning Politician-Issued Meme Coins

California’s AB 2409 has cleared both the State Assembly and Senate, bringing restrictions on government-linked meme coins a step closer. The bill is being finalized for the governor’s consideration it is not law yet. 

If enacted, it would prohibit California state and local officials, along with government employees who make decisions on bids and contracts, from issuing meme coins.

The restrictions would also reach crypto platforms: they could not list qualifying meme coins for California residents to buy or sell if those tokens were issued on or after January 1, 2027 and offered by, or in partnership with, federal, state or local officials. 

This is not a blanket ban on meme coins. The bill targets government-linked tokens and the conflicts of interest that can arise when public office becomes a vehicle for private financial gain.

Biting the forbidden fruit: A detransitioner's story of regret and faith
By Chloe Cole, Op-ed contributor Thursday, August 27, 2026

After-school hangouts, sleepovers, even just feeling like anyone was on my team were all things I thought I may only ever dream of, growing up. It proved much easier to get lost in the internet, video games, or my own creativity than to try being part of the world around me. After all, many of my closest “friends” would only be there out of pity, ridicule, to erase the artwork that I worked hard on, or pressure me into downing 3 shots of liquor for the first time when we were only 11 so they could laugh at me while I stumbled. In a world so cruel, why would I want to be there at all?

I felt different — broken, even. Eventually, I came to the belief that perhaps I had been born wrong altogether.

In the Garden of Eden, humanity’s first temptation was rooted in the belief that what God had given us was insufficient. The devil’s first tactic was to convince us that we could grasp something else and become something more if we just looked elsewhere.

The online trans community offered a respite from this brokenness. Piled on top of that affirmation, doctors too offered a treatment for it. I was just 12 years old, and before I could blink an eye, I found myself in the juxtaposition of being born a girl, yet feeling like happiness could only be found on the other side.

At the time, I had no reason to question the medical authorities telling my family that transition was the answer. They had plenty of evidence and studies to recite. After all, they were known as the best provider in California for treating gender-distressed youth. I certainly couldn’t have understood the larger system operating behind the exam-room doors. Years later, I dedicated my life to exposing just how deep that system goes.

Last week, the Department of Health and Human Services released “Wolves in White Coats: How Doctors and Hospitals Pushed and Profited from the Fraud of ‘Gender Medicine.’” Its findings are not surprising to detransitioners like me. I have long known that the gender medical industry is built upon false premises. But this report goes further, presenting evidence of fraudulent billing practices and financial incentives inside the medical institutions entrusted with vulnerable children.

As one of those former vulnerable children, I can attest to this egregious behavior. When my parents sought help for me, they were made to believe that withholding transition could mean losing me. The statistic that dominated the conversations in so many of those sterile exam rooms like mine? 41%. That’s the likelihood of suicide, parents were told — in story after story, time and time again — if they did not allow their child to undergo irreversible medical procedures like hormones and surgeries.

This stat is misleading at best, if not incredibly manipulative. The number came from a survey of trans-identifying and gender-nonconforming adults, 41% of whom reported having attempted suicide at some point in their lives. What it did not establish was that 41% of gender-distressed children would attempt suicide without hormones or surgery — much less that medical transition would prevent those deaths.

Yet parents with a distressed child heard a far more manipulative message: affirm and transition or begin preparations for a funeral.

Countless other families say they were presented with the horrifying choice of a “live son or a dead daughter.” Desperate to keep their child alive, they were coerced into medical interventions.

When you present a desperate mother and father with a choice between transition and death, I do not believe you are obtaining consent in any meaningful sense. You’re exploiting a parent’s greatest fear.

For the record, a healthy individual does not need affirmation of their identity, or the allowance of elective surgeries, in order to prevent self-harm and assure life. That in itself should have been a red flag to those involved.

The deeper I look at what happened to myself and my fellow victims of minor transitions, the more difficult it becomes to reconcile this movement’s claims with the basic principles of medicine.

Absurdly enough, my double mastectomy at age 15 happened at the height of the pandemic. While Americans weren’t able to say goodbye to their dying loved ones, weren’t able to get quality-of-life procedures done like knee and hip surgery, somehow, my elective, cosmetic procedure was greenlit. My healthy body became collateral damage in the gender ideology movement.

The HHS report alleges that pediatric gender programs exploded between the 2010s and the 2020s. It cites nearly $120 million in submitted charges since 2019, encompassing 5,747 minors who underwent surgeries and 8,579 who received hormones and puberty blockers.

More disturbing are the report’s findings concerning medical coding. HHS presents evidence suggesting that providers have used diagnoses such as “endocrine disorder, unspecified” to obtain coverage for puberty blockers even though gender dysphoria itself is not an endocrine disorder. Its claims analysis identified nearly $50 million billed for puberty blockers for minors carrying “endocrine disorder” or “precocious puberty” diagnoses to ensure providers get reimbursed through insurance.

This evident misuse of medical authority is exactly why exposing these practices matters. It seems that every time we shine light on the gender medical industrial complex, hundreds of cockroaches come scurrying out. We must continue exposing the darkness until every single roach disappears for good.

I never imagined we would have a presidential administration willing to confront these institutions on behalf of children and families. Now, the Trump administration has directed investigations and enforcement efforts, and the Justice Department has issued more than 20 subpoenas to doctors and clinics involved in performing these procedures on children.

For years, I searched for an explanation of why I felt so uncomfortable being myself. I wanted desperately for there to be some straightforward, scientific answer for my struggles while growing up and finding my life’s purpose.

I knew I was broken, but I was looking in the wrong places to put the pieces back together. I had unknowingly confused the consequences of living in a fallen, broken world with evidence that my creator had somehow made a mistake when He made me female.

For me, transitioning became my own act of biting into forbidden fruit. For a season, living a life that was not meant to be my own felt good. But it would never satisfy me — I would forever be trapped in a cycle of searching for the next change.

I kept running into brick walls because I was trying to create my own selfish answer instead of accepting His.

I still struggle fitting into a narrow box, and I think I always will. Christianity never promises to erase the difficulties of this world and the life that God has called you to. No matter what “identity” you have — male or female, white collar or blue collar, academically smart or street smart — life will come with its challenges. The answer to those challenges is to embrace the story that God has written for you, and to embrace your weaknesses. In 2 Corinthians, Paul writes of pleading with God to remove his “thorn,” only to receive the answer: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.”

The world told me my weakness meant my body needed changing. God has taught me that weakness could become the very place where His grace was most visible.

Behind every statistic in this report is a child asking questions much larger than medicine — and larger than themselves or any name, haircut, or clothing they could try on. They’re searching for meaning. For purpose. Why am I hurting? Why am I different? Who even am I? Will I ever belong somewhere?

Thousands of those children have been enticed by medical institutions looking for the answers to those questions. We cannot allow those institutions to tell another generation that the answer is to wage war against their own bodies. There is a better answer: You were not born a mistake. Your body is not an accident. And the God who created you loves you and wants to heal what you hate.

Chloe Cole is an Independent Women ambassador and detransitioner who is a prominent advocate against “gender-affirming” procedures for children. She shared her story of undergoing gender-transition surgeries and hormone therapy as a minor in IW Features’ “Identity Crisis” series.

text:
Gene Fullmer (black trunks with white stripe), 49-4-0 coming in, TKO's Carmen Basilio in the 14th round on August 28, 1959, for the vacant Middleweight title, at the Cow Palace in Daly City, California.

The title had been  declared "vacant"  due to inactivity by Sugar Ray Robinson.

Sugar Ray had only fought once in 1959, a 10-round non-title TKO of Bob Young in the 2nd round, and he'd not make another title defense until January of 1960 against Paul Pender. That would make 22 months between title defenses as he was still recognized as the titlist by the NYSAC and the state of Massachussetts.

Fullmer came into this one on a 9-fight winning streak, his last loss had been to Sugar Ray in May of 1957, including solid wins over proven contenders Ralph "Tiger" Jones, Chico Vejar and Spider Webb.

Basilio, who'd lost his middleweight title to Robinson in March of 1958, would get a rematch with Fullmer in June of 1960 but, this time, be TKO'd again (in 12).
----------------------------------------------------------
Once bitter rivals, two of today's subjects, (the third pic of this post) Carmen Basilio (left) and Gene Fullmer would come to later exchange pleasantries instead of punches.

Excerpts following are from Gare Joyce's 2007 article for ESPN titled 'Fight Club: After Trying To Break Each Other's Heads, Sworn Boxing Enemies Break Bread Together' describing a Friday night at Graziano's Casa Mia in Canastota, New York during the IBHOF's  induction weekend:

Befitting their status as boxing royalty, a couple of middleweight champions from the '50s have their entourages. 
Gene Fullmer is flanked by his younger brothers, Don and Jay. 
Carmen Basilio is with his family from around Canastota. 
The strain is starting to show on the two oldest boxing legends to make it out for the weekend. They get around all right -- every once in a while, a fan extends a hand for shaking, and Basilio gives him a fist in the solar plexus and a gentle slap before the fan can react. Sometimes, though, it seems like only the muscles have memories. They need a break. Don and Jay Fullmer help their 76-year-old brother up the stairs to a private room in the clubhouse. A few minutes later, Basilio's nieces show the way for the 80-year-old family patriarch.
The fighters' families sit them together at a table and fetch some fried chicken. A private moment during a very public weekend seems to stir memories. "I remember when we fought and at the end of the fight my mother jumped into the ring to hug me and hugged you instead," Fullmer says.
It would have seemed hard to mistake one for the other, Fullmer with a crew cut and surprising brawn, Basilio with dark eyes and a character actor's tough-guy countenance. They knew each other a bit out of the ring back in their primes, enough to know they came from a distance apart but there was common ground. They grew up on farms, Fullmer in Utah, Basilio just outside Canastota. "I was sugar beets, and he was onions," Fullmer says. "That's all you need to know about us."
They might not have had an occasion to meet all these years after the height of their fame if it hadn't been for a story in the paper in Oneida back in 1982, a celebration of the 25th anniversary of Basilio's 15-round victory over Sugar Ray Robinson. 
The story spurred townspeople in Canastota to set up a modest showcase to pay tribute to Basilio and the other homegrown champion, Billy Backus, Basilio's nephew, who won the welterweight title back in the '70s. 
Over the years, the showcase for Basilio and Backus, just another roadside attraction off the New York State Thruway, evolved into a small boxing museum and by the early '90s, into the International Boxing Hall of Fame. 
That's when Fullmer first made it out to Canastota and got to know Basilio. "They musta liked him," Fullmer says. "They put up a big statue for him."
If you're a reporter looking to fill a notebook with stories of the golden age of boxing, you're likely to get more out of the statue than out of Basilio. Ask him about the old days and he'll ask, "Who wants to know?" Or offer a couple of profanities in Italian. Or flip you the bird. Whether he can't go back or won't, it's hard to say.
Fullmer will reflect, but it's so hard you feel guilty asking him to try. His right hand, the one that rained down on Sugar Ray Robinson in their four fights, trembles. Every word is a struggle out of a clinch, and his voice is barely louder than a whisper. The mind is there, though, and at the right moment he winks knowingly, just like he's giving a sign to his corner that he's all right.
----------------------------------------------------------
We would lose Carmen Basilio in 2012 and Gene Fullmer in 2015.

(I'll try to post the whole article for you guys and gals in the comments section of my FB group. It's a good, quick read)

text: Respectfully, not sure about that. The Raiders have moved on and will forever be the Las Vegas Raiders. As a person who grew up in the Bay Area, too many things have happened in the game itself and the rules, everything has changed. No disrespect meant as we have a beautiful state of the art home. This team now is located in a destination that is so popular that it will never make economic sense to move from this location ever again. The team is found its home. With that scenario there will never be the intimate feeling and the home-field advantage that was felt in all those glorious years playing at the Oakland Alameda County Colosseum. That environment, that spirit, that intensity, and thus pre-tailgates, well never be forgotten or duplicated. However, in Las Vegas the Raiders well begin new traditions and will raise more Super Bowl trophies again. Las Vegas gave the Raiders a solid financial future that Oakland in the end could never offer them. It's nobody's fault it's just the economic fact of life that California is economically bankrupt and NFL team owners better have a healthy money stream non-dependent on city governments helping fund teams in that state. I really do feel that both teams have moved on. The 49ers will always feel that the Raiders were a stepchild and never was the favorite team of the area. Fans can debate that statement tell the end of time but from a Raiders perspective the history, the drama, the atmosphere, will never be duplicated by the 49ers or any other NFL team. The Raiders in Oakland will always be one of the greatest legacies in the history of NFL football.

text:
Chula Vista real estate agent buys a boarded-up property. Walks in to find a squatter who refused to leave.

She offered cash for keys. He declined.

He damaged the property. Spray-painted graffiti on the walls. Had utilities turned on in his name while she paid the HOA fees that covered his water.

She filed an unlawful detainer case. The court process took nearly 10 months before the Sheriff's Department finally removed him.

Ten months.

San Diego Superior Court handled over 9,000 unlawful detainer cases in 2025. All assigned to a single judge.

One judge for 9,000 cases. That's why it takes 6-12 months to remove someone who broke into a boarded-up property and refused to leave.

Property owners have limited options when dealing with squatters. Police won't intervene. The court system is the only recourse.

By the time she got her property back, it was trashed. Damaged walls, garbage everywhere, slurs spray-painted inside.

This is what property owners are dealing with in California. Someone breaks into your property, and you have to spend months and thousands of dollars to get them out. Plus pay the mortage, property taxes, and insurance.

text:
Could Nepal’s catastrophic flood provide the excuse for an American military presence that later becomes permanent?

Washington has already announced emergency funding and offered to deploy a disaster response adviser. The United States has spent years trying to build ties with the Nepali Army through officer training, equipment grants, disaster exercises and high-altitude military cooperation.

Nepal’s strategic importance lies not only in its proximity to Tibet, but also in its reported potential reserves of uranium, lithium, rare earths, copper, iron and zinc.

In 2022, Nepal rejected the US State Partnership Program amid fears that a partnership presented as disaster preparedness could compromise its neutrality and establish an enduring American presence. Significantly, the current Prime Minister, Balen Shah, has now rejected offers of foreign search-and-rescue assistance following the flood, insisting that Nepal’s own security forces can manage the operation.

This suggests the new government understands the risks and is determined, at least for now, to protect Nepal’s sovereignty. But the pressure will undoubtedly continue, particularly as the scale of reconstruction becomes clear.

text:
“Down Fishing Creek”

On 18 August 1780, noon, just above the mouth of Fishing Creek.
Two days after Horatio Gates’s army came apart at Camden, Thomas Sumter’s column…about eight hundred militia and a thin spine of Continentals, two small guns, wagons of captured stores, and British prisoners taken at Carey’s Fort, halted on the west bank of the Catawba. 

The heat in the South Carolina backcountry in mid-August is not weather. It is an occupation. Men stacked their muskets. Some cooked. Some slept. Some went into the creek. Sumter, by more than one account, lay under a wagon. 

Across the river that morning, Banastre Tarleton had already done the thing Sumter assumed he would not do so quickly…crossed, discarded most of his infantry, and come on with roughly 160 men, about a hundred Legion dragoons and sixty foot riding double. He cut down the American sentries before they could give a proper alarm. Then he charged the stacked arms. 

That is the documented battle. It lasted minutes, not hours. American losses ran on the order of 150 killed or wounded and about 300 captured. Tarleton’s casualties were a handful. He recovered the wagons, the guns, the horses, the prisoners. Sumter got away coatless on an unsaddled horse and reached Charlotte two days later. The rest of the command scattered into the woods and water. battlefields.

Family tradition places Jacob Myers, born in Germany, brought over as a child, later a landholder in the Saxe Gotha country….among those men, serving under Sumter, about forty years old, an officer in a militia that had just learned, again, how expensive a noon rest can be. A later compiled note says he was with Sumter at ‘Fishing Creek’ “when he was surprised and his command badly used up and scattered by Tarleton.” That is not a muster roll. 

It is the kind of sentence families keep when the army’s paperwork burned with the wagons. A Captain Jacob Myers does appear later with the Camden District Regiment, in 1782. Rank in 1780 is harder to pin. The user remembers lieutenant. Tradition later says major. The battle itself does not name him. 

What the creek would have offered a man who still had his legs is not mystery. ‘Fishing Creek’ meets the Catawba north of present-day Great Falls. Downstream the Catawba takes the name Wateree. 

In August the water is warm, the banks thick, the swamps south of there a geography the British Legion hated and the Whigs used. 

Tarleton’s name, after Waxhaws that May, traveled ahead of his horses: Tarleton’s Quarter…the reputation, fair or inflated, that surrender was a poor bet. Patrols looking for stragglers would have been the second half of the fight. 

Reuben Harrison is easier to put on a map. He was a young Whig of the Wateree settlements in Fairfield District, later paid for militia service in 1781 under General William Henderson and Captain Thomas Starke on the Four Holes and Edisto. His land, over the years, sat on the Wateree and its creeks….Goose, Morrison’s, Dutchman’s, Thorntree. 

The plantation that family memory says hid a fleeing militiaman is the right neighborhood and the right politics. A document that he hid Jacob Myers specifically has not turned up in the public record. The friendship is tradition. The geography is not. 

The story can be told without inventing a diary is this….
A German-born militiaman in Sumter’s beaten column does what several hundred others did when the Legion came through the stacked muskets: he runs toward water. 

He works downstream, creek to river, river to swamp, while August does its work…heat, insects, the smell of a camp that has become a slaughter-yard in the time it takes to wake from a nap. 

The British and Loyalist riders comb the roads. The Wateree bottoms swallow a man who knows enough to stay off the high ground. 

@KickRocks2026

text:
Real-world results from the first legal psilocybin program in the United States show that guided psychedelic sessions can offer powerful, life-changing support for mental health. A comprehensive study published in JAMA Network Open by researchers at Oregon Health and Science University followed 346 adults who received psilocybin at licensed service centers across the state. The findings reveal that structured psychedelic experiences in community settings can deliver profound emotional relief outside of traditional hospital laboratories.

​Just one month after a single supervised session, an extraordinary 92.2 percent of participants reported that the experience had brought direct, positive benefits to their lives. Nearly sixty percent went a step further, describing their session as one of the ten most meaningful events of their entire lifetime. These outcomes highlight how intentional preparation, professional facilitation, and safe environments combine to help people process deep emotional burdens and discover renewed clarity.

​The positive effects extended well beyond the initial weeks, creating lasting improvements in everyday well-being over three months of structured follow-up. Participants experienced a sixty percent reduction in moderate to severe depression, alongside a seventy-one percent decrease in severe anxiety. Individuals navigating post-traumatic stress saw their symptom severity drop by sixty-five percent, accompanied by significant gains in daily emotional resilience and life satisfaction.

​Safety records throughout the statewide program proved equally remarkable, closely mirroring the rigorous standards established in clinical university trials. Fewer than two percent of participants experienced acute distress requiring medical evaluation, demonstrating that non-medical community frameworks can operate safely when led by trained, state-licensed professionals. As communities around the globe explore new solutions for mental well-being, Oregon’s real-world model provides compelling scientific evidence that regulated psychedelic care can expand mental health support safely and effectively.

Link to study: Korthuis PT, Cook RR, Gregoire D, et al. Safety and Mental Health Outcomes of Oregon State-Regulated Psilocybin Services. JAMA Network Open. 2026;9(8):e2630608. DOI: 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.30608.
