text:
Leo Frank Trial Dispute: The Blood Stains on the Machine Department Floor

By Dan Garcia

In the Atlanta Constitution of August 15, 1913, factory mechanic Charley Lee was called by the defense to explain the blood found on the second floor of the National Pencil Company near the ladies’ dressing room. The defense thesis was that these stains could have originated from an old workplace accident rather than from the murder of Mary Phagan on Saturday, April 26, 1913.

Lee testified about an accident involving factory worker J. E. Duffy on October 4, 1912, nearly eight months before Mary’s murder. Lee said Duffy “was cut on the finger and bled freely.” In the official Brief of Evidence, Lee described the injury as severe enough that the blood “spouted out,” and he said there was considerable blood on the floor near the dressing-room area.

On cross-examination, Solicitor Hugh Dorsey asked Lee what had happened to the blood.

“Who cleaned up the blood you are speaking of?”

“It wasn’t cleaned up.”

“Why?”

“They don’t clean up that way. The place is swept out once a week.”

“Can you go there now and find this blood?”

“No.”

The defense thesis therefore asked the jury to connect the suspicious stains found after Mary Phagan’s murder with an accident that had occurred nearly eight months earlier.

That explanation faced a serious difficulty when J. E. Duffy himself testified for the prosecution in rebuttal. Duffy confirmed that he had cut his fingers and bled, but his description of where the blood fell differed from Lee’s. Duffy testified, “A few drops of blood dropped on the floor at the machine where I was hurt.” He said the blood did not fall elsewhere and repeated on cross-examination that he had never seen his blood anywhere except at his machine.

The stains discovered after Mary’s murder were described by several witnesses who saw the machine department before or shortly after the crime.

Robert Pittman Barrett, a factory machinist, discovered the principal stain Monday morning, April 28. Barrett testified that he found an unusual spot near the west end of the ladies’ dressing room that he had never seen before. He said it had not been there when he worked Friday. Barrett described one principal spot approximately four or five inches across, accompanied by several smaller spots. Asked what it was, Barrett answered, “It was blood.” He also testified that a white substance appeared to have been wiped or smeared over the area with something resembling a coarse broom.

Mell Stanford provided particularly important testimony because he had personally swept the metal-room floor on Friday morning, April 25, the day before the murder. Stanford testified that the disputed spot was absent when he swept the floor. When he returned Monday, he saw what appeared to be blood near the dressing room with white haskoline spread over it. A large cane broom was nearby, and Stanford believed marks on the floor indicated that the broom had been used to spread the white substance. He said the blood spots were “right in front of the ladies’ dressing room” and “led right up to the door.”

Mrs. George W. Jefferson gave one of the clearest descriptions of the stains. Jefferson testified that she and Barrett saw the spot Monday morning. She described the stains as “dark red in color” with a white substance over them. Jefferson was familiar with the red paints and varnishes used in the factory and said the stains did not resemble the maroon red, red line, or bright red paint used there.

On cross-examination, Jefferson gave an especially important description:

“The white stuff there didn’t hide the red at all. You could see it plainly.”

N. V. Darley, who supervised manufacturing and labor at the factory, also examined the area Monday morning. Darley testified that the spots looked like blood with something white spread over them. He said, “The white stuff practically hid the spots,” but added that the stains could still be seen.

Darley then described what he believed the appearance suggested:

“It looked like there had been an attempt to hide them, but you could see the spots.”

Darley also described what appeared to be a smearing motion over the stains. His testimony gave the prosecution theory direct support that the white substance had been spread over the blood in an attempt to conceal it.

City Detective J. N. Starnes also saw the stains Monday morning. He described “splotches that looked like blood” near the end of the dressing room. Starnes testified that the principal splotch had a white substance over it and said, “The splotch looked as if something had been swept over it.” Portions of the stained floor were later removed for examination.

Atlanta Police Chief James Lafayette Beavers inspected the area as well. He testified that he saw what he considered “a splotch of blood,” together with several smaller spots extending toward the dressing room. Under cross-examination, Beavers acknowledged that he could not scientifically prove by sight alone that the substance was blood, although he said, “It looked like blood.”

Magnolia Kennedy also saw the dark spots and the white material covering them. She testified that the stains could be plainly seen from approximately ten or twelve feet away and said she had never previously noticed anything like them in the metal room.

Other defense witnesses acknowledged seeing the disputed area while questioning what the stains represented. Wade Campbell saw the spots near the ladies’ dressing room but could not identify them as blood. Lemmie Quinn also saw the area Monday and argued that the dirty factory floor made it difficult to determine whether the stains were blood, varnish, or oil.

The physical samples eventually reached Dr. Claude Smith, Atlanta’s city bacteriologist and chemist. Smith examined pieces cut from the floor and found blood corpuscles on one specimen. His examination established the presence of blood on that sample. He could not determine whether it was human blood, how old it was, or precisely how much blood had originally been present.

The Phagan family preserved an additional description of the scene through family oral history. According to that account, the white powder placed over the blood took on different shades of pink, crimson, and maroon where the blood showed through it. This description belongs to the Phagan family oral tradition and should be kept separate from the surviving sworn testimony.

The courtroom testimony itself still paints a striking picture. Jefferson described dark-red stains that remained plainly visible despite the white covering. Darley said the white substance nearly concealed the spots but left them visible and testified that the scene looked like an attempt to hide them. Barrett described the white substance as having been smeared or wiped over the blood. Stanford believed a large broom had been used to spread haskoline over the area. Starnes independently described something white as having been swept over bloodlike splotches.

The defense thesis that these stains originated with Duffy’s October 1912 injury was therefore difficult to accept. Lee described considerable bleeding and placed Duffy near the dressing-room area, while Duffy himself testified that only a few drops fell at his machine and that he never saw his blood anywhere else. Barrett and Stanford also testified that the suspicious spot had not been present when they were in the area on Friday, April 25.

The defense offered additional explanations, including the possibility that some of the discoloration resulted from varnish or other factory substances. The prosecution theory was that the stains represented recent blood associated with the crime and that the white substance had been spread over them in an effort to conceal them.

Taken together, the testimony of Barrett, Stanford, Jefferson, Darley, Starnes, Beavers, Kennedy, Duffy, and Dr. Smith gave the prosecution theory substantial support. Several witnesses described bloodlike or dark-red stains near the ladies’ dressing room. Two witnesses who knew the floor before the murder said the principal spot had not been there Friday. Multiple witnesses described white material spread over the stains. Darley explicitly said the appearance suggested an attempt to hide them. Laboratory examination later confirmed that blood was present on at least one of the floor samples.

The defense thesis required the jury to trace the stains back nearly eight months to an accident whose injured worker testified that his blood fell only at his machine. That contradiction, combined with the testimony concerning the newly appearing stains and the white substance spread over them, left the old-blood explanation with substantial weaknesses.

Transcript

Leo Frank Defense: Factory Mechanic Tells of Blood on Floor From Mans Wounded Hand

Atlanta Constitution

August 15th, 1913

Charley Lee, a mechanic in the pencil factory, who admitted on cross-examination that he had received a raise in salary within the past two weeks, was called to testify to a number of accidents on the second floor from which blood had been spilled in vicinity of the dressing rooms where blood spots were found after the tragedy.

“Do you remember an accident in the metal room on October 4, 1912?”

“Yes, a man named Duffy was cut on the finger and bled freely.”

“Was his finger cut to the bone?”

“Yes.”

“Did he go to the ladies’ dressing room while his finger was bleeding?”

“Yes.”

Solicitor Dorsey on cross-examination:

“What do you get for wages?”

“Thirty-two and a half cents an hour?”

“How long have you been getting that rate?”

“For two weeks.”

“What did you get prior to that?”

“Thirty cents an hour.”

“Did you tell anybody what you were going to swear in this trial?”

“Nobody.”

“How did they know what you were going to say, then?”

“I made a written statement.”

“Who cleaned up the blood you are speaking of?”

“It wasn’t cleaned up.”

“Why?”

“They don’t clean up that way. The place is swept out once a week.”

“Can you go there now and find this blood?”

“No.”

⚽️ FOLLOW BARCELONA ON COUNTERPRESS WITH THE 1899 ⚽️

Calling all Culers, a new way to follow FC Barcelona is launching on CounterPress in time for the new La Liga season. 

The 1899, named after the year Joan Gamper founded the Catalan giants, launches later this month with a mission to deliver the best English-language coverage of Barcelona.

The site is fronted by journalists Tom Sanderson, Neal Gardner and Pol Ferré Martínez.

After previously living in São Paulo and becoming The Guardian’s lead writer on Brazilian football, Tom has held the same function at Forbes on FC Barcelona since 2019 when he moved to the Catalan capital. He’s also had Spanish content editorial roles at The Daily Mail, and written for other outlets including The i Paper and The Blizzard.

Neal is a freelance football writer and content creator. An avid Barça supporter since childhood, he began sharing his thoughts on the club on Twitter during the pandemic, initially as little more than a passion project and a way to connect with fellow fans.

What started as a search for community has since grown into an audience of more than 205,000 followers. At the heart of Neal’s work remains the same passion that started it all: a love for Barça, football, and thoughtful discussion around the game.

Pol is a UAB journalism graduate that has recently completed an internship at one of the biggest radio stations in Spain, Onda Cero. 

He’s heavily involved in Catalonia’s grassroots system as a league-winning coach leading teams for eight years, or since he was 16. Growing up and living in Barcelona, he’s a lifelong Culer and member with a love of FC Barcelona passed down to him by his ancestors.

The 1899’s members can look forward to analysis, features, news, opinion and historical pieces related to the Blaugrana.

Tom said: "I promise that we’ll deliver Culers authentic, local, in-depth coverage from the Camp Nou press box and the stands of the Gol Sud to the best of our ability as not just journalists but also members of the club."

Neal added: “My goal with this project is to produce football writing that goes beyond the surface. In an environment increasingly driven by immediacy, headlines and clickbait, I want to create work built around nuance, context and genuine depth."

While Pol added: “Growing up in Barcelona, Barça have always been a part of my life. Having the chance to now combine my love with journalism and build a new media project around the club is something I’m incredibly excited about.

"Our goal is to offer Culers more than just the latest news. We want to bring a local perspective to widespread coverage, and stories told with the passion we feel for Barça."

The 1899’s early interest waiting list is now open, ahead of a full launch later this month. 

Barcelona supporters keen to explore the platform can secure an exclusive discount on membership by adding their details to the mailing list today.

text:
Little wonder there's so little trust in this agency, even now after nearly 2 years?
Daily Wire Bombshell Leads To Report Finding FEMA Illegally Skipped Trump Supporters’ Homes
By Jacob Wheeler
In a scandal first uncovered by The Daily Wire, a new Department of Homeland Security inspector general report found that a FEMA disaster response crew illegally skipped Florida homes displaying signs supporting President Donald Trump, as workers surveyed damage from Hurricane Milton without proper training.

In November 2024, The Daily Wire first exposed the FEMA scandal after multiple federal employees confirmed that a supervisor ordered disaster relief workers to “avoid homes advertising Trump” as they canvassed Lake Placid, Florida, to identify residents eligible for federal aid. Internal messages obtained by The Daily Wire showed that supervisor Marn’i Washington issued the directive both verbally and in a group chat used by the relief team, according to multiple government employees.

“This situation eroded public trust in FEMA’s ability to treat everyone impartially, offer unbiased and consistent assistance, and ensure equal access to resources and tools,” the inspector general’s report said.

The 25-page investigation concluded that the discrimination violated both FEMA policy and the Hatch Act. The 1939 federal law prohibits government employees from using their positions or government resources for partisan political activity.

FEMA disaster relief crews canvassed more than 744,000 homes and other locations after Hurricanes Helene and Milton. But a DHS watchdog found that workers deliberately skipped 11 homes displaying signs supporting then-presidential candidate Donald Trump.

Images obtained by The Daily Wire showed workers documenting the homes in the government system with messages such as “Trump sign no entry per leadership.”

Microsoft Teams chat used by FEMA workers.

“These issues occurred due to weaknesses in FEMA’s training, documentation, and oversight,” the inspector general’s report concluded. “FEMA DSA [Disaster Survivor Assistance] crews did not receive ethics and Hatch Act training before deploying to disasters, DSA policies and procedures did not require crews to explain why they skipped homes, and DSA crew leaders were not required to conduct quality control reviews of survivor interactions.” 

Investigators also interviewed 18 random FEMA Disaster Survivor Assistance crew members deployed during the natural disasters and found 11 who said they never received Hatch Act training.

Hurricane Helene slammed into Florida’s Gulf Coast as a Category 4 storm on September 26, 2024, unleashing catastrophic flooding and devastation that killed hundreds and caused billions of dollars in damage from the Gulf Coast to the mountains of North Carolina. Less than two weeks later, Hurricane Milton struck near Siesta Key, Florida, as a Category 3 storm, battering communities still reeling from Helene. 

President Biden quickly approved major disaster declarations for Florida, North Carolina, and Tennessee, unlocking federal aid to help survivors clean up and begin rebuilding.

As FEMA scrambled to respond to the back-to-back disasters, the agency called on a DHS Surge Capacity Force, drawing volunteers from other DHS agencies to bolster its understaffed workforce ahead of Hurricane Milton.

“I know they’re short-staffed, I thought we could go help and make a difference,” one of the employees told The Daily Wire at the time. “When we got there we were told to discriminate against people. It’s almost unbelievable to think that somebody in the federal government would think that’s okay.” 

The employee said it felt wrong to discriminate against Trump supporters when they were at their “most vulnerable.” 

“I volunteered to help disaster victims, not discriminate against them,” the employee said. “It didn’t matter if people were black, white, Hispanic, for Trump, for Harris. Everyone deserves the same amount of help.”

The guidance came as the Biden administration faced mounting criticism over what many rural communities described as a lackluster response to Hurricane Helene. In Roan Mountain, Tennessee, for example, residents told The Daily Wire that it took nearly two weeks for FEMA to arrive. Carter County, where the town is located, voted 81% for Trump.

The FEMA workers ordered to bypass homes displaying Trump signs were operating in Highlands County, a deep-red region of south-central Florida that backed Trump with 70% of the vote. The county was battered by tornadoes, torrential winds and rain, and flooding when Hurricane Milton struck in October.

The inspector general’s report laid out the limited exceptions in which FEMA workers could skip homes, including “hostile” interactions with residents, no-trespassing or private-property signs, hazardous debris, or purple paint marking a property as off-limits.

Political signs supporting Trump were not among the exceptions.

The inspector general reviewed thousands of FEMA canvassing records and identified 11 cases with notes indicating potential political bias. The workers logged the skipped homes under generic categories such as “Not Able to Access Property” and “Private Property.” 

“However, in the notes field all 11 surveys included the name of then-presidential candidate Donald Trump to explain the reason for skipping the homes,” the investigation found. 

One of the homes skipped by FEMA/ FEMA app tracking what homes were visited.

The report could not determine whether FEMA workers used similar discriminatory tactics elsewhere in the country as communities reeled from hurricane devastation.

“We could not determine if crews skipped locations for unallowable reasons during other disasters because the support contract for FEMA’s Field Assessment and Collection Tools ended in September 2025 when then-Department of Homeland Security Secretary Noem did not act on FEMA’s request to fund it before expiration,” investigators said.  

Looking forward, the inspector general issued four recommendations: strengthen ethics and Hatch Act training before deployments, create a system to document survivor interactions, and require FEMA crews to standardize how they record skipped homes and the reasons for doing so. 

After The Daily Wire broke the story, a FEMA spokesman said the agency was “deeply disturbed” and “horrified” by the employee’s actions, and that it has “taken extreme actions to correct this situation.”

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters headed into his traditional preseason round table facing some probing questions which didn’t, for once, exclusively revolve around unresolved financial charges.

After a World Cup which delivered on its hype, littered with gripping games and glittering star names, could the Premier League provide a compelling follow-up act?

Masters wasn’t impressed.

“I’m absolutely confident that what people are going to see is a fantastic competition,” he declared in no uncertain terms. Whether that assurance will hold throughout the coming 10 months remains to be seen, but the opening round of fixtures didn’t let him down.

There was some dazzling play spread across the first 10 games, several giants were toppled and a man even got a haircut. What more could you really ask for? Unai Emery admitted that Aston Villa “lost our balance emotionally” after falling 1–0 down to Brighton & Hove Albion. The humiliation which followed inside the opening half-hour proved his point, but the prickly manager looked to have lost the wrestling match with his own emotions in a bizarre prematch interview.

To answer the question of why top scorer Ollie Watkins had been omitted, Emery simply refused to offer anything more than a single word: “Silence.” It was easy to mistakenly think that Igor Tudor was grimly pacing Tottenham Hotspur’s technical area at the Gtech Community Stadium on Sunday rather than Roberto De Zerbi. A pitiful display befitting the short-lived interim’s disastrous tenure was made all the more embarrassing by the $300 million transfer spend which came before it. Michael Carrick insisted that he was not as calm as his outward demeanor may have suggested in the wake of a humbling defeat to newly promoted opposition on Saturday. If only his players had not done such a good job of disguising any whisper of energy or endeavor themselves.

United’s vulnerability in transition, toothlessness in attack and the unorthodox approach of grappling their own teammates, rather than the opposition, at set pieces all tested Carrick’s control over his calm exterior.

text:
Florida voters mostly delivered a series of  setbacks Tuesday to antisemitic and anti-Israel candidates, while  handing decisive primary victories to several prominent pro-Israel  candidates in widely watched contests that offered a sigh of relief to  supporters of the Jewish state.

The clearest rejection came in Florida’s 6th  Congressional District, where incumbent Republican Rep. Randy Fine, a  Jewish and strongly pro-Israel lawmaker, overwhelmingly defeated  social-media personality Dan Bilzerian. Fine received 56.9 percent of  the vote, compared with just 18.7 percent for Bilzerian.

Bilzerian’s campaign became nationally notorious for its antisemitic rhetoric,  including praise for Adolf Hitler and attacks targeting Fine’s Jewish  identity. His campaign also used AI-generated imagery to mock the  congressman. The rhetoric drew condemnation from both Republican House  Speaker Mike Johnson and Democratic Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries.

Bilzerian, a scandal-plagued social media personality, largely  centered his campaign around his virulent hatred of Jewish people. He  diagnosed that the key issues for the US can be sourced to “the real  root cause of the problem, which is Jewish supremacy.” He wrote that his  campaign would aim to “End Jewish Supremacy” and proclaimed that “this  country is being run into the ground by Jewish Special Interests.”

Fine’s victory was particularly significant  because the race offered Republican primary voters an unusually stark  choice. Fine has himself attracted criticism for inflammatory statements  concerning Muslims and Palestinians, but Bilzerian made antisemitism a  conspicuous feature of his campaign. In the end, nearly three times as  many Republican voters chose Fine as chose Bilzerian.

Another prominent figure on the far-right  fringe, James Fishback, also failed to break through in the Republican  gubernatorial primary. Fishback, who had attracted attention for  inflammatory rhetoric and associations with the online far right,  finished a distant third with 10.5 percent of the vote, far behind US  Rep. Byron Donalds (47.8 percent) and Lt. Gov. Jay Collins (25.2  percent).
Fishback has drawn criticism for relentlessly attacking Israel and veering, at times, into antisemitic discourse. While addressing  students at the University of Central Florida back in February, Fishback  said he “will not visit the country of Israel under any circumstances.”  The candidate went on to mock the Western Wall, calling it a “stupid  wall.”

Fishback has also criticized Donalds for arranging a forum at a south  Florida synagogue, accusing the congressman of expressing favoritism  toward Jewish people. The insurgent candidate further came under fire  for praising supporters of antisemitic social media personality Nick  Fuentes as “patriots” and “civil.” He has accused Israel of committing  genocide in Gaza and stated that the supposed “genocide” should be  taught in Florida public schools. The failed candidate also disparaged  the food quality in the state’s public schools as “goyslop,” an  antisemitic term popularized online.

The Republican results were matched by a series of victories for pro-Israel Democrats.

Rep. Jared Moskowitz, one of the Democratic  Party’s most outspoken supporters of Israel and a prominent Jewish voice  in Congress, decisively defeated Democratic Socialists of  America-backed challenger Oliver Larkin in the Democratic primary for  Florida’s 25th Congressional District. Moskowitz won 63.5 percent of the  vote, dealing a significant blow to the effort by the party’s activist  left to unseat him. According to reports, Moskowitz dominated in heavily  Jewish regions of the district such as Palm Beach.

Larkin had criticized US military assistance to  Israel and campaigned from the party’s progressive left. He accused  Israel of committing a “genocide” in Gaza. Moskowitz, by contrast, has  consistently defended Israel and has emerged as one of the Democratic  Party’s most prominent congressional advocates for the US-Israel  relationship. His fierce defense of Israel has made him somewhat of an  outlier in a party increasingly critical of the Jewish state.

The victory was particularly notable because  the redrawn 25th District is significantly more competitive in November,  meaning Democrats will need a candidate capable of holding the seat in a  difficult general election. US President Donald Trump won the district  by 9 points in the 2024 election. Moskowitz will now face Republican  Scott Singer in this year’s general election.
Corey Walker, The Algemeiner

text:
Shaquem Griffin ran a 4.38 forty at the NFL Combine.

That was the fastest time by a linebacker in fifteen years.

He also benched 225 pounds twenty times, using a prosthetic to attach his left arm to the bar.

Because Shaquem Griffin does not have a left hand.

He was born with amniotic band syndrome, a condition that occurs in about one in every 1,200 births, where fibrous bands in the womb constrict a developing limb. His left hand never formed properly and the fingers caused him constant pain.

And here's the detail that tells you who this kid was at four years old.

One night the pain was so bad that Shaquem got out of bed, walked into his family's kitchen, and grabbed a knife with the intention of removing his own hand.

His parents had it amputated the next day.

He kept playing football anyway, alongside his identical twin brother Shaquill, who is one minute older.

Coaches doubted him at every level. Youth football. High school. College recruiting.

And when Shaquill started getting offers, including from his dream school Miami, he told the recruiters something.

If you want me, you take my brother too.

Central Florida's coach said yes to both.

At UCF, Shaquem became the American Athletic Conference Defensive Player of the Year in 2016 and defensive MVP of the Peach Bowl in UCF's undefeated 13-0 season.

And the NFL still didn't invite him to the Combine. He only got in as a late addition on January 30.

Then he went to Indianapolis and broke it.

The 4.38 was the same time his twin brother had run the year before, and Shaquem is 33 pounds heavier.

Richard Sherman tweeted that if he didn't get drafted in the first two days, the system was broken.

Pete Carroll, after the Seahawks interviewed him: "I don't know if I've ever been in a more inspirational interview that we do at the combine than that one."

On the third day of the 2018 draft, Seattle took him 141st overall.

The same team his brother played for.

His reaction: "It was literally like a dream. It was unexplainable. I couldn't ask for anything in the world than to be with my brother."

He became the first player with one hand to be drafted in the modern era, and then he started in his very first NFL game.

He wasn't a feel-good story who got cut in camp. He made the roster twice, was one of Seattle's best special teams players, had a sack in a playoff game against Green Bay, and generated the pressure that led to a pick six against the Rams.

Two brothers made a deal as kids that they would do it together.

They did.

text:
Stanley Schachter told volunteers they were about to be given an electric shock, then offered them a choice about where to wait. The women chose to sit with strangers. The men chose to sit alone.

That result sat as a curiosity for decades, until Shelley Taylor's group at UCLA went back through hundreds of stress studies and found the same split everywhere they looked.

Fight or flight was described in 1932 and became the account of how a body handles threat. It was also built almost entirely on male subjects. Taylor's argument, published in Psychological Review in 2000, is that the physical surge holds for everyone while the behaviour splits.

Her name for the female pattern is tend and befriend. Under stress, protect the young, then go and find other women.

The chemistry proposed underneath is oxytocin, the same hormone that runs between a mother and her infant, working alongside oestrogen and the body's own opioids. Oxytocin turns the stress response down. Taylor's team suggested that friendship between women may have been built on top of the mother-infant machinery, borrowing a system that already existed.

Rena Repetti found the behavioural version in ordinary households. After a hard day at work, women came home and turned toward their children. Men came home and withdrew.

The theory has had pushback, particularly on how well it travels outside Western samples, and one study of 237 young adults found both sexes reported tending and befriending more than any other response.

What nobody disputes is the starting point. The textbook account of how a human body handles fear was written from men, and the other half was left to be discovered in 2000.

Frances Tiafoe has withdrawn from the U.S. Open mixed-doubles event because of the hand/wrist problem he has been managing for several weeks. He is still entered in the U.S. Open singles draw.

Betting implication: Tiafoe’s singles status has not changed, but the mixed-doubles withdrawal confirms the injury is still active enough to affect workload decisions. He should not be treated as fully healthy in early-round singles pricing, especially in long matches where serving, forehand acceleration and cumulative hand stress could become limiting factors.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL — Memphis at UNLV, Saturday 10:00 ET — UNLV PLANS QB SPLIT

UNLV is expected to split quarterback work between Jackson Arnold and Alex Orji in the opener against Memphis rather than commit immediately to one full-time starter.

That creates a materially different offensive setup from a conventional QB1 arrangement because the two quarterbacks offer different skill sets and could be used situationally.

The current market is roughly UNLV -4.5 to -5.5, with the total approximately 56.5 to 60 depending on the book.

Betting implication: A planned quarterback rotation increases offensive variance and complicates first-half and player-prop projections. It is not automatically a downgrade, but any handicap assuming Arnold would operate the entire offense should be adjusted. The wide total range across books also makes line shopping especially important before assigning meaning to any apparent move.

text:
ベッセント米財務長官が、なぜ日本の円買い介入について異例ともいえる長い説明をする必要があったのか

発端は円安そのものではなく、米議会から「なぜ米国の公的資産を使って日本円を買ったのか」と正式に説明を求められたことです

民主党のエリザベス・ウォーレン上院議員は8月13日、上院銀行委員会の民主党筆頭委員としてベッセント氏に書簡を送り、米財務省が7月末の円買い介入にESF＝為替安定化基金を使った理由、介入額、米国側のコスト、法的根拠、ECBとの事前協議などについて回答を要求しました

回答期限は8月28日でした

つまり今回の書簡は、28日に円安が進んだから突然出されたものではなく、議会監督への回答という性格が強いものです

問題になったのはESFという仕組みです

ESFは財務長官が大統領の承認を得て外国為替などを取引できる基金で、通常の歳出のように個別案件ごとに議会の新たな予算承認を取る仕組みではありません

実際、財務省は既に保有していた外貨資産を円へ交換したと説明しており、日本政府に資金を貸したわけではありません

この点ではウォーレン氏の書簡冒頭にあった「日本が返済できなければ米国納税者が負担する」という前提は取引の性質と一致しておらず、ベッセント氏は「日本は財務省に何も借りていない」と強く反論しました

ただし、それで議会側の問題提起がすべて消えるわけではありません

ESFは財務長官に大きな裁量が認められている一方、法律上は取引状況を議会へ報告する制度があり、今回のような約30年ぶりの異例の円買いについて「米国の国益として何を守ったのか」を議会が問うこと自体には重要な意味があります

そこでベッセント氏が示した最大の正当化理由が、円相場と米国債市場のつながりです

日本は米国債の主要保有国であり、ベッセント氏は円相場が無秩序になれば市場参加者のポジションが強制的に巻き戻され、世界の金融市場が不安定化し、最終的には米国の家計や企業の借入コスト上昇につながり得ると説明しました

これは非常に重要です

米国が円を買った理由を単純に「日本を助けるため」と見ると本質を見誤ります

ベッセント氏が議会に示した論理は、円市場の混乱を放置すれば米国債の需給や長期金利にまで波及し、結果として米国自身がコストを負う可能性があるため、その連鎖を防ぐことが米国の利益になるというものです

つまり今回ベッセント氏が弁明を迫られた本当の理由は、日本支援の是非だけではありません

議会の個別承認を必要としない強力なESFを使い、外国通貨である円を買うという異例の政策判断について、「なぜそれが米国の国益なのか」を説明する必要が生じたからです

そして今回の回答から見えてくるのは、米財務省が円相場をもはや日本だけの問題ではなく、米国債市場と米国の長期金利にも波及し得る金融安定上の問題として捉えているという点です

text:
Everyone knows Jackie Robinson broke baseball's color line in 1947.

That same year, a 5'7 Japanese American from Ogden, Utah broke basketball's.

His name was Wataru Misaka, and almost nobody has heard of him.

He was born in 1923 to Japanese immigrants. His father was a barber who died when Wat was 15. He grew up in an Ogden that one account described as virtual apartheid.

Then December 7, 1941 happened, and being Japanese American in this country became something else entirely.

The government forced tens of thousands of Japanese Americans into incarceration camps. Misaka's family avoided it only because Ogden sat outside the exclusion zone.

His teammates weren't all so lucky. And that matters in a minute.

He played at Weber Junior College, won two championships, and transferred to the University of Utah in 1943.

In 1944, as a freshman contributor, Utah went to Madison Square Garden and beat Dartmouth 42-40 in overtime for the NCAA championship.

It was the first title game in history to require overtime. The next one wouldn't happen until 1957.

It remains the only national championship in University of Utah history.

At the victory parade back home, Misaka's mother pulled him aside to tell him he'd been drafted into the United States Army.

He went. He served in military intelligence as an interpreter in East Asia. He rose to Staff Sergeant. He was sent into Hiroshima after the bomb and saw what was left of it.

A Japanese American soldier, fighting for the country that had imprisoned his neighbors, walking through the ruins of the country his parents came from.

Now the part that will get you.

Every player on that 1944 championship team received a red blanket, embroidered with a white U and a championship emblem. A keepsake.

Misaka's teammate Masateru Tatsuno had family locked in the Topaz internment camp in the Utah desert.

So Misaka took Tatsuno's blanket to Topaz and gave it to his family himself.

A national championship blanket, hand delivered into a prison camp, so a family behind barbed wire could hold the thing their son had won.

Misaka came home from the war, returned to Utah, and led the Utes to the 1947 NIT title, which at the time was as prestigious as the NCAA tournament.

In that final against Kentucky, Misaka guarded Ralph Beard, the national player of the year.

He held him to ONE POINT.

That summer, the New York Knicks drafted him in the first ever BAA draft, the league that became the NBA.

Wataru Misaka became the first non-white player in the history of professional basketball. Three years before Earl Lloyd became the first Black player in the NBA.

He played three games and scored seven points.

Then, after the team's first road trip, Knicks boss Ned Irish cut him. No explanation was ever given.

He was 24 years old. The Harlem Globetrotters offered him a spot. He turned it down.

He went home to Utah, became an engineer, and lived a quiet life there for the next seventy years.

When NPR interviewed him decades later, he described being drafted into the NBA as an insignificant event.

He genuinely did not think it was a big deal.

Wataru Misaka died in November 2019 at 95 years old.

Utah's athletic director said it right: he was bigger than the game of basketball, blazing trails into places nobody of his descent had gone before.

Three games. Seven points. A door that has never closed since.

text:
🚨 The Joke’s on Us: Musk, Tehran, and the Transatlantic Network Behind the Weaponised Meme.

Elon Musk has reposted a video to his own @X feed, credited to the account @BasedMikeLee, showing his own face grafted onto footage of a 1960s dance sequence, styled after Austin Powers. The caption read: “ELON MUSK: man who bought the UK.”

Within hours it had racked up 4.7 million views, 142,000 likes and 14,00000 reposts on Musk’s own account alone.

@BasedMikeLee is not an anonymous meme account. It is the personal X account of Mike Lee, the sitting senior US Senator for Utah, run by Lee himself since 2022. That reframes what happened here: a sitting foreign legislator, not a random amplifier, gave the video its first serious push before Musk gave it its enormous one.

The two men have a documented mutual-admiration habit on the platform; two months before the Austin Powers repost, Musk had already publicly praised one of Lee’s threads as deeply insightful. Lee is no marginal figure inside the Republican party.

A Brigham Young University study identified him as the most ideologically extreme senator of the 113th Congress, and he has spent the past several years amplifying Infowars content and Jan. 6 conspiracy theories, on top of rejecting the scientific consensus on climate change and calling the concept of the US as a democracy an active danger to be avoided.

He currently sits on the advisory board of the Alliance for Responsible Citizenship (ARC), alongside Sir Paul Marshall, lead investor in GB News, and Alan McCormick, the channel’s chairman. A US senator with that profile amplifying an AI-generated claim that Musk owns Britain, on the same advisory board as two of the men who bankroll and chair one of Britain’s own news channels, is not incidental context. It is the Transatlantic network the ‘joke’ travels through.

The video did not originate with Musk, or with Lee, either. It was first posted the previous evening by an account called DFF, @DumbFxckFinder, a Los Angeles-based operation that describes its own output as “fighting DumbF*ckery 24/7 via AI-powered music vids & memes.” DFF has built a following of close to 60,000 on a diet of exactly this kind of content, at volume, since April 2025.

The video’s actual path is therefore four links long: a dedicated AI-content account manufactures the clip, a sitting US senator with a track record of conspiracy amplification and a seat on a UK-media-linked advisory board gives it its first serious reach, and the owner of the platform itself then reposts that repost to roughly 210 million followers.

This was not a stray algorithmic boost or a like Musk forgot to hide. It was a deliberate act, at the top of a laundering chain running through elected office and media ownership networks on both sides of the Atlantic, that took a small studio’s output and gave it the reach of a head-of-state-adjacent global platform in a matter of hours.

DFF is not a neutral joke account that happened to catch Musk’s eye. Fact-checkers at Snopes traced a fabricated image purporting to show New York mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani as a child alongside Jeffrey Epstein, Ghislaine Maxwell, Bill Clinton and Bill Gates back to the account, complete with a Google SynthID watermark confirming it was AI-generated; when the image recirculated later, the small “DFF” watermarks the account had originally attached were gone, stripped in a way that made the fake harder to identify as such.

Tommy Robinson has separately praised and shared a DFF video called “Welcome to Islamington,” urging his own followers to give the account a follow. And in March 2026, DFF was producing mocking AI content aimed at Iran’s leadership over the death of the country’s supreme leader. This is an account with a settled political alignment and a documented history of content mistaken for real, not an aimlessly funny meme farm that happened to make a video about Musk.

Taken alone it looks like just another entry in a long run of Musk-adjacent deepfakes aimed at the UK, from the fabricated Farage-Bailey brawl footage that circulated earlier this year to the AI-generated image of Keir Starmer in a bikini that Musk himself posted, and, in the same window as the Austin Powers clip, a second AI video of Musk performing a stunt jump in a Union Jack-liveried Cybertruck.

Taken as part of a pattern, it looks like something else: a deliberate application of a #propaganda technique already road-tested on a much larger stage.

That stage is the Iran-US-Israel information war. Since the conflict escalated last year, pro-Iranian accounts, several believed by researchers to be linked to Tehran, have flooded English-language social media with AI-generated Lego-style animations.

Set to rap soundtracks and built around cartoon figures of Trump, Netanyahu and assorted devils, the videos mock American power, accuse Washington of running on Epstein-file corruption, and frame the war as a doomed imperial venture against a seven-thousand-year civilisation.

#Propaganda researchers who have studied the genre note its sophistication is deliberate: catchy, funny, and disposable enough to spread on its own momentum, while carrying genuinely inflammatory claims underneath the cartoon gloss. As one scholar told the Associated Press, the strategy exploits popular culture against the country that arguably invented it.

The Austin Powers video works on exactly the same principle, and that is the point worth dwelling on. It is not an isolated bit of billionaire trolling, and the fact that Musk sits at the end of a laundering chain rather than having built the edit himself does not weaken the point; if anything it sharpens it.

This is precisely how the format is designed to work: a dedicated content account produces material that is deniable and disposable, a credentialed amplifier gives it a first push and a veneer of institutional legitimacy, and the powerful amplifier at the top lends it overwhelming reach while retaining the “I just shared a joke” plausible deniability defence at every stage.

It’s the same mechanic, adapted to a domestic British target, deployed by a platform owner who reporting in the @FT says actively discussed ways to destabilise the Starmer government and has floated replacing Farage with a more pliable Reform leadership, and passed through a sitting senator whose own record of amplifying conspiracy content is well established.

Musk did not stumble into meme warfare. He owns the platform where it circulates, he has posted fabricated images of the former UK PM, and his own site has hosted AI-generated smears of Farage and Bailey severe enough that Farage himself had to publicly disown them. Treating the Austin Powers video as comedy rather than strategy misreads what it is for.

The 4chan lineage

None of this technique is new in form, only in scale and sponsorship. Meme warfare as a deliberate tactic, using humour, irony and plausible deniability to spread ideas that could not survive being stated plainly, has its modern roots in 4chan’s /pol/ board, where the “just joking” register was refined precisely because it let extreme content travel under the protection of ambiguity. Anyone offended could be told they had failed to get the joke.

What has changed is who now uses the technique, with what resources, and at what scale. DFF is a small, obviously commercial version of the same production logic Iranian researchers attribute to Akhbar Enfejari: a dedicated account, openly branded around manufacturing this content, pumping out AI-generated attack material on a rolling basis for whichever audience will share it.

Akhbar Enfejari does it for an anti-American, pro-Tehran audience; DFF does it for whichever side of Anglophone online politics is currently amplifying it, in this instance Musk himself. The ideological content differs. The production model does not.

It also has a domestic British face. The Crewkerne Gazette account, revealed this year to be run by Joshua Bonehill-Paine, produces exactly this kind of satirical AI-adjacent political content, and has built a genuine following on X and YouTube for AI-generated videos depicting real politicians.

Bonehill-Paine is widely described in UK coverage as a former neo-Nazi activist; he has a 2014 conviction for malicious communications over a hoax that led to death threats against the owners and staff of a Leicester pub and was jailed in 2015 for a racially aggravated harassment campaign against the Jewish former Labour MP Luciana Berger, having previously described himself as a proud antisemite.

Despite that record, the Conservative Party selected him this month as its candidate for Crewkerne South on Somerset Council in the 2027 local elections, a decision Kemi Badenoch has publicly defended, and which has drawn condemnation from the Board of Deputies of British Jews and others. Bonehill-Paine says he has now withdrawn from next  year’s local elections, and that the Conservative leader had instead asked him to become an adviser to the party’s culture and integration  commission, where he will focus on how young men become radicalised.

The pipeline from openly fascist activism to “just a satire account” to selection as a mainstream party candidate runs through the same laundering mechanism that makes the Musk, DFF and Iranian videos work: humour as cover, virality as validation, and “it’s a parody” as a legal and rhetorical shield that arrives pre-loaded whenever anyone objects.

The Legatum thread

Lee’s presence on the ARC board is not the only tie worth tracing. Christopher Chandler, the New Zealand-born billionaire who made his fortune in Russian gas and founded the Dubai-based investment firm Legatum in 2006, is himself one of ARC’s co-founders and he also sits on its advisory board, alongside McCormick, a Legatum partner, and Marshall.

ARC’s co-founder and executive chair, Baroness Philippa Stroud, previously served as chief executive of the Legatum Institute, the same body that later became the Prosperity Institute. Legatum’s philanthropic arm has funded that think tank since 2007, originally under the Legatum Institute name and renamed the Prosperity Institute in January 2025; the renamed body remains, by its own account, funded overwhelmingly by Legatum.

Matt Goodwin, now a GB News presenter, was the institute’s founding director of its Centre for UK Prosperity before his GB News career, and he stood earlier this year as Reform UK’s candidate in the Gorton and Denton by-election. During that campaign, Tommy Robinson endorsed Goodwin unprompted on X. 

Reform’s own spokesman publicly rejected the endorsement, saying Robinson “isn’t welcome in the party,” and Farage has separately called Robinson “not what we need.” Goodwin himself never repudiated Robinson by name. When Labour’s deputy leader Lucy Powell wrote to him directly asking him to condemn the endorsement and remove Robinson-linked supporters from his campaign, Goodwin replied only that he “reject[s] all extremism” in general terms, without naming Robinson or clarifying whether his supporters would be excluded.

This is the same Tommy Robinson who separately promoted the DFF account that made the Musk video.

Two further ARC advisory board members hold live positions inside Reform UK itself: Danny Kruger, who defected from the Conservatives, now heads the party’s transition-to-government operation, and James Orr, the Cambridge philosopher who joined ARC’s advisory board before becoming Farage’s senior adviser in October 2025, was appointed Reform UK’s head of policy in February 2026.

Farage himself has gone well beyond engaging with the Prosperity Institute from a distance. He spoke at ARC’s February 2025 conference in London, where Marshall, ARC’s director, had personally donated £1 million the previous year, and was interviewed on stage by Jordan Peterson, the controversial Canadian psychologist who co-founded ARC alongside Stroud. On his podcast, Jordan Peterson has also interviewed Tommy Robinson, painting him as a heroic, persecuted truth-teller rather than a divisive, multiply convicted far-right criminal with a history of violence.

In the ARC interview, Farage told Peterson he was not a scientist and could not say whether carbon dioxide was driving warming, while in the same breath dismissing the idea that CO2 counts as a pollutant and crediting sunspots and underwater volcanoes with more climate influence than humanity, a claim that climate scientists have long rejected. He later returned to the Prosperity Institute directly, delivering a speech on economic policy in April 2026 that the institute’s own site wrote up approvingly.

These high-profile appearances do crucial ideological work: they build the institutional credibility that allows an outrage-generating or ‘parody’ meme/video to land not as fringe internet noise, but as a legitimate political signal.

Farage’s own record of climate denial, aired from ARC’s stage, sits alongside Lee’s rejection of the same scientific consensus and McCormick’s history of sharing climate-sceptic content, a strand of shared conviction running through the network as well as a shared address book.

Marshall’s own financial position gives that conviction a harder edge. A Guardian and DeSmog investigation published in July 2026 found that Marshall Wace, the hedge fund Marshall chairs, had almost tripled its declared fossil fuel holdings to $2.8 billion (£2.1 billion) by the end of the first quarter of 2026, with its stake in Chevron alone growing from $196 million to $864 million over three months. Over the same period, the fund’s holdings in renewable energy and battery companies fell by 30 percent, to $415 million.

Marshall Wace called the analysis partial and inaccurate but did not offer alternative figures. Yet it is precisely this underlying financial scale that underwrites the entire media ecosystem; without this balance sheet, the platforms and networks that normalise and amplify disposable AI clips simply would not exist.

GB News, the channel Marshall part-owns and McCormick chairs, is widely reported to give regular airtime to guests who question climate science and oppose net zero policy, criticism that predates this investigation but that the fund’s own trading now gives a concrete financial backdrop.

None of this is proof of a coordinated operation; think tanks, TV channels and advisory boards routinely share personnel and funders without anyone directing traffic between them.

But it is a documented, densely overlapping network: Legatum’s money, ARC’s platform, GB News’s airtime and Reform’s front bench all run through a small number of the same people, and the Austin Powers video landed inside it rather than beside it. This ecosystem acts as an echo chamber that strips away the origin story of a 10-second AI clip, transforming a disposable bit of digital chaff into potent, weaponised political media.

Why the format matters

None of this network made the Austin Powers video, and none of it needs to have known the video existed for the point to stand. What Lee’s ARC seat, Farage’s own turn on ARC’s stage, and the Legatum money running underneath both show is that the joke did not arrive into a vacuum. It arrived into an already-built infrastructure of mutual amplification, shared donors and overlapping advisory boards that spans a US senator, a British party doing well in the polls, and the news channel that covers that party most favourably, all of it bound together in part by a shared willingness to dismiss inconvenient science, whether about the climate or, in DFF’s case, about what is real and what is generated.

What connects Tehran’s Lego animations, Musk’s Austin Powers skit and Bonehill-Paine’s output is not ideology, obviously, Iran and the Anglophone right are not, in most respects, natural allies.

What connects them is a shared recognition that comedy formats are currently the most efficient vector for political content on social platforms, precisely because media literacy training, platform moderation and journalistic fact-checking are all built to catch claims, not ‘jokes’.

A claim can be debunked. A joke can only be called unfunny, which changes nobody’s mind and does nothing to the algorithm that is busy rewarding it with engagement.

This matters more, not less, because the actors involved are so different. State information operations, platform-owner activism and home-grown extremist content creators are usually analysed as separate problems, requiring separate frameworks: foreign interference law for one, platform policy for another, domestic extremism monitoring for the third.

But the technique underneath all three is converging, and the fact that it is converging is itself informative. It suggests less a coordinated conspiracy than a shared, correctly identified gap: British and American publics, and the institutions meant to inform them, currently have no good answer to propaganda that arrives as ‘just a joke’.

The instinct to shrug off Musk’s Austin Powers video as an eccentric billionaire’s idea of a joke is exactly the instinct these formats are built to exploit. The Lego videos survive scrutiny for the same reason. So does the Crewkerne Gazette.

Calling all three what they are, a coordinated exploitation of the humour loophole in how democracies police political communication, is a necessary first step in closing the loophole.

Starmer accused Musk in January 2025 of spreading lies and misinformation that undermine British democracy, and returned to similar language over Musk’s amplification of the grooming-gangs scandal. Farage, for his part, has spent the past eighteen months alternately courting Musk’s money and being publicly humiliated by him, including being told by Musk that Reform “needs a new leader.”

A video captioned “man who bought the UK,” laundered through a partisan AI content farm and amplified by Musk himself to millions, arrives into that history rather than starting a new one. It reads less like a joke about Musk’s influence than an assertion of it, one that Starmer and Farage have already, in effect, conceded in their own responses to him.

The video may be funny, but it’s no laughing matter.

text:
Rant incoming: I love Kalani too. But I genuinely don’t know how to view this as anything other than a massive misplay on his part.

If BYU isn’t delivering things it committed to in the new deal, then Kalani better have exhausted EVERY option internally before airing dirty laundry 3 weeks before the season.

And honestly, I find it completely implausible that BYU just signed him to a massive new contract and then immediately decided, “Nah, we’re not honoring it.”

We also just did this 8 months ago. The Penn State circus happened the week of BYU’s biggest game in decades. Kalani engaged with them. It became a massive distraction. Players admitted afterward it affected preparation. Then BYU got absolutely waxed by Texas Tech.

And somehow the lesson from that is…let’s create another public firestorm right before the next season?

That’s what I don’t get.

And I REALLY don’t buy this narrative that BYU refuses to invest in football.

Kalani just got a monster raise.

ARod was pursued hard by Utah. He didn’t stay for free.

BYU was willing to spend huge money to keep Jay Hill from Michigan and nearly pulled it off.

Bear Bachmeier’s camp says an SEC school offered him $5M to enter the portal. He stayed.

Satuala had Michigan and others coming after him. He stayed.

LJ got NFL-level money to stay and not enter the draft (I’m hearing north of $2 million).

Ryder Lyons had every elite program in America chasing him. He signed with BYU.

Then look around the building. New weight room. Facilities. Nutrition. Players’ meals. Offices. Entrance. Staffing. Everything.

Did all of that happen because BYU suddenly became really good at asking people to take discounts?

Come on.

Maybe Kalani wants MORE. Fine! Heck, give football every dollar BYU can responsibly throw at it.

But “I want more resources” is VERY different from “BYU hasn’t stepped up” or “Santiago broke his promises.” And people are treating those as interchangeable without actually knowing what’s going on.

And this goes way beyond Kalani just implicating Brian too.

Has Kalani taken this to Keith Vorkink? Shane Reese?

If not, what the heck is he doing talking to the media about it?

And if he HAS, and it still hasn’t happened, then maybe…just maybe…this isn’t Brian Santiago sitting in his office stroking a white cat and refusing to give football money.

Maybe there are legitimate reasons why his demands aren’t being met.

Yet Cougar Nation has somehow skipped discovery, trial and deliberation and gone straight to hanging Santiago in the town square because somebody’s buddy’s donor’s barber has “sources.”

I like Kalani. I want him here. I think the last two years have been tremendous.

But reputation doesn’t give him a blank check either.

He’s the head coach. Fall camp is underway. This might be the most anticipated season in BYU history.

At some point, whatever grievance you have, your responsibility is to the 100+ guys in that building preparing to play football.

So what exactly is the endgame here?

Because I cannot figure out how publicly undermining your own athletic department 3 weeks before kickoff gets BYU one inch closer to winning a Big 12 championship this season.
