text:
My Adventures in LA LA Land Part 8

The multiple-engagement funeral scandal of legendary Los Angeles financier Roger Mathers didn't merely make the news.
It exploded.
Within a matter of days, the story had gone from an unbelievable rumor whispered at a funeral to a full-blown national media circus. Every television station in Los Angeles had a reporter assigned to it. Instagram was overflowing with memes. TikTok creators were reenacting the scandal. Facebook was hosting heated arguments between people who had never met Roger Mathers and were now absolutely convinced they knew everything about him. Even Twitter—where outrage was practically a competitive sport—was having a field day.
The headline was simple:
DEAD FINANCIER EXPOSED AS SECRET FIANCÉ TO FOUR WOMEN.
And the women of Los Angeles were furious.
Then the story took an even darker—and considerably more bizarre—turn.
Somebody discovered Roger Mathers' gravesite.
Before long, angry women were showing up with cans of spray paint, leaving messages on his headstone such as:
CHEATING DOG.
F-BOY.
And, perhaps most succinctly:
YOU GOT WHAT YOU DESERVED, ROGER.
It became so bad that cemetery security had to be increased, and the Los Angeles Police Department was asked to keep an eye on the grave.
Apparently, even death had not provided Roger Mathers with a sufficient cooling-off period.
But the person caught squarely in the middle of this media hurricane was none other than Bianca Rosario.
To the television cameras, Bianca was no longer simply a glamorous and ambitious Los Angeles councilwoman.
She was now The Other Woman.
The Hussy.
The Temptress.
The Alleged Homewrecker.
And because Bianca was already a well-known Southern California political figure, controversy seemed to follow her around like a thundercloud looking for a lightning rod.
KTLA — SIX O'CLOCK NEWS
The scene opened outside Los Angeles City Hall.
Bianca was making her way toward the entrance for the evening City Council meeting when a crowd of angry women gathered behind police barricades began shouting at her.
"Homewrecker!"
"Other woman!"
"How could you do that to those women?"
"She stole Roger!"
One woman held up a cardboard sign:
BIANCA — FOUR WOMEN CAN'T ALL BE WRONG!
Another read:
ROGER'S FIANCÉE #4!
Bianca kept walking.
She had learned long ago that when surrounded by television cameras, protesters and microphones, the safest facial expression was one that said absolutely nothing.
Unfortunately, that was difficult to maintain when twenty angry women were yelling your name.
CUT TO KTLA NEWS DESK
Anchor Joe Birdwell sat behind the desk, wearing the grave expression normally reserved for earthquakes, wildfires and politicians caught doing something embarrassing.
"Good evening. The Roger Mathers scandal continues to grow tonight as new allegations have surfaced involving Los Angeles Councilwoman Bianca Rosario."
Joe shuffled his papers dramatically.
"According to sources familiar with the investigation, Councilwoman Rosario allegedly knew that the late financier was romantically involved with another woman when she began dating him—and may have deliberately pursued Mathers anyway."
He looked directly into the camera.
"Those allegations have not been independently confirmed."
A pause.
"But they have certainly made for a fascinating evening of television."
Joe turned toward the monitor beside him.
"KTLA's Katlyn Morales is standing by live outside Los Angeles City Hall."
CUT TO LIVE REMOTE
Katlyn Morales stood on the sidewalk, microphone in hand, with a cameraman behind her and the unmistakable chaos of City Hall unfolding in the background.
"And Joe, things are getting very heated here tonight."
Behind her, another protester could be heard shouting:
"ASK HER ABOUT THE OTHER FIANCÉE!"
Katlyn turned toward the approaching Bianca.
"Councilwoman Rosario!"
Bianca kept walking.
Katlyn followed.
"Councilwoman Rosario, were you aware that Roger Mathers was allegedly engaged to another woman when you began dating him?"
Bianca didn't stop.
"Councilwoman, did you know about the other women?"
Nothing.
"Did Roger Mathers tell you that he was engaged to three other women?"
Bianca continued toward the City Hall entrance.
"Councilwoman Rosario, did you deliberately pursue Mr. Mathers after learning about his other relationships?"
Bianca finally stopped.
For one brief second, she turned toward the cameras.
Her expression was perfectly composed.
"No comment."
And then she walked through the doors.
Katlyn turned back toward the camera with the satisfied expression of a reporter who had just obtained exactly the eight seconds of television she needed.
"There you have it," she said.
"Councilwoman Bianca Rosario, when asked whether she knew that Roger Mathers was engaged to other women, declined to comment."
Katlyn paused.
"Back to you, Joe."
BACK TO THE NEWS DESK
Joe Birdwell nodded solemnly.
"Katlyn Morales reporting live from Los Angeles City Hall."
He looked down at his notes.
"And coming up after the break: Who were the four women Roger Mathers was allegedly engaged to—and why did none of them know about each other?"
A dramatic musical sting played.
Joe smiled faintly.
"Stay with us."
The screen faded to commercial.
And somewhere in Los Angeles, Roger Mathers was probably wishing he had been cremated.
It was a chilly Saturday morning in Southern California, the kind where the air carried a crisp edge even under the bright sun. Rene Twistylegger walked along the wide jogging and biking path, her two schnauzers trotting ahead on their leashes. Foxie wore a burnt-orange Texas Longhorns dog sweater that stood out against her wiry coat, while her other schnauzer Moxie sported a blue-and-silver Dallas Cowboys sweater. In the background, kids shouted and laughed as they played soccer and softball on the nearby fields. Adults jogged past or glided by on bikes, the path busy with weekend energy.
Coming toward them from the opposite direction was a very handsome man walking two sturdy Airedale terriers—Fluffy and Muffy—while two small children trailed alongside him. The four dogs spotted one another and slowed, tails up, noses working as they sized each other up. True to form, they circled and began sniffing each other’s rumps with focused curiosity.
Rene reined in her leashes and offered an apologetic smile. “Sorry about my dogs. They’re big on curiosity and just love to smell each other’s rumps all the time.”
The man chuckled, keeping a relaxed hold on his own dogs. “Nah, don’t worry. That’s just what dogs do—it’s like a doggie form of a handshake between people. By the way, my name’s Bill Sternhagen. What’s yours?”
“Rene. Rene Twistylegger. Glad to meet you.” They shook hands briefly while the dogs continued their thorough introductions.
Rene glanced at the two children. “Are these your kids?
“Yes, they are. We’re out for a morning walk with the dogs.”
“Where’s Mrs. Sternhagen?” she asked lightly.
Bill’s expression stayed easy. “Oh, she’s not here. We’re divorced, and I get the kids on the weekends.”
“I see,” Rene said with a nod.
Bill’s gaze drifted to the colorful sweaters on her schnauzers. “By the way, where did you get those doggie sweaters? Texas Longhorns and Dallas Cowboys, huh? You from Texas?”
“Well, Austin to be more precise,” Rene replied. “I got those from my ex-boyfriend back in Austin.”
“Really? Is he still around in the picture?”
“No,” she said. “We broke up years ago. He was a really great guy, but we’re no longer together.”
“Well, that sounds interesting,” Bill said with a small smile.
One of the kids tugged at his sleeve. “Daddy, can we go? You promised some ice cream cones.”
Bill laughed. “That’s my cue. Nice to meet you.”
“Likewise,” Rene answered.
As they started to move past each other, Bill paused and turned back. “So… would you like to have dinner with me tomorrow night?”
Rene hesitated for a moment, then found she couldn’t quite resist the combination of a good-looking man and the easy way he was with his kids. She accepted, and they quickly exchanged phone numbers before the little group continued on their way toward ice cream, the dogs giving one last sniff over their shoulders.

The next night, René and Bill were having dinner together when Bill finally brought up the question that had been nagging at him.
"Okay, I have to ask you something," he said. "Who's this mysterious doggie-sweater benefactor of yours? The guy who apparently keeps your dogs better dressed than most people in Los Angeles?"
René laughed.
"That would be an ex-boyfriend."
"An ex-boyfriend?" Bill raised an eyebrow. "Judging by those sweaters, he must have been one hell of an ex-boyfriend."
"He was," René said, smiling wistfully. "His name was Barrington Swenson Lasstier. He was an older man, very handsome, very kind, and incredibly generous. Super intelligent a man with a quick whit and super sharp brain. We were together for almost two years."
She paused for a moment.
"And honestly, Bill, he was a real Prince Charming."
Bill leaned back in his chair.
"Okay. I'm listening."
"He was always sweet and romantic with me. He was affectionate, attentive, and constantly making me feel beautiful. He'd hug me, cuddle with me, kiss my neck and shoulders, and tell me how much he adored me. At night, he'd hold me close and tell me I was the girl of his dreams and that someday he wanted us to have a serious, long-term relationship."
René smiled.
"I loved that man. I really did."
"Sounds pretty serious."
"It was."
She took a sip of her wine.
"I'll never forget Valentine's Day. I woke up that morning and found a little arrangement beside the bed. There were Hershey's Kisses, rose petals, and a handwritten note."
"What did it say?"
René smiled as she recited it from memory.

"Some girls are kind,
some girls are really sweet,
and some girls are as beautiful as they can be.
But if you're lucky, you'll meet a girl like René—
who just so happens to be all three."

Bill shook his head.
"Okay. That's actually pretty damn good."
"My heart melted."
She laughed softly.
"He was always doing things like that. When I was working at Hooters on Riverside, in Austin he'd sometimes show up during my break with a Frappuccino or my favorite sushi. He knew exactly what I liked."
"That's dangerous," Bill said. "A man who knows your favorite sushi order."
René laughed.
"Then there were the late-night IHOP dates."
"IHOP dates?"
"Romantic blueberry-pancake dinners after my shift."
Bill stared at her.
"Blueberry pancakes?"
"Don't laugh. At midnight, after working a long shift, those pancakes tasted like filet mignon."
"Fair enough."
"And the funny thing is, for the entire two years we were together, he never cheated on me. Not once."
Bill nodded thoughtfully.
"So who exactly was this guy? Because, René, you're making him sound like a pretty tough act to follow."
René's smile faded slightly.
"Well, there's a story behind why he was the way he was."
"I'm listening."
"Before me, Barrington had a girlfriend named Monica. And he wasn't good to her."
"How bad?"
"He was struggling with drugs and alcohol at the time. He treated her terribly. She left him because of his drugs and alcohol addition problems. It devastated him to lose her, but he learned his lesson the hard way."
René looked down at her plate.
"So then he went into rehab. During one of the group meetings, he made a promise—an oath, really—that he would never mistreat a woman he loved again."
Bill nodded slowly.
"And he kept that promise?"
"With me, absolutely."
She smiled.
"If anything, I think he overcompensated. He wanted to make sure I never doubted for one second that I was loved."
"Wow," Bill said. "So the Prince Charming routine wasn't just an act."
"No. Not with me."
René paused before continuing.
"And then there was Francesca."
"Another girlfriend?"
"Yes. After Monica, Barrington dated Francesca. Her mother owned a real-estate business, and Francesca helped promote it. Her mother would have these little promotional items made—pens, notepads, things with the company's logo on them."
Bill smiled.
"Old-school advertising."
"Exactly. Around Halloween she'd get Halloween pens. Christmas brought Christmas pens. Fourth of July meant patriotic pens."
René laughed.
"And Barrington would help Francesca distribute them to local businesses and people around town. They'd go around together handing out pens and trying to drum up business for her mother's company."
Bill nodded.
"So what's the connection to Barrington now?"
René's expression became more serious.
"One night, Francesca got drunk and decided to drive."
Bill's smile disappeared.
"Barrington tried to stop her. He did everything he could to convince her not to get behind the wheel."
"But she drove anyway."
René nodded.
"She was killed in a terrible drunk-driving crash. And so were three other people."
Bill sat quietly for a moment.
"That's horrible."
"It devastated him. For the longest time he blamed himself for not doing more to take away her car keys that night"
René stared toward the restaurant window.
"I don't think he ever completely got over it. Even years later, till this day he still gives away those promotional pens—to schoolchildren, to people in businesses, to anyone who will take one."
"Why?"
"To honor Francesca's memory."
Bill was silent.
René smiled faintly.
"That's Barrington. He's made mistakes. Big ones. But when he loves someone, he loves them completely. And when something terrible happens, he carries it with him."
She looked back at Bill.
"So yes. The doggie sweaters were from Barrington."
Bill chuckled.
"Well, René, I have to admit something."
"What?"
"I thought you were going to tell me about some rich guy who spoiled you and your dogs."
"He did."
Bill laughed.
"But apparently I was getting the abridged version."
René smiled.
"You asked."
"Yeah," Bill said. "And now I understand why you still have such a soft spot for the guy."
René nodded.
"I'll always have a soft spot for Barrington."
She looked down at her plate and smiled.
"Some people come into your life and leave you with memories."
"And Barrington?"
"Barrington left me with memories—and two very well-dressed dogs.”
"So why did you break up with him?" Bill asked.
René was quiet for a moment.
"It was me."
Bill looked surprised. "You?"
"Yes. Me."
She slowly set down her fork.
"I just wasn't used to having a man treat me that way. All the other guys I'd been with were jerks and losers. Most of them seemed interested in only one thing—getting me into bed. Barrington was completely different, and honestly, I didn't know how to handle it."
Bill listened without interrupting.
"I think the root of my problem goes all the way back to my childhood. I had what people would probably call 'daddy issues.' My father was a drug addict and an alcoholic, and when I was very young, he was killed during a high-stakes poker game."
Bill's expression changed.
"That's a lot for a little girl to deal with."
"It was."
René took a breath.
"I felt abandoned. And then my stepfather came into my life, and for years he was a jerk to me. So I grew up carrying all this emotional baggage. Daddy issues, abandonment issues—you name it. I was basically riding the struggle bus with a monkey on my back."
Bill gave her a sympathetic smile.
"And then along came Barrington."
"Exactly."
She smiled sadly.
"Here was this man who was patient with me. Kind to me. Affectionate. He wanted to make me feel safe and loved. He wasn't trying to use me. He wasn't playing games. He actually wanted a future with me."
"So why couldn't you accept it?"
"Because I didn't know how."
René looked down at the table.
"I think some part of me was so accustomed to being disappointed by men that when somebody finally treated me well, I didn't trust it. I kept waiting for the other shoe to drop."
She sighed.
"I couldn't bring myself to love Barrington the way I knew I should have. And that's probably the saddest part. He deserved somebody who could love him without being afraid of being loved."
Bill was quiet.
"So you left."
"I did."
"Where did you go?"
"Los Angeles."
She smiled.
"I came out here to start over. I wanted to pursue acting, build my yoga business and become the person I'd always wanted to be."
Bill nodded.
"And Barrington?"
René's expression softened.
"He moved to El Paso to help his mother run the family business."
"And did he ever find somebody else?"
René smiled.
"Yes."
"Who?"
"A UTEP cheerleader."
Bill laughed.
"You're kidding."
"Nope."
She laughed too.
"They met in El Paso, fell in love, and they've been happily married ever since."
Bill shook his head.
"Well, I guess he did all right."
"He did better than all right."
René paused.
"He found exactly what he was looking for."
"And you?"
René gave him a bittersweet smile.
"I found Los Angeles."
Bill smiled.
"That's not exactly the same thing."
"No," René said softly. "It isn't."
She looked down for a moment before adding:
"Barrington was the one I let get away."
Bill didn't say anything.
René continued.
"And now, looking back, I realize something."
"What's that?"
"Sometimes the person you think you have to leave behind is actually the person who was trying to help you become who you were supposed to be."
She smiled sadly.
"I regret leaving him."
Bill leaned back in his chair.
"So the doggie sweaters..."
René laughed.
"Yes. They're from the one who got away."
Bill shook his head.
"Well, René, after hearing this story, I think those dogs aren't wearing sweaters."
"What are they wearing?"
"Memorials to the greatest romantic blunder in Los Angeles history."
René burst out laughing.
"Bill!"
"What? I'm just saying."
He raised his glass.
"To Barrington."
René raised hers.
"To Barrington."
They clinked glasses.
"And to the ones who got away," Bill added.
René smiled.
"Especially those."

A week later, the four amigas—René, Carlotta, Bianca and Maggie—were having lunch together when René suddenly leaned across the table with a mischievous smile.
"I have news."
Carlotta immediately perked up.
"Uh-oh. That sounds dangerous. What happened?"
"I'm dating a new man."
"Tell us everything," Carlotta said.
René smiled.
"His name is Bill. He's a single father of two, and he's a mathematics professor at UCLA. He's intelligent, sweet, funny, and incredibly handsome."
Bianca raised an eyebrow.
"So what's the catch?"
René sighed.
"His children."
Maggie laughed.
"Children? That's the catch?"
"Trust me," René said. "Children can be very enthusiastic about expressing their opinions at the worst possible moment."
Bianca leaned forward.
"Okay. Now you've got my attention. How bad could it possibly be?"
René looked around the table.
"Let me put it this way. Bill and I were having a very hot sex in his bedroom when suddenly—"
She paused for dramatic effect.
"—his two kids burst through the door."
Carlotta nearly spit out her drink.
"No!"
"Yes!"
René continued.
"They started jumping on the bed like it was a trampoline."
Maggie started laughing.
"What were they doing?"
"They were yelling, 'Daddy! Take us to the beach!'"
Bianca covered her mouth.
"While you two were in bed?"
"Unfortunately, yes."
René shook her head.
"And because the mattress was bouncing underneath us, the entire bed started moving up and down like some kind of amusement-park ride."
Carlotta was laughing now.
"So basically you and Bill were getting bounced around by the kids?"
"Exactly!"
René pointed at her.
"Except there was nothing romantic about it. We were both getting knocked around like clothes in a dryer."
Maggie wiped a tear from her eye.
"So you two accidentally invented Trampoline Romance."
"Trust me," René said, "there was nothing romantic about it."
Bianca laughed.
"How did the kids react?"
"Well, eventually one of them stopped jumping and looked at us."
René paused.
"Then came the question."
Carlotta grinned.
"Oh, no."
René nodded.
"He looked at us and said, 'Daddy... are you two having SEX?'"
The entire table erupted.
Maggie nearly fell out of her chair.
"What did Bill say?"
"I don't know!" René said. "I was too busy trying to disappear underneath the blankets."
Bianca was laughing so hard she could barely speak.
"And then?"
"Then the kid asked, 'Is that how you're supposed to have sex? By bouncing up and down on the bed like you're riding a trampoline?'"
Carlotta slapped the table.
"Children really do ask the questions adults desperately don't want to answer."
René shook her head.
"Bill looked like he wanted the earth to open up and swallow him."
Maggie grinned.
"Well, you never know. Maybe you and Bill have just pioneered a revolutionary new California lifestyle."
Carlotta joined in.
"Forget yoga. Forget Pilates. Forget SoulCycle."
She raised her glass.
"Introducing Trampoline SEX Romance: the newest workout sweeping Southern California!"
Bianca laughed.
"Ten minutes a day and you'll strengthen your core, improve your balance and completely traumatize your children."
René groaned.
"You girls are terrible."
Maggie leaned back with a grin.
"Hey, in Los Angeles, anything can become a business opportunity."
Bianca nodded solemnly.
"That's true."
Maggie looked at her.
"Especially if Bianca's grandmother can supposedly invent a secret cake recipe involving a dolphin."
Bianca stared at her.
"Please don't bring Grandma into this."
The four women burst into laughter.
René shook her head.
"I swear, I tell you girls one embarrassing story and somehow it turns into a new California fitness craze."
Carlotta raised her glass.
"That's friendship, honey."
Maggie nodded.
"And market research."
The four amigas clinked their glasses together.
And René suddenly realized that dating a single father might be considerably more complicated than she had originally imagined.

ChiChiMarieMcGulliacudy 
was a psychic witch—stunningly beautiful long raven haired brunette, sharp-eyed, and thoroughly mischievous. She delighted in causing harmless, hilarious chaos wherever she went, and restaurants were her favorite playground.
With a simple wiggle of her magic nose she could lift food right off someone’s plate and deposit it onto her own. One moment a perfectly good meatball sat in front of a diner; the next it was gone, already halfway to ChiChi’s mouth. She had perfected the art of mooching without ever leaving her seat.
One evening she spotted a couple at a nearby table enjoying sushi. With a quick nose-wiggle she floated several pieces onto her own plate, took a neat bite out of each, then sent the half-eaten sushi gliding silently back. The man looked down, frowned, and turned to his wife.
“Ethel, why did you take chomps out of my sushi?”
Ethel stared at the plate in genuine confusion. “I didn’t touch it!”
He scowled, shoved the plate toward her, and muttered, “Here—you eat it then.”
Another night ChiChi grew bolder. She levitated half-eaten pieces of steak, lobster tail, and dinner rolls from one diner’s plate and gently dropped them into the open purse of the woman sitting beside him. Later that evening the woman arrived home, opened her purse, and discovered the stolen leftovers. Convinced her date had been sneaking food off other people’s plates to smuggle home, she was furious. She marched him straight to the door and threw him out of her apartment.
And that is how ChiChiMarieMcGulliacudy—the beautiful, troublemaking psychic witch—makes her entrance in the next chapter of My Adventures in LA LA Land.

text:
**Dolly Parton founded the Dollywood Foundation in 1988 and built extensive philanthropy focused on education/literacy (especially for children), medical research, disaster relief, and community support in her native East Tennessee and beyond.**

### Dollywood Foundation and Education Initiatives
She created the foundation shortly after opening Dollywood to inspire educational success in Sevier County, Tennessee (her home area). Early efforts included the Buddy Program, which offered $500 to seventh- and eighth-graders who graduated high school; this helped drop the local dropout rate from about 35% to 6%.

The foundation also provides the Dolly Parton Scholarship (typically $15,000 each to five Sevier County high school seniors annually) and has supported employee education (e.g., covering tuition/fees/books for Dollywood workers pursuing college).

### Imagination Library (Signature Program)
Launched in 1995 through the Dollywood Foundation and inspired by her father Robert Lee Parton’s illiteracy, this program mails one free, age-appropriate book each month to registered children from birth to age 5 (regardless of income). It began locally in Sevier County and expanded nationally then internationally (U.S., Canada, UK, Ireland, Australia).

By 2025–2026 it had gifted more than 300 million books (with reports of over 3 million per month at peak and totals cited around 300–332 million). It includes options like braille/bilingual books and has been a major focus of the foundation’s spending.

### Medical Research and Health Causes
- In 2020 she donated $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville, supporting research that contributed to the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine.
- Additional gifts to Vanderbilt included $1 million (around 2017) for the Monroe Carell Jr. Children’s Hospital and another $1 million (2022) for pediatric infectious disease research.
- She has supported breast cancer awareness (e.g., via benefit performances and recognition from Susan G. Komen) and other health efforts, including contributions tied to women’s services at local medical centers.

### Disaster Relief
- **2016 Sevier County/Smoky Mountains wildfires**: Created the My People Fund, which provided monthly aid (e.g., $1,000/month for months to hundreds of families who lost homes) plus a final payment; total relief reached roughly $9–12.5 million, bolstered by a telethon that raised over $13 million.
- **2024 Hurricane Helene floods** (East Tennessee and nearby): Personal $1 million gift to the Mountain Ways Foundation, matched by another $1 million from her businesses and the Dollywood Foundation (total ~$2 million).

### Other Efforts and Recognition
Additional work has included animal/wildlife support (e.g., bald eagle sanctuary efforts at Dollywood, earning a U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Partnership Award), hospital fundraising, and various community causes. In 2022 she received the Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy and the Bezos Award for Courage and Civility (which included $100 million directed to charities of her choice via her foundation). She was also recognized in TIME’s philanthropy lists.

Her giving has often started locally (“charity begins at home”) and scaled globally, with a consistent emphasis on literacy, opportunity for children, and helping “her people” in times of need. The Dollywood Foundation remains the primary vehicle.

text:
We Know How to Solve the Housing Crisis. We Just Have to Remember.

NYT Gift Article link
Listen · 7:48 min
23AUG2026,
By Christopher Serkin & Daniel J. Sharfstein
https://t.co/AKbiqmMgc4
Mr. Serkin and Mr. Sharfstein are professors at Vanderbilt Law School.

In a housing crisis that has now stretched across two decades, Americans have spent years arguing about the local regulations governing what and where people can build.

Should suburbs allow homeowners to add garage apartments?

Should cities continue setting aside land for parking spaces?

Should it be easier to approve the construction of apartment towers?

These are important debates, but they also reveal how narrow our imagination has become.

Millions are struggling to afford rent or buy a home.

Policy responses thus far have mostly amounted to crossing out onerous rules in the hope that profit-minded developers will then build more housing.

Even Congress’s newly passed bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act focuses mostly on streamlining regulations to stimulate more private building.

The act includes many important reforms and is an excellent start, but it does not go nearly far enough to address the scale of the problem.

We forget that America once confronted a housing crisis with far more urgency and ambition.

As World War II raged across the globe, millions flooded into industrial centers to build ships, tanks and airplanes.

Workers slept in trailers, cars and overcrowded rooms, and rents skyrocketed. Housing shortages became so severe that they threatened the war effort itself.

So the federal government responded by treating housing as critical national infrastructure.

Washington reformed mortgage markets to allow more people to borrow more money.

It subsidized rental housing and capped rents.

It experimented with prefabricated construction techniques to reduce building costs and speed production.

In Virginia, for example, the government tried a new building process that involved spraying a concrete mixture onto spherical balloon forms, creating bubble houses that went up quickly and minimized the use of scarce war material.

And, crucially, the government directly built housing itself.

It converted hotels and school buildings into apartments and partnered with leading architects and planners to design new forms of housing to foster community engagement and improve workers’ quality of life.

Reformers advocated designs that could have had an enduring impact on postwar housing, planning entire neighborhoods with new kinds of homes that offered models for the future.

Credit...Xi Li for The New York Times

Talwani and Boasberg or two of a handful of judges who have gained notice by being openly defiant to not just the Executive powers of the President but the Supreme Court.

text:
There is a potentially quite remarkable argument and acknowledgment in yesterday's SCOTUS opinion.  I'm going to study this a bit more before I write on it it length, but all six of the Justices in the majority signed off on it by joining the Opinion.  Because it is per curiam, the point made can't be attributed to just one of them -- but it is probably better that all six in the majority are seen as the "author" in this regard.

The point is that the Executive branch can suffer "irreparable harm" at the hands of district judges who meddle and interfere with Executive branch operations at the very beginning of Executive branch activity such as that involved here.  

The three liberals response to that was "Well, what the Executive was about to do is patently illegal so interfering right at the start is justified."  

But the Majority disagreed -- whether the proposed conduct would ultimately be illegal is a question for another day.  The instructions to the subordinate officials was to act lawfully.  Maybe they do nothing, maybe they do something.  It is not for district judges' to prejudge prior to anything taking place.

This point can be extrapolated across much of the lawfare being waged against the Trump Admin. as it changes federal policy on a range of issues. 

I could be wrong, but this is the first outright expression by SCOTUS that lower court judges who act without jurisdiction are -- themselves -- doing "irreparable harm" to the Administration.

That goes beyond merely defining and enforcing the law.  It is a direct challenge by the six Justices to judicial activism at the district court level.

text:
It Is Time to Truly Wake Up

After respectfully listening to the Dharma discourse “Focusing Primarily on Cultivating One’s Own Dharma and Conduct” imparted by Namo H.H. Dorje Chang Buddha III, I came to a profound realization: It is time to truly wake up!

I am deeply grateful for the blessings of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!

Although I had listened to this Dharma discourse before, it seemed to have left almost no impression on me. Just as my Buddha Master said, it went in one ear and out the other. As soon as I finished listening, I forgot what I had heard. The teachings neither entered my mind nor touched my heart. I am truly ashamed of myself.

After listening to this Dharma discourse again, I came to understand more deeply the preciousness of Buddha Dharma, the true meaning of liberation, and how I should make use of my limited lifetime.

First, we must understand that Buddha Dharma is extremely precious and difficult to encounter. Why? Because only Buddha Dharma can enable us to end the cycle of birth and death and transcend the six realms of samsara in which we now exist.

In the past, when Dharma Master Nenghai listened to Geshe Jangba expound the Dharma, he could hear only one sentence each day and had to make a round trip of about 25 miles. It took him half a year to finish listening to that Dharma teaching.

There are also many people who learn Buddhism by studying Buddhist scriptures. Because many scriptures are written in classical Chinese, their meanings can be very difficult to understand. Even when someone can understand the words, the scriptures were compiled by the Five Hundred Arhats based on their recollections of the Dharma expounded by Namo Shakyamuni Buddha. Therefore, deviations in the meaning of the Dharma could inevitably have occurred, and what was recorded may not fully convey the perfect Dharma meaning spoken by the Buddha.

Today, we are able to listen directly to the perfect Dharma teachings of unsurpassed, complete enlightenment expounded by my Buddha Master（H.H. Dorje Chang Buddha III）. This is truly rare, precious, and extraordinarily auspicious!

When my Buddha Master （H.H. Dorje Chang Buddha III）expounds the Dharma, profound principles are explained in simple and accessible language, almost like having an everyday conversation. Deep principles of Buddha Dharma are presented to us clearly and understandably, enabling people of different levels of good roots to gain understanding according to their capacities.

Therefore, we must cherish every opportunity to listen to the Dharma!

Second, we must understand how swiftly impermanence can arrive. How much time do I really have left to waste? Impermanence can take my life at any moment, for death makes no distinction between the young and the old.

Since I have already encountered the true Dharma of H.H. Dorje Chang Buddha III, I must make good use of my time and genuinely cultivate myself according to the Dharma principles taught by my Buddha Master. I must integrate Buddha Dharma into my everyday life.

At every moment, I should recall the Dharma principles taught by H.H. Dorje Chang Buddha III and use them to examine my every word, action, and thought:

Do I truly have compassion?

Have I practiced patience and forbearance?

Have I let go of greed, anger, and ignorance?

Am I still entangled in worldly grievances and disputes over right and wrong?

Are the things I am doing bringing me step by step closer to accomplishment and liberation?

A human existence endowed with the freedoms and favorable conditions for learning the Dharma is difficult to obtain. Even more difficult is the opportunity to hear directly from H.H. Dorje Chang Buddha III the perfect Dharma teachings that enable living beings to end the cycle of birth and death!

All worldly phenomena are illusory and ultimately unreal. What, then, is there to cling to?

Isn’t that true?

The people and possessions I cherish most, everything I have worked so hard to obtain—I carefully protect them, constantly afraid that I might lose them. Joy, worry, and anxiety accompany me all the time.

But has this attachment really brought me happiness?

Is this truly the happiness I have always longed for?

Have I actually obtained it?

At the very moment I take my last breath, will any of these things still belong to me?

Therefore, I must clearly establish the true goal of my life: to end the cycle of birth and death and attain liberation.

On the path toward liberation, I must not keep looking around—admiring the scenery here one moment and envying someone else’s treasures the next. Doing so only delays my journey and wastes my precious life and time.

Cultivation means cultivating oneself.

I must listen to the Dharma teachings frequently, and whenever I understand even one principle, I should put it into practice through my actions, speech, and thoughts—the three karmas.

I must constantly examine myself:

Have I let go of greed, anger, and ignorance?

Am I practicing the Six Paramitas and the myriad Bodhisattva practices?

I should begin with the people closest to me. It is in front of those closest to us that we remove our disguises and reveal our true selves. In those relationships, all our shortcomings are exposed most clearly.

I asked myself sincerely: Am I truly compassionate toward my family?

Suppose I have just finished mopping the floor, and suddenly a large footprint appears on the spotless surface. At that very instant, anger and irritation arise within me. I glare angrily at the person responsible, only to receive a casual response:

“Just wipe it again. What’s the big deal?”

Not only was my effort unappreciated, but I also felt that it had been disrespected. My anger immediately intensified, and I raised my voice:

“Why don’t you clean it yourself?”

Such a trivial incident exposed the selfishness within me.

First, my effort was not truly selfless. I expected praise and respect in return. Second, I lacked tolerance and understanding. When someone failed to respect the results of my labor, instead of responding with compassion and patience, I gave rise to anger and resentment.

At the root of the problem was my failure to truly understand the impermanence of all phenomena. I had failed to realize that I should be selfless, compassionate, and forbearing, and that I should do only those things that benefit others.

Instead, I had neglected what was truly important while clinging to things that offered no help whatsoever toward my accomplishment and liberation—my pride, my dignity, my boundaries, and so on.

It is truly time for me to wake up completely.

I must make full use of this limited lifetime, take my Buddha Master (H.H. Dorje Chang Buddha III) as my role model, establish unwavering faith, rely upon correct understanding and correct views, and diligently cultivate my own conduct and practice my own Dharma.

I will strive to end the cycle of birth and death and attain liberation as soon as possible.

Written by: Qingxin Edited by: Sayi

text:
America's most advanced AI chips are going to a foreign spy chief who paid Trump's family $263 million.

Washington had blocked those chips for years. But the block came off right after the money landed.

Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan is the UAE's national security adviser. He runs the country's intelligence services, he's the brother of its president, and he controls its largest wealth fund. 

The press calls him the Spy Sheikh.

He also chairs G42, the Emirati AI company.

In January 2025, four days before the inauguration, an investment vehicle backed by Tahnoon put $500 million into World Liberty Financial, the Trump family's crypto company, for a 49% stake.

Trump's own financial disclosure shows $263 million of that went to Trump family entities.

Four months later Trump toured the Gulf, and Washington signed a preliminary agreement letting the UAE import 500,000 of Nvidia's most advanced chips a year.

Before that trip, the number under discussion for the whole country had been 100,000.

Under the new deal, G42 alone was earmarked for 100,000 a year. Tahnoon's own company got what the ENTIRE country had been offered.

To picture what that buys: 

G42 is building a five gigawatt AI campus in Abu Dhabi that could eventually hold up to 2.5 million of Nvidia's top chips. That's larger than any AI site announced anywhere on Earth, including Stargate.

And those chips were restricted for one documented reason: American intelligence believed they could reach China and end up strengthening the Chinese military.

The rule sorted countries into tiers, and the UAE landed in a restricted one specifically because of G42.

In 2022, US intelligence collected information suggesting G42 had passed flight software technology to Huawei. That technology allegedly turned up in Chinese air-to-air missiles.

That's the company that got the chips.

And the relationship kept going:

MGX, another firm Tahnoon chairs, settled a $2 billion investment into Binance using World Liberty's own stablecoin, handing the Trump-linked token its first real use -> Binance had paid $4.3 billion to settle American money laundering charges -> its founder pleaded guilty and served prison time -> Trump pardoned him later that year

In November 2025, Commerce issued the first actual license under that framework, clearing G42 to buy the equivalent of 35,000 Blackwell chips. Last month the administration eased the limits again.

Then on August 14 the Comptroller of the Currency gave World Liberty preliminary approval to run a federally chartered national bank.

And the Wall Street Journal reported Thursday who actually owns it. Tahnoon's vehicle holds 49%. The Trump family entity holds 38%.

None of that proves a trade, and the honest version has to say so. 

There's no evidence the money moved the chip decision, and a person close to the investment told the Journal it was never discussed with Trump. The White House denies any conflict. 

G42's imports carry security and reporting requirements built with the Commerce Department, and for every data centre G42 builds in the UAE it has to build one in America. The administration's AI czar David Sacks says the old controls were "never intended to capture friends, allies, strategic partners." And there's a real case that if America won't sell, Huawei will.

But strip the politics out and one fact is still standing:

The most strategically valuable product this country makes is being allocated to a foreign intelligence chief who has paid the sitting president's family hundreds of millions of dollars.

That's not a left or right problem. A national security restriction came off, and the payment that preceded it sits in the president's own disclosure.

What do you think of this?

text:
< Be Felix Frankfurter
< Born 1882, Vienna, Austria
< Your family is Jewish. Your father sells furs
< You speak no English when you arrive in New York at age twelve
< The Lower East Side swallows you whole
< You learn English from the streets, from the newspapers, from sheer will
< City College of New York, then Harvard Law School
< You graduate first in your class, 1906
< The most elite Wall Street firms see your credentials
< They also see your name. Your accent. Your face
< No offers
< You take a job with the U.S. Attorney's office instead
< Henry Stimson becomes your mentor. You become his weapon
< Prosecuting antitrust cases, corporate fraud, customs violations
< You discover you love the machinery of government
< 1914, Harvard Law School offers you a professorship
< You accept. You will stay for twenty-five years
< Your classroom becomes a forge
< You train an entire generation of lawyers who will remake America
< Dean Acheson. Alger Hiss. Tommy Corcoran
< They call themselves "Frankfurter's Happy Hot Dogs"
< You place them throughout the Roosevelt administration
< FDR calls you constantly. You never hold an official position
< You are the most powerful man not on any org chart
< You help draft the Securities Act of 1933
< You advise on labor policy, judicial appointments, everything
< 1939, FDR nominates you to the Supreme Court
< The first naturalized citizen ever appointed
< You replace Benjamin Cardozo. Another Jew. The seat becomes "the Jewish seat"
< Everyone expects you to be a flaming liberal
< You have spent decades defending civil liberties, fighting for labor
< You co-founded the ACLU
< Now you have real power. Lifetime tenure. No elections to worry about
< Here is where the story turns
< You become the Court's most aggressive advocate for judicial restraint
< The legislature decides. Not you. Not any judge
< Your former students are stunned
< West Virginia v. Barnette, 1943. Jehovah's Witnesses refuse to salute the flag
< You dissent. You think the school board can compel it
< You, the immigrant. You, the Jew. Siding with forced patriotism
< Your former allies accuse you of betrayal
< Hugo Black becomes your nemesis. You despise each other
< The Warren Court expands civil rights. You often stand apart
< The man who built the liberal legal movement watches it leave him behind
< 1962, you suffer a stroke. You retire
< 1965, you die in Washington
< Your former students run the government. Your philosophy does not

Felix Frankfurter spent his whole life believing that democracy meant trusting the people's representatives, not unelected judges.

The cruel joke is that his own disciples used judicial power to do what legislatures would not.

He trained the army that ignored his battle plan.

text:
Agree, SF is the worst place to build a tech company.

...at least for the first 1-3 years (if you're not already here).
- SF is expensive (good luck getting a house!)
- SF talent is hard to hire! (hard to convince ppl to join your startup for long hours and low pay if you haven't worked with them in the trenches before somewhere else and the labs are throwing them massive offers)

so yeah if you're a founder who 
- lives somewhere else
- has a nice house
- has a strong network there

...SF is a terrible idea for the first 1-3 years.  

The magic is what happens after the first 3 years.  

networks compound.  ideas compound.

also, the reality is most startups fail.  

Even if you don't think SF is best place to build a successful company...I think I convince you that SF is the best place to build a failed company.  

SF rewards founders for trying.  if you failed at your startup now you can
- get acquihired
- go to YC
- start a new company (now you are a repeat founder!)

Most ecosystems if you fail there is no good path to taking a step up. in SF, failure as a founder is an amazing way to advance your career!

I know failed founders who got acquihired by
- athropic / openai
- stripe
etc etc

if you fail in wisconsin...where do you go?

play that out over an entire ecosystem and you start to understand the magic.  

So yeah, SF sucks for 1-3 years.  don't let that deter you.  

you should be thinking in 10-30 year time horizons across multiple companies (failed and successful).

And if you do that, SF is obviously the best place.

don't get stuck in a short term local minima b/c change is hard.

Do you have to move to San Francisco to build a tech company?

"The common mantra is, 'Oh, the outcomes in SF are just so much bigger. That’s what its all about. You’ve got $100 billion companies, and I can’t name a single tech company in Wisconsin. So why would you waste time there? Just move to SF.'

But then you start pushing down. Where’s the most valuable cloud computing company in the world? What part of SF is it in? Seattle.

Or you’re like, it’s Silicon Valley, what part of SF is the largest manufacturer of silicon based in? Oh, they’re actually based in Taiwan.”

The next-generation social network that the whole world is clamoring for. What part of SF are they based in? Singapore.

The next great music company? Stockholm.

You start to find these all over. There's so much cognitive dissonance around these things. When you’re in SF, it’s a giant echo chamber."

text:
OttoGeoGraphica 
August 24, 2026
At Toll Rock and the Palisades 
(photo taken last sunset)
Green River, Wyoming

When accompanying surveyors to the Yellowstone area in 1871, landscape painter Thomas Moran painted “The Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone” with Lower Falls being the focal point. In 1872, Yellowstone became the country's first national park. See:
https://t.co/FShVMYWYF5

Moran arrived at Yellowstone from its southern entrance, reaching the west by rail, departing for Yellowstone here at Green River. He was familiar with these Green River cliffs then, but didn't actually paint “Green River Cliffs” until 1881. 

The cliffs are located west of the town, between Green River and Jamestown, and currently Interstate 80 passes between the two major rock formations in the painting (the big trucks visible on the highway offer perspective). The closest monolith is fittingly called Toll Rock. In 1974, my brother and I parked on the shoulder of eastbound I-80 and climbed a steep rise to Toll Rock’s north face, and from there, with some primitive rock climbing abilities, we summited, walking across its flatness and lay on our bellies to stare down at the river below.

The second rock formation(s), in the painting to Toll Rock's left, are called The Palisades, actual cliffs that are part of the western White Mountain escarpment.

The City of Green River has their Visitor Center near the spot where Mr. Moran set up his easel. 

The actual painting, “Green River Cliffs”, is proudly on display at The National Gallery of Art in Washington DC.

Read Thomas Moran's biography:

Markets Wrap. Asian stocks edged lower, with the artificial intelligence trade in focus during a week set to be shaped by earnings from chip bellwether Nvidia Corp. and the Federal Reserve’s annual gathering. Oil fell. MSCI’s Asia Pacific equities gauge slipped 0.2%, with tech shares leading the losses. The Kospi Index — a bellwether for AI investments — fell 1.4%, with Samsung Electronics Co. slumping over 6% after announcing plans to return as much as 110  trillion won ($80 billion) to investors this year. Equity-index futures for US stocks declined in early Asian trading on Monday.

Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.’s HK$80 billion ($10.2 billion) share sale to compete for global leadership in AI and SoftBank Group Corp.’s plans for a record ¥1 trillion ($6.3 billion) retail bond offering in Japan kept attention on the tech sector. Nvidia also notified customers about price hikes.

Elsewhere, Brent fell 1.5% to $93 a barrel ahead of Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s press conference detailing a plan to economically isolate Iran. Treasuries advanced across the curve, with the yield on the benchmark 10-year falling two basis points to 4.71%. Government bonds in Australia and New Zealand also advanced.

It’s a crucial week for markets, with investors looking to Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s comments at Jackson Hole, Wyoming, for clues on the path for interest rates as elevated oil prices stoke inflation pressures and bond yields soar to multi-decade highs. Traders are also bracing for Nvidia’s earnings and guidance to gauge whether this year’s rally in artificial intelligence  shares has further to run.

Early attention in Asia is on Alibaba. The online retail giant-turned-AI player said Sunday it’s offering 710 million shares at HK$112.7 each. That represents a discount of 3.6% to the closing price of Alibaba’s  American depositary receipts on Friday.

Meanwhile, Nvidia’s price hikes will go into effect on systems shipped early next year and will impact systems including those with the flagship Vera Rubin and Grace Blackwell chips, according to people familiar with the process. The increases will depend on the generation of Nvidia chips and the memory configurations, they said.

The developments add to already brewing concerns over the sustainability of the AI spending boom, with soaring hardware costs threatening returns just as companies commit ever-larger sums to the technology.

In other corners of the market, the Canadian dollar weakened following the sudden collapse of trade talks with the US late Friday that saw Washington place a 50% duty on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods. Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada will apply counter-tariffs on $20 billion of US products on Sept. 8. in response.

Gold held its gains from last week, trading around $4,605 an ounce.

Attention is also on Bessent Monday and his economic isolation plans for Iran.

“At dawn begins an economic D-Day — the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary,” Bessent wrote in a Financial Times article.

Traders are also watching Bessent’s fiscal consolidation plans after last week’s announcement of increased buybacks of long-term bonds whipsawed the Treasury market.

While Bessent has attempted to ease concerns over US fiscal policy, the Congressional Budget Office offers little evidence of fiscal consolidation, projecting large budget deficits and debt rising to a record 120% of GDP in 10 years, Elias Haddad, global head of markets strategy at Brown Brothers Harriman, wrote in a note to clients.

Oklahoma: Tulsa, OK features Art Deco architecture, an Arts District, and the Gilcrease Museum.

text:
A cowboy from Texas...

A cowboy, who just moved to Wyoming from Texas, walks into a bar and orders three mugs of Bud.

He sits in the back of the room, drinking a sip out of each one in turn.

When he finishes them, he comes back to the bar and orders three more.

The bartender approaches and tells the cowboy, "You know, a mug goes flat after I draw it. It would taste better if you bought one at a time..."

The cowboy replies, "Well, you see, I have two brothers. One is an Airborne Ranger, the other is a Navy Seal, both serving overseas somewhere.

When we all left our home in Texas, we promised that we'd drink this way to remember the days when we drank together.

So I'm drinking one beer for each of my brothers and one for myself."

The bartender admits that this is a nice custom, and leaves it there.

The cowboy becomes a regular in the bar, and always drinks the same way.

He orders three mugs and drinks them in turn.

One day, he comes in and only orders two mugs.

All the regulars take notice and fall silent.

When he comes back to the bar for the second round, the bartender says, "I don't want to intrude on your grief, but I wanted to offer my condolences on your loss."

The cowboy looks quite puzzled for a moment, then a light dawns in his eyes and he laughs.

"Oh, no, everybody's just fine," he explains, "It's just that my wife and I joined the Baptist Church and I had to quit drinking."

"Hasn't affected my brothers though...."

text:
The Bureau of Land Management (BLM) regularly gathers (rounds up) excess wild horses and burros from public rangelands in the Western U.S. and sells some of them through its official Sale Program.

The BLM conducts gathers when herd numbers exceed Appropriate Management Levels (AML) set to protect rangeland health, water, vegetation, and other wildlife. Methods include helicopter-assisted drives and bait trapping. Gathered animals go to off-range holding corrals.

Recent and ongoing 2026 examples include:
Piceance-East Douglas/West Douglas (Colorado): Operations underway as of late August 2026, with hundreds gathered so far.
Lahontan HMA (Nevada): Completed in July 2026 (about 700 horses removed).
Lake Pleasant HMA (Arizona, burros): Completed earlier in 2026.
Others planned or recently finished in Wyoming, Montana, and Nevada complexes.

There are currently around 58,000 animals in off-range holding, at an annual cost of roughly $100 million. On-range estimates are in the 70,000–85,000 range depending on the survey date.

Sales
Congress authorized sales in 2004 for animals that are over 10 years old or have been offered for adoption at least three times without success. These are sold “without limitation” to qualified buyers who get immediate ownership. Standard sales start at $125 (sometimes less for events), with limits of four animals per buyer every six months; larger group sales are possible.

The BLM’s stated policy is that it does not sell animals to slaughterhouses or “kill buyers.” Buyers sign agreements pledging humane care and that they will not knowingly transfer the animals for commercial processing. Once sold, the animals lose federal “wild horse” protections and the BLM does not track them.

Sales volume rose sharply in recent years (about 3,700 animals in FY 2025). A separate Adoption Incentive Program that paid adopters was restricted by a court in 2025. Adoption events continue independently.

Advocacy groups and recent reporting (including a New York Times investigation) argue that the sale process has created a loophole: some buyers resell animals quickly to intermediaries who then send them to slaughter plants in Canada or Mexico. The BLM disputes that it intends or authorizes this and says it investigates credible violations.

In short, gathering excess animals and offering some for sale (or adoption) is standard, ongoing BLM policy under the 1971 Wild Free-Roaming Horses and Burros Act, as amended. The debate is over how many of the sold animals ultimately end up slaughtered despite the stated restrictions.

text:
Stanford: "A blueprint for mapping melting ice sheets," by Corey Binns.

"Ice-penetrating radar is a core tool used by glaciologists monitoring how ice sheets contribute to rising sea levels." Researchers in the Stanford Radio Glaciology lab use radio waves to understand rapidly changing ice sheets and their contributions to global sea-level rise. This technique has revealed open water beneath Greenland, the long-term impacts of extreme melt, a process that could accelerate ice sheet mass loss, in Antarctica, the potential instability of an ice sheet that could raise sea levels by 10 feet, and more.

Now, PhD students within the group have created an open-source tool so other scientists can construct ice-penetrating radar systems at a fraction of the cost of current methods. "The Open Radar Code Architecture (ORCA) offers scientists a cheaper, easier, + more efficient way to build both airborne + ground-based radars, even if they lack a technical engineering background."

Ice-penetrating radars can cost tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars, while the lowest-cost version of the team’s open-source radar costs only $1,500—not that you will find these in a big box store near you anytime soon.

'The ice sheets + glaciers atop Greenland + Antarctica are critically important, providing habitats to wildlife, storing > half of the planet’s freshwater, and contributing to evolution of the climate.' They are major contributors to the sea-level rise that threatens the 680 M people who live in low-lying coastal zones—yet the uncertainty of projections may be underestimating that threat. Earth’s ice sheets represent the largest contribution to uncertainty in average sea-level rise by 2100, according to Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) models.

“I think we’re going to see some really exciting and first-of-their kind experiments enabled by this system,” said Principal Investigator Dustin Schroeder, whom I met at a school reunion well over a decade ago.

text:
Orchids are the most prolific con artists in evolutionary history.
Cattleya cernua produces dazzling vermilion blossoms that offer visiting pollinators exactly zero nectar—pure chromatic fraud.
Total biological freeloading, wrapped in vintage elegance.
Are you backing the ruthless floral grifter or the honest working plant?
https://t.co/bjiRAjUhz2

Botanists classify this energetic swindle as non-rewarding deceptive pollination: an evolutionary gambit where the flower mimics calorie-rich flora so flawlessly that foraging pollinators burn flight fuel doing cross-pollination for free. Perched high in the canopy of Brazil’s Atlantic Forest, Cattleya cernua anchors its pseudobulbs to bare bark and exposed granite, subsisting on humid mist, leaf litter, and unyielding insolence. Nineteenth-century collectors lost both fortunes and decorum during the heights of Orchidelirium, scouring coastal cliffs for these fiery dwarf epiphytes. There is something delightfully grotesque about a plant that conquered the canopy through an aristocratic disdain for dirt and an airtight refusal to provide fair compensation. It makes a wonderfully subversive talisman for recording your own audacious schemes, field observations, or daily marginalia.

text: Has anyone polled the homeless addicts and asked them, if they were offered treatment, would they take it? I spent years volunteering in the homeless community in Colorado Springs and most of the people I helped did not want to be housed nor give up their lifestyle. Most had been living in parks, etc. for years and while they were happy to accept help of clothing and food, they did not want their lifestyle altered. People who have never been addicted to drugs, with good intentions, saying that the homeless should receive treatment for drugs and enroll in job training do not understand the true drug addict. Their goal is not to quit drugs, get a job or find housing. Their goal is - where am I getting my next fix. Rehab, for most, is not on their list of things to accomplish. Sure, you may get a few of them to clean up but that decision must be theirs. Forcing a drug addict, or anyone addicted to anything, into rehab against their will does not work. Unless that person comes to the decision on their own and truly wants to quit, forced rehab will fail. I have personal knowledge of both sides of this coin. Give me a shout if you would like me to give you some insight on this.

text:
Mortgages might be the most underappreciated part of the entire $OPEN thesis — @ericjackson $82 target starts to make more sense if Opendoor executes.

The market still looks at Opendoor and sees an iBuyer.

Buy a house → resell it → make a thin spread.

But Opendoor 2.0 is trying to build something much bigger:

SELL → BUY → FINANCE → TITLE → ESCROW → CLOSE

The cash offer isn't necessarily the end product.

It's CUSTOMER ACQUISITION.

And Carvana already showed why this model can become incredibly powerful.

Look at $CVNA's economics.

In 2025, Carvana generated:

$1.98 BILLION of retail vehicle gross profit.

But its “other” businesses — primarily gains from financing receivables + complementary products like protection plans and insurance — generated another:

$1.73 BILLION of gross profit.

Think about that.

The high-margin businesses surrounding the car generated almost as much gross profit as selling the cars themselves.

That's the playbook $OPEN investors should be studying.

Except Opendoor is applying the concept to a transaction measured in HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS OF DOLLARS.

And we're already seeing early evidence.

COLORADO:
More than HALF of scheduled Opendoor resale closes are expected to use Opendoor Home Loans.

TEXAS:
Nearly 1 in 5 after just SIX WEEKS.

And that's with a mortgage product management itself describes as still unoptimized.

No FHA yet.
No VA yet.
No ARMs yet.

Those are coming.

Management expects mortgage licensing to reach roughly 35–40 states by year-end.

Even more interesting:

Opendoor says there are roughly 65–85 basis points of structural costs embedded in the traditional mortgage process that its vertically integrated model can potentially eliminate and pass back to customers.

That's the advantage of controlling the transaction.

Opendoor already has:

The house.
The buyer.
The property data.
The timeline.
The closing process.

So instead of spending heavily to find a random mortgage customer, the mortgage customer can arrive through an Opendoor home transaction.

That creates the flywheel:

More acquisitions
→ more inventory
→ more buyers
→ more mortgages
→ more title/escrow opportunities
→ more economics per transaction
→ better conversion
→ potentially faster closes
→ faster inventory turns
→ more capital recycled.

This is where Eric Jackson's $82 by 2028 thesis gets interesting.

Jackson currently assigns a 60% probability to $82 by the end of 2028.

He's not valuing $OPEN as simply a better house flipper.

The thesis depends on Opendoor becoming infrastructure for the housing transaction itself.

And remember: Jackson was publicly bullish on Carvana around $15 before its massive turnaround.

The parallel isn't that houses are cars.

It's the BUSINESS MODEL.

The physical asset brings the customer into the ecosystem.

Then vertically integrated services dramatically increase the economic value of that customer.

Carvana:

CAR → financing → protection products → insurance → trade-in

Opendoor:

HOME → mortgage → title → escrow → future financial/transaction services

And there's potentially an even bigger second act:

Why @HyperliquidX Should Acquire Gemini: The Regulated HIP-3/4 Deployer in the US

Hyperliquid is engaging with the CFTC/SEC to enable U.S.-regulated companies to offer perpetual futures that trade and settle on its public blockchain.

I think Hyperliquid should take that ambition one step further: Acquire a regulated U.S. platform like Gemini and turn it into the de facto regulated HIP-3 and HIP-4 venue in the U.S.

Gemini went public in September 2025 at a $3.3B valuation. Today, it trades at roughly $450M, down more than 85% from its IPO valuation.

The core business is clearly struggling. Gemini is too small to compete effectively with the major U.S. exchanges for spot or derivatives flow. It has no meaningful liquidity moat and limited crypto-native distribution. The company has already started diversifying toward its credit card and prediction markets businesses.

More telling is that Gemini is in outright shrinking mode. It has wound down its UK, EU, and Australia operations, cut headcount roughly 40% from peak to about 402 employees, and guided to lower compensation and technology spend for the year. Assets on platform fell from $18.2B to $8.4B year over year and spot volume dropped 66%. This is a company retreating to its core and cutting burn.

But what looks like a challenged standalone business could be a strategic asset at a fire-sale price.

For roughly $450M, Hyperliquid could acquire Gemini's entire U.S. regulatory stack, which I think could be worth ~$200M on its own:

- NYDFS Trust Charter: custody + New York exchange authority (2015)
- DCM: Gemini Titan, CFTC-regulated derivatives venue (Dec. 2025)
- DCO: Gemini Olympus, CFTC clearing license (Apr. 2026)
- FCM: in progress, completing the CFTC derivatives stack
- MTLs: money-transmitter licenses across nearly all U.S. states
- Broker-dealer: rails for regulated equities

For context, @krakenfx's parent paid up to $550M for Bitnomial, effectively acquiring a regulatory and derivatives infrastructure asset with little operating business attached. Gemini's entire market cap is now below that.

Yes, Hyperliquid would inherit a business currently losing roughly $30–40M per quarter operationally. But it would also acquire a meaningful operating footprint:

- 580K monthly transacting users (Q2'26)
- 1.72M lifetime transacting users
- $8.4B of assets on platform
- $3.8B quarterly spot volume
- $3.1B institutional / -= $0.7B retail
- $45.5M quarterly revenue, or ~$180M annualized
- 106K active card users
- ~$485M quarterly card spend and ~$220M of receivables
- A regulated prediction-markets business with 27K+ traders and 225M+ contracts since launch

At a $450M valuation, that's roughly $290 per funded customer.

For comparison, @Robinhoodapp paid roughly $400 per funded customer for Bitstamp, despite acquiring about half the revenue and no comparable U.S. federal license stack. Kraken paid roughly $790 per funded user for NinjaTrader.

And Gemini's users already hold an average of roughly $14.5K of assets on platform. In other words, you could argue that the regulatory stack alone goes a long way toward underwriting the purchase price, while the users, assets, revenue, card business, and prediction markets come on top.

The most interesting part is that Hyperliquid could potentially finance the acquisition without touching a single burned HYPE token and using a very small % of the FDV supply.

The community reserve holds roughly 389M HYPE. Spending ~7.9M HYPE at $70 would represent approximately $550M — just 2.0% of the reserve, under 1% of max supply, and roughly 3% of HYPE's ~$18.5B circulating market cap — enough to acquire Gemini outright at a ~20% premium to its current market cap. Hyperliquid could then redirect a portion of protocol buybacks toward rebuilding the reserve. At the current fee run rate, the reserve could potentially be replenished within 12–18 months.

The strategic logic is bigger than simply buying an exchange. Hyperliquid would be buying the regulatory bridge between HIP-3/4 and the U.S. market.

Gemini could become one of Hyperliquid's HIP-3 and HIP-4 markets, the regulated U.S. deployer, handling KYC, custody, fiat rails, brokerage, clearing, and compliance while the L1 provides the underlying market infrastructure, liquidity, and onchain settlement.

Mechanically, this transaction is far simpler than most public-company M&A. Gemini's dual-class structure gives Class B shares ten votes each, and the Winklevoss twins hold all of them, roughly 94.7% of total voting power. It is a Nasdaq-designated controlled company. There is no proxy fight, no activist interloper, no drawn-out process. Board approval and a majority of voting power both run through two people. The entire negotiation is whether Cameron and Tyler want to convert a controlling stake in a declining exchange into a meaningful HYPE position and the distinction of bringing Hyperliquid onshore.

On structure, the buyer wouldn't be the protocol or the foundation directly. NYDFS probabl wants a US entity with named officers, not an offshore foundation. The path is a Delaware HoldCo, funded by the Hyper Foundation but legally distinct, that acquires Gemini and keeps the regulated subsidiaries intact. The L1 stays a separate permissionless layer that never touches a US customer.

Polymarket already ran this playbook. Offshore, non-KYC, with a CFTC settlement on its record, it bought QCEX (a licensed DCM/DCO) for $112M in July 2025, ring-fenced it as a US entity, and relaunched onshore in December. Hyperliquid starts from a better position: no enforcement history, US users geofenced, and active dialogue with both agencies.

Hyperliquid generates substantial cash flow and sits on an enormous treasury. It should be much more aggressive about deploying both strategically. let's stop the buy back and burns and play offense.

My thinking: Potential SpaceX-Tesla Merger Premiums price 494-512 dollar: Lessons from Past Deals.

Elon Musk has a history of high-profile acquisitions involving premium valuations. Looking at past transactions and current market conditions raises an interesting hypothetical about a possible SpaceX-Tesla combination. Here is a structured breakdown of the key points.

1. The 2016 SolarCity Acquisition Set a Precedent for Premiums
In 2016, Tesla acquired SolarCity in an all-stock deal valued at roughly $2.1–2.6 billion. The initial offer carried a premium of about 21–30% (with some contemporary reports describing it as high as ~35%) over SolarCity’s pre-announcement trading price.

Critics called it an overpayment or “bailout,” but Delaware courts later ruled the deal entirely fair. This established a pattern of Musk-linked deals involving notable premiums when strategic synergies (in this case, integrating solar, batteries, and EVs) were the justification.

2. The Twitter (X) Buyout Showed Even Higher Premiums
When Elon Musk acquired Twitter in 2022 for $44 billion ($54.20 per share), the offer represented approximately a 38% premium over Twitter’s closing price on the day before his stake was publicly disclosed (and a higher ~54% premium relative to earlier levels). Many observers described it as more than 40% in broader market discussions.

The deal was highly controversial at the time, with claims of overpayment, yet it highlighted Musk’s willingness to pay substantial premiums for control of transformative assets.

3. Tesla’s Current Valuation Provides the Baseline
As of mid-August 2026, Tesla stock trades around $341 per share (fluctuating in the $336–$341 range recently), giving the company a market capitalization in the vicinity of $1.3–1.34 trillion.

This serves as the reference point for any hypothetical valuation discussions involving SpaceX.

4. A Hypothetical SpaceX-Tesla Merger at 45–50% Premium
Suppose SpaceX were to acquire or merge with Tesla and apply a premium in the 45–50% range—higher than the SolarCity deal and comparable to or slightly above the Twitter transaction.

At today’s(2026-08-19) ~$341 share price, that would imply a deal value of roughly:
45% premium → about $494 per share
50% premium → about $511–$512 per share
This range reflects the kind of control premium often seen in strategic, founder-driven combinations where synergies in energy, autonomy, AI, and space technologies could be cited as justification.

5. Rising Tesla Share Price Would Push the Final Deal Higher
Acquisition or merger prices are typically tied to the target’s stock price at announcement or closing (or a volume-weighted average). If Tesla’s share price climbs to $380 before any deal is finalized, the same 45–50% premium would translate to a significantly higher figure:
45% premium → approximately $551 per share
50% premium → approximately $570 per share

In other words, any upward movement in Tesla’s stock would automatically inflate the ultimate transaction value under a fixed-percentage premium structure.6. Broader Context and Caveats

These calculations are purely illustrative. No official SpaceX-Tesla merger has been announced, and any real deal would depend on valuations, regulatory approval, shareholder votes, exchange ratios (if all-stock), synergies, and market conditions.

Past deals show that premiums can compress by closing if the acquirer’s or target’s stock moves, and courts or markets may later debate whether the price was “fair.” Still, the historical pattern of 30%+ premiums in Musk’s major transactions makes the 45–50% range a reasonable speculative benchmark for https://t.co/5mk5MDAd5e summary, the SolarCity (~35% initial premium range) and Twitter (~38–40%+) deals illustrate Musk’s approach to paying up for strategic assets.

Applying a similar or slightly higher 45–50% premium to Tesla at ~$341 yields a hypothetical $494–$512 range—rising further if the stock advances to $380 or beyond.

No agency retainer
No MCP

I just ran Claude Code straight out of my terminal (I used the Claude Code extension in Antigravity lol)

Here is how I set it up:

1. Most people use AI wrong, for ads. 

Because they use it to write ad copy and create AI slop creatives.

This is how I’ve been using it:

- Setting up campaigns with my naming conventions

- Analyzing campaigns, audiences and ads

- Creating new assets and uploading them

-Setting budgets and targeting

- Checking if dimensions match the placements.

Clicking around Ads Manager for an hour is a waste of your time

So I hooked Claude Code up to the Meta Ads CLI and a few basic Python scripts.

2. I gave it eyes for creatives

Before anything gets uploaded, Claude inspects the files.

I plugged in a vision model to scan the creatives first:

- Checks if the aspect ratio fits 9:16 vs 1:1
- Makes sure the text on the image/video is actually readable

- If an asset looks broken, it flags it to you

Activation commands are blocked

Claude can build the campaign, format the copy and push the assets.

Every single campaign uploads as 𝗣𝗔𝗨𝗦𝗘𝗗

The AI does the heavy lifting but I control the budget.

Past winning angles
Product margins and offers
Naming conventions
Tone of voice guidelines

Claude reads that folder before it touches anything so it builds campaigns like someone who actually knows the business.

5. The daily workflow

Now launching ads takes about two minutes

I type /build with the offer, audience and budget

Claude builds the full structure in the background.

Later in the week, I run /analyze and it pulls the account data to tell me what to cut, keep running or scale

You don’t need to hand your ad account over to a black box

text:
Michael Alden of The London Lounge once gave what I think is the perfect description of the drape cut. "It was a hit with critics," he said, "but a flop at the box office."   

First, some background. The term "drape" can describe many things, including how fabric hangs. But in tailoring, "drape cut" refers to something specific. In the early 20th century, a Dutch-English tailor named Frederick Schlote devised a new method of making suits and sport coats so the chest puffed out a little. The fullness in the chest resulted in extra fabric that "draping" near the armhole, hence the term "drape cut."   

If you were to list the most stylish men of the 20th century, you may be surprised how many wore a drape cut. Such a list would include the Duke of Windsor, Cary Grant, Fred Astaire, Gary Cooper, Laurence Olivier, Douglas Fairbanks, and others. In this sense, Alden is correct that it was a hit with critics — the drape cut is sometimes seen as a connoisseur's cut — but it was never really something adopted by the mass market or fashion brands. I think that's to its credit.  

I happen to love the drape cut and think Edwin DeBoise makes one of the best versions. His illustrious career includes cutting for the late, great Edward Sexton and Anderson & Sheppard before founding his own firm in the 1990s. You can see his house style below: a relatively soft shoulder (for British tailoring) teamed with a full chest, nipped waist, and close skirt. The style gives the wearer an almost heroic figure.   

The firm offers full bespoke and made-to-measure services so that you can choose different price points. The upside of using a bespoke tailor's MTM service, of course, is that they are technically trained, so they can spot and address issues that lesser-skilled MTM shops may miss. Consider them if you, like me, love classic English style.
