text:
In 1998, Warren Buffett gave a 1-hour masterclass on how to never lose money investing.

Here are the 22 most valuable lessons from his lecture:

1. You only have to get rich once. If you have $100 million and can make 10% unleveraged or 20% leveraged, the difference between $110 million and $120 million at year-end means nothing to your life, your family, or anything. But the downside, especially with other people's money, is disgrace, humiliation, and facing the friends whose money you lost. The equation never makes sense.

2. To make money they did not need, they risked money they did have and needed. That is just plain foolish, Buffett says, regardless of your IQ. If you hand him a gun with a million chambers and one bullet and offer him any sum to put it to his temple and pull once, he will not do it. There is nothing on the upside that justifies the downside. People do this financially all the time without thinking.

3. The smartest people in finance went broke, and that is the most fascinating story Buffett knows. Long-term Capital Management had 16 people with possibly the highest average IQ of any business in the country, 350 to 400 combined years of experience, and most of their own net worth in the firm. They still went bankrupt. Buffett says if he ever wrote a book, it would be called why smart people do dumb things.

4. Beta and sigmas tell you nothing about the real risk of going broke. The LTCM team relied heavily on mathematics and believed a six- or seven-sigma event could not touch them. They were wrong. History does not tell you the probabilities of future financial events. The real risk is not volatility. It is a permanent, irreversible blind spot in something crucial, often caused by knowing a great deal about something else.

5. Invest only in businesses you can understand. That one rule narrows the field by about 90%, and that is fine. Buffett can understand Coca-Cola. he cannot value an internet company, and he says if a student handed him a valuation of one on a final exam, he would flunk them. People thought Enron was incredible because it had a good track record, but almost nobody understood how it made money. That was the signal to avoid it.

6. You want a business that is a castle with a wide moat around it. Inside the castle, you want an honest, able, hard-working duke. The moat can be low cost, like Geico in auto insurance, or brand, or patents, or location. But a wonderful castle will always be attacked, so the job of every manager Buffett owns is one thing: widen the moat. Throw crocodiles and sharks into it to keep competitors out.

7. Moats change slowly and invisibly, but they change. Thirty years ago, Kodak's moat was as wide as Coca-Cola's. They had share of mind; the little yellow box meant best in everyone's head. Then they let Fuji into the Olympics and narrowed their own moat. Coca-Cola's moat, by contrast, is wider now than 30 years ago. Every time infrastructure gets built in a country that is not yet profitable, the moat widens a little. You cannot see it day by day, but in 10 years, the difference is enormous.

8. Share of mind beats share of market. When you say Disney, every person in the room has something in their head. Say Universal Pictures or 20th Century Fox, and you have nothing. A mother with two kids will pick the $17.95 Disney video over the $16.95 alternative because she knows it will be fine and does not want to preview ten videos to decide. That little bit of certainty in the customer's mind is worth a fortune.

9. The best businesses have pricing power and require little capital. see's candy sold 16 million pounds at $1.95 when Buffett bought it for $25 million. The entire thesis was whether the price could go to $2.25 without hurting sales. It could, because nobody wants to hand their valentine a box of candy and say, "This year I took the low bid." Today, See's makes $60 million on the same formulas and still takes almost no capital. Compare that to GM, which had to reinvest every dollar into better factories and whose stock barely moved over 50 years.

10. The best businesses earn a royalty on other people's capital. Coca-Cola sells a formula and collects a royalty on every drink. American Express takes a few percent of every dollar you spend. You put up the capital, they take a cut. Low capital intensity is one of the most underrated qualities in a business and one of the surest paths to durable wealth.

11. Define your circle of competence and stay inside it. The size of the circle does not matter. Staying inside, it does. If you know which 30 companies out of thousands you actually understand, you are fine. Buffett understood H.H. brown shoes and Frank Rooney, so he closed that deal in five minutes. If you do not know enough to understand a business instantly, you will not understand it in a month either.

12. Ignore the macro entirely. Buffett has never bought or skipped a business because of a feeling about interest rates, the economy, or any macro forecast. If Alan Greenspan and Bob Rubin both whispered exactly what they would do for the next 12 months, it would not change what he pays for anything. You want to focus on what is important and knowable. The macro is important but not knowable, so you ignore it.

13. Inactivity is the strategy, not a flaw. Wall Street makes money on activity. You make money on inactivity. A broker is like a doctor paid by how often he changes your pills. If everyone in a room trades their portfolio with everyone else every day, they all end up broke, and the intermediary keeps the money. Buffett looks for one good idea a year and rides it to its full potential. He measures Berkshire by how little turnover there is, like a church where the same people fill the seats every Sunday.

14. If you understand businesses, diversification is a mistake. For the 99% who will not evaluate businesses, Buffett recommends a low-cost index fund and extreme diversification. But if you bring real intensity to evaluating companies, owning more than six is a terrible idea. Very few people got rich on their seventh best idea. A lot of people got rich on their best one. Buffett keeps about half his money in what he likes best.

15. Buffett's biggest mistakes are mistakes of omission, not commission. The times he understood a business well enough to act and instead sat there sucking his thumb. He passed on healthcare stocks during the Clinton plan and on Fannie Mae in the mid-eighties, each a multi-billion-dollar miss. Accounting never captures these. The $2,000 he put into a Sinclair service station as a young man, money he lost, has an opportunity cost of about $6 billion today.

16. Focus on what will happen, not when. Coca-Cola went public in 1919 at $40 a share and dropped to $19 within a year. There was always a reason not to buy: the great depression, world war, sugar rationing, thermonuclear weapons. But one share bought then and reinvested would be worth about $5 million. If you are right about the business, you will make a lot of money. The timing is the tricky part, so do not focus on it.

17. When hiring, look for integrity, intelligence, and energy. But if the person lacks the first one, you actually want them dumb and lazy. Because a person with intelligence and energy but no integrity will destroy you. Buffett borrowed this from Pete Kiewit. The trait everyone screens for last is the one that matters most.

18. Here is a thought experiment Buffett gives students. Imagine you could own 10% of one classmate for the rest of their life. You would not pick the highest IQ or the best grades. You would pick the person you respond to best, the one who is generous, honest, gives credit to others, and has leadership qualities. Now imagine you also had to short one classmate. You would pick the egotistical, greedy, slightly dishonest one. The qualities that decide both are not talent. They are character.

19. Every quality on the admirable side is achievable, and every quality on the repellent side is removable. The things that make you want to own 10% of someone are not the ability to throw a football or run fast; they are behavior, temperament, and character, all of which anyone can choose. Buffett's point: you already own 100% of yourself, so you might as well become the person worth betting on.

20. The chains of habit are too light to be felt until they are too heavy to be broken. Buffett sees people in their forties and fifties trapped by self-destructive patterns they can no longer change. At a young age, you can choose any habits you want. Ben Franklin and Ben Graham both did exactly this, looking at people they admired and simply deciding to behave like them. There was nothing impossible about it.

21. Take a job you would take if you were already independently wealthy. Buffett told a 28-year-old at Harvard who wanted a consulting job "to look good on his resume" that it was like saving up sex for your old age. There comes a time to just start doing what you love. Buffett offered to work for Ben Graham for free, was told he was overpriced, and kept pestering him for years. Take the job you would jump out of bed for. You cannot miss.

22. You won the ovarian lottery, and that should shape how you think. Buffett imagines a genie 24 hours before your birth letting you design the world's rules, with one catch: you do not know which of 5.8 billion balls you will draw. Born here or in Afghanistan, with an IQ of 130 or 70, male or female, able-bodied or not. If you could put your ball back and draw one of 100 random others, most people would not, because they are already in the luckiest 1%. Buffett knows he is perfectly wired for a market economy that pays him like crazy, while an equally good citizen leading scout troops and teaching Sunday school is not, purely by luck.

text:
To the Anti-Defamation League,

I am writing concerning the death of Leo Frank near Marietta, Georgia, on August 17, 1915, and the modern tendency to portray both his 1913 prosecution and his subsequent extrajudicial hanging primarily through the lens of antisemitism.

The Phagan family rejects private vengeance and extralegal punishment. The men who entered the Georgia State Prison Farm at Milledgeville, removed Frank from state custody, transported him across Georgia, and hanged him possessed no lawful authority to execute him. Governor John Marshall Slaton had already commuted Frank's death sentence to life imprisonment. Frank was therefore legally entitled to remain in state custody and serve that sentence. Our family would have preferred that he remain imprisoned under his murder conviction rather than be abducted and killed by private citizens.

Recognizing the illegality of the hanging, however, does not require speculative mind-reading or the assignment of motives that the surviving historical evidence cannot establish.

The documentary record surrounding the Mary Phagan case is immense. The Atlanta Constitution, Atlanta Journal, and Atlanta Georgian covered the investigation, hearings, trial, appeals, and subsequent controversy in exceptional detail. Team Phagan has transcribed more than 2,000 newspaper articles published between April 1913 and August 1915, created audio editions of those articles, produced more than 1,000 newspaper-clipping videos, and processed more than 10,000 pages of newspapers, magazines, court records, and related historical documents.

After years of examining these sources alongside the trial transcript, the Brief of Evidence, and the appellate record, I do not find adequate evidence for treating antisemitism as the dominant explanation for Frank's 1913 prosecution, the guilty verdict returned against him, or the motives of every man connected with his 1915 extrajudicial hanging. Frank was prosecuted for the murder of Mary Phagan. A jury found him guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. The Georgia Supreme Court later concluded that the evidence presented at trial was legally sufficient to sustain the verdict. My own review of the Brief of Evidence has likewise led me to conclude that the evidence supports Frank's guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

Antisemitic language certainly appeared during the wider controversy, particularly in portions of Thomas E. Watson's post-trial writings. Those writings should be confronted directly, quoted accurately, dated carefully, and placed within their actual historical setting. They should not be transferred wholesale or projected backward onto jurors, prosecutors, witnesses, public officials, Georgians generally, or the men who later abducted Frank unless independent contemporary evidence demonstrates that they shared the same motive. The prejudice of one writer or political faction cannot reasonably be transformed into the mentality of an entire state.

Georgia's Jewish history also deserves closer examination before the state of 1913 is characterized broadly as consumed by antisemitism. Georgia's Jewish population continued to grow after the Frank case, and Jewish communities became increasingly established within the state's civic, commercial, religious, and cultural life. I encourage the ADL to examine Jewish demographic growth in Georgia before and after 1913 to 1915 rather than relying upon generalized descriptions of the period. If antisemitism was as pervasive as is sometimes claimed, the subsequent growth and integration of Georgia's Jewish population require explanation.

During my own lifetime, instances of antisemitism in Georgia have been rare compared with the ordinary experience of Jewish and Christian families living, working, worshipping, marrying, and participating in community life together. The prevalence of interfaith marriages and congregations welcoming interfaith families provides additional evidence that Jewish-Christian relations in Georgia cannot fairly be reduced to the occasional examples of Jew-hatred that have occurred.

The ADL's "Hang the Jew" Claim

A particularly revealing example of the danger of retrojecting antisemitism onto the 1913 trial is the famous claim that people gathered outside the Fulton County courthouse shouted to the jury, "Hang the Jew or we'll hang you!"

The ADL has repeated a version of this account in an article titled "Hang the Jew, Hang the Jew," presenting such a cry as part of the atmosphere surrounding Frank's trial. (ADL, 5)

Steve Oney, author of the 742-page And the Dead Shall Rise, reached a different conclusion after seventeen years of research. In a February 5, 2004 interview with the Jewish Journal, Oney addressed the allegation directly:

"In my book I say it didn't happen."

Oney explained that the story surfaced years after the original events and was repeated by later writers until it gradually became accepted as part of the conventional account. (Oney, 6)

Atlanta Magazine similarly summarized Oney's research in 2013 by reporting that there was no evidence supporting the later assertion that the jury had been threatened with the words, "Hang the Jew, or we'll hang you." (Atlanta Magazine, 7)

This episode illustrates a larger historical problem. Claims about the past should rest first upon contemporary documentation. A vivid quotation does not become authentic simply because it has circulated for decades through books, documentaries, classrooms, museums, newspapers, or advocacy literature. If the surviving record from 1913 does not corroborate the famous "Hang the Jew" story, it should not be presented as settled evidence that antisemitism controlled the trial.

The Legal Record

The legal sequence is equally important.

On May 8, 1913, the coroner's jury voted 6 to 0 to hold Frank for investigation by the grand jury.

On May 24, 1913, the grand jury indicted him for Mary Phagan's murder by a vote of 21 to 0.

On August 25, 1913, a Fulton County trial jury returned a guilty verdict by a vote of 12 to 0.

The presiding judge denied Frank's motion for a new trial on October 31, 1913.

On February 17, 1914, the Georgia Supreme Court affirmed the conviction and ruled that the evidence was sufficient to sustain the verdict.

Frank continued pursuing legal remedies. His federal habeas case eventually reached the United States Supreme Court. On April 12, 1915, the Court rejected his challenge in Frank v. Mangum by a vote of 7 to 2. (SCOTUS, 1)

Frank then sought executive clemency. The Georgia Prison Commission considered his application and declined, by a vote of 2 to 1, to recommend commutation. The final decision rested with Governor John Marshall Slaton.

Governor Slaton's Professional Conflict

Slaton's professional relationship with Frank's defense counsel deserves close examination.

In June 1913, the Atlanta firms of Rosser & Brandon and Slaton & Phillips announced their consolidation as Rosser, Brandon, Slaton & Phillips. Luther Z. Rosser subsequently became one of Frank's principal trial attorneys. Slaton entered the governorship while his name and longstanding professional associations remained attached to the same legal organization.

Contemporary announcements stated that Slaton would neither actively practice law with the firm nor participate in its current earnings while serving as governor. That qualification should be stated fairly. Even so, his established clientele, longtime partners, professional reputation, name, and anticipated return to private practice remained connected with the organization.

On June 21, 1915, one day before Frank's scheduled execution and five days before Slaton was due to leave office on June 26, the governor commuted Frank's death sentence to life imprisonment.

Slaton unquestionably possessed constitutional authority to grant clemency and later published an extensive justification for his decision. He did not claim that he was formally overturning the jury's verdict or reversing the judgments of the courts.

The ethical question is different: should a governor whose own law practice had been consolidated with the firm of the condemned man's principal trial attorney have personally exercised the final clemency power in that case?

To Frank's opponents, the circumstances appeared deeply compromised. A jury had convicted him. The trial judge had refused a new trial. Georgia's appellate process had left the conviction intact. The United States Supreme Court had rejected his federal challenge. The Prison Commission had declined to recommend commutation. Slaton, professionally associated with Rosser's firm, then intervened at the final stage and prevented the execution.

That sequence forms the immediate background to what occurred approximately eight weeks later.

The men who removed Frank from Milledgeville appear to have believed that they were enforcing a sentence already imposed through Georgia's judicial system and subsequently frustrated by political intervention. Their belief supplied no legal authority. Their conduct remained kidnapping followed by an unlawful execution. Yet proving that their actions were illegal is not the same as proving that religious hatred inspired them.

The 1983 and 1986 Pardon Proceedings

The later pardon proceedings require the same degree of care.

The first effort to obtain a posthumous pardon and exoneration failed in December 1983. The Georgia State Board of Pardons and Paroles declined to clear Frank because the Board could not conclusively determine whether he was guilty or innocent, despite testimony offered approximately seventy years after the murder.

A second application produced a posthumous pardon on March 11, 1986. Once again, the Board deliberately declined to resolve whether Frank had murdered Mary Phagan. Its order specifically stated that it acted "without attempting to address the question of guilt or innocence." The pardon rested upon Georgia's failure to protect Frank while he remained in state custody, the loss of his opportunity to pursue additional legal remedies following his death, and the state's failure to prosecute those responsible for his hanging. (NGE, 2)

The Anti-Defamation League itself has acknowledged the limited character of the 1986 decision, stating that the pardon "did not exonerate Frank and prove his innocence." (ADL, 3)

Georgia law also distinguishes clearly between a pardon and an exoneration. The Georgia State Board of Pardons and Paroles describes a pardon as official forgiveness. A pardon does not erase, expunge, or remove the underlying conviction. Georgia further advises that a pardoned person who is asked whether he or she has previously been convicted of a crime must still answer yes. (GSBPP, 4)

The March 11, 1986 action therefore did not vacate Leo Frank's 1913 murder conviction, did not declare him innocent, and did not exonerate him. His conviction has never been judicially overturned or vacated. In that precise legal sense, Leo Frank remains a convicted murderer in Georgia's legal record. Describing the 1986 pardon as an exoneration gives the Board's action a conclusion it expressly declined to reach.

History Should Follow the Evidence

The same evidentiary discipline should govern discussion of both the 1913 trial and the August 1915 hanging.

The Phagan family does not excuse Frank's abduction or death at the hands of private citizens. We reject vigilantism. Condemning that unlawful act, however, does not justify assigning antisemitic intentions to historical figures without contemporary proof.

Where anti-Jewish prejudice appears in the record, it should be documented plainly. Watson's rhetoric deserves exactly that treatment. Where such evidence is absent, historians should resist filling the silence with assumptions created afterward.

The historical distortion begins when later commentary is projected backward onto the Fulton County courtroom, the prosecution, the jury, or the participants in Frank's hanging and is then repeated as though it were contemporary evidence. Repetition by authors, journalists, educators, institutions, historians, filmmakers, or advocacy organizations cannot replace documentation from the period itself.

The events of August 17, 1915, cannot be understood adequately without first examining June 21, 1915: Slaton's commutation, his relationship with Rosser, Brandon, Slaton & Phillips, the failure of Frank's successive legal challenges, the Prison Commission's refusal to recommend clemency, and the belief among Frank's opponents that political intervention had displaced the sentence imposed through the courts.

None of these circumstances legitimizes Frank's extrajudicial hanging. They do, however, require separating three distinct historical questions: whether an act was lawful, what motivated the people who committed it, and what later generations subsequently claimed about those motives.

The Phagan family therefore asks the Anti-Defamation League to apply a consistent historical standard. Condemn vigilantism whether in Israel-Palestine or the United States. Identify genuine antisemitism wherever contemporary evidence demonstrates it. At the same time, do not import Jew-hatred for political expediency into episodes where the surviving record does not establish it.

I also extend an invitation to the Anti-Defamation League and its interested members to read the revised 2025 edition of my book, The Murder of Little Mary Phagan. The book examines the Leo Frank case through the trial record, appellate decisions, contemporary Atlanta newspapers, witness testimony, primary documents, Governor Slaton's commutation, the 1915 hanging, the pardon proceedings, and more than a century of subsequent controversy.

Agreement is not a prerequisite for serious historical discussion. What is required is a willingness to examine the surviving evidence, including material that may challenge familiar interpretations. I would welcome members of the ADL reading the book and engaging with the Phagan family in a substantive discussion about the case and the way its history has been preserved, interpreted, and taught.

The Phagan family rejects vigilante justice. We also reject the alteration of history through unsupported attribution of motive. Leo Frank's extrajudicial hanging should be condemned as unlawful. The 1913 trial and the events of August 1915 should likewise be described from evidence produced during the period itself, rather than through later attempts to retroject antisemitism or Jew-hatred onto people whose documented words and actions do not establish those motives.

History should follow the evidence, even when the evidence complicates a familiar story.

Respectfully,

Mary Phagan-Kean

Dear Jonathan Greenblatt, CEO and National Director, Anti-Defamation League of B'nai B'rith(ADL),

I am writing to you about the extrajudicial hanging of Leo Frank near Marietta, Georgia, on August 17, 1915, and the way this event has increasingly been presented as the culmination of an antisemitic prosecution and an antisemitic lynching.

The Phagan family opposes vigilante justice. The men who removed Frank from the Georgia State Prison Farm at Milledgeville and hanged him had no lawful authority to do so. Governor John Marshall Slaton had commuted Frank's death sentence to life imprisonment, making him a prisoner of the State of Georgia. The family would have preferred that he remain imprisoned under his murder conviction rather than be killed by private citizens.

Condemning the hanging, however, does not require rewriting the motives behind it or projecting unsupported narratives onto historical actors.

The surviving contemporary record is enormous. The Atlanta Constitution, Atlanta Journal, and Atlanta Georgian reported the investigation and trial in extraordinary detail. Team Phagan has transcribed more than 2,000 newspaper articles concerning the case between April 1913 and August 1915, produced audio versions and more than 1,000 newspaper-clipping videos, and transcribed more than 10,000 pages of newspapers, magazines, legal records, and related historical material.

After examining this record alongside the trial and appellate documents, I do not believe the evidence supports treating antisemitism as the controlling force behind the 1913 prosecution, verdict, or the motives of every participant in Frank's 1915 hanging. Leo Frank was prosecuted for the murder of Mary Phagan, tried before a jury, and convicted. The Georgia Supreme Court subsequently held that the evidence was legally sufficient to sustain the guilty verdict. Claims raised by Frank's defense concerning mob pressure and prejudice failed to overturn his conviction.

Antisemitic rhetoric did appear in the broader controversy, particularly in some of Thomas E. Watson's post-trial writings. It should be acknowledged, quoted, dated, and examined in its proper setting. It should not be projected backward onto every juror, prosecutor, witness, Georgian, political leader, or participant in Frank's hanging unless contemporary evidence establishes such a motive. The prejudice of one person or political faction cannot automatically be treated as the belief of an entire population.

One of the clearest examples of this problem is the oft-repeated story that crowds outside the Fulton County courthouse shouted at the jurors, "Hang the Jew or we'll hang you!" The ADL continues to present a version of this claim on its own website, including an archived retrospective titled "Hang the Jew, Hang the Jew," which describes such a cry as coming from the crowd outside Frank's 1913 trial. (ADL, 5)

Yet Steve Oney, author of the 742-page And the Dead Shall Rise, reached a different conclusion after seventeen years of research. In a February 5, 2004 interview with the Jewish Journal, Oney addressed the story directly: "In my book I say it didn't happen." He explained that the allegation appeared years after the crime and was subsequently repeated until it became accepted as part of the narrative. (Oney, 6)

Atlanta Magazine likewise summarized Oney's research in 2013 by stating that there was no evidence for the later claim that crowds threatened the jury with "Hang the Jew, or we'll hang you." (Atlanta Magazine, 7)

This illustrates why contemporary evidence should take precedence over later repetition. A dramatic quotation does not become an actual historical event simply because it is reproduced for generations in books, articles, museums, documentaries, or advocacy materials. If the contemporary record does not substantiate the famous "Hang the Jew" chant, it should not be presented as established evidence that antisemitism controlled the 1913 trial.

The legal chronology preceding the hanging is equally important. On May 8, 1913, the coroner's jury voted 6 to 0 to bind Frank over for grand jury investigation. On May 24, the grand jury indicted him 21 to 0 for Mary Phagan's murder. On August 25, a Fulton County jury convicted him 12 to 0. The presiding judge denied his motion for a new trial on October 31, 1913.

On February 17, 1914, the Georgia Supreme Court affirmed the judgment and held that the evidence was sufficient to sustain the conviction. Frank's legal challenges continued until Frank v. Mangum, when the United States Supreme Court rejected his federal habeas challenge 7 to 2 on April 12, 1915. (SCOTUS, 1)

Frank then sought executive clemency. The Georgia Prison Commission declined, 2 to 1, to recommend commutation. The final decision passed to Governor John Marshall Slaton.

At this point, Slaton's professional relationship with Frank's defense counsel becomes significant.

In June 1913, the Atlanta firms of Rosser & Brandon and Slaton & Phillips announced their consolidation as Rosser, Brandon, Slaton & Phillips. Luther Z. Rosser became one of Frank's principal trial attorneys. Slaton entered the governorship with his name and longstanding professional interests associated with the same firm.

Contemporary announcements stated that Slaton would neither actively practice nor participate in the firm's current earnings while governor. That qualification should be acknowledged. His partners, established clientele, name, and anticipated return to private practice nevertheless remained connected with the firm, and his name continued as part of its identity after his gubernatorial term.

On June 21, 1915, one day before Frank's scheduled execution and five days before Slaton was due to leave office on June 26, Slaton commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment.

Slaton possessed the constitutional authority to do so and issued an extensive explanation of his decision. In his commutation statement, he made clear that he was not purporting to overturn the jury's verdict or the judgments of the courts. The ethical question is separate: should a governor whose professional practice had been joined with the firm of the condemned man's principal trial attorney have personally exercised the final clemency power in that case?

To Frank's opponents, the appearance was deeply troubling. A jury had convicted him, the trial judge had denied a new trial, the Georgia appellate process had left the conviction standing, the United States Supreme Court had denied federal relief, and the Prison Commission had declined to recommend clemency. Slaton, professionally connected with Rosser's firm, then intervened at the final stage and prevented the execution.

This sequence provides essential context for what followed approximately eight weeks later. The men who seized Frank appear to have regarded themselves as carrying out a sentence they believed the judicial process had imposed and political intervention had frustrated. Their belief gave them no lawful authority. Kidnapping remained kidnapping, and an extrajudicial hanging remained illegal. But the illegality of their conduct does not, by itself, establish religious hatred as their motive.

The same precision is necessary when discussing Frank's posthumous pardon.

The first attempt to obtain a posthumous pardon and exoneration failed in December 1983. The Georgia State Board of Pardons and Paroles declined to exonerate Frank because it could not conclusively determine his guilt or innocence, despite recollections offered approximately seventy years after the murder.

A second application resulted in a posthumous pardon on March 11, 1986. The Board again deliberately declined to decide whether Frank had murdered Mary Phagan. Its order was issued "without attempting to address the question of guilt or innocence." The stated grounds concerned Georgia's failure to protect Frank while he was in state custody, the loss of his opportunity to pursue further legal remedies, and the state's failure to prosecute those responsible for his hanging. (NGE, 2)

The Anti-Defamation League itself acknowledges this limitation, stating that the 1986 pardon "did not exonerate Frank and prove his innocence." (ADL, 3)

The legal distinction is important. The Georgia State Board of Pardons and Paroles describes a pardon as official forgiveness. A pardon does not erase, expunge, or clear the underlying conviction. Georgia further instructs a pardoned person who is asked whether he or she has been convicted of a crime to answer yes. (GSBPP, 4)

The 1986 pardon therefore did not vacate Frank's 1913 conviction, declare him innocent, or exonerate him. His conviction has never been overturned or vacated. In that precise legal sense, Leo Frank remains a convicted murderer in Georgia's legal record. Describing the pardon as an exoneration assigns it a meaning the Board expressly refused to give it.

The same standard should govern descriptions of the 1913 trial and the events of August 1915.

The Phagan family does not defend Frank's unlawful seizure and killing. Rejecting vigilante justice, however, does not require assigning antisemitic motives to historical actors without contemporary evidence.

Antisemitism should be identified wherever the record establishes it. Watson's anti-Jewish rhetoric should be confronted directly. The reverse is equally important. Later rhetoric cannot simply be retrojected onto the 1913 courtroom, its jury, the prosecution, or the men involved in Frank's 1915 hanging and then presented as established fact. Repetition by writers, journalists, professors, institutions, or advocacy organizations cannot substitute for historical evidence.

The events of August 17, 1915, cannot be fully understood without examining June 21, 1915: Slaton's commutation, his relationship with Rosser, Brandon, Slaton & Phillips, the exhaustion of Frank's legal challenges, the Prison Commission's rejection of clemency, and the belief among Frank's opponents that political intervention had displaced the sentence imposed through the judicial process.

None of this makes Frank's hanging lawful. It requires us to distinguish an illegal act from the motive attributed to those who committed it, documented antisemitic rhetoric from demonstrated antisemitic motivation, and a pardon from an exoneration.

The Phagan family asks for a historically responsible standard: condemn vigilante justice, acknowledge genuine antisemitism wherever the contemporary record establishes it, and do not manufacture or retroject it where the evidence does not.

I personally invite you, Mr. Greenblatt, and interested members of the @ADL to read the revised 2025 edition of my book, The Murder of Little Mary Phagan. It examines the Leo Frank case in great detail through the 1913 trial record, appellate proceedings, contemporary Atlanta newspapers, witness testimony, primary documents, Governor Slaton's commutation, the 1915 hanging, the pardon proceedings, and the continuing controversy surrounding the case.

Whether we ultimately agree or disagree about Leo Frank, serious discussion should begin with the surviving historical record and a willingness to examine evidence that may challenge long-established interpretations. I would welcome members of the ADL reading the book and engaging with the Phagan family in a thoughtful discussion about how this history should be understood and remembered.

The Phagan family opposes vigilante justice, but we also oppose the falsification of history. The unlawful hanging of Leo Frank should be condemned for what it was. Neither the 1913 trial nor the events of August 1915 should be rewritten by retrojecting Jew-hatred or antisemitism onto historical actors without evidence demonstrating that those were their motives.

If this history is going to be told, it should be told as it happened.

Respectfully,

Mary Phagan-Kean

text:
The Mary Phagan Case: Leo Frank Mounts the Witness Stand: His Unsworn Statements of August 18 and August 20, 1913

On Monday, August 18, 1913, Leo M. Frank mounted the witness stand in Fulton County Superior Court in Atlanta, Georgia, and personally addressed the twelve jurors who would decide whether he was guilty of murdering 13-year-old Mary Phagan.

Frank’s appearance was different from the testimony given by the other witnesses during the trial. He did not take an oath and did not become an ordinary sworn witness. Under Section 1036 of the Georgia Penal Code of 1910, a criminal defendant was permitted to make an unsworn statement directly to the court and jury. The defendant could give his version of events without being required to submit to ordinary cross-examination by the prosecution. Defense counsel also did not conduct a normal direct examination of the defendant. Frank therefore presented his account largely as a prepared narrative to the jury. (1)(2)

Georgia law gave the jury broad freedom in deciding how much weight to give such a statement. The jurors could accept all of it, reject it, accept portions of it, and could even believe the defendant’s unsworn statement in preference to sworn testimony if they found it more convincing. (1)

This procedure seems unusual today because Georgia law in 1913 did not allow a criminal defendant to take the stand as an ordinary sworn witness in his own defense. Georgia retained this unusual system for decades. Following the United States Supreme Court’s 1961 decision in Ferguson v. Georgia, the state changed its law, and beginning in 1962 defendants could choose to testify under oath in the manner familiar in modern criminal trials. (2)

Frank Gives His Account of April 26

Frank’s August 18 statement was longwinded, verbose, loquacious, mind-numbing and largely irrelevant or immaterial. He took the jury through his pencil accounting calculous, and his movements on Saturday, April 26, 1913, the day Mary Phagan was killed at the National Pencil Company. He described his morning at the factory, the employees and visitors he remembered seeing, his encounter with Mary when she came for her pay, his office work that afternoon, his trip home for dinner, his return to the factory, and the events following the discovery of Mary’s body in the basement early the next morning. (3) He went through his pencil accounting work in mind-numbing detail to suggest to the jury that he was too busy to have had time to kill Mary Phagan, but this was a flawed approach because his accounting work only required a few hours, and many of the accounting pages as exhibits he presented to the jury, had dates earlier than April 26, 1913, , on them suggesting that some of the work had already been accumulated in prior days, which might have been a strategic or tactical blunder, as the jury was zoning-out on his explanations of his work he did that day. Saturday was also a State holiday and the presumption was he wasn't supposed to be working that afternoon, especially since most people even when it wasn't a holiday, only worked half days on Saturdays that ended at about noon.

Because Frank could not be forced into ordinary cross-examination, the prosecution had to attack his account through the testimony already before the jury, rebuttal witnesses, physical evidence, and later closing argument.

This makes Frank’s statement most useful when it is read beside the other evidence.

The Five Minutes of Monteen Stover

One of the most important conflicts involved 14-year-old Monteen Stover.

Two days after the murder, on Monday, April 28, Frank gave Chief of Detectives Newport Lanford an account of Mary Phagan’s visit. Frank said Mary entered his office “between 12:05 and 12:10, maybe 12:07.” He said he was sitting in his inner office, paid Mary her wages, and watched her leave. The statement was later introduced at the trial as State’s Exhibit B. (4) At the Coroner's inquest, Frank bounced between 12:05 pm and 12:10 pm as the arrival time for Mary Phagan, even though he seemed to lean more in the 12:10 pm direction, the 12:05 number came up.

Monteen Stover described those same five minutes very differently.

She testified that she entered the factory at 12:05 p.m. to collect her pay. She went upstairs, entered Frank’s outer office, walked into the inner office, and found no one there. She said she saw and heard nobody. After waiting several minutes, she left at 12:10 p.m. Stover said she had looked at the clock when she arrived and again when she departed. (5)

The conflict was simple and potentially important. Frank’s April 28 statement placed himself and Mary Phagan in his office during approximately the same five-minute period when Stover said she walked through those offices and found them empty. That became the crux of the case.

Things changed at the trial though. Frank decided to move Mary's arrive to after Monteen Stover reported time of arrival and departure.

By August 18, Frank described Mary’s arrival differently. Instead of repeating the precise 12:05 to 12:10 estimate, he connected her arrival to the departure of stenographer Hattie Hall, saying Mary came about ten to fifteen minutes after Hall left. (3)

Hall testified that she left at noon but came back for an umbrella and then left at 12:02 p.m. when she departed. Using Hall’s time, Frank’s later estimate would place Mary’s arrival at roughly 12:12 to 12:17 p.m. This calculated range comes from comparing their statements and was not an exact time Frank himself gave. (3)(6)

Frank also addressed why Stover might have found his office empty. He said that, to the best of his memory, he had remained in his inner office during the noon period, but allowed for the possibility that he had gone to the toilet in the machine department in response to a “call of nature,” (to poop) or urinate. He explained that such a routine trip might have been made without leaving a distinct memory. (3)

The jury therefore had several pieces to compare: Frank’s early 12:05 to 12:10 statement, Stover’s 12:05 to 12:10 visit to an empty office, Hattie Hall’s 12:02 time punch (which seemed like an embellishment), and Frank’s August 18 explanation of a possible trip away from his office to a location in the building where hair on a lathe and blood on the floor were found in the machine department.

Jim Conley Versus Leo Frank

The greatest conflict before the jury was between Frank and Jim Conley.

Conley testified under oath for the State and accused Frank directly. He said Frank arranged for him to watch the first-floor entrance on April 26. Conley described Lemmie Quinn visiting the factory, Mary Phagan arriving and going upstairs, sounds from the upper floor going to the machine department, a woman screaming, Monteen Stover entering and leaving, and Frank later calling him upstairs. (7)

According to Conley, Frank told him that he had struck a girl after she resisted his sexual advances. Conley claimed he found Mary’s body in the metal department near the entryway to the men's toilet and later helped Frank carry it to the elevator and take it into the basement. He also described ghost writing the notes that were later found beside Mary’s body and written as if they were coming from her. (7)

Frank denied the entire story.

In his August 18 statement he said he had never seen Conley in the factory on April 26 and knew nothing about Mary’s death after she left his office. Frank called Conley’s account a “tissue of lies.” (3)

Conley presented the jury with a serious credibility problem of his own. He admitted that he had lied during earlier statements to investigators and that his story had changed. His first accounts denied being at the factory. Later statements placed him there a day before, and then the day of which gradually added details about Frank, Mary’s body, the notes, and the alleged disposal of the body. Conley explained that he had lied because he wanted to protect himself and Frank, who he thought would come get him out, and later was frightened even more because he might be accused of the crime itself and did not initially want to admit his own involvement. (7)

The jury had to decide whether Conley’s later account represented the mainthrust of truth finally being disclosed or another version from a witness who had already admitted giving earlier false statements.

Frank and Conley contradicted each other, and thus could not both be telling the truth about their encounter that day. Conley said they worked together to move Mary’s body. Frank said he never saw Conley at all.

Lemmie Quinn and the Late Noon Timeline

Lemmie Quinn, foreman of the metal department, supplied another important time point.

Quinn testified for the defense that he visited the factory at approximately 12:20 p.m. and spoke with Frank in his office. He did not see Mary Phagan, Jim Conley, or Monteen Stover. Under cross-examination, Quinn acknowledged that he had reconstructed the time afterward rather than checking the office clock at the moment of his visit. (8) He also gave his arrival time, as something the authorities regarded as a fabrication, because he gave it in a suspicious way. He said things about that late arrival which made the authorities doubt its authenticity.

Frank said Mary had been gone only a short time when Quinn arrived. His August 18 version of Mary arriving about ten to fifteen minutes after Hattie Hall’s 12:02 departure fits more closely with Quinn’s estimated visit than Frank’s earlier statement that Mary arrived between 12:05 and 12:10. (3)(6)(8)

Conley gave a different sequence. He placed Quinn’s visit before Mary Phagan entered the building. (7) Conley did not see Quinn come back to the factory.  (There are actually two situations where people later tell every one they had "come back" to the benefit of Leo Frank, one is Lemmie Quinn, a week late, and the other is Alonzo Mann in 1982, 70 years late.)

Once again, the jury was left to compare remembered times and the order of events.

Mrs. J. Arthur White

Mrs. J. Arthur White placed Frank near his office later in the noon period.

She testified that when she returned to the factory at about 12:30 p.m., Frank was near the office and safe. She spoke with him before going upstairs to see her husband, who was working on the fourth floor. Mrs. White later testified that, as she was leaving the building, she saw a Black man sitting on a box near the first-floor stairway. She could not identify the man as Jim Conley, but presumably it was him. (9)

Frank referred to Mrs. White in his own statement and acknowledged that her memory of seeing him near the office during this period might have been better than his own. (3)

Her testimony supported Frank’s presence around the second-floor office later in the noon hour while also establishing that an unidentified Black man was present on the first floor before she left.

Robert Pittman Barrett and the Metal Department

The jury also had physical evidence to consider.

Robert Pittman Barrett, a machinist in the metal department, testified for the State that on Monday morning, April 28, he discovered what appeared to him to be blood spots on the floor near the women’s dressing room. He described one larger spot with smaller spots nearby and said a white substance appeared to have been spread over part of the area. (10)

Barrett also found several strands of hair on the handle of his bench lathe. He said the hair had not been there when he left work Friday evening, April 25. (10)

This was important because Conley placed Mary’s body in the metal department before he said it was carried to the basement. (7)

The defense challenged the meaning of Barrett’s discoveries. Witnesses described the metal-room floor as dirty and stained from industrial work. Quinn testified about previous injuries and blood in the department, while the defense questioned whether the stains and hair could be connected to Mary with certainty. (8)

The jurors therefore had to decide how much weight to give the physical evidence and whether it supported Conley’s account of what happened upstairs.

Harry Denham and the Elevator

Conley claimed he and Frank used the factory elevator to take Mary’s body from the second floor to the basement. (7)

Harry Denham, who was working with Arthur White on the fourth floor that Saturday, testified that he did not remember hearing. Denham also acknowledged that he and White were hammering and making considerable noise while they worked. (11)

His testimony gave the defense an argument against Conley’s elevator story, while his description of the noise weakened any claim that he necessarily would have heard every movement elsewhere in the building.

The Medical Evidence

Dr. Henry F. Harris, secretary of the Georgia State Board of Health, gave the jury medical testimony concerning Mary’s injuries and digestion.

Harris testified that Mary had suffered a blow to the back of her head and had been strangled. His examination of her stomach showed cabbage and bread that were only partly digested. Based on the condition of the food, he believed the attack or death had occurred relatively soon after her meal. He acknowledged that digestion varies among individuals and that an exact time of death could not be established from stomach contents alone. (12) he placed the time of death in a 15 minute range from noon to 12:15 pm.

This testimony helped the jury consider the likely time window of the attack, although it could not identify who attacked Mary.

Frank Returns to the Stand

Frank’s longwinded August 18 statement was not his final appearance before the jury.

On Wednesday, August 20, 1913, as the evidentiary portion of the trial was drawing to a close, Frank mounted the witness stand again.

Attorney Reuben R. Arnold told Judge Leonard S. Roan that accusations introduced during the State’s rebuttal required a personal response from Frank. Solicitor General Hugh M. Dorsey objected, but Judge Roan permitted Frank to speak. (13)

This second unsworn statement was brief.

According to The Atlanta Constitution, Frank denied the testimony of Willie Turner, denied claims that witnesses had seen him talking with Mary Phagan in the manner they described, and denied an accusation that he had entered a dressing room with another female employee (Rebecca Carson). He then returned to his seat. (13)

Frank was the last person to address the jury from the witness stand before the evidence closed. Like his August 18 appearance, his final statement was unsworn.

This date is sometimes confused because the newspaper reports describing the event were published on Thursday, August 21. The second statement itself was made on Wednesday afternoon, August 20, 1913. Contemporary reporting confirms that both sides completed the presentation of evidence that Wednesday. (13)(14)

Twenty-Four Days of Evidence

The evidentiary phase of the Leo Frank trial began on Monday, July 28, 1913, and ended on Wednesday, August 20, 1913, a span of 24 calendar days.

Closing arguments began the following morning, Thursday, August 21.

The lawyers then addressed the jury over several days. The arguments continued through the morning of Monday, August 25, 1913, when Judge Roan charged the jury and the case was submitted for deliberation.

Frank’s two appearances therefore came very near the end of a long trial. His principal statement on August 18 gave the jury his complete account. His brief return on August 20 allowed him to deny new accusations before the evidence closed.

Listen to Frank and Weigh the Evidence

In just a few days, August 18, 2026, marks 113 years since Leo Frank made his principal unsworn statement to the jury.

This abstract montage video from The American Mercury was originally created for the 2013 centennial of the Leo Frank trial. It recreates the setting of Frank’s August 18 appearance and presents his words as part of the surviving historical record.

Listen first to the analysis and then listen to Frank in his own words.

Put yourself in the jury box.

Compare what Frank told the jury with his earlier April 28 statement. Consider Monteen Stover’s five minutes in the apparently empty office from 12:05 to 12:10. Place Hattie Hall’s 12:02 time punch beside Frank’s later estimate of Mary’s arrival. Examine Lemmie Quinn’s approximately 12:20 visit and Mrs. White’s presence around 12:30. Compare Frank’s complete denial of seeing Jim Conley with Conley’s detailed accusations and Conley’s admitted earlier lies. Consider Barrett’s discoveries in the metal department, Denham’s testimony about the elevator, the medical evidence, and the testimony offered by witnesses for both the State and the defense.

Frank had the opportunity to speak directly to the twelve men who would decide his fate, without being placed under oath or compelled to undergo ordinary cross-examination. The jury had heard weeks of sworn testimony against which they could measure his account.

The question they faced was the same question that remains available to anyone studying the surviving record today:

How well did Leo Frank’s own account fit the evidence surrounding him?

text:
The American Mercury presents Bradford L. Huie’s four-part abridged audiobook, The Leo Frank Trial: Four Weeks from the 1913 Brief of Evidence.

Based on the official 1913 Brief of Evidence from the trial of Leo M. Frank, this audiobook follows the case week by week through the Fulton County Superior Court in Atlanta, Georgia.

The Brief of Evidence is a digest of the testimony and evidence presented during the trial. It was prepared as part of the legal record following the conviction, agreed upon by counsel for the prosecution and defense, and approved by the trial judge. This makes it an important surviving record of what witnesses actually testified to under oath in the courtroom. Georgia appellate practice required a brief of evidence used in this manner to be agreed to by counsel and approved by the court.[1]

From July 28 through August 25, 1913, jurors heard four weeks of testimony, cross-examinations, conflicting accounts, physical evidence, and arguments in the murder trial of 13-year-old Mary Phagan.

Presented in four abridged parts, the audiobook carries the listener through the trial as it unfolded: from the first witnesses in Week One, through the prosecution and defense cases, to the final testimony, closing arguments, jury deliberations, and verdict in Week Four.

Four Weeks. Four Parts. One Month-Long Trial.

Drawn from the official 1913 Brief of Evidence agreed upon by the prosecution and defense and approved by the trial judge.

Tune in and hear the Leo Frank trial unfold from the surviving courtroom record itself.

References

Supreme Court of Georgia. (1954). Heard v. Helms, 210 Ga. 242. The court discusses the requirement that a brief of evidence be agreed to by counsel and approved by the court.

The world’s busiest airport is tapping the municipal bond market for more than $1 BILLION.

Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport is issuing debt to help fund its massive $13 billion expansion.

Some of the 2036 bonds are being offered at a 3.84% yield.

But for a high-income Georgia investor, that number is misleading.

Because qualifying Georgia municipal bond interest can be exempt from both federal and Georgia state income taxes, a 3.84% tax-free yield can be equivalent to roughly a:

6.4% taxable yield

That’s assuming a 37% federal tax bracket and roughly 5% Georgia state income tax.

The bonds are also rated:

AA+ by Kroll
AA by S&P
AA by Fitch

This is why you cannot compare municipal bond yields directly with Treasury or corporate bond yields.

A 3.84% muni yield can effectively compete with a 6%+ taxable bond once taxes are considered.

The yield you keep matters more than the yield you see.

text:
Mary Phagan Autopsy Report

Dr. H. F. Harris Testifies for the State at the 1913 Leo Frank Trial

This lip-sync video is an early demonstration prototype recreating the testimony of Dr. H. F. Harris at the 1913 trial of Leo M. Frank. More work still needs to be done on the facial movements, timing, synchronization, and overall presentation. The voice is also temporary. A later version will use a more historically appropriate Southern accent and improved vocal delivery to better reflect how an Atlanta physician of Harris’s era may have sounded. The present video is intended primarily to demonstrate the concept and bring the surviving courtroom testimony to life.

Dr. H. F. Harris, Secretary of the Georgia State Board of Health, was one of the prosecution’s principal medical witnesses at the trial in the Fulton County Superior Court Annex in Atlanta, Georgia. Judge Leonard Strickland Roan presided over the trial, which began Monday, July 28, 1913.

Harris first took the stand on Friday afternoon, August 1, 1913, the fifth day of the trial. H. L. Parry, the court stenographer, testified immediately before him. Harris became ill while testifying and was unable to complete his examination that afternoon. G. C. Febuary, stenographer for Atlanta Chief of Detectives Newport Lanford, followed him on the stand.

Harris later returned to complete his testimony and undergo cross-examination. On Thursday, August 7, he finished his evidence shortly before the prosecution rested its main case. City Detective L. S. Rosser had testified immediately before Harris returned. Dr. Leroy W. Childs followed Harris as the first witness called by the defense and was used in part to challenge Harris’s conclusions concerning digestion and the estimated interval between Mary Phagan’s last meal and her death.

Harris held a unique place among the physicians involved in the case. Dr. J. W. Hurt examined Mary’s body after it was discovered, but Harris performed the detailed autopsy after her body was disinterred on May 5, 1913. He removed and examined organs and stomach contents and carried the examination into the laboratory, using chemical tests and a microscope to study tissues and other material taken from Mary’s body.

One of Harris’s most important findings concerned Mary’s final meal. Her mother, Mrs. J. W. Coleman, testified that Mary ate cabbage and bread at their home at 146 Lindsey Street at about  a.m. on Saturday, April 26, 1913. Mary left home around  a.m. to travel downtown to the National Pencil Company at 37-41 South Forsyth Street, where she intended to collect her pay envelope.

During the autopsy, Harris removed about 160 cubic centimeters of cabbage and bread from Mary’s stomach. His examination showed that the meal had undergone very little digestion. Under the microscope, he found little alteration in the starch, while his chemical examination showed only limited digestive activity. He also testified that none of the food had passed into the small intestine.

Harris did not claim that he could calculate the exact minute Mary died. His conclusion was expressed as a range. From the condition of the stomach contents, he believed Mary had either been rendered unconscious or killed within approximately thirty to forty-five minutes after eating.

Using Mrs. Coleman’s testimony that Mary ate at about  a.m., Harris’s estimate placed the critical period roughly between noon and  p.m. His medical findings therefore became an important part of the prosecution’s attempt to establish when Mary died after reaching downtown Atlanta.

Harris also examined the injuries to Mary’s head and neck. After removing the skull, he found hemorrhaging beneath the area where she had been struck on the back of the head. He believed the blow could have rendered her unconscious, but concluded that strangulation by the cord around her neck caused her death.

His microscopic examination went beyond what could be seen with the naked eye. Harris examined tissues taken from the vagina and uterus and testified concerning hemorrhage, dilated blood vessels, and changes visible under magnification. His testimony was therefore based on an autopsy, laboratory testing, and microscopic examination of the body and its tissues.

The defense devoted considerable attention to attacking Harris’s estimate concerning digestion. Dr. Leroy W. Childs was called immediately after the State rested and emphasized the variations that can occur in digestion, particularly with foods such as cabbage. Yet Harris had never claimed that stomach contents could establish an exact clock time. He offered a medically based range derived from the condition of the food he personally removed and examined.

This reconstruction attempts to give viewers a sense of how Harris’s testimony may have sounded in the Fulton County courtroom in August 1913. It remains a rough prototype. The lip synchronization, facial animation, voice performance, and historical presentation will continue to be refined, and the final voice will need a more convincing Southern accent appropriate to the period and setting.

text:
Why Dr. Henry F. Harris’s Examination Was Different

Dr. Henry F. Harris conducted the most detailed medical examination of Mary Phagan’s body presented by the State at Leo Frank’s 1913 trial. Mary’s body had been found early Sunday morning, April 27, in the basement of the National Pencil Company in Atlanta. It was taken to P. J. Bloomfield’s undertaking establishment, where undertaker W. H. Gheesling prepared and embalmed it. Fulton County physician Dr. John W. Hurt examined the body there that morning. Hurt observed the cord around Mary’s neck, the head wound, blackened eye, scratches, blood, and the condition of the genital area. He concluded that she had died from strangulation. The official Brief of Evidence, however, shows that Hurt’s examination was much more limited than the examination Harris later performed.

On Monday, May 5, 1913, Mary’s body was exhumed at the city cemetery in Marietta. Coroner Paul Donehoo, Dr. Hurt, and Dr. Harris were present. Harris then conducted the post-mortem examination that became the foundation of his trial testimony. Contemporary newspaper reporting stated that the stomach contents were taken to the laboratory of the Georgia State Board of Health at the State Capitol in Atlanta for further study.

Harris did something the earlier examination had not done. He opened and examined the body internally and studied tissue and stomach material under a microscope. At Frank’s trial, the official Brief of Evidence records Harris saying, “I made a microscopic examination of the vagina and uterus.” He also explained that the swelling and enlargement of certain blood vessels “could be seen only with a microscope.”

This distinction is important. A doctor examining a body with the naked eye can see bruises, cuts, blood, swelling, and obvious injuries. A microscope allows the examiner to study changes occurring at the level of the tissue itself. Harris reported that the epithelium, the thin layer of cells lining the vaginal wall, had been loosened and in places completely detached. He also described dilated blood vessels, meaning vessels that had widened, and hemorrhage in the surrounding tissues, meaning blood had escaped into nearby tissue. Harris interpreted those changes, together with inflammation, as evidence that genital trauma had occurred while Mary was still alive and shortly before her death.

Harris did not find sperm cells, which physicians of the period called spermatozoa. His examination therefore did not establish ejaculation or sexual intercourse. What he testified to was physical evidence of injury. He believed the tissue changes showed that “violence,” the word used in the 1913 testimony for physical trauma, had occurred in the genital area before death. He estimated the interval at perhaps ten to fifteen minutes, although that timing was a medical opinion and became a point of dispute during the trial.

Dr. Hurt’s testimony shows why Harris could reach conclusions Hurt could not. Hurt acknowledged in the Brief of Evidence that he had made no examination of the blood vessels of the uterus or womb and had never examined Mary’s lungs. Hurt had performed what he called a digital and ocular examination. “Digital” meant examining with a finger, while “ocular” meant examining by sight. He found no outward signs from which he was willing to conclude that rape had occurred, and he could not determine when the hymen had been ruptured. Hurt was present when Harris later performed the post-mortem examination, but Hurt had not conducted Harris’s microscopic tissue analysis himself.

Harris also examined Mary’s skull and internal organs. He found a small hemorrhage beneath the skull corresponding to the blow on the back of her head. He believed the blow was strong enough to render her unconscious, although he did not consider the head injury itself fatal. His conclusion was that Mary died from strangulation by the cord around her neck.

His examination of the stomach added another layer of forensic evidence. Harris found about 160 cubic centimeters, roughly 5.4 fluid ounces, of cabbage and bread or biscuit. He studied the contents microscopically and chemically and found very little digestive change. Since Mary’s mother, Mrs. J. W. Coleman, testified that Mary had eaten cabbage and bread at about 11:30 a.m. at their home at 146 Lindsey Street before leaving for the factory, Harris used the state of digestion to estimate how soon afterward Mary had become unconscious or died. He placed the interval at roughly thirty to forty-five minutes, while acknowledging under cross-examination that digestion varies from person to person.

Dr. Claude A. Smith, Atlanta’s city bacteriologist and chemist, also used laboratory methods in the investigation, but his work was different. Smith examined suspected blood on wooden floor chips from the National Pencil Company and stains on a shirt associated with Newt Lee. He was analyzing physical evidence collected from the investigation, not performing a microscopic examination of Mary Phagan’s internal tissues.

Later in the trial the defense called physicians including Dr. George Bachman, Dr. Thomas H. Hancock, Dr. Willis Westmoreland, and Dr. John C. Olmstead to challenge portions of Harris’s medical reasoning, especially his conclusions about digestion and the timing of the injuries. Their testimony was expert criticism of Harris’s conclusions. They had not performed Harris’s May 5 autopsy or his microscopic examination of Mary’s tissues.

The basic difference is therefore straightforward. Dr. Hurt gave the jury valuable firsthand observations from his early examination of Mary’s body. Dr. Smith performed laboratory tests on evidence collected elsewhere in the investigation. The defense physicians later offered competing medical opinions. Dr. Harris, however, examined Mary internally, studied her tissues and stomach contents under magnification, and used those findings to address three major forensic questions: what caused her death, whether the blow to her head could have rendered her unconscious, and whether the genital injuries occurred before she died. His testimony went beyond what could be seen on the surface of the body and gave the jury the most extensive microscopic and post-mortem evidence presented in the case.

References

[1] Harris, H. F. (1913). Testimony for the State, State of Georgia v. Leo M. Frank, Brief of Evidence. Leo Frank Trial Brief of Evidence. Dr. H. F. Harris trial testimony

[2] Hurt, J. W. (1913). Testimony for the State, State of Georgia v. Leo M. Frank, Brief of Evidence. Leo Frank Trial Brief of Evidence. Dr. J. W. Hurt trial testimony

[3] Smith, Claude. (1913). Testimony for the State, State of Georgia v. Leo M. Frank, Brief of Evidence. Leo Frank Trial Brief of Evidence. Dr. Claude Smith trial testimony

[4] The Atlanta Journal. (1913, August 2). Dr. Harris collapses on stand as he gives sensational evidence. Original August 2, 1913 newspaper PDF

HIGH-PRODUCTION GUARD WITH A DEVELOPING CROSS-CONTEXT UPSIDE CASE

Meyerkorth enters the evaluation with a stronger foundation than early recruiting visibility alone. She has produced at essentially the same scoring level across two varsity seasons, earned statewide recognition, contributed to postseason success, and now carries Nike Girls EYBL exposure through Missouri Phenom.

PRODUCTION / OFFENSIVE ANALYSIS

As a freshman, Meyerkorth averaged 17.7 PPG, 4.4 RPG, 2.0 APG and 2.8 SPG. Her sophomore season remained stable at 17.0 PPG, 3.5 RPG and approximately 2.3–2.4 APG across 32 games.

That consistency is the primary signal.

She also owns a verified 30-point sectional performance and surpassed 1,000 career points during her sophomore season. The unresolved layer is efficiency. Verified shooting splits, shot distribution, turnover data and assist-to-turnover ratio remain unavailable.

FACILITATING / BASKETBALL INTELLIGENCE

Her PG/SG designation suggests functional role flexibility, but available evidence does not establish her as a true primary initiator. The assist production supports secondary creation activity without proving advanced lead-guard processing.

DEFENSIVE / COMPETITIVE CHARACTER

Steal production of 2.8 SPG as a freshman and 2.0 SPG as a sophomore creates a legitimate defensive-event signal. Film is still required to identify whether that production comes primarily from anticipation, ball pressure, scheme or risk-taking.

RECRUITMENT MARKET ANALYSIS

Northern Iowa is the first publicly announced Division I offer. Reported contact with Iowa State adds market visibility but should not be treated as an offer.

COMPETITIVE INFRASTRUCTURE

Rock Port’s Missouri Class 1 setting requires contextual calibration, not automatic discounting. Her school résumé is strengthened by postseason success and statewide honors, while Missouri Phenom now supplies the higher-density evaluation environment needed to test translation.

THE BEECHUM VERDICT

Meyerkorth belongs on the active watch board because the résumé has moved beyond speculative potential. She has produced, won, accumulated recognition and entered the Division I market.

The next question is translation.

text:
Uso Seumalo played six games of high school football.

Four of them were EIGHT-MAN football.

He's now a 330 pound nose tackle in camp with the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks.

Start with where he's from, because it explains everything.

Molokai is one of the most rural islands in Hawaii. About 7,300 people. Molokai High School in Ho'olehua has roughly 380 students, and it's the only public high school on the entire island.

The school didn't even have a sanctioned football team for more than 50 years. They brought the program back around 2012.

And when they did, they couldn't field 11-man. Not enough bodies. So the Molokai Farmers played eight-man football in the Maui Interscholastic League against Lanai and Hana.

Now here's Vaai Jericho Seumalo, who everyone calls Uso.

He wasn't a football player. He played volleyball and basketball, and he was good enough to earn honorable mention all-state honors in both.

Football wasn't happening, because his parents didn't want him playing it.

So as a senior, in 2019, he talked them into it.

That season Molokai went 4-0 in the league and won their fifth straight MIL eight-man championship. They also played two non-league 11-man games against bigger schools and lost both.

Six games. That's the entire high school football career of Uso Seumalo.

In those six games he made first team all-conference and got picked for the All-Hawai'i Bowl.

Then he flew to Garden City, Kansas. Roughly 3,700 miles and one ocean from home, to play junior college football in the middle of the American prairie.

Two seasons there: 47 tackles and five sacks. ESPN ranked him the 31st best junior college prospect in the country and the second best defensive tackle in his class.

Kansas State's defensive line coach saw the film and brought him in for a workout.

His high school coach Mike Kahale's version of it: "Uso did not disappoint. They were really impressed with his footwork and athleticism and made him an offer."

When he signed, Uso Seumalo became the first Division I scholarship football player in the history of Molokai High School.

Not the first in a decade. The first ever.

He played four years at Kansas State. Fifty games in the Big 12. He was in the middle of the goal line stands in the Big 12 Championship Game.

Think about that jump. Eight-man football on Molokai to the Big 12 in about three years.

And on May 1 of this year, after the draft ended and his name was never called, the Seattle Seahawks signed him as an undrafted free agent.

He reported to rookie minicamp in Renton two days later and reportedly opened eyes right away.

But before that, he went home. He flew back to Molokai and visited his old school in Maunaloa.

On the local Molokai sports report, the host signed off with five words.

"Uso, live your dream, young man."

And what Seumalo keeps talking about isn't himself. It's the kids back on that island.

"It just goes to show that everybody's been there for me. The support, the prayers. A lot of these kids don't realize it until it actually happens. The chance of making something this big is possible."

And: "The value of belief is huge. If you don't believe in yourself, you won't accomplish what you want."

He's wearing 92 and fighting for a roster spot on a team that just won a Super Bowl.

He might make it. He might not. Undrafted nose tackles are long odds by definition.

But somewhere on Molokai there's a kid playing eight-man football on a field where nobody has ever done this.

And he's watching.

Exiting the train at 75th Avenue, a deserted station just after 11:00 pm, ascending the stairs, a weary 52-year-old author unintentionally letting her guard down, unzips her black bag, emblazoned with MARC JACOBS NEW YORK in gold lettering, anxious to rid her hands of repulsive train crud.

Her heart thrumps in her chest like a jackrabbit when she spies a 30-something disheveled man wearing a camouflage jacket, black pants, and matching shoes lurking near the exit. A devil in disguise. A native New Yorker, she’s well-aware that means trouble. He approaches, eager for a handout. “Hey, goodnight…hey goodnight,” he squawks urgently, like a demented parrot, bouncing on the balls of his feet. Polly wants a cracker!

She averts her gaze quickly downward. A maroon splotch the size of a plumb makes her queasy. Is that blood fresh, the woman wonders, as she weighs her options — Queens Boulevard, North side — her usual point of egress — and Queens Boulevard, South side, which requires her to cross eight lanes of treacherous traffic to reach her apartment safely. The meddlesome man paces between the two. Caught between the devil and the deep blue sea, quick like a bunny, she scampers to the North side. Outside, the woman glances over her shoulder. Luckily, she’s alone, for now…
.

Amy Grech has sold over 100 stories to various anthologies and magazines including: 10 by 10 Flash Fiction Stories, Apex Magazine, Gamut Magazine, Punk Noir Magazine, Roi Fainéant Press, Space & Time Magazine, Tales from the Canyons of the Damned, Yellow Mama, and many others. A Dish Served Cold

by Madeleine Armstrong / @Madeleine_write
.

Every summer, my in-laws throw a family garden party and everyone brings a dish. In previous years I slaved over rich curries, crispy bhajis and sweetly spiced cardamom cakes, but they always turned their noses up, muttering about the funny foreign flavours when they thought I wasn’t listening.

This year, I can’t be arsed.

“I’m making salmagundi,” I announce during our weekly call.

“Salma-what now?” my father-in-law says.

“Is it ethnic?” my mother-in-law asks. “After your last curry I was on the loo for days.”

Why do old people think everyone wants to know about their bowel habits?

“It’s like a salad,” I say. “Not spicy.”

Their relief washes down the phone line.

When the big day comes, I take my time over the dish: layer upon layer of wafer-thin ham, topped with succulent tomatoes and crunchy lettuce, finished with pimento-stuffed olives, quartered hard-boiled eggs, and the pièce de résistance: some carefully selected prawns.

Beautiful, if I say so myself.

When I place the salmagundi on the heaving picnic table everybody coos, all the aunts and uncles and cousins crowding around in a way they never did with my other dishes. My in-laws take the choicest ingredients, including most of the prawns, and tuck in as I nibble on breadsticks and supermarket tzatziki. My husband, with his aversion to shellfish, steers clear.

It takes less than an hour for my mother-in-law to turn green. She rushes inside, holding her mouth, before we hear the strains of her vomiting through the open bathroom window. That sets off my father-in-law who, with nowhere else to go, retches into a manicured flower bed, splattering the begonias with salmagundi chunks.

“Oh dear – something you ate?” I ask.

The aunts and uncles and cousins look panicked. There’s just one prawn left on top of my salad. I’m surprised no one noticed how out of date they were – but then, my in-laws never did have much taste.
.

Madeleine is a Pushcart Prize-nominated author who dreams of food-based revenge. She lives in London. Twitter/X @Madeleine_write; Bluesky @madeleinewrite. bsky. social

The Weight of Yesterday

by Karen Grose / @kgrose2
.

Long gone, Gran’s love knew no bounds
a smile of stardust
her hugs shelter, soft and safe
her kindness my first taste of home.
Gran’s hands were always moving
quick and practiced
blue-green veins bulging under peppery skin,
all-purpose, baking cookies and then knitting striped socks afterward while I waited at her elbow.
My childish mouth watered as she prattled, the needle’s staccato click-clack keeping time with what Gran liked to call her tales
wartime stories, family secrets,
opinions
unfulfilled dreams,
hopes
a desire for a better world.

Older now, I wish I’d listened more carefully
to have lingered in those moments together instead of being mesmerized by the shiny cabinetry on the seafoam cupboards and too focused on how long it may take those cookies to cool before I could grab one off the counter and run outside to play.
Today I yearn for those stories
I’d give anything to hear Gran’s tales one more time
to lean in and ask questions
to hold her gnarled hands
to feel her magic, my source of strength.
I wish I could have slowed down back then
I wish I could have been more present
I wish I could return.
.

Karen Grose is a crime fiction writer from Toronto, Canada. Her debut novel, The Dime Box, was selected by Amnesty International for its 2021 Book Club.
