First Real Job

by Paul MacDougall / @franeymountain
.

They warned me about the rats. Bloody big things that would bite if aggravated. Best to avoid at all cost and wear thick, leather, steel-toed workbooks just in case you have to boot one out of the way. Boots with good soles so you don’t slip.

Bats were different. Odds are they wouldn't bite me, but their guano could carry some deadly fungi called Cryptococcus. If you breathed in the shit you could get meningitis and die, or maybe survive but be blind. Who needed that. Avoid bat guano at all costs. Wear gloves and a dust mask. Plus the mask can help keep out the smells. It's a sewer after all. The place stinks no matter what good it does by carrying away storm water and human waste. It still stinks.

Then there were the odd critters dummies let loose after their life as house pets expired. All manner of snakes, lizards, iguana-type things. You name it. They were down there. Not as many as the rats, but plenty big enough. Once I saw a six foot snake just a few yards in front of me. Talk about near messing your pants for sure.

The biggest problem was the gases that might be present. Methane could blow you up, carbon monoxide could asphyxiate you and sulphur smells make you wretch. But that's the life of a big city sewer inspector. How you going to know if the concrete is giving way, a pipe is going to burst or a huge disaster is right below your feet. There were a lot of risks alright. But I took the right safety courses, wore the proper clothes, carried gloves and masks, had my inoculations.

I never saw it coming. I roamed down the wrong tunnel. Perturbed a pretty messed up junky. They live down here too. Shoot up in the sewers. Carry knives. Stick people. The one hazard I was never warned about. Two-legged kind. I'm in no shape to inspect pipes and drains or do anything now. It was the last real job I ever had.
.

Paul MacDougall is a writer, playwright and columnist from Cape Breton, Nova Scotia. He writes fiction and non-fiction and has had numerous plays produced in Cape Breton.

Chopped Fine

by Ashley Mangtani / @Bookish_Ash
.

The death house sent up its order, and nobody in the kitchen could place the word. Duplantier thumbed it into his phone by the fryers. An old English supper, chopped meat, anchovies, boiled eggs, onion, grapes, whatever the larder held, served on one plate. He soaked raisins for the grapes the commissary lacked and laid his anchovies out like commas.

Renee Ostrander, twenty-four, drove Dawn Marie Cole home after close. Dawn Marie, nineteen, ran her nursing flashcards in the passenger seat. Emory Dean Hatch had cut the battery cable in the lot. He offered a jump. He drove them to the Bonnet Carré levee. Raped them on the riprap. Strangled Renee with her lanyard, then held Dawn Marie under the shallows until the cards came loose and floated. A catfish trotline brought them up, day eleven.

His grandmother had made salmagundi in Ascension Parish from church-supper leftovers, chopped fine so charity reached the table as plenty. Nine years old, holding the bowl steady, asking to do the chopping. The state asked him what he wanted. Renee's last meal was half a sandwich eaten standing at the register. Dawn Marie's was gas station coffee, most of it still in the cup holder.

He ate almost all of it. The raisins had swollen. Exactly right, he said, tell the cook.

On the witness side, Renee's mother and Dawn Marie's grandmother sat at a table laid with no cutlery. The warden asked for last words. He said forgive me, Renee. He was looking at Dawn Marie's grandmother when he said it.

One plate. Everyone eats.

His fist came open at 12:19. The plate came back at 12:31.

Duplantier scraped the rest, a coin of egg, the tail of one small fish, into the bin with everything else, chopped fine, past telling the meal from the man.
.

Revised Parameters

by Patricia Russo / @BlaiseMarcc
.

I had a thought, he says. Don’t laugh, that still happens sometimes. It occurred to me that under the grass, there is more grass, we just can’t see it. Though not under, exactly. I don’t mean like it’s elephants all the way down. It’s more like sideways, but not exactly that, either. Sideways in all directions. This hidden grass, this additional grass, is softer than the grass we can see, more tender. You could lie down in it, and float, the way you can in an ocean, or in a dream.

He looks at me, but I’m busy recording the readings for this timemark, which again indicate that all systems are functioning within the revised parameters. Not the original ones, but most definitely within the revised ones. I’m about to make a comment about this when he asks, Could you open the windows please, and I have to tell him again that it isn’t possible to do that. But you can look out of them, I say. There’s one right beside you, and you never look out of it. You can’t see vacuum, he replies, then, after a moment, adds, And the stars are so very far away.
.

A Hive That Burns

by Zary Fekete / @ZaryFekete
.

My name is Elaine, the mercury has hit 100 every day this week, and I have done everything that I can for my bees. Every afternoon I sit in the backyard, close enough to the hive to hear the soft murmur of their wings. They speak this quiet language to one another every day, a low vibration that thrums right through the soles of my shoes.

All of the books say that bees don’t do well with weather over the mid 90s. I thought about trying to move them today, but the books also recommend not doing that. You shouldn't disrupt them when they're already stressed.

This one is the third hive I’ve attempted. The first two died away, leaving nothing but empty, waxen ghost towns. Hives require a lot of work and often the bees can’t seem to make a go of it. They are expensive, and people grow frustrated quickly. But this hive, this third one, crackles like a fire. They have a will to live that matches the heat.

Yesterday, that fire spilled over the fence. My neighbor marched down the street to my front door, her face was red with heat and anger. She informed me that her son had been stung three times in the past week.

“The audacity!” she had shouted, her voice cutting through the heavy summer air. “That you should keep that hive! That you could pretend to control so many thousand!”

Now, I am back in the grass, near to my hive, near to my queen. She hadn’t meant wrong, my queen. On hot days like this, bees are commanded to stop focusing on nectar and to start bringing water back to cool the hive. The neighbor's boy must have stood between them and a puddle. They probably felt threatened. Bees become more defensive when it’s hot, and they want to protect their queen.

I understand. That’s what I’d want.
.

Cave Dweller

by M.E. Proctor / @MEProctor3
.

There used to be bears and mountain lions. Many of them. And packs of wolves. We, I, don’t smell them anymore. Coyotes still roam. Less of them it seems, from the yips and howls. Small fare comes this way, occasionally, to find coolness in the heat of summer. The slithery, the crawling, and the furry keep me, us, fed.

The hive doesn’t need much. Scarcity makes the hive drowsy. I, we, can sleep for so long, time has no meaning. Time only matters for the prey. They live and breathe, do their foraging and hunting, and then they are no more. The hive is as old as the mountain, born from molten rock and part of it, as ancient as the world. We, I, have memories of turmoil and destruction, of the hive being much bigger. The world itself must have been bigger then, before it started feeding on itself and shrinking.

Maybe I, we, are doomed to become smaller too and disappear like all creatures of wonder. But not for eons more, because something new is hovering near our domain. It’s smaller than a bear, noisier than anything we’ve fed on before, and its smell is strong.

The edges of the hive, awake now, vibrate with the scent of flesh and blood. Maybe the prey will be curious and explore, all prey are curious. Maybe it will seek shelter from the sun, the cold, or the rain.

And if it doesn’t, the hive can wait. Prey always come back.
.

M.E. Proctor writes the Declan Shaw PI series. Book 3, The Way You Say My Name, comes out in September. She’s the author of two short story collections, and the co-author of the retro-noirs Bop City Swing and Kansas City Breakdown. She’s a Derringer and Shamus Award nominee.

The Happiest Kingdom

by Tejaswinee Roychowdhury / @TejaswineeRC
.

Azad Bose didn’t know the ‘when’ of the thin air that spat him out on a stone road draped in sunset, but he knew it was time travel for two reasons. First, the place looked like a period-piece film set. And second, just moments ago, he was outside the United Science Organization HQ, leading a protest against the Time-Travel and Teleportation Project.

By evening, the locals had absorbed him completely, though neither side understood the other’s language. They dressed him in a patchwork bottom drape like themselves, and brought him charred meat and slices of a strange lemon. He would have been flattered by their hospitality if he weren’t unnerved by their oddly serene faces and thoughtless eyes.

They marched him to the palace and introduced him as “A Sad.” The king, an equally serene-looking character, hopped forward, hugged him tight, and squealed, “A Sad!”

“AZAD!” he protested.

“A SAD! A SAD! A SAD!” The palace echoed amidst claps.

Frustrated by the dystopia and his inability to snap back into his timeline, Azad decided to do what he did best.

He shot out of the palace into the market square and climbed onto a stack of crates. Without the luxury of words, he resorted to mime. He let out a battle cry and pointed aggressively to the palace gates where the king now stood. He then ran around the market collecting props. He placed a roasted goat leg on a table and, from a wicker basket, hurled randomly at it: potatoes, tomatoes, onions, cucumbers, the strange lemons, and a couple of boiled eggs. Azad looked at the crowd—clearly inspired by his performance, he thought—pumped his fists into the air, and roared victoriously.

Just then, the king emerged and threw a block of cheese at the goat leg, and the crowd erupted.

Celebrations continued through the night. Everyone got a plate of this new dish.

Azad looked at his portion, and hunger hit him like a bag of bricks. Through a mouthful, he finally smiled.
.

Revel

by Merlin Flower / @merlinflower
.

The injustice of the plate was overwhelming.

I looked at the leaves. Five of them, three brown and two green. When the grays went from zero to eight in an otherwise ordinary night, I had used the henna leaves from the garden and Indigo powder to convert them to a different color. However, in the alchemy between the leaves, they cancelled out each other leaving me with the exact number of white hairs. Surprise!

Rubbing salt to the wound, there was no dressing on the plate. I checked again.

Five raw leaves with a sliver of a tomato. Did they really cut it into five million pieces?

‘How is it?’ asked the chef who somehow materialized nearby while I was deep in thoughts. The chef smiled at me like an astronaut re-entering the planet, as his assistant joined him. At 900 Aussie dollars this was eating money. Follows that, I should just chew them with eyes closed. But still, leaves?

‘Fantastic, Any dressing,?’ I asked, adding, ‘I wouldn’t mind a pizza underneath these leaves. Like a hibernating frog emerging to find a floor of concrete, he gasped. I saw the cunningness in the eye of the hunter changing as one of us become the prey.

In slow motion, he looked at his assistant, aghast.  Faster than Houdini, both vanished from sight.

‘Did you know? Snippid is the smell of wet leaves?’ I told my eight-year-old niece. She shrugged, not wanting anything to interfere with the taste of roo meat in the mouth.

I dreamt of a simple burger filled to the gills with red or white – edible-moisturizer. Like, not all em dashes are ai generated. And, not all moisturizers are edible.

Only the assistant came back.

‘I love the plate but even a small slice of bread or breadstick would be great,’ I said averting my eyes to hide the dishonesty.

‘Didn’t you order salad?’ asked the assistant. Between the dispatch and receiving, the message had been lost.

‘No, Salmagundi,’ my niece clarified with a laugh.
.

Ricochet: Salma Who?

by Offer Kuban / @OfferKuban
.

Two MI5 officers stood below the large Borough Market sign. To the right, in the background, The Shard reached into the London sky, stark against its blueness. London Bridge lay nearby. Even at the entrance, the market teemed with activity.

“Well, he couldn’t have picked a more public spot,” said Morse.

“I don’t like it.” Shae scanned the crowd, pinching the cigarette tight between his fingers before discarding it. “Not one sodding bit.”

Morse glanced at his wristwatch. “What about Tactical?”

“Have them stand by, especially their armoured unit. Armed coppers running about will terrify the public enough.”

Deeper into the crowd, Shae’s mind spun through various scenarios. None of them appealed. An evac order might cause panic, or worse, be too late. If there was a bomb, a shooting, anyone died, or fuck if the intel was shite, every newsie would decry the Service was screwing the pooch.

“Where are we meeting the asset?” Morse asked.

“Asset,” Shae scoffed. “He’s in the Market Kitchen. Imagine, this bloody Russian agent wants to chat over a pint. In public.”

The radio in Morse’s pocket chirped, and he muttered something into his lapel mic.

“Ricochet, the Met are getting a little jumpy waiting—”

“Don’t call me that,” Shae said. “Tell them to keep it in their pants. When we know, they’ll know.”

“It’s time.” Morse tapped his watch.

“Come on, boyo.” Shae moved through the market’s hodgepodge of colours, sounds, and smells of produce, fishmongers, and cheesemongers. “Salmagundi in here, innit?”

They’d crossed over Middle Road to the communal dining area of Market Kitchen, and Morse’s head was on a swivel.

“Who, the author?” he said, befuddled. “Don’t you mean, Salman Rushdie?”

Shae stopped. “Your mum, she drop you on your head a few times, did she?” He rolled his eyes, turning to enter the Kitchen. “Ah, there’s the bastard now,” he pointed.

“So, not Rushdie, then?”

“Don’t be twee, and let’s not make a balls of it.”
.

US Manufacturing Is Booming, Thanks to AI Data Centers | Matt Vespa, Townhall

American manufacturing is showing signs of renewed life, powered in part by the nationwide race to build AI data centers.

Manufacturing activity recently climbed to its highest level since 2022. And according to The Wall Street Journal, the data-center boom and related AI industries are fueling that demand, that has spurred manufacturing across the industrial economy. Not only has the AI industry’s soaring demand for power equipment boosted American manufacturing, but it has also helped manufacturers weather inflation, elevated interest rates, and mounting materials costs.

Several companies have already shifted major parts of their business models to capitalize on the AI-driven economic shift.

Caterpillar offers a clear example.

Its power-generation business, once a secondary line beside its iconic construction equipment, has become its most profitable segment, propelled by data-center demand. Generators are now indispensable to both Caterpillar’s growth strategy and the AI industry’s buildout. The company is spending $725 million to expand generator production at an Indiana plant and has converted a Kansas facility to build turbine engines also popular with data centers.

Ford Motor is another major company moving to support the data-center buildout. Its new Ford Energy subsidiary expects to spend $2 billion redirecting battery capacity toward electricity storage for data centers and other large industrial power users.

Several other companies, including Cummins, Eaton, Vertiv, Modine Manufacturing, Trane Technologies, Samsung Electronics, and Micron, are also shifting their operations to meet surging demand from the AI data-center buildout.

This underscores a broader free market economic point: what is good for one industry is often good for many others. AI’s rapid expansion is not confined to Silicon Valley or the technology sector; it is pumping new demand into American manufacturing, supporting factory jobs, and drawing fresh investment into the industries that build the physical backbone of the digital economy.

Payton said he removed Coleman early from the preseason opener because three weeks of work had already provided enough evidence of what the running back could do. (Zac Stevens)

🟤 Cleveland Browns

– KC Concepcion expected to be an offensive weapon
Todd Monken said Cleveland wants to get Concepcion the ball as often as possible. Concepcion also said he takes pride in never being tackled by a cornerback. (Daniel Oyefusi; Scott Petrak)

– Quinshon Judkins’ movement bears watching
Jeff Mueller, PT, DPT thought Judkins looked less confident planting his right foot for sharp cuts and showed less burst around the edge than Cam Skattebo did in preseason Week 1. Mueller had previously thought Judkins looked further along based on camp video, making the preseason tape notable.

🐆 Jacksonville Jaguars

– Jaguars starters trending toward playing
Liam Coen said Jacksonville’s starters were trending toward participating in preseason Week 2.

– Travis Hunter competing with Parker Washington off the field
Hunter described a competition with Washington to see who can arrive at the team facility first.

🧀 Green Bay Packers

– Tucker Kraft extension viewed as a matter of price
Ian Rapoport said Kraft is healthy and framed a potential extension as a question of how high the tight-end market will go rather than whether Green Bay wants to extend him.

– Packers plan to keep feeding MarShawn Lloyd
Matt LaFleur wants Lloyd to receive more touches in the next preseason game and said the team will continue feeding him as he stacks healthy days. (Ryan Wood)

🇺🇸 New England Patriots

– Patriots backfield could feature a fairly even split
Rhamondre Stevenson projects for early-down and short-yardage work, while TreVeyon Henderson could handle long-yardage situations if his pass protection holds up. Stevenson received the first red-zone reps and currently appears to have the edge. (Andrew Callahan; Chad Graff)

– Drake Maye connects deep with A.J. Brown
Maye found Brown on a deep completion during Monday’s practice.

– Kyle Williams will have an offensive role
Williams is expected to contribute despite what Chad Graff described as a quiet training camp.

– Romeo Doubs emerging as the clear WR2
Doubs has strung together productive practices and developed chemistry with Maye. His usage has him positioned for a high route share in an offense expected to utilize plenty of two-receiver personnel.

✈️ New York Jets

– Breece Hall’s groin injury considered minor
Follow-up testing indicated Hall’s strained groin is a weeks-not-months injury and he should be ready for the opener. Jeff Mueller, PT, DPT expects roughly 2-3 weeks of healing and does not view the injury as a reason to fade Hall in drafts. (Connor Hughes; Jeff Mueller)

– Hall’s preseason usage supports a lead role
Hall played 10 of 11 offensive snaps before leaving the preseason game, an encouraging sign for his workload despite talk of a three-back approach.

– Garrett Wilson misses practice due to illness
Wilson did not practice Monday because he is sick.

🗽 New York Giants

– Najee Harris visits the Giants
The free-agent running back visited New York on Monday. (Adam Schefter)

– Malik Nabers returns to team drills
Nabers participated in 11-on-11 work for the first time and remains expected to play in Week 1. John Harbaugh said Nabers is not yet operating at full speed. (Art Stapleton)

– Odell Beckham Jr. receives increased first-team work
Beckham logged his most team-drill reps with Jaxson Dart this summer and connected with him for approximately 40 yards after Dart extended the play. (Art Stapleton)

– Malachi Fields pushing for the WR2 job
Fields has mixed in with the starters, drawn strong reviews for his blocking and impressed during the preseason opener. Connor Hughes said the starting job opposite Nabers might be his to lose.

– Cam Skattebo continues trending upward
Skattebo received a stock-up grade for his preseason performance and said his previous ankle injury never entered his mind during the game. Tyrone Tracy’s stock dipped primarily because of a pass-protection rep for which he accepted responsibility.

🏹 Kansas City Chiefs

– Emmett Johnson making a push for the RB2 role
Johnson received the next 9-on-7 touch after Kenneth Walker and has been taking first-team reps behind him. His recent usage puts him firmly in the mix for the RB2 job. (Pete Sweeney)

– Cyrus Allen pushing for a rotational role
Allen produced a notable one-handed catch in practice. Matt Verderame believes he could work as Kansas City’s WR4 or push for WR3 snaps, potentially playing ahead of Royals.

☠️ Las Vegas Raiders

– Malik Benson receives rotational first-team work
Benson and Jack Bech rotated with the first-team offense. Tucker and Nailor remain the clear top two receivers, but Benson still has an opportunity to earn a role. (Levi Edwards)

🐏 Los Angeles Rams

– Puka Nacua remains sidelined by groin soreness
Sean McVay said Nacua is still dealing with groin/psoas soreness and might not practice this week.

🌉 San Francisco 49ers

– Christian McCaffrey’s absence is injury-related
Ian Rapoport clarified that McCaffrey is dealing with physical tightness—not a contract-related absence—and said it does not appear concerning.

– Khalil Herbert released as RB2 competition continues
San Francisco released Herbert while Jordan James and Kaelon Black remain sidelined. James remains a name to watch in the potentially valuable backup role behind McCaffrey. (Adam Schefter; Matt Barrows)

– Deebo Samuel seeing substantial backfield work
Samuel has reportedly played primarily running back during camp, possibly because of the injuries throughout San Francisco’s backfield. The usage could point toward a more specialized role than currently expected. (Grant Cohn)

– De’Zhaun Stribling gains fantasy appeal
With injuries affecting several other rookie receivers, Stribling’s productive preseason debut has made him a more interesting late-round fantasy target.

🟡 Pittsburgh Steelers

– Rico Dowdle and Jaylen Warren could form a true split
Dowdle returned to practice and led the run-period carry order ahead of Warren. The two backs currently appear closely matched for fantasy purposes. (Alex Kozora)

– Kaleb Johnson and Eli Heidenreich face roster uncertainty
Alex Kozora’s latest projection had both players as less likely to make Pittsburgh’s roster. Johnson could become an interesting name to watch elsewhere if released.

🌊 Seattle Seahawks

– Jadarian Price returns to full participation
Price was full-go Monday and currently projects as the likely Week 1 lead back amid Seattle’s backfield injuries.

– George Holani could remain involved
Backfield injuries contributed to Holani’s heavy preseason workload, but his dependable play could keep him involved even after Price returns.

⚔️ Tennessee Titans

– Tony Pollard and Nicholas Singleton miss practice
Pollard was listed with a foot injury, while Singleton also remained absent. No timetable was reported. (Turron Davenport)

– Carnell Tate evaluated after a hard collision
Tate held on for a first down after colliding with two defenders but reportedly felt dizzy afterward. Jeff Mueller, PT, DPT believes he was likely evaluated for a concussion, although no diagnosis has been reported. (Easton Freeze; Turron Davenport; Jeff Mueller)

– Cam Ward finds Tyjae Spears in the red zone
Ward checked down to Spears for a touchdown during low-red-zone 7-on-7 work. (Turron Davenport)

– Will Levis participates in throwing work
Levis took part in a net-throwing drill Monday. (Connor Nute)

🐾 Carolina Panthers

– Darren Waller’s debut remains undetermined
The Panthers have not decided when Waller will make his debut. He was assigned No. 35. (Alex Zietlow; Mike Kaye)

🦁 Detroit Lions

– Jameson Williams dealing with a minor shoulder injury
Williams has missed the past two practices with a shoulder injury, but Dan Campbell described it as minor and said Williams is “good to go.” Williams was at Monday’s practice helping receivers through drills without a brace or sling, though it remains unclear whether he’ll play in Detroit’s second preseason game.

🦅 Philadelphia Eagles

– DeVonta Smith returns to practice
Smith was spotted participating Monday after dealing with a hamstring injury. (Dave Zangaro)

– Makai Lemon continues side-field rehabilitation
Lemon did not practice but ran routes during rehabilitation work. He remains a name to monitor as he works his way back. (Brandon Gowton)

– Dontayvion Wicks positioned as a top-three receiver
Wicks rested with the starters during preseason Week 1 and appears to be firmly positioned among Philadelphia’s top three receivers, making him an intriguing late-round target.

🐂 Houston Texans

– Jaylin Noel’s absence leaves the slot role unsettled
Noel is expected to miss several weeks with hamstring and right-pinky injuries. Houston’s increased use of 12 personnel further clouds the WR3/slot projection. (Aaron Wilson)

🏴‍☠️ Tampa Bay Buccaneers

– Emeka Egbuka’s toe injury carries early-season concern
Egbuka is day-to-day with a toe sprain, but Jeff Mueller, PT, DPT believes it should be treated as turf toe given Todd Bowles’ uncertainty around his Week 1 status and the rigid brace Egbuka was wearing. Surgery is not expected, but Mueller projects a possible 3–6 week recovery from the injury date, potentially extending into Weeks 1–2, with an elevated risk of reinjury, compensation and reduced production over his first four-plus games back.

– Jalen McMillan considered day-to-day
Todd Bowles also listed McMillan as day-to-day.

– Baker Mayfield will play in preseason Week 2
Mayfield is scheduled to play Saturday, potentially giving us a better look at Tampa Bay’s offense depending on receiver availability.

⚜️ New Orleans Saints

– Jordyn Tyson expected to miss roughly two months
Tyson suffered another hamstring injury and could begin the season on short-term injured reserve. His history includes major knee-ligament tears in 2022, a fractured collarbone in 2024, an ankle injury and two hamstring strains in 2025, and the current 2026 strain. (Ian Rapoport; Mike Garafolo)

– Tyson’s repeated right-hamstring injuries remain concerning
Jeff Mueller, PT, DPT pushed back on describing Tyson’s latest injury as completely “unrelated,” noting the hamstring muscles function together and this is now his fourth right-hamstring injury since October 2025. If the latest strain is at a different site, Mueller considers that preferable to repeatedly tearing scar tissue at the same location, but believes compensation from the previous injuries could still be contributing and cautions that the reported two-month timetable could ultimately be longer.

– Saints face an unsettled receiver rotation behind Chris Olave
Nick Underhill said it would be difficult to overstate how well Tyson played in camp. With Tyson sidelined, New Orleans’ other options include Devaughn Vele, Barion Brown, Bryce Lance, Mason Tipton and Trey Palmer.

– Tyson falls into WR5-plus range
The extended absence pushed Tyson into the 120-plus range of one fantasy ranking, where his upside remains appealing without managers having to depend on him immediately.

text:
The Anthropocene and the Unliberated Intellect
Why humanity can alter the planet while remaining remarkably poor at judging the consequences

“The ugliest word in the English language is Anthropocene.”

AJJ leaves that line hanging at the end of Normalization Blues. The word has become shorthand for a disturbing fact about our time: human activity now affects climate, ecosystems and the conditions of life on a planetary scale.
What makes the idea even more unsettling is that our ability to alter the planet has not been matched by an equally impressive ability to judge the consequences of what we do.
A 2026 study in Nature Sustainability examined what the researchers call carbon competence, meaning people’s understanding of the relative climate impact of different actions. Across three preregistered studies involving 2,924 participants, people estimated the mitigation potential of 34 actions, including recycling, reducing meat consumption, improving insulation, using public transport, avoiding flights, buying renewable electricity and living without a car.
The estimates were strikingly inaccurate. In the first study, the correlation between what people thought would reduce emissions and the actual mitigation potential was only r = 0.06, an extremely weak relationship. Put simply, people’s estimates were barely aligned with the real differences between the actions. Familiar low and medium impact actions were often rated too highly, while several much more consequential actions were underestimated. The pattern became even more revealing when the researchers looked at what people were already doing. Across the 34 actions, the more commonly an action was adopted, the lower its mitigation potential tended to be, with a correlation of r = -0.51.
Recycling, reducing waste and other modest actions still have environmental value. The point is about proportion. Someone may make a sincere effort to live responsibly and still have very little idea which changes make the largest difference. Governments, industry and infrastructure obviously matter enormously as well. The study concerns individual judgement within that much larger picture.
Wanting to reduce one’s impact is one thing. Knowing where the largest effects lie is another.
Bad climate maths
The problem had already appeared clearly two years earlier.
In 2024, Eric Johnson and colleagues asked people to rank behaviours, companies and industries according to their emissions or mitigation potential. In several tasks, participants did little better than chance. They recognised some obvious cases, particularly airlines, but their understanding deteriorated when the differences were less visible.
One behavioural study produced an average rank correlation with the emissions benchmark of essentially zero. Another behavioural task produced a small positive correlation. When participants judged companies, familiarity and company size seemed to provide clues, but those clues did not reliably tell them which firms had the greatest emissions intensity.
Johnson and his colleagues suggested attribute substitution as part of the explanation. Carbon accounting is difficult. When people cannot answer a difficult question directly, they may answer a nearby, easier one without being fully aware of the substitution.
How often have I heard this behaviour recommended?
How familiar is this company?
How large does this industry seem?
Those are much easier questions than calculating tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent.
The researchers even offered financial incentives for greater accuracy. It made little difference. People could be encouraged to try harder, but effort could not supply information they did not possess. A later German replication broadly found the same problem, although the level of accuracy differed across behaviours and industries.
The 2026 research took the next step and examined what was associated with the estimates themselves.
Actions that were easier to bring to mind were judged as more effective. Participants also assigned greater impact to actions they already performed. Stronger environmental values predicted higher impact estimates across actions. Numeracy worked differently: participants with greater numerical ability showed somewhat better correspondence between estimated and actual impact.
The researchers connect these patterns with the availability heuristic and motivated reasoning. They are appropriately cautious about causality. Their evidence for those psychological mechanisms is mostly correlational, and they explicitly call for further experiments that manipulate availability and self-relevant motivation directly.
Even with that qualification, the pattern raises an uncomfortable question.
Suppose someone recycles carefully, buys second-hand clothes and avoids unnecessary packaging. Over time, these practices may become part of that person’s understanding of what it means to be environmentally responsible. It would be easy to assume that the actions occupying so much moral and mental space must also occupy a similarly large place in the emissions picture.
The numbers may say otherwise.
The 2026 team also tried to improve people’s estimates. Participants were given rules of thumb based on behavioural cost or social prevalence. Another group was directly told which actions had the highest mitigation potential. The effects were uneven. One intervention made estimates worse. More elaborate versions helped some participants but not others. Even direct information about the most effective actions produced only limited average improvement.
Lack of information is therefore only part of the difficulty. New information is interpreted through habits, expectations, values and assumptions that are already there.
When evidence becomes personal
Research outside climate psychology helps to show why this matters.
David Eil and Justin Rao conducted a laboratory experiment in which participants received information about their relative rank in intelligence or attractiveness. Before receiving feedback, each participant gave a probability distribution representing where they believed they ranked. The researchers could therefore calculate how that person’s beliefs should change after each piece of information according to a Bayesian model.
Favourable and unfavourable information were handled differently.
When participants received good news, their revisions followed the statistical strength of the evidence relatively closely. Bad news produced noisier responses and less sensitivity to how informative the signal actually was.
The experiment included a useful control. Participants also completed a ranking task involving an arbitrary random number that carried no personal significance. The same good-news/bad-news asymmetry did not appear there.
The obvious difference was that intelligence and attractiveness mattered to the participants in a way that a random number did not.
Another part of the experiment concerned whether participants wanted to learn their true rank. Those who had come to believe they might rank poorly were often less willing to pay for that information, with some preferring to be compensated before finding out. This was not a clean experiment on information avoidance, so the result should be treated cautiously, but it fits the wider pattern.
Eil and Rao interpreted their results in terms of the psychological cost of unwelcome information about valued aspects of the self. Their design did not prove that self-esteem protection was the cause, and later work suggests that this kind of asymmetry is sensitive to context. It does not simply appear whenever news is good or bad.
What their experiment does show rather clearly is that evidence can be processed differently when it concerns something personally important.
That has consequences far beyond intelligence tests and attractiveness rankings.
Moral commitments often become part of identity. Once that happens, criticism of a judgement may be experienced as criticism of the person making it. There is then a subtle shift from asking whether an action is actually beneficial to preserving the conviction that one is the sort of person who acts beneficially.
Under those conditions, moral conviction can begin to protect self-image rather than examine conduct.
This can happen in almost any milieu. Environmental movements are susceptible to it, but so are political parties, professions, religious communities, academic cultures, spiritual organisations and communities built around scepticism or anti-establishment thinking. Even the identity of being the person who “sees through things” can become difficult to question.
The common factor is not the content of the belief. It is the point at which reconsidering the belief begins to feel personally costly.
What intelligence does and does not protect us from
There is a familiar argument that intelligent people are simply better at rationalising. Because they have more cognitive resources, they can invent better reasons for whatever they already want to believe.
Research gives a much less tidy picture.
Ben Tappin, Gordon Pennycook and David Rand examined cognitive sophistication and politically motivated reasoning across three large studies. Their interest centred on a problem that is easy to overlook: political identity and prior factual belief are related, but they are not the same thing.
Consider two people who disagree about gun control. Their political identities may differ, but they may also begin with genuinely different beliefs about whether particular laws reduce gun violence. If they later evaluate new evidence differently, it is not enough to notice that one is liberal and the other conservative and declare the difference tribal reasoning.
Tappin and his colleagues measured both political identity and issue-specific prior beliefs.
When political identity was considered by itself, cognitively sophisticated participants sometimes appeared more polarised. Once prior factual beliefs were entered into the same models, however, the interaction between sophistication and political identity disappeared. The relationship with prior belief remained. In the third study, this pattern held across four different measures of cognitive sophistication.
Their experiments did not measure whether participants ultimately arrived at the objectively correct belief. They measured how participants evaluated evidence. So it would be wrong to conclude that sophisticated people became more inaccurate.
What the study suggests is that sophisticated reasoners may pay greater attention to whether new evidence fits the factual picture they already hold.
That can be entirely reasonable. Prior knowledge is supposed to matter. A doctor should not abandon decades of established medical evidence because of one weak study. The difficulty arises when a mistaken prior belief receives the same protection. A person can then build an impressively consistent interpretation around an inaccurate starting point.
Internal consistency is useful, but it cannot tell us by itself whether the starting assumptions were sound.
A study by Federico Vegetti and Moreno Mancosu adds another complication. More than 3,000 Italian participants judged the plausibility of real and fabricated political stories. Participants with greater political knowledge were better at distinguishing real from false stories in some conditions. Yet their evaluations still showed partisan patterns. The researchers had predicted that political sophistication would weaken motivated reasoning, but the relevant interaction was not statistically significant.
So greater knowledge can improve discrimination between true and false information without removing every partisan influence on judgement.
This is why sweeping claims about intelligence and bias are not very helpful. Education, knowledge, numeracy and reasoning ability clearly improve judgement in many circumstances. People with those advantages are still people, carrying prior beliefs, loyalties and self-images into the act of reasoning.
The more interesting question is not whether intelligent people are biased. Of course they can be. The question is what happens when a genuine capacity for analysis operates alongside a strong prior commitment.

Sarkar and rationalistic mentality

P. R. Sarkar approached a related problem from a philosophical direction. He was writing in a very different context, but his account of rationality, sentiment and conscience speaks directly to the difficulty these studies expose and offers a useful framework for thinking about what follows.
In The Liberation of Intellect: Neohumanism, Sarkar describes rationalistic mentality as a process.
One begins by studying. The positive and negative sides must then be examined and a logical conclusion reached. Even at that point the work is unfinished. The conclusion has to be considered in relation to its consequences for welfare. Sarkar identifies this final discriminating function with conscience, and calls the completed process “awakened conscience” or “rationalistic mentality”.
In the same discourse, delivered in Calcutta on 22 March 1982, he warns:
“You must never merely applaud after hearing others’ words or reading books.”
He also cautions against giving undue importance to any person or any theory.
There is something quite demanding in that instruction. It applies just as much when the person is someone we admire, when the theory belongs to our own movement, or when a new scientific result says exactly what we hoped it would say.
Sarkar did not equate rationality with emotional detachment. In Subháśita Saḿgraha Part 12 he says that “sentimental support must be based on rationality”, and contrasts this with sentimentality that becomes distorted into dogma.
This is a useful distinction in the climate context.
Concern for other people, animals and the natural world gives climate action its moral urgency. Nothing in the research suggests that such concern should be weakened. The difficulty begins when conviction is allowed to answer questions that require empirical investigation.
The relative effects of flying, driving, heating, diet, electricity use and consumption are not settled by how strongly we care about them. Their consequences have to be measured, and those measurements will sometimes challenge habits that have acquired considerable symbolic importance.
Sarkar’s account of rationalistic mentality adds another question after the analysis: what serves welfare?
That prevents rationality from becoming merely technical. An accurate emissions calculation can tell us the consequences of an action, but it does not by itself provide the ethical reason to care about those consequences. The concern and the analysis belong together, provided neither is asked to do the other’s work.
In that sense, seeing oneself as moral is a poor substitute for continuously examining whether one’s decisions actually contribute to welfare.
AI makes this newly relevant
Generative AI adds a modern complication to a very old human tendency.
Anyone who has used a conversational AI for long enough will know how easy it is to ask for arguments supporting a position. If the first answer is unsatisfactory, the question can be reframed. Supporting evidence, alternative formulations and increasingly polished justifications can be produced almost without limit.
An overly agreeable system makes this worse. What appears to be independent confirmation may sometimes be the model elaborating assumptions supplied by the user.
There is another way to use the same technology. One can ask for contrary evidence, request the strongest objection, demand primary sources, check whether a result has replicated, or ask the system to distinguish carefully between what a study measured and what someone later inferred from it.
The difference lies partly in model design and partly in the habits of the user. A conversational system that is very good at constructing arguments becomes especially useful when it is asked to test them rather than merely decorate them.
This deserves more empirical study. It is included here because the practical risk is already easy to recognise: technologies that make information retrieval effortless can also make selective information retrieval effortless.
What the Anthropocene asks of us
Climate change is usually discussed through physical quantities: tonnes of emissions, atmospheric concentrations, temperature increases, energy use, land conversion and rates of species loss. Those numbers describe effects that continue regardless of how the people causing them understand themselves.
Sincerity matters when we judge intention and character. It cannot alter a physical consequence. Carbon released into the atmosphere has the same climatic effect whether it came from ignorance, indifference or a decision made with excellent intentions. Environmental damage is not reduced merely because the person responsible believed that some other action compensated for it.
The studies discussed here do not reveal a uniquely foolish species. They show ordinary human judgement working under conditions for which intuition is often badly equipped. People rely on familiar cues. They interpret evidence through prior beliefs. Personally important information can receive different treatment from neutral information. Knowledge helps, although it does not remove every bias. Corrective information helps some people more than others.
There is no reason to expect a permanent cure for this. Being rational at one moment says little about how we will respond when the next piece of evidence threatens something we value.
Sarkar’s phrase liberation of intellect is useful because it describes an ongoing task rather than an intellectual status. Education and argumentative skill are poor measures of freedom if a person cannot seriously reconsider a belief when the evidence turns against it.
Human beings have acquired extraordinary power over natural systems. Exercising that power responsibly requires a willingness to find out when our preferred account of ourselves, our habits or our causes does not match what is actually happening.
If concern for the living world is what moved us to act in the first place, then evidence that corrects us is not an enemy of that concern. Sometimes remaining faithful to a principle requires letting go of an opinion we had attached to it.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has granted a $16.7 million no-bid contract for 6,000 gloves that can deliver electric shocks.

Dubbed the G.L.O.V.E., or Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, the device operates as a conventional patrol glove until an officer activates its "electrical mode." Once activated, the device must make direct contact with a person's skin to deliver a painful shock designed to force compliance.

In contract paperwork released on a federal database Thursday, ICE describes the gloves as "conductive distraction and de-escalation devices," and says the new technology will offer personnel a lower-impact option during arrests, detainee transports and disturbances surrounding detention facilities. According to the agency's procurement rationale, the gloves may be used when a person is "actively or passively resisting" and an officer needs to gain control quickly.

Federal records show ICE signed the contract Wednesday with a Kentucky-based company known as Compliant Technologies LLC, but formally posted the award Thursday. The six-month deal includes the gloves, support equipment and services. The gloves themselves cost $2,495 apiece.

The agency argues the devices reduce agency reliance on physical force and, in more dangerous encounters, grant officers an alternative to resorting to a firearm.

text:
I added a more powerful intro going after the hypocrisy of Doug Wilson exegetically and politically:  The Hypocritical and Unbiblical Pattern of These Men

This is not the first time this same circle, headed in significant measure by Andrew Sandlin, has resorted to a public declaration as a tool of boundary enforcement and scapegoating. Not long ago the same network produced a contradictory and divisive statement condemning full preterism. In that earlier document Gary DeMar was cast as the primary scapegoat and target—portrayed as a dangerous influence whose views threatened the faith. The critique was exegetically shallow, historically selective, and theologically inaccurate. It misrepresented the full-preterist reading of the time-texts, the fulfillment of the Old Covenant in AD 70, and the present reality of the Kingdom. Now, with the Antioch Declaration, the same pattern reappears. Pastor Joel Webbon and those associated with similar concerns have been positioned as the new scapegoats—labeled “wolves” for raising questions the establishment prefers to silence. In both cases the signers stand on the wrong side of the exegetical and historical debate. In both cases they unnecessarily sow division in the body of Christ, elevating institutional control and personal platforms above the plain teaching of Scripture and the finished work of Christ. The consistent thread is not defense of the gospel but the protection of a particular postmillennial, establishment consensus that cannot tolerate either the full implications of AD 70 or honest examination of the theological and historical issues surrounding modern Israel and the Talmud.  I have covered both of these topic in detail in my books, "Armageddon Deception" and "In the Land vs. In Christ" and they inevitably overlap.

The parallel is striking and damning. In the earlier public letter signed by many of the same men (Jason Bradfield, Uri Brito, Ardel Caneday, Jeff Durbin, John Frame, Sam Frost, Ken Gentry, Phillip Kayser, Brian Mattson, Andrew Sandlin, Keith Sherlin, Jeffery Ventrella, James White, and Doug Wilson), they demanded that DeMar answer their questions or face withdrawal of support from American Vision—because they “love” him.  The letter then moved to another declaration - A Statement on Unorthodox Eschatology. DeMar’s “crime” was simply stating that the debate between partial and full preterism should continue, that both sides needed to hash out issues, and that he wanted the freedom to study these matters for himself. He had unanswered questions for them (such as the clear parallels between Matthew 24 and 1 Thessalonians 4–5) that they refused to address publicly. It was a one-way street. They claim to embrace “Scripture alone,” “Reformed and always reforming,” the “priesthood of all believers,” and the Westminster Confession’s own acknowledgment that creeds may err and are subject to revision by the Word of God. Yet when someone exercises those principles on eschatology, the hyper-creedalists demand silence or face their wrath. Some of them claim to be public apologists yet have offered no consistent defense of their futurist “hope” (or challenges from myself to debate)--against the imminent time-texts of the New Testament. The original context of 1 Peter 3:15 was first-century believers prepared to give an answer concerning the imminent hope of Christ’s coming in their generation—a hope realized in AD 70. The signers of both letters promote a delayed, sick hope (Proverbs 13:12) that they are unwilling and unable to defend consistently.  None of the signers are willing to debate me publicly to defend their claims.

Worse still, the signers of that earlier letter were (and remain) a house divided among themselves on the very texts that determine the debate. text:
⚔️📖 PROPHECY LANGUAGE VS. MYSTERY LANGUAGE — LEARN TO HEAR THE DIFFERENCE! 👀🔥

(James sounds like PROPHECY. Ephesians sounds like MYSTERY.)

(KJV / Mid-Acts 9 / Rightly Divided)

One of the clearest ways to recognize right division is to pay attention to the LANGUAGE God uses. 📖🔍

When you study James and then study Ephesians, you are not merely reading two writers with different personalities.

You are reading language that reflects two different programs:

🏛️ PROPHECY — God’s revealed purpose concerning Israel and the earth.

✨ MYSTERY — God’s previously hidden purpose concerning the Body of Christ and the heavenly places.

And once you learn to recognize the vocabulary, the distinction starts jumping off the page. 👀🔥

⚔️ FIRST — PROPHECY WAS SPOKEN; THE MYSTERY WAS KEPT SECRET 📖🔒

This distinction begins with two incredibly important verses.

📖 Acts 3:21 KJV
“Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began.”

That’s PROPHECY.

God had been speaking about Israel’s coming kingdom program since the world began.

Now compare that with Paul:

📖 Romans 16:25 KJV
“…according to the revelation of the mystery, which was kept secret since the world began.”

🔥 DO NOT MISS THAT CONTRAST!

✅ PROPHECY: spoken since the world began.
✅ MYSTERY: kept secret since the world began.

You cannot make “spoken” mean “kept secret.”

Those words are opposites! ⚔️📖

And that distinction helps us understand why James sounds so different from Ephesians.

⚔️ SECOND — LOOK AT THE VERY FIRST VERSE OF JAMES! 👀🇮🇱

Before building doctrine from James, READ THE MAILING LABEL.

📖 James 1:1 KJV
“James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad, greeting.”

WHO? 🤔

Not “the church, which is his body.”

Not “one new man.”

Not “fellowheirs of the same body.”

James explicitly identifies:

🔥 THE TWELVE TRIBES.

That’s Israel!

James doesn’t hide his audience. People erase the address and then wonder why James doesn’t sound like Paul’s revelation concerning the Body of Christ.

⚔️ THIRD — JAMES SPEAKS THE LANGUAGE OF ISRAEL’S PROPHETIC PROGRAM 🇮🇱📜

Watch the terminology throughout James.

📖 James 2:2 KJV
“For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring…”

The underlying setting is thoroughly Jewish; the KJV’s “assembly” corresponds to synagōgē—the word commonly rendered synagogue. 🚨This is not the same context as ἐκκλησία and that’s the point! 

Then:

📖 James 2:12 KJV
“So speak ye, and so do, as they that shall be judged by the law of liberty.”

James speaks repeatedly about law, judgment, works, endurance, Israel’s fathers, and the coming of the Lord.

📖 James 2:21 KJV
“Was not Abraham our father justified by works, when he had offered Isaac his son upon the altar?”

📖 James 2:24 KJV
“Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only.”

Then James points to another distinctly Old Testament example:

📖 James 2:25 KJV
“Likewise also was not Rahab the harlot justified by works…?”

And look at the prophetic expectation:

📖 James 5:7-8 KJV
“Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord… for the coming of the Lord draweth nigh.”

This language fits naturally within Israel’s prophetic expectation. 📜🇮🇱

⚔️ FOURTH — JAMES EVEN SOUNDS LIKE CHRIST’S EARTHLY KINGDOM MINISTRY 👑

This shouldn’t surprise us!

James belongs with the Hebrew epistles and addresses the twelve tribes scattered abroad.

Compare:

📖 James 2:5 KJV
“…Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he hath promised to them that love him?”

HEIRS OF WHAT?

👑 THE KINGDOM.

That language fits the prophetic kingdom hope repeatedly proclaimed to Israel.

Christ’s earthly ministry was explicitly directed to Israel:

📖 Matthew 15:24 KJV
“I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

Cont…

1. An immigration system overhaul that only allows immigration that serves the national interest.  

Admission to the United States is not an entitlement. Prioritize people who obey the law, can support themselves, and are willing to assimilate rather than importing violent extremism or open hostility.

2. Secure borders. enforce  immigration laws, remove people without a legal right to remain, and prevent trafficking, smuggling, and unlawful entry.

3. Get ideological and therapeutic mission-creep out of K–12 schools. Parents, not school bureaucracies, should have primary authority over a child’s moral and emotional formation.

4. Return public education to academics. Reading, writing, mathematics, science, history, civics, art, and serious literature. Controversial political, sexual, or philosophical theories should not be smuggled in. Teach students how to reason and evaluate arguments instead of requiring ideological conformity.

5. Overhaul higher-education incentives. Universities should be free to teach unusual or unpopular subjects, but taxpayers do not have to subsidize them. Federal support should be tied to transparency, measurable educational outcomes, viewpoint protections, financial accountability, and actual value to students.

Stop using federal money to underwrite institutions that charge enormous tuition while producing America hating communists who are not employable. If a university wants to offer highly specialized degrees with little economic demand, it can. Not on our dime though. 

6. Establish clear, viewpoint-neutral protections for minors in public spaces. Sexually explicit material should be subject to meaningful age restrictions where minors are concerned. The standard should be based on content and age, not whether the material comes from the political left, right, or any religion.

7. Strong parental-rights laws. Parents should have access to curricula, reading lists, surveys, counseling policies, and major decisions involving their children.

8. Real school choice. Parents should not be trapped in a failing or ideologically hostile school because of their ZIP code. Expand charters, vouchers or education-savings accounts where constitutionally permissible, and protect homeschooling and private religious education from unnecessary interference.

9. Restore discipline and safety in schools. Enforce rules against violence, threats, chronic disruption, drugs, and harassment.

10. Religious liberty and free speech protections. Christian students, teachers, organizations, businesses, and churches should receive the same constitutional protections as everyone else. Government should not be allowed to punish Christians for holding orthodox beliefs about marriage, sexuality, or human nature.

11. Stop compelled ideological speech. Nobody should be required by a public institution to affirm a political, racial, sexual, or religious proposition as a condition of education or employment.

12. Transparency in government-funded institutions. If taxpayers fund a school, university, library, nonprofit, or program, taxpayers should be able to see where the money goes, what is being taught, what outcomes are produced, and what policies govern children.

13. Protect minors online as well as physically. Enforce existing obscenity and exploitation laws, pursue traffickers and predators aggressively, and develop constitutionally sound age protections for genuinely adult content without turning government into a general censor of lawful adult speech.

14. Rebuild civic education. Children should actually know the Constitution, separation of powers, federalism, due process, religious liberty, American history, and the responsibilities of citizenship. You can’t preserve a constitutional republic if students are never taught how one works.

15. End government favoritism toward any ideology forever.

16. Require fiscal accountability everywhere. Universities, NGOs, school systems, and public agencies need transparency.

„Starbase Louisiana“ - SpaceX plans 100 billion space center

SpaceX is investing up to $100 billion in a new space center in Louisiana/USA. Ten launch pads and thousands of annual launches are planned.

The private space company SpaceX has announced far-reaching plans for the construction of a new rocket launch site in the US state of Louisiana. The project, called "Starbase Louisiana", provides for investments of up to 100 billion US dollars. The Space Center is also to be used for military purposes.

The company thus underlines its ambitions to massively increase the frequency of orbital launches and to secure the necessary infrastructure for future missions in the long term.
The space center is to be built on a site of approximately 125,000 acres in Vermilion Parish. The core of the area is Pecan Island, where SpaceX, among other things, acquired a former site of the energy company Exxon for 100 million US dollars. The geographical location of the site near the Intracoastal Waterway is considered strategically advantageous, as it offers ideal conditions for launches into polar orbits.

Technical planning provides for an infrastructure that goes far beyond existing facilities. Five launch complexes with a total of ten launch ramps are planned. SpaceX aims to create capacity at this location for thousands of rocket launches per year. In order to increase logistical independence, the site should also have its own fuel production and a low-water port. 

SpaceX's announcement of investing up to $100 billion in a new space center in Louisiana marks a turning point for commercial space travel. Those who now understand the strategic levers can benefit from this mega project – before the competition reacts.

Elon Musk already described the area as the largest starting point on earth.

A New Orleans high school teacher used his job as cover, then got 33 years for s*x traff*cking a 16-year-old runaway.

Aaron Terod Johnson, a U.S. citizen and former teacher, is now starting that sentence after a federal jury convicted him of s*x traff*cking a minor and coercing a minor into prostitution.

He spotted the girl after she ran away in February 2024, saved a screenshot of her social media page, and contacted her in March when she was stranded in Vicksburg, Mississippi.

That night he drove from Louisiana, picked up the teen and a friend, and told her he wouldn’t hurt her “because he was a teacher and his students were her age.”

He offered alcohol and mar*juana, took her to his apartment, and s*xually abused her. After she left, he kept trying to reach her even after she blocked him. Within two weeks he abused her again.

Trial evidence also showed he later tried to pay a different girl for s*x after she said she was 15.

U.S. Attorney David I. Courcell said, “As an educator, Johnson violated the trust bestowed upon him to protect children; instead he preyed upon a 16-year-old runaway.”

ICE Homeland Security Investigations worked the case with the Ouachita Parish Sheriff’s Office, the U.S. Marshals Service, and ATF. The school where he taught has not been named in public reports.

This is what happens when a pr*dator hides behind a classroom title. Credit the investigators who built the case and made sure he doesn’t walk back into a school.

text:
SpaceX just committed $100 billion to turn a quiet stretch of Vermilion Parish marsh into the largest launch site on Earth.
That single decision creates one of the largest sustained demand shocks Louisiana has ever seen.
In an underdeveloped coastal area with limited industry beyond oil, gas, hunting, and fishing, the project brings:
•3,000 direct high-wage jobs averaging nearly $93,000 (with SpaceX signaling the long-term number could approach 10,000 and 60-80% local hiring)
•More than 8,000 indirect and construction jobs
•Over $645 million in direct local tax payments across 25 years
•Continuous multi-year demand for structural fill, limestone base, sand, concrete, asphalt, road construction, heavy equipment, housing, food service, logistics, and skilled trades
For local businesses the opportunities are immediate and structural. Aggregate suppliers, earthwork contractors, concrete plants, trucking firms, welders, electricians, pipefitters, and equipment rental companies will face years of elevated volume. Service businesses from catering to housing to vehicle maintenance will expand to support thousands of new workers. Companies that join Source Louisiana and position themselves early will have preferred access to contracts.
For individuals the path is equally clear. High school graduates and trade workers in Acadiana now have a multi-decade pipeline of well-paid technical and industrial jobs that do not require leaving the region. Training programs, FastStart workforce partnerships, and on-the-job pathways will convert local talent into the core workforce. Entrepreneurs who open housing, restaurants, transportation, or specialty services near the site stand to build lasting businesses in a place that previously offered few such options.
Lafayette sits 45 to 50 miles north as the nearest major city and regional economic center. The impact will be substantial. Lafayette will absorb significant spillover demand for professional services, higher-end housing, healthcare, education, retail, and entertainment. Engineers, managers, and specialized contractors will base themselves in the Lafayette metro while commuting or staging work south. Local banks, real estate, and commercial developers will see increased activity. The city becomes the natural support hub for a project whose scale exceeds anything previously located in the parish.
This is not a temporary construction boom. It is the creation of a permanent, high-cadence industrial and aerospace complex in a region that has long sought economic diversification. The demand is real, the wage levels are transformative for the local labor market, and the geographic concentration of activity will pull Lafayette deeper into the daily economic orbit of the project.
The window for local businesses and workers to position themselves is open now. Those who move early will define the next chapter of Acadiana’s economy.

A federal appeals court stayed the nationwide injunction, so every Class of 2022 athlete who was covered as a class member is ineligible again. And a judge in Louisville granted a TRO to ten players who filed their own suit back on the 14th.

He finds out in December, when the call doesn't come.

text:
A Letter Home from the Mexican-American War (1846–1848)

Extracted by S.L. Baker and transcribed by the late Betty Bowman Gabbard from the Benton Tribune, Kentucky, May 23, 1894.

This letter was written by Elisha Bowman Treadway (born 1824), Second Lieutenant in the 3rd Regiment, Kentucky Volunteers, during the Mexican-American War. He later served as Captain and Major in the 7th Kentucky Infantry (Union) in the Civil War, where he was wounded seven times. He is remembered without doubt as the Hero of Owsley County, Kentucky.

Elisha Bowman Treadway — whose mother was a Bowman and who was named after his Grandfather Bowman — is a cousin through the Bowman line to Vice President JD Vance.

He wrote to his father, William Walton Treadway, from three miles west of Vera Cruz on November 20, 1847:

Three Miles West of Vera Cruz, Nov. 20, 1847. – I take this opportunity of writing to you informing you of my good health and trusting you have the same.

I will begin at the first day of the month and give you a history of my movements down to the present date.

On the first day we (i.e., Capt. L. M. Cox, John Smith and Wm. P. Chiles) started for this place. We arrived at New Orleans on the first Saturday of this inst. and reshipped aboard the barque Paoli for Vera Cruz. We lay there aboard the barque until Sunday evening, when the steamer Daniel Webster towed us to the gulf, at which place we arrived on Monday about 11 o’clock. Immediately we launched into the gulf some of the boys commenced to vomit and in the course of an hour they were all at it with the exception of Henry Thomas and Capt. Cox. Henry Thomas never got sick during the voyage, but Capt. Cox fell about 2 o’clock that night. I did not stand up so long. I fell in the course of an hour and remained in a fallen condition for two days vomiting. The sea-sick is the sickest sick on land or water. “Tis worse than chewing tobacco, smoking cigars, riding on a horse-mill, or anything else. Some fell flat on their faces and laid so three hours at a time; some begged the sailors to throw them overboard; some wished to be knocked on the head with an axe; some cried like children and others said they would give all they were worth to be in Kentucky. Some offered the steward a dollar for a drink of water or a dish of soup, for he was the only cook on board that could walk for the first two days.

Well, at length we grew better, and seeing the porpoise, flying fish and one whale and a few vessels rather contributed to our health than otherwise. Well, we sailed on for five days without anything material taking place, but on the fifth night a “nor’wester” blew up and lasted three days, during which time we arrived at the harbor of Vera Cruz, cast anchor Sunday morning, under the castle and lay there until the next Tuesday, for the breakers would leap 15 feet high. A portion of us landed, that is Sunday from each company and a lieutenant from the same. I was first to get ashore, but could not walk without reeling about for some time.

We landed the troops on what is called the Mole; it runs out into the gulf 80 yards and is 50 feet wide and five feet high, all square blocks of stone. Just back of that stand the custom houses. They are the strangest houses I ever saw. In fact, the city is equally as strong. All along the beach is a solid fort of stone and cement, and on the back of the city there are two gates opening out to the country, also one opening to the gulf. In fact, every inch of the city is walled in and the walls are surmounted with cannons.

I have seen many of the Mexican women in splendor, and as many in degradation and squalor. I have seen the green headed/horned scorpion that weighs three pounds. I also saw a snake yesterday eight feet long and as large as your thigh. The common black bird is as large as our French crow. There is not a stick of timber here except small shrubbery and the castor bean and chaparral, etc.

I met with John Scott from Scott County in Louisville and took a parting glass with him; he sends his respects to you.

I would like to give you a full history of this country, but you can get it from the papers better than I could give it. Don’t know when we’ll leave here. When we do we start for the city of Mexico.

It is very warm, as warm as in Kentucky in August, although the nights are cool.

I am in good health, in fact I never was in better, for in crossing the gulf it acted on me as an emetic and a purgative; it has also given me a distaste for smoking and drinking anything but cider or wine.

I want you take particular care of my tools until I return. Be certain and send the children to school; be industrious and sober and you can make a living there better than any place in the world. As soon as I get Santa Anna’s scalp I will return to the U. S. and live with you, for that is a country blessed with pure water, plenty of wood and you have good health. Here they needs must cook with charcoal, go to the beach and a few poles, set up and interweave it with brush and cover it with grass or what is called thatching. If I had the timber here that is on my land it would be worth a million dollars.

Stephen Scoffield deserted us at Louisville, and the company are glad of the riddance. H. H. Mize sends his respects to you. I must stop. Farewell.

E. B. TREADWAY, 2nd Lieut.  
Of 3rd Reg. Ky. Volunteers  

To W. W. TREADWAY

The 3rd Kentucky Volunteers arrived after the fall of Mexico City and performed occupation duty. This letter remains a vivid primary source of a Kentucky soldier’s journey, the Gulf crossing, Vera Cruz, and his longing for home.

I hold 247 pages of his pension file, cleaned the graveyard where he is buried, and obtained his military monument. 
Grateful to Betty Bowman Gabbard for the careful transcription that helped preserve this record.

Paul Healey Sr:
Somerset, MA - PUBLIC UPDATE — PROPOSED SALT COD BATTERY STORAGE PROJECT

Today, August 24, 2026, I submitted Public Comment / Recommendations to the Somerset Zoning Board of Appeals, Town leaders and departments, Town Counsel, Flatiron/Somerset Energy Storage, and the Town’s technical peer reviewers a detailed recommendation concerning the proposed Salt Cod Battery Energy Storage System at 1606 Riverside Avenue, Somerset, MA 02726.

The submission adapts the Massachusetts Energy Facilities Siting Board’s recently updated Uniform Set of Baseline Health, Safety, Environmental, and Other Standards to the specific circumstances of the Salt Cod project.

I recommended that the ZBA use these statewide standards as a minimum completeness and decision-making framework. I asked the Board to require Flatiron to provide a project-specific compliance matrix identifying, for every applicable standard:
Whether the standard applies;
What documents and technical evidence demonstrate compliance;
Which qualified professional is responsible for the information;
Which Town department or independent consultant should review it;
Whether the matter must be resolved before the ZBA completes its review; and
What enforceable permit condition would apply.
The recommendation addresses fire and emergency response, battery testing and certification, toxic-gas and plume analysis, protection of nearby residents and emergency responders, stormwater and emergency firewater containment, contaminated soil and groundwater, the Massachusetts Contingency Plan, cybersecurity, equipment and battery-cell changes, decommissioning, insurance, financial assurance, and protection of the Taunton River and surrounding environment.

This submission is not a request for automatic approval or denial. It is a request for a complete, transparent, and site-specific record before the ZBA closes its review or makes findings.

The central question is whether Flatiron can demonstrate—with final plans, complete technical evidence, independent review, and enforceable conditions—that the project will adequately protect the health, safety, and welfare of the public, emergency responders, neighboring properties, and the environment. If important questions remain unanswered, the ZBA should identify and resolve them before acting.

The EFSB material is being offered as a persuasive statewide benchmark—not as a claim that draft state guidance automatically controls Somerset’s local proceeding. The public deserves to know what has been demonstrated, what remains unresolved, who is reviewing each issue, and which protections will be enforceable before construction and operation.

Submitted by Dr. Healey as a Somerset resident and retired public-health physician specializing in Occupational and Environmental Medicine. The submission is informational public-health and environmental research and is not legal advice. 
- Paul Healey Sr

𝐒𝐂𝐎𝐓𝐔𝐒 𝐆𝐑𝐄𝐄𝐍-𝐋𝐈𝐆𝐇𝐓𝐒 𝐓𝐑𝐔𝐌𝐏'𝐒 𝐌𝐀𝐈𝐋-𝐁𝐀𝐋𝐋𝐎𝐓 𝐎𝐑𝐃𝐄𝐑 𝟔—𝟑 — 𝐀𝐍𝐃 𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐃𝐈𝐒𝐒𝐄𝐍𝐓 𝐈𝐒 𝐋𝐎𝐍𝐆𝐄𝐑 𝐓𝐇𝐀𝐍 𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐑𝐔𝐋𝐈𝐍𝐆

On Monday the Supreme Court granted the Trump administration’s emergency application 6–3, staying the Massachusetts district-court injunction that had frozen the President’s March mail-ballot executive order since June. For the first time, the order can move — with 71 days until the midterms.

Strip away the commentary and read what the order actually does. It directs 𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬: 𝐚 𝐃𝐇𝐒-𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐢𝐥𝐞𝐝 𝐟𝐞𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐜𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐳𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩 𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐭 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬, 𝐉𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐨𝐧 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥𝐬 𝐰𝐡𝐨 𝐢𝐬𝐬𝐮𝐞 𝐛𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐨𝐭𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐯𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐏𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐫𝐮𝐥𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧 𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐥-𝐛𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐨𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐠𝐧. Three moving parts, one question behind all of them: is the person holding the ballot eligible to hold it?

The Court did not rule the order legal — it ruled that the 23 Democratic-led states who sued did so before the order had done anything to them. Justice Sotomayor, joined by Justice Kagan, dissented that the harms are already real and the case should be decided on the merits now. That is the actual legal fight: not whether eligibility checks are constitutional, but whether you can sue a list into oblivion before it exists.

Then there is Justice Jackson — alone.
