Subject: Massachusetts Kratom Ban 

- Please Stop Making Medical Decisions for Veterans Like Me Without Hearing From Us

To Governor Healey, Commissioner Goldstein, Members of the Massachusetts Legislature, and other officials responsible for Massachusetts kratom policy:

I am writing because the decision to prohibit kratom in Massachusetts is not an abstract policy debate for me. It directly affects my life.

I am a United States Navy veteran.

For years, I have dealt with the reality of going to the VA looking for help and being offered prescription medications. I have taken medications that left me with side effects, brain fog, and the feeling that the treatment itself was making it harder for me to function.

Then I discovered kratom.

I am not claiming that kratom is perfect, harmless, or appropriate for every person. I am telling you something much simpler:

It works for me.

I have used traditional kratom for years. I can think. I can function. I don't experience the same brain fog that I experienced with medications prescribed to me.

That experience matters.

Yet now Massachusetts is taking away my ability to purchase the product that has actually helped me while the healthcare system remains perfectly willing to send me back toward medications that did not.

Please explain how that improves my health?

I understand that government has a legitimate responsibility to protect people from contaminated products, misleading medical claims, dangerous concentrations, synthetic compounds, and irresponsible manufacturers.

Then regulate those things.

Require laboratory testing.

Establish purity standards.

Require accurate labeling.

Set age restrictions.

Establish limits on concentrated 7-hydroxymitragynine products.

Punish companies that adulterate their products or deceive consumers.

But please do not take legitimate concerns about some products and use them to eliminate access to traditional botanical kratom for responsible adults.

That distinction has become even more important as federal regulators themselves have increasingly distinguished traditional botanical kratom from highly concentrated 7-OH and synthetic products.

I also ask you to remember something that statistics can easily erase:

There are human beings on the other side of this policy.

Some of us are veterans.

Some are people living with chronic pain.

Some are people desperately trying to stay away from more dangerous substances.

Some tried conventional medications and found that they simply did not work well for them.

We are not numbers on a government spreadsheet.

We are adults trying to manage our own lives.

I am tired of having other people's irresponsible behavior used as justification for restricting choices that I have responsibly made for myself.

If someone abuses alcohol, we do not prohibit responsible adults from drinking alcohol.

If someone misuses prescription medication, we do not conclude that every patient should lose access to that medication.

If a supplement is contaminated, the rational response should be to remove the contaminated product and establish better manufacturing standards, not automatically condemn every responsible consumer of the underlying botanical.

Why should kratom be treated differently?

I am especially troubled by the span of Massachusetts' action when the scientific and regulatory debate has increasingly recognized meaningful differences between traditional botanical kratom, concentrated extracts, artificially elevated 7-OH products, and synthetic derivatives.

Those distinctions should matter when government is considering something as serious as criminal prohibition.

I am therefore asking Massachusetts officials to reconsider the blanket prohibition and replace it with an evidence-based regulatory framework that protects consumers without eliminating responsible adult access to traditional botanical kratom.

At minimum, I am asking you to hear directly from veterans and other responsible kratom consumers before making permanent decisions about our lives.

Please do not tell me that government knows what works better for me simply because government has the authority to prohibit my choice.

I have lived in my body.

I experienced the prescription medications.

I experienced their side effects.

And I experienced the difference when I found something that worked better for me.

I am not asking government to guarantee that kratom is safe.

I am asking government to respect my ability as an informed adult to weigh risks and benefits for myself while establishing reasonable safeguards against genuinely dangerous products.

Protect us from deception and contamination. Give us accurate information. Establish reasonable standards. But stop treating responsible adults as though we are incapable of making decisions about our own lives.

For me, this is personal.

Please stop playing with my health by taking away something that has helped me and leaving me with options that have already failed me.

I served my country.

Now I am asking the people governing it to listen.

Regulate responsibly. Distinguish the plant from dangerous derivatives. Protect consumers without criminalizing responsible adults. And give veterans like me a voice before taking away something that is actually helping us.

- A U.S. Veteran

The Pontifical Swiss Guard,[note 1] also known as the Papal Swiss Guard or simply Swiss Guard,[3] is an armed forces, guard of honour, and protective security unit, maintained by the Holy See to protect the Pope and the Apostolic Palace within the territory of the Vatican City State. Established in 1506 under Pope Julius II, it is among the oldest military units in continuous operation[4] and is sometimes called "the world's smallest army".[3]

The Swiss Guard is recognised by its Renaissance-era dress uniform, consisting of a tunic striped in red, dark blue, and yellow; high plumed helmet; and traditional weapons such as the halberd. Guardsmen perform their protective duties in functional attire and with modern firearms. Since the assassination attempt on Pope John Paul II in 1981, the Guard has placed greater emphasis on its nonceremonial roles and has sought more training in anti-irregular military counterintelligence, commando-style raids, counter-sniper tactics, counterterrorism, close-quarters battle, defusing and disposal of bombs, executive protection, hostage rescue, human intelligence, medical evacuation, reconnaissance, tactical driving, tactical medical services, and tactical fast shooting by small arms.

As I thought, your quote is a fabrication. 
Clinton has long maintained that Arafat rejected a viable path to a Palestinian state (details of the exact percentages and maps have been debated by participants and historians, with some Palestinian accounts contesting the generosity or completeness of the offer). 
The circulating quote, however, is a misleading rewording rather than a faithful record of his words. Correct attribution of remarks Bill Clinton actually https://t.co/KOxg2Zu7pJ Snopes and other fact-checkers have rated versions of this exact (or nearly exact) claim as an “Incorrect Attribution” or false. 
The viral wording, I.E. YOUR LIE: —“I offered Palestine all of Gaza and 97% of the West Bank, but they never really wanted a homeland for themselves. They just wanted to kill the Jews”—does not match what Clinton https://t.co/3bTivgKwNM 
What Clinton actually said In an October 30, 2024, speech in Michigan: He described the proposed deal (roughly a Palestinian state on ~96% of the West Bank plus land swaps equivalent to the rest, all of Gaza, and a capital in East Jerusalem, accepted in principle by Barak’s government). He noted the Palestinians said no, then added: “And I think part of it is that Hamas did not care about a homeland for the Palestinians. They wanted to kill Israelis and make Israel uninhabitable.” https://t.co/4w0xqJdiwH
Key differences: 
* Clinton referred to Hamas (not  “Palestine”/Palestinians as a whole) as not caring about a homeland.
* He said they wanted to kill Israelis, not “the Jews.”

The land figures are close to what he and others have described for the Clinton Parameters (typically framed as 94–97% of the West Bank with swaps totaling near equivalence, plus Gaza), but the surrounding attribution and conclusion are altered.

The viral version conflates or invents phrasing that broadens the target and changes the language in a more absolute and inflammatory way.

text:
@GrahamAllen 

You might rethink your comment.

When Carney stood at that podium Saturday and said the Americans “asked too much and offered too little,” everyone assumed he was talking about dairy quotas and hockey stick tariffs.

He wasn’t.

Over the weekend, between Carney’s own words at that press conference and the reporting out of the Globe and Mail’s sources inside the room, the actual shape of what the United States demanded came into focus. And once you lay it all out in one place, you realize this was never a trade negotiation.

This was an annexation attempt with a cover page.

Trump couldn’t take Canada with the 51st state garbage. He couldn’t take it with tariffs, because we matched him and the Supreme Court took his favourite toy away in February. 

So he and his team tried to take it with a pen, in the final hours of a negotiation, after he’d already announced “DEAL!” on his failing social media site, betting that our negotiators were too exhausted to read what they were signing.

They read it.
What they actually demanded. The verified list.

I want to be precise here because there’s a document floating around on social media claiming to summarize the US demands, and about half of it is fabricated. 

Ignore it. You don’t need the fake version. The real version, confirmed by Carney’s own mouth and sourced reporting, is damning enough on its own.

Here’s what we know the United States put on that table.

One. They demanded control over who Canada trades with. This came straight from Carney on Saturday: “The U.S. introduced at the last hour, in the last hour, efforts to restrict our ability to have other trade deals.” Not tariff levels. Not quotas. The United States demanded a say in Canada’s trade relationships with the rest of the planet. That is not a term you put to a trading partner. That is a term you put to a territory.

Two. They came for the French language. This is the one that should make every Canadian’s blood run cold, and Carney laid it out in detail. The Americans had “issues” with Canada’s subsidies for French culture. With the prevalence of French-language media online. And, I’m not making this up, with the requirement that products sold in Canada carry bilingual labels. Carney’s words: “It was unacceptable right from the start, but the Americans kept trying and trying and we said no.” American negotiators sat across from Canadian officials and demanded we water down the legal protections for one of our two founding languages. In a trade deal. About tariffs.

Three. They tried to rig the auto sector to strip our jobs. Carney said the US wanted to treat Canadian-made parts unfairly and to exempt some cars and pickup trucks from tariffs but not others, without explaining the logic. There was a logic. The logic was to pick which assembly lines live in Michigan and which ones die in Ontario, and to write it into a treaty.

Four. They demanded we dismantle our own domestic policies, right down to the provincial level. Per the Globe’s sourcing: kill the retaliatory tariffs on American autos, rewrite how dairy licences are allocated under supply management to Washington’s interpretation, force provinces to end their bans on American booze, and scrap Buy Canadian procurement rules. The United States demanded that Canadian provinces change their liquor store policies. Doug Ford’s LCBO decisions were on a term sheet in Washington.

Five. The resource grab was queued up for “phase two.” The Globe reported that US negotiators raised critical minerals, oil exports, the F-35 purchase, and Golden Dome missile defence in the talks, with the understanding that Canada’s flexibility on those files would shape the deal. Translation: sign away autos, dairy, culture and procurement now, and then we’ll discuss how much of your lithium, uranium and crude you get to keep.

Six. The snapback. The remote-control tariff. Sign all of the above away permanently, and in exchange receive tariff relief that Trump can revoke any afternoon he wakes up feeling “aggrieved.” I covered this yesterday. It’s the mechanism that makes everything else a one-way door.

Add it up. Control over our foreign trade relationships. Control over our language and culture. Control over our auto industry. Control over provincial policy. First position on our resources. And a kill switch held by one man.

There’s a word for an arrangement where a larger country controls a smaller country’s trade, culture, industry and resources while holding a unilateral punishment mechanism over its head.

Annexation.

Why now? Look at the CUSMA calendar.

Here’s the context the cable networks keep missing.
CUSMA review is right there on the horizon, and Trump refused to renew it. That was a choice. A renewed CUSMA means rules, panels, dispute resolution, three parties at the table, and Mexico watching everything. A dead CUSMA means bilateral knife fights where the biggest guy sets the terms.

So the play was obvious in hindsight. Kill the framework. Manufacture a tariff emergency under a 1930 statute nobody’s ever used this way. 

Drag Canada into a bilateral “deal” under deadline pressure. Load the deal with sovereignty concessions that would be impossible to claw back once CUSMA talks eventually happened, because Canada would already be locked in. 

Get the Prime Minister’s signature before anyone reads page 40.

This wasn’t a negotiation that went sideways at the end. 

The end WAS the negotiation. Everything before it was theatre designed to exhaust our side and set up the midnight switch. 

You don’t accidentally demand bilingual label changes and veto power over a G7 nation’s trade relationships in the final hour. You hide it there.

They bet the former Governor of the Bank of England and the Bank of Canada wouldn’t read the fine print. 

For the second time in two days I get to type this sentence: he read the fine print.

The find-out portion begins now

So where does this go? Let me tell you where it goes, and why I think Trump folds before the leaves change.

Expect a fury of announcements this week.

Start with what Carney has already announced, on the record. Dollar-for-dollar retaliation on Trump’s $28 billion, coming September 8, targeted at steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics. 

Focused, surgical, aimed at red-state supply chains, with more support for Canadian workers layered on top of the $25 billion already deployed.

That’s the announced part. Now the part I believe is coming, and why the math forces it.

For eighteen months, Carney has resisted the export tax. Reporters have asked him about it since the Trudeau days, when Ottawa first war-gamed export levies on oil, uranium and potash. 

As recently as late July, standing in Alberta, he waved it off: “I don’t see the value of it.” Reliable supplier. People trust us. All of that.

But listen to what he said next, because Carney never wastes a sentence: “There’s other things we can do if we need it.”

And then listen to what he said Saturday, after they came for our sovereignty: “Canada fuels American growth. I don’t think they want us to stop sending any of that.” And in his address to the country: “Canada has what the world wants. And we will not allow any nation to determine our future.”

The reliable-supplier doctrine was built for a trade dispute. This stopped being a trade dispute the moment American negotiators demanded control over our language laws and our trade relationships. 

You don’t owe reliability to a counterparty who just tried to paper-annex you. Every constraint that kept the energy weapon in its holster died at midnight Friday. The premiers are already screaming for it. Ford listed the arsenal out loud: oil and gas, critical minerals, electricity, potash, uranium. 

The only person who was holding it back was Carney, and the Americans just spent two weeks teaching him why he shouldn’t.

Now flip the board and look at Trump’s side of it, because this is where it gets genuinely dark for the White House.

He is running a 50% tariff war against his largest energy supplier during an oil shock. Hormuz has been functionally closed to commercial traffic for five months. 

The Strategic Petroleum Reserve is sitting at 293 million barrels, the lowest since Reagan’s first term, drained at record pace and pumping at 61% of design capacity. 

There is no cavalry. The Gulf isn’t coming. OPEC isn’t coming. The only country on Earth with millions of barrels a day of spare heavy crude, pipelined directly into US refineries that were literally built to run on it, is the one he just tried to annex with a term sheet.

Midwest refineries cannot substitute Canadian heavy crude. That’s not politics, that’s chemistry. An export levy on Canadian oil doesn’t hurt Alberta; American refiners eat it and pass it straight to the pump in Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania. 

Ten weeks before a midterm. Same story with uranium for their reactors, potash for their farms, and the electricity keeping the lights on across the northern border states.

And behind all of it, the thing I’ve been writing about since April 2025: the bond market. 

The 30-year at levels not seen since 2007. Bessent’s emergency buybacks erased by the market in 48 hours. 

Japan, China and the UK all selling at once. Foreign central banks dumping $230 billion since February. 

A president who, asked about Treasury yields, threatened to use the military on his own creditors. And Canada sitting quietly on $460 billion of that debt, fifth-largest holder on the planet, having added over $100 billion to the position since I started telling you this was the play.

Carney’s Checkmate: How Canada’s Quiet Bond Play Forced Trump to Drop Tariffs

Trump needs Canadian oil to keep the pump price down. He needs Canadian creditors to hold his bonds. He needs a deal to hold his midterm. 

Canada needs none of those things this week. 

That asymmetry is the entire story, and it’s why I think he caves, publicly, dressed up as some “beautiful new framework” he’ll claim was his idea, before September 8 makes the front page of every swing-state paper.

He walked into this thinking he was shaking down a branch plant. He was actually picking a fight with his gas station, his grocer, his power company and his banker, all of whom turned out to be the same guy, and that guy ran two central banks.

The bill, updated

Understand what almost happened Friday night. A foreign government attempted to acquire, by contract, control over Canada’s trade relationships, cultural protections, official languages policy, auto industry, and provincial procurement, with a unilateral-enforcement whip attached, and they tried to do it in the dark, at midnight, on a deadline they manufactured.

The 51st state thing was never a joke. It was a mission statement. Friday was the paperwork.

It failed because one guy read the document. Now comes the invoice, and it gets paid in September tariffs, in energy leverage, and in Ottawa, no longer having any reason to hold back, and in a bond market that just watched the United States try to defraud its fifth-largest creditor at a signing table.

I’m telling you now: Trump just started a sovereignty fight with the one country that can raise his gas prices, his food prices, his electricity bill and his borrowing costs simultaneously, and the man deciding how hard to squeeze spent his whole life learning exactly where the arteries are.

The reliable-supplier doctrine was built for a trade dispute. This stopped being a trade dispute the moment American negotiators demanded control over our language laws and our trade relationships. 

You don’t owe reliability to a counterparty who just tried to paper-annex you. Every constraint that kept the energy weapon in its holster died at midnight Friday. 

The premiers are already screaming for it. Ford listed the arsenal out loud: oil and gas, critical minerals, electricity, potash, uranium. 

The only person who was holding it back was Carney, and the Americans just spent two weeks teaching him why he shouldn’t.

Now flip the board and look at Trump’s side of it, because this is where it gets genuinely dark for the White House.

He is running a 50% tariff war against his largest energy supplier during an oil shock. Hormuz has been functionally closed to commercial traffic for five months. 

The Strategic Petroleum Reserve is sitting at 293 million barrels, the lowest since Reagan’s first term, drained at record pace and pumping at 61% of design capacity. 

There is no cavalry. The Gulf isn’t coming. OPEC isn’t coming. The only country on Earth with millions of barrels a day of spare heavy crude, pipelined directly into US refineries that were literally built to run on it, is the one he just tried to annex with a term sheet.

Midwest refineries cannot substitute Canadian heavy crude. That’s not politics, that’s chemistry. 

An export levy on Canadian oil doesn’t hurt Alberta; American refiners eat it and pass it straight to the pump in Ohio, Michigan, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania. 

Ten weeks before a midterm. Same story with uranium for their reactors, potash for their farms, and the electricity keeping the lights on across the northern border states.

And behind all of it, the thing I’ve been writing about since April 2025: the bond market. 

The 30-year at levels not seen since 2007. Bessent’s emergency buybacks erased by the market in 48 hours. Japan, China and the UK all selling at once. 

Foreign central banks dumping $230 billion since February. A president who, asked about Treasury yields, threatened to use the military on his own creditors. 

And Canada sitting quietly on $460 billion of that debt, fifth-largest holder on the planet, having added over $100 billion to the position since I started telling you this was the play.

Carney’s Checkmate: How Canada’s Quiet Bond Play Forced Trump to Drop Tariffs

Trump needs Canadian oil to keep the pump price down. He needs Canadian creditors to hold his bonds. He needs a deal to hold his midterm. 

Canada needs none of those things this week. 

That asymmetry is the entire story, and it’s why I think he caves, publicly, dressed up as some “beautiful new framework” he’ll claim was his idea, before September 8 makes the front page of every swing-state paper.

He walked into this thinking he was shaking down a branch plant. He was actually picking a fight with his gas station, his grocer, his power company and his banker, all of whom turned out to be the same guy, and that guy ran two central banks.

The bill, updated

Understand what almost happened Friday night. A foreign government attempted to acquire, by contract, control over Canada’s trade relationships, cultural protections, official languages policy, auto industry, and provincial procurement, with a unilateral-enforcement whip attached, and they tried to do it in the dark, at midnight, on a deadline they manufactured.

The 51st state thing was never a joke. It was a mission statement. Friday was the paperwork.

It failed because one guy read the document. Now comes the invoice, and it gets paid in September tariffs, in energy leverage, and in Ottawa, no longer having any reason to hold back, and in a bond market that just watched the United States try to defraud its fifth-largest creditor at a signing table.

I told you about the bonds eighteen months ago. I told you about the snapback yesterday. I’m telling you now: Trump just started a sovereignty fight with the one country that can raise his gas prices, his food prices, his electricity bill and his borrowing costs simultaneously, and the man deciding how hard to squeeze spent his whole life learning exactly where the arteries are.

When Carney stood at that podium Saturday and said the Americans “asked too much and offered too little,” everyone assumed he was talking about dairy quotas and hockey stick tariffs.
He wasn’t.
Over the weekend, between Carney’s own words at that press conference and the reporting out of the Globe and Mail’s sources inside the room, the actual shape of what the United States demanded came into focus. And once you lay it all out in one place, you realize this was never a trade negotiation.

This was an annexation attempt with a cover page.

Trump couldn’t take Canada with the 51st state garbage. He couldn’t take it with tariffs, because we matched him and the Supreme Court took his favourite toy away in February. 

So he and his team tried to take it with a pen, in the final hours of a negotiation, after he’d already announced “DEAL!” on his failing social media site, betting that our negotiators were too exhausted to read what they were signing.

They read it.

What they actually demanded. The verified list.

To be precise here because there’s a document floating around on social media claiming to summarize the US demands, and about half of it is fabricated. 

Ignore it. You don’t need the fake version. 

The real version, confirmed by Carney’s own mouth and sourced reporting, is damning enough on its own.

Here’s what to know the United States put on that table.

One. They demanded control over who Canada trades with. This came straight from Carney on Saturday: “The U.S. introduced at the last hour, in the last hour, efforts to restrict our ability to have other trade deals.” Not tariff levels. Not quotas. The United States demanded a say in Canada’s trade relationships with the rest of the planet. That is not a term you put to a trading partner. That is a term you put to a territory.

Two. They came for the French language. This is the one that should make every Canadian’s blood run cold, and Carney laid it out in detail. The Americans had “issues” with Canada’s subsidies for French culture. 

With the prevalence of French-language media online. And, I’m not making this up, with the requirement that products sold in Canada carry bilingual labels. Carney’s words: “It was unacceptable right from the start, but the Americans kept trying and trying and we said no.” 
American negotiators sat across from Canadian officials and demanded we water down the legal protections for one of our two founding languages. In a trade deal. About tariffs.

Three. They tried to rig the auto sector to strip our jobs. Carney said the US wanted to treat Canadian-made parts unfairly and to exempt some cars and pickup trucks from tariffs but not others, without explaining the logic. There was a logic. The logic was to pick which assembly lines live in Michigan and which ones die in Ontario, and to write it into a treaty.

Four. They demanded we dismantle our own domestic policies, right down to the provincial level. Per the Globe’s sourcing: kill the retaliatory tariffs on American autos, rewrite how dairy licences are allocated under supply management to Washington’s interpretation, force provinces to end their bans on American booze, and scrap Buy Canadian procurement rules. 

The United States demanded that Canadian provinces change their liquor store policies. Doug Ford’s LCBO decisions were on a term sheet in Washington.

Five. The resource grab was queued up for “phase two.” The Globe reported that US negotiators raised critical minerals, oil exports, the F-35 purchase, and Golden Dome missile defence in the talks, with the understanding that Canada’s flexibility on those files would shape the deal. Translation: sign away autos, dairy, culture and procurement now, and then we’ll discuss how much of your lithium, uranium and crude you get to keep.

Six. The snapback. The remote-control tariff. Sign all of the above away permanently, and in exchange receive tariff relief that Trump can revoke any afternoon he wakes up feeling “aggrieved.” This was covered  yesterday. It’s the mechanism that makes everything else a one-way door.

Add it up. Control over our foreign trade relationships. Control over our language and culture. Control over our auto industry. Control over provincial policy. First position on our resources. And a kill switch held by one man.

There’s a word for an arrangement where a larger country controls a smaller country’s trade, culture, industry and resources while holding a unilateral punishment mechanism over its head.

Annexation.

Why now? Look at the CUSMA calendar.
Here’s the context the cable networks keep missing.
CUSMA review is right there on the horizon, and Trump refused to renew it. 

That was a choice. 

A renewed CUSMA means rules, panels, dispute resolution, three parties at the table, and Mexico watching everything. A dead CUSMA means bilateral knife fights where the biggest guy sets the terms.

So the play was obvious in hindsight. Kill the framework. Manufacture a tariff emergency under a 1930 statute nobody’s ever used this way. 

Drag Canada into a bilateral “deal” under deadline pressure. Load the deal with sovereignty concessions that would be impossible to claw back once CUSMA talks eventually happened, because Canada would already be locked in. Get the Prime Minister’s signature before anyone reads page 40.

This wasn’t a negotiation that went sideways at the end. 

The end WAS the negotiation. Everything before it was theatre designed to exhaust our side and set up the midnight switch. You don’t accidentally demand bilingual label changes and veto power over a G7 nation’s trade relationships in the final hour. 

You hide it there.

They bet the former Governor of the Bank of England and the Bank of Canada wouldn’t read the fine print. 

Carney read the fine print.

The find-out portion begins now

text:
What’s happening in Michigan?
What are Michigan senior citizens on fixed incomes experiencing? 

Many of them are barely making it, and the data support that concern. Nearly 40% of Michiganders are struggling to afford basic needs as of August 2026. For seniors living primarily on Social Security, pensions, or retirement savings, increases in utilities, groceries, housing costs, insurance, and health care can be especially difficult because their income doesn’t automatically rise when those expenses do. 

Energy costs are serious enough that the Michigan Public Service Commission recently told state leaders that there is still significant unmet need among households that earn slightly too much to qualify for some low-income programs. Michigan has expanded eligibility for the Michigan Energy Assistance Program to 60% of state median income, roughly comparable to 200% of the federal poverty level. 

For a senior trying to survive on a modest fixed income, the monthly budget can become a series of tradeoffs: pay the electric/gas bill, buy groceries, fill prescriptions, pay property taxes/insurance, or cover an unexpected home or car repair. University of Michigan researchers specifically note that increases in groceries and health-care costs can push fixed-income seniors toward financial instability or poverty. 

There is assistance, although qualifying and navigating the programs can be difficult. Michigan offers MEAP and State Emergency Relief for energy costs, a Home Heating Credit, utility senior credits for customers 65+, and winter shutoff protection for seniors. Michigan’s SNAP rules also allow certain medical expenses to be considered for people 60+, and the Commodity Supplemental Food Program provides qualifying seniors 60+ with monthly USDA food packages. 

So the answer to “How are they surviving?” is unfortunately: many are cutting discretionary spending to almost nothing, relying on assistance or family, using food programs, postponing purchases, and stretching a fixed monthly check further than it was designed to go. Assistance helps, but it doesn’t mean Michigan seniors aren’t experiencing a genuine affordability problem.

Are you proud of this landscape in Michigan?

Looking forward to this symposium on Terrorism in Question: Decolonizing Anthropology & the Study of Islam [Oxford, NY: Berghahn, 2026] set for day after tomorrow and organized by Centre For Bengal Studies, Dhaka. 

Book Symposium on 'Terrorism in Question: Decolonizing Anthropology and the Study of Islam' by Dr. Irfan Ahmad.

How do state power, law, and media construct the label of "terrorism"? Rather than asking the standard question—"Who is the terrorist?"—Prof. Dr. Irfan Ahmad's work poses a foundational decolonial query: "Who needs the category of the terrorist?"
In his latest work, Terrorism in Question: Decolonizing Anthropology and the Study of Islam, Prof. Ahmad offers a ground-breaking critique of post-9/11 counterterrorism discourses. By examining how state institutions deploy the label of terror, his scholarship shifts our focus away from orientalist depictions and toward the structural power configurations that produce them.

Centre For Bengal Studies is hosting a Book Symposium to discuss this vital work and its implications for modern anthropology and political theory.

text:
Polymarket Review by casinobillionaire blog
    - Is this prediction market legit? Dive into its legitimacy, how to trade, and what to expect from its platform

Polymarket returned to American screens after a $1.4 million CFTC settlement, a $112 million QCEX purchase in July 2025, and a December 2025 relaunch that now sits under federal oversight as a CFTC-regulated designated contract market.

Share prices still read as implied probabilities from $0.01 to $0.99, the international venue still settles in USDC on Polygon, and the Polymarket us app lets eligible traders fund in dollars, claim a 20 trading bonus after a $10 deposit, and trade sports, politics, crypto, and culture.

     Key Takeaways

     - Polymarket is a peer-to-peer exchange, not a house book, so you buy Yes or No shares against other traders and a winning contract pays $1.00 when the market resolves.
     - Federal status improved after Polymarket acquires QCEX, yet state eligibility still shifts, so you should confirm access inside the app before you send money.
     - New accounts can use a Polymarket promo code for a 20 trading bonus after a $10 deposit, then fund with cards, ACH, or crypto rails depending on the venue.
     - Polymarket charges a variable taker fee on many books, geopolitics is often fee-free, and a patient limit order can cut cost versus hitting the spread.
     - Trustpilot currently sits near 1.4/5 from 600-plus reviews, mostly about resolution fights and slow replies, while the US venue holds dollars under exchange custody rules.

     What Polymarket Is and Why I Still Watch the Tape

I treat this Polymarket review like a hotel walk-through: I open the lobby, time the check-in, then see if the room matches the brochure.

Shayne Coplan founded the brand in 2020 in New York, and Polymarket is a blockchain-based venue that made its name during the 2024 election cycle with crowded presidential books.

The international site remains a decentralized prediction market on Polygon, while the US product runs as a regulated derivatives exchange with identity verification and dollar balances.

Polymarket is a decentralized matching engine at heart, even after the American rebuild, because prices still come from traders rather than a house line.

Each event contract is a binary share in a real-world outcome, from an NFL winner to a Fed decision to a coin-price print, and that share pays $1.00 if you are right or $0.00 if you are wrong.

A 72-cent Yes price is the crowd saying there is about a 72% chance, and that is the whole product in one number.

Politics built the fame, sports volume then surged, and culture plus geopolitics keep the board noisy around the clock.

This prediction market platform processed about $6 billion in the first half of last year, then scaled again as the American door reopened.

Intercontinental Exchange, owner of the New York Stock Exchange, put serious money behind the firm, with reports of a $600 million check inside a larger pledge.

     How prices and payouts actually move

You pick a market, you buy Yes or No at the live price, and you can sell before settlement if the tape moves your way.

The order book matches buyers and sellers, so you are trading with people, not fading a bookmaker.

Always read the resolution text first, because the rule sheet beats the headline every time.

Global tickets go through the UMA optimistic oracle, where a proposer posts a bond and a dispute can go to token holders.

American tickets sit under a filed rulebook and federal oversight, which is the cleaner path if you live here.

That split is the first thing older write-ups miss, and this Polymarket review starts there on purpose.

      Legal Status, Access, and Whether I Trust the Desk

Federal clearance for the US product is real, with caveats I will not sand off.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission fined the company in 2022 for running an unregistered book, then Americans were geo-blocked for nearly four years.

Access came back through paperwork rather than a workaround: CFTC approval of an amended designation, QCEX as the licensed vehicle, and a waitlist that later dropped for verified accounts.

Polymarket is legal at the federal level as a CFTC-regulated venue, and Polymarket operates through that licensed structure for American flow.

State attorneys general still fight sports contracts as gambling, so the map moves.

Nevada is the consistent hard no in most roundups I checked, and Arizona, Illinois, Maryland, Michigan, Montana, Ohio, and a few others have shown restrictions depending on the week.

Minnesota even passed a ban that a federal judge then paused, which tells you the fight is live.

Friends in California or Texas hear the same line from me: the app's eligibility screen is the only list that counts on the day you sign up.

Markets do settle and winners do get paid, which is my baseline for calling the shop genuine.

Custody on the US side follows exchange rules, while the global book sits in a wallet with on-chain settlement.

Wired also flagged that US users still appear to dominate parts of the banned tape, and I treat that as a compliance cloud rather than a how-to.

       Fees, Spreads, and the Cost of Being Impatient

Search Polymarket fees and you will not get one clean number, because cost lives in three places.

Posted commissions peak near 50-cent prices and shrink at the extremes, with a common US formula in the 0.04 to 0.072 range, or about $1.50 on 100 contracts at $0.50 under one published schedule.

Makers who add depth can earn a rebate, and some geopolitics books stay at zero.

Spreads are the silent tax.

Thin culture markets can cost more in slippage than the trading fee on the ticket.

Funding is the third slice: MoonPay or Coinbase on-ramps can skim a few percent on the international rail, while the US cashier moves dollars through ACH, debit, and wires with hold times.

Post a resting bid, wait, and let someone come to you.

Crossing the spread for an instant fill is how casual size leaks money.

Buy 100 shares at 97 cents and you risk $97 to make $3.

Win that thirty times and you are up $90.

Lose it once and that single miss wipes the streak.

      Market Categories I Actually Click

Market variety is the reason I keep the app on my phone.

Politics still draws the cameras: elections, shutdowns, nominations, and messy news-cycle side markets.

Polymarket sports coverage now includes NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL, soccer, and championship outrights, with live trading so you can exit after a turnover or a bullpen change.

Digital-asset books print Bitcoin and Ethereum thresholds, even five-minute candles if you like speed.

Economics lists Fed moves, CPI, and jobs, though Kalshi still feels deeper on pure macro prints.

Culture, awards, box office, and geopolitics fill the overnight hours, and those are the rooms where global liquidity often looks thicker than the US-only shelves.

Market types also include trending, new, and breaking shelves, which is useful when a headline hits and you want the freshest ticket.

Some states only see sports, New Jersey being the usual example, so market coverage is not uniform.

I still call this one of the best prediction market apps for breadth, as long as you accept that niche books can be thin.

Traders who already follow American sports odds on a traditional book will recognize the subjects and then notice there is no juice baked into the number.

      How Polymarket Stacks Up Against the Dollar-First Rival

Polymarket vs Kalshi is the comparison every new account asks me, and I keep both funded.

The dollar-first exchange was built with bank rails, 1099s, and a larger promo ceiling that can randomize up to hundreds of dollars after you trade a set amount.

Polymarket and Kalshi now share federal oversight on the US side, yet the plumbing differs.

Global tickets still run on token rails with USDC, while the rival stays in dollars from the first click.

Commissions here are usually kinder to makers, with 15% to 25% rebate talk on filled size, and takers often pay less than the rival's peak near $1.75 per 100 contracts at coin-flip prices.

Market selection on Polymarket skews faster and more global: internet culture, geopolitics, and odd news.

Kalshi skews cleaner on NFL boards, CPI, and Fed tickets that look like a brokerage.

Sites like Polymarket now include CryptoCom, Coinbase, FanDuel Predicts, and Gemini, so the prediction market space is no longer a two-horse race.

Deep worldwide tape still sends me here first, while the fattest sign-up lottery sends me to the other desk.

      The App, the Cashier, and How I Fund

The Polymarket app is the US front door, and I recommend it over the waitlist-era desktop flow.

Apple users currently rate the iOS app near 4.6 to 4.7 on the App Store from tens of thousands of reviews, while Android scores have lagged because of queue complaints.

Screens stay clean, books load quickly, and you can trade from a phone without touching a self-custody wallet on the US build.

A dedicated mobile app matters here, because prices jump on breaking news and I want an exit in my pocket.

Polymarket payment options on the US cashier include debit, ACH, wire, and Apple Pay, with a $10 floor if you want the bonus.

International users still move USDC on Polygon, often via Coinbase or MoonPay, then withdraw back to a wallet in minutes when the network is quiet.

A Polymarket deposit on the US side can sit as funds in flight for three to four business days on cards and ACH, even while you are allowed to trade.

Withdrawals follow a first-in, first-out original-source rule, so your first $100 out may return to the same debit card that sent it.

Readers who already keep a wallet for Bitcoin and stablecoins will find the global rail familiar, while dollar users should stay on the US cashier.

     Bonus, Promo, and the Fine Print I Actually Read

Polymarket offers a straightforward starter credit rather than a mystery draw.

Put in $10, complete checks, and the extra 20 trading bonus posts so you sit near $30 in buying power.

I called the Polymarket welcome package predictable, which is the point for a first test ticket.

Terms say 18+, new accounts, KYC, and not available in all jurisdictions, with 100% loss possible.

Liquidity rewards also pay daily credits if you rest orders inside the spread, which is how the book stays tight.

Promo funds are extra risk capital in my book, never a free roll, and I follow the same bankroll rules I use on any responsible gambling checklist.

      Trustpilot Notes and the Front Desk

Guest books matter before I recommend a stay, and the Trustpilot page is a 1.4 score from about 613 reviews, with most of the last year's notes sitting at one star.

One reviewer wrote that positions looked wrong and called a $15 loss the site's fault.

Another said a Costa Rica football ticket sat on a match that never kicked off, then live chat promised ten minutes and never came back.

Resolution anger is the repeating theme: UMA token votes, whales, and markets that close on a reading the crowd did not expect.

One user thanked an agent named CC for staying on a messy case even off the US team.

Another credited an engineer named Jax with helping recover funds.

Those two posts sit inside a pile of "no reply" stories, which matches my own wait on email.

The website has live chat, the Help Center is decent, and the app often pushes you to email at support [at] Polymarket [dot] com.

Polymarket customer support is the weakest room in this property, and I say that as someone who still uses the product.

      Who Should Sign Up

After weeks on both venues, I would send a curious beginner to the US app with a small test deposit, and I would send a high-volume news trader to the global book if they are outside the blocked map.

          What works

     - Peer-to-peer pricing with no hidden vig, plus early exit before settlement.
     - Broad catalogs across politics, sports, digital assets, economics, and culture.
     - Federal path for Americans, dollar cashier, and a small starter bonus that actually posts.
     - Maker rebates and tight books on the names that matter.
     - A usable iOS build and fast coin withdrawals on the international rail.

         What still nags me

     - State blocks and sports-only shelves in some places.
     - UMA dispute optics on the token venue and a handful of lawsuits over resolved books.
     - FIFO cash-out rules and multi-day holds on card deposits.
     - Slow human replies and a Trustpilot page that the brand barely answers.
     - A learning curve if you have never seen shares priced as percents.
     - Latest Polymarket headlines I tracked while writing include ICE's check, the MLB deal, tighter insider-trading rules after suspicious Iran-war flow, and a New York suit over a Strategy Bitcoin-sale market seeking millions.

Polymarket's blockchain rail still gives the global book a transparency edge I like, as long as you accept oracle drama on messy headlines.

I keep a second login at the dollar-first shop for Fed days, and I read the rule text before the price.

      A Final Word About It

Polymarket earns a stay on my home screen as a top prediction venue with a 4.6 out of 5 from me for product and a 3.0 for service.

The trading floor is sharp, the federal rebuild is real, and the catalog still beats most copies.

Service, state chaos, and oracle drama keep it from a perfect score, the same way a grand hotel with a brilliant suite can still lose me at the front desk.

Open the US build if you pass KYC and your state is green.

Stay on the international site if you already live in wallets and your jurisdiction allows it.

Skip it if you want parlays, same-game combos, or a clerk who picks up the phone in two minutes.

This Polymarket review covers the two-product split on purpose, because judging the old website when you can only trade the app is how people get lost.

Trade on Polymarket with size you can lose, verify the market's source, and treat every price as a crowd guess rather than a promise of a future result.

      Polymarket FAQs

     - How does Polymarket work?
You buy Yes or No shares priced between one cent and 99 cents, the price is the crowd's implied chance, and a correct share pays $1.00. You can sell before the event ends, which is how I lock a gain or cut a loss without waiting for the final whistle.

     - Is Polymarket legal in the US?
The US product sits under federal designation after the QCEX deal, but several states still restrict sports or all contracts. Check the app during sign-up, because a static article cannot beat a live geo check.

     - Is Polymarket safe for my money?
Custody depends on the venue: the US exchange holds dollars under federal customer-fund rules, and the global site holds a dollar-pegged token on-chain. Trading risk is separate, and a wrong share still goes to zero.

     - How do the two big American books differ?
The dollar-native shop is built around bank transfers and a bigger randomized promo ceiling. Polymarket uses token rails globally, lists faster culture and geopolitics books, and usually prices takers cheaper while paying makers to quote.

     - How do I claim the starter credit?
Create a new Polymarket account in the app, pass identity checks, enter your partner code, and deposit at least $10. Profits on winning bonus trades can be withdrawn as cash, and Nevada is typically excluded.

     - Can I trade from a phone?
Yes. Download the iOS or Android build, complete KYC, and you can bet on Polymarket from the same screens I use for live news tickets. Desktop still wins for charts, and some regions remain view-only on Polymarket website.

     - How is a Polymarket prediction settled?
Each ticket follows the written source in the market rules. The US book uses a regulator-filed process, while the international book uses a bonded proposal and, if challenged, a token-holder vote that has drawn whale-vote criticism.

     - Where can Americans open an account?
Polymarket is available in most U.S. states plus D.C., with Nevada and a rotating set of court fights as the usual exceptions. Sports-only shelves also appear in places such as New Jersey, so your catalog may be smaller than the homepage implies.

     - Are winnings taxable, and how slow are cash-outs?
Profits can be taxable as capital gains or miscellaneous income depending on your facts, and I am not your accountant. US cash-outs wait for funds to clear, then return FIFO to the original method, while coin withdrawals are usually fast once you paste a wallet address.

     - Should I pick this exchange or a regular book?
Use Polymarket when you want a probability you can sell, a news market a book will never list, or access in a state with no legal sports betting. Stick with a sportsbook if you want parlays, props depth, and a cashier that feels like a bank app.

     - Is Polymarket legit after the 2022 fine?
Yes for the regulated American product: contracts settle, winners are paid, and customer dollars sit under exchange rules. Keep the 2022 penalty, the moving state map, and messy oracle votes on the international venue in view before you size up.

HOW TO USE

- Fleet / Teslaconomics (Mar 2026): ~$30k/yr net profit per Robotaxi to owner is a base-case assumption from analyst models + Tesla long-term vision — after platform fee, charging, tires, maintenance, insurance, cleaning. No official real-world owner earnings in this dump. Profit/mile chatter ~$0.25–$0.50 after costs at 50k–100k+ miles/yr in high-demand areas.

SAFETY

Facts matter. 
Wild horse adoption refers primarily to the U.S. Bureau of Land Management (BLM) Wild Horse and Burro Program, which places excess animals removed from public rangelands into private homes. These animals are feral descendants of domestic horses (mostly of Spanish and later ranching origin), legally protected as “wild free-roaming horses and burros” under the 1971 Wild Free-Roaming Horses and Burros Act. 

https://t.co/2Vcg2ZZlpp

Population Reality and Why Adoption ExistsOn-range estimates as of March 1, 2026, were 85,466 wild horses and burros on BLM-managed lands in 10 Western states, compared to a nationwide high Appropriate Management Level (AML) of 25,592. Nevada holds the largest share. Populations grow 15–20% annually without effective predators. Excess numbers lead to overgrazing, water competition, habitat degradation for other wildlife, and eventual starvation or poor body condition in drought years. 

https://t.co/2Vcg2ZZlpp

The BLM removes animals exceeding AML via gathers (often helicopter-assisted) and offers them for adoption or sale. Roughly 58,000–63,000 animals remain in off-range corrals and pastures at any time, costing taxpayers over $100 million per year. Since 1971, more than 290,000–320,000 have been placed into private care. 

https://t.co/2Vcg2ZZlpp

How Adoption WorksBase adoption fee is typically $125.
Adopters must be 18+, have no animal-abuse convictions, provide at least 400 sq ft of corral space per animal, meet fence-height rules (6 ft for adult horses), and use appropriate trailers.
Title transfers after one year of documented good care; BLM may conduct compliance checks. Animals generally cannot be sold or given away during that period and must stay in the U.S.
Animals 11+ years old or previously offered for adoption at least three times may be sold instead, with immediate title transfer. 

https://t.co/2Vcg2ZZlpp

In FY2025, more than 8,000 animals found private homes (4,330 adoptions + 3,718 sales + transfers), a 20% increase from the prior year and the highest since 2021. BLM estimated this saved $121 million in lifetime holding costs. 

https://t.co/2Vcg2ZZlpp

The 2019 Adoption Incentive Program paid $1,000 to adopters of untrained animals and more than doubled placement rates. A federal court vacated it in March 2025 on procedural grounds (lack of proper rulemaking and environmental review) after groups documented abuse. New incentive payments stopped; adoptions themselves continue without the cash bonus.

What are the new heaven and the new earth?
Answer
In Revelation 21:1, John sees something spectacular: “Then I saw ‘a new heaven and a new earth,’ for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.” This new earth and new heaven are sometimes referred to as the “eternal state.” As seen in Revelation chapters 21—22, the new earth will be the eternal dwelling place of believers in Jesus Christ. Scripture gives us a few details of the new heaven and new earth.

The current heaven and earth have long been subject to God’s curse because of mankind’s sin. All creation “has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth” (Romans 8:22) as it awaits the fulfillment of God’s plan and “the children of God to be revealed” (verse 19). Heaven and earth will pass away (Mark 13:31), and they will be replaced by the new heaven and the new earth. At that time, the Lord, seated on His throne, says, “I am making everything new!” (Revelation 21:5). In the new creation, sin will be totally eradicated, and “there shall be no more curse” (Revelation 22:3, NKJV).

The new heaven and new earth are also mentioned in Isaiah 65:17; 66:22; and 2 Peter 3:13. Peter says that the new heaven and new earth will be “where righteousness dwells.” Isaiah says that “the former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind.” Things will be completely new, and the old order of things, with the accompanying sorrow and tragedy, will be gone.

The new earth will be free from sin, evil, sickness, suffering, and death. It will be earth as God originally intended it to be, prior to the curse of sin. It will be Eden restored.

A major feature of the new earth will be the New Jerusalem. John calls it “the Holy City . . . coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband” (Revelation 21:2). This glorious city, with its streets of gold and pearly gates, is situated on a new, glorious earth. The tree of life will be there (Revelation 22:2). This city represents the final state of redeemed mankind, forever in fellowship with God: “God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. . . . His servants will serve him. They will see his face” (Revelation 21:3; 22:3–4).

In the new heaven and new earth, Scripture says, there are seven things notable for their absence—seven things that are “no more”:
• no more sea (Revelation 21:1)
• no more death (Revelation 21:4)
• no more mourning (Revelation 21:4)
• no more weeping (Revelation 21:4)
• no more pain (Revelation 21:4)
• no more curse (Revelation 22:3)
• no more night (Revelation 22:5)

The creation of the new heaven and new earth brings the promise that God “will wipe every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4). This event comes after the tribulation, after the Lord’s second coming, after the millennial kingdom, after the final rebellion, after the final judgment of Satan, and after the great white throne judgment. The brief description of the new heaven and new earth is the last glimpse into eternity that the Bible gives.

My father had lost a massive chunk of his savings in a failed real estate venture in Nevada, while my mother had been maintaining her high-society lifestyle entirely on credit cards. To keep Chloe afloat, they had taken out high-interest personal loans against their own house.

I wasn’t the daughter who needed their help. I was the last remaining asset they had left to exploit.

When I froze my credit and refused to co-sign the refinance, the bank rejected their application. My parents were forced to put their vacation property on the market to cover their debts. Meanwhile, the bank repossessed Chloe’s vehicle after she failed to refinance it under her own name.

She called me over twenty times until I finally answered.

“What do you want, Chloe?” I asked flatly.

“You destroyed my credit!” she shrieked. “I can’t pay back $18,400!”

“Then present a realistic repayment plan.”

“I’m your sister! You can’t treat me like a collection agency!”

“You treated me like an ATM for six years.”

Silence stretched over the line.

“Dad made the decision about the dinner menu, Clara, not me!” she whined.

“You fed your dog prime steak while handing my six-year-old son dry bread.”

“Coco has a strict veterinary diet!” she snapped back.

The excuse was so absurd it almost made me laugh. “Thank you, Chloe.”

“For what?!”

“For reminding me why I should never feel a single second of guilt.”

Two weeks later, my parents’ attorney requested a formal mediation settlement. We met at Uncle Richard’s law office. My father looked visibly aged; my mother wore dark sunglasses inside the conference room; Chloe sat quietly without her phone.

Their initial offer was to pay back $10,000 over three years in exchange for me surrendering the original black ledger and signing a mutual non-disparagement agreement.

“The original ledger stays with my attorney,” I stated firmly.

“That book is private property!” my father protested.

Uncle Richard raised a hand. “If we go to court over the book, Arthur, we will also subpoena Chloe’s bank records, the unauthorized credit card usage, and the fraudulent loan applications. I strongly advise you not to open that door in front of a judge.”

My father sank back into his leather chair, completely defeated.

Polymarket Full Review 📊 Prediction Markets Guide #Polymarket

Here's the twist everyone misses: Polymarket isn't gambling disguised as trading—it's information arbitrage in its purest form. When you buy a "yes" share at 80 cents, you're not betting against a house, you're buying probability from someone who values it differently.

Core thesis: Polymarket functions as a real-time sentiment exchange where information asymmetry creates edge. Unlike fixed-odd books with built-in margins, this peer-to-peer model lets you trade the delta between public perception and actual probability.

Signals: Market depth shows 80-cent pricing implies roughly 80% probability. Welcome offer gives 100% bonus up to $50 with code CGDEALS for eligible US users. Price movements can occur within minutes of breaking news. Excluded states: Arizona, Illinois, Massachusetts, Maryland, Michigan, Montana, New Jersey, Nevada, Ohio.

Between the lines: The platform's settlement rules vary by market type—some resolve on official announcements, others on media reports. This creates timing edges if you understand resolution hierarchies. The bonus structure suggests they're actively funding liquidity acquisition.

Risk: Settlement delays when official sources conflict. Market rules can be updated mid-event, though rarely. Verification depends on designated sources—check each market's fine print before entry.

Flip triggers: Major election updates, surprise court rulings, unexpected economic data releases, sudden candidate withdrawals, regulatory announcements, or significant polling shifts.

Trade: Enter on information gaps—when news breaks but markets haven't fully priced it. Add positions on confirmation volume. Invalidation occurs when designated resolution sources contradict your thesis. Working window: 24-72 hours for news-driven events.

Watch: Rule amendment notices, volume spikes on thin markets, cross-market correlations, settlement source credibility, and timing differences between official announcements and market resolution.

Bottom line: Trade information, not odds. The edge lives in understanding resolution mechanics faster than the crowd.

text:
New Mexico Friends

The Catch

The New Homes for New Mexico program offers 0% down-payment loans of up to $50,000 ($75,000 in Santa Fe, Taos, and Los Alamos) for first-time buyers of new starter homes. Here are the main limitations that determine who can actually use it and how far it stretches.
•  Scale is small. The program was capitalized with a one-time appropriation in the $10–25 million range. At $50,000 per household that covers only a few hundred buyers statewide before funds run out. It is not a revolving program that automatically refills.
•  Homes must be brand-new and built by competitively selected participating builders. Existing homes, resale properties, and new homes from non-participating builders do not qualify.
•  Size restrictions are tight. The house cannot exceed 1,800 square feet and the lot cannot exceed 5,000 square feet. Larger or more typical suburban lots are ineligible.
•  Eligibility is narrow. Buyers must never have owned a home, must earn at or below 120% of area median income (calculated for a family of four), and must occupy the property as their primary residence.
•  The loan is not forgiven. It carries 0% interest but must be repaid in full when the home is sold or if the owner stops living there as their primary residence.
•  Timing and availability are constrained. Housing New Mexico is still writing program rules and selecting builders through an RFP process. Construction of each home must finish within three years of builder selection, so inventory will arrive gradually rather than immediately.
•  It does not solve supply by itself. The program only works if builders choose to participate, find small lots, and price the homes so the assistance plus a conventional or FHA first mortgage is affordable. Broader housing shortages, construction costs, and land prices remain outside its scope.
These rules mean the program can meaningfully reduce cash-to-close for a limited number of first-time buyers who find a qualifying new small home from a participating builder. It is not available for most homes on the market and will reach only a fraction of New Mexico households facing high down-payment requirements.

#MRFResearchWednesday -- For the next installment of our spotlight on #melanoma research, we are proud to recognize Surya Veerabagu, MD of the University of New Mexico HSC as a recipient of our 2026 Resident/Fellow Award with funding provided in memory of Lynn Kessler.

Dr. Veerabagu's research project titled, "Cutaneous Genital and Acral Melanoma Treatment Trends and Outcomes," will use national cancer registry and insurance claims data to compare treatment outcomes on the national level for Mohs versus traditional WLE for cutaneous melanomas of the face, hands, feet and genitalia. 

Related to her work, Dr. Veerabagu offers, "Traditional surgery (wide local excision, WLE) for cutaneous melanoma removes the tumor visible to the human eye with a surrounding margin of normal skin that is then sent to the laboratory for evaluation. If tumor remains, it must be re-excised at a later date. For melanomas on the trunk and limbs, the risks of cancer remaining at the surgical margins, finding more advanced disease, or the melanoma returning is approximately 2%. However, for melanomas of the face, hands, feet, and genitalia, these risks increase to 10%. Since 2020, national guidelines have included Mohs micrographic surgery (Mohs) as a treatment option for certain melanomas in these cosmetically, functionally, and anatomically sensitive areas. Smaller studies have reported recurrence rates of approximately 0.5–1% after Mohs in these sensitive areas, compared with about 10% after traditional WLE, but larger national studies are lacking. We hope to determine whether the promising results seen with Mohs translate into lower recurrence rates and improved overall survival for patients."
