text:
Economists Say World Population May Have Already Crossed into Below Replacement Fertility, Faster Than U.N. Estimates | Tibi Puiu, ZME Science

Humanity may be crossing a demographic line it has never crossed before at a planetary scale: the world population may now be having too few children to replace itself.

But the more surprising part of a new analysis is not the threshold itself. It is where the collapse is happening.

Thailand’s fertility rate has fallen below one child per woman. Colombia is hovering around one. Tunisia is faring better at around 1.5 but still below the minimum 2.1 needed for net-zero replacement. These are not rich societies following Japan and Italy into old age. They are middle-income countries reaching extraordinarily low fertility while still earning a fraction of American incomes.

In a new paper, economists Jesús Fernández-Villaverde of the University of Pennsylvania and Patrick Norrick of Northwestern University argue that the conventional story of fertility decline (parents in rich countries have fewer children while those in poorer countries have many) is breaking down. Their statistical model covers 236 countries and territories from 1950 through 2023. It finds declining country-specific fertility trends in 219 of them, with no sign in the data that those declines are leveling off. Even more unexpectedly, some of the fastest falls are occurring in countries in the middle of the global income distribution rather than at the top.

The authors go further. They argue that humanity is probably already below replacement fertility (they estimate the current global replacement fertility rate at roughly 2.20), and that world population could peak around 2056 at nine billion, almost three decades earlier than the United Nations’ central projection.

The Big Surprise Is Not Low Fertility, It Is Where Fertility Is Falling

Demographers have known for generations that fertility falls as societies modernize.

Historically, families had many children partly because many children died. Before industrialization, up to 50% of children died before reaching the age of 5, which counts to a misleadingly low life expectancy you often hear about, between 30 and 40 years. Adults who survived childhood frequently lived into their 50s or 60s, though overall adult mortality risk remained relatively high across all ages.

As mortality declined, urbanization spread and education became more valuable, parents shifted toward having fewer children and investing more in each of them. Economists have built models that explained much of this first demographic transition reasonably well.

For a long time, the implicit expectation was that fertility would eventually settle somewhere around replacement.

Instead, Japan and Italy plunged well below it. South Korea went lower still. Then China followed. Now remarkably low fertility is appearing in Latin America, Southeast Asia and parts of the Middle East.

Lower Than Expected

A 2026 analysis in the Journal of Economic Perspectives by Michael Geruso and Dean Spears concluded that persistent low global fertility is likely, noting that once cohort fertility — the number of children women actually have over their lifetimes — has fallen to very low levels, it has generally failed to rebound. A large 2024 Lancet study separately projected that 155 of 204 countries would be below replacement by 2050 and 198 by 2100.

Fernández-Villaverde and Norrick’s new contribution is partly to emphasize just how quickly the geography of low fertility is changing.

Their model finds a common global fertility component that peaked around 1978. Since then, however, increasingly divergent country-specific trajectories have done much of the work. Thailand, China, Tunisia, Algeria and Iran stand among the countries with especially steep long-run declines.

Fernández-Villaverde and Norrick also offer a surprisingly simple reason fertility can fall dramatically without everyone suddenly deciding not to have children.

Imagine 100 women. In the authors’ example, 15 have no children, 10 have one, 60 have two, 10 have three and five have four. The average works out to 1.8 children per woman.

Now increase childlessness from 15 women to 26, move 13 more women into the one-child group and eliminate the four-child families. Three-quarters of women still behave exactly as before.

Yet fertility falls to 1.3.

The point is that small shifts around the margins — from three children to two, two to one, or one to none — can produce startling changes in the national average.

Is the United Nations Missing Part of the Crash?

The most contentious claim concerns the United Nations’ World Population Prospects, the standard global demographic dataset.

The U.N.’s 2024 central projection has world population rising from about 8.2 billion in 2024 to roughly 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s before edging down. These projections represent a range of plausible futures, not a single certain outcome.

Fernández-Villaverde and Norrick think the central path is too high.

They compare the U.N.’s 2024 projections with subsequently reported births for 37 countries with populations above one million and birth-registration systems that the U.N. rates as at least 90 percent complete.

Together, those countries recorded about 16.05 million births, compared with 17.70 million in the U.N. projection — a shortfall of roughly 1.65 million, or 9.3 percent. Colombia came in 36.5 percent below the projection, South Africa 33.4 percent below it and Thailand 24.1 percent below it. Only four of the 37 countries recorded more births than projected.

A spot check against national sources supports some of those underlying numbers. Türkiye’s official statistics agency reported 937,559 births in 2024, exactly the figure used in the paper. Statistics South Africa reported 787,933 babies born and registered that year, again matching the author’s data. Colombia’s statistical agency likewise publishes final 2024 birth-registration data through its official DANE series.

The U.N. does not simply add up registered births. Its methodology combines censuses, surveys, registration systems and other data through Bayesian models, correcting for estimated biases and incomplete registration.

Fernández-Villaverde and Norrick argue that these corrections can leave fertility too high in countries whose registration systems have rapidly improved. At least, that is their interpretation.

One important disagreement is about whether today’s record-low birth rates are temporary or the new normal.

The U.N.’s population model assumes that when fertility falls extremely low, it will usually recover somewhat over time. In other words, it does not expect countries such as South Korea or China to remain indefinitely at today’s extraordinarily low levels. For South Korea, for example, the U.N. estimates fertility at 0.72 births per woman in 2023, then projects it rising to 0.79 by 2028 and eventually to about 1.30 by 2100.

Fernández-Villaverde and Norrick think that assumption may be too optimistic. Their objection is simple: the recent data do not yet show the rebound the U.N. model expects. In several countries, fertility has continued falling instead. If those extremely low rates persist for longer than the U.N. assumes, the world population would peak earlier and at a lower level than the U.N.’s central forecast.

Still, the authors’ alternative is not that far outside the U.N. envelope. The U.N.’s low variant itself peaks around 2053 at roughly 8.95 billion people, close to their forecast of a roughly nine-billion-person peak around 2056.

Housing, Smartphones and Money Explain Pieces of the Puzzle — But Not the Whole Thing

Finding that fertility is falling is easier than explaining why.

“Many commentators do not seem to understand the difference between proximate causes and ultimate causes,” Fernández-Villaverde wrote in his X post.

Suppose fewer babies are being born because fewer people marry or form long-term relationships. That identifies the immediate mechanism. It does not explain why relationships declined.

Perhaps people stay in education longer. But then, Fernández-Villaverde argues, the question simply moves backward another step: why has education expanded in this way, and why has the same broad shift occurred in societies with radically different economies, religions and political systems?

“Once you start down the whole chain of reasoning, things become much harder than they seem,” he wrote.

Housing clearly matters in some places, but the effect size cannot be clearly disentangled. Research reviewed by the two economists finds that higher house prices can increase births among homeowners, who become wealthier, while reducing them among renters trying to buy larger homes. Child care, employment insecurity, contraception and the cost of education can likewise explain the timing of particular national declines. But none obviously explains why fertility has moved in the same general direction across such different societies.

Smartphones offer an especially tempting explanation. The economists cite recent U.S. research estimating that iPhone diffusion may account for a substantial share of the fertility decline among women of reproductive age. The main idea is that smartphones have reduced in-person interactions and increased pornography use. But the authors note that Italy already had a fertility rate around 1.2 in 1995, more than a decade before the iPhone existed.

Their preferred interpretation is that digital technology accelerated the spread of changing norms rather than created them.

What remains is a much broader — and much harder to test — hypothesis.

The authors call it modernity.

Their Boldest Explanation May Also Be the Hardest One to Prove

By “modernity,” the authors mean societies increasingly organized around formal education, credentials, specialized careers, large institutions and individual economic independence.

In such a world, they argue, a third child becomes expensive while having no children at all increasingly becomes the easiest choice.

Children today require years of schooling and intensive parental investment. Careers often have rigid timelines that collide with reproductive biology. Extended families play a smaller role in daily child care. Pensions and public health systems reduce the economic need to have adult children who can support parents later in life.

Then there is gender.

Women’s educational and professional opportunities have changed far faster in many countries than expectations about who cooks, cleans and raises children. The new study draws heavily here on Claudia Goldin, whose new NBER working paper likewise argues that expanding female autonomy can depress fertility when men’s participation in domestic life fails to keep pace.

That could help explain a strange trajectory. In highly traditional societies, men may once have had enough bargaining power to sustain high fertility. As women acquire more autonomy, they can increasingly reject arrangements that ask them to participate in traditional domestic workloads. Fertility can then swing unusually low.

“Modernity” bundles together dozens of social changes that are difficult to separate statistically. But a theory broad enough to explain South Korea, Colombia, Italy, Thailand and Tunisia risks becoming broad enough to explain almost anything.

The authors recognize the problem. They say their preference-and-norms explanation survives partly by elimination rather than conviction.

A Shrinking Population Is Not the Same Thing as a Collapsing Standard of Living

If the authors are right about the direction, what happens next?

The simplest effect is arithmetic. An economy’s total output depends partly on how many people are working. If the labor force shrinks, aggregate economic growth slows unless productivity rises enough to offset it.

Japan is a good example.

From 1991 to 2023, Japan’s real GDP grew by only 0.79 percent a year, compared with 2.60 percent in the United States. But measured per working-age adult, Japan grew by 1.33 percent annually versus 1.73 percent in the United States. Much of the enormous gap therefore reflects demographics rather than a corresponding collapse in individual economic performance.

A country like Japan shows that a shrinking workforce doesn’t necessarily mean its citizens will get poorer.

But governments cannot ignore aggregate output. Public debts, pensions, health systems and defense budgets have to be financed from the total economic pie. A society approaching one retiree for every worker faces a distributional problem even if each worker is highly productive. That worker who needs to support a pensioner and eventually children as well would have to be extremely productive. You might think this is where AI will come in, but the supposed prosperity gains are uncertain from an income distribution standpoint. If AI makes a ton of money, who’s to say that won’t simply make a lot of tax-dodging trillionaires, while leaving labor and governments holding the bag.

Pros and Cons of a Smaller Population

Fernández-Villaverde and Norrick also worry that smaller generations could produce fewer entrepreneurs, scientists and transformative inventions, although those effects are much less certain than the basic labor-force arithmetic. Other economists have argued that labor scarcity could instead accelerate automation and raise productivity. The historical evidence, Fernández-Villaverde and Norrick note, comes mostly from fertility rates far above the extraordinary levels now seen in East Asia.

And a smaller population has advantages. It can reduce pressure on housing and infrastructure, make it easier to invest more in each child and lower environmental pressures. The authors also point to the enormous decline in unintended teenage pregnancy as an example of falling fertility that should not be regarded as a social failure.

In other words, population decline is not necessarily catastrophic.

Humanity may be entering a demographic regime for which history provides almost no direct experiment. We do not know yet how low fertility can sustainably fall. We do not know whether today’s ultra-low rates will rebound (but they might). And we still do not know which policies can substantially change the number of children people ultimately choose to have.

There may not even be a natural mechanism that returns fertility to replacement. As Fernández-Villaverde and Norrick put it, “nothing in an economy pushes fertility back to replacement,” although the two also mention “Much of what we write is, at best, educated conjecture.”

More About The Study

The new study, Terra Incognita: The Economics of a Shrinking World, was “prepared for” the peer-reviewed journal Annual Review of Economics. Annual Reviews says articles undergo editorial or external review before publication, but it also permits authors to circulate preprints that have not yet undergone that process.

Both Fernández-Villaverde and Norrick are affiliated with the American Enterprise Institute (AEI), a center-right think tank. AEI has published strongly worded arguments about a global fertility crisis. AEI says it is nonpartisan, takes no institutional positions, is financed primarily through donations from individuals, foundations and corporations, and leaves research conclusions to its scholars.

There has also been public pushback against Fernández-Villaverde’s earlier demographic claims. In 2024, the population and environmental advocacy group Population Matters published a fact-check disputing several of his arguments, including his inference from discrepancies in national birth registrations to errors in U.N. global fertility estimates and his earlier prediction of a much earlier population peak.

text:
Last week I posted a new paper with Patrick Norrick: “Terra Incognita: The Economics of a Shrinking World.”

We chose the title deliberately. No society in history has experienced the fertility levels now seen in South Korea, China, Thailand, Colombia, Chile, and many other countries. Our knowledge of the causes (and of the economic consequences) remains far more limited than most public discussion acknowledges. Much of what we write is, at best, educated conjecture.

The paper also struggles against a space limit. We wrote 20,000 words, far from the 250,000 or so we would need to address some issues in more detail (if I had the time and resources to hide away for a year, I could do that, but not now). That means some ideas are only sketched.

Nonetheless, we emphasize several important points.

First, fertility has fallen very fast everywhere: rich and poor countries, east and west, north and south, conservative and liberal societies, religious and non-religious societies (with the exception of the Jewish population of Israel; fertility has also collapsed among the Muslim population within the pre-1967 borders), you name it. Even in sub-Saharan Africa we see fast and unprecedented drops in fertility (alas, from a high initial level).

Second, and this is really interesting, the fertility collapse has been concentrated in poor and lower-middle-income countries much more than in rich countries. By now, income per capita and fertility are positively correlated within OECD countries. We conjecture this will hold globally in a few decades.

Third, and related to the second point, the fertility collapse has been concentrated among poor and lower-middle-income women within countries. In countries such as the U.S., the rich and highly educated now have more children than the poor and less educated.

Fourth, we document why we do not understand the data from the U.N. World Population Prospects. See, for example, Tables A.1 and A.2.

Fifth, we explain why some proposed mechanisms struggle when confronted with the data.

A more subtle point is at work here. Many commentators do not seem to understand the difference between proximate causes and ultimate causes. Yes, births might have gone down because fewer women are in long-run relationships. That is the proximate cause. But you need to explain why fewer women are in long-run relationships (the ultimate cause), and saying that they spend more years in school, to take one example, does not get us very far. Why do they spend more years in school? Once you start down the whole chain of reasoning, things become much harder than they seem.

A love letter to Arvind Dharmapuri and the BJP.

You and your party have given yourselves far too much importance.

At some point, you appear to have decided that patriotism belongs to you. That you will decide who is nationalist, who is anti-India, which academic an Indian leader may meet, which elected representative is sufficiently loyal to the country, and what exactly constitutes the “national interest”.

Arvind Dharmapuri now attacks Revanth Reddy for meeting Professor Maya Tudor at Oxford, calling her an “anti-India force”.

Except BJP’s own (at some point) K. Annamalai met the very same Maya Tudor at the very same Blavatnik School of Government and proudly described their interaction as an “insightful discussion” on India, democracy and geopolitics.

So which is it?

Was Annamalai meeting an “anti-India force” too?

Or does somebody magically become anti-national the moment a Congress Leader enters the room?

This selective nationalism would be laughable if the consequences of your politics were not so ugly.

You want to teach us what is patriotic?

To us, watching young Indians take to the streets because they have lost faith in examinations, recruitment and the systems supposed to secure their futures is not patriotic.

Watching a 19-year-old student end up with more than 200 pellets lodged in his body after a protest, his eyesight badly damaged, is not patriotic. An FIR had to be fought for after weeks of protest and political pressure. 

A government presiding over paper-leak, student despair and young people having to fight on the streets for something as elementary as a fair examination does not get to look those same students in the eye and lecture them about nationalism.

Patriotism is not a certificate issued from BJP headquarters.

It is what you do for Indians.

Which brings us to Revanth Reddy.

He travelled to the UK as part of the TelanganaRising mission and was scheduled to continue to the United States. His US programme included engagements with Harvard, MIT, Northeastern University and Virginia Tech as Telangana pursued educational partnerships and MoUs aimed at bringing some of the world’s best academic opportunities closer to students here. The UK leg was approved. The US leg was denied political clearance. 

And now we are told that a proposed meeting with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani was among the reasons the Centre objected to the visit. 

Again, who gave you the right to decide that an elected Chief Minister of an Indian state cannot meet an elected Mayor of one of the world’s most important cities? Need we remind you of what you have done to India’s foreign policy during something as recent as the US-Iran war, you will teach the Congress, the ones who fought for this country what foreign engagement and nationalism should like?

More importantly, look at the breathtaking hypocrisy.

BJP leaders have had no difficulty sending their own children to universities across America and Britain.

Harvard is good enough for their children.

Oxford is good enough for their children.

Carnegie Mellon, Georgetown, Northwestern, NYU and the rest are good enough when access to them belongs to the political and economic elite.

But when a Chief Minister says: why should the ordinary child in Telangana have to cross an ocean for these opportunities? Why can we not bring the world’s finest institutions, programmes, faculty, research and skills partnerships to India?

Suddenly he must be stopped.

How dare you?

Your children can inherit access to the best education the world has to offer, but an Indian Chief Minister cannot fight to expand that access to everybody else’s children?

That is why TelanganaRising will continue.

The Centre may have denied the Chief Minister clearance to travel to America, but he has instructed Telangana’s officials to proceed with the US programme and continue the proposed institutional engagements and MoUs. 

You cannot stop Telangana from reaching for the world.

The framework is particularist by design. It is a standard, a living cultural aspiration for Northwestern Europe. Other peoples are free, and expected, to cultivate parallel ideals from their own traditions. Reciprocity is assumed. The Ideal does not rank the world’s populations in a hierarchy of inherent biological worth. It simply asserts that a people may deliberately orient itself toward the best of its own inheritance.

The same pattern appears across cultures and is nowhere else regarded as inherently exclusionary. Japanese bushidō elevates discipline, loyalty and honour within a specifically Japanese historical frame. Classical Roman virtus and later romanitas served the same function for Rome. Various steppe, African and Near Eastern codes have long done likewise for their own peoples. In each case the ideal is particular: it is offered to those who inherit or deliberately orient themselves toward that tradition. No serious observer treats the existence of bushidō as a claim that the Japanese are inherently superior, or the cultivation of Roman virtue as a denial of everyone else’s right to their own standards. The Hyperborean Ideal would operate on exactly the same principle. It is one people’s curated inheritance among many, one rooted in and suited to our particular people.

The purpose is constructive. Too much of the dissident right can find themselves trapped in negation, defining themselves by what they oppose. The Hyperborean Ideal would supply positive content: a coherent ethical and aesthetic orientation that can be practised, taught and refined. It keeps a clean terminological firewall. It rejects the reductive elements that made the historical National Socialist definition of the Volk unworkable. And it remains open to anyone of the historic population who chooses to orient themselves toward the standard, Christian and pagan alike.

A YEAR AGO SHE RAN A 1/2 MARATHON- TODAY, SHE NEEDS A DOUBLE LUNG TRANSPLANT.

Kelsey Flake is a 39-year-old Utah mother of five battling Stage 4 lung cancer, despite never smoking a cigarette in her life.

“Kelsey has never smoked a cigarette in her life. Today, she has Stage 4 lung cancer,” her brother wrote in a fundraiser for the family.

Kelsey was born with a rare genetic variant that predisposes her to lung damage and lung cancer. She was diagnosed in 2024 and went through chemotherapy, surgery and immunotherapy. For a time, scans showed no evidence of active disease.

Then, in January, the cancer returned in both lungs. Her family says she now has just 41% lung capacity and relies on oxygen full time.

After exhausting other options, her family found the DREAM Program at Northwestern Medicine in Chicago, which offers double-lung transplants to a highly selected group of patients with advanced cancer confined to the lungs.

“This work changes what we can imagine for a highly selected group of patients who were previously considered beyond the reach of curative-intent intervention,” Dr. Ankit Bharat, chief of thoracic surgery at Northwestern’s Canning Thoracic Institute, said.

Kelsey and her husband, Jacob, are now facing months in Chicago for the transplant and recovery, while trying to keep life as normal as possible for their five children, ages 6 to 15.

Kelsey started the process Tuesday in Chicago.

Her family has launched a fundraiser to help with the cost of temporarily relocating a family of seven.

“Right now, she is the one who needs people to show up for her,” her brother wrote.

More on Kelsey’s journey, the groundbreaking research behind transplanting donor lungs into patients with Stage 4 lung cancer and what this opportunity could mean for her family in comments

text:
**The Attack in Northern Syria: The Struggle for an Air Route to Iran and the Future of Syria**

In the early morning hours of August 18, 2026, Israeli aircraft attacked the Abu al-Duhur military airbase in the eastern Idlib district of northwestern Syria. According to official Syrian media, about eight strikes hit runways and storage facilities. However, it can be assumed that the runways themselves were not the true target. There were no reports of casualties, but heavy infrastructure damage was caused.

After initial ambiguity, the Prime Minister's Office clarified that this was a response to a violation of the security status quo—primarily due to the deployment of Turkish forces at the base, despite repeated warnings from Jerusalem.

The base, located just 70 kilometers from the Turkish border, had been out of service as an active facility since 2013 and changed hands many times during the civil war. Since the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024, the site has served as a training center for the "New Syrian Army" under the administration of Ahmed al-Shara (formerly Abu Mohammad al-Julani). The Israeli attack early this morning came following a visit by a Turkish military delegation intended to advance the rehabilitation of the runways, and against the backdrop of the first Syrian aerial exercises since the change of government.

### The Strategic Axis: Syria as an Air Corridor to Iran

The incident at Abu al-Duhur is not just a local incident, but a direct result of Israel’s exclusive interest: **preserving the eastern air route toward Iran.**

Syrian airspace constitutes the shortest, most efficient, and most critical corridor for the Israeli Air Force on its way to targets deep within Iranian territory, while bypassing complex geographical and political obstacles. Based on this perception, Israel views any attempt to revive the Syrian Air Force or deploy air defense systems within it as a direct threat to the freedom of action it requires against Tehran.

Following the extensive wave of bombings in December 2024, Damascus—with close Turkish assistance—attempted to rehabilitate facilities, train pilots, and conduct exercises. The attack on al-Duhur was intended to clarify that Israel will not tolerate such a process. The message broadcast was unequivocal: **Any rebuilding of aerial capability or air defense batteries that could endanger the air corridor to Iran will be met with force.** This is a direct continuation of Israel’s prevention policy, which aims to prevent a situation where Syria returns to serving as an operational obstacle or shield for Iran and its proxies.

### Current Reference Threat: Air Defense and UAVs, Not MiGs

On a tactical level, the nascent Syrian Air Force does not pose a real threat to the IDF. Recent Syrian activity has been limited to a pair of MiG-29s, a pair of obsolete Sukhoi-20s, a pair of L-39 training aircraft, and several Mi-8 and Mi-17 helicopters—a meager order of battle that has not threatened the Israeli Air Force since the attack on Egyptian Spitfires and Dakotas in Tel Aviv during the War of Independence.

The real threat to Israeli freedom of movement to Iran is not Syrian planes, but two other factors:

1. **Rehabilitation of Syrian air defense systems or the deployment of advanced Turkish air defense batteries.**
2. **Change in Syrian armament perception:** As a result of lessons from the wars in Ukraine and the Strait of Hormuz, it is likely that Damascus will forgo expensive aircraft and focus on extensive equipping with Turkish UAVs, rockets, and a large ground army.

### The Turkish Angle and Tension with Washington

Turkey, the central ally of the new regime in Damascus, aspires to expand its influence southward. Rehabilitating bases like Abu al-Duhur allows Ankara to establish a military presence, offer logistical assistance, and *de facto* harm Israeli freedom of action. For Israel, this is a double threat: strengthening the Syrian army and creating a Turkish "umbrella" that will complicate any future sortie eastward. The attack clarifies to Ankara that Israel will not allow the establishment of an aerial infrastructure that will serve Turkish expansion at the expense of Israeli security.

However, the Israeli move has a diplomatic price. The attack reinforces the international argument that Israel acts unilaterally in Syria even in the era after Assad. Strong criticism from Washington—as expressed by President Trump’s envoy to Syria and Iraq, Tom Burke, who called the attack an "unnecessary escalation that does not promote stability"—illustrates the disconnect with the American administration, which prefers dialogue and support for the new government in Damascus.

### Summary and Outlook

For the al-Shara (al-Julani) regime, the event presents a difficult dilemma. On the international level, Damascus can present itself as a victim and garner condemnations from Turkey, the Arab world, and the UN (as was done in the sharp condemnation by the Syrian Foreign Ministry). But at the operational level, the military weakness and dependence on the Turks limit the ability to respond, harm aerial reconstruction efforts, and highlight the inability to defend national sovereignty.

In conclusion, the attack at Abu al-Duhur is not an isolated move but part of a continuous strategic battle over **the skies of the Middle East and the route to Iran**. Israel is proving that it is determined to preserve its air superiority and eastern strike routes at any cost, even in the face of international criticism.

The central question that remains open is how Israel will act if the Turks—with the agreement of Damascus and quiet American support—deploy mobile air defense systems in Syria under a Syrian umbrella, directly challenging the air corridor to Iran.

## התקיפה בצפון סוריה: המאבק על נתיב אווירי לאיראן ועתיד סוריה

בשעות הבוקר המוקדמות של 18 באוגוסט 2026 תקפו מטוסים ישראליים את בסיס התעופה הצבאי אבו א-דהור שבמזרח מחוז אידליב, בצפון-מערב סוריה. לפי דיווחים בתקשורת הסורית הרשמית, כשמונה תקיפות פגעו במסלולי ההמראה ובמתקני אחסון. אך ניתן להניח כי לא המסלולים עצמם היו המטרה האמיתית. לא דווח על נפגעים, אך נגרם נזק כבד לתשתיות. 

לאחר עמימות ראשונית, הבהירה לשכת ראש הממשלה כי מדובר בתגובה להפרת הסטטוס-קוו הביטחוני — בעיקר בשל פריסת כוחות טורקיים בבסיס, חרף אזהרות חוזרות ונשנות מצד ירושלים.

הבסיס, הממוקם כ-70 קילומטרים בלבד מגבול טורקיה, יצא מכלל שימוש כמתקן פעיל עוד ב-2013 ועבר ידיים רבות במהלך מלחמת האזרחים. מאז נפילת משטר אסד בדצמבר 2024, שימש המקום כמרכז אימונים עבור הצבא הסורי החדש תחת ממשל אחמד א-שרע (לשעבר אבו מוחמד אל-ג'ולאני). התקיפה הישראלית לפנות בוקר הגיעה בעקבות ביקור של משלחת צבאית טורקית שנועד לקדם את שיקום המסלולים, ועל רקע תרגילים אוויריים סוריים ראשונים מאז חילופי השלטון.

---

### הציר האסטרטגי: סוריה כפרוזדור האווירי לאיראן

האירוע באבו א-דהור אינו רק תקרית מקומית, אלא נגזרת ישירה של האינטרס הישראלי הבלעדי: **שימור הנתיב האווירי מזרחה לעבר איראן.**

המרחב האווירי הסורי מהווה את המסדרון הקצר, היעיל והקריטי ביותר עבור חיל האוויר הישראלי בדרכו למטרות בעומק שטח איראן, תוך עקיפת מכשולים גיאוגרפיים ומדיניים מורכבים. מתוך תפיסה זו, ישראל רואה בכל ניסיון לחדש את חיל האוויר הסורי או להציב בו מערכי הגנה אווירית - איום ישיר על חופש הפעולה הנדרש לה מול טהראן.

לאחר גל ההפצצות הנרחב בדצמבר 2024, ניסתה דמשק — בסיוע טורקי צמוד, לשקם מתקנים, להכשיר טייסים ולקיים תרגילים. תקיפת א-דהור נועדה להבהיר כי ישראל לא תסבול תהליך כזה. המסר ששודר חד-משמעי: **כל בנייה מחדש של יכולת אווירית או סוללות הגנ"א שעלולות לסכן את המסדרון האווירי לאיראן — תיענה בכוח.** זהו המשך ישיר של מדיניות המניעה הישראלית, שמטרתה למנוע מצב שבו סוריה חוזרת לשמש כמכשול מבצעי או כמגן עבור איראן וגרורותיה.

---

### איום ייחוס עדכני: הגנה אווירית וכטב"מים, לא מיגים

ברמה הטקטית, חיל האוויר הסורי המתחדש אינו מהווה איום ממשי על צה"ל. הפעילות הסורית הוגבלה לאחרונה לזוג מטוסי מיג-29, זוג מטוסי סוחוי-20 מיושנים, זוג מטוסי אימון L-39 ומספר מסוקי מי-8 ומי-17 - סד"כ דל שכמוהו לא סיכן את חיל האוויר הישראלי מאז תקיפת הספיטפיירים והדקוטות המצריים בתל אביב במלחמת העצמאות.

האיום האמיתי על חופש התנועה הישראלי לאיראן אינו המטוסים הסוריים, אלא שני גורמים אחרים:

1. **שיקום מערכי ההגנה האווירית הסוריים או הצבת סוללות הגנ"א טורקיות מתקדמות.**
2. **שינוי תפיסת ההתחמשות הסורית:** כתוצאה מלקחי המלחמות באוקראינה ובמצר הורמוז, סביר כי דמשק תוותר על מטוסים יקרים ותתמקד בהצטיידות נרחבת בכטב"מים טורקיים, ברקטות ובצבא יבשה גדול.

---

### הזווית הטורקית והמתח מול וושינגטון

טורקיה, בעלת הברית המרכזית של המשטר החדש בדמשק, שואפת להרחיב את השפעתה דרומה. שיקום בסיסים כמו אבו א-דהור מאפשר לאנקרה לבסס נוכחות צבאית, להציע סיוע לוגיסטי ולפגוע ד-פקטו בחופש הפעולה הישראלי. עבור ישראל מדובר באיום כפול: חיזוק הצבא הסורי ויצירת "מטריה" טורקית שתסבך כל גיחה עתידית מזרחה. התקיפה מבהירה לאנקרה כי ישראל לא תאפשר הקמת תשתית אווירית שתשרת את ההתפשטות הטורקית על חשבון הביטחון הישראלי.

עם זאת, למהלך הישראלי יש מחיר דיפלומטי. התקיפה מחזקת את הטיעון הבינלאומי כי ישראל פועלת באופן חד-צדדי בסוריה גם בעידן שאחרי אסד. הביקורת החריפה מצד וושינגטון — כפי שביטא שליח הנשיא טראמפ לסוריה ועיראק, טום ברק, שכינה את התקיפה "הסלמה מיותרת שאינה מקדמת יציבות" — ממחישה את הנתק מול הממשל האמריקני, המעדיף דיאלוג ותמיכה בממשל החדש בדמשק.

---

### סיכום ומבט לעתיד

עבור משטר א-שרע (אל-ג'ולאני), האירוע מציג דילמה קשה. במישור הבינלאומי, דמשק יכולה להציג עצמה כקורבן ולגייס גינויים מטורקיה, מהעולם הערבי וממהאו"ם (כפי שנעשה בגינוי החריף של משרד החוץ הסורי). אך ברמה המבצעית, החולשה הצבאית והתלות בטורקים מגבילות את יכולת התגובה, פוגעות במאמצי השיקום האווירי ומבליטות את חוסר יכולתה להגן על הריבונות הלאומית.

לסיכום, התקיפה באבו א-דהור אינה מהלך מבודד אלא חלק מקרב אסטרטגי מתמשך על **שמי המזרח התיכון והנתיב לאיראן**. ישראל מוכיחה כי היא נחושה לשמר את עליונותה האווירית ואת נתיבי התקיפה מזרחה בכל מחיר, גם מול ביקורת בינלאומית.

השאלה המרכזית שנותרה פתוחה היא כיצד תפעל ישראל אם הטורקים — בהסכמת דמשק ובתמיכה אמריקאית שקטה — יציבו בסוריה מערכי הגנה אווירית ניידים תחת חסות סורית, ויאתגרו ישירות את המסדרון האווירי לאיראן.

text:
One of the strangest rules in Irish folklore: never eat in the Otherworld.

Be polite, fascinated even, but remain hungry.

There are recorded stories of people being taken by the fairies, brought into their halls & offered a feast. The warning is always the same: “eat their food and you may lose your way back to the human world.”

One Sligo story tells of a woman who had been taken by the fairies but secretly returned home each night to eat the ordinary food there. She explained that if she ate fairy food, she would never be able to return.

The symbolism is beautiful, despite the darker turns, but still there’s something very old encoded in it. 

Food is communion. To eat what belongs to another realm is to participate in its order, accept its hospitality, & perhaps become subject to its laws.

So if I ever disappear into a fairy hill, you’ll know where I went.

And if they offer me a plate, I’m bringing my own snacks.

text:
Ireland is taking a much more rigid, mandate-heavy approach compared to the market-driven design in ERCOT.

@ESBNetworks recently rolled out a Demand Flexibility Product that issues "dynamic operating envelopes" to service providers in constrained areas to manage local distribution congestion. Conceptually, these operating envelopes sound a lot like the conditional operating band between  #PCLR’s Low Power Consumption (LPC) and Maximum Power Consumption (MPC) design. 

However, the entry point to grid flex is more stringent and administratively mandated. 

EirGrid recently published its new Data Centre Connection Offer Process and Policy (DCCOPP Version 3) in May 2026. Under it, large data centers are mandated to provide dispatchable onsite or proximate generation/storage that exactly matches their Maximum Import Capacity (MIC).

The Irish Model: Load is forced to build or contract 1-to-1 generation/storage capacity just to get a connection offer. So, RA takes precedence over Transmission headroom utilization. (Makes sense, their grid is way tighter to start).

The #PCLR Model: PCLR doesn't force a site to build a battery or gas turbine. It simply registers the load in ERCOT’s SCED, placing the operational risk of curtailment on the developer. The private developer decides exactly how much physical mitigation is worth financing to protect their operations.  

PCLR architecture places the load directly inside ERCOT's 5-minute Security-Constrained Economic Dispatch (SCED), using tools like the Adjusted Bid Cap to respond to dynamic, nodal network conditions. 

In Ireland, ESB Networks relies on 15-year medium-duration contracts and targeted tenders for flexibility, which operates closer to a traditional capacity mechanism than a fluid, highly locational spot market. I'm not sure what the notice period for loads will be when constraints bind, but that piece seems crucial to understand.

text:
There is something surreal about being lectured on the defining principles of a political tradition by someone who openly places another ideology ahead of it. Some thoughts:

• The Subhas Chandra Bose comparison is especially strange. Bose explicitly described his preferred political philosophy as "a synthesis between National Socialism and Communism", met both Hitler and Hideki Tojo and led an army of tens of thousands alongside the Axis against Britain.

Yet Corkery can still recognise Bose as an "anti-colonial revolutionary", with collaboration merely constituting "a stain on his legacy". Russell, who showed no comparable ideological identification with National Socialism (and even categorically denied holding such views) somehow becomes "Ireland's Quisling".

I regard both men as patriots of their respective nations. But I would be interested to know what principle makes Bose's collaboration compatible with remaining an anti-colonial revolutionary while Russell's supposedly consumes his entire political identity.

• On the Zionist collaboration hypothetical, my answer is perfectly consistent. If assistance from any foreign power materially advanced the cause of Irish freedom without subordinating the Irish cause to that power's political project, I would not reject it merely because I disliked the government offering it.

That is the distinction between cooperation and subordination which my original article actually argued. Although anyone familiar with the geopolitical alignments involved will know it is as hypothetical as a question can get.

• I mentioned Coventry twice in my article. Corkery did not mention it once in her original piece, yet now accuses "Russell's defenders" of hiding Republicanism's "dirty laundry" and says my response contained no new information.

The main contemporary dispute within the IRA was not "fascists versus anti-fascists". Russell's opponents objected above all to his strategy of bombing England and argued instead for concentrating military action against British rule in the Six Counties. The Coventry bombing itself occurred before Britain and Germany were even at war.

• The section of the article demanding unsparing honesty about Republican history is oddly charitable to Frank Ryan by her own logic. Although Ryan initially ended up in Germany involuntarily, he offered to act as a liaison between Germany and the IRA.

• The deeper disagreement is that Corkery consistently evaluates Republican history entirely through a socialist and anti-fascist lens and then treats that framework as constitutive of Republicanism itself. This is simply not the case.

Irish Republicanism has contained socialists, conservatives, liberals, secularists, third positionists, Catholics and virtually everything in between. What gives the Irish Republican tradition coherence is the national question and the question of who holds legitimate authority in Ireland, both of which supersede any social agenda.

In that respect, Republicanism has a strong structural similarity to Jacobitism. Military defeat and the establishment of a successful de facto constitutional order do not, by themselves, extinguish the legitimacy of the authority to which allegiance is considered due.

Anyone is perfectly entitled to condemn Russell from a socialist or anti-fascist perspective. Corkery even explicitly says that she is "first of all a socialist" and throughout this article she subjects the national question to that ideological framework rather than the other way around. On any meaningful understanding of Irish Republicanism in which the national question must always come first, that is not a Republican analysis.

text:
DC Coaching Breakdowns for 2026

Dallas Cowboys 
Christian Parker, Defensive Coordinator 

Christian Parker is in his first season as defensive coordinator for the Dallas Cowboys under head coach Brian Schottenheimer. Hired in January 2026, the 34-year-old is the youngest DC in franchise history. He previously served as the Philadelphia Eagles’ passing game coordinator and defensive backs coach (2024–25), where his secondary ranked among the league’s best, and spent time as defensive backs coach with the Denver Broncos under Vic Fangio.

Scheme Overview Parker is a teaching-first coach who emphasizes player understanding and post-snap disguise rather than rigid system dogma. Key elements include:
•Multiple 3-4 hybrid — Base 3-4 principles mixed with 4-3 spacing and heavy 4-2-5 Nickel packages.
•“Eraser” secondary focus — Strong emphasis on zone-match coverage, post-snap rotations, and eliminating options for the quarterback (drawing from his Fangio and Eagles background).
•Interior-driven pressure — Relies on dominant interior play to create one-on-one opportunities for the edge rotation rather than depending on a single superstar edge rusher.
•Pass-rush-by-committee approach with versatile front-seven roles.
The identity prioritizes communication, disguise, and maximizing the strengths of a rebuilt unit.

Top 3 IDP Targets in the Parker Defense

1. Caleb Downs (S) – The Versatile Chess Piece The 2026 first-round pick (Ohio State) is a high-upside, multi-role safety who can play deep, in the box, or as a hybrid defender. In Parker’s multiple, disguise-heavy scheme that values secondary versatility and “eraser” play, Downs is positioned for elevated snaps, tackle opportunities, and big-play production as a rookie. Target if: You want a high-ceiling DB1 with the athleticism and scheme fit to deliver early returns in a system that moves safeties around.

2. DeMarvion Overshown (LB) – The Green-Dot Leader Overshown has assumed communication duties and fits Parker’s preference for athletic, hybrid linebackers who can cover, spy, and play near the line of scrimmage. His speed and range make him a natural fit in the zone-match and multiple looks. Target if: You want a high-floor, high-upside LB with every-down potential and the ability to produce tackles plus big plays in a versatile role.

3. Quinnen Williams (DT) – The Interior Engine Acquired in a major trade from the Jets, Williams is the cornerstone of Parker’s interior-driven front. His presence is designed to collapse pockets, stop the run, and free up the edge rotation. He projects as a high-volume disruptor with elite TFL and sack upside for a defensive tackle. Target if: You play in DT-required leagues or need a true elite interior presence who benefits from a scheme built around him.

Bonus Target: Rashan Gary (EDGE) Gary was added to help rebuild the edge after the Parsons departure. In Parker’s multiple 3-4 and pressure-by-committee approach, he has a clear path to meaningful snaps and sack production as a primary stand-up or hand-in-the-dirt rusher. Target if: You want EDGE upside in a scheme that creates one-on-ones through interior dominance and creative alignments.

IDP Strategy Note
Parker’s first-year defense is in rebuild mode after a poor 2025, which creates both risk and potential value. Caleb Downs offers the highest upside as a first-round safety in a secondary-focused, multiple scheme. DeMarvion Overshown provides the most reliable linebacker floor and leadership role, while Quinnen Williams is the clear interior anchor. Rashan Gary is a key edge piece to monitor in the rotation. The unit’s improved talent on the interior and secondary should create clearer production paths once the scheme settles.

text:
🎥 Nathan Peterson Exclusive Interview
https://t.co/dH91q0Jq8g

One of the things I really enjoyed hearing about from Nathan Peterson was his decision to come to Oklahoma State.

He grew up an OSU fan.  His mom and dad are Alumni, and he also had an uncle who went to OSU as well. And he was a BIG recruit coming out of Union and had offers from OU, Texas A&M, Tennessee, Nebraska, and a bunch of other schools. So while OSU was where he was always going to end up, he said those offers definitely made him stop and think about it.

But when it came down to it, he said there was really nowhere else he could go.

“Deep down I knew there was nowhere else I could go.”

Peterson also made the decision early, the summer before his senior year, because he wanted to get the recruiting part over with and just play football with his friends his senior year. He's not a big "hype" type of guy, he just wanted to play football. So getting that decision out of the way before his Senior year eliminated all of those possible distractions.

Then he did something pretty unusual, but it started becoming more common at the time. He graduated early and came to Stillwater for the spring semester of what should have been his last semester as a High Schooler. Imagine playing in the playoffs for your High School, then about 60 days later bumping into grown men on a College campus.

He said the speed, the pace, the physicality... all of it hit him in the face, and he didn't really know what he'd gotten himself into. But he knew what he wanted, which was to play football at Oklahoma State.

And once he got here, guys like Marquee Fountain, Trumaine Carroll, Paul Duren, Clay Coe, and Jerry Don Bray helped him make that transition.

Peterson got to campus, had a great start, then hurt his knee, then overcame, and then ended up having the career we all hoped he'd have. The one he deserved, and he tells the story about all of it. 

🎥 Check out the full interview on OState Daily!

text:
Happy birthday to former Booker T. Washington, Notre Dame and professional running back Tony Brooks, born on this day in 1969 in Tulsa.

Brooks was an All-Region, All-State, AP Super Team and Gatorade Oklahoma Football Player of the Year selection as a senior at Booker T. Washington after rushing for 1,638 yards and 19 touchdowns, helping the Hornets go 12-and-2 and advance to the Class 5A state championship game.

He was also a standout linebacker for the Hornets, who allowed just 10.7 points per contest.

In his three seasons on varsity, teams Brooks played for were 35-4, won the 1984 state championship and were runner-ups in 1986.

Brooks chose Notre Dame over numerous other offers, including those from Georgia, UCLA, Oklahoma and Oklahoma State.

With the Fighting Irish, Brooks rushed for 262 yards and a touchdown as a freshman and was second only to quarterback Tony Rice with 667 yards rushing as Notre Dame went undefeated and won the 1988 national championship.

Brooks' 1989 season was over before it began after he was suspended following a minor accident in which Brooks left the scene. He faced misdemeanor charges of leaving the scene of an accident and driving with a suspended license and withdrew from school.

He returned to Notre Dame in 1990 and rushed for 451 yards and six touchdowns as the backup to Ricky Watters. A year later, he again found himself behind a future NFL star in Jerome Bettis, but still led the team with a 6.1 yards per carry average and was second with 894 yards rushing, helping the Irish go 10-3.

In 1992, Brooks was selected by the Philadelphia Eagles in the fourth round of the NFL Draft. He played in five games as a rookie, but suffered a back injury that cost him the entire 1993 season. He was waived prior to the 1994 season.

Brooks returned to the field on the world stage with the London Monarchs of the World Football League, earning the Player of the Year award by the American Football Writers Association of Britain after finishing second in the league with 480 yards and two touchdowns and adding 249 yards and two touchdowns receiving.

text:
Barry Sanders spent two years at Oklahoma State as a backup running back.

The guy playing ahead of him is also in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

Then Barry got the job and had the greatest season in the history of college football.

Start with how little anybody wanted him.

At Wichita North High School, Barry Sanders did not become the starting tailback until the FOURTH GAME of his senior year. He was 5'8 and coaches thought he was too small.

He rushed for 1,417 yards in the final seven games and made all-state anyway.

It didn't matter. He got three scholarship offers total. Emporia State, Tulsa and Oklahoma State.

He picked Oklahoma State, where the starting running back was Thurman Thomas, a first team All-American who would go on to a Hall of Fame career with the Buffalo Bills.

So for two full seasons, one of the greatest running backs who has ever lived sat behind another one.

He returned kicks instead. As a sophomore in 1987 he led the entire nation in kickoff return average at 31.6 yards while rushing for just 603 yards as a backup.

And there is one perfect story from those years.

Oklahoma coach Barry Switzer was watching film to prepare for Oklahoma State. His entire staff was locked in on how to stop Thurman Thomas.

Switzer noticed something else.

His recollection: "I saw this back run a kickoff back 100 yards. Then a little while later, he did it again. I walked over to our coaches in another room and I told them, 'You'd better hope Thurman Thomas doesn't get hurt.'"

His staff thought he'd lost his mind.

Thomas graduated after 1987. Everyone spent that offseason asking how Oklahoma State would possibly replace an All-American.

Then Barry Sanders played the 1988 season.

He opened the year by returning the first kickoff of the season 100 yards for a touchdown.

He rushed for 2,628 yards. He scored 39 total touchdowns. He averaged 238.9 rushing yards PER GAME. He had four separate 300 yard games. He set 34 NCAA records in a single season.

And that 2,628 doesn't even count the bowl game, because the NCAA didn't include bowl statistics until 2002. Add his 222 yards and five touchdowns in the Holiday Bowl and it's 2,850 yards and 44 touchdowns.

Nobody in the 38 years since has come close.

His own head coach Pat Jones put it bluntly: it's the greatest season any individual has ever had, and maybe in any sport.

His quarterback that year was Mike Gundy, who now coaches Oklahoma State. His verdict: there won't be another one like it.

He won the Heisman Trophy that December, and he's the only winner in history to be notified in Tokyo, Japan, where the team was playing its final game.

Then Detroit took him third overall, and he made the Pro Bowl in all ten of his NFL seasons and won MVP in 1997 with a 2,053 yard year.

Then, at 30 years old and roughly 1,400 yards from the all-time rushing record, Barry Sanders just walked away.

Two Pro Football Hall of Fame running backs on the same college roster at the same time.

One of them couldn't get on the field.

text:
Three men convicted of murder were executed by lethal injection on Thursday, August 13, 2026, in Oklahoma, Tennessee and Alabama — the first time three U.S. states have carried out executions on the same day since January 7, 2010. 
Death penalty observers, including Death Penalty Information Center Executive Director Robin Maher, described the simultaneous schedule as highly unusual and largely the result of coincidental timing rather than coordinated policy. Most U.S. execution days involve one inmate; doubles are uncommon and triples rarer still. 
Oklahoma:
Carlos Cuesta-Rodriguez, reported as 70, was pronounced dead at 10:13 a.m. CT at the Oklahoma State Penitentiary in McAlester. He was sentenced to death for the 2003 fatal shooting of his common-law wife, Olimpia Fisher, 43, at their Oklahoma City home. Court records and reports state he shot her during an argument; one of Fisher’s daughters witnessed the first shot. 
In a July 2026 appearance before the Oklahoma Pardon and Parole Board, Cuesta-Rodriguez declined to seek clemency. He told the board he did not deserve mercy and stated it was time for him to pay for what he had done, addressing Fisher’s daughters.
Attorneys had cited his background, mental health history and remorse in arguments for sparing his life. The board denied clemency. He offered no formal last words from the gurney but mouthed “I love you” to relatives present. 
Tennessee:
Anthony Darrell Hines, 66, was pronounced dead at 10:43 a.m. CT at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. He was convicted and sentenced to death for the 1985 stabbing death of Catherine Jean Jenkins, 54, a mother of four who worked as a motel maid. Prosecutors said Hines stabbed Jenkins while she cleaned a room, took cash and left in her car. Hines admitted stealing the vehicle but maintained throughout that he did not kill her. 
His final words included a message to his son. The execution proceeded after legal challenges related to Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol, including issues raised after a previous attempted execution earlier in 2026.
Alabama:
Jeremy Williams, 42, was pronounced dead at 6:16 p.m. CT at William C. Holman Correctional Facility. He was convicted in the December 2021 kidnapping, r-pe and murder of 5-year-old Kamarie Holland. According to court records and police accounts cited in reporting, Williams obtained the child from her mother, Kristy Siple (who later pleaded guilty to human s-x trafficking of her daughter and received a 20-year sentence), after agreeing to pay for access. Authorities said Williams forced the child to use methamphetamine, sexually assaulted her, strangled her and continued to abuse her body after death. He filmed portions of the crimes. 
Williams pleaded guilty, requested that his attorneys present no defense at trial and waived appeals of the death sentence, resulting in a significantly shorter time between crime and execution than is typical in capital cases.
The last triple-execution day occurred on Jan. 7, 2010, involving inmates in Ohio, Texas and Louisiana. In July 2026, Florida carried out two lethal injections on the same day — the first double execution in that state in nearly a decade — involving James Duckett and Dominick Occhicone.

text:
From a scouting perspective, Justin King was an explosive, versatile defensive back whose speed, movement skills and athletic background consistently showed up at every level

At @GatewayGatorsFB, King was one of the top prospects in the country and a dominant two-way athlete. He rushed for 1,763 yards and 29 touchdowns as a junior, then 1,902 yards and 33 rushing touchdowns as a senior while also adding 180 receiving yards and three scores

He finished his Gateway career with 4,519 rushing yards and 59 total touchdowns, earned 2004 Gatorade Pennsylvania Player of the Year honors, was a Parade All-American and reportedly held more than 50 scholarship offers. His track background, including a reported 10.45 100-meter time, showed up in his burst and long speed

At @PennStateFball, King initially contributed on offense, defense and special teams before developing into a full-time cornerback. As a freshman, he totaled 227 rushing yards, 126 receiving yards, two receiving touchdowns and 40 kickoff-return yards, earning Freshman All-America recognition as an all-purpose player

Once focused primarily on defense, King became one of the better cover corners in the Big Ten. He finished his Penn State career with 90 tackles, three interceptions and 23 passes defended in 38 games with 31 starts. His best traits were his recovery speed, ability to carry receivers vertically, closing burst and comfort playing in space

Pre-Draft Testing:

• Height: 5’10⅞”
• Weight: 192 lbs
• Arms: 31⅝”
• Hands: 8½”
• 40-Yard Dash: 4.31
• Bench: 14 reps
• Vertical: 37.5”
• Broad: 10’7”
• Short Shuttle: 4.31
• 3-Cone: 6.91

The @RamsNFL selected King 101st overall in the fourth round of the 2008 NFL Draft. He went on to appear in 38 NFL games with 19 starts, including 12 starts in 2011

King’s evaluation is a strong example of how a complete athletic background can help explain a defensive back’s ceiling beyond just his listed position

Inspired by the author’s love of the fall season—with its vibrant colors, crisp air, and sense of harvest and gratitude—the book offers forty days of gentle spiritual nourishment. Each entry includes a daily Bible verse, a peaceful and thought-provoking observation, and soft reflections designed to refresh faith and cultivate joy. McDonald encourages readers to pause amid life’s busyness, sit quietly or take a walk, and intentionally harvest God’s steadfast love and boundless grace. It serves as a humble, encouraging guide that can be used in autumn or anytime throughout the year. Readers looking for a calming, faith-centered companion will find it uplifting and accessible.

- Also check Amazon and other retailers for paperback or additional formats as they become available.

About the author
C.S. McDonald taught dance and choreographed shows for twenty-six years before turning to writing. She lives with her husband Bill and their dogs on a Thoroughbred farm near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. She is the author of the popular clean Fiona Quinn Mysteries (cozy mysteries featuring a kindergarten teacher turned sleuth) and the Owl’s Nest Mysteries, as well as children’s books inspired by farm life. In recent years she has added devotionals, including *Harvesting Grace*, as part of her spiritual writing. She is a wife, mom, grandma, dog lover, and self-described helpless chocoholic.
